Surat al-Nisa'
One hundred and seventy-five verses, and it is Medinan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate, and from the two of them scattered many men and women. And fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs. Indeed God is ever watchful over you.﴾ ﴿And give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the bad for the good, and do not devour their property along with your own property. Indeed, that is a great sin.﴾ [al-Nisa': 2] ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans, then marry from among the women what is good for you, two, three, or four. But if you fear that you will not be just, then one, or what your right hands possess. That is more suitable that you not deviate.﴾ [al-Nisa': 3] ﴿And give the women their dower as a gift. But if they give you something of it willingly, then consume it with satisfaction and ease.﴾ [al-Nisa': 4] ﴿And do not give the foolish your property which God has made a means of support for you, but provide for them from it and clothe them, and speak to them with kind words.﴾ [al-Nisa': 5] ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age. Then if you perceive in them maturity of judgment, release to them their property. And do not consume it excessively and hastily before they grow up. And whoever is wealthy should refrain, and whoever is poor may eat according to what is reasonable. And when you release their property to them, have witnesses over them. And sufficient is God as Reckoner.﴾ [al-Nisa': 6] ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, whether it is little or much, an obligatory share.﴾ [al-Nisa': 7] ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives, orphans, and the needy, provide for them from it and speak to them with kind words.﴾ [al-Nisa': 8] ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them fear God and speak words of appropriate justice.﴾ [al-Nisa': 9] ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a Blaze.﴾ [al-Nisa': 10]

Al-Raqib (the Watchful): an intensive form (fa'il for mubalagha) from raqaba, yarqubu, raqban, ruquban, riqban, meaning he fixed his gaze on a matter to verify it as it is. It is accompanied by protection (hifz), and from this comes the saying for the one who watches for the arrow's release: raqib.

Abu Dawud said:
"Like the seats of the watchers for the gazelles, their hands are...".

Al-raqib is also the third of the seven arrows that have shares. Al-raqib is also a kind of snake. Al-marqab is the high, elevated place where the watcher stands. Al-irtiqab means waiting.

Al-huib: sin. It is said: haba yahubu hawban and huban and haban and hu'ub and hiyaba. Al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di said:
"Let time not admit me to your grave with sin, for you will meet it, and it will hold you to account."

Another said:
"If you migrate, you will restrain it, its... it has erred and sinned."

It is said: al-hawb with an open ha' is the verbal noun, and with a dammed ha' is the noun. Tahawwaba al-rajul means he cast off sin from himself, like tahannatha, ta'ththama and taharraja. And so-and-so yatahawwabu from such-and-such means he anticipates it. The root of al-huib is driving camels, so sin is called huib because one is driven away from it. From it comes al-hawba: need. In supplication: "To You I raise my need." It is said: God inflicted upon him al-hawba, that is, poverty and need.

﴿Mathna wa-thula' wa-ruba'﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]: these are forms deviated from ithnayn ithnayn (two by two), thalatha thalatha (three by three), and arba'a arba'a (four by four). The deviated-from form is not intended for emphasis. What is intended is repetition of the number up to the limit of the counted items, as in His saying: "They drove a camel, camel by camel," (p. 151) and "I detailed the account for you, door by door."

It is obligatory to prohibit their declension on account of this deviation and the descriptive quality, according to the view of Sibawayh, al-Khalil, and Abu 'Amr. Al-Farra' permitted declension, but prohibition of declension is preferable in his view. The reason for prohibition in his view is deviation and definiteness by the intention of al-alif wa-al-lam. Their being annexed was prohibited in his view, because they are in the intention of al-alif wa-al-lam, and the appearance of al-alif wa-al-lam was prohibited because they are in the intention of annexation. We have mentioned the refutation of this in our book al-Takmil.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They are prohibited from declension only because of the two deviations they contain: their deviation from their form, and their deviation from their repetition. They are indefinite nouns that become definite by the definite article. It is said: so-and-so marries al-mathna, al-thula', and al-ruba'. End of his statement.

What he holds regarding the prohibition of declension because of the two deviations, deviation from their form and deviation from their repetition, I do not know of anyone who held that. Rather, the reported views on the reason for prohibiting declension are four. The first is what we reported from Sibawayh. The second is what we reported from al-Farra'. The third is what is reported from al-Zajjaj, namely that they are deviated from ithnayn ithnayn, thalatha thalatha, and arba'a arba'a, and that it is a deviation from the feminine. The fourth is what Abu al-Hasan reported from some grammarians, that the preventing reason for declension is the repetition of deviation in them, because it deviated from the word ithnayn and deviated from its meaning. That is because it is not used in a place where undeviated numbers are used. You say: "Two men and three came to me," and it is not permissible to say: "Mathna and thula' came to me," unless a plural precedes it, because this pattern was made to explain the arrangement of the action. If he says: "The people came mathna," it conveys that the arrangement of their coming was two by two. As for undeviated numbers, their purpose is informing about the quantity of the counted items only. It has become clear from what we mentioned that they differ in meaning, and therefore it is permissible for one reason to take the place of two reasons, since each requires a different ruling. End of what was established for this view.

People have refuted al-Zajjaj's statement that it is a deviation from the feminine with what is found in books of grammar. As for al-Zamakhshari, he did not follow any of these reported reasons. If someone before him said this, then he followed him; otherwise it is something he uniquely stated. As for his statement that they become definite by the article, one says: so-and-so marries al-mathna, al-thula', and al-ruba', it is objectionable on two counts. One: his claim that they become definite by the definite article, which no one has held. Rather, they have not been used in the Arabic language except as indefinite nouns. Two: he gave an example with them, and they came after governing words in his saying "so-and-so marries al-mathna," whereas they do not come after governing words; rather what precedes them is what comes after governing words, and they only occur as predicates, as in the saying: "The night prayer is mathna." Or as a circumstantial qualifier, like: ﴿What is good for you of women, mathna﴾ [al-Nisa': 3], or as a descriptive qualifier, like: ﴿Possessors of wings, two, three, or four﴾ [Fatir: 1], and his saying:
"Wolves seeking people, mathna and mawhida."

(p. 152) They occasionally come annexed, as in the saying of another:
"With mathna al-zuqaq, the full skins, and with al-juzur."

Some have mentioned that they come after governing words rarely, and it may be cited as evidence for this in the saying of the poet:
"I struck khumas with a strike of an Abshami, who turned sudas, that they would not stand straight."

Among the rulings of this deviated form is that it is not feminized. So you do not say: mathnah, nor thulathah, nor rubba'ah, but it applies without a ta' to masculine and feminine alike.

'Ala ya'ulu 'awlan and 'iyalah: he inclined. The scale of so-and-so is 'a'il (tilted). 'Ala al-hakim in his judgment: he was unjust. Abu Talib said of the Prophet (ﷺ):
"For him is a witness from himself, not inclining."

Ibn al-A'rabi reported that the Arabs say: 'ala al-rajul ya'ulu, meaning his dependents increased. It is also said: 'ala ya'il, meaning he became poor and became dependent. 'Ala al-rajul 'iyalahu ya'ulahum: he supported them. From this comes: "Begin with yourself, then with those you support." Al-'awl in the inheritance shares is its exceeding the limit of the fixed shares. The summary of what is said about 'ala: it is intransitive and transitive. The intransitive meanings are: inclined, was unjust, his dependents increased, became great, and this is its present tense ya'ulu. 'Ala al-rajul: became poor, and 'ala fi al-ard: went about in the land, whose present tense is ya'il. The transitive meanings are: burdened, and was supported by the burden. And it became dominant: u'ila sabri (my patience was overwhelmed) and u'jiza (was exhausted). When it means a'jaza (overcame), it is from the ya' roots: 'alani al-shay' yu'ilu ni 'ayl and ma'il, meaning it overcame me. The rest of the transitive forms are from the waw roots.

Al-sadaqah, on the pattern of samurah: the dower. The dal may be sukun, and dammed with fatha on the sad is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. It is said: sadqah on the pattern of ghurfah. Its dal may be dammed, so it is said: sadquh, and asdaqaha: gave her a dower.

Al-nihlah: a gift given willingly. Al-nihlah also means creed, and the nihlah of Islam is the best of creeds. So-and-so yanhalu bi-kadha: he adheres to such-and-such.

Hanii'an mari'an: two adjectives from hani'a al-ta'am and mari'a: when food is pleasant with no disturbance in it. It is said: hana yahna without hamza, and hanna'ani al-ta'am and marra'ani. When you do not mention hanna'ani, you say: am'ara'ani in the quadriliteral form, and it was used with hanna'ani in the trilateral form for assonance. Sibawayh said: hanian mari'an are two adjectives they put in the accusative as the accusative of verbal nouns invoked by a verb not used with its display, abbreviated, for the indication present in speech about it, as if they said: that is established hanian mari'an. End of his statement. Kuthayyir said:
"Hanian mari'an, not an incurable disease infecting what our honors have made lawful to Azzah."

It is said: the derivation of hani' is from the hina' of a camel, which is the medicine applied to it for mange and placed in its wound. From it is his saying:
"Dishevelled, his good qualities appear, placing the hina' in the places of the cracks."

Al-mari': what goes down the throat, and from it the gullet, the passage of food from the throat to the mouth of the stomach, is called al-mari'. Anasa kadha: perceived it and felt it. He said:
"I perceived a sheep, and the hunter frightened it at afternoon when evening had drawn near."

Al-Farra' said: found. Al-Zajjaj said: knew. 'Ata' said: saw. Ibn 'Abbas said: recognized. These sayings are close in meaning. Al-sadid of speech is what agrees with the truth in it.

He said:
"I teach him archery every day, but when his forearm grew strong, he shot at me."

The meaning: when it matched the targets he aimed at. Sala bi-al-nar: he was heated by it, and salaytuhu: I brought him near to it. Al-tasir: glowing embers kindled, from sa''artu al-nar: I lit the fire, and from it: mis'ar harb (a war's kindler).

(p. 153) ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate, and from the two of them scattered many men and women.﴾ The majority hold that this surah is Medinan except for His saying: ﴿Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa': 58]. Al-Nahhas said: it is Meccan. Al-Naqqash said: it was revealed at the time of the migration from Mecca to Medina. End of his statement. There is no dispute that it contains what was revealed in Medina. In al-Bukhari: the last verse revealed was ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: God gives you a ruling concerning the kalalah﴾ [al-Nisa': 176].

Relation of this surah to what precedes it: when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the states of the polytheists, the hypocrites, the People of the Book, and the believers who possess understanding (ulu al-albab), and drew attention through His words, "Indeed I do not waste the work of any worker among you" (Qur'an 3:195), to recompense, and informed that some of them are from others in terms of procreation, He, exalted is He, at the beginning of this surah drew attention to the origination of the origin and the branching of the human world from it, in order to urge agreement, mutual affection, compassion, and the avoidance of disagreement. By this He also draws attention to the fact that the origin of the human species was worshipping Allah, singling Him out with monotheism and piety, obedient to Him; so likewise its offshoots that arose from it should be. Thus He called out with a general call to the people and commanded them to piety (taqwa), which is the foundation of the matter, and He made the reminder by Him that He originated them and brought them into being from a single soul a cause for piety. Whoever is capable of such a wondrous origination and of annihilating these forms, and of benefit and harm, is deserving of being feared. Through His words, "from a single soul," He drew attention to what is fixed in natures of the inclination of some kinds toward others and their attachment to one another rather than to others, so that by that He may unite His servants upon His piety. The apparent meaning of "people" (al-nas) is generality, because the definite article in it indicates that; and the command to piety and the reason are likewise general, since they are not restricted but are general. It was said: the intended meaning of "people" is the people of Makkah, as if the proponent of this view looks at His words, "by whom you ask one another, and the wombs" (4:1), because the Arabs are the ones who ask one another by that, saying: "I adjure you by Allah and by the womb." It was also said: the intended meaning is the believers, in view of His words, "The believers are but brothers" (49:10) and the saying (ﷺ): "The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim." The more prevalent practice is that when the address and the call are with "O you people" and it is for the disbelievers only, or for them along with others, He follows it with proofs of divine oneness (wahdaniyya) and lordship (rububiyya), because they do not know Allah, so they are alerted to reflect upon that in order to come to know; like: "O people, indeed the promise of Allah is true" (35:5), "O people, worship your Lord" (2:21). And when the address is to the believers, it is followed by mention of the blessings, because they know lordship.

It was said: He made this opening (matla') an opening for two surahs: one of them is this one, which is the fourth of the first half; and the second is Surat al-Hajj, which is the fourth of the second half. Here He gave as the reason for the command to piety that which indicates knowledge of the origin (mabda'), and there that which indicates knowledge of the return (ma'ad). He began with the origin because it is first. The apparent sense of the command to piety is that it is a general piety regarding whatever is to be guarded against, of what brings punishment; and for this reason it was explained as abstaining from what has been threatened in it. It was said: it is possible that He intended by piety a specific piety, namely that they be mindful of Him regarding what relates to preserving the rights among them, so that they do not sever what is obligatory for them to maintain. It was said: "Fear your Lord who joined you together by making you branches (sinwan) springing from one root (aruma wahida) in what is due from some of you to others and from others to some; so guard it and do not neglect it." This meaning accords with the meanings of the surah.

Ibn Abbas said: the intended meaning of piety is obedience. Muqatil said: fear (khashya). It was said: avoiding major and minor sins. The intended meaning of His words "from a single soul" is Adam. The majority read "wahidatin" with a ta' marbuta, in accordance with the feminine form of the word nafs. Ibn Abi Abla read "wahidin" in consideration of the meaning, since what is intended by it is Adam; or because nafs may be masculine or feminine, so his reading follows the masculine form of nafs. The meaning of creation (khalq) here is origination by way of branching and return to a single origin, as the poet said:

"Until the roots of the earth, and my roots have grown, and this death strips me of my youth."

He said, in Rayy al-Zam'an: the construction indicates the permissibility of attributing a thing to the origin to which it returns, and that this returning is considered as procreation, succession, and sequence. And [it indicates] that we are not in it as some of the materialists (al-dahriyya) claimed; for otherwise He would have said, "He brought you out from a single soul," so He attributed our creation to Adam, even though we were not from his very self, but were from a single drop which came about through those who were connected to him of his descendants; but he is the origin. End of quote. Al-Asamm said: reason does not indicate that the created beings were created from a single soul; rather, revelation (al-sam') does. Since he was unlettered and did not read a book, the meaning of "He created you" is a proof of monotheism, and "from a single soul" is a proof of prophethood. End of quote.

In His words "from a single soul" there is an indication of abandoning boasting and arrogance, since He informs them that they are from a single origin; and it is an indication of the return (ma'ad), because the One who is able to bring forth distinct persons from one person is even more able to revive them.

"And its mate" (zawjaha) refers to Hawwa'. It is apparent from it that the beginning of Hawwa's creation was from his self, and that he is her origin from which she was brought forth and produced. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi said this, and al-Suddi (repeated): they said that Allah created Adam as a solitary being in Paradise alone, then he slept, and Allah took out one of his short ribs from his left side. It was said: from his right side; so from it He created Hawwa'. Ibn Atiyya said: what strengthens this view is the sound hadith in which he, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed the woman was created from a crooked rib; if you try to straighten it you will break it, and breaking it is divorcing it." End of quote. It is possible that this is by way of illustration for the instability of their characters, and that they do not remain in one state; that is, they are difficult in dealing; so she is like the crooked rib, as in the verse, "Man was created of haste" (21:37). This interpretation is supported by his saying "indeed the woman", where he used the genus and did not say "indeed Hawwa'." It was said: there is an omitted element (hadhf mudaf), the estimate being: "and He created from its kind its mate", as said by Ibn Bahr and Abu Muslim, based on His words, "from yourselves He made for you spouses" (16:72) and "a messenger from among them" (2:129). Al-Qadi said: the first view is stronger, for if Hawwa' had been created initially, then people would have been created from two selves, not from a single self. It may be answered that the particle "min" indicates the starting point, so when the beginning of creation fell upon Adam, it is correct to say "He created you from a single self." And since He was capable of creating Adam from dust, He was capable of creating Hawwa' likewise as well. It was said: there is no omission, and the pronoun in "minha" does not refer to nafs, but refers to the clay that was separated from Adam's clay, and Hawwa' was created from it, i.e., she was created from that from which Adam was created. The apparent sense of the words of Ibn Abbas and those before him is that she was created while Adam was in Paradise, and Ibn Mas'ud said this. It was said: before his entry into Paradise; this was said by Ka'b al-Ahbar, Wahb, and Ibn Ishaq. The "wa" (and) in conjoining this clause has been taken in one of its possible senses, namely that the creation of Hawwa' occurred before the creation of people, since "wa" does not indicate temporal sequence, as has been established in the science of Arabic grammar. The clause concerning the creation of people was mentioned first, even though its meaning occurred after the creation of Hawwa', because they are the ones addressed, commanded to fear their Lord; so mentioning what concerns them first is more emphatic. A parallel is: "O people, worship your Lord who created you and those before you" (2:21); and it is known that their creation came after the creation of those before them. But since they are the ones commanded to worship and addressed for its sake, He took care to mention their origination first, then mentioned the origination of those who preceded them. Al-Zamakhshari went to great lengths to establish that what is conjoined with "wa" is later than what it is conjoined to, so he postulated an omitted antecedent conjoined to, which precedes the conjoined in time, saying: it is conjoined to an omitted element, as if it were said: "from a single self which He originated or initiated, and from it He created its mate," and it was omitted because the meaning indicates it. The meaning: your branches are from a single self whose attribute is this, namely that He originated it from dust and created from it its mate, Hawwa', from one of its ribs. There is no need to strain this interpretation when the view we mentioned is permissible according to what Arabic requires. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that view, saying: it is conjoined to "He created you," and the address in "O people" is to those to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent. The meaning: He created you from the self of Adam, since they are among the category of the kind branched from him, and from it He created your mother Hawwa'. End of quote. It is also permissible that His words "and from it He created its mate" be conjoined to the active participle which is "wahida", the estimate being "from a self that has become single (wahadat)", i.e., it was alone (infarada), and from it He created its mate; so it would be like "in ranks and those who grip" (67:19). The Arabs say: "wahada yahidu wahdan and wahdatan," meaning "infarada" (was alone).

Among the strange interpretations is that by "self" (nafs) he meant the spirit (ruh), which is mentioned in what is said: he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Indeed Allah created the spirits before the bodies by such-and-such years." And by "its mate" he meant the body, and by "creation" he meant composition (tarkib). To something similar He alluded by His words, "And of everything We created pairs" (51:49), and His words, "Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, of what the earth grows and of themselves" (36:36). This cannot apply to plants except in the sense of composition. He began with mentioning the pair and the pairs in things, on the basis that they are never free of composition, while the One who is truly one is none other than Allah, exalted is He. End of quote. This is contrary to the words of the earlier scholars. Some of them said: by His words "and created from it its mate" He drew attention to its deficiency and perfection, because she is a part of it.

"And He spread forth from both of them" means: from that self and its mate, i.e., He dispersed and scattered them into existence. It is said: "abatha Allah al-khalq" (quadriliteral) and "batha" (triliteral); the latter is what occurs in the Qur'an: "men in great number and women" (4:1). It was said: it was indefinite because of the generality (shuyu') inherent in indefiniteness, yet it did not suffice with generality until it explicitly stated multitude; and the men were placed first because of their superiority over women. "Men" was specifically qualified with the description of multitude, and it was said: the description of the second was omitted because the description of the first indicates it; the estimate is "and women in great number." It was also said: the description is not to be estimated, even if the meaning in it is sound, because He drew attention, by the specific quality of men with the description of multitude, to the fact that what is fitting for their state is fame, going out, and prominence, while what is fitting for the state of women is obscurity and concealment. In the division of what He created from Adam and Hawwa' into men and women there is evidence for the negation of the hermaphrodite (khuntha), since He limited what He created to these two kinds; so if something is found whose appearance is problematic, it must be reduced to one of these two kinds. It was read: "wa khaliqun minha zawjaha wa babithun" in the active participle form, being the predicate of an omitted subject whose estimate is "wa huwa khaliq" (and He is the Creator).

* *

"And fear Allah, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs." He repeated the command to piety for emphasis of the first. It was said: it is due to the difference in the reason (ta'lil). And He mentioned first "the Lord" (al-Rabb), which indicates beneficence and nurture, and second "Allah," which indicates subjugation and awe. He built the first on encouragement and the second on warning, like His words, "They call upon their Lord in fear and hope" (32:16) and "They call upon Us in desire and awe" (21:90). It is as if He said: He is your Lord who has done good to you, so beware of opposing Him; and if you do not fear Him for that, then fear Him, for He is severe in punishment. The majority of the seven read "tasa'alun" (with a doubled sin). The Kufans read with a lightened sin, and its origin is "tatasa'alun."

Ibn Atiyya said: that is because they deleted the second ta' for lightness; this ta' is the ta' of "tatafa'alun," which is assimilated in one dialect and deleted in another, due to the convergence of similar letters. Abu Ali said: when similar letters converge, they are lightened by deletion, assimilation, and substitution, as they say "tast" (basin), where they substituted a ta' for one of the two sins, since the original is "tass." Al-Ajjaj said:

"If she had appeared to a priest, a shaven-headed one, disheveled in his sanctuary, he would have longed for her as the longing of the basin."

[End of quotation.] As for Ibn 'Atiyya's statement, "they deleted the second *ta'*" (*hadhafū al-ta' al-thaniya*), this is the view of the grammarians of Basra. Hisham ibn Mu'awiya al-Darir al-Kufi held that the deleted letter is the first one, which is the *ta'* of the present tense (*ta' al-mudari'a*). This is a disputed question, and its evidence is set out in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*).

As for his statement, "This is the *ta'* of *tatafa'alūna*; it is assimilated (*tudghamu*) in one dialect and deleted (*tuhdhafu*) in another," he should have pointed out that the form with the letter retained (*al-ithbat*) is permissible, and it is the original form. Assimilation (*al-idgham*, merging two identical or similar consonants into one) is close to the original, since the letter has not disappeared except by replacing it with a letter identical to the one following it and assimilating it into that letter. Deletion (*al-hadhf*) occurs because of the meeting of two identical letters. The apparent sense of his words is that assimilation and deletion are specific to *tatafa'alūna*, and that is not the case. Assimilation is not specific to it; rather, it occurs in the imperative, the present, the past, the active participle, the passive participle, and the verbal noun. Deletion, however, is specific to the forms to which the *ta'* has been prefixed in the present tense. His statement "because of the meeting of close letters" (*li-ijtima' huruf mutaqaribah*) apparently gives as the reason for deletion alone, because of their closeness, or gives it as the reason for both deletion and assimilation. Neither is correct. If it is taken as the reason for deletion alone, that is not correct either: rather, deletion results from the meeting of identical letters, not close ones. If it is taken as the reason for both, then assimilation is correct but deletion is not, as we have explained.

As for Abu 'Ali's statement, "When close letters meet, it is such-and-such," it does not mean that this is a necessary rule. It means only that lightening may occur by such-and-such a means. Many instances of close letters meeting have not been lightened by deletion, assimilation, or substitution. As for his illustration with *tast* in *tass* (a basin, where the *t* is substituted for a letter), substitution here is not due to a meeting of letters; rather, this is a meeting of two identical letters, like the saying *lasṭ* for *laṣṣ* (a thief).

The meaning of *yatasā'alūna bihi* is that they exchange the request with it, so that some of you ask others [by it]; or each says, "I ask you by God to do such-and-such." The apparent sense of the form *tafā'ala* is reciprocity: you ask him by God, and he asks you by God. A group said its meaning is: you ask one another your rights, making Him the one who is revered in them. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read *tas'alūna bihi*, the present of the basic triliteral *sa'ala*. It was also read *tasalūna*, with the *hamzah* deleted and its vowel transferred to the *sin*.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of "*tasa'alūna bihi*" is that you show compassion to one another (*tata'aṭafūna*). Al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: you make covenants with one another and bind yourselves to one another (*tata'aqadūna wa-tata'ahadūna*). Al-Zajjaj said: you seek your rights by it (*tatatallabūna bihi huquqakum*).

*Wa-al-arḥām* ("and the wombs/kinship ties"): the majority of the Seven read it with the accusative (*naṣb*) of the *mim*.

Hamzah read it in the genitive (*jarr*). This is also the reading of al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, and al-A'mash.

Al-A'mash ibn Yazid read it in the nominative (*ḍamm*).

As for the accusative, its apparent sense is that it is coordinated (*ma'ṭuf*) with the word of majesty (*lafẓ al-jalālah*, i.e., Allah), and this would be with an omitted noun (*ḥadhf muḍāf*, deletion of a genitive-modified word). The meaning is: "Fear Allah and [fear] severing the wombs." On this meaning Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, and others interpreted it.

What unites the fear of God and the fear of the wombs is this shared aspect, even though the two kinds of fear differ in meaning. The fear of God is by upholding His obedience and avoiding His disobedience, while the fear regarding the wombs is by maintaining (*an tūṣala*) them and not severing them, in what is due to them of goodness and kindness. By taking the shared aspect as the meaning, the objection of the judge (al-Qadi) is answered: "How can one word be intended with different meanings?" We also say that in reality this is from the type of coordinating the specific with the general (*'aṭf al-khāṣṣ 'alā al-'āmm*), since the meaning is: "Fear God," that is, "Beware of opposing God." Coordinating the wombs with the name of God indicates the gravity of the sin of severing the ties of kinship. Consider His words: ﴿Worship none but Allah, and show kindness to parents and to the near of kin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83], and how He joined that with the worship of God in the taking of the covenant.

There is a hadith: "Who deserves my goodness most?" He said: "Your mother." And in it: "You and your wealth belong to your father." And God, in condemning those of the wicked whom He misguided, said: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification, and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27].

It has been said that the accusative is coordinated with the position (*mawḍi'*) of *bihi* (the preposition phrase), as you say: "I passed by Zayd and 'Amr" (with *'Amr* in the accusative, coordinated with the position of the preposition phrase). When it does not share the case-form in the matter of following (*al-ittiba' 'alā al-lafẓ*), it is made to follow the position. This view is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah: *tasa'alūna bihi wa-bi-al-arḥām* ("you ask one another by Him and by the wombs").

As for the nominative, it is explained as a subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of a nominal sentence) whose predicate (*khabar*, the comment of a nominal sentence) is omitted. Ibn 'Atiyya supplied it as: "And the wombs are worthy that they be maintained." Al-Zamakhshari supplied it as: "And the wombs are among what is feared, or among what is asked by." His supplying is better than Ibn 'Atiyya's, since he supplied what the preceding word indicates, while Ibn 'Atiyya supplied something from the meaning.

As for the genitive, its apparent sense is that it is coordinated with the attached pronoun in the genitive without repeating the preposition. On this interpretation al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, and Mujahid explained it. It is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah: *wa-bi-al-arḥām* ("and by the wombs"). They used to adjure one another by mentioning God and the kinship tie.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is not sound," meaning the genitive as coordination with the pronoun. He said: "Because the attached pronoun is attached like its noun, and the preposition with its object is like one word. So in your saying *marartu bihi wa-Zayd* ("I passed by him and Zayd") and *hādhā ghulāmuhu wa-Zayd* ("this is his servant and Zayd"), they are very closely attached. When the attachment is strengthened by its repetition, coordination on part of a word is confused, so it is not put in the genitive, and the repetition of the governing element is required, as in your saying *marartu bihi wa-bi-Zayd* ("I passed by him and by Zayd") and *hādhā ghulāmuhu wa-ghulāmu Zayd* ("this is his servant and Zayd's servant"). Do you not see the correctness of *ra'aytuka wa-Zaydan* ("I saw you and Zayd") and *marartu bi-Zayd wa-'Amr* ("I passed by Zayd and 'Amr"), since the attachment is not strong, because it is not repeated?" He had recourse to contrivance (*tamaḥḥala*) to validate this reading, saying it is on the assumption that the preposition is repeated. A parallel to this is the verse of the poet:

*fa-mā bika wa-al-ayyāmi min 'ajab*
("So what is wrong with you and with the days of wonder?")

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This reading is not permitted according to the leading grammarians of Basra, because they do not allow a noun to be coordinated with a pronoun in the genitive. Al-Zajjaj reported from al-Mazini: 'Because the coordinated and the coordinated-upon are partners, each of which may occupy the position of the other. Just as it is not permitted to say *marartu bi-Zayd wa-ka* ("I passed by Zayd and you"), so it is not permitted to say *marartu bika wa-Zayd*.'" As for Sibawayh, it is in his view ugly and not permitted except in poetry, as he said:

*fa-al-yawma qad bitta tahjūnanā wa-tashtimunā*
*fa-idh-hab fa-mā bika wa-al-ayyāmi min 'ajab*
(Now you have spent the night reviling us and insulting us; so go, for what is wrong with you and with the days of wonder?)

And as he said:

*tu'allaqu fī mithli al-sawāri suyūfunā*
*wa-mā baynahā wa-al-kaffu ghawṭun ta'ānafu*
(Our swords are hung on pillars like these, and between them and the palm is a valley that is stretched out.)

Some grammarians found it easy. [End of Ibn 'Atiyya's statement.] The reasoning of al-Mazini is open to objection: it is permitted to say *ra'aytuka wa-Zaydan*, but it is not permitted to say *ra'aytu Zaydan wa-ka*. So by analogy, *ra'aytuka wa-Zaydan* should not be permitted either.

Ibn 'Atiyya also said: "The pronoun in the genitive is not separated, so it is like a letter of the word, and one does not coordinate upon a letter."

In my view, this reading is refuted on grounds of meaning by two considerations. The first: mentioning the wombs as among the things by which one asks one another has no sense in exhorting to the fear of God, Most High, and there is no benefit in it beyond informing that the wombs are things by which one asks one another. This introduces a separation in the meaning of the speech and diminishes its eloquence, since eloquence lies in mentioning the wombs as having an independent benefit. The second: mentioning them in that way implies the supposition of asking by them and swearing by their sanctity, and the authentic hadith refutes this in his words: "Whoever swears, let him swear by God or let him keep silent." [End of his statement.]

Some hold that the *wa-* in *wa-al-arḥām* is the *wa-* of oath, not the *wa-* of coordination, and what the oath governs is the sentence after it. God may swear by whatever He wills of His creatures, as is found in more than one verse of the Book of God. They adopted this analysis to avoid coordinating upon an attached pronoun in the genitive without repeating the preposition, and because swearing by them indicates their connection and magnifies their status, and that they hold a place with God, Most High. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is a view that the structure and the purpose of the speech reject." [End of his statement.]

What the grammarians of Basra held, and what al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya followed them in, namely the prohibition of coordinating upon an attached pronoun in the genitive except by repeating the preposition, and their reasoning for it, is not correct. Rather, the correct view is that of the Kufans on this matter, that it is permitted. I have already extended the argument on this at the words of God, Most High: ﴿and disbelief in Him and the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], and I mentioned that this is attested in the language of the Arabs, both in prose and in verse, so that suffices here and need not be repeated.

As for Ibn 'Atiyya's statement, "Two considerations refute this reading in my view," it is an ugly audacity on his part, unbecoming of his position and the purity of his tongue. He went to a mutawatir reading (one transmitted by a multitude so that its transmission cannot be doubted) from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), which the early generations of the community recited, and which is connected to the great reciters among the Companions who received the Qur'an directly from the mouth of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) without an intermediary: 'Uthman, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, the most accomplished reciter among the Companions. He set out to refute it with something that came to his mind. This audacity befits none but the Mu'tazilites, like al-Zamakhshari, who often impugns the transmission of the reciters and their recitation. Hamzah, may God be pleased with him, took the Qur'an from Sulayman ibn Mihran al-A'mash, Humran ibn A'yan, Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, and Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, and Hamzah did not recite a single letter of the Book of God except on the basis of an authentic transmission. Hamzah was righteous, pious, and trustworthy in hadith. He belongs to the third generation. He was born in the year eighty (AH), mastered the recitation when he was fifteen years old, and led the people in prayer in the year one hundred. Several of his contemporaries received the Qur'an from him, including Sufyan al-Thawri and al-Hasan ibn Salih. Among his students was the imam of Kufa in recitation and Arabic, Abu al-Hasan al-Kisa'i. Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, and Yahya ibn Adam said: "Hamzah surpassed the people in the Qur'an and the laws of inheritance." I mention this and extend it only so that no ignorant person will look at the words of al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya concerning this reading and think ill of it and of its reciter, and so come close to falling into disbelief through disparaging it. We are not bound by the view of the grammarians of Basra or of anyone who opposed them. How many rulings have been established by the transmission of the Kufans from the speech of the Arabs which the Basrans did not transmit, and how many rulings have been established by the transmission of the Basrans which the Kufans did not transmit. Only one who has deep immersion in the science of Arabic knows this, not the people of the churches (*kanānīs*), who occupy themselves with various sciences and take from books rather than from teachers.

*Inna Allāha kāna 'alaykum raqīban* ("Indeed Allah has been watching over you"): the word *kāna* ("has been") is not intended to restrict the predicate to the subject in past time that has ended, in the case of God, Most High, although the function of *kāna* is that. Rather, the meaning is continuous (*al-daymūmah*): He, Most High, is watchful over us in the past and otherwise. The *raqīb* (watcher, guardian) has been explained earlier in the vocabulary section. Some said: here it means the All-Knowing (*al-'Alīm*), and the meaning is: He observes you, and nothing of your affairs is hidden from Him, so fear Him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 2:

﴿And give the orphans their property﴾. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning a man from Ghatafan who had a great deal of wealth belonging to his orphaned nephew. When the boy reached [adulthood] and asked for his property, he withheld it from him. Its connection to what precedes it is that when [the surah] had enjoined joining the ties of kinship, it followed this with [the matter of] orphans, because they had come to be in a state where no guardian was left for them, so their condition differed from that of one who has a близкий kinsman. Its apparent meaning is a command to give orphans their property.

Yutm (orphanhood) among the children of Adam is the loss of the father, and it is a collective noun that includes males and females. This designation ends in the Sharia upon puberty (bulugh), so there must be a metaphor (majaz). It may be in "al-yatama" (the orphans), by applying it to adults on account of consideration and naming them by what they were in the Sharia before puberty, the name of orphanhood; so the guardians are commanded not to delay their property beyond the limit of puberty, nor to procrastinate with them if maturity of judgment (rushd) is perceived in them. Or the metaphor may be in (utu, "give"), and the meaning of giving them their property would be spending on them from it bit by bit, and that the guardians and executors should not covet it, and should restrain their wrongful hands from it. On both meanings the address is to the one who has lawful custody of the orphan's property. Ibn Zayd said: the address is to those whose custom among the Arabs was that a small child among the children did not inherit alongside an adult; so it was said to them: give them their inheritance, and do not, O adults, leave your portions, [which are] lawful and good, in exchange for what is unlawful and foul, so that your action becomes a substitution. It was also said: a guardian used to earn profits on his orphan's property, and those profits would consume the orphan's property, so they were forbidden from this.

Abu Bakr al-Razi (p-160) argued from this verse that the foolish person (safih) is not to be placed under restriction after reaching the age of twenty-five. He said: because "And give the orphans" is unrestricted, encompassing the foolish and others, whether maturity of judgment has been perceived in them or not. The action was abandoned before the stated age by consensus that the perception of maturity before reaching this age is a condition for handing over the property to him; and this consensus is not found after this age, so it is obligatory to apply the command after this age according to its apparent ruling. It was answered that this verse is general and has been specified by His saying: ﴿And test the orphans﴾ [al-Nisa: 6] and ﴿And do not give the foolish their property﴾ [al-Nisa: 5], and there is no doubt that the specific takes precedence over the general.

﴿And do not substitute the foul for the good﴾. Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: some of them would exchange a fat sheep from the orphan's property for a lean one from their own, and a good dirham for a counterfeit one from their own. Mujahid and Abu Salih said: the meaning is: do not hasten to consume the foul from their property, and abandon waiting for the lawful provision from Allah. It was said: the meaning is, do not consume their property, which is foul, and leave your property, which is good. It was said: the meaning is, do not take the orphan's property, which is foul, so that your property, which is good, may be taken from you. It was said: do not consume their property in this world, for it becomes fire that you consume, and you leave what is promised to you in the Hereafter, because of retaining the foulnesses and prohibited things. It was said: do not substitute the foul matter, which is the appropriation of orphans' property, with the good matter, which is preserving it and abstaining from it. Here tafa"ala carries the meaning of istaf"ala, as ta"ajjala and ta'akhkhara carry the meanings of isti"jal and isti'khar. Its apparent meaning is that "foul" and "good" are attributes of the substances being exchanged and the substances exchanged for, so either this is in linguistic terms, and they mean the disliked and the pleasant, or it is in Sharia terms, and they mean the unlawful and the lawful. As for their being attributes of the appropriation and preservation of property, this is clearly remote, although it has some connection with His saying: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾.

Ibn Muhaysin recited (wa la tabaddalu) with the assimilation of the first tා' into the second.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 3 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾ [An-Nisa: 2]. When they were forbidden to exchange the bad of their property for the good of the orphans' property, he (God) escalated the prohibition to what is more grievous than exchange, namely consuming the property of orphans, and they were forbidden from it. As for the meaning of ﴿along with your own property﴾ [An-Nisa: 2], it was said: "together with your property." It was also said: "ila" (to) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), the implied meaning being: "added to your property." It was also said: it relates to "ta'kulu" (consume) by way of tadmin (implicit meaning), i.e., "do not add their property in consumption to your property." The wisdom of ﴿along with your own property﴾ [An-Nisa: 2], although they were forbidden from consuming the property of orphans without right, is that it is an alert to the wealth of the guardians. As if it were said: "Do not consume their property while you possess wealth," i.e., while you are rich; for the guardian who is poor has been permitted to eat in a reasonable manner (bil-ma'ruf). This is a explicit text on the prohibition of consumption, and within its ruling is the appropriation of wealth in all its forms.

Mujahid said: the verse forbids mixing in expenditure, for the Arabs used to mix their expenditure with the expenditure of their orphans, so they were forbidden from that, then the prohibition was abrogated (naskh) from it by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 220]. Al-Hasan said something close to this.

He said: People interpreted from this verse the prohibition of mixing, so they avoided it out of their own scruples, and so it was lightened for them in the verse of al-Baqarah. Al-Zamakhshari endorsed this view by saying: "Its reality is: do not add them to them in expenditure, so that you do not distinguish between your property and their property, out of carelessness about what is not lawful to you, and equating it with the lawful." He said: If you ask, "It has been forbidden to them to consume the property of orphans alone and together with their own property, so why was the prohibition on consuming it together with theirs mentioned?" I answer: Because when they were independent of the orphans' property through the lawful wealth God had provided them, yet they still coveted it, the ugliness was greater and the blame more fitting. And because they used to do this, so He censured their action and made it audible to them, so that it would be a stronger deterrent for them. End of his words. Its summary is: that His saying ﴿along with your own property﴾ [An-Nisa: 2] is not a restrictive qualifier; it came to denounce their action, and so that it would be a prohibition of the actual occurrence, being like His saying: ﴿doubled and redoubled﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 130], though usury is forbidden in all its states. As for what we have put forward, that qualifier is restrictive: when the guardian is poor, it is permissible for him to eat in a reasonable manner, so the prohibition applies to consuming the property of an orphan for one who is rich, like His saying: ﴿And whoever is rich, let him abstain﴾ [An-Nisa: 6].

﴿Indeed, it is a great sin (huban kabiran)﴾ [An-Nisa: 2]. The majority of reciters read the ḥa' with a ḍammah (ḥūb), while al-Hasan read it with a fatḥah (ḥaub), which is the dialect of Banu Tamim and others, and some reciters read: (innahu kana ḥaban kabiran). All of them are verbal nouns (maṣādir). Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and others said: al-ḥūb is sin. It was also said: injustice. It was also said: loneliness (waḥsha). The pronoun in (innahu) refers to the consumption. It was also said: it refers to the exchange. Its reference to the consumption is closer, due to its proximity to it, though it could refer to both. As if it were said: "That is as the poet said:
"On them are lines of black and white, as if on the skin is the spreading of leprosy."
i.e., as if that (were so)...

﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what is good for you of women, two, three or four﴾. It is recorded in Sahih Muslim from 'A'isha that she said: It was revealed concerning the guardians of orphans who were attracted by the beauty of their wards and wished to cheat them in the bridal gift (mahr) because of their guardianship over them. It was said to them: "Be just in their bridal gifts; whoever fears that he will not be just, let him marry what is good for him of the women outside (of his guardianship) who bargain over their rights." Rabi'a also said this. 'Ikrima said: It was revealed concerning the Quraysh, where a man would marry ten or more or fewer, and when his wealth ran short, he would take from the wealth of his orphan and marry with it. It was said to him: "If you fear that your wealth will fall short, so that you will be unjust to the orphans, then limit yourselves." Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi said: The Arabs were scrupulous regarding the property of orphans but not scrupulous regarding justice among wives; they would marry ten or more, so it was revealed concerning that: just as you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, so be scrupulous with women, and marry within the limit that keeps injustice far away. Mujahid said: the verse is only a warning against fornication and a deterrent from it, just as you are scrupulous regarding the property of orphans, so be scrupulous regarding fornication, and marry within what has been set as a limit for you. According to these views other than the first, the orphans are not specific to females or males; but according to what is narrated from 'A'isha, it is specific to females, as if it said: concerning the orphan women.

The apparent meaning of these views is that the implied sense is: "And if you fear that you will not act justly in marrying orphan women, then marry others of what is good for you." Since they were commanded to give orphans their property and forbidden from the aforementioned exchange and from consuming the property of orphans, there was in that an extra concern for orphans and caution against wronging them, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [An-Nisa: 10]. So the guardians of orphan women, or people, were addressed with His saying: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans﴾, i.e., in marrying orphan women, so marry others than them. According to this which we have chosen, that the meaning concerns marrying orphans: if "orphans" is meant in the legal sense, it applies to girls who have not reached puberty.

Abu Hanifa has used this as evidence for the permissibility of marrying a young orphan girl before puberty, and said: After puberty she is no longer an orphan, as evidence that if she wished to reduce her bridal gift below the equivalent (mahr al-mithl), it would be permissible for her. Contrary to Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority, who said: it is not permissible. If what is meant is the linguistic sense of orphanhood, then it includes those who have reached puberty, and it is permissible to marry a woman who has reached puberty for less than the equivalent bridal gift if she consents; so what sense is there in turning to marrying others? The answer: the turning was only because the guardian takes advantage of her and controls her wealth, while she cannot resist him. When what is meant by orphans here is those who have reached puberty, there is no proof for Abu Hanifa in the verse for the permissibility of marrying a young girl who has not reached puberty.

The meaning of (khiftum) is "you feared," and it is in its linguistic usage, since fear is caution. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of khiftum here is "you were certain," and khafa can mean "ayqana" (was certain), and his evidence is the poet's verse:
"So I said to them: be certain (khafū) of two thousand armored men."
What he said is not valid; it is not established in the speech of the Arabs that khafa means "certain," rather khafa is among verbs of anticipation, and in it assumption may lean toward one of two possibilities. That verse is also narrated as: "So I said to them: suppose (zunnū) two thousand armored men." This narration is more famous than "khafū." Al-Raghib said: fear is said of what has some hope in it, which is why one does not say: "I feared that I would not be able to reach the sky, or move the mountains," end of quote.

The meaning of ﴿that you will not act justly﴾ is: that you will not be equitable, i.e., "and if you fear injustice." Aqsata means "adala" (was equitable). Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wassab read (tuqsitu) with a fatḥah on the tā' from qasata, whereas the well-known meaning of qasata is "jara" (acted unjustly). Al-Zajjaj said: it is also said qasata in the sense of aqsata, i.e., "adala." If this reading is taken according to the well-known usage of the language, then (lā) is superfluous, i.e., "and if you fear that you will act unjustly," since the meaning is not complete without considering it superfluous. If it is taken as "an tuqsitu" meaning "an tuqsitu" (that you act justly), then (lā) is for negation, as in "tuqsitu."

Ibn Abi 'Abla read (man ṭāba). The majority read (mā ṭāba). It was said: (mā) means (man), and this is the view of those who permit (mā) to refer to individual rational beings, which is a weaker view. It was said: He expressed with (mā) for women, because female rational beings, due to the deficiency of their intellects, take the place of non-rational beings. It was said: (mā) refers to a category, i.e., "marry the category of women that is good for you," and this is the statement of our companions: that (mā) can refer to kinds of rational beings. Abu al-'Abbas said: (mā) is for generalizing the genus with emphasis, and this statement seems to be the one before it. It was said: (mā) is verbal-masdarial, the verbal noun being implied as an active participle: meaning, "marry the marriage that is good for you." It was said: (mā) is an indefinite descriptive, i.e., "marry a kind or a number that is good for you." It was said: (mā) is temporal and verbal-masdarial, i.e., "for the duration of the goodness of marriage for you." The apparent view is that (mā) is the object of "fankihu" (marry), and that (min al-nisā') means "of the adult women." The (min) in it is either to specify the kind, due to the vagueness in (mā) according to the view of those who accept this meaning for it, or partitive, relating to an omitted verb, i.e., "being of the women," and in the position of a circumstantial phrase. As for when (mā) is verbal-masdarial or temporal, the object of "fankihu" is "min al-nisā'," as you say: "I ate from the bread," the implied meaning being: "some of the bread." It is not permissible for the object of "fankihu" to be "matnā," because this numerical form turned from its base does not come before operators, as established in the discussion of the individual words.

Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Jahdari and al-A'mash read (ṭāba) with imala (inclination). In Ubayy's codex it is (ṭība) with a yā', which is evidence for the imala. The apparent sense of "fankihu" is obligation, and the people of the apparent (Zahiris) held this view, relying on this imperative and on other evidence. Others said: it is recommended for some, and permissible for others, according to the circumstances of the person; and marriage in general is recommended. The meaning of "mā ṭāba" is "what is lawful," because the forbidden women are many, as said by al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik. It was also said: what the soul finds pleasing and the heart inclines to. They said: "fankihu" does not include slaves (al-'abīd).

Since His saying ﴿what is good for you of women﴾ is general for all numbers, it is specified by His saying ﴿two, three or four﴾. The apparent meaning of this specification is the division of the women to be married: that we may marry two by two, three by three, and four by four, but it is not permissible for us to marry five by five, nor any numbers beyond that. This is like saying: "I divide the dirhams between Zayd and Zayd, two dirhams each, three each, and four each," meaning that the division is to occur according to this breakdown and not otherwise. So it is not permissible for us to give any of those to whom it is divided five each, and it is not appropriate to put (aw, "or") here in place of (wa, "and"), because then the meaning would be that they all marry only one of the named numbers, and they would not have the option of making some two, some three, and some four; for (aw) is for one of two things or things. Whereas (wa) indicates general combination, so the marrying people may take whomever they wish to marry in combination, if they wish varying in those numbers, or if they wish agreeing in them, while what exceeds is forbidden to them. Some of the Shi'a went to the view that marriage is permitted without any number, just as concubinage is permitted without any number. The verse does not indicate a fixed limit in number, but indicates permissibility, like your saying: "Take what you like, one, two or three." Mentioning some of what the general implies came by way of explanation and does not require restriction to it. Some went to the view that it is permissible to marry nine, because (wa) indicates combination, so the meaning of "two, three and four" is two and three and four, which totals nine; and they reinforced this by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) died leaving nine wives. Some went to the view that these numbers, and their being joined by (wa), indicate the permissibility of marrying eighteen, because each number among them is a repetition of a doubled form, and when those repeated forms are added together they amount to eighteen. The discussion of these views, both in argument and refutation, is mentioned in the books of disputed jurisprudence.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 3 (part 2 of 3):

The jurists of the major cities have agreed that it is not permissible to exceed four wives. The apparent meaning is that marrying two, three or four is not permitted except for one who fears he will not be just towards the orphans, because the condition is attached to it. As for one who does not fear this, the implication of the condition indicates that it is not permitted for him. The consensus is against what the apparent meaning indicates, namely that the permission is restricted to the one who fears injustice. The Muslims have agreed that one who does not fear injustice regarding the wealth of orphans may marry more than one: two, three or four, just as one who fears may. So this shows that the verse is an answer to one who fears that, and its ruling is more general.

Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Thabbat read (ورُبَعَ) without the alif, just as it was omitted in His saying (وحَلَيانًا بَرَدًا), meaning (بارِدًا, cold). If we parse (ما) in (ما طابَ) as an object (maf'ul) — and it is a relative pronoun — then the accusative of (مَثْنى) and what follows it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is a hal from "al-nisa'" (the women). Ibn Atiyya said: its place in i'rab is accusative as a substitute (badal) for (ما طابَ), and they are indefinite nouns that do not take inflection because they are diptotes (ma'dula) and adjectives. End of quote. These are two weak parsings. As for the first, the thing spoken of is (ما طابَ), and (﴿مِنَ النِّساءِ﴾) comes as a specification (tabyin) and is not the thing spoken of, so it cannot be a hal from it, although restricting it by the hal would entail restricting the women who are married. As for the second, the badal is intended as a repetition of the governing verb, and so it would follow that the governing verb directly governs it; but it has been established in the Mufradat that the governing verb does not directly govern it. Also, he said they are indefinite and adjectival, and whatever is indefinite and adjectival, when it comes as a follower of an indefinite noun, is an adjective of it, as in His saying (﴿أُولِي أجْنِحَةٍ مَثْنى وثُلاثَ ورُباعَ﴾ [Fatir: 1]), and whatever is an adjective of an indefinite noun is a hal of a definite noun. And (ما طابَ) is definite, so (مَثْنى) must be a hal.

﴿فَإنْ خِفْتُمْ ألّا تَعْدِلُوا فَواحِدَةً أوْ ما مَلَكَتْ أيْمانُكُمْ﴾ — meaning: if you fear that you will not be just between two if you marry both, or between three or four if you marry them, in division, maintenance or clothing, then choose one, or what your right hands possess. This is if we take (فانْكِحُوا) to mean "marry"; if we take it to mean "sexual intercourse," we supply the verb governing (فَواحِدَةً): "then have intercourse with one, or with what your right hands possess." It may also be of the type of (عَلَفْتُها تِبْنًا وماءً بارِدًا) according to one of its two analyses, and the estimate is: "then marry," i.e., marry one, or have intercourse with what your right hands possess. He did not restrict the slave women owned by the right hand to a number, so it is permissible for him to have intercourse with as many of them as he wishes, because justice among them is not obligatory, neither in division, nor in maintenance, nor in clothing.

Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Abu Ja'far and Ibn Hurmuz read (فَواحِدَةٌ) with a nominative. Ibn Atiyya explained this as nominative by way of the inchoative (mubtada'), with an implied predicate: "one is sufficient." Al-Zamakhshari explained it as nominative as a predicate: "then [what suffices you is] one," or "then one is enough for you, or what your right hands possess." The (أوْ) here is for one of two things: either for choice (takhyir) or for permission (ibahah).

It is narrated from Abu 'Amr: (فَما مَلَكَتْ أيْمانُكم), meaning the female slaves, and the sense according to this is: if he fears he will not be just in treating one, then what his right hand owns. Ibn Abi 'Abla read (أوْ مَن مَلَكَتْ أيْمانُكم), and attributed the possession to the right hands, because it is a term of praise, and the right hand is specially associated with noble qualities. Do you not see that it is the one that spends, in his saying: (حَتّى لا تَعْلَمَ شِمالَهُ ما تُنْفِقُ يَمِينُهُ), and it is the one that pledges and receives the banners of glory, and the one commanded to eat food with it, and forbidden from cleaning oneself with it. These are two independent conditions, each having an independent answer. The first of the two conditions is: (﴿وإنْ خِفْتُمْ ألّا تُقْسِطُوا﴾), and its answer: (فانْكِحُوا). It directed those who fear injustice regarding marrying orphans to marrying those of them who are adults and others, and mentioned those numbers. The second of the two conditions is His saying: (﴿فَإنْ خِفْتُمْ ألّا تَعْدِلُوا﴾), and its answer: (﴿فَواحِدَةً أوْ ما مَلَكَتْ أيْمانُكُمْ﴾). It directed those who fear injustice in marrying the number mentioned to marrying one, or to concubinage with what one possesses; and this is by way of kindness to the responsible person, gentleness toward him, and compassion toward women and consideration for them.

Some people said that these clauses contain one condition and a parenthetical clause. The condition is (﴿وإنْ خِفْتُمْ ألّا تُقْسِطُوا﴾), and its answer is: "then one." The parenthetical clause is His saying: (﴿فانْكِحُوا ما طابَ لَكم مِنَ النِّساءِ مَثْنى وثُلاثَ ورُباعَ﴾), and the condition is repeated with His saying: (﴿فَإنْ خِفْتُمْ ألّا تَعْدِلُوا﴾), because the speech was lengthened by the parenthetical clause, its meaning being as in (﴿فَلَمّا جاءَهم ما عَرَفُوا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]) after (﴿ولَمّا جاءَهم كِتابٌ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]), since the separation between (لَمّا, lamma) and its answer was long, so it was repeated. Likewise (﴿فَلا تَحْسَبَنَّهم بِمَفازَةٍ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 188]) after (﴿لا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 188]), since the separation by what follows lengthened between (لا تَحْسَبَنَّ) and (بِمَفازَةٍ), so the clause was repeated. The meaning on this estimate becomes: if you cannot be just, then marry one. He said: It is established that they cannot be just, by His saying (﴿ولَنْ تَسْتَطِيعُوا أنْ تَعْدِلُوا بَيْنَ النِّساءِ ولَوْ حَرَصْتُمْ﴾ [al-Nisa': 129]). End of this view, which is attributed to Abu 'Ali. But it is likely that this is not authentically from him, for Abu 'Ali was of high standing in the science of grammar, and this view corrupts the compositional structure of the Qur'an and nullifies the legal rulings, because if one derives from these two verses and His saying (﴿ولَنْ تَسْتَطِيعُوا﴾ [al-Nisa': 129]) what follows from them, it requires that it is not permissible to marry more than one, or to take concubines with what one's right hand owns. And the separation by the parenthetical clause between the condition and its answer would remain mere superfluity with no benefit, on his claim. The justice whose capability is negated is other than the justice negated here: that is justice in the inclination of the heart, which has been lifted as a burden from a person; and this is justice in division and maintenance. For this reason its capability is negated there, and here it is conditioned upon fear of its absence, because fear in it is hope and, generally, assumption.

Al-Shafi'i derived from His saying (﴿فَواحِدَةً أوْ ما مَلَكَتْ أيْمانُكُمْ﴾) that occupation with voluntary acts of worship is superior to occupation with marriage, contrary to Abu Hanifa, who reversed this. The basis of his derivation and his argument from the verse is that He, exalted is He, gave the choice between marrying one and concubinage; and choice between two things indicates equality between them in the sought wisdom, and the wisdom is the tranquility of the soul through spouses, the protection of religion and the interests of the household, and all of this is achieved by both methods. We agree that occupation with voluntary worship is superior to concubinage, so it must be superior to marriage, because what exceeds two equals must necessarily exceed the second equal.

(﴿ذَلِكَ أدْنى ألّا تَعُولُوا﴾) The demonstrative refers to choosing the single free woman or the slave woman. (أدْنى): from "dunuww," meaning closer. (أنْ لا تَعُولُوا): meaning that you not deviate from the truth. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Abu Malik, and al-Suddi. Mujahid said: "not go astray." Al-Nakha'i said: "not betray."

A group, among them Zayd ibn Aslam, Ibn Zayd, and al-Shafi'i, said: its meaning is "that your dependents not increase." This view of al-Shafi'i was rejected both in meaning and in wording. As for the meaning, Abu Bakr ibn Dawud and al-Razi said, in substance: al-Shafi'i erred, because the owner of slave women has dependents just as the owner of wives does. Al-Zajjaj said: God has permitted a multitude of concubines, and in that there is an increase of dependents, so how could it be closer to their not increasing? The author of al-Nazm said: He said "or not" (أوْ لا) — "that you not be unjust" — so the opposite of justice must be injustice. As for the wording, which also requires rejection on the level of meaning: al-Shafi'i's explanation of (تَعُولُوا) as (تُعِيلُوا). They said: one says "a'ala yu'ilu" when his dependents increase; it is thus from the ya'-root, not from the waw-root, so the two differ in their root, and the meaning of (تَعُولُوا) is not (تُعِيلُوا). Al-Razi also said about al-Shafi'i that he opposed the exegetes. What he said is not correct; rather, Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Zayd said his statement, as we have already mentioned, and others as well. As for his explanation of (تَعُولُوا) by (تُعِيلُوا), there is no evidence that he meant that (تَعُولُوا) and (تُعِيلُوا) come from one root and share one derivation; rather, two words may have one meaning without sharing one derivation, such as their saying: "dumtu" and "dashir," and "sibt" and "sibta." Likewise here.

Ibn al-A'rabi transmitted "'ala al-rajul ya'ulu," meaning his dependents increased, as we mentioned in al-Mufradat. Al-Kisa'i also transmitted it, saying: it is an eloquent dialect. Al-Kisa'i said: the Arabs say "'ala ya'ulu" and "a'ala yu'ilu," meaning his dependents increased. Abu 'Amr al-Duri the reciter, who was an unchallenged imam in the language, also transmitted it, saying: it is the dialect of Himyar.

Abu 'Amr recited as evidence for it:

And death takes every living being without doubt, even if he be wealthy in livestock or has many dependents.

(amsha: his livestock increased; 'ala: his dependents increased.) Al-Zamakhshari took al-Shafi'i's statement and his explanation of (تَعُولُوا) as "that your dependents increase," by making it from your saying: "'ala al-rajul 'iyalahu ya'ulahum." He said: it should not be supposed of him that he changed (تُعِيلُوا) into (تَعُولُوا), and he praised al-Shafi'i as being too high in standing and too broad in command of Arabic speech for something like this to be hidden from him. He said: But scholars have methods and styles, and he followed in the explanation of this word the method of kinayat (allusion). As for what Ibn Dawud, al-Razi and al-Zajjaj rejected, Ibn 'Atiyya said: this objection — pointing to the objection of al-Zajjaj — is not correct, because concubines are only property that may be disposed of by sale, whereas the dependents that burden are free women with their obligatory rights.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The purpose of marriage is procreation and offspring, unlike concubinage. For this reason it is permissible to practice withdrawal (al-'azl) with concubines without their permission, so concubinage is likely to produce fewer children compared with marriage, and one wife compared with marrying four. Al-Qaffal said: if concubines multiply, he may require them to work, so they spend on themselves and on their master as well, and dependents decrease. As for when she is a free woman, the matter is not like that. End of quote. It is also narrated from al-Shafi'i that he explained the saying of God, exalted is He, (أنْ لا تَعُولُوا) as meaning "that you not become poor," and he did not intend that (تَعُولُوا) derives from (تُعِيلُوا); from (عال يَعِيلُ) when one becomes poor. He intended only allusion as well, because the multiplying of dependents causes poverty. The apparent meaning is that the choice of the single free woman or the slave woman is closer to the absence of injustice, since that is the feared outcome on whose fear the mentioned choice is conditioned. That is, he expressed "that you not be unjust" by "that your dependents not increase," as he expressed the cause by its effect, because a multitude of dependents results in injustice.

Talhah read (أنْ لا تَعِيلُوا), with a fatha on the ta', meaning: that you not become poor, from al-'ayla (poverty), as in His saying (﴿وإنْ خِفْتُمْ عَيْلَةً﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]). And the poet said:

The poor man does not know when his wealth will come, and the rich man does not know when he will become poor.

Tawus read (أنْ لا تُعِيلُوا) from (أعالَ الرَّجُلُ), when his dependents increased, and this reading supports al-Shafi'i's explanation in the meaning he intended. And (أنْ) is connected to (أدْنى), and it is in a place of accusative or genitive according to the difference of opinion, since the estimate is: "closer to that you not be unjust." And the comparative form (أفْعَلُ التَّفْضِيلِ), when the verb is transitive by a preposition, is transitive by that same preposition. You say: "dunawtu ila kadha" (I drew near to such-and-such), so the estimate was "closer to that you not be unjust." It is also permissible that the omitted particle is the lam of purpose, because you say: "dunawtu li-kadha."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 3 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And give the women their dower (ṣadaqāt) as a gift (niḥlah).﴾ [An-Nisa: 4] The apparent meaning is that the address is to the husbands, because the address before it is to them. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jurayj. It was said: a man would marry without a dower, saying, "I will inherit you and you will inherit me," and she would say, "Yes." So they were commanded to hasten in giving the dowers. It was also said: the address is to the guardians of the women, for it was the custom of some Arabs that a woman's guardian would consume her dower, and God removed that with Islam. This was said by Abu Salih, and al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah preferred it. It was also said: the intent of the verse is to abandon what those who practised shighar (shighar, an exchange of wives without dower) used to do, and they were commanded to give dowers. This was said by Hadrami. The command to give women their dowers as a gift encompasses all these cases.

The ṣadaqāt are the dowers. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: (niḥlah) means an obligation (farīḍah). It was said: a gift of ownership (ʿaṭiyyat tamlīk), said by Abu al-Kalbi and al-Farra'. It was said: a law and a religion, said by Ibn al-Aʿrabi. Al-Raghib said: niḥlah is more specific than hibah (gift), since every hibah is a niḥlah but not vice versa, and the dower was called niḥlah because, in exchange for it, nothing more is required than enjoyment without a financial return. As for one who says niḥlah means obligation, he looked to the ruling of the verse, not to the root meaning and derivation of the word, and the verse requires that they give the dower. End of quotation. This command indicates caution about encroaching upon women's dowers, just as the command in: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [An-Nisa: 2] does, and the two are equal in prohibition. When permission was given to marry up to four, he commanded husbands and guardians to avoid what they had been doing of the customs of the Jahiliyyah.

The Jumhur read ﴿ṣadaqātihinna﴾ [An-Nisa: 4] as the plural of ṣadaqah, on the pattern of samurah. al-Suddi and others read it with the dal sukun and the ṣad damma (ṣudqāt). Mujahid, Musa ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, Fayyad ibn Ghazwan and others read it with damma on the ṣad. al-Nakhaʿi and Ibn Wththab read (ṣadaqatahinna) with damma and in the singular. (niḥlah) is in the accusative as a verbal noun not from its own root, since the sense of (wa-ātū) is "give as a gift" (inḥalū), so the accusative is governed by (ātū). It was also said it is governed by an implied (inḥalūhunna). It was also said it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), either from the agents, meaning "giving as a gift" (nāḥilīn), or from the first or second object, meaning "given as a gift" (manḥūlāt). It was also said it is accusative by an implied verb with the meaning of "legislate" (sharaʿa), meaning God made that a gift, that is, legislated it as a law and religion. It was also said that if it means a law (shirʿah), it may be accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlih) or as a circumstantial accusative of the ṣadaqāt. In the words ﴿And give the women their dowers﴾ [An-Nisa: 4] there is evidence that the dower is obligatory for the woman, and this is agreed upon, except what was narrated from some Iraqi scholars: that when a master marries his slave to his slave-woman, no dower is due. The verse does not address the amount of the dower, nor any of its rulings. Some exegetes have spoken about that here, but the proper place for discussion of that is the books of fiqh.

The address in this (﴿فَإنْ طِبْنَ لَكم عَنْ شَيْءٍ مِنهُ نَفْسًا فَكُلُوهُ هَنِيئًا مَرِيئًا﴾, "But if they give you willingly of it, from something of it, then consume it with satisfaction and pleasure") is disputed: is it addressed to the husbands or to the guardians (awliya', sing. wali)? This dispute is based on the disagreement over ﴿وآتُوا النِّساءَ﴾ ("And give the women their dowries"). Al-Hadrami said: the occasion of its revelation was that some people were reluctant for anything they had given to their wives to come back to them. The pronoun in (مِنهُ, "of it") refers to the dower (ṣadaq), as said by Ikrimah. If (صَدُقاتِهِنَّ, "their dowries") had been placed in its position, it would have been permissible, and it would be like the saying: "He is the best of youths and the most beautiful of them," since "he is the best youth" is also acceptable.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the masculine form of the pronoun is used so that it refers to a single dower, and thus it covers part of it. If it had been feminine, its apparent meaning would cover the gift of the whole dower, because some of the dowries are one or more of them. End of quotation.

I say: the masculine form of the pronoun is good, because the meaning of ﴿فَإنْ طِبْنَ﴾ is: if each one of them is pleased. Therefore he said (مِنهُ), that is, of her dower. This is similar to ﴿وأعْتَدَتْ لَهُنَّ مُتَّكَأً﴾ ("and she prepared for them a couch," Yusuf 31), meaning for each one of them; for this reason (مُتَّكَأً, "couch") is singular.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to (صَدُقاتِهِنَّ) treated as if it were a demonstrative noun, as if it were said: "of some of that." A demonstrative noun, even if singular, may refer to a plurality, as in His saying: ﴿قُلْ أؤُنَبِّئُكم بِخَيْرٍ مِن ذَلِكُمْ﴾ ("Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that?" Al-Imran 15). And many things have preceded it.

Ru'bah was asked: "How did you say:

"As if on its skin were the spotting of leukoderma (bahaq)"

and it had been mentioned before:

"In it are lines of black and of white."

He said: "I meant: that was it."
