It has been said that it refers to the property (al-mal), which is not mentioned, but is indicated by (صَدُقاتِهِنَّ). It has been said that it refers to the giving (al-iita'), which is the verbal noun indicated by (وآتُوا, "and give"). This was said by al-Raghib, and Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned it. The two prepositional phrases are connected to the verb (طِبْنَ, "they are pleased"), and (مِنهُ, "of it") is in the position of a qualifier for (شَيْءٍ, "something"), so it is connected to an omitted element. The apparent meaning of (مِنِ, "of") is partitive. In this there is an indication that what she gives is a part of the dower. For this reason al-Layth ibn Sa'd held that her giving to him is not permitted except for a small amount.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Here (مِن, "of") implies the category (jins). Likewise it is permissible for her to give him the entire dower; if (مِن) had indicated partiality, that would not be permissible.

The word (نَفَسًا, "willingly") is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz, "clarifying accusative"), and it is a tamyiz transferred from the subject (al-tamyiz al-manqul min al-fa'il). When a tamyiz comes after a plural and is in the accusative in respect of the complete sentence, it either agrees in meaning with what precedes it or differs from it. If it agrees, it matches it in plurality, as in: "The men were noble as men," just as it would agree if it were a predicate. If it differs, then either its referent is singular or its referents vary. If its referent is singular, the word must be singular, as when you say of the sons of one man: "The sons of so-and-so were noble in origin and in father," and as when you say: "The pious became pious in piety, and the clever excelled in understanding." This is when you do not intend, by the verbal noun, the variety of kinds because of the variety of its loci. If its referents vary, then either their singular form would be confusing or it would not be. If it would be confusing, agreement is required, as in: "The men were noble as fathers," meaning: the fathers of the men were noble. If you said: "The men were noble as a father," it would give the false impression that their father was one person described as noble. If it would not be confusing, both singular and plural are permitted, but the singular is preferred, as in His saying: ﴿فَإنْ طِبْنَ لَكم عَنْ شَيْءٍ مِنهُ نَفْسًا﴾, since it is known that each has a self, and that they do not share one self. One may say: "Their eyes were cool (qarra al-zaydun 'aynan)," and it is also permitted to say "anfusan" (selves) and "a'yunan" (eyes).

What also makes the singular suitable in the verse is what we mentioned earlier concerning the reason for the masculine and singular pronoun: the meaning is, "if each one of them is pleased with something of it, willingly."

Some of the Basran grammarians said: By (النَّفْسِ, "self") he meant desire (al-hawa). Desire is a verbal noun, and verbal nouns are neither dualized nor pluralized.

The answer of the conditional clause is ﴿فَكُلُوهُ﴾ ("then consume it"), which is an imperative of permission. The meaning is: benefit from it. He expressed it by "eating" because it is the principal form of benefit.

﴿هَنِيئًا مَرِيئًا﴾ means: healing and smooth. Abu Hamzah said: "Hanian" means without sin in it, "marian" means without sickness in it. It has been said: "hanian" means delicious, "marian" means praiseworthy in outcome. It has been said: "hanian marian" means without any turbidity. It has been said: it goes down smoothly and no one who swallows it chokes on it. It has been said: "hanian marian" means lawful and good.

Al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read (هَنِيًّا مَرِيًّا, without hamzah), replacing the hamzah which is the final radical of the word with a yā', and assimilating the long vowel yā' into it.

The accusative of (هَنِيئًا) is either as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "consume it with a pleasant consumption," or as a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun object. This is how al-Zamakhshari and others parsed it. But this view contradicts the view of the leading grammarians of Arabic, because according to Sibawayh and others, it is accusative by a verb that is omitted and may not be expressed. We have already quoted Sibawayh's text on this in the section on vocabulary. According to what the leading grammarians of Arabic say, ﴿هَنِيئًا مَرِيئًا﴾ is a separate sentence from His saying ﴿فَكُلُوهُ هَنِيئًا مَرِيئًا﴾, and it has no grammatical connection to it, only a connection in meaning.

The summary of the discussion on (هَنِيئًا) is that it is a circumstantial accusative standing in place of the subject that governs it. When it is said, "So-and-so obtained good," and you say "hanian lahu dhalik" ("may that be wholesome for him"), the underlying form is "thabata lahu dhalika hanian" ("that became his, wholesome"), with (ثَبَتَ, "became established") omitted and (هَنِيئًا) put in its place. They then disagreed about what (dhalika) is raised by. Al-Sirafi held that it is raised by that omitted verb (ثَبَتَ), and (هَنِيئًا) is a circumstantial accusative of it, and in (هَنِيئًا) there is a pronoun referring to it. If you say (هَنِيئًا) and do not say (لَهُ ذَلِكَ), but limit yourself to "hanian," then there is a hidden pronoun referring to the one described, which is the subject pronoun hidden in the omitted (ثَبَتَ).

Al-Farisi held that when you say "hanian lahu dhalika," it is raised by (هَنِيئًا), which stands in place of the omitted verb, because it has become its substitute, so it works as the verb would. Just as when you say "Zayd is in the house," the prepositional phrase raises the pronoun that was raised by the implied predicate, because it is a substitute for it. In (هَنِيئًا) there is no pronoun, because it has raised the explicit noun, which is the demonstrative. When you say "hanian" alone, there is a subject pronoun in it, namely the pronoun that is the subject of (ثَبَتَ), and "hanian" has taken the place of the omitted verb as a derivative from the verb.

When you say "hanian marian," they disagreed about the accusative of (مَرِيءٍ, "marian"). Some held that it is an adjective of "hanian," and among those who held this was al-Hawfi. Al-Farisi held that its accusative is like the accusative of "hanian," so the implied sense is "thabata marian" ("became smooth"). According to him it cannot be an adjective of (هَنِيئًا), because (هَنِيئًا), since it is a substitute for the verb, has the same rule as the verb it replaces, and a verb cannot be described; likewise it cannot be described.

Al-Zamakhshari touched on some of what the grammarians said about (هَنِيئًا), but he distorted it. After first stating that its accusative is as a qualifier of the verbal noun, or as a circumstantial accusative of the pronoun in (فَكُلُوهُ, "consume it"), that is, "consume it while it is wholesome and smooth," he said: It may be stopped upon at (فَكُلُوهُ) and then begin with (هَنِيئًا مَرِيئًا) as a supplication, and as two adjectives placed in the position of a verbal noun, as if it were said: "hana'an mara'an." End of quotation. His distortion is that he made them stand in the position of a verbal noun, so their accusative is the accusative of a verbal noun. For this reason he said "as if it were said: hana'an mara'an" ("a pleasant and smooth [act]"), so it becomes like your saying "saqyan wa ra'yan," meaning "watering and grazing." The grammarians make the accusative of (هَنِيئًا) a circumstantial accusative, and the accusative of (مَرِيئًا) as described in the disagreement mentioned: either as a circumstantial accusative or as a qualifier.

What shows the corruption of al-Zamakhshari's distortion and the correctness of the grammarians' view is that the apparent nouns occur after ﴿هَنِيئًا مَرِيئًا﴾ in the nominative. If the two words were in the accusative as verbal nouns used as supplications, it would be permitted to say, with them: "saqyan laka wa ra'yan" (watering and grazing for you), but it would not be permitted to say "saqyan Allahu laka" or "ra'yan Allahu laka," even though "saqahu Allahu wa ra'aahu Allahu" ("may God water him and pasture him") is permitted in the verb form. The evidence for the permissibility of raising the apparent nouns after them is the poet's saying:

"Wholesome and pleasant, without any hidden sickness,
is what Izzah has made lawful from our honor."

Here (ما, "what") is raised by what was mentioned before, namely (هَنِيءٍ, "wholesome") or (مَرِيءٍ, "pleasant"), or by the omitted (ثَبَتَ), according to the disagreement of al-Sirafi and Abu 'Ali, by way of the grammatical principle of operation (i'mal, one word governing another). The operation was permitted in this issue even though there is no coordinating conjunction between them, because (مَرِيئًا) is used only as a follower of (هَنِيئًا), so they are as if they were linked by that. If this were in a verb, it would not be permitted: if you said "qama kharaja Zayd" ("stood up went out Zayd"), it would not be valid as operation except with the intention of a coordinating particle.

Some held that (مَرِيئًا) is used alone and is not a follower of (هَنِيئًا), and that this is not preserved in the speech of the Arabs, and that "hanian marian" are two intensive active participles. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that they are two verbal nouns that came in the pattern fa'il, like (الصَّهِيلِ, "neighing") and (الهَدِيرِ, "roaring"), and they are not of the type in which fa'il is regularly used as a verbal noun.

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that if a woman gives her husband something of her dower, willingly, with her self pleased and not compelled to do so by insistence, ill temper, or bad companionship, then it is permitted for him to take it from her, to possess it and to benefit from it. This giving is not limited by a time, and no exception to it implies a right of return.

Al-Awza'i held that her giving is not permitted until she has borne a child or has lived in her husband's house for a year. If she takes it back after the gift, Shurayh and 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said: she has the right to take it back. The same was reported from 'Umar. 'Umar wrote to his judges: "Women give out of desire and out of fear, so whichever woman gives her husband something and then wishes to take it back, she has that right." Shurayh said: "If her self were pleased, she would not take it back." 'Abd al-Malik said: God the Exalted said: ﴿فَلا تَأْخُذُوا مِنهُ شَيْئًا﴾ ("then take not from it anything," al-Nisa 20). Both of these views contradict the apparent meaning of this verse.

Making acceptance depend on the pleasure of the self, rather than using the word "gift" or "remission," indicates the necessity of caution in taking, and informs that what is considered is her being pleased with what is given. In His saying ﴿هَنِيئًا مَرِيئًا﴾ there is an emphasis on permission, acceptance, and the removal of any liability.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 4, Verse 5:**

﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made for you a means of sustenance (qiyaman).﴾ Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and others said: it was revealed concerning a man's young children and his wife. Ibn Jubayr said: concerning those placed under guardianship (al-mahjurin). Mujahid said: concerning women specifically. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, al-Tabari and others said: it was revealed concerning everyone who has the attribute (al-sifah) that Allah stipulated as foolishness, whoever he may be. Mujahid's view that it refers to women is weakened by the fact that the word is the plural of safihah (foolish, feminine), and the Arabs normally pluralize fa'ilah as fa'a'il or fa'ilat. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. However, it has been reported that the Arabs pluralized safihah as sufaha', so this word has been used by the Arabs for the feminine, and Mujahid's view is therefore not weakened. Even if the plural of the feminine adjective fa'ilah (fa'ilah) is rare, it has been reported specifically for this word. Ibn 'Atiyyah's restriction of the plural of fa'ilah to fa'a'il or fa'ilat is not sound, because fi'al is regularly used for it, as in zarifah and ziraf, and karimah and kiram, and this agrees with the masculine. His unrestricted use of fa'ilah without specifying that it does not carry the meaning of maf'ulah (passive), as in qatilah, is also not sound, because fa'ilah in that sense is not pluralized as fa'a'il.

It was also said: by "the foolish" is meant the heirs whose condition is known to be that they act foolishly in using whatever comes into their hands, so He forbade the accumulation of property that the foolish inherit. The foolish (al-sufaha') are those who squander property by spending it on what is not fitting, and who have no ability to manage it, to develop it, or to dispose of it properly. The apparent meaning of His words "your property" (amwalakum) is that the property is attributed to the addressees mentioned in "do not give." Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: He forbade giving the foolish any of another person's property. If this prohibition applies to that, then prohibiting giving them any of one's own property is more fitting and more deserving of the prohibition. According to this view, that the address is to the owners of the property, it was said that this indicates that bequesting to a woman is permissible, and this is the view of the majority of the scholars. 'Umar bequeathed (his affairs) to Hafsah. It is reported from 'Ata' that a woman cannot be an executor (wasi). He said: if she did so, it would be transferred to a man from her people.

It was said: the ignorant person who does not know the rules of trade is also included under this, and it is reported from 'Umar that he said: "Whoever has not gained understanding of the religion, let him not trade in our markets." The unbelievers are also included. The scholars disliked that a Muslim should appoint a dhimmi (non-Muslim protected subject) as agent for buying and selling, or give him property to trade on his behalf (yudarribahu). Ibn Jubayr said: it means the property of the foolish, and it was attributed to the addressees in order to make them value the property, that is: it belongs to them when they need it, just as your own property protects your honour, guards you, and enhances your standing. Of the same kind is ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ (An-Nisa 4:29), and what is similar to it. This view was mentioned first by al-Zamakhshari, who said: the address is to the guardians, and the property was attributed to them because it is of the kind by which people sustain their livelihoods, just as He said ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ (An-Nisa 4:29) and ﴿So from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾ (An-Nisa 4:25). The evidence that the address is to the guardians regarding the property of orphans is His words ﴿and provide for them from it and clothe them﴾.

Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i recited (al-lati) with the form ﴿allati﴾. The majority recited ﴿allati﴾ (alladhi). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Property (al-amwal) is a plural for non-rational things, so the recitation of the majority is more correct." End of quote. Allati is a plural in meaning of alla, so its analogy would be that it should not be used to describe the female slaves in the way its singular is described with allati. The masculine is not described with allati, whether it is rational or non-rational, so the analogy for its plural is that it should not be described with the plural of allati, which is allati. Description with allati operates like description with other attributes that take the feminine ta' marbuta. When we have a plural of a non-rational thing, the description may be applied to it as it is applied to a feminine singular, and it may also be applied to it as it is applied to plurals of feminine nouns. You may say: "I have broken trunks (judhu' munkasirah)" just as you say "a tall woman (imra'ah tawilah)," and "broken trunks (judhu' munkasirat)" just as you say "righteous women (nisa' salihat)," so the description operates in this respect as the verb does. The better usage is to treat it as one treats what applies to the feminine singular. This applies when the plural of the non-rational thing is a plural of abundance (jam' al-kathrah). When it is a plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah), the opposite ruling is better: "ajdha' munkasirat" is better than "ajdha' munkasirah." This applies to what has both plurals: the plural of paucity and the plural of abundance. As for what is pluralized only in one of them, its ruling should follow what is intended by it of paucity or abundance. Once this is established, it follows that alati is more appropriate than allati, because it follows a plural of a non-rational thing. Property is not pluralized as anything else, and it is not intended to mean paucity, because the description operates with it as a description with an attribute that takes the feminine ta'. Therefore the recitation of the majority is more correct.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say "allati" for women more often than "alati," and for property they say "alati" more often than "allati," and both are permissible in both cases. It was recited irregularly (shadhdhan) as "al-lawati," which is also in meaning a plural of alati.

The meaning of ﴿qiyaman﴾ is: you stand by them and are sustained by them, and if you were to waste them your conditions would be ruined. Al-Dahhak said: Allah made them a means of support (qiyam) because by them the Hajj and jihad are established, the completion of righteousness is achieved, and by them the freeing of necks from slavery and from the Fire is accomplished. The early generations used to say: "Property is the believer's weapon," and "Leaving what Allah will hold me accountable for is better than my needing people." It is reported from Sufyan al-Thawri, who had merchandise that he turned over (in trade), that he said: "If it were not for it, the Banu al-'Abbas would have (wrongfully) devoured (me)," meaning the Banu al-'Abbas. They used to say: "Trade, for you are in a time when, if one of you is in need, the first thing devoured is his religion."

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿qiyaman﴾ as ﴿qiyaman﴾ (qiyam, with a short vowel), the majority of the Seven recited ﴿qiyaman﴾ (qiyam), al-A'mash ibn 'Umar recited ﴿qiwaman﴾ with a kasrah on the qaf, and al-Hasan and 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited ﴿qawaman﴾ with a fathah on it. It was also reported from Abu 'Amr. It was recited irregularly as ﴿qiwaman﴾ (with the vowel on the second letter). As for ﴿qiyaman﴾ (the form with the fathah and the ya), it is considered a verbal noun (muqaddar) like qiyam and qiyam; this was said by al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Akhfash, and it is not a contraction of qiyam. It was said that it is a contraction of it. They said: the alif was dropped as it was dropped in khiyam, whose original form is khiyam (tents), or it is the plural of qimah, like diyam, the plural of diymah. This was said by the Basran grammarians other than al-Akhfash. Abu 'Ali rejected this, saying: it is described by it in His words ﴿dinan qiyaman﴾ (religion, upright), and qiyam is not described by it; rather, it is a verbal noun in the sense of qiyam, which is intended to mean steadfastness and permanence. This was rebutted: if it were a verbal noun it would not have undergone i'lal (morphological alteration), just as they did not alter hiwal and 'iwad, because it is not on the pattern of the verb, especially the unaugmented triliteral. The answer is: it followed its verb in i'lal and so was altered, because it is a verbal noun in the sense of qiyam; just as qiyam was altered, so it was altered. Al-Akhfash reported qiyaman and qiwaman, and said: the analogy is to keep the waw sound, but it underwent i'lal irregularly, as in their saying tirah, and the saying of the Banu Dabbah tiyal (plural of tawil), and the saying of all (of them) jiyad (plural of jawad). If they altered diyaman because of the i'lal of diymah, then the i'lal of a verbal noun because of the i'lal of its verb is more appropriate. Do you not see the soundness of the plural despite the i'lal of its singular in ma'ishah and ma'a'ish, and maqamah and maqawim, while they did not keep sound a verbal noun whose verb had undergone i'lal? It was said: it is possible here that it is the plural of qimah, though it cannot bear this meaning in ﴿dinan qiyaman﴾ (An-Am 6:161). As for qiyam, it clearly is the verbal noun. As for qiwam, it was said to be the verbal noun of qawama. It was also said that it is a noun that is not a verbal noun, meaning that by which something is upheld, like your saying: "He is the mainstay of the matter (mulak al-amr), by which it is held." As for qiwam, Abu Hatim considered it an error, and said: qiwam means the stature of the body (imtidad al-qamah). Al-Kisa'i permitted it, and said: it has the meaning of qawam, meaning that it is a verbal noun. It was also said: it is a noun for the verbal noun. It was said: qiwam means stature (al-qamah), and the meaning is: the property which Allah made the cause of the continuance of your statures.

﴿And provide for them from it and clothe them﴾: that is, feed them and make for them a share. It was said: its meaning concerns those whose maintenance a man is obliged to provide, namely his wife and his young children. Ibn 'Abbas said: do not deliberately destroy the thing that Allah made your livelihood, so that you give it to your wife or your children and then look at what is in their hands; rather, keep that and manage it, and you yourself spend on them for their provision, their clothing and their sustenance. It was said: it concerns those placed under guardianship, and this is a difference of opinion based on the difference over who is addressed in His words "and give to those who..." The meaning according to this view is: make it a place of their provision, by trading with it and making profit, so that their maintenance comes from the profits and not from the principal, so that spending does not consume it. It was said: He said "in it" (fiha) and did not say "from it" (minha), as an indication of what the peace be upon him said: "Seek trade in the property of orphans, so that zakat does not consume it." The recommended course is that the spending on them be from its acquired surplus. It was also said: "fi" here has the meaning of "min," that is, "from it."

﴿And speak to them a kind word﴾: Al-ma'ruf (the kind) is what souls find agreeable, are at ease with, and what the Shari'ah requires. If the intended meaning of "the foolish" is those placed under guardianship, then part of the kind word is promising them the good promise that when you become mature we will hand over your property to you. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata', Muqatil and Ibn Jurayj. 'Ata' said: "When I profit, I will give you (a share), and when I gain booty in my campaign, I will make a portion for you." If the intended meaning is the women, the young children, and the foolish strangers, then you pray for them: "May Allah bless you, and protect you," or something similar. This was said by Ibn Zayd. Al-Dahhak said: it is a graceful refusal. When Allah the Exalted first commanded giving orphans their property in His words ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ (An-Nisa 4:2), and commanded a second time giving women their bridal gifts in His words ﴿And give the women their dowries﴾ (An-Nisa 4:4), and this was general without specification, He clarified in this verse that such giving is only for other than the foolish. He particularized that generality and restricted the unrestricted command to give.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 6 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age. Then if you perceive in them sound judgment, release their property to them.﴾ It is said: Rifa'a died and left behind his son Thabit, who was a young child. [Rifa'a's brother] asked: "My nephew is in my care. What is lawful for me from his property, and when should I hand over his property to him?" So this was revealed. It is also said: Aws ibn Thabit died, or it is said Aws ibn Suwayd, leaving his wife Umm Kajja, three daughters, and two cousins (sons of his paternal uncle), Suwayd and [another]. It is also said that al-Suddi and Arfaja took his property and gave nothing to the woman or the daughters. It is also said that the one who prevented their inheritance was the paternal uncle of the sons, whose name was Tha'laba. In the pre-Islamic period they did not give inheritance to women, to daughters, or to young sons who were male, so Umm Kajja complained of the two of them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he summoned them. He said: "No, O Messenger of Allah, her son does not ride a horse, does not carry a burden, and does not confront an enemy." He said: "[Go away until I see what Allah will bring about]." So this was revealed.

The testing of orphans means examining their intellects. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, Muqatil, and Sufyan. Or it means [examining] their intellects and their religion, their preservation of their property, and their good management of it. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. The manner of testing a young boy is to hand him a small amount of property to dispose of, while the guardian observes his conduct in it, lest he waste it. The testing of a young girl is to entrust her with the affairs of the household and with overseeing spinning, in terms of its output, its wage, and its completion. The testing of each of them varies according to what suits him or her and according to the tasks and trades he or she undertakes. When sound judgment is perceived in him or her after reaching puberty and after the testing, the property is handed over, and witnesses are called upon it. This is the apparent meaning of the verse, and it follows the handing over. The "calling of witnesses" is the required perceiving [of sound judgment]. Ibn Sirin said: The property is not handed over after the perceiving and testing mentioned until a year has passed over him, and the four seasons have cycled through it. The verse does not address the age of puberty or by what [sign] it occurs. Some exegetes have spoken about this here. The discussion of puberty is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence. The apparent meaning of the verse is that if sound judgment is not perceived in him, he remains under restriction (hajr) permanently, and the property is not handed over to him. This is the view of the majority. Al-Nakha'i and Abu Hanifa said: He is awaited for twenty-five years, and his property is handed over to him whether sound judgment is perceived in him or not. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the guardian (wasi) is independent in the handing over and autonomous in it. A group said: It requires that he hand it over to the ruler and establish his sound judgment before him, or that he be one whom the judge trusts. The general application of the term "orphans" includes daughters under this ruling, so their ruling is the same as that of sons in this respect. It is said: Their sound judgment is considered, even if they have not married upon reaching puberty. It is said: The period after consummation is five years. It is said: one year. It is said: seven years for the one with a father, and one year for the orphan girl who has no guardian.

Here "ḥattā" (until) indicates the end point (ghāyah) of the testing. It has entered upon the conditional particle "idhā" (when). Its response is "fa-in ānastum" (then if you perceive), and its response, along with the response of ﴿Indeed, Allah...﴾ [al-Nisa': 1], is "fa-idfa'ū" (then release). The perceiving of sound judgment is contingent upon reaching marriageable age, so it must be after it. When "ḥattā" enters upon a conditional, it does not govern [the conditional particle]; rather, it is what is followed by full clauses, as in his saying:

*"Even the thoroughbreds are not led by their reins."*

And his saying:

*"Even the water of the Tigris is turbid."*

However, in this matter there is a disagreement. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Durustawayh held that the clause is in a genitive position, while the majority held that it is not governing at all. In His saying ﴿reached marriageable age﴾ there is an omitted element, which is: "reached the limit of marriageable age or its time." Ibn Abbas said: The meaning of "ānastum" is "you knew." Ata' said: "you saw." (p-172) al-Farra' said: "you found." al-Zajjaj said: "you knew." These statements are close in meaning.

Ibn Mas'ud read: "fa-in aḥastum" (then if you sense), meaning "aḥsastum." He omitted the middle radical of the word. This omission is anomalous and occurs only in a few words. Other than Sibawayh has related that it is the dialect of Sulaym, and that it applies regularly to the middle radical of every doubled verb when it is joined to the suffix of the feminine or the plural nūn. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Abu al-Sammal, and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "rashadan" with two fatḥas. It was read anomalously as "rushudan" with two ḍammas. "Rushdan" is indefinite because its meaning is a kind of sound judgment, a portion and a sign of its signs, and one does not wait for its full completion. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Malik holds both conditions, reaching puberty and sound judgment, and then the property is handed over. Abu Hanifa holds that the property is handed over on the basis of one condition alone, as long as no foolishness is observed in him, just as the taking of a concubine is permitted on the basis of one condition alone. The Book of Allah has restricted this by the absence of ability to marry freely and the fear of sin. In my view, the analogy regarding handing over property based on the succession of two conditions is not valid, because reaching puberty is not presented by the verse as a cause of the condition. Rather, it is the state in which human intellects generally become mature, and it is the time at which the condition of sound judgment is considered only at that time. So it says: when he reaches that time, then let him look to the condition, which is sound judgment at that time. The eloquence of the speech indicates this, because the timing by puberty came with "idhā" (when), while the conditional came with "in" (if), which is the basic conditional particle. "Idhā" is not a conditional particle in the sense that what follows it occurs; Sibawayh permitted its use as a conditional in poetry. He said: They did this out of necessity, and it was made conditional only because it requires a response, and because the verb follows it, whether expressed or implied. Khalil argued against its being a conditional particle because what follows it occurs. Do you not see that you say: "I will come to you when the unripe dates turn red," and you do not say: "if the unripe dates turn red"? End of his statement. His statement indicates that "idhā" is a temporal adverb devoid of conditional meaning, and this contradicts the statements of the grammarians. Rather, the grammarians are virtually in agreement that "idhā" is a temporal adverb for what is future, in which the meaning of a condition is generally present. If anyone among them explicitly stated that it is not a conditional particle, he only meant that it does not apocopate (jazm) like conditional particles do, not that it never comes for a condition. How could one say that, when it is usually a conditional? The verse does not address the ruling concerning one in whom sound judgment is perceived after reaching puberty and whose property is handed over to him, and who then reverts to foolishness: does restriction return to him or not? On this there are two opinions. Malik said: it returns. Abu Hanifa said: it does not return. Both opinions are reported from al-Shafi'i.

﴿And do not consume their property extravagantly and hastily, [fearing] that they will grow up.﴾ It was previously stated that "consuming" is used figuratively for "taking," because consuming is the greatest way of benefiting from what is taken. This sentence is independent. He, exalted is He, forbade them from consuming the property of orphans and destroying it through poor management. It is not joined to the response of the conditional, because that and its condition are dependent upon reaching marriageable age. It also conflicts with His saying ﴿and hastily, [fearing] that they will grow up﴾, which entails hardship regarding what is dependent upon it, and that is impermissible. By what we have established, the error of one who took ﴿and do not consume it﴾ as coordinated with "release" becomes clear. Restricting the prohibition to consuming the property of orphans under these two circumstances is not something that permits consumption without them, so it is not an instance of "dalil al-khitab" (argument from the implication of the address). Extravagance (isrāf) is excessiveness in spending, and "saraf" is error in the places of spending. He said:

*"They gave Hunayda, with eight camels driven before her, and in their giving there is neither reproach nor extravagance."*

That is, they do not err in the places of giving. Ibn Abbas and others said: Hastening to their growing up means that the guardian seizes the property of his ward and consumes it, saying: "I hasten its growing up, lest he become sound in judgment and take his property." Both "isrāfan" and "bidāran" are in the accusative as two verbal nouns in the position of the circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning "extravagantly" and "hastily." "Bidār" is the verbal noun of "bādara," and it is of the form of reciprocal action (mufā'alah) that occurs between two parties, because the orphan hastens toward growing up, and the guardian hastens toward taking his property, so it is as if they are racing. It may also be from one party. It is permitted that both be in the accusative as the object of purpose (maf'ūl min ajlih), meaning "for your extravagance and your hastening." "An yakbarū" (that they grow up) is the object of the verbal noun, meaning "their growing up," as in His saying: "or feeding an orphan" [al-Balad: 14]. There is a disagreement about giving effect to an indefinite verbal noun. It is also said that the estimated phrase is "for fear that they grow up," so that "an yakbarū" would be the object of purpose, and the object of "bidāran" is omitted.

(p-173) ﴿And whoever is wealthy, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat according to what is reasonable.﴾ The apparent meaning of this sentence indicates that it is a division of the state of the guardian regarding the orphan. So He, exalted is He, commanded him to abstain from his property if he is wealthy, and to be content with what Allah, exalted is He, has provided of wealth. He permitted him to eat from the orphan's property according to what is reasonable if he is poor, in such a way that he takes sustenance carefully estimated. The apparent meaning of this permission is that there is no liability upon him, and no debt is incurred in his obligation for what he took to satisfy his hunger, provided it is not fine clothing, and he is not required to repay if he becomes well-off. This was said by Ibrahim, Ata', al-Hasan, and al-Suddi, and the jurists follow this view. Umar, Ibn Abbas, 'Ubayda, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliyya, and Ibn Jubayr said: He must repay if he becomes well-off, and he should not borrow more than his need. This is also the view of al-Awza'i. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Abu al-'Aliyya, al-Hasan, and al-Sha'bi: He only eats according to what is reasonable if he drinks from the milk and eats from the dates, enough to heal the mangy camel, line the trough, and pick the dates and similar things. As for the principal property itself and its capital, the guardian has no right to take it.

A group said: What is reasonable is that he should have a wage according to the amount of his work and service. This is a narration from Imam Ahmad. Al-Hasan ibn Hayy made a distinction and said: If he is the guardian appointed by a father, then he may eat reasonably; if he is the guardian appointed by a judge, then he has no access to the property in any way, and his wage is paid from the public treasury (bayt al-mal). Abu Hanifa and his two companions made a distinction and said: If the guardian of the orphan is resident, it is not permissible for him to take anything from his property; if he is traveling, he may take what he needs, but he may not accumulate anything. Al-Sha'bi made a distinction and said: If he is in a state of dire need, like the one permitted to eat carrion, he eats an amount according to his need and repays when he finds means; otherwise he should not eat at all, neither while traveling nor while resident. Mujahid said: This permission is abrogated (naskh, meaning its ruling is cancelled by a later revelation) by His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly...﴾ [al-Nisa': 10]. Abu Yusuf said: It may be abrogated by His saying: ﴿And do not consume your properties among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188], so he may not take a loan or anything else. Ibn Abbas and al-Nakha'i also said: This command is not connected to the property of the orphan. The meaning is that the wealthy one abstains by his wealth, and as for the poor one, he eats reasonably from his own property, and he maintains himself by his own property so that he does not need the property of his orphan. Al-Kiya al-Tabari from the Shafi'is chose this view. It was also said: If the orphan's property is large and requires much management, such that it occupies the guardian away from his own affairs and important matters, then a wage for his work is assessed from the orphan's property. If it does not occupy him, then he should take nothing from it, except that it is recommended for him to drink a little milk and eat a little food and ghee, provided it does not harm the property and is not excessive, according to what custom and tolerance have established. A group, including Rabi'a and Yahya ibn Sa'id, said: This is a division of the state of the orphan, not of the state of the guardian. The meaning is: whoever among them is wealthy, let him abstain with his property, and whoever among them is poor, let him be frugal with it reasonably and moderately. This is a second-person address with a specific referent intended for a general meaning (khitab al-'ayn, yurādu bihi al-ghayr). The orphans are addressed with abstinence and eating reasonably, but what is meant is the guardians, because the orphans are not among those addressed. So it is as if He said to the guardians and trustees: if the orphan is wealthy, then spend on him as one who is abstemious and moderate, lest his property be lost through extravagance in spending on him; and if he is poor, then spend on him according to the amount of his property, lest it be lost and he remain as a weak, burdensome dependent.

Thus these are the opinions, summarized: Is the division concerning the guardian or the orphan? There are two views. If it concerns the guardian, is the command directed at the guardian's own property or the orphan's property? There are two views. If it is directed at the orphan's property, is that abrogated (naskh) or not? There are two views. If it is not abrogated, is the distinction with respect to the eating or the thing eaten? There are two views. If it concerns the eating, is it specific to the father's guardian, or to the traveler, or to the one under compulsion, or to the one occupied with managing the property to the neglect of his own affairs? There are several views. If it concerns the thing eaten, is it specific to what is trivial or does it extend to other things? There are two views. If it extends to other things, is it a wage or not? There are two views. If it is not a wage and he took it, does a debt become binding on him that must be repaid when he becomes well-off or not? There are two views. The evidences for these views are mentioned in the books on the disputed questions (masa'il al-khilaf). The phrase ﴿فَلْيَسْتَعْفِفْ﴾ (fal-yasta'fif, "let him seek abstinence") is more emphatic than فَلْيَعِفَّ (fal-ya'iff, "let him be chaste"), because it implies a request for an increase in chastity.

﴿When you hand over their property to them, then call witnesses against them﴾. God, exalted is He, commanded the calling of witnesses (al-ishhad) to cut off the source of dispute, of suspicion toward them, and to secure safety from liability and penalty should the orphan deny the handover. It also comforts the orphan's heart by lifting the restriction (hajr) on him and integrating him into the ranks of those who transact and are transacted with. If the guardian does not call witnesses and the orphan sues him, then according to Abu Hanifa and his companions, the guardian is believed with his oath. According to Malik and al-Shafi'i, he is not believed except with proof (bayyinah). Thus calling witnesses protects against the oath that leads to accusation, or against the obligation of liability when no proof is produced. The apparent meaning of the command is that it is obligatory. Some people said it is recommended (nadb).

The apparent meaning of the verse is the command to call witnesses against them when one hands over their property, and this property is what is commanded to be handed over in His saying: ﴿Then if you perceive in them maturity of judgment, hand over their property to them﴾. 'Amr ibn Jubayr said: this calling of witnesses is only for the guardian's repayment of what he borrowed from the orphan's property during his poverty, when he becomes well-off. It was also said: the verse indicates the obligation of restitution upon one who ate from the orphan's property. The meaning: whether you borrowed or ate, then call witnesses when you pay it back. It was also said: the meaning is that when you spend something on the one under guardianship, then call witnesses, so that if a dispute arises, proof can be produced, for property received in trust (amanah) by testimony is not discharged from except by testimony of its return.

﴿And sufficient is God as Reckoner﴾, i.e., sufficient as a witness against you. Its meaning: one who reckons (muhsib), from "ahsabani kadha," i.e., it sufficed me. This was said by al-A'mash and al-Tabari. So it is fa'il in the sense of muf'il, or it means muhasib (one who calls to account), or hasib (one who reckons) your deeds, rewarding you for them. Therefore, be truthful and beware of lying. In this is a warning to one who denies the truth.

Hasib is fa'il in the sense of mufa'il, like jalis (companion) and khalit (associate), or in the sense of fa'il, transformed for emphasis in reckoning. Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Muqatil said: the meaning of hasiban is shahid (witness). Regarding kafa there is a dispute: is it a verb of naming (ism fi'l) or a verb? The correct view is that it is a verb, its subject is the name of God, and the ba' is superfluous. It was also said that the subject is a pronoun implied, the pronoun of sufficiency (damir al-iktifa'), meaning: "he sufficed," i.e., sufficiency by God, and the ba' is not superfluous, so (bi-Allah) is in the position of an accusative and is connected to the subject. This view is valid only according to the Kufan grammarians, who permit the verbal noun's pronoun to govern as its apparent form does. If by implied one means elision, then this involves governing with a verbal noun that is connected (to its object), and retaining its object, which according to the Basran grammarians is impermissible, namely, eliding the subject and eliding the verbal noun. (Hasiban) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), since min can be introduced before it. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Here kafa is transitive to one object, which is elided, the sense being: "and God suffices you as Reckoner." It also occurs in other senses, transitive to two objects, as in His saying: ﴿So God will suffice you against them﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 137].

﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave, and for women there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave, whether it be little or much, an obligatory share﴾. It was said: the occasion of its revelation was the report of Umm Kajja, which has already been mentioned. This was narrated by ʿIkrima, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Al-Marwazi said: The Greeks (al-Yunan) used to give the entire property to the daughters, because a man is not incapable of earning, whereas a woman is incapable. The Arabs did not give anything to the daughters, so God refuted both groups. By "men" is meant the males, and by "women" the females, as in His saying: ﴿And from the two He spread forth many men and women﴾ [al-Nisa larger: 1].

He left the word "share" (nasib) indeterminate, and "of what he left" (mimma taraka) is in the position of a qualifier of "share." It was also said that it is connected to the word "share," so it is part of its completion. "The two parents" (al-walidan) means the parents of the men and the women, namely their fathers and mothers. The father was called a walid (parent) because the child comes from him, and from the mother as well. The distinction between the two is made by the feminine ending (the taʾ) for the sake of commonality, as in His saying: ﴿A mother shall not be harmed on account of her child﴾ [al-Baqara: 233]. It was also made into the plural by the suffix of alif and taʾ by analogy, as in His saying: ﴿And the mothers﴾ [al-Baqara: 233]. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: As the poet said:

*Where the egg-laying raven builds its nest*

because the egg comes from both the female and the male. End of quotation. It is not necessary that "the raven" here be understood as the male, because the word "raven" applies to both male and female, and it is not one of those words that are distinguished from their feminine by the taʾ. It is like the word "ruʿub" (a woman who is lively and talkative), which applies to both male and female. Describing it as "egg-laying" does not favor its being male, for the description is in the masculine form, which may be taken as a male by following the wording, since no sign of the feminine appears in it. Just as the masculine is made feminine by following the wording of the feminine in His saying, "and ʿAntara al-Falhaʾ (the one with the cleft lip)," and in the poet's saying:

*Your father is an ally, whom another woman bore.*

"The close relatives" (al-aqrabun) are those who inherit from among the kin. He left the word "the close relatives" indeterminate, just as he left "share" indeterminate, and in the verses after it He specified the heir and the amount. His saying ﴿of what little of it﴾ is a substitution (badal) for His saying "of what he left" in the last instance, and the preposition was repeated with it. The pronoun in "of it" (minhu) refers to "what" (ma) in His saying "of what he left" in the last instance. He was content with mentioning it in this sentence, though it is intended in the first sentence, and it was not necessary to mention it again because the substitution came in the manner of emphasis, for there is nothing in it except clarifying that by His saying "of what he left" the generality of what is left is intended. In this substitution is the mention of both kinds of what is left, whether little or much.

Abu al-Baqaʾ said: ﴿of what little﴾ may be a circumstantial (hal) construction from the omitted pronoun in "he left," meaning: of what he left, established as little.

The meaning of ﴿an obligatory share﴾ is: a portion determined definitely, which they must take possession of. Al-Zajjaj and Makki said: "A share" (nasiban) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). The meaning: for these there are portions, as we have mentioned here, in the state of being obligatory. Al-Farraʾ said: It was put in the accusative because he brought it out in the manner of a verbal noun (masdar), and for this reason he made it singular, as when you say to someone: "On me is such-and-such, an incumbent right," and similar to it: ﴿an obligation from God﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 11]. If it were a fixed noun it would not be put in the accusative; you do not say: "For you upon me is a right, a dirham." End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said something close to this view: He said: It is permissible that it be in the accusative in the manner of a verbal noun emphasizing His saying ﴿an obligation from God﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 11], as if it were an obligatory division. Ibn ʿAtiyya said something similar to al-Zajjaj's words: He said: It is only a noun put in the accusative as a verbal noun is put in the accusative in the position of a circumstantial state; its estimated form is "obligation." For this reason its accusative is permissible, just as you say to him: "On me is such-and-such, a binding right," and were it not for the meaning of the verbal noun contained in it, this accusative would not be permissible for a noun that is not a verbal noun; rather its proper case is the nominative. End of his words. This is a combination of the words of al-Zajjaj and al-Farraʾ, and the two are different, for the accusative as a circumstantial state is distinct from the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun, and opposed to it. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿an obligatory share﴾ is in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas, a construction in which a noun is singled out by an accusative), meaning: I mean an obligatory, definite, binding share. End of quotation. If by "specification" he means what the grammarians have agreed upon, then it is rejected, because the word is indefinite, and the grammarians have stated that the accusative of specification cannot be indefinite. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a pure verbal noun, since it is a verbal noun, meaning: its share is a share. It was said: it is a circumstantial state of an indefinite noun, since it has been qualified. It was said: it is governed by an omitted verb, its estimated form being: I made it, or I made obligatory for them a share. It was said: it is a circumstantial state of the agent in "whether little or much."

By the apparent meaning of this verse, the division of inheritable rights is obligatory when they are distinct and can be divided, and when each of the two partners demands it, without disagreement. They differed regarding dividing what is left in the case of the fixed shares, when the division cannot be made without altering its state, such as a bathhouse, a mill, a well, and a house whose benefits are nullified by the separation of the shares. Malik, al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifa said: it is divided. Ibn Abi Layla and Abu Thawr said: it is not divided. Ibn al-Mundhir said: This is the more correct of the two opinions. It is also cited as evidence for the obligation of a brother inheriting from the deceased along with a daughter: when she takes half, he takes the remainder. They differed concerning two paternal cousins, one of whom is a maternal brother. ʿAli and Zayd said: the maternal brother has a sixth, and what remains is divided equally between them. This is the view of the jurists of the major cities. ʿUmar, al-Aʿmash, Shurayh and al-Hasan said: the property belongs to the maternal brother.

﴿And when the division is attended by the close relatives, the orphans and the needy, provide for them from it and speak to them a kind word﴾. It was said: it was revealed concerning the owners of property who divide it when death is present, in a bequest and to causes they choose, and relatives who are barred from inheritance attend them, so they bequeath to strangers and leave out those who are barred, so they are deprived of both inheritance and bequest. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Zayd and Abu Jaʿfar. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the owners of fixed shares, to whom a barred person also comes, so they were commanded to give them something from what God has bestowed on them. It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn al-Musayyib that it is abrogated (mansukha, subject to naskh, abrogation), and ʿIkrima and al-Dahhak said the same. They said: it was a division which God made into three categories, then that was abrogated by the verse of inheritance, which gave each possessor of a share his share, and made the bequest for those who are deprived and do not inherit. It was also said: it is muhkam (not abrogated). God commanded that whoever is entitled to an inheritance, and a relative, orphan or needy person who does not inherit attends the division, should not be deprived if the property is abundant, and that apologies be offered to them if it is little. Abu Musa al-Ashʿari commanded this. Al-Hasan and al-Nakhaʿi said: The believers used to do this: they would give them from the silver and gold coins, and when they divided the lands and slaves they would say to them a kind word: "May blessing be upon you." Al-Aʿmash ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr did this, and recited this verse. If the heir is a minor who cannot dispose of property, does the guardian do this or not? There are two opinions. The apparent sense of this verse, in the context following what precedes it, is that it concerns the heirs and not the dying testators. What is apparent from the word "qisma" (division) is that it is a verbal noun in the sense of "qasam" (dividing), as He said: ﴿That is then an unjust division﴾ [al-Najm: 22].

It was said: "qisma" means the thing divided. It was also said: "qisma" is a noun from "iqtisam" (apportioning), not from "qasm," like "khira" from "ikhtiyar." The eloquent do not usually say "qasamtu baynahum qisma" (I divided among them a division), and al-Kisaʾi transmitted this. Your "qisma" is what you have taken of the portions, and its plural is "qisam." Al-Khalil said: "al-qasm" is the share and portion of a part; it is said: "qasamtu falanan al-mal, wa-taqasamnahu, wa-iqtasamnahu" (I divided so-and-so's property with him, and we divided it mutually), and "al-qasm" is the one who shares with you.

The apparent meaning of His saying "fa-arzuquhum" (provide for them) is obligation. This was held by a group, including Mujahid, ʿAta and al-Zuhri. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan said: it is recommended (nadb). In His saying "fa-arzuquhum" there is the attribution of provision to other than God Most High, as He said: ﴿And God is the best of providers﴾ [al-Jumuʿa: 11]. It was said: this was obligatory for the heirs, and the verse of inheritance abrogated it. The pronoun in "minhu" (from it) refers to the property divided, which the division indicates, because the division, being a verbal noun, indicates its object, which is the property. It was also said: it refers to "what" (ma) in His saying: ﴿of what the parents and the close relatives leave﴾. Whoever said "the division is the thing divided" made the pronoun refer to the division in the sense of masculine gender, since what is meant is the thing divided. He placed the orphans before the needy, because their weakness is greater and their need more severe, so placing charity with them is more excellent and greater in reward. The apparent sense is that they are provided for from the very property divided. ʿUbayda and Ibn Sirin held that the provision in this verse means that a meal is prepared for them to eat, and they did this, and slaughtered a sheep from the estate. With ʿUbayda, property of an orphan was divided, and he bought a sheep from it and slaughtered it, and ʿUbayda said: "If not for this, it would have been from my own property." His saying "minhu" (from it) indicates partialness (tabʿid), and there is no estimate in it by consensus, and this is among the things that indicate recommendation. For if these people had a definite right, God would have specified the amount of that right, as He specified it in the other rights. On this basis, the jurists of the major cities hold that if the heirs are adults, it is so; but if they are minors, then there is only the kind word.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿and speak to them﴾ refers to what the pronoun in "fa-arzuquhum" referred to, namely: the close relatives, the orphans and the needy. Ibn Jarir said: The verse is muhkam (unabrogated) regarding bequest, and the pronoun in "fa-arzuquhum" refers to the close relatives to whom a bequest is made, and the pronoun in "lahum" (for them) refers to the orphans and the needy. He commanded that a kind word be said to them. It was also said with a splitting of the pronoun, so that what is meant by the close relatives are those who inherit, and what is meant by the orphans and needy are those who do not inherit. Thus His saying "fa-arzuquhum" refers to the close relatives, and His saying "lahum" refers to the orphans and the needy. What is said about splitting the pronoun is arbitrary, with no evidence for it.

The "kind word" (qawlan maʿrufan) was explained here by Ibn Jubayr as saying to them: "This property belongs to absent people, or to young orphans, and you have no right in it." It was also said: it is a prayer for them for provision and wealth. It was also said: it is the speech indicating that what they were given to them is a gift, and this was narrated from Ibn Jubayr. It was also said: it is a good promise, by saying: "These are young orphans; when they come of age we will command them to recognize your right," as ʿAta ibn Yasar said, from Ibn Jubayr. It was also said: the kind word is whatever gives comfort, such as a supplication or other. The apparent sense of the speech is that the three categories are combined in receiving both provision and the kind word. It was also said: either they are given, or a kind word is said to them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿an obligatory share﴾ is in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas, a construction in which a noun is singled out by an accusative), meaning: I mean an obligatory, definite, binding share. End of quotation. If by "specification" he means what the grammarians have agreed upon, then it is rejected, because the word is indefinite, and the grammarians have stated that the accusative of specification cannot be indefinite. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a pure verbal noun, since it is a verbal noun, meaning: its share is a share. It was said: it is a circumstantial state of an indefinite noun, since it has been qualified. It was said: it is governed by an omitted verb, its estimated form being: I made it, or I made obligatory for them a share. It was said: it is a circumstantial state of the agent in "whether little or much."

By the apparent meaning of this verse, the division of inheritable rights is obligatory when they are distinct and can be divided, and when each of the two partners demands it, without disagreement. They differed regarding dividing what is left in the case of the fixed shares, when the division cannot be made without altering its state, such as a bathhouse, a mill, a well, and a house whose benefits are nullified by the separation of the shares. Malik, al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifa said: it is divided. Ibn Abi Layla and Abu Thawr said: it is not divided. Ibn al-Mundhir said: This is the more correct of the two opinions. It is also cited as evidence for the obligation of a brother inheriting from the deceased along with a daughter: when she takes half, he takes the remainder. They differed concerning two paternal cousins, one of whom is a maternal brother. ʿAli and Zayd said: the maternal brother has a sixth, and what remains is divided equally between them. This is the view of the jurists of the major cities. ʿUmar, al-Aʿmash, Shurayh and al-Hasan said: the property belongs to the maternal brother.

﴿And when the division is attended by the close relatives, the orphans and the needy, provide for them from it and speak to them a kind word﴾. It was said: it was revealed concerning the owners of property who divide it when death is present, in a bequest and to causes they choose, and relatives who are barred from inheritance attend them, so they bequeath to strangers and leave out those who are barred, so they are deprived of both inheritance and bequest. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Zayd and Abu Jaʿfar. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the owners of fixed shares, to whom a barred person also comes, so they were commanded to give them something from what God has bestowed on them. It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn al-Musayyib that it is abrogated (mansukha, subject to naskh, abrogation), and ʿIkrima and al-Dahhak said the same. They said: it was a division which God made into three categories, then that was abrogated by the verse of inheritance, which gave each possessor of a share his share, and made the bequest for those who are deprived and do not inherit. It was also said: it is muhkam (not abrogated). God commanded that whoever is entitled to an inheritance, and a relative, orphan or needy person who does not inherit attends the division, should not be deprived if the property is abundant, and that apologies be offered to them if it is little. Abu Musa al-Ashʿari commanded this. Al-Hasan and al-Nakhaʿi said: The believers used to do this: they would give them from the silver and gold coins, and when they divided the lands and slaves they would say to them a kind word: "May blessing be upon you." Al-Aʿmash ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr did this, and recited this verse. If the heir is a minor who cannot dispose of property, does the guardian do this or not? There are two opinions. The apparent sense of this verse, in the context following what precedes it, is that it concerns the heirs and not the dying testators. What is apparent from the word "qisma" (division) is that it is a verbal noun in the sense of "qasam" (dividing), as He said: ﴿That is then an unjust division﴾ [al-Najm: 22].

It was said: "qisma" means the thing divided. It was also said: "qisma" is a noun from "iqtisam" (apportioning), not from "qasm," like "khira" from "ikhtiyar." The eloquent do not usually say "qasamtu baynahum qisma" (I divided among them a division), and al-Kisaʾi transmitted this. Your "qisma" is what you have taken of the portions, and its plural is "qisam." Al-Khalil said: "al-qasm" is the share and portion of a part; it is said: "qasamtu falanan al-mal, wa-taqasamnahu, wa-iqtasamnahu" (I divided so-and-so's property with him, and we divided it mutually), and "al-qasm" is the one who shares with you.

The apparent meaning of His saying "fa-arzuquhum" (provide for them) is obligation. This was held by a group, including Mujahid, ʿAta and al-Zuhri. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan said: it is recommended (nadb). In His saying "fa-arzuquhum" there is the attribution of provision to other than God Most High, as He said: ﴿And God is the best of providers﴾ [al-Jumuʿa: 11]. It was said: this was obligatory for the heirs, and the verse of inheritance abrogated it. The pronoun in "minhu" (from it) refers to the property divided, which the division indicates, because the division, being a verbal noun, indicates its object, which is the property. It was also said: it refers to "what" (ma) in His saying: ﴿of what the parents and the close relatives leave﴾. Whoever said "the division is the thing divided" made the pronoun refer to the division in the sense of masculine gender, since what is meant is the thing divided. He placed the orphans before the needy, because their weakness is greater and their need more severe, so placing charity with them is more excellent and greater in reward. The apparent sense is that they are provided for from the very property divided. ʿUbayda and Ibn Sirin held that the provision in this verse means that a meal is prepared for them to eat, and they did this, and slaughtered a sheep from the estate. With ʿUbayda, property of an orphan was divided, and he bought a sheep from it and slaughtered it, and ʿUbayda said: "If not for this, it would have been from my own property." His saying "minhu" (from it) indicates partialness (tabʿid), and there is no estimate in it by consensus, and this is among the things that indicate recommendation. For if these people had a definite right, God would have specified the amount of that right, as He specified it in the other rights. On this basis, the jurists of the major cities hold that if the heirs are adults, it is so; but if they are minors, then there is only the kind word.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿and speak to them﴾ refers to what the pronoun in "fa-arzuquhum" referred to, namely: the close relatives, the orphans and the needy. Ibn Jarir said: The verse is muhkam (unabrogated) regarding bequest, and the pronoun in "fa-arzuquhum" refers to the close relatives to whom a bequest is made, and the pronoun in "lahum" (for them) refers to the orphans and the needy. He commanded that a kind word be said to them. It was also said with a splitting of the pronoun, so that what is meant by the close relatives are those who inherit, and what is meant by the orphans and needy are those who do not inherit. Thus His saying "fa-arzuquhum" refers to the close relatives, and His saying "lahum" refers to the orphans and the needy. What is said about splitting the pronoun is arbitrary, with no evidence for it.

The "kind word" (qawlan maʿrufan) was explained here by Ibn Jubayr as saying to them: "This property belongs to absent people, or to young orphans, and you have no right in it." It was also said: it is a prayer for them for provision and wealth. It was also said: it is the speech indicating that what they were given to them is a gift, and this was narrated from Ibn Jubayr. It was also said: it is a good promise, by saying: "These are young orphans; when they come of age we will command them to recognize your right," as ʿAta ibn Yasar said, from Ibn Jubayr. It was also said: the kind word is whatever gives comfort, such as a supplication or other. The apparent sense of the speech is that the three categories are combined in receiving both provision and the kind word. It was also said: either they are given, or a kind word is said to them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 9:

﴿Let those fear [Allah] who, if they were to leave behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them be mindful of Allah and let them speak words of rectitude.﴾

The apparent meaning of this sentence is that He commanded the fear of Allah and mindfulness of Him. As for "words of rectitude" (al-qawl al-sadid), it refers to one who looks at the condition of weak offspring, to alert him that he himself is leaving weak offspring behind. This includes the guardians of orphans, and Ibn 'Abbas interpreted it this way. It also refers to one who forbids the dying person from bequeathing to his relatives, and to one who deserves and is fitting to withhold [property] for his kin and children. Miqsam and Hadrami also interpreted it this way. It also refers to one who commands the dying person to bequeath to so-and-so and so-and-so, and reminds him to send ahead [good deeds] for himself, while his aim is to harm his heirs by doing so. Ibn 'Abbas also interpreted it this way, as did Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Mujahid.

A group said: the intended meaning is all people. They were commanded to be mindful of Allah concerning orphans and the children of others, even if those orphans are not in their custody, and that they should speak to them with rectitude as they would like their own children to be treated.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that it connects to what precedes it, and that it is a command to the heirs to show compassion toward those who attend the division [of the estate] among the weak of their relatives, orphans and the needy. And [it means] that they should imagine that if these were their own children left behind them, abandoned and needy, would they fear for them deprivation and want?" End of his words. And it is possible that this is what is intended.

Al-Qadi said: "What best fits what precedes and what follows is that it is among the verses concerning orphans. Thus, the last of what He called them to, in order to preserve the property of the orphan, is that He alerts them to the condition of their own selves and their offspring, if they imagine it. There is no doubt that this is among the strongest motives toward this aim, namely caution in the matter."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Its estimation is: if they left [the children] behind, they would have betrayed [them]." It is permissible to omit the lam in the response of "law" (if), as you say: "law qama Zayd la-qama 'Amr" and "law qama Zayd qama 'Amr." End of his words. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is: let those fear whose attribute and condition is that, if they were about to leave behind them weak offspring, which is at the time of their death, they would fear for them loss after them, due to the departure of their guardian and earner, as the poet said:

"Children have increased life for me in love; they are indeed among the weak.
I fear that after me they will inherit misery, and drink turbid water after clear."

End of his words.

Others said: "Law tarakû" — "law" is used to prohibit one thing because of the prohibition of another, and "khafû" is the response of "law." End of words.

The apparent meaning of these texts is that "law" here is the one that expresses a conditional in the past, which Sibawayh describes as a particle for what would have happened due to the occurrence of something else. Others describe it as a particle indicating the prohibition of one thing due to the prohibition of another. The author of al-Tashil held that "law" here is conditional with the meaning of "in" (if), so that it turns the past into the sense of the future, and the estimation is: "let those fear who, if they leave behind them..." He said: "If a present-tense verb follows this 'law,' it has a future meaning, just as it does after 'in,' as the poet said:

"Those who hope in you will not find you except displaying
the character of the generous, even if you were destitute."

It seems that the speaker of this thought imagined that since they were commanded to fear, and the command is in the future, and the object of the command is the relative clause, the relative clause could not be past in a sense that indicates non-existence, which would contradict the fulfilment of the command. And the word "in" was considered a suitable replacement for "law," so he said: "It is a conditional concerning the future, and it means 'in.'" It seems that al-Zamakhshari also had this same imagining, which is why he said: "Its meaning is: let those fear whose attribute and condition is that they were about to be left [in such a state]," so "law" did not enter upon the future, but was applied to "shārafû" (were about to), which is a past verb attributed to the relative pronoun in the state of command. And what they imagined is not necessary in the relative clause unless the clause is past in meaning, actually occurring. For the meaning of "law tarakû min khalfihim" is: if they died and left behind them, so if it were so, it would necessitate that "law" be interpreted as "in," since the command cannot be combined with the actual occurrence of the act of one who has died. But if it is past by an estimation that allows it to be a relative clause, and the operator of the relative pronoun is a future verb, such as your saying: "Let visit us the one who, if he had died yesterday, we would have wept for him." The original of "law" is that it is a conditional concerning the past, and it is not taken to mean the future with the sense of "in," except when a context indicates it, like the verse mentioned above, because the response of "law" in it is an omitted future, due to the futurity of what it indicates, which is his saying: "lā yulfika" (will not find you). Likewise his saying:

"A people who, when they wage war, tighten their waistcloths,
apart from women, even if they spend the night in purity."

because what follows it falls within the scope of "idha" (when), and "idha" is for the future. If a speaker said: "law qama Zayd qama 'Umar," it would immediately come to mind that it is a conditional concerning the past, not the future.

"Min khalfihim" is connected to "tarakû." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from "dhurriyyatan."

Al-Jumhur read "di'afan," the plural of "da'if," like "zarif" and "zirafun." Hamzah inclined the fatha of the 'ayn. Its plural on the pattern "fi'al" is analogical. Ibn Muhaysin read "du'uffan" with two dammas and nunation on the fa'. 'A'ishah, al-Sulami, al-Zuhri, Abu Hayawah and Ibn Muhaysin also read "du'afa'" with a damma on the dad and a long vowel, like "zarif" and "zurafa'," and this too is analogical. It was also read "du'afa" and "da'afa" with inclination, like "sukara" and "sukara." Hamzah inclined "khafû" because of the kasra that occurs for him in words like "khiftu."

Consider the excellent ordering of these commands, for it begins first with fear (khashyah), whose locus is the heart, which is the avoidance of a thing by the dictate of knowledge, and which is what leads to piety (taqwa). Then it commands piety second, which results from fear, since it is the placing of oneself in protection from what one fears. Then it commands words of rectitude, which is what appears of action arising from piety, which arises from fear. It is not intended to restrict "words of rectitude" alone, but the meaning is on both action and speech of rectitude. The reason it is limited to words of rectitude is the ease of that for a person, as if it were said: the least that should be followed is words of rectitude. Mujahid said: "They say to those who distribute the wealth: increase so-and-so, and give to so-and-so." It is also said: it is the command to give out only a third. It is also said: it is prompting the dying person to the testimony of faith. It is also said: truthfulness in testimony. It is also said: what agrees with the truth. It is also said: justice. It is also said: moderation. All of these are close in meaning.

"Al-sadad" is evenness in speech and action. The root of "al-sadd" is removing disorder. "Al-sadid" is used in the sense of the active and in the sense of the passive. A "rajul sadid" is one who is between the two meanings, for he is made straight by the one he follows, and he makes straight for the one who follows him.

﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a Blaze﴾. It was revealed concerning the polytheists who used to consume the property of orphans and did not give them, or the women, any inheritance. This is related from Ibn Zayd. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Handhalah ibn al-Shamardal, who was the guardian of an orphan and consumed his property. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Zayd ibn Zayd al-Ghatafani, who was the guardian of his nephew's property and consumed it; this is related from Muqatil. Most scholars said: it was revealed concerning the guardians who consume from the property of orphans what is not permitted to them. The verse encompasses every unjust consumption that is not by a guardian. The word ﴿unjustly﴾ (ظلمًا) is in the accusative either as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), or as an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlihi). The predicate of ﴿Indeed﴾ (inna) is the clause ﴿they only consume﴾. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of a clause introduced by ﴿inna﴾ serving as the predicate of ﴿inna﴾, though there is a difference of opinion on this. What made it acceptable here is the separation between the two, since the subject of ﴿inna﴾ is a relative pronoun, so the sentence is lengthened by mentioning its relative clause. The phrase ﴿into their bellies﴾ means "filling their bellies"; one says "he ate into his belly" and "into part of his belly," as the poet said:

"Eat into part of your bellies, so you may be chaste, for your time is a lean time."

The apparent connection is that ﴿into their bellies﴾ is linked to ﴿they consume﴾, and this is said by al-Hawfi. Abu al-Baqa' said it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier of the word ﴿fire﴾. By his saying ﴿into their bellies﴾ he drew attention to their baseness, and to their description with gluttony in eating and eagerness to obtain what is forbidden on account of the belly. How can these people compare with the words of the poet:

"You see him lean in the belly, while provisions are present,"

and the saying of al-Shanfara:

"Even if hands reach out to the food, I will not be the quickest of them; when the people are most greedy, they are the quickest."

The apparent meaning of his saying ﴿fire﴾ is that they literally consume fire. In the hadith of Abu Sa'id concerning the night of the Night Journey, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I saw a people who had lips like the lips of camels, and an angel had been assigned to them who would seize their lips, then place in their mouths a rock of fire that would come out from their lower parts. I said, 'O Jibril, who are these?' He said, 'They are those who consume the property of orphans unjustly.'" Some said that they literally consume fire. It was also said that it is figurative: since consuming an orphan's property leads to the fire and to being punished by it, this was expressed as eating into the belly, and it drew attention to what drives one to take property, which is the belly, the basest of things for which property is benefited, since what is put into it ends in dissolution and disappearance in a short time. Therefore he said: "A human has filled no vessel worse than his belly."

The majority recited ﴿they will burn﴾ (وسيصلون) as active from the triliteral verb. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr recited it with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fatḥah on the lām, as passive from the triliteral verb. Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited it with a ḍammah on the yā', a fatḥah on the ṣād and lām, with the lām doubled, as passive. The word ṣalā means warming oneself near a fire, while iḥrāq (burning) means destroying a thing by fire. He expressed by ﴿being burnt by the fire﴾ the lasting punishment by it, since the fire does not annihilate their essences entirely; rather, as He said: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted, We replace them with other skins so that they may taste the punishment﴾ [an-Nisa': 56]. This is a great threat for this disobedience. ﴿They consume﴾ came in the present tense without the sīn of futurity, while ﴿they will burn﴾ came with the sīn. If the consumption into the fire is literal, then it is future, and he dispensed with restricting it by the sīn through coordinating the future with it. If it is figurative, then it is not future, since the meaning is: they consume what leads to the fire and is a cause of punishment by it. Since the word "fire" in His saying ﴿they only consume into their bellies fire﴾ is unrestricted, it was restricted in His saying "a blaze," since it is the blazing ember.

These verses contain varieties of rhetorical eloquence: antithesis (ṭibāq) in ﴿single﴾ and ﴿its mate﴾, in ﴿wealthy﴾ and ﴿poor﴾, and in ﴿little or much﴾. Repetition (takrār) in ﴿fear Allah﴾, in ﴿created﴾, in ﴿you fear﴾, and ﴿that you not act justly﴾ and ﴿that you not be equitable﴾ in terms of meaning, in ﴿orphans﴾, in ﴿women﴾, in ﴿then hand over to them their property﴾ [an-Nisa': 6], ﴿so when you hand over to them their property﴾ [an-Nisa': 6], in ﴿a share of what the parents and the relatives leave﴾ [an-Nisa': 7], and in His saying ﴿and let them fear﴾ and ﴿fear﴾, in terms of meaning according to those who make them synonymous.
