He said: The verse ﴿And those two of you who commit it﴾ was revealed concerning the people of sodomy (liwāṭ). The [verse] in Sūrat al-Nūr concerns the adulterous woman and the adulterous man, and he opposed the majority of the exegetes. Abū Muslim built this on a principle of his own, which is that there is no abrogating (nāsikh) and no abrogated (mansūkh) [verse] in the Qurʾān.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He, exalted is He, commanded kindness to women, mentioning the giving of their dowries and their inheritance, and they had not been inherited from in the Jāhiliyyah, He mentioned the severity against them for the immorality they commit. In reality this is a kindness to them, since it is a concern for their Hereafter, and lest it be supposed that kindness to them means that the prescribed punishments should not be applied to them, which would lead to their falling into various kinds of corruption. Also, when He, exalted is He, mentioned His limits and pointed with "those" to everything that had occurred from the beginning of the sūrah up to the place of the reference, the beginning of the sūrah was about protecting oneself through marriage and permitting what He permitted of marrying up to four for those permitted to do so. Then He digressed after that to the ruling concerning those who violate what Allah commanded regarding marriage, namely the adulteresses. He singled them out first because they are, as it has been said, more prone to the matter of desire than men. Then He mentioned them a second time together with the adulterous men in His saying: ﴿And those two of you who commit it﴾. Thus the mention of adulterous women occurs twice: once in the singular and once in the inclusive plural.

Al-lātī (feminine plural) is a plural in meaning of allatī, and it has many plurals, the strangest of which is al-āt. Its inflection follows that of al-hindāt (the grammatical pattern of sound feminine plurals).

The meaning of ﴿they commit lewdness﴾ is: they come to it and cover themselves with it. Here al-fāḥishah is adultery by the consensus (ijmāʿ, scholarly agreement) of the exegetes, except what is reported from Mujāhid, whom Abū Muslim followed, that it means musāḥaqah; the discussion with him on this will follow. The term fāḥishah was applied to adultery because it exceeds many vices in ugliness. It has been said: If it is asked, "Killing and disbelief are greater than adultery," the answer is: The powers that govern the body are three: the rational (nāṭiqah), whose corruption is through disbelief and innovation and the like; the irascible (ghaḍabiyyah), whose corruption is through killing, anger, and the like; and the appetitive (shahwāniyyah), whose corruption is through adultery, sodomy, and sorcery. The last is the lowest of these powers, so its corruption is the lowest kind of corruption. Therefore this act was specified as lewdness. Abū Muslim's argument that the lewdness is sihāq (lesbianism) is His saying: ﴿those who commit it, from among your women﴾, and for men: ﴿those two﴾ and ﴿from among you﴾; its apparent meaning is specification. He also argued that this does not involve abrogation and does not necessarily involve repetition. Furthermore, interpreting the "way" (sabīl) as stoning, flogging, or exile, according to those who hold that the verse concerns adultery, would make it apply against them rather than for them, whereas on our view the way is the facilitation of desire for them through marriage. They responded to Abū Muslim that what he said had not been said by any exegete, so it was invalid. He answered that Mujāhid had said it, so it was not a consensus. And interpreting the way by the authentic ḥadīth: "Allah has made a way for them. The married person (thayyib) is stoned, and the virgin is flogged," indicates that this refers to fornicators. He answered that this implies abrogating the Qurʾān by a solitary report (khabar al-wāḥid), which is impermissible. Further, the Companions disagreed about the rulings on the practitioners of sodomy, and none of them relied on His saying: ﴿And those two of you who commit it﴾, which indicates that it does not concern them. He answered that what the Companions sought was whether the prescribed punishment (ḥadd) is to be applied to the sodomite, and there is no indication in the verse either by negation or affirmation of that; therefore they did not refer to it. End of what Abū Muslim argued, what was argued against him, and what he answered with. What the apparent wording requires is the view of Mujāhid and others: that allātī is specific to women and is general, whether they are married or not. And that ﴿those two﴾ is specific to males and is general, whether they are married or not. So the punishment for women is confinement, and the punishment for men is harm. These two verses and the verse of Sūrat al-Nūr together cover all categories of fornicators. This apparent meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿from among your women﴾ and His saying: "from among you." It cannot be said that musāḥaqah and liwāṭ were not known among the Arabs or in the Jāhiliyyah, because they existed among them, though they were rare. Among examples of this is the saying of Ṭarafah ibn al-ʿAbd:
"You are the king of the day, while you are a prostitute at night,
with the semen of men on your thighs like curds."
And the rajaz poet said:
"Oh, how strange are the women who rub against each other with saffron,
who place the vulva upon the vulva!"

Al-A'mash read: (wal-lati ya'tina bil-fahishah). As for His saying ﴿min nisa'ikum﴾ (from among your women), there has been disagreement over whether what is meant is wives, or free women, or believing women, or married women (thayyibat) to the exclusion of virgins (abkar), since the word "women" (nisa') is in common usage specific to married women. There are several opinions. The first is that of Qatadah, al-Suddi and others. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His saying ﴿min nisa'ikum﴾ is an attribution carrying the sense of Islam, because a disbelieving woman may be among the women of Muslims by lineage, yet this ruling does not apply to her; end of quote. The apparent usage of "women" attributed to the believers refers to wives, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who swear off relations with their wives (min nisa'ihim)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226], and ﴿Those who divorce by zihar from their wives﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 3]. That what is meant is wives, and that the verse concerns them, is the view of the majority of the commentators. Exalted is He commanded the calling of four witnesses as a strengthening against the accuser and as a concealment of this sin. It was also said that two witnesses are required for each one. His saying "against them" (alayhinna) means: against their committing the fahishah. The apparent meaning is that this is restricted to male believers, based on His saying: ﴿four of you﴾ (arba'atan minkum), and that testimony is permitted for direct observation of adultery. And if one deliberately looks at the private part, this does not impair one's integrity ('adalah) when it is for the sake of establishing adultery.

Grammatically, (al-lati) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿fastashhidu﴾ (then call for testimony). The entry of the fa' into the predicate is permitted, although "Zayd fadribhu" (Zayd, so strike him) is not permitted as a subject-predicate construction, because the subject is a relative pronoun joined to a verb that requires the predicate, and it fulfills the conditions of what the fa' may enter the predicate of; the relative is therefore treated in that respect as a conditional noun (ism al-shart). Since it has been treated as such through the entry of the fa', it cannot be governed in the accusative by an implied verb that is explained by ﴿fastashhidu﴾, which would make it a case of ishtighal (occupation of the verb), because ﴿fastashhidu﴾ cannot validly operate on it, since it functions like a conditional noun; so it cannot be explained in this way. Some said: Some people permitted the accusative with an omitted verb, its estimate being: "Intend the (women) who..." It was also said: the predicate of al-lati is omitted, its estimate being: "In what is recited to you, the ruling concerning those who commit fahishah," like the statement of Sibawayh regarding His saying: ﴿As for the thief, male and female (al-sariqu wal-sariqah)﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38], and regarding His saying: ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress (al-zaniyatu wal-zani)﴾ [al-Nur: 2]; and Sibawayh interpreted it in this way. ﴿min nisa'ikum﴾ is connected to an omitted element, because it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the subject in "ya'tina," its estimate being: "being from among your women." ﴿minkum﴾ may be connected to ﴿fastashhidu﴾, or to an omitted element so that it is a qualifier of "arba'atan," meaning: "being from among you."

﴿Then if they testify, confine them to houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way﴾, meaning: if four of you testify against them. Those addressed by this command: are they the husbands, who were commanded to do this when the wife showed the fahishah of adultery, ﴿and do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], as a punishment for them, which was of the same kind as their crime? Or the guardians (awliya'), when it appears from those who have guardianship and authority over them, that they be confined until they die? Or the rulers (ulu al-amr) among the governors and judges, since they are those who establish the hudud and forbid the fawahish? There are three opinions. The apparent meaning is that confinement in the houses until the stated limit was a form of hadd for them, and that their hadd was this until it was abrogated, and this is the sound view, related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. Confinement in a house is more painful and more agonizing than beating and humiliation, especially when taking the dowry is added to that, as mentioned by al-Suddi, because the pain of confinement is continuous, whereas the pain of beating passes. Ibn Zayd said: They were prevented from marriage until they died as a punishment for them, when they sought marriage in an illicit manner. Some said: It is not a hadd; rather it is keeping them confined after the Imam has applied the hadd to them, in order to protect them from falling into the same situation that befell them due to going out of the houses; and according to this, confinement is not a hadd. When (yatawaffa) means "causes to die," the estimate is: "until the Angel of Death takes them." This omitted genitive has been stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who is charged with you will take you (yatawaffakum)﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11]. If the meaning of taking is simply seizing, then there is no need to omit a genitive, as the estimate becomes: "until death seizes them." The way that Allah ordained for them depends on the difference over what is meant by the verse. It was said: it is marriage, which protects them and makes them independent of illicit intercourse; and this is according to the interpretation that the address is to the guardians, the rulers or the judges, not to the husbands. It was also said: the way is what the ruling on adultery has settled upon as hadd, namely: "For a virgin with a virgin, a hundred lashes and exile for a year; for a married person with a married person, stoning." The interpretation of the way with this is established by the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit in Sahih Muslim from the Prophet (ﷺ), so it is obligatory to adopt it. The hadith of 'Ubadah does not abrogate this verse, nor is it abrogated by the lashing; rather, it explains an ambiguity in this verse, since it limited their confinement in the houses until Allah ordains for them a way, and it particularizes the generality of the verse of lashing. On this basis, the criticism of Abu Bakr al-Razi against al-Shafi'i, in his saying that the Sunnah does not abrogate the Qur'an, by his claim that the verse of confinement is abrogated by the hadith of 'Ubadah, while the hadith of 'Ubadah is abrogated by the verse of lashing, does not hold; this would entail abrogation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah and of the Sunnah by the Qur'an, contrary to al-Shafi'i's position. Rather, explanation and particularization are more appropriate than claiming abrogation three times, as the companions of Abu Hanifah held, since they claimed that the verse of confinement is abrogated by the hadith, that the hadith is abrogated by the verse of lashing, and that the verse of lashing is abrogated by the verse of stoning.

﴿And the two of you who commit it among you, harm them both﴾. The statement of Mujahid was mentioned earlier, and Abu Muslim's choice is that it refers to sodomy (liwat), which is supported by the apparent dual form. The apparent meaning of "among you" in this case is in reality for males, while the majority hold that it refers to both male and female fornicators. "Al-lani" (the two who) is intended to mean the male adulterer and the female adulteress, and the masculine is given precedence over the feminine. The harm is ordained upon committing the fahishah, and it is restricted by testimony regarding its commission, which was clarified in the preceding verse: the testimony of four. The command to harm is a substitute for harm in general, by word or deed or both.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is reviling (nayl) with the tongue and hand, striking with sandals and the like. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: it is reproach and censure. Some said: it is with action rather than speech. A group said: it is cursing and harshness without reproach. It was also said: the harm commanded is combining the two punishments: lashing and stoning; this is the view of 'Ali, who did this in the case of the Hamdaniyyah: he lashed her and then stoned her.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and the two of you who commit it﴾ is generality. Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and others said: the second verse concerns the virgin man and woman, while the first concerns married women; and those who are chaste among men are included with them in meaning. Al-Tabari preferred this view. They agreed that these two verses are abrogated by the verse of lashing, except for 'Ali's interpretation of harm, which is not abrogated, and except for the view of the one who said that harm by reproach together with lashing remains, so there is no abrogation in his view, since there is no contradiction, rather both are combined upon one person. If the two verses are taken to refer to adultery, then the first verse indicates confinement of adulteresses, and the second indicates harming them and harming him, so harm is shared between them, while confinement is specific to the woman, so she is subjected to both confinement and harm; this is the apparent meaning of the wording. It was also said: the punishment of the woman was made confinement so that the source of this sin would be cut off, and the punishment of the man was harm; and confinement was not imposed on him because he needs to go out and earn a living. As for the view of Qatadah and al-Suddi, that the first verse concerns the married and the second concerns virgin men and women, then the objects of the two punishments differ, so harm is not shared. Al-Hasan held that this verse came before the preceding verse, and then ﴿confine them to houses﴾ was revealed, meaning: if they do not repent and persist, then confine them until their condition becomes clear; but this view entails disruption of the order, so it is far-fetched. According to these opinions, the repetition has benefits; according to the view of Qatadah and al-Suddi there is no repetition, and likewise there is no repetition according to the view of Mujahid and Abu Muslim.

The grammatical analysis of ﴿wal-lani﴾ is the same as that of (wal-lati). Al-Jumhur read ﴿wal-lani﴾ with a light nun. Ibn Kathir read it with a doubled nun. The commentators mentioned the reason for omitting the ya' and the reason for doubling the nun, and the subject of that belongs to the science of grammar. Al-A'mash read: (wal-ladhina yaf'aluna-hu minkum), which is a reading that contradicts the consonantal text of the Imam's codex and is inconsistent with what follows it, since this is a plural with a plural pronoun, while what follows is a dual pronoun. But it is interpreted with some strain: that the plural "alladhina" includes the two categories of males and females, so the pronoun after it returns as a dual with regard to the two categories, just as the pronoun returned as plural to the dual, in view of the fact that under the dual there are many individuals, which carry the sense of the plural, as in His saying: ﴿If two groups of the believers fight﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9], and ﴿These two disputants who dispute﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. The preferable view is to hold that the reading of 'Abd Allah is by way of explanation, and that the dual refers to generality among the adulterers. It is also read: (wal-ladha'anni) with a hamzah and a doubled nun. The justification for this reading is that when the nun was doubled, two consonants met, so the reciter avoided their meeting by replacing the alif with a hamzah, likening it to the alif of the fa'il whose 'ayn is doubled in its lam, just as it was read: "wa la al-dallin wa la jann." The discussion of this has already been presented at length in the commentary on His saying: ﴿wa la al-dallin﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7] in al-Fatihah.

﴿Then if they repent and reform, leave them alone﴾, meaning: if they repent from the fahishah and reform their conduct, then abandon harming them. The meaning is: turn away from harming them. It was said: the command to refrain from harming them is abrogated by the verse of lashing. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The force of the wording contains a rebuke of the fornicators even if they repent, because leaving them is only a turning away. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]? This turning away in the two verses is not a command to boycott, but is leaving alone one who turns away, and in it is a demeaning of them because of the earlier sin; end of his words.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾, meaning: He returns His servants from His disobedience to His obedience, and is merciful to them by leaving off harming them when they repent.

(p-193) ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness, bring against them four witnesses from among you. If they testify, then confine them to their houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way.﴾ ﴿And the two of you who commit it, harm them. If they repent and amend, then leave them alone. Indeed, Allah is ever Accepting of repentance, Merciful.﴾ ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon. Those are the ones whose repentance Allah accepts, and Allah is ever Knowing, Wise.﴾ [al-Nisa': 17] ﴿Repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers. For those We have prepared a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Nisa': 18] ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by force, nor to restrain them in order to take back part of what you have given them, unless they commit a clear immorality. And live with them in kindness. If you dislike them, perhaps you dislike something in which Allah has placed much good.﴾ [al-Nisa': 19] ﴿And if you wish to replace one wife with another, and you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take back anything from it. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾ [al-Nisa': 20] ﴿And how could you take it, when you have been intimate with one another and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?﴾ [al-Nisa': 21] ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an immorality and hatred and an evil way.﴾ [al-Nisa': 22] ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, your sisters' daughters, your foster mothers, your foster sisters, your wives' mothers, your stepdaughters in your guardianship born of the wives with whom you have consummated marriage (but if you have not consummated, there is no blame on you), the wives of your sons who are from your loins, and combining two sisters, except what has already passed. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ [al-Nisa': 23] ﴿And [also forbidden are] married women, except those whom your right hands possess. This is the decree of Allah upon you. Lawful for you is what is beyond that, that you seek with your wealth, chaste and not fornicating. So whatever you enjoy from them, give them their due compensation as an obligation. And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree after the obligation. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Wise.﴾ [al-Nisa': 24] ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women, then [he may marry] from what your right hands possess of your believing young women. And Allah is most knowing of your faith; you are of one another. So marry them with the permission of their families and give them their compensation in kindness, [they being] chaste, not fornicating and not taking secret lovers. And when they are married and then commit immorality, their punishment is half that of free women. That is for one of you who fears hardship; but to be patient is better for you. And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ [al-Nisa': 25] ﴿Allah wants to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways of those before you and to turn to you in forgiveness. And Allah is Knowing, Wise.﴾ [al-Nisa': 26] ﴿And Allah wants to turn to you in forgiveness, while those who follow their desires want you to deviate into a great deviation.﴾ [al-Nisa': 27] ﴿Allah wants to lighten [the burden] for you, and man was created weak.﴾ [al-Nisa': 28]

Al-ʿIshrah (ʿishrah, companionship and association): al-ṣuḥbah and al-mukhālaṭah (close association and mixing). It is said: ʿāsharū, taʿāsharū, and iʿtasharū (they associated with one another). That [word] derives from ʿashr al-judhūr (the division of the palm-stumps into shares), because it involves division and mixing.

Al-ifḍāʾ ilā al-shayʾ (al-ifḍāʾ, reaching something): arriving at a fiḍāʾ (open expanse) of it, that is, a wide, unbounded space. In the proverb "al-nās fawḍā fuḍḍiya," meaning the people are mixed together, each touching the other. It is said: faḍā yafḍū faḍāʾan, when it became wide; the alif of afḍā is converted from a yā' whose root is wāw.

Al-maqt (maqt, detestation): hatred combined with contempt, arising from a shameful act committed by its doer.

Al-ʿammah (paternal aunt): the father's sister. Al-khālah (maternal aunt): the mother's sister, and its alif is converted from a wāw; the evidence is their saying akhwāl in the plural of khāl, and rajul mukhwil, meaning a man with noble maternal uncles.

Al-rabībah (stepdaughter): the daughter of a man's wife from another husband.

Al-ḥijr (ḥijr, with the ḥāʾ either fatḥah or kasrah): the front of a person's garment and what lies before him of it while wearing it. The word was then used for guarding and keeping, because the one who wears it protects a child and similar things in that part of the garment. Its plural is ḥujūr.

Al-ḥalīlah (ḥalīlah, wife) and al-ḥalīl (husband). The poet said:
"I visit the young woman of the tribe in the presence of her husband,
but when he goes out to raid with the army, I do not visit her."
She is called ḥalīlah because she alights (taḥull) with the husband wherever he alights, so it is faʿīlah in the sense of fāʿilah. Al-Zajjāj and others held that it derives from the word ḥalāl (lawful), so she is ḥalīlah in the sense of muḥallalah (made lawful). It is also said that each of them unties the other's waistwrap.

Al-ṣulb (ṣulb, the back): the spine. Ṣalaba ṣalābah means he became strong and firm. Al-Farrāʾ mentions in his book Lughāt al-Qurʾān that al-ṣulb, the back, is on the pattern of qufl, and that this is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, while the Tamīm and Asad say al-ṣalab, with fatḥah on the ṣād and lām. He said: Someone recited to me:
"And a back like the supple, greased rein."
He said: Someone from Banū Asad recited to me:
"When I stand up, I complain about my back."

Al-muḥṣanah: a chaste woman. It is said: uḥṣinat, so she is muḥṣan, and ḥaṣunat, so she is ḥaṣān, meaning she refrained from suspicion and guarded herself against it. Shamir said: It is said, "a woman ḥaṣān and ḥāṣin." He said:
"And a guarded one, one of the guarded women, smooth, [protected] from harm and from separation from the Waqs."
The verbal noun of ḥaṣunat is ḥaṣn. Sibawayh said: Abū ʿUbaydah and al-Kisāʾī said: ḥaṣānah. It is said that the active participle of aḥṣana, asḥaba, and abʿaja is muftaʿil with a fatḥah on the middle radical; this is an anomaly transmitted by Thaʿlab from Ibn al-Aʿrābī. The root meaning of iḥṣān is prevention, and from it comes the word ḥaṣīnah for armour and for a city, and ḥiṣn (fortress), and "a horse ḥaṣān" (a chaste or well-protected horse).

Al-musāfaḥah and al-sifāḥ: fornication. Its root is from al-safḥ, which is pouring, because each of the two fornicators pours out his drop (nuṭfah).

Al-khidn and al-khadīn: the companion.

Al-ṭawl: superiority. It is said of it: ṭāla ʿalayhi yaṭūlu ṭawlan, meaning he surpassed him. Al-Layth and al-Zajjāj said: al-ṭawl is capability. End of quote. It is also said: ʿalayhi ṭawl, meaning an excess and superiority, and ṭālahu ṭawlan, so he is ṭāʾil. The poet said:
"Hatred of myself has increased for me, for I am
detested by every man who is not superior."
From it comes ṭūl in the body, because it is an addition to it, just as qiṣar (shortness) is a deficiency and shortfall in it.

Al-fatāh: a young person in the prime of youth; al-fatāʾ is youthfulness. He said: "Then chivalry and youthfulness have gone." Ibn Manṣūr al-Jawāliqī said: al-mutafattiyah and al-fatāh is the adolescent girl; al-fatā is the companion, and from it [comes the Qurʾanic phrase]: ﴿And when Moses said to his fatā﴾ [al-Kahf: 60]. Al-fatā also means the slave. From it [comes the Prophetic statement]: "None of you should say 'my slave' or 'my female slave,' but let him say 'my fatā' and 'my fatāt'."

Al-maylu: deviation from the path of straightness.

﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness, bring against them four witnesses from among you﴾. Mujāhid said, and Abū Muslim ibn Baḥr al-Iṣfahānī chose this view: this verse was revealed concerning women. The lewdness here means musāḥaqah (lesbianism), and their punishment was made confinement until they die or marry. He said: The verse ﴿And those two of you who commit it﴾ was revealed concerning the people of sodomy (liwāṭ). The [verse] in Sūrat al-Nūr concerns the adulterous woman and the adulterous man, and he opposed the majority of the exegetes. Abū Muslim built this on a principle of his own, which is that there is no abrogating (nāsikh) and no abrogated (mansūkh) [verse] in the Qurʾān.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He, exalted is He, commanded kindness to women, mentioning the giving of their dowries and their inheritance, and they had not been inherited from in the Jāhiliyyah, He mentioned the severity against them for the immorality they commit. In reality this is a kindness to them, since it is a concern for their Hereafter, and lest it be supposed that kindness to them means that the prescribed punishments should not be applied to them, which would lead to their falling into various kinds of corruption. Also, when He, exalted is He, mentioned His limits and pointed with "those" to everything that had occurred from the beginning of the sūrah up to the place of the reference, the beginning of the sūrah was about protecting oneself through marriage and permitting what He permitted of marrying up to four for those permitted to do so. Then He digressed after that to the ruling concerning those who violate what Allah commanded regarding marriage, namely the adulteresses. He singled them out first because they are, as it has been said, more prone to the matter of desire than men. Then He mentioned them a second time together with the adulterous men in His saying: ﴿And those two of you who commit it﴾. Thus the mention of adulterous women occurs twice: once in the singular and once in the inclusive plural.

Al-lātī (feminine plural) is a plural in meaning of allatī, and it has many plurals, the strangest of which is al-āt. Its inflection follows that of al-hindāt (the grammatical pattern of sound feminine plurals).

The meaning of ﴿they commit lewdness﴾ is: they come to it and cover themselves with it. Here al-fāḥishah is adultery by the consensus (ijmāʿ, scholarly agreement) of the exegetes, except what is reported from Mujāhid, whom Abū Muslim followed, that it means musāḥaqah; the discussion with him on this will follow. The term fāḥishah was applied to adultery because it exceeds many vices in ugliness. It has been said: If it is asked, "Killing and disbelief are greater than adultery," the answer is: The powers that govern the body are three: the rational (nāṭiqah), whose corruption is through disbelief and innovation and the like; the irascible (ghaḍabiyyah), whose corruption is through killing, anger, and the like; and the appetitive (shahwāniyyah), whose corruption is through adultery, sodomy, and sorcery. The last is the lowest of these powers, so its corruption is the lowest kind of corruption. Therefore this act was specified as lewdness. Abū Muslim's argument that the lewdness is sihāq (lesbianism) is His saying: ﴿those who commit it, from among your women﴾, and for men: ﴿those two﴾ and ﴿from among you﴾; its apparent meaning is specification. He also argued that this does not involve abrogation and does not necessarily involve repetition. Furthermore, interpreting the "way" (sabīl) as stoning, flogging, or exile, according to those who hold that the verse concerns adultery, would make it apply against them rather than for them, whereas on our view the way is the facilitation of desire for them through marriage. They responded to Abū Muslim that what he said had not been said by any exegete, so it was invalid. He answered that Mujāhid had said it, so it was not a consensus. And interpreting the way by the authentic ḥadīth: "Allah has made a way for them. The married person (thayyib) is stoned, and the virgin is flogged," indicates that this refers to fornicators. He answered that this implies abrogating the Qurʾān by a solitary report (khabar al-wāḥid), which is impermissible. Further, the Companions disagreed about the rulings on the practitioners of sodomy, and none of them relied on His saying: ﴿And those two of you who commit it﴾, which indicates that it does not concern them. He answered that what the Companions sought was whether the prescribed punishment (ḥadd) is to be applied to the sodomite, and there is no indication in the verse either by negation or affirmation of that; therefore they did not refer to it. End of what Abū Muslim argued, what was argued against him, and what he answered with. What the apparent wording requires is the view of Mujāhid and others: that allātī is specific to women and is general, whether they are married or not. And that ﴿those two﴾ is specific to males and is general, whether they are married or not. So the punishment for women is confinement, and the punishment for men is harm. These two verses and the verse of Sūrat al-Nūr together cover all categories of fornicators. This apparent meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿from among your women﴾ and His saying: "from among you." It cannot be said that musāḥaqah and liwāṭ were not known among the Arabs or in the Jāhiliyyah, because they existed among them, though they were rare. Among examples of this is the saying of Ṭarafah ibn al-ʿAbd:
"You are the king of the day, while you are a prostitute at night,
with the semen of men on your thighs like curds."
And the rajaz poet said:
"Oh, how strange are the women who rub against each other with saffron,
who place the vulva upon the vulva!"

Al-A'mash read: (wal-lati ya'tina bil-fahishah). As for His saying ﴿min nisa'ikum﴾ (from among your women), there has been disagreement over whether what is meant is wives, or free women, or believing women, or married women (thayyibat) to the exclusion of virgins (abkar), since the word "women" (nisa') is in common usage specific to married women. There are several opinions. The first is that of Qatadah, al-Suddi and others. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His saying ﴿min nisa'ikum﴾ is an attribution carrying the sense of Islam, because a disbelieving woman may be among the women of Muslims by lineage, yet this ruling does not apply to her; end of quote. The apparent usage of "women" attributed to the believers refers to wives, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who swear off relations with their wives (min nisa'ihim)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226], and ﴿Those who divorce by zihar from their wives﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 3]. That what is meant is wives, and that the verse concerns them, is the view of the majority of the commentators. Exalted is He commanded the calling of four witnesses as a strengthening against the accuser and as a concealment of this sin. It was also said that two witnesses are required for each one. His saying "against them" (alayhinna) means: against their committing the fahishah. The apparent meaning is that this is restricted to male believers, based on His saying: ﴿four of you﴾ (arba'atan minkum), and that testimony is permitted for direct observation of adultery. And if one deliberately looks at the private part, this does not impair one's integrity ('adalah) when it is for the sake of establishing adultery.

Grammatically, (al-lati) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿fastashhidu﴾ (then call for testimony). The entry of the fa' into the predicate is permitted, although "Zayd fadribhu" (Zayd, so strike him) is not permitted as a subject-predicate construction, because the subject is a relative pronoun joined to a verb that requires the predicate, and it fulfills the conditions of what the fa' may enter the predicate of; the relative is therefore treated in that respect as a conditional noun (ism al-shart). Since it has been treated as such through the entry of the fa', it cannot be governed in the accusative by an implied verb that is explained by ﴿fastashhidu﴾, which would make it a case of ishtighal (occupation of the verb), because ﴿fastashhidu﴾ cannot validly operate on it, since it functions like a conditional noun; so it cannot be explained in this way. Some said: Some people permitted the accusative with an omitted verb, its estimate being: "Intend the (women) who..." It was also said: the predicate of al-lati is omitted, its estimate being: "In what is recited to you, the ruling concerning those who commit fahishah," like the statement of Sibawayh regarding His saying: ﴿As for the thief, male and female (al-sariqu wal-sariqah)﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38], and regarding His saying: ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress (al-zaniyatu wal-zani)﴾ [al-Nur: 2]; and Sibawayh interpreted it in this way. ﴿min nisa'ikum﴾ is connected to an omitted element, because it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the subject in "ya'tina," its estimate being: "being from among your women." ﴿minkum﴾ may be connected to ﴿fastashhidu﴾, or to an omitted element so that it is a qualifier of "arba'atan," meaning: "being from among you."

﴿Then if they testify, confine them to houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way﴾, meaning: if four of you testify against them. Those addressed by this command: are they the husbands, who were commanded to do this when the wife showed the fahishah of adultery, ﴿and do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], as a punishment for them, which was of the same kind as their crime? Or the guardians (awliya'), when it appears from those who have guardianship and authority over them, that they be confined until they die? Or the rulers (ulu al-amr) among the governors and judges, since they are those who establish the hudud and forbid the fawahish? There are three opinions. The apparent meaning is that confinement in the houses until the stated limit was a form of hadd for them, and that their hadd was this until it was abrogated, and this is the sound view, related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. Confinement in a house is more painful and more agonizing than beating and humiliation, especially when taking the dowry is added to that, as mentioned by al-Suddi, because the pain of confinement is continuous, whereas the pain of beating passes. Ibn Zayd said: They were prevented from marriage until they died as a punishment for them, when they sought marriage in an illicit manner. Some said: It is not a hadd; rather it is keeping them confined after the Imam has applied the hadd to them, in order to protect them from falling into the same situation that befell them due to going out of the houses; and according to this, confinement is not a hadd. When (yatawaffa) means "causes to die," the estimate is: "until the Angel of Death takes them." This omitted genitive has been stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who is charged with you will take you (yatawaffakum)﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11]. If the meaning of taking is simply seizing, then there is no need to omit a genitive, as the estimate becomes: "until death seizes them." The way that Allah ordained for them depends on the difference over what is meant by the verse. It was said: it is marriage, which protects them and makes them independent of illicit intercourse; and this is according to the interpretation that the address is to the guardians, the rulers or the judges, not to the husbands. It was also said: the way is what the ruling on adultery has settled upon as hadd, namely: "For a virgin with a virgin, a hundred lashes and exile for a year; for a married person with a married person, stoning." The interpretation of the way with this is established by the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit in Sahih Muslim from the Prophet (ﷺ), so it is obligatory to adopt it. The hadith of 'Ubadah does not abrogate this verse, nor is it abrogated by the lashing; rather, it explains an ambiguity in this verse, since it limited their confinement in the houses until Allah ordains for them a way, and it particularizes the generality of the verse of lashing. On this basis, the criticism of Abu Bakr al-Razi against al-Shafi'i, in his saying that the Sunnah does not abrogate the Qur'an, by his claim that the verse of confinement is abrogated by the hadith of 'Ubadah, while the hadith of 'Ubadah is abrogated by the verse of lashing, does not hold; this would entail abrogation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah and of the Sunnah by the Qur'an, contrary to al-Shafi'i's position. Rather, explanation and particularization are more appropriate than claiming abrogation three times, as the companions of Abu Hanifah held, since they claimed that the verse of confinement is abrogated by the hadith, that the hadith is abrogated by the verse of lashing, and that the verse of lashing is abrogated by the verse of stoning.

﴿And the two of you who commit it among you, harm them both﴾. The statement of Mujahid was mentioned earlier, and Abu Muslim's choice is that it refers to sodomy (liwat), which is supported by the apparent dual form. The apparent meaning of "among you" in this case is in reality for males, while the majority hold that it refers to both male and female fornicators. "Al-lani" (the two who) is intended to mean the male adulterer and the female adulteress, and the masculine is given precedence over the feminine. The harm is ordained upon committing the fahishah, and it is restricted by testimony regarding its commission, which was clarified in the preceding verse: the testimony of four. The command to harm is a substitute for harm in general, by word or deed or both.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is reviling (nayl) with the tongue and hand, striking with sandals and the like. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: it is reproach and censure. Some said: it is with action rather than speech. A group said: it is cursing and harshness without reproach. It was also said: the harm commanded is combining the two punishments: lashing and stoning; this is the view of 'Ali, who did this in the case of the Hamdaniyyah: he lashed her and then stoned her.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and the two of you who commit it﴾ is generality. Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and others said: the second verse concerns the virgin man and woman, while the first concerns married women; and those who are chaste among men are included with them in meaning. Al-Tabari preferred this view. They agreed that these two verses are abrogated by the verse of lashing, except for 'Ali's interpretation of harm, which is not abrogated, and except for the view of the one who said that harm by reproach together with lashing remains, so there is no abrogation in his view, since there is no contradiction, rather both are combined upon one person. If the two verses are taken to refer to adultery, then the first verse indicates confinement of adulteresses, and the second indicates harming them and harming him, so harm is shared between them, while confinement is specific to the woman, so she is subjected to both confinement and harm; this is the apparent meaning of the wording. It was also said: the punishment of the woman was made confinement so that the source of this sin would be cut off, and the punishment of the man was harm; and confinement was not imposed on him because he needs to go out and earn a living. As for the view of Qatadah and al-Suddi, that the first verse concerns the married and the second concerns virgin men and women, then the objects of the two punishments differ, so harm is not shared. Al-Hasan held that this verse came before the preceding verse, and then ﴿confine them to houses﴾ was revealed, meaning: if they do not repent and persist, then confine them until their condition becomes clear; but this view entails disruption of the order, so it is far-fetched. According to these opinions, the repetition has benefits; according to the view of Qatadah and al-Suddi there is no repetition, and likewise there is no repetition according to the view of Mujahid and Abu Muslim.

The grammatical analysis of ﴿wal-lani﴾ is the same as that of (wal-lati). Al-Jumhur read ﴿wal-lani﴾ with a light nun. Ibn Kathir read it with a doubled nun. The commentators mentioned the reason for omitting the ya' and the reason for doubling the nun, and the subject of that belongs to the science of grammar. Al-A'mash read: (wal-ladhina yaf'aluna-hu minkum), which is a reading that contradicts the consonantal text of the Imam's codex and is inconsistent with what follows it, since this is a plural with a plural pronoun, while what follows is a dual pronoun. But it is interpreted with some strain: that the plural "alladhina" includes the two categories of males and females, so the pronoun after it returns as a dual with regard to the two categories, just as the pronoun returned as plural to the dual, in view of the fact that under the dual there are many individuals, which carry the sense of the plural, as in His saying: ﴿If two groups of the believers fight﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9], and ﴿These two disputants who dispute﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. The preferable view is to hold that the reading of 'Abd Allah is by way of explanation, and that the dual refers to generality among the adulterers. It is also read: (wal-ladha'anni) with a hamzah and a doubled nun. The justification for this reading is that when the nun was doubled, two consonants met, so the reciter avoided their meeting by replacing the alif with a hamzah, likening it to the alif of the fa'il whose 'ayn is doubled in its lam, just as it was read: "wa la al-dallin wa la jann." The discussion of this has already been presented at length in the commentary on His saying: ﴿wa la al-dallin﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7] in al-Fatihah.

﴿Then if they repent and reform, leave them alone﴾, meaning: if they repent from the fahishah and reform their conduct, then abandon harming them. The meaning is: turn away from harming them. It was said: the command to refrain from harming them is abrogated by the verse of lashing. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The force of the wording contains a rebuke of the fornicators even if they repent, because leaving them is only a turning away. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]? This turning away in the two verses is not a command to boycott, but is leaving alone one who turns away, and in it is a demeaning of them because of the earlier sin; end of his words.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾, meaning: He returns His servants from His disobedience to His obedience, and is merciful to them by leaving off harming them when they repent.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 17:

﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon. Those - Allah will turn to them in forgiveness. And ever is Allah Knowing and Wise.﴾

The discussion of "innama" (indeed, only) and its indication of restriction (hasr) has already preceded: whether this is from the standpoint of its lexical coinage (wad') or of usage (isti'mal), or whether it has no such indication at all. The discussion of repentance and its conditions has also preceded, so there is no need to repeat it.

His saying, ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah﴾, involves the elision of a modifier (mudaf) from the subject and predicate; the implied meaning is: "Indeed, the acceptance of repentance is conditional upon the bounty of Allah," so that "ʿalā" (upon) remains in its original usage. Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is, acceptance and forgiveness are obligatory upon Allah the Exalted for these people." What he said follows the path of the Mu'tazila. What we believe is that nothing is obligatory upon Allah the Exalted by way of reason ('aql). As for what apparently implies obligation by way of revelation (sam') upon Himself, such as the eternal punishment of the disbelievers and the acceptance of faith from a disbeliever upon its condition, that is certainly realized. As for the acceptance of repentance, it is not obligatory upon Allah by reason; but by way of revelation, the apparent meanings of the verses and the Sunna converge on Allah's acceptance of repentance, and they convey certainty in this. Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni and others went to the view that these apparent meanings only convey a predominance of opinion (ghalabat al-zann), not certainty, regarding the acceptance of repentance. Repentance is an obligation by the consensus of the community, and it is valid even if one breaks it at a later state by returning to the sin, and even if one persists in some other sin, contrary to the Mu'tazila and those who follow their path among those who ascribe themselves to the Sunna, for they held that one who persists in a sin is not a penitent.

It was said that "ʿalā" here means "ʿinda" (with/at). Al-Hasan said it means "min" (from). "Evil" (al-su') encompasses disbelief, and other than it, sins; it is so named because its consequence is bad (tasu'u ʿāqibatuhu).

The position of "bi-jahāla" (in ignorance) is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: ignorant, possessing foolishness and little attainment, since the committing of evil (al-su') occurs only when desire overcomes reason; reason calls to obedience, while desire and appetite call to disobedience, so every disobedient person is ignorant in this interpretation. Here "ignorance" (jahala) does not mean deliberate intent, as al-Dahhak held. It was also reported from Mujahid; but there is consensus of the Muslims that whoever commits a sin deliberately and then repents, Allah accepts his repentance. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed that every act of disobedience is "in ignorance," whether deliberate or from unawareness. Abu al-Kalbi said: "in ignorance" means that he does not fail to know that it is a sin, but he does not know the reality of the punishment. ʿIkrima said: "All the affairs of this world are ignorance," meaning whatever is specific to it and departs from obedience to Allah. Al-Zajjaj said: his ignorance lies in that he preferred fleeting pleasure over lasting pleasure, and immediate gain over deferred gain. It was said: ignorance is persistence in disobedience, and for this reason He followed it with His saying: ﴿then repent soon﴾. It was said: its meaning is that he did it without persisting in it, so he resembled the ignorant one who does not intentionally do a thing. Al-Tirmidhi said: "ignorance of the act" is committing it without intention, so the intended meaning would be pardon for error; and it is possible that the intention is to do the act while being ignorant of its status, i.e., that it is forbidden, or of the degree of its prohibition, so he commits it in ignorance of its state, not with intent to make light of it or to be careless about it. Acting in ignorance may arise from overpowering desire, so he acts to satisfy the demand of desire, in the hope that he will repent afterward and become righteous; and it may arise from hope of forgiveness and reliance on His mercy and generosity. Ignorance may also be ignorance of the punishment for it.

The meaning of ﴿soon﴾ (min qarib) is: from a near time. Nearness here is relative to the time of the sin, which is the remainder of his life until he is at the death rattle (yughargir), or relative to the time of the soul's departure. If his repentance is accepted at this time, its acceptance before it is more fitting; and the extreme limit of the prohibition of accepting repentance has been explained in the verse after it, by the presence of death. It was said: before evil encompasses his good deeds, i.e., before his evil deeds multiply and exceed his good deeds, so that he is left as though he had no good deeds. It was said: before the darkness of his heart accumulates through the multitude of his sins, and that leads him to encompassing disbelief. ʿIkrima, al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Qays, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn Zayd and others said: before witnessing the angels and the driving. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi said: before sickness and death. Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned the best times for repentance, while those before him mentioned its last time. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: before the authority of death descends upon him. Abu Ayyub narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah accepts the repentance of the servant as long as he has not yet reached the death rattle." And it is narrated from al-Hasan that Iblis said when he was sent down to the earth: "By Your might, I will not leave the son of Adam as long as his spirit is in his body." He (Allah) said: "By My might, I will not close the door of repentance upon him as long as he has not reached the death rattle." It was said: this period was called "near" because the appointed term is coming, and everything that is coming is near; and as an alert that the period of a human's life, however long, is little and near, and because a person anticipates the descent of death upon him every moment, and whoever is in such a state is described as near.

The nominative "repentance" (al-tawba) is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "upon Allah." "For those" (lilladhina) is connected to what "upon Allah" is connected to, and the implied meaning is: "Repentance is only established by the bounty and kindness of Allah for those who..." Abu al-Baqa' said: in this view, ﴿for those who do evil﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in His saying "upon Allah," and the governing element in it is the adverbial and the stability (al-istiqrar), meaning: established for those. Abu al-Baqa' said this, but this strained construction is not needed. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that the predicate be "for those," with "upon Allah" connected to an elided element, and that it be a circumstantial clause from an elided element also; the implied meaning being: "Repentance, when it is, or when it is, upon Allah." "Idha" and "idh" are two adverbs governed by "for those," because the adverb is governed by the meaning even if it precedes it. "Kana" is complete (tamma), and the circumstantial element's subject is the pronoun of the subject of "kana." He said: it is not permissible for "upon Allah" to be a circumstantial clause governed by "for those," because it is a semantic governor (ʿamil maʿnawi), and a circumstantial clause does not precede a semantic governor. A parallel to this issue is the saying: "This, unripe, is better than it, ripe." He said this, but it is an artificial grammatical construction that is not clear in meaning. "Bi-jahala" in the position of a circumstantial clause means: accompanied by ignorance. In my view it is permissible that the "ba" be causal (ba' al-sabab), meaning: what moves them to do evil is ignorance; for if they were knowing of what follows from disobedience, mindful of it at the time of committing the disobedience, they would not have done it, as in his saying (no fornicator fornicates while he is a believer), because reason at that time is overpowered or taken away. The "min" in His saying ﴿from soon﴾ is connected to "they repent," and there are two views regarding it: the first is that it is partitive, meaning part of a near time, so that whatever part of this time one repents in, one is a penitent "from soon." The second is that it is for the beginning of the limit, meaning he begins repentance from a time near to the sin, so as not to fall into persistence. The implication of the beginning of the limit is that if he repents from a distant time, he is excluded from those who were specified with the honour of the seal of acceptance of repentance upon Allah mentioned in the verse with "upon," in His saying "upon Allah," and His saying ﴿Allah will turn to them﴾, and he would be among those promised with the word "perhaps" in His saying ﴿Perhaps Allah will turn to them﴾ [al-Tawba: 102].

The entry of the initial "min" (from) upon a time-word is not permitted by the Basrans; and the qualified noun here, which is a time, is elided, and the adjective which is "near" took its place, which is not analogical. Because this adjective, namely "near," is not among the adjectives that may be elided by analogy, since it is not used in the manner of nouns, so its qualified noun is not pronounced, like "al-Abtah" and "al-Abraq"; nor is it specific to a class of the qualified noun, as in "I passed by an engineer"; nor has its qualified noun been previously mentioned, as in "give me water, even if cold." Whatever is not like this, in which the adjective is a noun and the qualified noun is elided and its adjective placed in its stead, is not analogical.

﴿Those - Allah will turn to them﴾: when He the Exalted mentioned that the acceptance of repentance is upon Allah for those mentioned, He mentioned that He Himself is inclined toward them and shows mercy to them; for this reason the two complements of "repentance" differ with the difference of the prepositional phrases: the first is "upon Allah," and the second is "upon them," so each is explained in what suits it. When "yatubu" (turns) was made to imply the meaning of what is transitive with "ʿalā," it was made transitive with "ʿalā," as if he said: "He inclines toward them." In the first "ʿalā," the elided modifier was taken into account, which is "acceptance." Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿Those - Allah will turn to them﴾ after His saying ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah﴾ for them? I say: His saying ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah﴾ is an announcement of its being obligatory upon Him, just as some acts of obedience are obligatory upon the servant; and His saying ﴿Those - Allah will turn to them﴾ is a promise that He will fulfil what is obligatory upon Him, and an announcement that forgiveness is certainly to come, just as one promises a servant to fulfil the obligatory. End of his words. He is pointing to the path of the Mu'tazila in their saying that Allah is obligated. Their view on this has already been mentioned. Muhammad ibn ʿUmar al-Razi said, in summary: His saying ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah﴾ is an announcement that its acceptance is necessary as a matter of kindness, not of entitlement; and ﴿He turns to them﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 128] is an informing that He will do that. Or the first may mean guidance to repentance and direction, and ﴿He turns to them﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 128] means: He accepts their repentance.

﴿And ever is Allah Knowing and Wise﴾: that is, Knowing of who obeys and who disobeys; "Wise" means He places things in their proper places, so He accepts the repentance of whoever turns back to Him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 18–19 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And repentance is not [accepted] from those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor from those who die while they are disbelievers.﴾ The Exalted has negated that repentance belongs to the sinner who is in the state of despair of life, nor to the one who dies upon disbelief. The first is like Pharaoh, when his faith did not benefit him while he was drowning in the surge of water, and like those about whom God said: ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment﴾ (Ghafir 40:85). The approach of death is the first of the conditions of the Hereafter. Just as repentance is not accepted in the Hereafter from one who dies in disbelief, so too is this one whom death has approached. Al-Zamakhshari said: He equated those who postponed their repentance until the presence of death with those who died in disbelief, in that neither has repentance, because the presence of death is the first of the conditions of the Hereafter. Just as the one who dies in disbelief has certainly lost repentance, so too the one who postpones it until the presence of death, because each of them has passed the time of obligation and choice. End of his words. This is in the way of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school). The Mu'tazilah claimed that knowledge of God in the abode of obligation may be speculative, and when knowledge of God becomes necessary, obligation falls away. The people of the Hereafter, because of their witnessing of its terrors, know God by necessity, and therefore obligation falls away. Likewise the state in which knowledge of God arises by compulsion. What the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) have said is: that proximity to death does not prevent the acceptance of repentance, because a group of the Children of Israel were caused to die by God, then He revived them and imposed obligations upon them, which shows that witnessing death does not nullify obligation. Also, the hardships one undergoes near death are no greater than those endured through colic, labour pains and other such things, and none of these prevents the continuation of obligation; so likewise that. Also, near death one becomes compelled, and that would be a cause for acceptance. But God does what He wills. He promised the acceptance of repentance at some times, and in His justice He informed of its non-acceptance at another time. He may make the accepted rejected and the rejected accepted: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:23). He has refuted the Mu'tazilah in their claim that obligation falls away when knowledge of God becomes necessary, and in their claim that witnessing the states of the Hereafter necessitates knowledge of God by compulsion.

Al-Rabi' said: It was revealed as "And repentance is not [accepted]" concerning the Muslims, then it was abrogated by: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:48). Thus He decreed that He would not forgive the disbelievers, and left the believers to His will. Ibn Zayd was criticised on the grounds that the verse is a statement (khabar), and statements are not abrogated (naskh, abrogation). It was answered: it includes the affirmation of a legal ruling (hukm shar'i), and that ruling may be abrogated, and there is no need to claim abrogation, because this verse does not state that the one for whom repentance is not accepted among the believers is not forgiven, so that it would need to be abrogated by His saying: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:48).

The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿and nor those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ is that these are different from His saying: ﴿those who do evil deeds﴾ (al-'Ankabut 29:4). This is because the original principle of two conjoined items is that they are two different things; and for the emphasis conveyed by "lā" (neither/nor), which indicates the negation of the judgement from each one, you say: "This is not for Zayd and 'Amr, but for one of them," and "This is not for Zayd nor for 'Amr," so that it is negated from each of them. It is not permissible to say: "but for one of them" after "This is not for Zayd nor for 'Amr." When this is established, the weakness of al-Zamakhshari's statement becomes clear, where he said: If you say: Who is meant by "those who do evil deeds"? Are they the wrongdoers among the people of the qiblah (ahl al-qiblah, Muslims), or the disbelievers? I say: In this there are two aspects. One is that it refers to the disbelievers, given the apparent meaning of "and they are disbelievers"; and it may refer to the wrongdoers, because the discourse is about the two adulterers, and turning away from them is if they repent and reform. And His saying "and they are disbelievers" would be a statement given as a form of severity, like His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then God is Rich, independent of the worlds﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:97), and the saying: "Let him die, if he wishes, a Jew or a Christian," and "Whoever deliberately abandons the prayer has disbelieved." Because whoever is a believer and dies without entertaining repentance in his soul, his condition is close to that of the disbeliever, for only a hardened heart would dare to do that. End of his words. And this is in extreme confusion, because previously he had interpreted the verse as indicating two categories: one, those who postponed repentance until the presence of death; and two, those who died upon disbelief. In this answer, he interprets the verse as meaning one of the two categories: either the disbelievers alone, who according to him are described as those who do evil deeds and die upon disbelief, and he justified this aspect by his saying "for the apparent meaning of 'and they are disbelievers'", thus making this state an indication that by "those who do evil deeds" the disbelievers are meant; or the wrongdoers among the believers, in which case his saying "and they are disbelievers" does not mean disbelief in its literal sense, nor that they die upon disbelief in the literal sense, but rather that it came as a form of severity, in his view. So his explanation in this answer contradicts the opening of his explanation of the verse. All of this is a defence of his school, so that the punishment may be assigned either to the disbeliever or to the wrongdoer. Thereby he departed from the rules of grammar and from taking the words in their apparent sense, because his saying "and they are disbelievers" does not, in its apparent meaning, have any function other than a qualifier of His saying: ﴿nor those who die﴾, and its apparent meaning is dying upon disbelief in the literal sense. Just as He made it a condition for the non-acceptance of the repentance of those who do evil deeds that it be made at the time of the presence of death, so too He made it a condition in that case that their disbelief be at the time of death; and the apparent meaning of the conjunction is difference. Al-Zamakhshari, as the proverb says: "Your love for a thing blinds and deafens you."

The verb "they do" (ya'malūn) came in the present tense rather than the past, indicating that they persist in doing evil deeds until death approaches them. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I have repented now"﴾ is their repentance at the sight of death, as its interpretation has already been given, so their repentance is not accepted, because it is a repentance of avoidance (tawbat daf'). It was said: His saying "I have repented now" is a conditional repentance (tawbah shartiyyah), so it was not accepted, because he did not make it definite. His saying: ﴿And repentance is not [accepted]﴾ apparently negates its existence, and the meaning is the negation of its acceptance; that is, their repentance, even if it exists, is not accepted. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿nor those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ is the actual occurrence of death. So the meaning is: if they repent in the Hereafter, their repentance will not be accepted, because that cannot happen in this world, since they died connected to disbelief. It was said: It is possible that by His saying "those who die" is meant "those who draw near to death," as in His saying: ﴿when death approaches one of them﴾, that is, its signs. Just as repentance from disobedience is not accepted when near death, so likewise faith is not accepted when near death.

﴿Those — We have prepared for them a painful punishment.﴾ It is possible that the indication (ishārah) refers to the two categories, and they would both share in the preparation of punishment, even though the punishment of one of them is finite and the other eternal. And this would be a threat to the disobedient one who did not repent except at the sight of death, since He associated him with the one who died upon disbelief. It is also possible that "those" refers to the last category, since it is the nearest thing mentioned. The demonstrative (ism al-ishārah) functions like a pronoun, so it refers to the nearest thing mentioned, just as a pronoun refers to the nearest thing mentioned. And the preparation of punishment would be ordered upon dying in disbelief, since disbelief is the cutting off of hope in the pardon of God, the Exalted. The apparent meaning of "preparation" is that the Fire is created, and this matter has already been discussed.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those — We have prepared for them" in the threat, like His saying: ﴿Those — God will turn toward them﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:17) in the promise, so that it is clear that both matters are certain to occur. End of his words. Al-Zamakhshari subtly slipped in Mu'tazilism here, for he had established at the beginning of his statement that those whom He denied repentance are of two categories, then mentioned this immediately after, and it was understood from it that the threat concerning these two categories is certain, just as the promise to those whose repentance is accepted from the category mentioned before this verse is certain. So it indicates that the threat against disobedient sinners who have no repentance is certain alongside the threat against disbelievers, and this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. And despite the possibility that "those" refers to those who die upon disbelief, which is favoured by the fact that the act of the disbeliever is more heinous than the act of the wrongdoer, it is not necessary that the threat be definite for the wrongdoer. And even if the threat is for the wrongdoer who has no repentance, it does not follow that what it indicates must occur, since punishment is possible and pardon is possible. The benefit of its mention is the generation of fear in the wrongdoer. And every threat to the wrongdoers who died in Islam is restricted by His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:48), and this is the decisive verse (muhkam) to which one returns.

Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi and Sufyan al-Thawri held that His saying: ﴿those who do evil deeds﴾ refers to the hypocrites. Al-Marwazi chose this view and said: He distinguished them by the conjunction, and this indicates that the first category refers to the hypocrites, just as He distinguished between them in His saying: ﴿So today no ransom will be taken from you, nor from those who disbelieved﴾ (al-Hadid 57:15), because the hypocrite was outwardly different from the disbeliever in this world. The view that appears to be correct is that it refers to the sinful believers who repent in the state of despair of life, because the hypocrites are included in His saying: ﴿nor those who die while they are disbelievers﴾, so they are a part of the disbelievers and have no counterpart. It was said: Repentance is only upon God for minor sins; repentance is not for those who do evil deeds in major sins, nor for those who die while they are disbelievers in disbelief.

﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by force﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and Abu Mijlaz said: The guardians of a deceased man had more right to his wife than her own family; if they wished, one of them would marry her, or they would marry her to someone else, or they would prevent her. And his son by another wife would marry her, and this was obligatory among the Ansar, and permissible among the Quraysh. Mujahid said: The eldest son had more right to his father's wife, if she was not his mother. Al-Suddi said: If the guardian (wali) got there first and placed his garment upon her, he had more right to her; or if she got to her family first, she had more right to herself. So God removed that practice by this verse.

The address in this reading is to the guardians (awliya'), who were forbidden to inherit women left behind by the dead as though they were property. The intended meaning is the negation of inheritance in cases of both willingness and reluctance, not its permissibility when the women are willing, as some have argued from the verse. The mention of reluctance (*karh*) came out in the form of the usual case, because most women in that situation were coerced, since their guardians had a better right over them than their own kin did. It has also been said that the verse refers to a husband who keeps his wives without marrying them, so that he may inherit their wealth when they die. Or it refers to a man who has a female orphan under his guardianship who possesses wealth. He dislikes to marry her to someone else, out of protectiveness toward her property, so he marries her against her will for that reason. Or it refers to a man who has an old woman with wealth under him and longs for a young woman. He keeps the old woman for her wealth and does not approach her until she ransoms herself from him with her property, or until she dies and he inherits her property. The address is to husbands, and on this view and the one before it, what is inherited is their property, not the women themselves. *Karhan* (under compulsion) is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) relating to the women. It is therefore estimated as an active participle, meaning "unwilling," or as a passive participle, meaning "compelled." The two Ḥaramayn (the Makkan and Madinan readers) and Abu 'Amr read it with a *fatḥa* on the *kaf* wherever it occurs. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a *ḍamma*. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read it with a *fatḥa* in this surah and in al-Tawba, and with a *ḍamma* in al-Ahqaf and al-Mu'minun. Both are dialectal forms, like *al-ṣamt* and *al-ṣumt* (silence). This was stated by al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, and Abu 'Ali. Al-Farra' said that the *fatḥa* means coercion, while the *ḍamma* means an act one performs while disliking it without being compelled, like things that involve hardship and toil. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Ibn Qutayba also said this. The discussion of this word has already been covered at the verse ﴿And fighting is prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you﴾ (al-Baqara 2:216). It is also recited as *lā taḥillu lakum* with a *tā'* (the verb being feminine), on the estimate "the inheritance is not lawful for you," like the reading of the one who recited ﴿Then their trial was only that they said﴾ (al-An'am 6:23), meaning "their saying." The accusative of *al-nisa'* (the women) is as a direct object, either because the women themselves are the ones inherited, or by omission of a noun, meaning "the wealth of the women."

﴿And do not restrain them in order to take away part of what you have given them﴾ That is, do not confine them or constrict them (p. 203). The apparent address here is to husbands, because of the phrase "part of what you have given them," since the husband is the one who gave the dowry. A husband would dislike his wife's company while she still had a dowry owed to her by him, so he would confine her and beat her until she ransomed herself from him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi (again). Or a man marries a noblewoman who does not suit him, so he divorces her on the condition that she may not remarry without his permission, and he calls witnesses to this. Then when she is proposed to and he is satisfied, he permits her, and otherwise he restrains her. This was said by Ibn Zayd. Or it was their custom to prevent a divorced woman from remarrying her former husband after three divorces, and they were forbidden from this. It has also been said that the address is to guardians, as clarified by the phrase ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾. It is possible that the address is to both guardians and husbands in the phrase ﴿O you who have believed﴾, and that they were addressed together in this address and then each was addressed separately in the prohibition with what suits them. Guardians were addressed with ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾, and husbands were addressed with ﴿and do not restrain them﴾, so each address returned to the one it fits. The exegesis of *'adl* (restraining) has already been covered at al-Baqara 2:232, ﴿So do not restrain them﴾. The *bā'* in *bi-ba'ḍi mā ātaytumūhunna* is for transitivity, meaning "to take away part of what you gave them." It is also possible that the *bā'* is for accompaniment, meaning "to go away accompanied by part of what you gave them."

﴿except that they commit a clear immorality﴾ This is an exceptive construction that is connected (*istithna' muttaṣil*), and there is no need to claim it is disconnected (*munqaṭi'*), as some have claimed. It is an exception from a general time expression or from a cause. It is as if it were said: "Do not restrain them at any time except the time when they commit immorality," or "Do not restrain them for any reason except the reason that they commit immorality." The address in "and do not restrain them" appears to be to husbands, since a guardian does not have the right to confine a woman so as to take her property. This is agreed upon by the community (*ijma'*), and it is only the husband's right, as has been explained. *Al-fāḥisha* (immorality) here means fornication. This was said by Abu Qilaba and al-Hasan. Al-Hasan said: "If a virgin commits fornication, she is to be flogged one hundred times and banished for one year, and she is to return to her husband what she took from him." Abu Qilaba said: "If a man's wife commits fornication, there is no harm in his harming her and making things difficult for her until she ransoms herself from him." al-Suddi said: "If they do that, take their dowries." 'Ata' said: "This ruling was in effect, then it was abrogated (*nuskh*) by the prescribed penalties (*hudud*)." Ibn Sirin and Abu Qilaba said: "Khul' (divorce by ransom) is not lawful until a man is found upon her belly." al-Suddi said: "It is not lawful for him to confine her out of harm until she ransoms herself from him, meaning: even if she has committed fornication." Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'isha, al-Dahhak, and others said: "*Al-fāḥisha* here is *nushuz* (disobedience and rebelliousness). When she is rebellious, it becomes lawful for him to take her property." This is the position of Malik. Others said: "*Al-fāḥisha* is abusive speech with the tongue, and bad conduct in word and deed. This has the same meaning as *nushuz*." The meaning is: "except that the bad conduct is on both sides, so it is permissible to take their property by way of khul'." This meaning is supported by the reading of Ubayy: ﴿except that they behave immorally toward you﴾, and by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿except that they behave immorally toward you, and live with them honorably﴾. These are two readings that differ from the codex of the Imam, and al-Dani similarly reported them from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima. What should be understood is that this is by way of interpretation and clarification, not that it is itself Qur'an. Some held that a husband should not exceed what he gave her, relying on the phrase ﴿in order to take away part of what you have given them﴾. Malik said: "The husband may take from a rebellious wife all that she owns." The apparent meaning of the exception implies that it permits restraining her so that he may take back part of what he gave her for his own consumption, but not what he did not give her from his own wealth, if she commits a clear immorality. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read *mubayyina* here, and in al-Ahzab and al-Talaq, with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'*, meaning that whoever claims it makes it clear and explains it. The rest read it with a *kasra*, meaning "clear in itself and manifest." It is an active participle from *bayyana*, which is an intransitive verb meaning *bāna*, "to become apparent." The apparent sense of "and do not restrain them" is that it is not a prohibition. The verb is then jussive because of the *wa*, and the *wa* conjoins a declarative clause to a prescriptive clause. If we say that the condition for conjoining clauses is that they be suitably related, then the suitability is that the earlier declarative clause carries the meaning of a prohibition, as if it were said: "Do not inherit women by compulsion, for that is not lawful for you, and do not restrain them." If we say that suitability is not a condition for conjunction, which is the position of Sibawayh, then the matter is obvious. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that *tu'ḍulūhunna* (you restrain them) is in the accusative, conjoined to *tarithū* (you inherit), so that the *wa* is a coordinating conjunction joining one verb to another verb." Ibn Mas'ud read *wa-lā an ta'ḍulūhunna* (and that you not restrain them), and this reading strengthens the possibility of the accusative, and that restraint is something not lawful by explicit text. On the reading of the jussive, it is a prohibition that compensates for the lack of signs of prohibition or reprehensibility. The possibility of the accusative is stronger. This ends what he mentioned about permitting this aspect. However, this is not permissible, because when you conjoin a verb negated with *lā* to an affirmed verb, and both are in the accusative, the governing particle is only estimated after the conjunctive particle, not after *lā*. So when you say: "I want to repent and not enter the Fire," the estimate is: "I want to repent and that I not enter the Fire," because the first verb is sought affirmatively and the second negatively. The meaning is: "I want repentance and the negation of my entering the Fire." If the verb governing the two conjoined items is negated, then it is the same.
