If you estimate this estimate in the verse, it does not work: if you say "It is not lawful for you that you do not restrain them," it does not work, unless you make *lā* an extra particle and not a negative one, which goes against the apparent meaning. As for estimating *an* after the negative *lā*, that is not correct. When you estimate *an* after *lā*, this is conjoining a estimated verbal noun to another estimated verbal noun, not conjoining a verb to a verb. Ibn 'Atiyya was confused by the two conjunctions and thought that because it is possible to estimate *an* after *lā*, it would be a conjoining of a verb to a verb. There is a difference between your saying "I do not want that he stand and that he not go out" and your saying "I do not want that he stand nor that he go out." In the first, there is a negation of the desire for his standing and a desire for the negation of his going out, so he wants his going out. In the second, there is a negation of the desire for his standing and his going out, so he does not want either standing or going out. In this understanding there is some obscurity for anyone who has not practiced the science of Arabic grammar.

﴿And live with them honorably﴾ This is a command to good companionship. The apparent address is to husbands, because the obligation of companionship is generally on husbands, and they used to treat women badly. *Bi-l-ma'rūf* (honorably) means fairness in the night spent with them and in maintenance, and gentleness in speech. It is said: "A woman grows fat from her ear," meaning that a woman responds to kind words.

﴿But if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes in it much good﴾ God, exalted is He, educated His servants with this. The meaning is that dislike should not lead you to bad companionship, for a person's dislike of something does not indicate the absence of good in it. As God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ (al-Baqara 2:216). Perhaps what the soul dislikes is more right in religion and better in outcome, and what it loves is the opposite. Since *'asā* (perhaps) is a rigid verb, the response particle *fa-* enters upon it. *'Asā* here is a complete verb, so it does not need a subject and predicate. The pronoun in *fīhi* refers to "a thing," meaning: God places in that disliked thing (much good). It has also been said that it refers to *al-karh* (dislike), the verbal noun understood from the verb. It has been said that it refers to patience (*al-ṣabr*). Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi interpreted "good" as a righteous child, and this is by way of example, not restriction. Consider the eloquence of ﴿then perhaps you dislike a thing﴾, in that it attaches dislike to the word "thing," which includes everything in the manner of a substitute, rather than attaching dislike to the pronoun of "them." It would have been "then perhaps you dislike them." The context of the verse indicates that the meaning is encouragement to keep them and to remain in their company, even if a person dislikes some of their characteristics. This is why what follows is: ﴿And if you wish to replace a wife with another wife﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:20). It has been said that the meaning of the verse is: "And Allah makes in your separation from them much good for you and for them," like His saying: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:130). This was said by al-Asamm. But this view is far from the context of the verse, and what precedes and follows it indicates otherwise. Rarely will you see two companions each of whom is pleased with all of the other's character. It is said: "No two people live together except that one of them overlooks something of the other." In Sahih Muslim: "A believing man should not hate a believing woman; if he dislikes one of her characteristics, he will be pleased with another." They recited, on this meaning:

"Whoever does not close his eye on his friend and on some of what is in him dies while still blaming."

"Whoever searches diligently for every slip finds it, and no companion is safe from time."

﴿And if you desire to exchange a wife for another wife, and you have given one of them a qintar, then do not take back anything from it﴾ [4:20]. When He permitted [the husband] to harm them [by taking back their gifts] if they committed a flagrant indecency, so that he would take back part of what he had given her, He based the prohibition of that on a situation other than the situation of flagrant indecency, and He placed the intention (al-irada) in the position of the act. It is as if He said: "And if you have exchanged [a wife for another]." Or He omitted a conjoined element, meaning: "and you have exchanged." The apparent meaning of His words "and you have given" (wa-ataytum) is that the wāw is for the circumstantial clause (lil-hal), meaning "and you have already given." It has also been said that it is conjoined to the verb of the condition (fi'l al-shart), but this is not the apparent meaning. Istibdal (exchange) is putting one thing in the place of another. The meaning is that if the separation comes from your choice, then do not take back anything from what you have given them.

He cited His words, ﴿and you have given one of them a qintar﴾ [4:20], as evidence for the permissibility of exaggeration in marriage gifts (mughalah fi al-sadaqat). The woman who addressed ʿUmar when he delivered a sermon and said, "Beware, do not exaggerate in the dowries of your women," also used this as evidence. Others said: it does not indicate exaggeration, because it is an illustration intended as an emphasis on abundance, as if it were said: "and you have given this great amount which no one gives." This is similar to his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever builds a mosque for Allah, even if it is as small as the nest of a sandgrouse (mafhas qata), Allah will build for him a house in Paradise." It is known that a mosque would not be as small as the nest of a sandgrouse; rather, this is an illustration for the extreme of smallness. He also said to someone who had given a dowry of two hundred [dirhams] and came seeking help with his dowry, and was angry: "It is as if you were cutting gold and silver from the side of a volcanic plain (min ʿurd al-harrah)." Muhammad ibn ʿUmar al-Razi said: there is no proof in it for exaggeration, because His words "and you have given" do not indicate the permissibility of giving a qintar, and making something a condition for another thing does not require that the condition itself be permissible to occur, as in His saying: "Whoever is killed, his family has a choice between two [options]" (man qutila lahu qatil fa-ahlihi bayn khiyaratayn). End of quote.

Since His words, "if you desire to exchange a wife for a wife," are addressed to a group, the object of the exchange is wives in place of wives. He was content with the singular instead of the plural because the plural of those being exchanged shows it, and because the wording "requiring the addressees to [take] one wife in place of one wife" would not cause confusion. And since the meaning of plurality is intended, the pronoun in His words "one of them" (iḥdāhunna) returns in the plural. The one He forbade us to take anything from is the wife who is being replaced, not the wife being taken as a replacement, since the former is the one to whom he gave the property, not the one he intends to bring into being. This is shown by His words: ﴿and how could you take it when you have already been intimate with one another﴾ [4:21]. He said "and you have given one of them a qintar" to show that His words "and you have given" mean that each one of you gave one of them, i.e. one of the wives, a qintar. He did not say "and you have given them a qintar" so that it would not be supposed that all the addressees had given the wives a qintar. The intended meaning is: each one gave his wife a qintar. So the word iḥdāhunna indicates that the pronoun in "you have given" means each and every one, just as the expression ﴿if you desire to exchange a wife for a wife﴾ [4:20] indicates that the intended meaning is exchanging wives for wives. Thus the singular here is intended to mean the plural, by the indication of "if you desire"; and by His words "and you have given" each one is meant, by the indication of iḥdāhunna, which is singular in that sense. This is one of the subtleties of eloquence (min latif al-balaghah), and this meaning cannot be expressed more concisely or more eloquently than this.

The discussion of qintar was given earlier at the beginning of Surat Al ʿImran, and the pronoun in minhu refers back to qintar. Ibn Muhaysin read the hamza of iḥdāhunna as connected (bi-wasl alif iḥdāhunna), just as it was read: ﴿Indeed it is one of the greatest [calamities]﴾ [74:35] with the alif connected. The alif was dropped as a matter of [linguistic] precision, as the poet said:

"And you hear from beneath the dust the clatter of it" (wa-tasmaʿu min taḥti al-ʿajaji lahā azmalā)

And he said:

"If I do not fight, then dress me in a veil (burqaʿ)."

The apparent meaning of His words, "do not take anything from it," is the prohibition of taking any part of what he gave her if the exchange of her place is by his own will. They said: this is restricted by His words, ﴿but if they willingly give you some of it, then consume it﴾ [4:4]. They said: consensus (ijma') has been reached on this. The khulʿ (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation) is treated in the same way, because she willingly gives the husband what she ransomed herself with. Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani said: do not take anything from the woman seeking khulʿ, because of His words: ﴿do not take anything from it﴾ [4:20]. He said the verse of al-Baqarah is abrogated (naskh) by this. The discussion of that was given in Surat al-Baqarah. The apparent meaning of His words, "and you have given one of them a qintar," together with the prohibition that follows it, indicates the generality of what he gave her, whether it was a dowry or something else.

[And] ﴿you have been intimate with one another﴾ [4:21]: this does not require that what he gave her was only a dowry. Rather the meaning is that there has come to be between them such mixing and union that it is not fitting for him to take back anything of what he gave her, whether it was a dowry or something else. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: it is not impossible that the beginning of the address is general in all that the term includes, while the element conjoined to it has a particular ruling; this does not necessitate the particularity of the first wording. The end of his statement. This is an acknowledgment from him that what is meant by His words ﴿how could you take it﴾ [4:21] is the dowry. We have shown that this does not necessarily follow.

Abu Bakr al-Razi also said: the verse indicates that whoever advances his wife her maintenance for a period, and she dies before the period ends, he does not reclaim anything from her inheritance of what he gave her, because of the generality of the wording. It is possible that he wishes to marry another after her death, substituting her for the first. The apparent meaning of the command covers this case. End of quote. This is not apparent, because istibdal requires the existence of both the replacement and that which is replaced. If the latter has ceased to exist, this is not valid, because the one who exchanges leaves this one and takes another in its place; so if it is non-existent, how can he leave it and take another in its stead?

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the prohibition of taking anything of what he gave her if he intends the exchange, and the end of the verse indicates through its reason, "intimacy," the generality of the ruling, both in the case of exchange and otherwise. The meaning of the conditional (mafhum al-shart) is not intended. It was singled out for mention because it is a situation in which one might suppose that, because of the exchange and the presence of another in her place, he may take her dowry and give it to the second wife, who is preferable to him than the one he divorces (tufariqa). So Allah made clear that he does not take anything from her. And if the one he exchanged is not permitted for him to take anything of what he gave her, despite the loss of his right to her body, then it is more fitting that it is not permitted for him to do so while his right and his enjoyment of her body remain, and while she is more fully available to him for benefit than the other.

Abu al-Sammal and Abu Jaʿfar read shayyan with a fatha on the yāʾ and tanwin, dropping the hamza and placing its vowel on the yāʾ.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 18–19 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And repentance is not [accepted] from those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor from those who die while they are disbelievers.﴾ The Exalted has negated that repentance belongs to the sinner who is in the state of despair of life, nor to the one who dies upon disbelief. The first is like Pharaoh, when his faith did not benefit him while he was drowning in the surge of water, and like those about whom God said: ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment﴾ (Ghafir 40:85). The approach of death is the first of the conditions of the Hereafter. Just as repentance is not accepted in the Hereafter from one who dies in disbelief, so too is this one whom death has approached. Al-Zamakhshari said: He equated those who postponed their repentance until the presence of death with those who died in disbelief, in that neither has repentance, because the presence of death is the first of the conditions of the Hereafter. Just as the one who dies in disbelief has certainly lost repentance, so too the one who postpones it until the presence of death, because each of them has passed the time of obligation and choice. End of his words. This is in the way of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school). The Mu'tazilah claimed that knowledge of God in the abode of obligation may be speculative, and when knowledge of God becomes necessary, obligation falls away. The people of the Hereafter, because of their witnessing of its terrors, know God by necessity, and therefore obligation falls away. Likewise the state in which knowledge of God arises by compulsion. What the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) have said is: that proximity to death does not prevent the acceptance of repentance, because a group of the Children of Israel were caused to die by God, then He revived them and imposed obligations upon them, which shows that witnessing death does not nullify obligation. Also, the hardships one undergoes near death are no greater than those endured through colic, labour pains and other such things, and none of these prevents the continuation of obligation; so likewise that. Also, near death one becomes compelled, and that would be a cause for acceptance. But God does what He wills. He promised the acceptance of repentance at some times, and in His justice He informed of its non-acceptance at another time. He may make the accepted rejected and the rejected accepted: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:23). He has refuted the Mu'tazilah in their claim that obligation falls away when knowledge of God becomes necessary, and in their claim that witnessing the states of the Hereafter necessitates knowledge of God by compulsion.

Al-Rabi' said: It was revealed as "And repentance is not [accepted]" concerning the Muslims, then it was abrogated by: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:48). Thus He decreed that He would not forgive the disbelievers, and left the believers to His will. Ibn Zayd was criticised on the grounds that the verse is a statement (khabar), and statements are not abrogated (naskh, abrogation). It was answered: it includes the affirmation of a legal ruling (hukm shar'i), and that ruling may be abrogated, and there is no need to claim abrogation, because this verse does not state that the one for whom repentance is not accepted among the believers is not forgiven, so that it would need to be abrogated by His saying: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:48).

The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿and nor those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ is that these are different from His saying: ﴿those who do evil deeds﴾ (al-'Ankabut 29:4). This is because the original principle of two conjoined items is that they are two different things; and for the emphasis conveyed by "lā" (neither/nor), which indicates the negation of the judgement from each one, you say: "This is not for Zayd and 'Amr, but for one of them," and "This is not for Zayd nor for 'Amr," so that it is negated from each of them. It is not permissible to say: "but for one of them" after "This is not for Zayd nor for 'Amr." When this is established, the weakness of al-Zamakhshari's statement becomes clear, where he said: If you say: Who is meant by "those who do evil deeds"? Are they the wrongdoers among the people of the qiblah (ahl al-qiblah, Muslims), or the disbelievers? I say: In this there are two aspects. One is that it refers to the disbelievers, given the apparent meaning of "and they are disbelievers"; and it may refer to the wrongdoers, because the discourse is about the two adulterers, and turning away from them is if they repent and reform. And His saying "and they are disbelievers" would be a statement given as a form of severity, like His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then God is Rich, independent of the worlds﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:97), and the saying: "Let him die, if he wishes, a Jew or a Christian," and "Whoever deliberately abandons the prayer has disbelieved." Because whoever is a believer and dies without entertaining repentance in his soul, his condition is close to that of the disbeliever, for only a hardened heart would dare to do that. End of his words. And this is in extreme confusion, because previously he had interpreted the verse as indicating two categories: one, those who postponed repentance until the presence of death; and two, those who died upon disbelief. In this answer, he interprets the verse as meaning one of the two categories: either the disbelievers alone, who according to him are described as those who do evil deeds and die upon disbelief, and he justified this aspect by his saying "for the apparent meaning of 'and they are disbelievers'", thus making this state an indication that by "those who do evil deeds" the disbelievers are meant; or the wrongdoers among the believers, in which case his saying "and they are disbelievers" does not mean disbelief in its literal sense, nor that they die upon disbelief in the literal sense, but rather that it came as a form of severity, in his view. So his explanation in this answer contradicts the opening of his explanation of the verse. All of this is a defence of his school, so that the punishment may be assigned either to the disbeliever or to the wrongdoer. Thereby he departed from the rules of grammar and from taking the words in their apparent sense, because his saying "and they are disbelievers" does not, in its apparent meaning, have any function other than a qualifier of His saying: ﴿nor those who die﴾, and its apparent meaning is dying upon disbelief in the literal sense. Just as He made it a condition for the non-acceptance of the repentance of those who do evil deeds that it be made at the time of the presence of death, so too He made it a condition in that case that their disbelief be at the time of death; and the apparent meaning of the conjunction is difference. Al-Zamakhshari, as the proverb says: "Your love for a thing blinds and deafens you."

The verb "they do" (ya'malūn) came in the present tense rather than the past, indicating that they persist in doing evil deeds until death approaches them. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I have repented now"﴾ is their repentance at the sight of death, as its interpretation has already been given, so their repentance is not accepted, because it is a repentance of avoidance (tawbat daf'). It was said: His saying "I have repented now" is a conditional repentance (tawbah shartiyyah), so it was not accepted, because he did not make it definite. His saying: ﴿And repentance is not [accepted]﴾ apparently negates its existence, and the meaning is the negation of its acceptance; that is, their repentance, even if it exists, is not accepted. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿nor those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ is the actual occurrence of death. So the meaning is: if they repent in the Hereafter, their repentance will not be accepted, because that cannot happen in this world, since they died connected to disbelief. It was said: It is possible that by His saying "those who die" is meant "those who draw near to death," as in His saying: ﴿when death approaches one of them﴾, that is, its signs. Just as repentance from disobedience is not accepted when near death, so likewise faith is not accepted when near death.

﴿Those — We have prepared for them a painful punishment.﴾ It is possible that the indication (ishārah) refers to the two categories, and they would both share in the preparation of punishment, even though the punishment of one of them is finite and the other eternal. And this would be a threat to the disobedient one who did not repent except at the sight of death, since He associated him with the one who died upon disbelief. It is also possible that "those" refers to the last category, since it is the nearest thing mentioned. The demonstrative (ism al-ishārah) functions like a pronoun, so it refers to the nearest thing mentioned, just as a pronoun refers to the nearest thing mentioned. And the preparation of punishment would be ordered upon dying in disbelief, since disbelief is the cutting off of hope in the pardon of God, the Exalted. The apparent meaning of "preparation" is that the Fire is created, and this matter has already been discussed.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those — We have prepared for them" in the threat, like His saying: ﴿Those — God will turn toward them﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:17) in the promise, so that it is clear that both matters are certain to occur. End of his words. Al-Zamakhshari subtly slipped in Mu'tazilism here, for he had established at the beginning of his statement that those whom He denied repentance are of two categories, then mentioned this immediately after, and it was understood from it that the threat concerning these two categories is certain, just as the promise to those whose repentance is accepted from the category mentioned before this verse is certain. So it indicates that the threat against disobedient sinners who have no repentance is certain alongside the threat against disbelievers, and this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. And despite the possibility that "those" refers to those who die upon disbelief, which is favoured by the fact that the act of the disbeliever is more heinous than the act of the wrongdoer, it is not necessary that the threat be definite for the wrongdoer. And even if the threat is for the wrongdoer who has no repentance, it does not follow that what it indicates must occur, since punishment is possible and pardon is possible. The benefit of its mention is the generation of fear in the wrongdoer. And every threat to the wrongdoers who died in Islam is restricted by His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:48), and this is the decisive verse (muhkam) to which one returns.

Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi and Sufyan al-Thawri held that His saying: ﴿those who do evil deeds﴾ refers to the hypocrites. Al-Marwazi chose this view and said: He distinguished them by the conjunction, and this indicates that the first category refers to the hypocrites, just as He distinguished between them in His saying: ﴿So today no ransom will be taken from you, nor from those who disbelieved﴾ (al-Hadid 57:15), because the hypocrite was outwardly different from the disbeliever in this world. The view that appears to be correct is that it refers to the sinful believers who repent in the state of despair of life, because the hypocrites are included in His saying: ﴿nor those who die while they are disbelievers﴾, so they are a part of the disbelievers and have no counterpart. It was said: Repentance is only upon God for minor sins; repentance is not for those who do evil deeds in major sins, nor for those who die while they are disbelievers in disbelief.

﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by force﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and Abu Mijlaz said: The guardians of a deceased man had more right to his wife than her own family; if they wished, one of them would marry her, or they would marry her to someone else, or they would prevent her. And his son by another wife would marry her, and this was obligatory among the Ansar, and permissible among the Quraysh. Mujahid said: The eldest son had more right to his father's wife, if she was not his mother. Al-Suddi said: If the guardian (wali) got there first and placed his garment upon her, he had more right to her; or if she got to her family first, she had more right to herself. So God removed that practice by this verse.

The address in this reading is to the guardians (awliya'), who were forbidden to inherit women left behind by the dead as though they were property. The intended meaning is the negation of inheritance in cases of both willingness and reluctance, not its permissibility when the women are willing, as some have argued from the verse. The mention of reluctance (*karh*) came out in the form of the usual case, because most women in that situation were coerced, since their guardians had a better right over them than their own kin did. It has also been said that the verse refers to a husband who keeps his wives without marrying them, so that he may inherit their wealth when they die. Or it refers to a man who has a female orphan under his guardianship who possesses wealth. He dislikes to marry her to someone else, out of protectiveness toward her property, so he marries her against her will for that reason. Or it refers to a man who has an old woman with wealth under him and longs for a young woman. He keeps the old woman for her wealth and does not approach her until she ransoms herself from him with her property, or until she dies and he inherits her property. The address is to husbands, and on this view and the one before it, what is inherited is their property, not the women themselves. *Karhan* (under compulsion) is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) relating to the women. It is therefore estimated as an active participle, meaning "unwilling," or as a passive participle, meaning "compelled." The two Ḥaramayn (the Makkan and Madinan readers) and Abu 'Amr read it with a *fatḥa* on the *kaf* wherever it occurs. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a *ḍamma*. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read it with a *fatḥa* in this surah and in al-Tawba, and with a *ḍamma* in al-Ahqaf and al-Mu'minun. Both are dialectal forms, like *al-ṣamt* and *al-ṣumt* (silence). This was stated by al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, and Abu 'Ali. Al-Farra' said that the *fatḥa* means coercion, while the *ḍamma* means an act one performs while disliking it without being compelled, like things that involve hardship and toil. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Ibn Qutayba also said this. The discussion of this word has already been covered at the verse ﴿And fighting is prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you﴾ (al-Baqara 2:216). It is also recited as *lā taḥillu lakum* with a *tā'* (the verb being feminine), on the estimate "the inheritance is not lawful for you," like the reading of the one who recited ﴿Then their trial was only that they said﴾ (al-An'am 6:23), meaning "their saying." The accusative of *al-nisa'* (the women) is as a direct object, either because the women themselves are the ones inherited, or by omission of a noun, meaning "the wealth of the women."

﴿And do not restrain them in order to take away part of what you have given them﴾ That is, do not confine them or constrict them (p. 203). The apparent address here is to husbands, because of the phrase "part of what you have given them," since the husband is the one who gave the dowry. A husband would dislike his wife's company while she still had a dowry owed to her by him, so he would confine her and beat her until she ransomed herself from him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi (again). Or a man marries a noblewoman who does not suit him, so he divorces her on the condition that she may not remarry without his permission, and he calls witnesses to this. Then when she is proposed to and he is satisfied, he permits her, and otherwise he restrains her. This was said by Ibn Zayd. Or it was their custom to prevent a divorced woman from remarrying her former husband after three divorces, and they were forbidden from this. It has also been said that the address is to guardians, as clarified by the phrase ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾. It is possible that the address is to both guardians and husbands in the phrase ﴿O you who have believed﴾, and that they were addressed together in this address and then each was addressed separately in the prohibition with what suits them. Guardians were addressed with ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾, and husbands were addressed with ﴿and do not restrain them﴾, so each address returned to the one it fits. The exegesis of *'adl* (restraining) has already been covered at al-Baqara 2:232, ﴿So do not restrain them﴾. The *bā'* in *bi-ba'ḍi mā ātaytumūhunna* is for transitivity, meaning "to take away part of what you gave them." It is also possible that the *bā'* is for accompaniment, meaning "to go away accompanied by part of what you gave them."

﴿except that they commit a clear immorality﴾ This is an exceptive construction that is connected (*istithna' muttaṣil*), and there is no need to claim it is disconnected (*munqaṭi'*), as some have claimed. It is an exception from a general time expression or from a cause. It is as if it were said: "Do not restrain them at any time except the time when they commit immorality," or "Do not restrain them for any reason except the reason that they commit immorality." The address in "and do not restrain them" appears to be to husbands, since a guardian does not have the right to confine a woman so as to take her property. This is agreed upon by the community (*ijma'*), and it is only the husband's right, as has been explained. *Al-fāḥisha* (immorality) here means fornication. This was said by Abu Qilaba and al-Hasan. Al-Hasan said: "If a virgin commits fornication, she is to be flogged one hundred times and banished for one year, and she is to return to her husband what she took from him." Abu Qilaba said: "If a man's wife commits fornication, there is no harm in his harming her and making things difficult for her until she ransoms herself from him." al-Suddi said: "If they do that, take their dowries." 'Ata' said: "This ruling was in effect, then it was abrogated (*nuskh*) by the prescribed penalties (*hudud*)." Ibn Sirin and Abu Qilaba said: "Khul' (divorce by ransom) is not lawful until a man is found upon her belly." al-Suddi said: "It is not lawful for him to confine her out of harm until she ransoms herself from him, meaning: even if she has committed fornication." Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'isha, al-Dahhak, and others said: "*Al-fāḥisha* here is *nushuz* (disobedience and rebelliousness). When she is rebellious, it becomes lawful for him to take her property." This is the position of Malik. Others said: "*Al-fāḥisha* is abusive speech with the tongue, and bad conduct in word and deed. This has the same meaning as *nushuz*." The meaning is: "except that the bad conduct is on both sides, so it is permissible to take their property by way of khul'." This meaning is supported by the reading of Ubayy: ﴿except that they behave immorally toward you﴾, and by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿except that they behave immorally toward you, and live with them honorably﴾. These are two readings that differ from the codex of the Imam, and al-Dani similarly reported them from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima. What should be understood is that this is by way of interpretation and clarification, not that it is itself Qur'an. Some held that a husband should not exceed what he gave her, relying on the phrase ﴿in order to take away part of what you have given them﴾. Malik said: "The husband may take from a rebellious wife all that she owns." The apparent meaning of the exception implies that it permits restraining her so that he may take back part of what he gave her for his own consumption, but not what he did not give her from his own wealth, if she commits a clear immorality. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read *mubayyina* here, and in al-Ahzab and al-Talaq, with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'*, meaning that whoever claims it makes it clear and explains it. The rest read it with a *kasra*, meaning "clear in itself and manifest." It is an active participle from *bayyana*, which is an intransitive verb meaning *bāna*, "to become apparent." The apparent sense of "and do not restrain them" is that it is not a prohibition. The verb is then jussive because of the *wa*, and the *wa* conjoins a declarative clause to a prescriptive clause. If we say that the condition for conjoining clauses is that they be suitably related, then the suitability is that the earlier declarative clause carries the meaning of a prohibition, as if it were said: "Do not inherit women by compulsion, for that is not lawful for you, and do not restrain them." If we say that suitability is not a condition for conjunction, which is the position of Sibawayh, then the matter is obvious. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that *tu'ḍulūhunna* (you restrain them) is in the accusative, conjoined to *tarithū* (you inherit), so that the *wa* is a coordinating conjunction joining one verb to another verb." Ibn Mas'ud read *wa-lā an ta'ḍulūhunna* (and that you not restrain them), and this reading strengthens the possibility of the accusative, and that restraint is something not lawful by explicit text. On the reading of the jussive, it is a prohibition that compensates for the lack of signs of prohibition or reprehensibility. The possibility of the accusative is stronger. This ends what he mentioned about permitting this aspect. However, this is not permissible, because when you conjoin a verb negated with *lā* to an affirmed verb, and both are in the accusative, the governing particle is only estimated after the conjunctive particle, not after *lā*. So when you say: "I want to repent and not enter the Fire," the estimate is: "I want to repent and that I not enter the Fire," because the first verb is sought affirmatively and the second negatively. The meaning is: "I want repentance and the negation of my entering the Fire." If the verb governing the two conjoined items is negated, then it is the same. If you estimate this estimate in the verse, it does not work: if you say "It is not lawful for you that you do not restrain them," it does not work, unless you make *lā* an extra particle and not a negative one, which goes against the apparent meaning. As for estimating *an* after the negative *lā*, that is not correct. When you estimate *an* after *lā*, this is conjoining a estimated verbal noun to another estimated verbal noun, not conjoining a verb to a verb. Ibn 'Atiyya was confused by the two conjunctions and thought that because it is possible to estimate *an* after *lā*, it would be a conjoining of a verb to a verb. There is a difference between your saying "I do not want that he stand and that he not go out" and your saying "I do not want that he stand nor that he go out." In the first, there is a negation of the desire for his standing and a desire for the negation of his going out, so he wants his going out. In the second, there is a negation of the desire for his standing and his going out, so he does not want either standing or going out. In this understanding there is some obscurity for anyone who has not practiced the science of Arabic grammar.

﴿And live with them honorably﴾ This is a command to good companionship. The apparent address is to husbands, because the obligation of companionship is generally on husbands, and they used to treat women badly. *Bi-l-ma'rūf* (honorably) means fairness in the night spent with them and in maintenance, and gentleness in speech. It is said: "A woman grows fat from her ear," meaning that a woman responds to kind words.

﴿But if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes in it much good﴾ God, exalted is He, educated His servants with this. The meaning is that dislike should not lead you to bad companionship, for a person's dislike of something does not indicate the absence of good in it. As God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ (al-Baqara 2:216). Perhaps what the soul dislikes is more right in religion and better in outcome, and what it loves is the opposite. Since *'asā* (perhaps) is a rigid verb, the response particle *fa-* enters upon it. *'Asā* here is a complete verb, so it does not need a subject and predicate. The pronoun in *fīhi* refers to "a thing," meaning: God places in that disliked thing (much good). It has also been said that it refers to *al-karh* (dislike), the verbal noun understood from the verb. It has been said that it refers to patience (*al-ṣabr*). Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi interpreted "good" as a righteous child, and this is by way of example, not restriction. Consider the eloquence of ﴿then perhaps you dislike a thing﴾, in that it attaches dislike to the word "thing," which includes everything in the manner of a substitute, rather than attaching dislike to the pronoun of "them." It would have been "then perhaps you dislike them." The context of the verse indicates that the meaning is encouragement to keep them and to remain in their company, even if a person dislikes some of their characteristics. This is why what follows is: ﴿And if you wish to replace a wife with another wife﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:20). It has been said that the meaning of the verse is: "And Allah makes in your separation from them much good for you and for them," like His saying: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:130). This was said by al-Asamm. But this view is far from the context of the verse, and what precedes and follows it indicates otherwise. Rarely will you see two companions each of whom is pleased with all of the other's character. It is said: "No two people live together except that one of them overlooks something of the other." In Sahih Muslim: "A believing man should not hate a believing woman; if he dislikes one of her characteristics, he will be pleased with another." They recited, on this meaning:

"Whoever does not close his eye on his friend and on some of what is in him dies while still blaming."

"Whoever searches diligently for every slip finds it, and no companion is safe from time."

﴿And if you desire to exchange a wife for another wife, and you have given one of them a qintar, then do not take back anything from it﴾ [4:20]. When He permitted [the husband] to harm them [by taking back their gifts] if they committed a flagrant indecency, so that he would take back part of what he had given her, He based the prohibition of that on a situation other than the situation of flagrant indecency, and He placed the intention (al-irada) in the position of the act. It is as if He said: "And if you have exchanged [a wife for another]." Or He omitted a conjoined element, meaning: "and you have exchanged." The apparent meaning of His words "and you have given" (wa-ataytum) is that the wāw is for the circumstantial clause (lil-hal), meaning "and you have already given." It has also been said that it is conjoined to the verb of the condition (fi'l al-shart), but this is not the apparent meaning. Istibdal (exchange) is putting one thing in the place of another. The meaning is that if the separation comes from your choice, then do not take back anything from what you have given them.

He cited His words, ﴿and you have given one of them a qintar﴾ [4:20], as evidence for the permissibility of exaggeration in marriage gifts (mughalah fi al-sadaqat). The woman who addressed ʿUmar when he delivered a sermon and said, "Beware, do not exaggerate in the dowries of your women," also used this as evidence. Others said: it does not indicate exaggeration, because it is an illustration intended as an emphasis on abundance, as if it were said: "and you have given this great amount which no one gives." This is similar to his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever builds a mosque for Allah, even if it is as small as the nest of a sandgrouse (mafhas qata), Allah will build for him a house in Paradise." It is known that a mosque would not be as small as the nest of a sandgrouse; rather, this is an illustration for the extreme of smallness. He also said to someone who had given a dowry of two hundred [dirhams] and came seeking help with his dowry, and was angry: "It is as if you were cutting gold and silver from the side of a volcanic plain (min ʿurd al-harrah)." Muhammad ibn ʿUmar al-Razi said: there is no proof in it for exaggeration, because His words "and you have given" do not indicate the permissibility of giving a qintar, and making something a condition for another thing does not require that the condition itself be permissible to occur, as in His saying: "Whoever is killed, his family has a choice between two [options]" (man qutila lahu qatil fa-ahlihi bayn khiyaratayn). End of quote.

Since His words, "if you desire to exchange a wife for a wife," are addressed to a group, the object of the exchange is wives in place of wives. He was content with the singular instead of the plural because the plural of those being exchanged shows it, and because the wording "requiring the addressees to [take] one wife in place of one wife" would not cause confusion. And since the meaning of plurality is intended, the pronoun in His words "one of them" (iḥdāhunna) returns in the plural. The one He forbade us to take anything from is the wife who is being replaced, not the wife being taken as a replacement, since the former is the one to whom he gave the property, not the one he intends to bring into being. This is shown by His words: ﴿and how could you take it when you have already been intimate with one another﴾ [4:21]. He said "and you have given one of them a qintar" to show that His words "and you have given" mean that each one of you gave one of them, i.e. one of the wives, a qintar. He did not say "and you have given them a qintar" so that it would not be supposed that all the addressees had given the wives a qintar. The intended meaning is: each one gave his wife a qintar. So the word iḥdāhunna indicates that the pronoun in "you have given" means each and every one, just as the expression ﴿if you desire to exchange a wife for a wife﴾ [4:20] indicates that the intended meaning is exchanging wives for wives. Thus the singular here is intended to mean the plural, by the indication of "if you desire"; and by His words "and you have given" each one is meant, by the indication of iḥdāhunna, which is singular in that sense. This is one of the subtleties of eloquence (min latif al-balaghah), and this meaning cannot be expressed more concisely or more eloquently than this.

The discussion of qintar was given earlier at the beginning of Surat Al ʿImran, and the pronoun in minhu refers back to qintar. Ibn Muhaysin read the hamza of iḥdāhunna as connected (bi-wasl alif iḥdāhunna), just as it was read: ﴿Indeed it is one of the greatest [calamities]﴾ [74:35] with the alif connected. The alif was dropped as a matter of [linguistic] precision, as the poet said:

"And you hear from beneath the dust the clatter of it" (wa-tasmaʿu min taḥti al-ʿajaji lahā azmalā)

And he said:

"If I do not fight, then dress me in a veil (burqaʿ)."

The apparent meaning of His words, "do not take anything from it," is the prohibition of taking any part of what he gave her if the exchange of her place is by his own will. They said: this is restricted by His words, ﴿but if they willingly give you some of it, then consume it﴾ [4:4]. They said: consensus (ijma') has been reached on this. The khulʿ (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation) is treated in the same way, because she willingly gives the husband what she ransomed herself with. Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani said: do not take anything from the woman seeking khulʿ, because of His words: ﴿do not take anything from it﴾ [4:20]. He said the verse of al-Baqarah is abrogated (naskh) by this. The discussion of that was given in Surat al-Baqarah. The apparent meaning of His words, "and you have given one of them a qintar," together with the prohibition that follows it, indicates the generality of what he gave her, whether it was a dowry or something else.

[And] ﴿you have been intimate with one another﴾ [4:21]: this does not require that what he gave her was only a dowry. Rather the meaning is that there has come to be between them such mixing and union that it is not fitting for him to take back anything of what he gave her, whether it was a dowry or something else. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: it is not impossible that the beginning of the address is general in all that the term includes, while the element conjoined to it has a particular ruling; this does not necessitate the particularity of the first wording. The end of his statement. This is an acknowledgment from him that what is meant by His words ﴿how could you take it﴾ [4:21] is the dowry. We have shown that this does not necessarily follow.

Abu Bakr al-Razi also said: the verse indicates that whoever advances his wife her maintenance for a period, and she dies before the period ends, he does not reclaim anything from her inheritance of what he gave her, because of the generality of the wording. It is possible that he wishes to marry another after her death, substituting her for the first. The apparent meaning of the command covers this case. End of quote. This is not apparent, because istibdal requires the existence of both the replacement and that which is replaced. If the latter has ceased to exist, this is not valid, because the one who exchanges leaves this one and takes another in its place; so if it is non-existent, how can he leave it and take another in its stead?

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the prohibition of taking anything of what he gave her if he intends the exchange, and the end of the verse indicates through its reason, "intimacy," the generality of the ruling, both in the case of exchange and otherwise. The meaning of the conditional (mafhum al-shart) is not intended. It was singled out for mention because it is a situation in which one might suppose that, because of the exchange and the presence of another in her place, he may take her dowry and give it to the second wife, who is preferable to him than the one he divorces (tufariqa). So Allah made clear that he does not take anything from her. And if the one he exchanged is not permitted for him to take anything of what he gave her, despite the loss of his right to her body, then it is more fitting that it is not permitted for him to do so while his right and his enjoyment of her body remain, and while she is more fully available to him for benefit than the other.

Abu al-Sammal and Abu Jaʿfar read shayyan with a fatha on the yāʾ and tanwin, dropping the hamza and placing its vowel on the yāʾ.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 20:

﴿Will you take it back by slander and a manifest sin?﴾ The root meaning of buhtan (slander, false accusation) is a lie that a person confronts his companion with by way of defiant denial, so that the one falsely accused is stunned (yubhat al-maktub alayhi). That is, he is left bewildered. Then every falsehood at whose baselessness one is bewildered was called buhtan. This interrogation is by way of denunciation, meaning: Do you do this while its ugliness is evident? It was called buhtan because, when they wanted to divorce a woman, they would accuse her of an immoral act so that she would fear and ransom her dowry from him. The verse thus follows the common situation. It has also been said: it was called buhtan because he had already fixed the dowry for her, and his seeking its return indicates that he is saying, "I did not fix it," and this is buhtan. Buhtanan and ithman are in the accusative as two verbal nouns (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the agent, the sense being: "bewildering [others] and sinning." Or they relate to the object, the sense being: "causing bewilderment, because of its heinousness and the ugliness of the rumour." Or they are two objects of purpose (maf'ulayn min ajlihima), meaning: "Will you take it for your slander and your sin?" Al-Zamakhshari said this, and said: "Even if it is not an object of purpose, as in your saying: he sat back from fighting out of cowardice."

This is a rhetorical question of denunciation as well. He first denounced the taking, and alerted to the impossibility of taking it by its being slander and sin. Second, he denounced the state of taking, and that it is not something that can be combined with the state of intimacy (al-ifda'), because al-ifda', which is direct contact and closeness with nothing closer beyond it, requires that nothing of what the husband gave be taken along with it. Then he joined to al-ifda' the women's taking of the solemn covenant (al-mithaq al-ghalith) from the husbands. Al-ifda' is intercourse (al-jima'), as said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi. Umar, Ali, a group of the Companions, Abu al-Kalbi, and al-Farra' said: it is seclusion (al-khalwa). The covenant is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then either retain them in kindness or release them with good treatment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Ibn Sirin, al-Suddi, and Qatadah. Qatadah said: It used to be said to the one contracting marriage in early Islam: "Upon you, you shall either retain them with kindness, or release them with good treatment." Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: the covenant is the word of Allah by which you made their private parts lawful to you, and it is the man's saying: "I have married (nakahtu) and I have acquired marriage (malaktu al-nikah)," and the like. 'Ikrimah said: it is his saying: ("Be good to women, for they are captives with you; you have taken them under the trust of Allah, and made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah"). Some said: the covenant is the child, since by it the causes of inviolability are reinforced and the motives of affection grow. It was also said: what was stipulated in the contract, that upon each of the two is the fear of Allah, goodness of companionship and association in kindness, and what goes in that direction. Al-Zamakhshari said: the solemn covenant is the right of companionship and lying together, as if it were said: "and they took from you a solemn covenant through the ifda' of some of you to others." He described it as solemn for its strength and greatness; they have said: "companionship for twenty days is kinship; how then with what passes between the spouses of union and mingling?" End of his words.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 22:

﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed.﴾ The reason for the revelation of this verse was mentioned earlier, in His words: ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾ [al-Nisa: 19]. The scholars have related stories, the gist of which is that some of the Arabs used to marry their father's wife, and they named a group who married their fathers' wives after their fathers' deaths. So God revealed the prohibition of that. The disagreement about *nikah* (marriage) was mentioned earlier: is it literally *wat'* (sexual intercourse), or *'aqd* (the marriage contract), or a term shared between both? They said: *nikah* does not come in the sense of the contract except in ﴿so marry them with the permission of their guardians﴾ [al-Nisa: 25]. This restriction is refuted by His words: ﴿When you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49].

There is a difference of opinion about the *ma* (what) in His words *ma nakaha* (what your fathers married). The first thing that comes to mind is that it is its object (*maf'ul*), and that it refers to the category, as in His words: ﴿so marry what is good for you of women﴾ [al-Nisa: 3]. That is, "Do not marry the kind of women whom your fathers married." It is established in the science of Arabic grammar that *ma* may refer to categories of rational beings. This is according to the view of those who forbid its use for individual rational beings. As for those who permit it, it becomes clear that *ma* in the verse is to be understood in this way, and it is claimed that this is the view of Sibawayh. On this understanding of *ma* as referring to the wives of fathers, the Companions received the verse and took it as evidence for the prohibition of sons marrying their fathers' wives. Ibn Abbas said: "The people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) used to forbid everything that is forbidden except the father's wife and the combining of two sisters, so this verse was revealed about that." Ibn Abbas also said: "Every woman whom your father married, whether he consummated the marriage with her or not, is forbidden to you."

Others said: *ma* is a masdar-forming particle (*masdariyya*), and the meaning is: "Do not marry the marriage of your fathers," that is, like the corrupt or unlawful marriage of your fathers which they practised in the Jahiliyyah, such as *shighar* (an exchange of wives without dower) and other things, just as you say, "I struck the strike of the prince," meaning "like the strike of the prince." That this was unlawful or corrupt is shown by His words: ﴿Indeed, it was an indecency﴾. Muhammad ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) chose this view and said: "If its meaning were 'Do not marry the women whom your fathers married,' then the position of *ma* would have to be *min* (of/from)." Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Suddi and Ata' understood *nikah* here as *wat'* (intercourse), because they used to inherit the wives of their fathers. Ibn Zayd, together with a group, said: what is meant is the valid contract, not what they did of fornication. End of quotation.

The exception in His words *illa ma qad salaf* (except what has already passed) is *munqati'* (disjunct, not connected to what precedes), since the present/future does not combine with the past, and the meaning is this: when He forbade them to marry what their fathers had married, this indicated that whoever engages in that after the prohibition is sinful. A doubt arose concerning what had happened from them before the prohibition, and what its ruling was. So it was said: ﴿except what has already passed﴾, that is, "but what has already passed," so no prohibition applied to it, and therefore there is no sin in it. Since Ibn Zayd understood *nikah* as the valid contract, he understood His words *illa ma qad salaf* as referring to what some of them had engaged in of fornication, and he said: "except what has already passed from the fathers in the Jahiliyyah of fornication with women; for that, their marriage to them is permitted to you in Islam, for it was an indecency and hatred." It is as if it were said: "Do not contract marriage with those whom your fathers contracted marriage with, except what has passed of their fornication, for it is permissible for you to marry them." On this reading the exception is *munqati'*.

It is also reported from Ibn Zayd that the meaning of the verse is the prohibition of a man having intercourse with a woman whom his father had intercourse with, except what has passed of the father's fornication with the woman in the Jahiliyyah, for then it is permitted for the son to marry her. On this reading ﴿except what has already passed﴾ is an exception that is *muttasil* (connected), since (what has already passed) falls under His words *ma nakaha* (what they married), as the intended meaning is: "what your fathers had intercourse with." And *ma wata'a* (what had intercourse with) includes the woman who was had intercourse with through fornication and otherwise. The implied meaning is: "What your fathers had intercourse with, except those whose intercourse with them was by fornication, from your fathers, so marry them." Whoever takes *ma* in His words *ma nakaha* as a masdar-forming particle, as we have explained, said: the meaning is "except what has already passed from you of those corrupt contracts, for it is permitted for you to continue in it in Islam, if it is among what Islam has established."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how did He make an exception of *ma qad salaf* from *ma nakaha abaukum*? I say: just as He made an exception of (*ghayra anna suyufahum*) from His words (*wa la 'ayba fihim*) [there is no fault in them, except that their swords...]." He means: "If it is possible for you to marry what has already passed, then marry it, but nothing else is lawful for you; and that is not possible." The purpose is to exaggerate its prohibition and to block the path to its permissibility, just as something is suspended in time without limit, as in the expressions "until the crow turns white" and "until the camel enters the eye of the needle." End of his words.

Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is: "You will be punished for it, except what has already passed, for God has removed that from you."

It was also said that there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in the verse, and its arrangement is: "Do not marry what your fathers married of women; indeed it was an indecency and hatred and an evil way, except what has already passed." This is ignorance of the science of grammar and the science of meanings (*ma'ani*). As for grammar, what falls within the scope of *inna* (indeed) may not precede it, and likewise the exception may not precede the sentence of which it is a complement, whether connected or disconnected, although there is a difference of opinion on this, and it should not be heeded. As for meaning, He informed that it is an indecency and hatred in the past time, so it is not valid for the past to be made an exception from it, for the meaning would become: "it is an indecency in the past time, except what happened from it in the past time, which is not an indecency." This is a meaning that cannot occur in the Qur'an or in Arabic speech, because it is incoherent. What appears from the verse is that every woman whom a man's father married, by contract or by ownership (of a slave-woman), is unlawful for him to marry, by contract or by ownership, because *nikah* applies to a woman who has been had intercourse with, by contract or by ownership, since there is only *nikah* or *sifah* (fornication). *Sifah* is fornication, and *nikah* is what is permitted. He indicated the prohibition of that by His words:

* *

﴿Indeed, it was an indecency and hatred and an evil way﴾. That is: the marriage of sons to their fathers' wives is an indecency, meaning extremely ugly. *Maqt* (hatred): God abhors its doer, as Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said; or the Arabs abhor it, meaning it is hated and despised among them. Some men of honour in the Jahiliyyah used to abhor it. Abu Ubaydah and others said: the Arabs used to call a child born from the husband of the mother *al-maqti* (the hated one), in reference to *maqt*. Whoever interpreted *illa ma qad salaf* as fornication made the pronoun in *innahu* (indeed it) refer to it, meaning: what has already passed of the fathers' fornication was an indecency. And *kana* (was) is often used in the sense of "has not ceased," so the meaning is: that has not ceased to be an indecency, but it is characterised by indecency in the past, present and future, so indecency is an inseparable attribute of it.

Al-Mubarrad said: *hiya* (it) is redundant (*za'ida*). He was answered by the existence of a predicate, since a redundant element has no predicate. His statement should be understood as meaning that *kana* is not intended to restrict the predicate to the past time only, so he regarded it as redundant from this perspective.

﴿And an evil way﴾: this is an exaggeration in censure, just as *bi'sa* (how evil) is used for exaggeration. If there is a pronoun in it that refers back to what the pronoun of *innahu* refers to, then it is not governed by the rules of *bi'sa*. If the pronoun in it is unspecified, as the people of Basra claim, then its explanation is *sabilan* (a way), and the subject of the censure in that case is omitted; the implied meaning is: "and evil is the way (sabil) of this marriage," just as it came: "evil is the drink," meaning: that water which is like molten metal. And He exaggerated in censuring this way, since it is a way that leads to the punishment of God.

Al-Bara' ibn Azib said: "I met my maternal uncle, and he had the banner with him. I said: 'Where are you going?' He said: 'The Messenger of God sent me to a man who married his father's wife after him, to strike off his neck.'"

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 23 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters﴾ Since the prohibition of marrying the wife of one's father was mentioned for a son, while she is not his mother, the prohibition of his own mother is more deserving of prohibition. This is not from the mujmal (the ambiguous), but rather this is one of those cases where the mudaf (the omitted noun, "marriage to") has been dropped because the meaning indicates it. For when it is said: "Wine is forbidden to you," what is understood from it is its drinking. And "Carrion is forbidden to you" means its eating. This is of the same kind, so the meaning is: marriage to your mothers. Also, what indicates it has already been mentioned, which is His saying: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾ [an-Nisa: 22].

Muhammad ibn Umar al-Razi said: "In it, in my view, there are investigations from several aspects. The first: the passive form of the verb does not explicitly state that the one who prohibits is Allah. The second: that "hurrimat" (was forbidden) does not indicate permanence, since it is possible to divide it into the permanent and the temporary. The third: that "alaykum" (to you) is a direct address, so it is restricted to those present. The fourth: that "hurrimat" is a past tense, so it does not encompass the present and the future. The fifth: that it implies that He prohibits for everyone all of their mothers. The sixth: that "hurrimat" by its apparent form suggests that permissibility preceded, for if it were forbidden, it would not have been said, 'was forbidden.' By these aspects it is established that the apparent meaning of the verse alone is not sufficient to establish the required ruling," and the end of his summarized words.

These investigations which he mentioned are not specific to this place, and there is no benefit in them. Among the reasons for omitting the agent is knowledge of it, and it is known that the one who prohibits is Allah, the Exalted. Do you not see the end of the verse, which is His saying: ﴿And that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, and He said afterward: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [an-Nisa: 24], according to the reading of the one who made it active. And whenever a prohibition comes from Allah, nothing is understood from it except permanence. If it has a state of permission, He has explicitly stated it, as in His saying: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173]. As for the claim that it is a past-tense form and so it restricts it, the verbs from which legal rulings are derived, even if they are in the past form, do not restrict it. They are like the statement "I swear that I will strike Zayd," which is not meant to indicate that an oath occurred in a past time. If the ruling was established before the verb was revealed, its benefit is confirming that established ruling; and if it was not established, its benefit is the establishing and renewing of that ruling. As for the claim that the apparent meaning is that He prohibits for everyone all of their mothers, it is not apparent, nor is it understood from the wording, because ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ is a general term, which is opposed by a general term, and the implication of generality is that each one is set against each one individually. As for taking it in the manner of collectivity, that is not so, because that is not the implication of a general term. Rather, what is understood is: it is forbidden to each one of you individually, each one's own mother. The meaning is: this one's mother is forbidden to him, and that one's mother is forbidden to him. The mother who is forbidden in the Sharia is every woman to whom your lineage traces by birth, whether through your father or through your mother. The word "umm" (mother) is literally applied to the one who gave birth to you herself. As for the application of the word "umm" to the grandmother: if it is by commonality (tawatu') or by homonymy (ishtirak), and it is permissible to apply it to both meanings, it is literal and the text includes her. If it is by metaphor, and it is permissible to apply it to both literal and metaphorical meanings, it is likewise. Otherwise, the prohibition of grandmothers is derived from consensus (ijma') or from another text.

The prohibition of mothers and daughters has been from the time of Adam, peace be upon him, until our present time. They mentioned that the reason for this prohibition is that intercourse is humiliation and degradation, so mothers are protected from it, since the mother's kindness to the child is the greatest form of kindness.

The forbidden daughter is every female whose lineage traces to you by birth, by one degree or several, whether through females or males. As for whether the daughter's daughter is called a daughter literally or metaphorically, the discussion of it is like the discussion of the grandmother. Among the Arabs there was one who married his daughter, namely Hajib ibn Zurara, who was a Magian. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl mentioned this in the Book of Mathalib (Shameful Deeds).

(And your sisters) The forbidden sister is every one who shares with you either a father (sulb) or a mother (batn).

* *

﴿And your paternal aunts and your maternal aunts﴾ The 'amma (paternal aunt) is the father's sister, and the khala (maternal aunt) is the mother's sister. He specified the prohibition of aunts and maternal aunts apart from their children. The father's aunt, the father's maternal aunt, the mother's aunt, the mother's maternal aunt, and the aunt's aunt are all forbidden. And the mother of the maternal aunt's... If the paternal aunt is a sister of the father through the mother, or through father and mother, then the maternal aunt of that aunt is not lawful, because she is the grandmother's sister. If the paternal aunt is only a sister of the father through the father alone, then her maternal aunt is a stranger to the sons of her brother, lawful to men, and it is permissible to combine her with women. As for the paternal aunt of the maternal aunt: if the maternal aunt is a sister of the mother through the father, then the paternal aunt of the maternal aunt is not lawful, because she is a sister of the grandfather. If the maternal aunt is only a sister of the mother through the mother alone, then her paternal aunt is a stranger to the sons of her sister.

* *

﴿And the daughters of the brother and the daughters of the sister﴾ Their daughters are forbidden, even if they descend further. The brother and the sister were stated in the singular and did not come in the plural, because the plural was attached to them, so the singular form is lighter, and by it is intended the genus which includes the single meaning and others. These are seven from lineage whose prohibition is permanent. As for those who became forbidden due to a later cause, the Qur'an mentions them as seven, and they are in His, the Exalted's, saying:

* *

﴿And your mothers who have nursed you, and your sisters through nursing﴾ He named the nursing women "mothers" for the sake of the prohibition, just as He named the wives of the Messenger of Allah "mothers of the believers." Since He named the nursing woman a mother, and the nursing woman together with the nursed child a sister, by this He drew attention to placing nursing in the position of lineage. This is because seven were prohibited by reason of lineage: two who are related by birth, namely the mother and the daughter; and five by way of siblinghood, namely the sister, the paternal aunt, the maternal aunt, the brother's daughter, and the sister's daughter. When He mentioned nursing, He mentioned from each of these two categories one example as an alert to the rest: from the category of kinship of children He mentioned mothers, and from the category of kinship of siblinghood He mentioned sisters, and by these two examples He drew attention to the fact that the situation in the matter of nursing is like the situation in the matter of lineage. Then He emphasized this by the clear saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "What is prohibited by lineage is prohibited by nursing," so the clear hadith corresponded to what the verse indicated. Thus the husband of the nursing woman is his father, her parents are his grandparents, and her sister is his paternal aunt. Every child born to her from someone other than the nursing woman, before the nursing or after it, they are his brothers and sisters through his father; the mother of the nursing woman is his grandmother, and her sister is his maternal aunt. Every child born to her from this husband, they are his brothers and sisters through his father and his mother. As for her child from someone else, they are his brothers and sisters through his mother.

They said: The prohibition by nursing is like the prohibition by lineage, except in two issues. The first: it is not permissible for a man to marry the sister of his son by lineage, but it is permissible for him to marry the sister of his son by nursing, because the reason in lineage is his having intercourse with her mother, and this reason does not exist in nursing. The second: it is not permissible to marry the mother of his brother by lineage, but it is permissible in nursing, because the impediment in lineage is the father's intercourse with her, and this reason does not exist in nursing. The apparent meaning of the words is the unrestricted application of nursing. The verse did not address the age of the nursling, nor the number of sucklings, nor the milk of the stallion (the father), nor a man's nursing with his own milk for a child, nor hiring him out for it, nor giving it to him as a drink in a way that reaches the stomach. In all of this there is a known disagreement mentioned in the books of jurisprudence. The majority read: ﴿allati arda'nakum﴾. Al-A'mash read "allay" with a ya'. Ibn Hurmuz read "allati". Abu Haywa read "min al-ridha'a" with a kasra on the ra'.

﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾ The majority hold that it is general. So whether he contracted marriage with her and did not consummate it, or consummated it, it applies. It is narrated from Ali, Mujahid and others that if he divorced her before consummation, he may marry her mother, and that in this matter she is in the position of the stepdaughter.

* *

﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is a condition for her prohibition that she be in his guardianship (hijr). This is the view of Ali, and Dawud and the people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Zahir) adopted it. So if she is not in his guardianship and he separated from her mother after consummation, it is permissible for him to marry her. They said: Allah prohibited the stepdaughter on two conditions: the first: that she be in the husband's guardianship; the second: consummation with the mother. If either condition is absent, the prohibition does not occur. They argued with his saying: ("If my stepdaughter were not in my guardianship, she would not be lawful to me; she is the daughter of my brother through nursing"), so he stipulated guardianship. Al-Tahawi and others said: Their attribution to guardianships is taken to mean the most common case of stepdaughters, though they are prohibited even if they are not in the guardianship. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the benefit of His saying "in your guardianships"? I say: its benefit is the explanation of the prohibition, and that they are as if they were in your embrace, or are in a state of being about to be in your embrace. And in the ruling of turning in your guardianships, when you have consummated with their mothers and the ruling of marriage is established by your consummation, their children take the place of your children, as if you, in contracting marriage to their daughters, were contracting marriage to your daughters. End of quote. There is some abridgement in it.

﴿From your women with whom you have consummated [the marriage]﴾ The apparent meaning of this is that it is connected only to the words "and your stepdaughters." "Allati" is an attribute of "nisa'ikum" governed by "min," and it is not permissible for "allati" to be an attribute of "nisa'ikum" in His saying "and the mothers of your women," since the governing element of the two modified nouns differs: this one is governed by "min," and that one is governed by the genitive construction (idafa). It is also not permissible for "min nisa'ikum" to be connected to an omitted element that encompasses the mothers of your women and your stepdaughters, because the meaning of the particle of jarr differs at that point: in relation to His saying "and the mothers of your women," "min nisa'ikum" is for clarifying the women and distinguishing those consummated with from those not consummated with. And in relation to His saying "and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, from your women with whom you have consummated," "min nisa'ikum" is for indicating the starting point, as you say: "This is my son from so-and-so." Al-Zamakhshari said: Except that I connect it to "the women" and "the stepdaughters," and make "min" denote connection, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The hypocrite men and hypocrite women are of one another﴾ [at-Tawbah: 67], and the verse of poetry:

*"Indeed, I am not of you, and you are not of me; I am not of Dadd, nor is Dadd of me."*

And the mothers of women are connected to women, because they are their mothers, just as the stepdaughters are connected to their mothers, because they are their daughters. End of quote. We do not know of anyone who held that one of the meanings of "min" is connection. As for what he compared it to from the verse, the poetry and the hadith, these are interpreted figuratively. And if we make "min nisa'ikum" connected to "the women" and "the stepdaughters" as al-Zamakhshari claimed, then it must be suitable for each of "the women" and "the stepdaughters." As for its construction with "stepdaughters," it is in the utmost eloquence and beauty, and that is the arrangement of the verse. As for its construction with His saying "and the mothers of your women," it would become: "and the mothers of your women from your women with whom you have consummated," and this is a construction that cannot occur in the Qur'an or in eloquent speech, since conveying this meaning does not require the phrase "from your women." And consummation here is a metaphor for intercourse, as they say: "he built upon her," and "he drew the veil over her."

The particle *bi* here expresses transitivity (*ta'diyah*), and the meaning is: "those whom you have entered under the veil (*al-sitr*)." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus and Ibn Dinar. So if he divorced her after consummation (*al-binā'*) but before intercourse (*al-jimā'*), it is permissible for him to marry her daughter.

'Ata', Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i and al-Layth said: if he touches her with desire (*bi-shahwah*), her mother and her daughter become forbidden to him, and she becomes forbidden to his father and his son. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i.

They differed concerning looking at her with desire. Ibn Abi Layla said: looking does not make her forbidden until he touches her, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Malik said: looking at her hair or at any of her beauty with pleasure makes her forbidden. The Kufans said: looking at her private part (*farj*) with desire makes her forbidden. Al-Thawri said: it makes her forbidden if he deliberately looked at her private part, and he did not mention desire. 'Ata' and Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman said: if a man looks at a woman's private part, he may not marry her mother or her daughter, and they extended this ruling to female slaves (*al-imā'*).

al-Hasan said: if a man owns a slave-girl and caresses her with desire, or uncovers her, or kisses her, she is never lawful to his son. Masruq ordered that his slave-girl be sold after his death, and said: "As for me, I did not have from her anything except what would make her forbidden to my son, namely touching and looking." 'Umar stripped a slave-girl whom he had been alone with, and a son of his asked to be given her; so he said: "She is not lawful to you."

* *

﴿And if you have not gone in to them, there is no blame upon you﴾, that is, in marrying the stepdaughters (*al-rabā'ib*). The permissibility of marrying stepdaughters is not conditional upon the absence of any kind of entering. Rather, a words must be understood as implied, and its estimate is: "And if you have not gone in to them and you have separated from them by divorce from you, or by death from them."

* *

﴿And the wives of your sons who are from your loins﴾. The scholars agreed upon the prohibition of what fathers have contracted (*'aqada*) for sons and what sons have contracted for fathers, whether or not intercourse (*wat'*) took place with the contract. The word *ḥalīlah* is a term specific to a wife, to the exclusion of ownership by the right hand (slave-women), and for this reason it is used regarding the wives of their adopted sons. Since the ruling of prohibition was linked to the designation (*al-tasmiyah*) and not to intercourse, it implies the prohibition of them by the contract, without requiring intercourse as a condition. The phrase ﴿who are from your loins﴾ qualifies "your sons," removing the metaphorical sense (*al-majāz*) which the word "your sons" may bear, since they used to apply the term to whomever the Arabs had adopted from others and made a son by adoption, just as they used to say "Zayd ibn Muhammad," until there was revealed: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any man among you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 40], and as the wife of Abu Hudhayfah said concerning Salim: "We used to regard him as a son."
