The Messenger of God (ﷺ) married Zaynab bint Jahsh al-Asadiyyah, who was the daughter of his paternal aunt Umayma bint 'Abd al-Muttalib, after Zayd ibn Harithah divorced her.

They agreed that the wife of a son by nursing (*min al-riḍā'*) is, in regard to prohibition, like the wife of a son by blood (*min al-ṣulb*), relying on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is prohibited by blood relationship is prohibited by nursing." The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and the wives of your sons﴾ is that this applies specifically to wives, as we have mentioned. They agreed that the mere act of purchasing a slave-girl does not make her forbidden to his father or his son. So if he touched her or kissed her, she becomes forbidden to his father and his son, and there is no disagreement about the prohibition of that. They differed regarding mere looking with desire.

* *

﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾. The phrase "that you combine" is in a position of nominative case (*raf'*), by being coordinated (*'atf*) with a nominative word. The meaning is: "And [prohibited to you is] that you combine two sisters in marriage," because the context of the verse is only about marriage, although combining two sisters is more general than being in two marriages or by ownership of the right hand. As for when it is by way of marriage, the community (*al-ummah*) agreed on the prohibition of contracting it, whether the two contracts occurred simultaneously or successively.

They differed regarding marrying a woman during the waiting period (*'iddah*) of her sister. It is narrated from Zayd, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ubaydah, 'Ata', Ibn Sirin, Mujahid and others among the Successors (*al-tābi'īn*) that this is not permissible. Some of them stated it absolutely as a waiting period, and some said: if it is from three [pronouncements], and this is the view of Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar, al-Thawri, and al-Hasan ibn Salih. It is narrated from 'Urwah, al-Qasim and Khilas that it is permissible for him if it is from an irrevocable divorce (*ṭalāq bā'in*), and this is the view of Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Layth and al-Shafi'i. It was reported differently from Sa'id, al-Hasan and 'Ata'. The permissibility is the apparent meaning of the verse, if the divorce was not revocable (*raj'iyyan*).

As for combining the two by ownership of the right hand, there is no disagreement about their purchase and their entry into his ownership. As for combining them in sexual intercourse (*al-wat'*), 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Zubayr, Ibn 'Umar, 'Ammar and Zayd went to the view that this is not permissible. Is this by way of disapproval (*karāhah*) or prohibition (*taḥrīm*)? Ibn al-Mundhir reported from the majority of the scholars that it is disapproval, and he reported from Ishaq that it is prohibition.

The one who sought victory in God (*al-Mustansir bi-Llah*), Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Amir Abi Zakariyya ibn Abi Muhammad ibn Abi Hafs, the ruler of Ifriqiya, had asked one of our shaykhs whom we met in Tunis, the devout shaykh who had withdrawn from the world, Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn 'Ali ibn Khalis al-Ishbili: "Do you not see the prohibition of combining two sisters by ownership of the right hand in intercourse?" He answered him with a prohibition, although another had given him a fatwa of permissibility. Our shaykh based the prohibition on the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾. It is narrated from 'Uthman and Ibn 'Abbas that this is permitted. And if the combining of them is also included by having intercourse with them by way of marriage and ownership of the right hand, then he has married one and owns her sister. The commentators (*al-mufassirūn*) have greatly expanded upon the legal derivations (*al-furū'*) here, and the place for that is the books of jurisprudence (*kutub al-fiqh*).

﴿Except what has already passed﴾. This is a disconnected exception (*istithnā' munqati'*) that relates to the last item, which is: "that you combine two sisters." The meaning is: "But what has passed of that and occurred, the Islamic law (*sharī'at al-Islām*) has removed its ruling, for God forgives it, and Islam cuts it off entirely." The absence of accountability for it is indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The meaning of His saying ﴿except what has already passed﴾ may also be that the contract with two sisters is not annulled by it; rather, he is given the choice between whichever of the two he wishes, so he divorces one and keeps the other, as came in the hadith of Fayruz al-Daylami: that he embraced Islam while he had two sisters, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "Divorce one of them and keep the other." The apparent meaning of the hadith of Fayruz is the giving of choice without regard to the time of the contract, and this is the view of Malik, Muhammad and al-Layth. Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf and al-Thawri went to the view that he chooses whichever of them was married first, and if both were in one contract, he is separated from both of them. 'Ata' and al-Suddi said: this exception indicates that what preceded the revelation of the prohibition was permissible. Ya'qub (peace be upon him) combined the mother of Yusuf and her sister. But this is weak, because the chain of transmission (*isnād*) of the story of Ya'qub regarding that is unlikely to be sound, and because this prohibition is connected to our law alone, and there does not appear from it any mention of a pardon for what others did.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 24 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the married women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾. Al-Ihsan (chastity, or being a muhsan/muhsanah): it means marriage, or freedom, or Islam, or chastity (iffah). This word is used in the Qur'an in these meanings, and each occurrence is interpreted according to what suits it among them. Abu Sa'id narrated that the verse was revealed on account of the fact that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent an army to Awtas, and they encountered an enemy and took captives, and those women had husbands among the polytheists, so the Muslims felt sinful about having intercourse with them, and so this was revealed." So al-muhsanat here means the married women. The exception is the captives (al-sabaya); so if a woman whose husband is still alive falls to someone's share, she is lawful to him. This was the view of Abu Sa'id, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Qilabah, Makhul, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Zayd, and this is as al-Farazdaq said:

Wa-dhat halilin ankahat-ha rima-hana halalun li-man yabni biha lam tutallaq
(And a woman with a husband whom our spears have made wed, she is lawful for whoever builds with her, she has not been divorced.)

It was also said: al-muhsanat are the married women, and the exception is the slave women; so married women are forbidden except those owned by way of purchase, gift, charity, or inheritance. Indeed, her owner has more right to her womb than the husband, and to selling her, gifting her, giving her in charity, and her inheritance is a divorce for her. This was the view of al-A'mash, Abu Jabir, Ibn 'Abbas as well, Sa'id, and al-Hasan. 'Amr ibn 'Abbas also held, as did Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Ubaydah, Tawus, Ibn Jubayr, and 'Ata': that al-muhsanat are the chaste women, and by it is meant that all women are forbidden, and all the sacred laws require that. The meaning of the exception is: except those your right hands possess, either by marriage or by ownership, so all of this falls under the possession of the right hand. With this interpretation the meaning is the prohibition of fornication (zina). It was narrated from 'Umar regarding al-muhsanat that they are the free women; according to this, His saying ﴿except those your right hands possess﴾ means: by marriage, if the exception is connected (muttasil); and if by it are meant the slave women, then it is disconnected (munqati').

It was said: what the word ihsan requires, if it is related to the common element among its meanings, is the four (meanings), even though the aspects of ihsan differ; and His saying ﴿except those your right hands possess﴾ is to be understood according to the apparent usage in the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and the custom of the scholars, that what is meant by it is the slave women, and the exception returns to what is valid for it to return to from the aspects of ihsan. And whatever ownership of it is valid as right-hand ownership, it becomes lawful for its owner, whether a captive or a slave woman who is married.

The seven readers did not differ on the vowelling of the sad in His saying ﴿wal-muhsanat min al-nisa'﴾, but they differed about other than this: al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the sad, whether it is definite with the article or indefinite. The rest of them, and 'Alqamah, read with a fatha, as in this agreed reading. Yazid ibn Qutayb read (wal-muhsunat) with a damma on the sad, in imitation of the damma on the mim, as they said (muntun); and they did not consider the intervening letter because it is quiescent, so it is a non-solid barrier (hajiz ghayr hasin). Makki said: the benefit of His saying ﴿min al-nisa'﴾ is that muhsanat applies to persons, so that His saying ﴿and those who accuse muhsanat﴾ [al-Nur: 4], if by it were meant women specifically, then whoever accused a man would not be punished with the hadd by the explicit text of the Qur'an, and they agreed that his hadd is by this explicit text.

﴿The Book of Allah upon you﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb, and it is a verb emphasizing the content of the preceding sentence, His saying ﴿Forbidden to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. As if it were said: Allah has prescribed upon you the prohibition of that as a Book. And whoever makes this dependent on His saying ﴿so marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four﴾ [al-Nisa': 3], as 'Abidah al-Salmani held, has gone far astray; and what al-Kisa'i held, that it is permissible to front the object in grammatical construction before the adverbials and prepositional phrases, citing this verse as evidence, since by his estimation the construction is: upon you the Book of Allah, i.e., adhere to the Book of Allah, does not complete as proof, because it is possible that it be an emphatic verbal noun (masdar) as we have mentioned. This interpretation is confirmed by the reading of Abu Haywah and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' al-Yamani: (Kataba Allahu 'alaykum), making it a past verb governing what follows it, i.e., Allah has prescribed upon you the prohibition of that. It was also narrated from Ibn al-Sumayqa' (p-215) that he read: (Kutubu Allahi 'alaykum) in the plural and nominative, i.e., these are the Books of Allah upon you, meaning His obligations and necessary matters.

* *

﴿And lawful to you is what lies beyond that, that you seek with your wealth, being chaste, not fornicating﴾. When He specified the forbidden ones in marriage, Allah the Exalted informed that He made lawful whatever is other than those mentioned, and the apparent meaning is generality. By this apparent meaning the Kharijites and those who agreed with them among the Shi'a argued for the permissibility of marrying a woman together with her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt, and combining the two. Abu Ja'far al-Tusi, one of the scholars of the Twelver Shi'a, extensively argued this in his tafsir, and the summary of what he said is: that the Qur'an is not opposed by a solitary report (khabar ahad), which is what was narrated that he said: (A woman is not to be married upon her paternal aunt or upon her maternal aunt). Rather, when a hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrives, it is presented to the Qur'an; if it agrees with it, it is accepted, and otherwise it is rejected. What they went to is not correct, because the hadith did not oppose the Qur'an; at most it is a specification of a general ruling, and most of the general rulings that came in the Qur'an necessarily have specifications, and the hadith is not a solitary report but is widely transmitted (mustafid), narrated from a group of the Companions: 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Musa, Abu Sa'id, Abu Hurayrah, and 'A'ishah. So much so that some scholars said it is mutawatir, binding for knowledge and practice. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned the consensus of the Ummah on the prohibition of combining them, and it seems he did not regard the disagreement of those mentioned because of its anomaly; and this specification is not considered abrogation (naskh) of the generality, contrary to some of them. Some have specified this generality by relatives other than those within the prohibited degrees, as if it were said: and lawful to you are your relatives beyond that, so it is lawful for you to marry them; this was the view of 'Ata' and al-Suddi. Al-Suddi specified it by slave women: i.e., and lawful to you is what lies beyond that of slave women. 'Ubaydah and al-Suddi went far in returning this to ﴿two, three, or four﴾ [al-Nisa': 3], meaning: and lawful to you is what is less than five, that you seek with your wealth in the manner of marriage. Al-Suddi also said regarding His saying ﴿what lies beyond that﴾ that it means marriage in what is other than the private part. The apparent meaning is generality, except what the widely transmitted Sunnah has specified (p-216) of the prohibition of combining a woman with her paternal aunt and combining a woman with her maternal aunt. Thus within this generality falls the combining of a woman with her paternal cousin, and of her with her paternal aunt's daughter, and of her with her maternal uncle's daughter, or her maternal aunt's daughter. The prohibition of this has been narrated from Ishaq ibn Talhah, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, and 'Ata'. Al-Hasan ibn Husayn ibn 'Ali married, in one night, the daughter of Muhammad ibn 'Ali and the daughter of 'Umar ibn 'Ali, thus combining two paternal cousins. Malik disliked this, and it is not forbidden in his view.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: I know of no one who invalidated this marriage, while both of them are included in what has been made permissible by marriage, not excluded from it by a Book, a Sunnah, or a consensus. The same goes for combining two daughters of paternal aunts or two daughters of maternal aunts. End. Also included within this generality: if a man commits zina with a woman, it is not forbidden to him to marry her because of his zina with her; likewise his wife is not forbidden to him if he commits zina with her mother or her daughter. If he commits zina with a woman and then wishes to marry her mother or her daughter, neither of them becomes forbidden to him by that, and this is the view of most of the people of knowledge. It was narrated from 'Imran ibn Husayn, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Sufyan, Ahmad, and Ishaq that both of them become forbidden to him, and Abu Hanifah also held this. Also included within this generality: if a man engages in sodomy with a man, his mother and his daughter do not become forbidden to him; this was the view of Malik, Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i and his companions, who said: sexual play with men does not prohibit marriage. Al-Thawri and 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan said: it is like intercourse with a woman, equal in prohibiting the mother and the daughter; so whoever becomes forbidden by this from women becomes forbidden from men. Al-Awza'i said regarding two boys, one of whom plays with the other so that a girl is born to the one who was acted upon: the doer may not marry her.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read: wa-uhilla (passive voice), and it is conjoined to His saying ﴿Forbidden to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. The rest of the Seven read (wa-ahalla) in the active voice, with the agent a pronoun referring to Allah the Exalted, and it is likewise conjoined to His saying: Forbidden. There is no difference in conjunction between the verb being active or passive. Congruence is not a condition, nor is it preferred, even if the implied agent differs due to the substitution of the object for the agent, and the agent to which the active verb is ascribed; how much more so when they are identical, as here, because it is known that the implied agent in (hurrimat) is Allah the Exalted, and it is the implied agent in (ahalla) in the active voice.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is ﴿and lawful to you﴾ conjoined to? I say: to the implied verb that governs ﴿the Book of Allah﴾: i.e., Allah has prescribed upon you the prohibition of that, and made lawful to you what lies beyond that. The reading of al-Yamani confirms it: Kataba Allahu 'alaykum wa-ahalla lakum. Then he said: Whoever reads wa-uhilla lakum in the passive, he has conjoined it to ﴿Forbidden to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. End of his words. Thus he distinguished in conjunction between the two readings, and what he chose from this distinction is not a preferred choice. Because the accusative of ﴿the Book of Allah upon you﴾ is only the accusative of the emphatic verbal noun for the content of the preceding sentence, His saying: Forbidden. So the verb governing it, which is (kataba), is only an emphasis of His saying: Forbidden. Thus this sentence was not brought as an establishing (ta'sis) of the ruling; the establishing is achieved by His saying: Forbidden, and this one was brought as an emphasis of that established sentence. What is of this manner is not suitable to be conjoined to it by a sentence that establishes the ruling; rather it is suitable to be conjoined to an establishing sentence like it, especially as the two sentences are contrasted: one is for prohibition, and the other for permission; so it is fitting that this be conjoined to that. Al-Zamakhshari permitted this in the reading of whoever reads wa-uhilla passively, so likewise it is permitted in the active. The object of (uhilla) is ﴿what lies beyond that﴾.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-waraa' in this verse is what is considered after the prohibited ones are considered, so it is beyond those in this respect. Al-Farra' said: ma wara'a dhalikum, i.e., ma siwa dhalikum (what is other than that). Al-Zajjaj said: ma duna dhalikum, i.e., what is after these things that were forbidden. Some of these explanations come close to others.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 24 (part 2 of 2):

The position of (an tabtaghu) is in the accusative, as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from ﴿what is beyond that﴾, and seeking (al-ibtigha') with wealth includes marriage (nikah) and purchase (shira'). It has been said: seeking with wealth is in the manner of marriage. Al-Zamakhshari said: (an tabtaghu) is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: He has made clear to you what is lawful from what is forbidden; (p-217) with the intention that your seeking be with your wealth which Allah has made a means of sustenance for you, while you are chaste (muhsinin), not fornicators (ghayra musafihin), so that you do not waste your wealth and impoverish yourselves in what is not lawful for you, and thus lose your worldly life and your religion; and there is no corruption greater than that which combines the two losses. End of his words. Look at the bombast of these expressions and their abundance, the loading of the Qur'anic wording with what it does not indicate, the explaining of the clear and evident by means of convoluted language, and the slipping of the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah secretly into the folds of these lengthy expressions, when he explained His words, ﴿and lawful for you﴾, as meaning: He has made clear to you what is lawful. He also made His words, (an tabtaghu), depend on the omission of two annexed terms: i.e., the intention that your seeking be, i.e., the intention of the existence of your seeking with your wealth. The wealth is then explained as dowries and what is spent in marriages, so his explanation implies that He, exalted is He, made clear to you what is lawful for the purpose of your seeking being with dowries, so that His intention is restricted to the lawful which is marriage, rather than fornication. The apparent meaning of the verse is other than what al-Zamakhshari understood, for the apparent meaning is that He, exalted is He, made lawful for us the seeking of what is other than the forbidden ones mentioned previously, with our wealth, in a state of chastity, not in a state of fornication. On this apparent meaning, (an tabtaghu) cannot be parsed as an object of purpose, as al-Zamakhshari held, because a condition of the object of purpose has been lost, namely the unity of the agent in the governing verb and in the object of purpose: the agent in (wa-uhilla) is Allah, exalted is He, while the agent in (an tabtaghu) is the pronoun of the addressees, so they differ. When al-Zamakhshari perceived this, if he did perceive it, he made ﴿an tabtaghu﴾ dependent on an omitted (iradah, "intention") so that the agent in (wa-uhilla) and in the object of purpose would be unified, and he did not make (an tabtaghu) an object of purpose except by omitting an annexed term and placing it in its position. All of this is a departure from the apparent meaning without any call for it. The object of (tabtaghu) is omitted for brevity, since it is a pronoun referring to (ma) in His words ﴿what is beyond that﴾, and its estimate is: an tabtaghuhu.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, where is the object of (tabtaghu)? I say: it is permissible for it to be understood, namely women, and it is better not to estimate it. It is as if it were said: an tukhriju amwalakum (that you spend your wealth). End of his words. As for his estimate, that if it is understood as "women," then since he made it an object of purpose he has distinguished between the object of the object of purpose and the object of the effect. As for his words, "it is better not to estimate it; it is as if it were said: an tukhriju amwalakum," this contradicts the apparent meaning, because the meaning of tabtaghu is not the meaning of tukhriju, and because the transitivity of tabtaghu to wealth by the preposition bi is not in the manner of the explicit direct object, as it is in (tukhriju). All of this is an artifice from which the Book of Allah should be exalted.

The apparent meaning of His words, "with your wealth," is that it applies to whatever is called wealth, even if small. This is the view of Abu Sa'id, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, 'Ata', al-Layth, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Thawri, al-Hasan ibn Salih, al-Shafi'i, and Rabi'ah. They said: marriage is permissible for a small amount of wealth or a large amount. It has been said: there is no dowry less than ten dirhams; this is narrated from 'Ali, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, and others among the Successors. It is also the view of Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, Zufar, al-Hasan, and Muhammad ibn Ziyad. Malik said: the least dowry is a quarter of a dinar or three dirhams. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: one who has a dirham or two dirhams is not said to have wealth. The apparent meaning of His words, "with your wealth," indicates that the dowry may not be a benefit (manfa'ah), such as teaching the Qur'an or anything else; yet a group of scholars permitted the dowry to be her service for a known period, and they have details on this. Al-Shafi'i permitted it to be teaching a chapter of the Qur'an, while Malik, al-Layth, Abu Hanifah, and Abu Yusuf prohibited that; their proofs are in the books of jurisprudence and in the books of the rulings of the Qur'an.

Ihsan (chastity) is fortification (al-fiqh) and guarding oneself against falling into what is forbidden. (Muhsinin) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and (ghayra musafihin) is an emphatic circumstantial clause, because chastity does not coexist with fornication. Likewise His words, ﴿nor those who take secret lovers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5]. The musafihun are the open, promiscuous fornicators, and likewise the musafihat are the open, promiscuous prostitutes who are a market for fornication.

(p-218) The takhidhu al-akhdan (secret lovers) are the concealed fornicators who keep company with one woman after another, and likewise the mutakhidhat al-akhdan are the concealed prostitutes who keep company with one man after another and commit fornication secretly. These two types existed in the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah), as said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, al-Dahhak, and others. The root of musafih is from al-saffh, which is the pouring of semen. The debauched man used to say to the debauched woman: "Musafihini" and "madhiyini," from al-madhy (pre-seminal fluid).

* *

﴿So for what you have enjoyed of them, give them their wages as an obligation﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd, and others said: the meaning is: when you have enjoyed a wife and intercourse has taken place, even once, then giving the wage, which is the dowry, becomes obligatory; and the word (ma) indicates that even slight intercourse necessitates giving the compensation. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿So for what you have enjoyed of them﴾ means from the women you have married, through intercourse or valid seclusion, or by the contract upon them, ﴿give them their wages for it﴾. End of his words. Valid seclusion (al-khalwah al-sahihah) was included in enjoyment according to the school of Abu Hanifah, since that is his view. Ibn 'Abbas and others explained enjoyment here as intercourse, because the full giving of the wage is only consequent upon it, and that is according to his view and the view of those who hold it.

Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others: the verse concerns temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah). Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Jubayr recited: ﴿So for what you have enjoyed of them up to a named term, give them their wages﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said to Abu Nadrah: "Thus did Allah reveal it." It is narrated from 'Ali that he said: "Were it not that 'Umar forbade temporary marriage, none but a wretch would commit fornication." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the permissibility of temporary marriage without restriction. It was also said of him: its permissibility in cases of necessity; the more correct report from him is his retraction to its prohibition. The jurists of the regions agreed on its prohibition. 'Imran ibn Husayn said: "The Messenger of Allah commanded us with temporary marriage, and he died after commanding us with it, and he did not forbid us from it." Then a man said afterward what he wished by his own opinion. A group of the People of the House (ahl al-bayt) and of the Successors held this view. Its prohibition has been established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ through the hadith of 'Ali and others. They differed about the abrogating text of temporary marriage, its manner, its conditions, and what follows from it regarding the attribution of a child or a legal penalty, as is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence and the books of the rulings of the Qur'an. The (ma) in His words ﴿so for what you have enjoyed of them﴾ is a subject (mubtada'). It may be conditional, with the predicate being the verb that follows it, and the response being ﴿give them﴾; in that case there must be a returning pronoun referring back to the conditional noun. If (ma) refers to the enjoyment, the returning element is omitted, its estimate being: give them their wages on account of it, i.e., on account of what you have enjoyed. If (ma) refers to the kind of wives enjoyed, then the returning element is the pronoun that is the object of the verb (ātūhunna), and he referred first in (bihi) to the wording of (ma), and referred to the meaning in ﴿give them﴾. The (min) in (minhunna) may on this account be partitive, and it has been said it may be explanatory. It is also permissible for (ma) to be a relative pronoun, with its predicate being (fa-ātūhunna), and the returning element being the accusative pronoun in (fa-ātūhunna) if (ma) refers to women, or omitted if (ma) refers to enjoyment, as explained earlier.

The wages (ujur) are the dowries. This is an explicit statement that the dowry is called a wage, since it is the counterpart of what is enjoyed. It has been disputed what is the object of the contract of marriage: is it the woman's body, or the benefit of a limb, or all of it? Al-Qurtubi said: the apparent view is the whole, since the contract requires all of this. If enjoyment here means temporary marriage, then the wage here is not meant as dowry but as compensation, as in His words ﴿that he may reward us the wage for what we gave to drink﴾ [al-Qasas: 25] and His words ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾ [al-Kahf: 77]. (p-219) The apparent meaning of the verse is that the named dowry is obligatory in a defective marriage, since it truly fits His words ﴿for what you have enjoyed of them﴾ with respect to it. The majority of scholars hold that in it only the equivalent dowry (mahr al-mithl) is obligatory, and the named dowry is not. Their proof is: "Any woman who marries herself without the permission of her guardian, her marriage is void; if he has consummated with her, then she has the equivalent dowry."

(Fariydatan) is in the accusative either as a circumstantial clause (hal) from (ujurihinna), or as a verbal noun (masdar) not of the same root (as the verb), meaning: give them their wages as a giving, since giving is obligatory; or as an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: He has made that an obligation.

* *

﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree upon after the obligation﴾. When they were commanded to give the wages of the women enjoyed, that would imply obligation, so He, exalted is He, informed that there is no hardship or sin in reducing what they agreed upon, or returning it, or delaying it, meaning men and women.

﴿After the obligation﴾: she may return it to him, reduce it, or delay it; this is what the context of the discourse indicates, and it is like ﴿And if they willingly give you of it anything, then consume it with pleasure and ease﴾ [al-Nisa': 4]. This is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. Al-Suddi said: it concerns temporary marriage. The meaning: what you mutually agree upon after the obligation, of an increase in the term and an increase in the dowry before the purification of the womb. Ibn 'Abbas said: concerning returning to them what you have given them. Ibn al-Mu'tamir said: concerning the reduction of the dowry when you are in hardship. It has been said: its meaning is the woman's release of the dowry, or her full payment of it, or the man's full payment of the whole dowry if he divorces before consummation. It has also been said: what you mutually agree upon after separation, or after residence following the payment of the obligation. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he cited His words, ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree upon after the obligation﴾, as evidence for the increase in dowry, saying: because (ma) is general in its reference to increase, decrease, deferral, reduction, and release; and generality of wording requires permissibility of all of these; and increase is more specific to it than the others we have mentioned, because release, reduction, and deferral do not require the man's consent for their occurrence, whereas restricting it to what was mentioned without increase would nullify the benefit of mentioning their mutual agreement. Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad held that an increase in the dowry after the marriage contract is permissible, and it is established if he consummates with her or dies leaving her; but if he divorces her before consummation, the increase is void. Malik said: the increase is valid; if he divorces her before consummation, what he added returns to him; and if he dies leaving her before she takes possession, she has nothing. Al-Shafi'i and Zufar said: the increase is in the position of a future gift; if he hands it over, it is valid, and otherwise it is void.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of what sets right the affairs of His servants.

(Wise) in His decree, His management, and His legislation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 25 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And whoever among you cannot afford the means to marry free, believing women, then let him marry from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾. Al-ṭawl (means, ability): abundance of wealth. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and Malik in al-Mudawwana. Ibn Masʿud, Jabir, ʿAtaʾ, al-Shaʿbi, al-Nakhaʿi, and Rabiʿa said: al-ṭawl here means endurance and patience for one who loves a slave woman and is so attached to her that he cannot marry anyone else, so he may marry her, even if he has the wealth to marry a free woman. Al-muḥṣanat here means free women; the division between them and slave women indicates this. Another group said it means chaste women, but this is weak.

They differed regarding the permissibility of marrying a slave woman for one who has the means to marry a free woman. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that whoever cannot afford what he would marry a free believing woman with, and fears ʿanat (sin), it is permissible for him to marry a believing slave woman. This is a specification of the generality of His saying: ﴿And marry the single among you and the righteous among your male and female slaves﴾ [al-Nur: 32]. It is thus a specification regarding the one who marries, on condition that he does not find the means to marry a free woman and fears ʿanat, and a specification regarding "your slaves" by His saying: "from your believing young women." The restriction of permissibility of marrying slave women to believing ones, for one who lacks the means to marry a free woman, is the position of the people of the Hijaz. Thus he may not marry a slave woman who is a People of the Book; this was said by al-Awzaʿi, al-Layth, Malik, and al-Shafiʿi. The Iraqis, namely Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Zufar, Muhammad, al-Hasan ibn Ziyad, and al-Thawri, and from the Successors al-Hasan and Mujahid, held that it is permissible. Marrying a believing slave woman is more excellent, so they interpreted it as preference, not obligation. They argued that faith is not a condition, from the fact that free women are described with it in His saying: ﴿to marry the chaste believing women﴾, and it is agreed that it is not a condition for them, though it is more excellent.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: God has made it easy for this community by permitting marriage to slave women, and to Jewish and Christian women. The early scholars differed greatly on this. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Jabir, Ibn Jubayr, al-Shaʿbi, and Makhul: one marries a slave woman only if he does not have the means to marry a free woman, and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. It is related from Masruq and al-Shaʿbi that marrying her is like carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine, meaning it is permitted in cases of necessity. It is related from ʿAli, Abu Jaʿfar, Mujahid, Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, and al-Zuhri that he may marry her even if he is wealthy. It is related from ʿAtaʾ and Jabir ibn Zayd that he may marry her if he fears he will commit fornication with her, even if he has a free wife under him. ʿAtaʾ said: he may marry a slave woman in addition to a free wife. Ibn Masʿud said: none may marry her in addition to a free wife except a slave. ʿUmar, ʿAli, Ibn al-Musayyab, Makhul, and others said: he may not marry her in addition to a free wife. This is what analysis requires, because the Qur'an indicates that one marries a slave woman only if he does not find the means to marry a free woman. So if he has a free wife, it is all the more so impermissible for him to marry a slave woman, because finding the means for a free woman is only a cause of obtaining her; if she is already his, it is more appropriate to prohibit it. Ibrahim said: he may marry a slave woman in addition to a free wife if he has a child by the slave woman. Ibn al-Musayyab said: he may not marry her in addition to a free wife unless the free wife consents, and he gives the free wife two days and the slave woman one day. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿from what your right hands possess﴾ is the permissibility, for one lacking the means to marry a free believing woman, of marrying up to four slave women if he wishes. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he may not marry more than one slave woman. If faith is not a condition for the slave woman, the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿from what your right hands possess of your young women﴾ is that if a female People of the Book has a non-believing master, her marriage is not permitted, because He addressed it by saying: ﴿from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾, so it is restricted to the young women of believers. It is related from Abu Yusuf that it is permitted, but disliked. If faith is not a condition for marrying a slave woman, then the apparent meaning is the permissibility of marrying a non-believing slave woman absolutely, whether she is a People of the Book, a Magian, an idolater, or other types of unbelievers.

* *

They agreed on the prohibition of marrying a non-Scriptural unbelieving slave woman, such as a Magian, an idolater, and others. As for sexual intercourse with a Magian woman by right of possession, Tawus, ʿAtaʾ, Mujahid, and ʿAmr ibn Dinar permitted it. The apparent meanings of the Qur'an supported this view, in the generality of "what your right hands possess" and the generality of ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Muminun: 6]. They said: this is an anomalous, abandoned view, which none of the jurists of the regions considered. And they said: it is not lawful for him to have intercourse with her until she becomes Muslim. They also said: marrying a slave woman was made inferior to marrying a free woman because of what it entails, namely that the child follows its mother in servitude, the owner's right over her and in her service, and her frequent coming and going; in this there is a diminishing of the marriage and its humiliation, since he accepted all of this, and honour is among the attributes of believers.

"Min" is a subject (mubtada'), and its apparent status is that it is a conditional particle. The fa' in "fa-min ma malakat" is the fa' of the response, and "min" is linked to an elided element, its estimate being: "then let him marry from what." It is possible that "man" is a relative pronoun, and the elided operative to which "min ma malakat" is connected is a clause in the position of the predicate. The conditions for the fa' to enter the predicate of the subject are present here. The apparent view is that the object of "yastaṭiʿ" is "ṭawlan," and "an yankiḥa" on this basis: they permitted that its underlying form had a preposition, so some estimated it as "ila" and some as "li," meaning: ability toward marrying, or for marrying. Then the preposition was deleted. If one estimates "ila," the meaning is: whoever among you does not have the ability to reach marriage. If it is estimated with "li," it is in the position of a qualifier: "ṭawlan," meaning a dowry suitable for marrying the chaste women. It was said: the estimated "li" is the "li" of purpose, meaning ability for the sake of marrying the chaste women. They also permitted that "an yankiḥa" be in the accusative position as object, governed by "ṭawl," since it is treated as the verbal noun of "ṭultu al-shay'," meaning I attained it. They said: from this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

Indeed al-Farazdaq is a rock of ʿAd, its height is such that the wild goats cannot reach it.

That is: it has extended beyond the wild goats. The estimate is then: "whoever among you does not have the ability to attain marriage with the chaste women." It makes the indefinite verbal noun govern an object, like his saying:

With strikes of swords upon heads of a people, we removed their skulls from their resting place.

This is according to the Basrans, who permitted the governing action of an indefinite verbal noun. Abu ʿAli in al-Tadhkira held that "ṭawlan" is the object of "yastaṭiʿ," and "an yankiḥa" is in the position of an object of "ṭawlan," since it is a verbal noun. They also permitted that "an yankiḥa" be a substitute for "ṭawl," saying: one thing substitutes for another, and they are one thing, since ṭawl is power and marriage is a power. They also permitted that the object of "yastaṭiʿ" be his saying "an yankiḥa." Regarding the accusative of "ṭawlan" there are two possibilities. One: that it is an object of purpose with an elided genitive, meaning: whoever among you does not have, for lack of means to marry the chaste women. The second, said by Ibn ʿAṭiyya: He said: it is also valid that "ṭawlan" is accusative as a verbal noun, with the governing element being "istiṭaʿa," because it is close in meaning. "An yankiḥa" in this case is the object of "istiṭaʿa" or of the verbal noun. End of his words. It seems he means that ṭawl is istiṭāʿa, so the estimate is: whoever among you does not have the capacity, the capacity to marry.

"Ma" in His saying ﴿fa-min ma malakat﴾ is a relative noun: meaning, "then let him marry from the category that your right hands possess." "Min fatayatikum" is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier of the elided pronoun in "ma malakat," returning to "ma." The object of the elided verb, which is "fa-l-yankiḥ," is elided, the estimate being: "then let him marry a slave woman from what your right hands possess." "Min" is partitive, as in: I ate from the loaf. It was said: "min" in "min ma" is extra, and the object of that verb is "ma" in His saying "ma malakat aymanukum." It was said: its object is "fatayatikum," with "min" being extra. It was said: its object is "al-mu'minat," the estimate being: "then let him marry from what your right hands possess of your young women, the believing young women." The more apparent view is that "al-mu'minat" is a qualifier of "fatayatikum." It was said: "ma" is a verbal-noun particle, the estimate being: from the possession of your faith. On this view "min fatayatikum" is linked to "malakat."

Among the strangest things recorded in books of tafsir and transmitted from al-Tabari's statement is that the doer of that elided verb is His saying ﴿some of you are from others﴾, and there is a fronting and deferment in the speech. The estimate is: "And whoever among you does not have the ability to marry the chaste believing women, then let some of them marry from some of the young women." This is an opinion that one should refrain from attributing to the Book of God, because it combines ignorance of the science of grammar and the science of meanings, and dismantles the structure of the Qur'an from its eloquent style. It should not be written down or given attention. "Minkum" is addressed to those who marry, and in "aymanukum min fatayatikum" the address is to the owners; the meaning is not that a man marries his own slave girl. This kind of expansion in language is common.

﴿And God knows best your faith﴾. When He addressed the believers with the ruling He mentioned, permitting one who lacks the means to marry a free believing woman to marry a believing slave woman, He drew attention to the fact that faith is an inward attribute and that the one who has knowledge of it is God. The meaning is: it is not required of the believing young women that they have certain knowledge of it, because that belongs only to God, and it suffices from them that they manifest it. So whoever manifests faith, her marriage is valid, even if she is mute, or newly captured and has displayed faith, and that suffices from her.

The address in "bi-imanikum" is to believers, males and females, free and enslaved, and faith is included in this address without singling out women. He did not say "bi-imanihinna," lest anyone else be excluded from this address. The intended point is the generality of the address, since all of them are subject to this ruling. How many a slave woman surpasses a free woman in faith and good deeds, and how many a woman surpasses a man in this! In this there is comfort for marrying slave women, and that the believer is not judged by the most noble lineage or ancestry: "Indeed the most honoured of you before God is the most pious. No Arab has merit over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, except through piety."

﴿Some of you are from others﴾. This is a nominal sentence of subject and predicate. Al-Tabari's statement has already been mentioned, that the raising of "ba'DuKum" is as subject of the elided verb. The meaning of this initial sentence is also comfort for marrying slave women, and that free persons and slaves are all connected, related, and return to one origin, and they share in faith, so marrying slave women does no harm. In it is also an accommodation for the Arabs, since in the pre-Islamic period they despised the child of a slave woman and called him the hajin. When the law came, it removed that. How excellent is what is related from ʿAli in his saying:

People, by way of comparison, are equals: their father is Adam and their mother is Eve.

﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾. This is a command of permission, and the meaning is: with the guardianship of their owners. By marriage here is meant the contract, and for this reason He mentioned the giving of their payment after it, that is, the dowry. The owners of slave women are called their "people" because they are like family, since the slave woman returns to her master in many rulings. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Charity is not lawful for Muhammad or the family of Muhammad." And he said: "The clients of a people are from among them."

And it was said: it is by elision of a noun, "with the permission of their guardians," and the guardians of their marriage are their owners. The implication of this address is that the permission of the master is a condition for the validity of the marriage. So if she marries without the permission of her master, the marriage is not valid, even if the master later approves it, unlike the slave. As for the male slave, if he marries without the permission of his master, the position of al-Hasan, 'Ata', Ibn al-Musayyib, Shurayh, al-Sha'bi, Malik and Abu Hanifah is that his marriage is suspended on the permission of his master: if the master approves it, it is valid, and if he rejects it, it is void. Al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and Dawud said: it is not valid, whether the master approves it or not.

The scholars agreed that a slave's marriage without his master's permission is not valid. Ibn 'Umar used to regard him as an adulterer and would impose the hadd (the prescribed punishment) on him, and this is the view of Abu Thawr.

'Ata' said: there is no hadd upon him, it is not zina, but he has violated the Sunnah (the prophetic practice). This is the view of most of the early generation (al-salaf). The apparent meaning of His words, "with the permission of their guardians," is that it includes owners, male and female, so the permission of the woman is required in marrying off her female slave. And if what is meant by "permission" is the contract itself, then it is permissible for a woman to marry off her female slave and to conduct the contract herself, just as it is permissible for a man. Al-Shafi'i said: it is not permissible; rather, she must appoint someone else to arrange the marriage. Al-Zamakhshari said: "with the permission of their guardians" makes the permission of the owners a condition for their marriage, and it is used as evidence for the view of Abu Hanifah that women may conduct the contract themselves, because it made the permission of the owners a requirement, not their contracting.

* *

﴿And give them their wages with fairness﴾. "Wages" here means the dowries. In this there is evidence for the obligation of giving a female slave her dowry, and that she has more right to her dowry than her master. This is the view of Malik, who said: the master may not take his female slave's dowry and leave her without provision. The majority of scholars hold that it must be paid to the master, not to her. It was said: slave women and what is in their hands are the property of their masters, so paying it to them is paying it to the masters. And it was said: it is by elision of a noun, meaning, "and give to their masters." And it was said: "with the permission of their guardians" was elided after His words, "and give them their wages," because of the indication in His words, "so marry them with the permission of their guardians." It is then like His words, "the men who guard their private parts and the women who guard [theirs]" [al-Ahzab: 35], meaning "their private parts," and "the men who remember Allah often and the women [who do]" [al-Ahzab: 35], meaning "Allah often."

Some said: "their wages" means their maintenance (nafaqat). That "wages" means dowries is the more apparent meaning, because maintenance is connected with the wife's availability to her husband, not with the contract. The apparent meaning of His words, "with fairness," is that it is connected with His words, "and give them their wages." It was said: its meaning is without delay, without harm, and without forcing them to demand it through pressure or insistence. And it was said: its meaning is according to the Law and the Sunnah, that is, the customary dowry of women like them who are equal to them in wealth and lineage. And it was said: "with fairness" is connected with His words, "so marry them," meaning, "so marry them with fairness, with the permission of their guardians, and at the customary dowry, and with witnesses to that." For that is what is customary in most marriages.

"Muhsanat" means chaste, and it may also mean Muslim women.

"Not fornicating" means not openly committing zina.

* *

﴿Nor those who take secret lovers﴾: that is, nor those who conceal their zina with their secret lovers. This is a division of what actually happens, for the adulteress either does not refuse the hand of any man who touches her, or she restricts herself to one man. On these two types was the zina of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period). Ibn 'Abbas said: some people used to forbid what was open of zina and permit what was hidden of it. The khidn (secret lover) is the friend of a woman who commits zina with her in secret. So Allah the Exalted forbade "the open and the secret" indecencies. The accusative of "muhsanat" is as a circumstantial state (hal). The apparent view is that its governing word is "and give them." It is also permissible in this view that the meaning of "muhsanat" is "married," meaning, "and give them their wages while they are married, not in a state of fornication or taking secret lovers." It was said: it is also possible that the governing word of "muhsanat" is "so marry them," meaning, "so marry them as chaste women, or Muslim women, not those who commit zina."

* *

﴿So when they are married, if they commit a flagrant immorality, then for them is half the punishment of free women﴾. The majority, including Ibn Mas'ud, said: the ihsan (chastity/protection) here is Islam. The meaning is that a Muslim slave woman receives half the hadd of a free Muslim woman. This view has been deemed weak, because the attribute of their belief has already been mentioned in His words, "from your believing young women," so how can it be said of believing women, "if they embrace Islam"? This was said by Isma'il al-Qadi. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: that is not necessary, for it is permissible to break off in speech and add. If they have this attribute of belief previously mentioned, then if they commit indecency, the punishment is upon them, and that is valid and sound. The end of his words. But his statement is not apparent, because "aslamna" (they embraced Islam) is a verb preceded by the particle of condition, so it is future, presumed to be renewed and to occur in what is to come. So it cannot be used to express Islam, because Islam is prior and precedes them. Moreover, it is a condition that came after His words, "so marry them," so it is as if it was said: "when they are made chaste by marriage, then if they commit..."

Those who explained ihsan here as Islam made it a condition for the obligation of the hadd. So if an unbelieving woman commits zina, she is not subjected to the hadd. This is the view of al-Sha'bi, al-Zuhri and others, and it has been narrated from al-Shafi'i. Another group said: it means marriage. So if a Muslim slave woman who has not married commits zina, there is no hadd upon her. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi. Another group said: it means marriage, and a Muslim slave woman is subject to the hadd by the Sunnah, whether she is married or not, based on the authentic hadith in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, which is that it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, if a slave woman commits zina and is not made chaste, what [is the punishment]?" Then he ordered the hadd upon her. Al-Zuhri said: a married woman is subject to the hadd by the Qur'an, and a Muslim woman who is not married is subject to the hadd by the hadith. This question from the Companions indicates that they understood the meaning of "when they are made chaste" as "when they are married." The Messenger's answer confirms this. There is no implied converse (mafhum) of the condition of ihsan, which is marriage, because the hadd was obligatory on her by the Sunnah even if she was not made chaste. Rather, attention is drawn to the state of ihsan, which is marriage, lest it be imagined that her punishment when married is like that of a free woman when made chaste, which is stoning. This misconception is removed by the statement that upon her is only half the punishment that is due upon free women who are not made chaste by marriage, which is flogging fifty lashes.

By "the punishment" is meant flogging, as in His words, "and let a group of the believers witness their punishment" [al-Nur: 2]. It cannot mean stoning, because stoning cannot be halved. By "indecency" here is meant zina, by the evidence of the imposition of the hadd. The apparent view is that half of what is due upon the free woman of punishment is obligatory, and the punishment of the free woman is a hundred lashes and exile for a year, so the hadd of the slave woman is fifty lashes and exile for six months. This was the view of a group of the Successors (tabi'un), and al-Tabari chose it. Ibn 'Abbas and the majority held that upon her there is only fifty lashes, and she is not exiled. If the definite article in "al-'adhab" (the punishment) refers to the punishment mentioned in the Qur'an, then it is the flogging alone. If it refers to the punishment established in the Law for free women, then it is flogging and exile. The apparent view is that the hadd is obligatory from His words, "then for them," so it is not permitted for the master to pardon his slave woman if she commits zina. This is the view of the majority. Al-Hasan held that the master may pardon, and the verse does not address who enforces the hadd upon her.

Ibn Shihab said: it has been the Sunnah that the masters of male and female slaves enforce the hadd upon them for zina, unless their case is referred to the ruler, and no one may usurp this from him. Ibn Abi Layla said: I saw the remnants of the Ansar beating their slave girls, when they committed zina, in their gatherings. A group of Companions enforced the hadd on their slaves, among them Ibn 'Umar and Anas. The apparent meanings of the hadiths support this, such as his saying: "If the slave girl of one of you commits zina, let him flog her with the hadd." This was also the view of al-Thawri and al-Awza'i. Malik and al-Layth said: the master enforces the hadd, except for amputation, which only the imam may carry out. Abu Hanifah said: the hadd upon slaves, male and female, is enforced only by the ruler and not by the owners. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the hadd is obligatory upon her while she is a slave. If she is freed before the hadd is enforced upon her, the hadd of a slave woman is enforced upon her, and this is agreed upon. The "muhsanat" here are the virgin free women, because the married woman's punishment is stoning. The apparent meaning of the verse is that only this hadd is obligatory. The Zahiris, among them Dawud, held that she must be sold if she commits zina a fourth time.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "ahsanna" (أحْصَنَّ) in the active voice, and the rest of the seven readers read it in the passive voice, except 'Asim, about whom the narrations differ. Whoever reads it in the passive voice is clearly referring to marriage. Reading it in the active voice supports this meaning as well, that is, "they made themselves chaste by marriage." The answer to "fa-idha" (when) is the conditional clause and its answer, which is His words, "then if they commit a flagrant immorality, then for them." The fa' in "fa-in ata'na" (then if they commit) is the fa' of the answer, not the fa' of coordination. For this reason the second condition and its answer are consequent upon the existence of the first, because the answer is consequent upon the condition in existence. It is like saying: "If you enter the house, then if you speak to Zayd, you are divorced." Divorce does not take effect unless she first enters the house and then speaks to Zayd second. If the fa' were dropped from the second condition, it would have a different ruling and a distinction mentioned in grammar. "Min al-'adhab" (of the punishment) is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun hidden in the relative clause of "ma" (what).

* *

﴿That is for one of you who fears hardship (al-'anat)﴾: "That" refers to marrying a slave woman for one who lacks the means to marry a free believing woman. Al-'anat means zina. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, 'Ata' al-'Awfi and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd. The root meaning of 'anat is hardship, and zina was called 'anat by the name of what follows it of hardship in this world and the Hereafter. Al-Mubarrad said: the root meaning of 'anat is that passion and sexual desire drive a person to zina, so he meets punishment in the Hereafter and the hadd in this world. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj said: 'anat means ruin. Another group said: it means the hadd. Another group said: it means the sin to which the overpowering of desire leads. The apparent meaning of this is that if he does not fear 'anat, it is not permissible for him to marry a slave woman. What the apparent Qur'an indicates is that it is not permissible for a free man to marry a slave woman except under three conditions: two concerning the one marrying, namely, lacking the means to marry a free believing woman and fearing 'anat; and one concerning the slave woman, which is that she is a believer.

* *

﴿But that you be patient is better for you﴾. Its apparent meaning is a report about a specific patience, which is refraining from marrying slave women. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi. The aspect of its being better is that the child is not born a slave, and that he (the man) does not degrade himself, and is not diminished in common estimation by marrying a slave woman. In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, from the hadith of Anas, he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Whoever wishes to meet Allah pure and purified, let him marry free women." It is also reported in a hadith: "Marry those who are equal (kufu'), and choose for your offspring (lit. seed)." It was said: the meaning is that if you are patient regarding zina by marrying slave women, it is better for you. According to this view, the superiority is clear. On this view, the verse has an element of encouragement toward marrying slave women and bringing one closer to it, since the Arabs used to shun it. If "but that you be patient" is taken in a general sense, it includes the particular patience, which is refraining from marrying slave women and from zina. For patience is better than its absence, because it indicates the courage of the soul, the strength of its resolve, the greatness of its refusal, and the intensity of its self-restraint. All of this reason approves of, and the Law recommends, and it may even make it obligatory in some situations. Allah the Exalted has made the reward of the patient one that is paid in full without reckoning. Some people of knowledge have said: all other acts of worship require patience. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45].

**﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾** When He urged, by His saying ﴿and that you be patient is better for you﴾, toward patience in refraining from marrying slave-women, it was as though this fell within the sphere of disliking it. So He came with the attribute of forgiveness, which indicates that this is among the things He has been lenient about, and with the attribute of mercy, in that He granted a concession for marrying them and permitted it.

[p. 225]

﴿Allah desires to make clear to you and guide you to the ways of those before you, and to turn to you in forgiveness.﴾ The object of (yatuba, "to turn [in forgiveness]") is omitted, and its implied object is: "Allah desires [that He turn to you]." This is the view of Sibawayh, as Ibn 'Atiyyah relates. That is: permitting what He permitted, prohibiting what He prohibited, and legislating what has been mentioned. The meaning is: Allah desires to impose upon His servants the obligations He has imposed, as mentioned, in order to make clear to them, through their guidance, so the object of the desire is other than the act of making clear and what is conjoined to it. This is the view of the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun). According to them, the object of the desire cannot be "making clear," because that would require the verb to govern its later object through the particle lam, and would require the elision of (an) after a lam that is neither lam al-juhud (the lam of denial) nor lam kay (the lam of purpose). Both of these are impermissible in their view. The view of the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun) is that the object of the desire is the act of making clear, and that the lam itself is the particle that governs the subjunctive, not an elided (an) after it. Some Basran grammarians said: when something like this occurs, the verb preceding the lam is taken as a verbal noun (masdar). The reading is: "the desire of Allah for what He desires, in order to make clear." Similarly, "I desire that he not forget its mention," meaning: "my desire that he not forget its mention." Likewise the verse ﴿We were commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ (6:71), meaning: "We were commanded with what we were commanded, in order that we submit." End of quotation. Ibn 'Isa attributed this view to Sibawayh and the Basrans, and it is a matter discussed in the science of grammar (ilm al-nahw).

Al-Zamakhshari said: the original is "Allah desires that He make clear to you," and the lam was added to emphasize the desire for making clear, just as it is added in "la aba laka" (may you have no father) to emphasize the attribution of the father. The meaning: Allah desires that He make clear to you what has been hidden from you of your interests and the excellent deeds you should do. End of his words. This departs from the views of both the Basrans and the Kufans. As for it departing from the Basran view, it is because he made the lam an emphasizing and strengthening particle for the transitivity of (yurid, "desires"), with the object coming later, and he presumed an elided (an) after this lam. As for it departing from the Kufan view, they hold that the accusative is governed by the lam, not by (an), whereas he makes the accusative governed by an elided (an) after the lam. Some grammarians held that the lam in His saying "li-yubayyina lakum" (in order to make clear to you) is the lam of consequence (lam al-aqibah), and he said: as in His saying ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ (28:8). The object of (yubayyin, "makes clear") is not mentioned.

'Ata' said: He makes clear to you what brings you closer [to Him]. Abu al-Kalbi said: He makes clear to you that abstaining from marrying slave women is better. It was also said: what He has detailed of the prohibited and the permitted. It was said: the legislated laws of your religion and the interests of your affairs. It was said: the path of those before you to Paradise. In my opinion it is permissible that this be of the type of al-i'mal (the grammatical construction in which two verbs share one object), so that the object of (li-yubayyin) is an elided pronoun explained by the object of (wa-yahdiyakum), as in: "I struck and insulted Zayd," the reading being: "in order that He make them clear to you and guide you to the ways of those before you," that is, "in order that He make clear to you the ways of those before you."

The word (sunan) is the plural of (sunnah), which means "way" or "path." The scholars differed regarding His saying ﴿the ways of those before you﴾: is it to be taken literally, as guidance to their ways, or as a comparison, meaning ways like the ways of those before you? Whoever held the first view meant that the "ways" are what is forbidden to us and to them through lineage, nursing, and affinity by marriage. It was also said that what is meant by "sunan" is what is referred to in His saying ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth﴾ (16:123). It was said that what is meant is what He mentioned in His saying ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ (42:13). It was said: the paths of those before you to Paradise. It was said: the methods of those prophets and righteous people who came before you, and the ways they followed in their religion so that you might follow them. This is close to what preceded it. According to these views, "those before you" means the prophets and the people of goodness. It was said that what is meant by "sunan" is the paths of the people of goodness, guidance, and misguidance, and of those before you from the people of truth and falsehood, so that you might avoid falsehood and follow truth.

Those who held that this is a comparison said: the meaning is that the paths of the earlier nations in their guidance came through sending messengers, revealing scriptures, and explaining rulings. Likewise, your path was made [to follow the same pattern]. So He willed to guide you to the laws of your religion and the rulings of your community through clarification and detail, just as He guided the believers among those before you. It was also said: guidance is in one of two respects. First, we are addressed in every narrative with a prohibition or a command, just as they were addressed in their narratives, and what was legislated for us is as what was legislated for them. So our guidance is their path in instruction, even if our rulings and their rulings differ. The second respect: our guidance in their path is that we heard and obeyed just as they heard and obeyed, and so there is similarity from this aspect.

The meaning of guidance here is instruction and clarification, and no other meaning is appropriate, given the context of "sunan." The "those before us" are the believers from every legislation. The author of Rayy al-Zam'an, who is Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi, said: His saying ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ means: He desires to make clear, or He desires the sending down of verses in order to make clear to you. As for His saying "and guide you," the exegetes said that the two have the same meaning and the repetition is for emphasis. This is weak. The truth is that the first refers to making the obligations clear, and then He said "and guide you." There are two views on this. One is that this is evidence that everything He made clear to us as prohibited and permitted regarding women in the preceding verses was also the ruling in all the legislations, even though they differed in themselves but agreed in the matter of benefits. End of quotation. The meanings of these views he mentioned have already been given. His statement "i.e., He desires to make clear" agrees with the words of al-Zamakhshari.

﴿and to turn to you in forgiveness﴾: that is, He brings you back from disobedience to Him to obedience to Him, and enables you to achieve it.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾: All-Knowing of your conditions and of the legislations and interests that have preceded, All-Wise, who places things in their proper places according to wisdom and perfection.

﴿And Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness, but those who follow their desires desire that you deviate into a tremendous deviation﴾: The desire is first connected to the turning in forgiveness as a causal relation, according to what we have chosen among the views, because His saying "and turn to you" is conjoined to the cause, so it is a cause. Its connection here is as an object, so the two connections differ, and there is no repetition. Just as He willed the cause of repentance, He also willed repentance toward them, since it is possible to will the cause without the act itself. Whoever held that the object of the desire is one in both places would consider His saying "Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness" a repetition of His saying "and turn to you," because His saying "and turn to you" is conjoined to an object, so it is an object. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the repetition of Allah's desire for His servants to repent is a strengthening of the first report, and the purpose of the verse is nothing but reporting the desire of those who follow their desires. So Allah's desire was placed first as a preliminary, revealing the corruption of those who follow their desires. End of his words. He chose the view of the Kufans, in that they took His saying "li-yubayyin" to mean "an yubayyin" (that He make clear), so it is an object of (yurid), and "and turn" is conjoined to it, so it is an object like it. For this reason he said: the repetition of Allah's desire for His servants to repent, and so on to the end of his words. He had reported the view of the Kufans and said: this is weak, and then he returned in the end to what he had labeled weak. He had earlier stated that Sibawayh's view is that the object of (yurid) is elided, the reading being: "Allah desires this making clear."

The word (shahawat) is the plural of (shahwah), which is that to which the soul is strongly drawn by love and desire. Since the legal obligations involve restraining the soul and turning it away from what it craves, following its cravings becomes a cause of every blameworthiness. Those who disbelieve and those who are sinful are described as "followers of desires," as He said ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected prayer and followed desires, so they will meet misguidance﴾ (19:59). Following desire in every situation is blameworthy, because that is obeying it in whatever desire calls for. But if following is by way of reason or the law, then that is following them, not following desire. Those who follow desires here are the fornicators, according to Mujahid, or the Jews and Christians, according to al-Suddi. Or the Jews specifically, because they wished that the Muslims would follow them in marrying sisters from the father's side. Or the Magians, who permitted marrying sisters from the father's side, and marrying daughters of a brother and daughters of a sister. When Allah prohibited these, they said: you permit marrying the daughter of your maternal aunt and paternal aunt, while the paternal aunt is forbidden to you, so marry daughters of brothers and sisters. Or those who follow every desire, according to Ibn Zayd, which al-Tabari preferred. Its apparent meaning is generality and inclination. If it is unrestricted, then what is meant here is inclining away from truth, which is oppression and departing from the intended path. For this reason, the desire of Allah is contrasted with the desire of those who follow desires, and how vast is the difference between the two desires. He emphasized the verb of inclining with a verbal noun for the sake of exaggeration, and did not stop at describing it as great. This is because inclinations differ: a person may abandon a good deed due to some obstacle that occupied him, or due to laziness, or due to sinfulness that he enjoys, or due to error, by having a prior bad belief. The levels of treating these matters vary, some being easier than others. Therefore such people are described as great, since it is the furthest inclination to treat, which is disbelief, as He said ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve﴾ (4:89) and ﴿They desire that you go astray from the way﴾ (4:44).

The majority of readers recited "an tamilu" with the feminine second-person plural (you). It was also read with the third-person (ya'), referring to those who follow desires, so the pronoun in (yamilu) returns to "those who follow desires." The majority recited "maylan" with a sukun on the ya'. Al-Hasan recited it with a fatha on the ya'. The first sentence was nominal, and the second verbal, in order to show the emphasis of the first sentence, because the nominal form indicates stability more. The name of Allah the Exalted is repeated in it in the manner of explicit mention and pronoun. The second sentence came verbal, indicating renewal, because their desire renews at every time. The waw in His saying "wa-yurid" is for conjunction according to what we have established. Al-Raghib permitted that the waw be for the circumstantial (hal), not for conjunction. He said, to indicate that He desires to turn to you in forgiveness at the time you desire to incline, and so he differentiated between the two reports by placing the subject first in the first sentences and delaying it in the second sentence, to show that the second is not in conjunction. This is not good, because His desire to turn to us in forgiveness is not restricted to the desire of others for inclination, and because the present tense is preceded by waw, which is not permitted. Something rare of this occurs that is interpreted as an elided subject before it, which the Qur'an should not be made to bear, especially when the speech has a sound and eloquent meaning. So taking it as the rare case is forced and impermissible.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 26–28 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Allah desires to lighten (yukhaffifa) for you﴾. He did not mention what the lightening relates to (muta'allaq al-takhfif), and on this there are several views:

First, that it lies in permitting marriage to slave women and in the other concessions (rukhas).

Second, that it lies in not imposing the burden of deliberation and removing confusion regarding what He has made clear to you of what is lawful for you in marriage and what is not.

Third, that it lies in the removal of the heavy burden (al-isr) that was prescribed for those before us, and in the coming of this upright religion (al-milla al-hanifiyya) as easy and tolerant.

Fourth, that it lies in bringing you to the reward for what He has imposed on you of bearing obligations.

Fifth, that it lies in His lightening for you the sin of the sins you commit out of your ignorance.

They parsed this clause (jumla) as a circumstantial clause (hal) from His saying ﴿and Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness﴾, and the governing element (al-'amil) in the circumstantial clause is (yurid, "desires"), the implied sense being: "and Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness, desiring to lighten for you." This parsing (i'rab) is weak, because it has separated the governing element from the circumstantial clause by a conjoined clause (jumla ma'tufa) upon the clause in which the governing element is embedded, and that clause is foreign to both the governing element and the circumstantial clause. Therefore it should not be permitted except on the basis of a report from the Arabs. Also, the verb that occurs as the circumstantial clause has raised an apparent noun, whereas it should raise its pronoun, not its apparent noun, so it becomes like the example: "Zayd goes out" or "Zayd strikes 'Amr" [i.e., an improper construction]. [p. 228] What has been heard of such usage is only in the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ibtida'iyya) or in some of its abrogating particles (nawasikh). As for the circumstantial clause, I do not know of such usage. The permissibility of that in what has come is eloquent only where exaltation and magnification are intended, so that the linking (rabt) in the clause that stands as a predicate (khabar) is by an apparent noun. As for the circumstantial clause or the qualifying clause (sifa), linking by an apparent noun in it requires a report from the Arabs. The best view is that the clause is a resumptive (mustaanifa), and so has no place in the parsing. He, exalted is He, informed us of it regarding His will to lighten for us, as in His saying: ﴿Allah desires ease for you and does not desire hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 185].

﴿And man was created weak﴾. Mujahid, Tawus and Ibn Zayd said: the report about the weakness of man is only in the matter of women, meaning: since We knew your weakness regarding women, We lightened for you by permitting slave women. Tawus said: man is not weaker than he is in the matter of women. Ibn al-Musayyib said: Satan never despaired of the sons of Adam except that he came to them through women. Eighty years have passed over me, one of my eyes has gone, and I am in love with the other; and indeed the thing I most fear for myself is the temptation of women.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "weak," not able to hold back from desires and from the hardships of acts of obedience.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: then, after this aim, namely Allah's lightening by permitting slave women, the verse takes the form of an act of grace (tafaddul), because it encompasses everything that Allah has lightened for His servants and made the religion ease. The report about man's weakness occurs in a general sense, according to what is in himself of weakness, as his desire tends to draw him in most cases.

Al-Raghib said: describing man as having been created weak is only with regard to his being considered in relation to the exalted assembly (al-mala' al-a'la), like: ﴿Are you a harder creation, or is the sky?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27]; or with regard to himself apart from what comes to him of the overflow of Allah's grace and help; or in consideration of the multiplicity of his needs and the dependence of some of them upon others; or in consideration of his beginning and his end, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah is He who created you from weakness﴾ [al-Rum: 54]. But when he is considered in terms of his intellect and of the strength He gave him by which he is enabled to act as Allah's vicegerent on His earth, and by which in the Hereafter he reaches His nearness, then he is the strongest thing in this world. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have preferred them over many of those We created, with preference﴾ [al-Isra': 70].

Al-Hasan said: "weak" because he was created from a degraded water. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He who created you from weakness﴾ [al-Rum: 54].

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid read: wa-khalaqa al-insana (with the verb in the active voice), attributed to the pronoun of the name of Allah, and the accusative of da'ifan (weak) is as a circumstantial accusative (hal). It was also said: it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), because it can be estimated as with min ("from"), but this is not valid. It was also said: it is in the accusative by dropping the preposition (harf al-jarr), the estimate being: "from a weak thing," i.e., from clay, or from a drop, a clinging clot, and a lump of flesh.
