When the qualified noun and the governing particle are omitted, the qualifying adjective takes the accusative by the verb itself.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is also valid that khalaqa be understood in the sense of ja'ala ("made"), so that it gives the verb the capacity to govern two objects (maf'ulayn), and then His saying da'ifan is the second object. End of quotation.

This is what he mentioned, that khalaqa is transitive to two objects by taking it in the sense of ja'ala. I do not know of any grammarian who went to that view. Rather, what people have mentioned is that among the uses of ja'ala is that it may mean khalaqa and be transitive to one object, as in His saying: ﴿and He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. As for the reverse, no one, as far as we know, has held that view, and later scholars who investigated these verbs did not mention it.

These verses also contain kinds of rhetorical eloquence (bayan) and figurative embellishment (badi'). Among them:

Metonymy (tajawwuz) by using the name of the whole for a part, in His saying: ﴿they commit the indecency (al-fahisha)﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], because the definite article (al-) embraces every indecency, and that is not what is meant, but rather some of it. The name of the whole was applied to a part only to magnify its ugliness and foulness. If the usage for "indecency" is adultery, then this is not of this type, since the alif and lam would then be for a known reference (al-'ahd).

Metonymy by the intended sense of the absolute being a part of its denotation, in His saying: ﴿harm them (fa-adhuhuma)﴾, when it is explained as reproach or beating with sandals, or as bringing them together; and in His saying: ﴿a way (sabilan)﴾, the intended meaning being the prescribed punishment (hadd) or stoning of the married person (muhsan); and in His saying: ﴿turn away from them (fa-a'ridu 'anhuma)﴾ [al-Nisa': 16], i.e., leave them.

Attribution of a verb to other than its agent, in His saying: ﴿until death takes them (yatawaffahunna al-mawt)﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], and in His saying: ﴿when death comes to one of them (hadara ahadahumu al-mawt)﴾ [al-Nisa': 18].

Paronomasia of difference (tajnis mughayir) in: ﴿if they repent (in taba)﴾, and ﴿Allah is ever Relenting (tawwaban)﴾ [al-Nisa': 16]; and in: ﴿they nursed you (arda'nakum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23] and ﴿of nursing (min al-rada'a)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]; and in: muhsanat, "married women," and fa-idha uhsinna ("when they are married").

Paronomasia of likeness (tajnis mumathil) in: ﴿if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing﴾ [al-Nisa': 19], and in: ﴿do not marry what your fathers married (ma nakaha)﴾ [al-Nisa': 22].

[p. 229] Repetition (takrar) of the name of Allah in several places; and in: ﴿the repentance (al-tawba) is only﴾ [al-Nisa': 17], ﴿and repentance is not (al-tawba laysat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 18]; and in: ﴿one spouse in place of another spouse﴾ [al-Nisa': 20]; and in: "your mothers" (ummahatukum) and ﴿and your mothers, those who﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]; and in: ﴿except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa': 22]; and in: "the believing [women]" (al-mu'minat) in His saying: ﴿chaste believing women (al-muhsanat al-mu'minat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and in: ﴿your believing slave girls (fatayatikumu al-mu'minat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]; and in: farida ("obligation") and ﴿after the obligation (min ba'di al-farida)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]; and in: ﴿the chaste women among the women (al-muhsanat min al-nisa')﴾ [al-Nisa': 24] and "the chaste ones" (al-muhsanat); and ﴿half of what is upon the chaste ones (nisf ma 'ala al-muhsanat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]; and in: ﴿some of you are from some (ba'dukum min ba'd)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]; and in: "desires" (yurid) in four places; and in: "turns [in repentance]" (yatubu) and "to turn" (an yatuba); and in the use of the imperfect for the past, in: ﴿and those women who commit the indecency (wa-allati ya'tina al-fahisha)﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], and in: ﴿and the two of you who commit it among you (wa-alladhani ya'tiyaniha minkum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 16], and in: ﴿who do evil (ya'malun al-su')﴾ [al-Nisa': 17], and in: ﴿then they repent (thumma yatubuna)﴾, and in: "desires" (yurid), and in: ﴿that He may make clear (liyubayyina)﴾, because Allah's will and His making clear are both eternal (qadimani), since His making clear is in His revealed books, and will and speech are among the attributes of His essence, which are eternal.

Allusion (ishara) and hinting (iyma') in His saying: ﴿by compulsion (karhan)﴾, since the prohibition of inheriting women by compulsion alludes to its permissibility by consent; this is stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿if they give consent (fa-in tibna)﴾, and in His saying: ﴿do not hinder them in order that you may go away with part of what you have given them﴾ [al-Nisa': 19]. He may hinder her in another manner for a benefit connected to her or to her wealth. And in: ﴿indeed it was an indecency﴾ [al-Nisa': 22], it hints at the custom in the Jahiliyya of sons marrying their fathers' wives. In: ﴿lawful for you is what is beyond that (uhilla lakum ma wara'a dhalikum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24] there is an allusion to what has preceded regarding the forbidden women. ﴿That is for one who fears hardship (dhalika liman khashiya al-'anata)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25] is an allusion to marrying slave women.

Hyperbole (mubalagha) in magnifying and emphasizing the matter in His saying: ﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold (qintaran)﴾ [al-Nisa': 20]; he magnified the matter until one is restrained from it.

Metaphor (isti'ara) in His saying: ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant (mithaqan ghalidhan)﴾ [al-Nisa': 21]. He used "taking" for holding firmly to the covenant and adhering to it, whereas the covenant is a meaning in which taking cannot literally occur. And in: ﴿the Book of Allah upon you (kitab Allah 'alaykum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], i.e., the obligation of Allah, He used the word "Book" as a metaphor for the obligation, because of its establishment and affirmation, thereby indicating the intelligible meaning by means of a perceptible matter. And in: muhsinin ("chaste"), He used the word ihsan, which is "being secured in a fortified place for protection by punishment," and he used "pouring" (al-safh) for the great amount of adultery, which is the pouring of water into rivers and springs with rushing and speed. Likewise: ﴿then give them their wages (fa-atuhunna ujurahunna)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], he used the word ujur ("wages") for the dowries (muhur), and ajr is what indicates a deed, so he made the woman's enabling of the man to benefit from her as though it were a deed she performs. And in His saying: tawlan, there is a metaphor for the dower, by which one attains the goal; and tawl, which is bounty, by which one attains lofty affairs. And in His saying: ﴿those who follow the desires (yattabi'una al-shahawat)﴾, he used following and inclining, which are literally of physical things, for agreeing with the desire of the soul, which leads to going out from the truth. And in His saying: an yukhaffifa, the lightening (takhfif) originally derives from lightness of weight and heaviness of body, and lightening of obligations is the removal of their hardships from the soul, and that belongs to the realm of meanings.

Naming a thing by what it will become: in His saying: ﴿that you inherit women by compulsion﴾ [al-Nisa': 19], the marrying of women or preventing them from marrying was called inheritance, because that was the cause of inheritance in the Jahiliyya. And in His saying: ﴿and man was created weak (wa-khuliqa al-insanu da'ifan)﴾, He described him as weak by the name of what he becomes, or by the name of his origin.

Inner antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi) in His saying: ﴿perhaps you dislike a thing while Allah places in it much good﴾ [al-Nisa': 19]; and "much good" has been explained as what is beloved. And in His saying: ﴿and the chaste women among the women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], meaning: it is forbidden to you; then He said: ﴿and lawful for you﴾. What appears is that it is verbal antithesis (tibaq lafzi), because the beginning of the verse is ﴿forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], then He listed the forbidden women, then He said: ﴿and lawful for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]; this is the antithesis. And in His saying: ﴿chaste, not fornicating (muhsinin ghayra musafihin)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]: the muhsin is one who guards his private part, and the musafih is one who expends it.

Precaution (ihtiras) in His saying: ﴿those with whom you have consummated (allati dakhaltum bihinna)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], he guarded against those with whom there was no consummation; and in: ﴿and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship (wa-rabaibukumu allati fi hujurikum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], he guarded against those who are not in one's guardianship. And in His saying: ﴿and the chaste women among the women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], since "chaste women" may be intended as chaste persons, which would include men; so he guarded against this with His saying: "among the women."

Interjection (i'tiraD) in His saying: ﴿Allah knows best your faith; some of you are from others﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. And the omission (hadhf) in places where the meaning is not complete without it.

[p. 225]

﴿Allah desires to make clear to you and guide you to the ways of those before you, and to turn to you in forgiveness.﴾ The object of (yatuba, "to turn [in forgiveness]") is omitted, and its implied object is: "Allah desires [that He turn to you]." This is the view of Sibawayh, as Ibn 'Atiyyah relates. That is: permitting what He permitted, prohibiting what He prohibited, and legislating what has been mentioned. The meaning is: Allah desires to impose upon His servants the obligations He has imposed, as mentioned, in order to make clear to them, through their guidance, so the object of the desire is other than the act of making clear and what is conjoined to it. This is the view of the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun). According to them, the object of the desire cannot be "making clear," because that would require the verb to govern its later object through the particle lam, and would require the elision of (an) after a lam that is neither lam al-juhud (the lam of denial) nor lam kay (the lam of purpose). Both of these are impermissible in their view. The view of the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun) is that the object of the desire is the act of making clear, and that the lam itself is the particle that governs the subjunctive, not an elided (an) after it. Some Basran grammarians said: when something like this occurs, the verb preceding the lam is taken as a verbal noun (masdar). The reading is: "the desire of Allah for what He desires, in order to make clear." Similarly, "I desire that he not forget its mention," meaning: "my desire that he not forget its mention." Likewise the verse ﴿We were commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ (6:71), meaning: "We were commanded with what we were commanded, in order that we submit." End of quotation. Ibn 'Isa attributed this view to Sibawayh and the Basrans, and it is a matter discussed in the science of grammar (ilm al-nahw).

Al-Zamakhshari said: the original is "Allah desires that He make clear to you," and the lam was added to emphasize the desire for making clear, just as it is added in "la aba laka" (may you have no father) to emphasize the attribution of the father. The meaning: Allah desires that He make clear to you what has been hidden from you of your interests and the excellent deeds you should do. End of his words. This departs from the views of both the Basrans and the Kufans. As for it departing from the Basran view, it is because he made the lam an emphasizing and strengthening particle for the transitivity of (yurid, "desires"), with the object coming later, and he presumed an elided (an) after this lam. As for it departing from the Kufan view, they hold that the accusative is governed by the lam, not by (an), whereas he makes the accusative governed by an elided (an) after the lam. Some grammarians held that the lam in His saying "li-yubayyina lakum" (in order to make clear to you) is the lam of consequence (lam al-aqibah), and he said: as in His saying ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ (28:8). The object of (yubayyin, "makes clear") is not mentioned.

'Ata' said: He makes clear to you what brings you closer [to Him]. Abu al-Kalbi said: He makes clear to you that abstaining from marrying slave women is better. It was also said: what He has detailed of the prohibited and the permitted. It was said: the legislated laws of your religion and the interests of your affairs. It was said: the path of those before you to Paradise. In my opinion it is permissible that this be of the type of al-i'mal (the grammatical construction in which two verbs share one object), so that the object of (li-yubayyin) is an elided pronoun explained by the object of (wa-yahdiyakum), as in: "I struck and insulted Zayd," the reading being: "in order that He make them clear to you and guide you to the ways of those before you," that is, "in order that He make clear to you the ways of those before you."

The word (sunan) is the plural of (sunnah), which means "way" or "path." The scholars differed regarding His saying ﴿the ways of those before you﴾: is it to be taken literally, as guidance to their ways, or as a comparison, meaning ways like the ways of those before you? Whoever held the first view meant that the "ways" are what is forbidden to us and to them through lineage, nursing, and affinity by marriage. It was also said that what is meant by "sunan" is what is referred to in His saying ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth﴾ (16:123). It was said that what is meant is what He mentioned in His saying ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ (42:13). It was said: the paths of those before you to Paradise. It was said: the methods of those prophets and righteous people who came before you, and the ways they followed in their religion so that you might follow them. This is close to what preceded it. According to these views, "those before you" means the prophets and the people of goodness. It was said that what is meant by "sunan" is the paths of the people of goodness, guidance, and misguidance, and of those before you from the people of truth and falsehood, so that you might avoid falsehood and follow truth.

Those who held that this is a comparison said: the meaning is that the paths of the earlier nations in their guidance came through sending messengers, revealing scriptures, and explaining rulings. Likewise, your path was made [to follow the same pattern]. So He willed to guide you to the laws of your religion and the rulings of your community through clarification and detail, just as He guided the believers among those before you. It was also said: guidance is in one of two respects. First, we are addressed in every narrative with a prohibition or a command, just as they were addressed in their narratives, and what was legislated for us is as what was legislated for them. So our guidance is their path in instruction, even if our rulings and their rulings differ. The second respect: our guidance in their path is that we heard and obeyed just as they heard and obeyed, and so there is similarity from this aspect.

The meaning of guidance here is instruction and clarification, and no other meaning is appropriate, given the context of "sunan." The "those before us" are the believers from every legislation. The author of Rayy al-Zam'an, who is Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi, said: His saying ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ means: He desires to make clear, or He desires the sending down of verses in order to make clear to you. As for His saying "and guide you," the exegetes said that the two have the same meaning and the repetition is for emphasis. This is weak. The truth is that the first refers to making the obligations clear, and then He said "and guide you." There are two views on this. One is that this is evidence that everything He made clear to us as prohibited and permitted regarding women in the preceding verses was also the ruling in all the legislations, even though they differed in themselves but agreed in the matter of benefits. End of quotation. The meanings of these views he mentioned have already been given. His statement "i.e., He desires to make clear" agrees with the words of al-Zamakhshari.

﴿and to turn to you in forgiveness﴾: that is, He brings you back from disobedience to Him to obedience to Him, and enables you to achieve it.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾: All-Knowing of your conditions and of the legislations and interests that have preceded, All-Wise, who places things in their proper places according to wisdom and perfection.

﴿And Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness, but those who follow their desires desire that you deviate into a tremendous deviation﴾: The desire is first connected to the turning in forgiveness as a causal relation, according to what we have chosen among the views, because His saying "and turn to you" is conjoined to the cause, so it is a cause. Its connection here is as an object, so the two connections differ, and there is no repetition. Just as He willed the cause of repentance, He also willed repentance toward them, since it is possible to will the cause without the act itself. Whoever held that the object of the desire is one in both places would consider His saying "Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness" a repetition of His saying "and turn to you," because His saying "and turn to you" is conjoined to an object, so it is an object. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the repetition of Allah's desire for His servants to repent is a strengthening of the first report, and the purpose of the verse is nothing but reporting the desire of those who follow their desires. So Allah's desire was placed first as a preliminary, revealing the corruption of those who follow their desires. End of his words. He chose the view of the Kufans, in that they took His saying "li-yubayyin" to mean "an yubayyin" (that He make clear), so it is an object of (yurid), and "and turn" is conjoined to it, so it is an object like it. For this reason he said: the repetition of Allah's desire for His servants to repent, and so on to the end of his words. He had reported the view of the Kufans and said: this is weak, and then he returned in the end to what he had labeled weak. He had earlier stated that Sibawayh's view is that the object of (yurid) is elided, the reading being: "Allah desires this making clear."

The word (shahawat) is the plural of (shahwah), which is that to which the soul is strongly drawn by love and desire. Since the legal obligations involve restraining the soul and turning it away from what it craves, following its cravings becomes a cause of every blameworthiness. Those who disbelieve and those who are sinful are described as "followers of desires," as He said ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected prayer and followed desires, so they will meet misguidance﴾ (19:59). Following desire in every situation is blameworthy, because that is obeying it in whatever desire calls for. But if following is by way of reason or the law, then that is following them, not following desire. Those who follow desires here are the fornicators, according to Mujahid, or the Jews and Christians, according to al-Suddi. Or the Jews specifically, because they wished that the Muslims would follow them in marrying sisters from the father's side. Or the Magians, who permitted marrying sisters from the father's side, and marrying daughters of a brother and daughters of a sister. When Allah prohibited these, they said: you permit marrying the daughter of your maternal aunt and paternal aunt, while the paternal aunt is forbidden to you, so marry daughters of brothers and sisters. Or those who follow every desire, according to Ibn Zayd, which al-Tabari preferred. Its apparent meaning is generality and inclination. If it is unrestricted, then what is meant here is inclining away from truth, which is oppression and departing from the intended path. For this reason, the desire of Allah is contrasted with the desire of those who follow desires, and how vast is the difference between the two desires. He emphasized the verb of inclining with a verbal noun for the sake of exaggeration, and did not stop at describing it as great. This is because inclinations differ: a person may abandon a good deed due to some obstacle that occupied him, or due to laziness, or due to sinfulness that he enjoys, or due to error, by having a prior bad belief. The levels of treating these matters vary, some being easier than others. Therefore such people are described as great, since it is the furthest inclination to treat, which is disbelief, as He said ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve﴾ (4:89) and ﴿They desire that you go astray from the way﴾ (4:44).

The majority of readers recited "an tamilu" with the feminine second-person plural (you). It was also read with the third-person (ya'), referring to those who follow desires, so the pronoun in (yamilu) returns to "those who follow desires." The majority recited "maylan" with a sukun on the ya'. Al-Hasan recited it with a fatha on the ya'. The first sentence was nominal, and the second verbal, in order to show the emphasis of the first sentence, because the nominal form indicates stability more. The name of Allah the Exalted is repeated in it in the manner of explicit mention and pronoun. The second sentence came verbal, indicating renewal, because their desire renews at every time. The waw in His saying "wa-yurid" is for conjunction according to what we have established. Al-Raghib permitted that the waw be for the circumstantial (hal), not for conjunction. He said, to indicate that He desires to turn to you in forgiveness at the time you desire to incline, and so he differentiated between the two reports by placing the subject first in the first sentences and delaying it in the second sentence, to show that the second is not in conjunction. This is not good, because His desire to turn to us in forgiveness is not restricted to the desire of others for inclination, and because the present tense is preceded by waw, which is not permitted. Something rare of this occurs that is interpreted as an elided subject before it, which the Qur'an should not be made to bear, especially when the speech has a sound and eloquent meaning. So taking it as the rare case is forced and impermissible.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 26–28 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Allah desires to lighten (yukhaffifa) for you﴾. He did not mention what the lightening relates to (muta'allaq al-takhfif), and on this there are several views:

First, that it lies in permitting marriage to slave women and in the other concessions (rukhas).

Second, that it lies in not imposing the burden of deliberation and removing confusion regarding what He has made clear to you of what is lawful for you in marriage and what is not.

Third, that it lies in the removal of the heavy burden (al-isr) that was prescribed for those before us, and in the coming of this upright religion (al-milla al-hanifiyya) as easy and tolerant.

Fourth, that it lies in bringing you to the reward for what He has imposed on you of bearing obligations.

Fifth, that it lies in His lightening for you the sin of the sins you commit out of your ignorance.

They parsed this clause (jumla) as a circumstantial clause (hal) from His saying ﴿and Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness﴾, and the governing element (al-'amil) in the circumstantial clause is (yurid, "desires"), the implied sense being: "and Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness, desiring to lighten for you." This parsing (i'rab) is weak, because it has separated the governing element from the circumstantial clause by a conjoined clause (jumla ma'tufa) upon the clause in which the governing element is embedded, and that clause is foreign to both the governing element and the circumstantial clause. Therefore it should not be permitted except on the basis of a report from the Arabs. Also, the verb that occurs as the circumstantial clause has raised an apparent noun, whereas it should raise its pronoun, not its apparent noun, so it becomes like the example: "Zayd goes out" or "Zayd strikes 'Amr" [i.e., an improper construction]. [p. 228] What has been heard of such usage is only in the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ibtida'iyya) or in some of its abrogating particles (nawasikh). As for the circumstantial clause, I do not know of such usage. The permissibility of that in what has come is eloquent only where exaltation and magnification are intended, so that the linking (rabt) in the clause that stands as a predicate (khabar) is by an apparent noun. As for the circumstantial clause or the qualifying clause (sifa), linking by an apparent noun in it requires a report from the Arabs. The best view is that the clause is a resumptive (mustaanifa), and so has no place in the parsing. He, exalted is He, informed us of it regarding His will to lighten for us, as in His saying: ﴿Allah desires ease for you and does not desire hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 185].

﴿And man was created weak﴾. Mujahid, Tawus and Ibn Zayd said: the report about the weakness of man is only in the matter of women, meaning: since We knew your weakness regarding women, We lightened for you by permitting slave women. Tawus said: man is not weaker than he is in the matter of women. Ibn al-Musayyib said: Satan never despaired of the sons of Adam except that he came to them through women. Eighty years have passed over me, one of my eyes has gone, and I am in love with the other; and indeed the thing I most fear for myself is the temptation of women.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "weak," not able to hold back from desires and from the hardships of acts of obedience.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: then, after this aim, namely Allah's lightening by permitting slave women, the verse takes the form of an act of grace (tafaddul), because it encompasses everything that Allah has lightened for His servants and made the religion ease. The report about man's weakness occurs in a general sense, according to what is in himself of weakness, as his desire tends to draw him in most cases.

Al-Raghib said: describing man as having been created weak is only with regard to his being considered in relation to the exalted assembly (al-mala' al-a'la), like: ﴿Are you a harder creation, or is the sky?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27]; or with regard to himself apart from what comes to him of the overflow of Allah's grace and help; or in consideration of the multiplicity of his needs and the dependence of some of them upon others; or in consideration of his beginning and his end, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah is He who created you from weakness﴾ [al-Rum: 54]. But when he is considered in terms of his intellect and of the strength He gave him by which he is enabled to act as Allah's vicegerent on His earth, and by which in the Hereafter he reaches His nearness, then he is the strongest thing in this world. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have preferred them over many of those We created, with preference﴾ [al-Isra': 70].

Al-Hasan said: "weak" because he was created from a degraded water. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He who created you from weakness﴾ [al-Rum: 54].

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid read: wa-khalaqa al-insana (with the verb in the active voice), attributed to the pronoun of the name of Allah, and the accusative of da'ifan (weak) is as a circumstantial accusative (hal). It was also said: it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), because it can be estimated as with min ("from"), but this is not valid. It was also said: it is in the accusative by dropping the preposition (harf al-jarr), the estimate being: "from a weak thing," i.e., from clay, or from a drop, a clinging clot, and a lump of flesh. When the qualified noun and the governing particle are omitted, the qualifying adjective takes the accusative by the verb itself.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is also valid that khalaqa be understood in the sense of ja'ala ("made"), so that it gives the verb the capacity to govern two objects (maf'ulayn), and then His saying da'ifan is the second object. End of quotation.

This is what he mentioned, that khalaqa is transitive to two objects by taking it in the sense of ja'ala. I do not know of any grammarian who went to that view. Rather, what people have mentioned is that among the uses of ja'ala is that it may mean khalaqa and be transitive to one object, as in His saying: ﴿and He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. As for the reverse, no one, as far as we know, has held that view, and later scholars who investigated these verbs did not mention it.

These verses also contain kinds of rhetorical eloquence (bayan) and figurative embellishment (badi'). Among them:

Metonymy (tajawwuz) by using the name of the whole for a part, in His saying: ﴿they commit the indecency (al-fahisha)﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], because the definite article (al-) embraces every indecency, and that is not what is meant, but rather some of it. The name of the whole was applied to a part only to magnify its ugliness and foulness. If the usage for "indecency" is adultery, then this is not of this type, since the alif and lam would then be for a known reference (al-'ahd).

Metonymy by the intended sense of the absolute being a part of its denotation, in His saying: ﴿harm them (fa-adhuhuma)﴾, when it is explained as reproach or beating with sandals, or as bringing them together; and in His saying: ﴿a way (sabilan)﴾, the intended meaning being the prescribed punishment (hadd) or stoning of the married person (muhsan); and in His saying: ﴿turn away from them (fa-a'ridu 'anhuma)﴾ [al-Nisa': 16], i.e., leave them.

Attribution of a verb to other than its agent, in His saying: ﴿until death takes them (yatawaffahunna al-mawt)﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], and in His saying: ﴿when death comes to one of them (hadara ahadahumu al-mawt)﴾ [al-Nisa': 18].

Paronomasia of difference (tajnis mughayir) in: ﴿if they repent (in taba)﴾, and ﴿Allah is ever Relenting (tawwaban)﴾ [al-Nisa': 16]; and in: ﴿they nursed you (arda'nakum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23] and ﴿of nursing (min al-rada'a)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]; and in: muhsanat, "married women," and fa-idha uhsinna ("when they are married").

Paronomasia of likeness (tajnis mumathil) in: ﴿if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing﴾ [al-Nisa': 19], and in: ﴿do not marry what your fathers married (ma nakaha)﴾ [al-Nisa': 22].

[p. 229] Repetition (takrar) of the name of Allah in several places; and in: ﴿the repentance (al-tawba) is only﴾ [al-Nisa': 17], ﴿and repentance is not (al-tawba laysat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 18]; and in: ﴿one spouse in place of another spouse﴾ [al-Nisa': 20]; and in: "your mothers" (ummahatukum) and ﴿and your mothers, those who﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]; and in: ﴿except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa': 22]; and in: "the believing [women]" (al-mu'minat) in His saying: ﴿chaste believing women (al-muhsanat al-mu'minat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and in: ﴿your believing slave girls (fatayatikumu al-mu'minat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]; and in: farida ("obligation") and ﴿after the obligation (min ba'di al-farida)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]; and in: ﴿the chaste women among the women (al-muhsanat min al-nisa')﴾ [al-Nisa': 24] and "the chaste ones" (al-muhsanat); and ﴿half of what is upon the chaste ones (nisf ma 'ala al-muhsanat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]; and in: ﴿some of you are from some (ba'dukum min ba'd)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]; and in: "desires" (yurid) in four places; and in: "turns [in repentance]" (yatubu) and "to turn" (an yatuba); and in the use of the imperfect for the past, in: ﴿and those women who commit the indecency (wa-allati ya'tina al-fahisha)﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], and in: ﴿and the two of you who commit it among you (wa-alladhani ya'tiyaniha minkum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 16], and in: ﴿who do evil (ya'malun al-su')﴾ [al-Nisa': 17], and in: ﴿then they repent (thumma yatubuna)﴾, and in: "desires" (yurid), and in: ﴿that He may make clear (liyubayyina)﴾, because Allah's will and His making clear are both eternal (qadimani), since His making clear is in His revealed books, and will and speech are among the attributes of His essence, which are eternal.

Allusion (ishara) and hinting (iyma') in His saying: ﴿by compulsion (karhan)﴾, since the prohibition of inheriting women by compulsion alludes to its permissibility by consent; this is stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿if they give consent (fa-in tibna)﴾, and in His saying: ﴿do not hinder them in order that you may go away with part of what you have given them﴾ [al-Nisa': 19]. He may hinder her in another manner for a benefit connected to her or to her wealth. And in: ﴿indeed it was an indecency﴾ [al-Nisa': 22], it hints at the custom in the Jahiliyya of sons marrying their fathers' wives. In: ﴿lawful for you is what is beyond that (uhilla lakum ma wara'a dhalikum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24] there is an allusion to what has preceded regarding the forbidden women. ﴿That is for one who fears hardship (dhalika liman khashiya al-'anata)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25] is an allusion to marrying slave women.

Hyperbole (mubalagha) in magnifying and emphasizing the matter in His saying: ﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold (qintaran)﴾ [al-Nisa': 20]; he magnified the matter until one is restrained from it.

Metaphor (isti'ara) in His saying: ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant (mithaqan ghalidhan)﴾ [al-Nisa': 21]. He used "taking" for holding firmly to the covenant and adhering to it, whereas the covenant is a meaning in which taking cannot literally occur. And in: ﴿the Book of Allah upon you (kitab Allah 'alaykum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], i.e., the obligation of Allah, He used the word "Book" as a metaphor for the obligation, because of its establishment and affirmation, thereby indicating the intelligible meaning by means of a perceptible matter. And in: muhsinin ("chaste"), He used the word ihsan, which is "being secured in a fortified place for protection by punishment," and he used "pouring" (al-safh) for the great amount of adultery, which is the pouring of water into rivers and springs with rushing and speed. Likewise: ﴿then give them their wages (fa-atuhunna ujurahunna)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], he used the word ujur ("wages") for the dowries (muhur), and ajr is what indicates a deed, so he made the woman's enabling of the man to benefit from her as though it were a deed she performs. And in His saying: tawlan, there is a metaphor for the dower, by which one attains the goal; and tawl, which is bounty, by which one attains lofty affairs. And in His saying: ﴿those who follow the desires (yattabi'una al-shahawat)﴾, he used following and inclining, which are literally of physical things, for agreeing with the desire of the soul, which leads to going out from the truth. And in His saying: an yukhaffifa, the lightening (takhfif) originally derives from lightness of weight and heaviness of body, and lightening of obligations is the removal of their hardships from the soul, and that belongs to the realm of meanings.

Naming a thing by what it will become: in His saying: ﴿that you inherit women by compulsion﴾ [al-Nisa': 19], the marrying of women or preventing them from marrying was called inheritance, because that was the cause of inheritance in the Jahiliyya. And in His saying: ﴿and man was created weak (wa-khuliqa al-insanu da'ifan)﴾, He described him as weak by the name of what he becomes, or by the name of his origin.

Inner antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi) in His saying: ﴿perhaps you dislike a thing while Allah places in it much good﴾ [al-Nisa': 19]; and "much good" has been explained as what is beloved. And in His saying: ﴿and the chaste women among the women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], meaning: it is forbidden to you; then He said: ﴿and lawful for you﴾. What appears is that it is verbal antithesis (tibaq lafzi), because the beginning of the verse is ﴿forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], then He listed the forbidden women, then He said: ﴿and lawful for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]; this is the antithesis. And in His saying: ﴿chaste, not fornicating (muhsinin ghayra musafihin)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]: the muhsin is one who guards his private part, and the musafih is one who expends it.

Precaution (ihtiras) in His saying: ﴿those with whom you have consummated (allati dakhaltum bihinna)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], he guarded against those with whom there was no consummation; and in: ﴿and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship (wa-rabaibukumu allati fi hujurikum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], he guarded against those who are not in one's guardianship. And in His saying: ﴿and the chaste women among the women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], since "chaste women" may be intended as chaste persons, which would include men; so he guarded against this with His saying: "among the women."

Interjection (i'tiraD) in His saying: ﴿Allah knows best your faith; some of you are from others﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. And the omission (hadhf) in places where the meaning is not complete without it.

[p. 225]

﴿Allah desires to make clear to you and guide you to the ways of those before you, and to turn to you in forgiveness.﴾ The object of (yatuba, "to turn [in forgiveness]") is omitted, and its implied object is: "Allah desires [that He turn to you]." This is the view of Sibawayh, as Ibn 'Atiyyah relates. That is: permitting what He permitted, prohibiting what He prohibited, and legislating what has been mentioned. The meaning is: Allah desires to impose upon His servants the obligations He has imposed, as mentioned, in order to make clear to them, through their guidance, so the object of the desire is other than the act of making clear and what is conjoined to it. This is the view of the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun). According to them, the object of the desire cannot be "making clear," because that would require the verb to govern its later object through the particle lam, and would require the elision of (an) after a lam that is neither lam al-juhud (the lam of denial) nor lam kay (the lam of purpose). Both of these are impermissible in their view. The view of the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun) is that the object of the desire is the act of making clear, and that the lam itself is the particle that governs the subjunctive, not an elided (an) after it. Some Basran grammarians said: when something like this occurs, the verb preceding the lam is taken as a verbal noun (masdar). The reading is: "the desire of Allah for what He desires, in order to make clear." Similarly, "I desire that he not forget its mention," meaning: "my desire that he not forget its mention." Likewise the verse ﴿We were commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ (6:71), meaning: "We were commanded with what we were commanded, in order that we submit." End of quotation. Ibn 'Isa attributed this view to Sibawayh and the Basrans, and it is a matter discussed in the science of grammar (ilm al-nahw).

Al-Zamakhshari said: the original is "Allah desires that He make clear to you," and the lam was added to emphasize the desire for making clear, just as it is added in "la aba laka" (may you have no father) to emphasize the attribution of the father. The meaning: Allah desires that He make clear to you what has been hidden from you of your interests and the excellent deeds you should do. End of his words. This departs from the views of both the Basrans and the Kufans. As for it departing from the Basran view, it is because he made the lam an emphasizing and strengthening particle for the transitivity of (yurid, "desires"), with the object coming later, and he presumed an elided (an) after this lam. As for it departing from the Kufan view, they hold that the accusative is governed by the lam, not by (an), whereas he makes the accusative governed by an elided (an) after the lam. Some grammarians held that the lam in His saying "li-yubayyina lakum" (in order to make clear to you) is the lam of consequence (lam al-aqibah), and he said: as in His saying ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ (28:8). The object of (yubayyin, "makes clear") is not mentioned.

'Ata' said: He makes clear to you what brings you closer [to Him]. Abu al-Kalbi said: He makes clear to you that abstaining from marrying slave women is better. It was also said: what He has detailed of the prohibited and the permitted. It was said: the legislated laws of your religion and the interests of your affairs. It was said: the path of those before you to Paradise. In my opinion it is permissible that this be of the type of al-i'mal (the grammatical construction in which two verbs share one object), so that the object of (li-yubayyin) is an elided pronoun explained by the object of (wa-yahdiyakum), as in: "I struck and insulted Zayd," the reading being: "in order that He make them clear to you and guide you to the ways of those before you," that is, "in order that He make clear to you the ways of those before you."

The word (sunan) is the plural of (sunnah), which means "way" or "path." The scholars differed regarding His saying ﴿the ways of those before you﴾: is it to be taken literally, as guidance to their ways, or as a comparison, meaning ways like the ways of those before you? Whoever held the first view meant that the "ways" are what is forbidden to us and to them through lineage, nursing, and affinity by marriage. It was also said that what is meant by "sunan" is what is referred to in His saying ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth﴾ (16:123). It was said that what is meant is what He mentioned in His saying ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ (42:13). It was said: the paths of those before you to Paradise. It was said: the methods of those prophets and righteous people who came before you, and the ways they followed in their religion so that you might follow them. This is close to what preceded it. According to these views, "those before you" means the prophets and the people of goodness. It was said that what is meant by "sunan" is the paths of the people of goodness, guidance, and misguidance, and of those before you from the people of truth and falsehood, so that you might avoid falsehood and follow truth.

Those who held that this is a comparison said: the meaning is that the paths of the earlier nations in their guidance came through sending messengers, revealing scriptures, and explaining rulings. Likewise, your path was made [to follow the same pattern]. So He willed to guide you to the laws of your religion and the rulings of your community through clarification and detail, just as He guided the believers among those before you. It was also said: guidance is in one of two respects. First, we are addressed in every narrative with a prohibition or a command, just as they were addressed in their narratives, and what was legislated for us is as what was legislated for them. So our guidance is their path in instruction, even if our rulings and their rulings differ. The second respect: our guidance in their path is that we heard and obeyed just as they heard and obeyed, and so there is similarity from this aspect.

The meaning of guidance here is instruction and clarification, and no other meaning is appropriate, given the context of "sunan." The "those before us" are the believers from every legislation. The author of Rayy al-Zam'an, who is Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi, said: His saying ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ means: He desires to make clear, or He desires the sending down of verses in order to make clear to you. As for His saying "and guide you," the exegetes said that the two have the same meaning and the repetition is for emphasis. This is weak. The truth is that the first refers to making the obligations clear, and then He said "and guide you." There are two views on this. One is that this is evidence that everything He made clear to us as prohibited and permitted regarding women in the preceding verses was also the ruling in all the legislations, even though they differed in themselves but agreed in the matter of benefits. End of quotation. The meanings of these views he mentioned have already been given. His statement "i.e., He desires to make clear" agrees with the words of al-Zamakhshari.

﴿and to turn to you in forgiveness﴾: that is, He brings you back from disobedience to Him to obedience to Him, and enables you to achieve it.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾: All-Knowing of your conditions and of the legislations and interests that have preceded, All-Wise, who places things in their proper places according to wisdom and perfection.

﴿And Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness, but those who follow their desires desire that you deviate into a tremendous deviation﴾: The desire is first connected to the turning in forgiveness as a causal relation, according to what we have chosen among the views, because His saying "and turn to you" is conjoined to the cause, so it is a cause. Its connection here is as an object, so the two connections differ, and there is no repetition. Just as He willed the cause of repentance, He also willed repentance toward them, since it is possible to will the cause without the act itself. Whoever held that the object of the desire is one in both places would consider His saying "Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness" a repetition of His saying "and turn to you," because His saying "and turn to you" is conjoined to an object, so it is an object. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the repetition of Allah's desire for His servants to repent is a strengthening of the first report, and the purpose of the verse is nothing but reporting the desire of those who follow their desires. So Allah's desire was placed first as a preliminary, revealing the corruption of those who follow their desires. End of his words. He chose the view of the Kufans, in that they took His saying "li-yubayyin" to mean "an yubayyin" (that He make clear), so it is an object of (yurid), and "and turn" is conjoined to it, so it is an object like it. For this reason he said: the repetition of Allah's desire for His servants to repent, and so on to the end of his words. He had reported the view of the Kufans and said: this is weak, and then he returned in the end to what he had labeled weak. He had earlier stated that Sibawayh's view is that the object of (yurid) is elided, the reading being: "Allah desires this making clear."

The word (shahawat) is the plural of (shahwah), which is that to which the soul is strongly drawn by love and desire. Since the legal obligations involve restraining the soul and turning it away from what it craves, following its cravings becomes a cause of every blameworthiness. Those who disbelieve and those who are sinful are described as "followers of desires," as He said ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected prayer and followed desires, so they will meet misguidance﴾ (19:59). Following desire in every situation is blameworthy, because that is obeying it in whatever desire calls for. But if following is by way of reason or the law, then that is following them, not following desire. Those who follow desires here are the fornicators, according to Mujahid, or the Jews and Christians, according to al-Suddi. Or the Jews specifically, because they wished that the Muslims would follow them in marrying sisters from the father's side. Or the Magians, who permitted marrying sisters from the father's side, and marrying daughters of a brother and daughters of a sister. When Allah prohibited these, they said: you permit marrying the daughter of your maternal aunt and paternal aunt, while the paternal aunt is forbidden to you, so marry daughters of brothers and sisters. Or those who follow every desire, according to Ibn Zayd, which al-Tabari preferred. Its apparent meaning is generality and inclination. If it is unrestricted, then what is meant here is inclining away from truth, which is oppression and departing from the intended path. For this reason, the desire of Allah is contrasted with the desire of those who follow desires, and how vast is the difference between the two desires. He emphasized the verb of inclining with a verbal noun for the sake of exaggeration, and did not stop at describing it as great. This is because inclinations differ: a person may abandon a good deed due to some obstacle that occupied him, or due to laziness, or due to sinfulness that he enjoys, or due to error, by having a prior bad belief. The levels of treating these matters vary, some being easier than others. Therefore such people are described as great, since it is the furthest inclination to treat, which is disbelief, as He said ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve﴾ (4:89) and ﴿They desire that you go astray from the way﴾ (4:44).

The majority of readers recited "an tamilu" with the feminine second-person plural (you). It was also read with the third-person (ya'), referring to those who follow desires, so the pronoun in (yamilu) returns to "those who follow desires." The majority recited "maylan" with a sukun on the ya'. Al-Hasan recited it with a fatha on the ya'. The first sentence was nominal, and the second verbal, in order to show the emphasis of the first sentence, because the nominal form indicates stability more. The name of Allah the Exalted is repeated in it in the manner of explicit mention and pronoun. The second sentence came verbal, indicating renewal, because their desire renews at every time. The waw in His saying "wa-yurid" is for conjunction according to what we have established. Al-Raghib permitted that the waw be for the circumstantial (hal), not for conjunction. He said, to indicate that He desires to turn to you in forgiveness at the time you desire to incline, and so he differentiated between the two reports by placing the subject first in the first sentences and delaying it in the second sentence, to show that the second is not in conjunction. This is not good, because His desire to turn to us in forgiveness is not restricted to the desire of others for inclination, and because the present tense is preceded by waw, which is not permitted. Something rare of this occurs that is interpreted as an elided subject before it, which the Qur'an should not be made to bear, especially when the speech has a sound and eloquent meaning. So taking it as the rare case is forced and impermissible.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 26–28 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Allah desires to lighten (yukhaffifa) for you﴾. He did not mention what the lightening relates to (muta'allaq al-takhfif), and on this there are several views:

First, that it lies in permitting marriage to slave women and in the other concessions (rukhas).

Second, that it lies in not imposing the burden of deliberation and removing confusion regarding what He has made clear to you of what is lawful for you in marriage and what is not.

Third, that it lies in the removal of the heavy burden (al-isr) that was prescribed for those before us, and in the coming of this upright religion (al-milla al-hanifiyya) as easy and tolerant.

Fourth, that it lies in bringing you to the reward for what He has imposed on you of bearing obligations.

Fifth, that it lies in His lightening for you the sin of the sins you commit out of your ignorance.

They parsed this clause (jumla) as a circumstantial clause (hal) from His saying ﴿and Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness﴾, and the governing element (al-'amil) in the circumstantial clause is (yurid, "desires"), the implied sense being: "and Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness, desiring to lighten for you." This parsing (i'rab) is weak, because it has separated the governing element from the circumstantial clause by a conjoined clause (jumla ma'tufa) upon the clause in which the governing element is embedded, and that clause is foreign to both the governing element and the circumstantial clause. Therefore it should not be permitted except on the basis of a report from the Arabs. Also, the verb that occurs as the circumstantial clause has raised an apparent noun, whereas it should raise its pronoun, not its apparent noun, so it becomes like the example: "Zayd goes out" or "Zayd strikes 'Amr" [i.e., an improper construction]. [p. 228] What has been heard of such usage is only in the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ibtida'iyya) or in some of its abrogating particles (nawasikh). As for the circumstantial clause, I do not know of such usage. The permissibility of that in what has come is eloquent only where exaltation and magnification are intended, so that the linking (rabt) in the clause that stands as a predicate (khabar) is by an apparent noun. As for the circumstantial clause or the qualifying clause (sifa), linking by an apparent noun in it requires a report from the Arabs. The best view is that the clause is a resumptive (mustaanifa), and so has no place in the parsing. He, exalted is He, informed us of it regarding His will to lighten for us, as in His saying: ﴿Allah desires ease for you and does not desire hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 185].

﴿And man was created weak﴾. Mujahid, Tawus and Ibn Zayd said: the report about the weakness of man is only in the matter of women, meaning: since We knew your weakness regarding women, We lightened for you by permitting slave women. Tawus said: man is not weaker than he is in the matter of women. Ibn al-Musayyib said: Satan never despaired of the sons of Adam except that he came to them through women. Eighty years have passed over me, one of my eyes has gone, and I am in love with the other; and indeed the thing I most fear for myself is the temptation of women.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "weak," not able to hold back from desires and from the hardships of acts of obedience.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: then, after this aim, namely Allah's lightening by permitting slave women, the verse takes the form of an act of grace (tafaddul), because it encompasses everything that Allah has lightened for His servants and made the religion ease. The report about man's weakness occurs in a general sense, according to what is in himself of weakness, as his desire tends to draw him in most cases.

Al-Raghib said: describing man as having been created weak is only with regard to his being considered in relation to the exalted assembly (al-mala' al-a'la), like: ﴿Are you a harder creation, or is the sky?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27]; or with regard to himself apart from what comes to him of the overflow of Allah's grace and help; or in consideration of the multiplicity of his needs and the dependence of some of them upon others; or in consideration of his beginning and his end, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah is He who created you from weakness﴾ [al-Rum: 54]. But when he is considered in terms of his intellect and of the strength He gave him by which he is enabled to act as Allah's vicegerent on His earth, and by which in the Hereafter he reaches His nearness, then he is the strongest thing in this world. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have preferred them over many of those We created, with preference﴾ [al-Isra': 70].

Al-Hasan said: "weak" because he was created from a degraded water. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He who created you from weakness﴾ [al-Rum: 54].

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid read: wa-khalaqa al-insana (with the verb in the active voice), attributed to the pronoun of the name of Allah, and the accusative of da'ifan (weak) is as a circumstantial accusative (hal). It was also said: it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), because it can be estimated as with min ("from"), but this is not valid. It was also said: it is in the accusative by dropping the preposition (harf al-jarr), the estimate being: "from a weak thing," i.e., from clay, or from a drop, a clinging clot, and a lump of flesh. When the qualified noun and the governing particle are omitted, the qualifying adjective takes the accusative by the verb itself.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is also valid that khalaqa be understood in the sense of ja'ala ("made"), so that it gives the verb the capacity to govern two objects (maf'ulayn), and then His saying da'ifan is the second object. End of quotation.

This is what he mentioned, that khalaqa is transitive to two objects by taking it in the sense of ja'ala. I do not know of any grammarian who went to that view. Rather, what people have mentioned is that among the uses of ja'ala is that it may mean khalaqa and be transitive to one object, as in His saying: ﴿and He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. As for the reverse, no one, as far as we know, has held that view, and later scholars who investigated these verbs did not mention it.

These verses also contain kinds of rhetorical eloquence (bayan) and figurative embellishment (badi'). Among them:

Metonymy (tajawwuz) by using the name of the whole for a part, in His saying: ﴿they commit the indecency (al-fahisha)﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], because the definite article (al-) embraces every indecency, and that is not what is meant, but rather some of it. The name of the whole was applied to a part only to magnify its ugliness and foulness. If the usage for "indecency" is adultery, then this is not of this type, since the alif and lam would then be for a known reference (al-'ahd).

Metonymy by the intended sense of the absolute being a part of its denotation, in His saying: ﴿harm them (fa-adhuhuma)﴾, when it is explained as reproach or beating with sandals, or as bringing them together; and in His saying: ﴿a way (sabilan)﴾, the intended meaning being the prescribed punishment (hadd) or stoning of the married person (muhsan); and in His saying: ﴿turn away from them (fa-a'ridu 'anhuma)﴾ [al-Nisa': 16], i.e., leave them.

Attribution of a verb to other than its agent, in His saying: ﴿until death takes them (yatawaffahunna al-mawt)﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], and in His saying: ﴿when death comes to one of them (hadara ahadahumu al-mawt)﴾ [al-Nisa': 18].

Paronomasia of difference (tajnis mughayir) in: ﴿if they repent (in taba)﴾, and ﴿Allah is ever Relenting (tawwaban)﴾ [al-Nisa': 16]; and in: ﴿they nursed you (arda'nakum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23] and ﴿of nursing (min al-rada'a)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]; and in: muhsanat, "married women," and fa-idha uhsinna ("when they are married").

Paronomasia of likeness (tajnis mumathil) in: ﴿if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing﴾ [al-Nisa': 19], and in: ﴿do not marry what your fathers married (ma nakaha)﴾ [al-Nisa': 22].

[p. 229] Repetition (takrar) of the name of Allah in several places; and in: ﴿the repentance (al-tawba) is only﴾ [al-Nisa': 17], ﴿and repentance is not (al-tawba laysat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 18]; and in: ﴿one spouse in place of another spouse﴾ [al-Nisa': 20]; and in: "your mothers" (ummahatukum) and ﴿and your mothers, those who﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]; and in: ﴿except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa': 22]; and in: "the believing [women]" (al-mu'minat) in His saying: ﴿chaste believing women (al-muhsanat al-mu'minat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and in: ﴿your believing slave girls (fatayatikumu al-mu'minat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]; and in: farida ("obligation") and ﴿after the obligation (min ba'di al-farida)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]; and in: ﴿the chaste women among the women (al-muhsanat min al-nisa')﴾ [al-Nisa': 24] and "the chaste ones" (al-muhsanat); and ﴿half of what is upon the chaste ones (nisf ma 'ala al-muhsanat)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]; and in: ﴿some of you are from some (ba'dukum min ba'd)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]; and in: "desires" (yurid) in four places; and in: "turns [in repentance]" (yatubu) and "to turn" (an yatuba); and in the use of the imperfect for the past, in: ﴿and those women who commit the indecency (wa-allati ya'tina al-fahisha)﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], and in: ﴿and the two of you who commit it among you (wa-alladhani ya'tiyaniha minkum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 16], and in: ﴿who do evil (ya'malun al-su')﴾ [al-Nisa': 17], and in: ﴿then they repent (thumma yatubuna)﴾, and in: "desires" (yurid), and in: ﴿that He may make clear (liyubayyina)﴾, because Allah's will and His making clear are both eternal (qadimani), since His making clear is in His revealed books, and will and speech are among the attributes of His essence, which are eternal.

Allusion (ishara) and hinting (iyma') in His saying: ﴿by compulsion (karhan)﴾, since the prohibition of inheriting women by compulsion alludes to its permissibility by consent; this is stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿if they give consent (fa-in tibna)﴾, and in His saying: ﴿do not hinder them in order that you may go away with part of what you have given them﴾ [al-Nisa': 19]. He may hinder her in another manner for a benefit connected to her or to her wealth. And in: ﴿indeed it was an indecency﴾ [al-Nisa': 22], it hints at the custom in the Jahiliyya of sons marrying their fathers' wives. In: ﴿lawful for you is what is beyond that (uhilla lakum ma wara'a dhalikum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24] there is an allusion to what has preceded regarding the forbidden women. ﴿That is for one who fears hardship (dhalika liman khashiya al-'anata)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25] is an allusion to marrying slave women.

Hyperbole (mubalagha) in magnifying and emphasizing the matter in His saying: ﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold (qintaran)﴾ [al-Nisa': 20]; he magnified the matter until one is restrained from it.

Metaphor (isti'ara) in His saying: ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant (mithaqan ghalidhan)﴾ [al-Nisa': 21]. He used "taking" for holding firmly to the covenant and adhering to it, whereas the covenant is a meaning in which taking cannot literally occur. And in: ﴿the Book of Allah upon you (kitab Allah 'alaykum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], i.e., the obligation of Allah, He used the word "Book" as a metaphor for the obligation, because of its establishment and affirmation, thereby indicating the intelligible meaning by means of a perceptible matter. And in: muhsinin ("chaste"), He used the word ihsan, which is "being secured in a fortified place for protection by punishment," and he used "pouring" (al-safh) for the great amount of adultery, which is the pouring of water into rivers and springs with rushing and speed. Likewise: ﴿then give them their wages (fa-atuhunna ujurahunna)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], he used the word ujur ("wages") for the dowries (muhur), and ajr is what indicates a deed, so he made the woman's enabling of the man to benefit from her as though it were a deed she performs. And in His saying: tawlan, there is a metaphor for the dower, by which one attains the goal; and tawl, which is bounty, by which one attains lofty affairs. And in His saying: ﴿those who follow the desires (yattabi'una al-shahawat)﴾, he used following and inclining, which are literally of physical things, for agreeing with the desire of the soul, which leads to going out from the truth. And in His saying: an yukhaffifa, the lightening (takhfif) originally derives from lightness of weight and heaviness of body, and lightening of obligations is the removal of their hardships from the soul, and that belongs to the realm of meanings.

Naming a thing by what it will become: in His saying: ﴿that you inherit women by compulsion﴾ [al-Nisa': 19], the marrying of women or preventing them from marrying was called inheritance, because that was the cause of inheritance in the Jahiliyya. And in His saying: ﴿and man was created weak (wa-khuliqa al-insanu da'ifan)﴾, He described him as weak by the name of what he becomes, or by the name of his origin.

Inner antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi) in His saying: ﴿perhaps you dislike a thing while Allah places in it much good﴾ [al-Nisa': 19]; and "much good" has been explained as what is beloved. And in His saying: ﴿and the chaste women among the women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], meaning: it is forbidden to you; then He said: ﴿and lawful for you﴾. What appears is that it is verbal antithesis (tibaq lafzi), because the beginning of the verse is ﴿forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], then He listed the forbidden women, then He said: ﴿and lawful for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]; this is the antithesis. And in His saying: ﴿chaste, not fornicating (muhsinin ghayra musafihin)﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]: the muhsin is one who guards his private part, and the musafih is one who expends it.

Precaution (ihtiras) in His saying: ﴿those with whom you have consummated (allati dakhaltum bihinna)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], he guarded against those with whom there was no consummation; and in: ﴿and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship (wa-rabaibukumu allati fi hujurikum)﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], he guarded against those who are not in one's guardianship. And in His saying: ﴿and the chaste women among the women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], since "chaste women" may be intended as chaste persons, which would include men; so he guarded against this with His saying: "among the women."

Interjection (i'tiraD) in His saying: ﴿Allah knows best your faith; some of you are from others﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. And the omission (hadhf) in places where the meaning is not complete without it.

[p. 230]

**The neighbour (al-jar):** the one who lives near your dwelling. Its *alif* is converted from a *waw*, as shown by their saying *jawartu* ("I lived as a neighbour"). It is pluralised as *jiran* and *jirah*. **Al-junub** means "the distant one." **Al-janabah** means "distance." He said:

*So do not deprive me of a gift out of distance, for I am a man, a stranger amid the tents.*

It derives from *al-ijtinab*, which is to leave a man to one side. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and keep me away﴾ (Ibrahim 14:35), meaning "distance me." It is a descriptive form on the pattern *fi'l*, like *naqah sarah* (a she-camel that roams freely).

**Al-mukhtal:** the arrogant one. It is the active participle of *ikhtala*, and its *alif* is converted from a *ya'*, as shown by their words *al-khuyala'* and *al-makhilah*. It is said: "*Khala al-rajul yakhulu khawlan*" when a man became proud and was pleased with himself. This would be a separate root, because the former is built from *khayal* (kh-y-l), while this is from *khawl* (kh-w-l). **Al-fakhur** is on the form *fa'ul* from *fakhara*. *Al-fakhr* is the enumeration of virtues with boastfulness and haughtiness.

**Al-qarin:** on the form *fa'il* meaning *mufa'il*, from *qaranahu* when he kept close to him and mixed with him. From it the wife is called *qarinah*. From it it is said of the camels and cattle that stay together that they are *qarinan*, and the rope with which they are tied together is a *qarn*. The poet said:

*And the son of a camel that is weaned, when he is bound in a rope, cannot withstand the charge of the stout, fierce camels.*

He also said:

*Like one who puts his head in, but none brings it near from the two yoked animals until the rope binds it.*

﴿O you who believe, do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood⦆ The explanation of the like of this sentence has already been given in His saying: ﴿and do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood, nor send it down to the authorities﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:188). The connection of this verse with what precedes it is as follows: when He, exalted is He, explained the manner of dealing with persons through marriage, He explained the manner of dealing with wealth that leads to marriage and to ownership by right hand, and that the dowries and prices paid in that are not to be acquired by falsehood. *Al-batil* (falsehood) is every means the Shariah has not permitted. It therefore includes theft, embezzlement, usurpation, gambling, usurious contracts, and the prices of invalid sales. It includes *bay' al-'urban* (the down-payment sale), which is that a man takes the commodity from you, rents the animal, and gives a dirham, for example, as *'urban* (earnest money). If he buys or rides, the dirham is part of the price of the commodity or the rent; otherwise it belongs to the seller. This is not valid and not permitted according to the majority of jurists, because it falls under consuming wealth by falsehood. A group, including Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Nafi' ibn 'Ubayd, and Zayd ibn Aslam, permitted the *bay' al-'urban* as described, and the proofs are in the books of jurisprudence.

The early scholars differed in explaining His saying *bil-batil* (in falsehood). Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: it is that he consumes it without an exchange. On this explanation Ibn 'Abbas said: the verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*, i.e. superseded by a later ruling), since consuming wealth without exchange is permissible when it is a gift, a charity, a grant of ownership, an inheritance, or something similar that the Shariah has permitted to be taken without exchange. Al-Suddi said: it is that he consumes by usury, gambling, defrauding, injustice, and other things by which Allah, exalted is He, has not permitted the consumption of wealth. On this explanation the verse is *muhkamah* (unabrogated), and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and the majority. Some said: the verse is *mujmalah* (general, requiring detail), because the meaning of His saying *bil-batil* is "by an unlawful way." Since this lawful way is not mentioned here in detail, the verse became general. The attribution of the wealth to the addressees means: the wealth of some of you, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿of what your right hands possess﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:25), and His saying: ﴿do not kill yourselves﴾. It was also said: His saying *amwalukum* (your wealth) includes the wealth of others and one's own wealth. So He forbade him to consume the wealth of another except by a lawful way, and forbade him to consume his own wealth by falsehood, which is spending it in disobedience to Allah, exalted is He. He expressed the taking of wealth here by "consuming," because consumption is one of the most prominent and most necessary of its purposes.

* *

﴿except that it be a trade by mutual consent from among you⦆ This is an exceptive clause that is *munqati'* (disconnected) for two reasons. First, trade is not included among the wealth consumed by falsehood, so that it could be excepted from it, whether you explain His saying *bil-batil* as "without exchange," as Ibn 'Abbas said, or as "by an unlawful way," as others said. Second, the exception falls only on the *kawn* (the being/occurrence), and *kawn* is one of the meanings and not a piece of wealth. Whoever holds that it is a *muttasil* (connected) exception is not correct, for the reason we have mentioned. This disconnected exception does not indicate restriction, in the sense that consuming wealth is permitted only through trade alone. Rather, it mentions the most common type of consuming wealth, which is trade, since most sources of livelihood are connected with it.

In His saying *'an taradin* (by mutual consent) there is an indication that whatever takes the form of trade requires mutual consent, and this comes from two parties: the one who pays the price and the seller of the item. Nothing other than mutual consent is mentioned in the verse. On this basis, the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that if he sold something worth a hundred for a dirham, it is permitted if they both consent to that, whether or not he knew the actual value. A group said: if he does not know the amount of the loss and it exceeds one third, the sale is rescinded. Its apparent meaning indicates that if they contract by words, that is mutual consent from both of them, and there is no option (*khiyar*) for either of them, even if they do not separate. Abu Hanifah and Malik held this view, and something similar is narrated from 'Umar. al-Thawri, al-Layth, 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan, and al-Shafi'i said: if they have concluded the contract, they have an option as long as they have not separated. They excepted cases in which separation is not required, and they differed about separation. It was said: separation is that each of them withdraws from the other. al-Layth said: it is by each of them rising from the session. Everyone who established the option of the session says: if one gives the other the choice in the session and he chooses, the sale becomes binding. The option of the session is also narrated from 'Umar. The commentators went at length in presenting the arguments for each of these schools, and the subject belongs in the books of jurisprudence.

*Tijarah* (trade) is a term applied to contracts of exchange whose purpose is seeking profits. The word *an takuna* is in the accusative position, meaning "but," i.e., "but the being of trade by mutual consent is not forbidden." The Kufans read *tijaratan* with the accusative, on the basis that *takuna* is *naqisah* (incomplete, i.e., requires a predicate), with a hidden pronoun in it that refers to the wealth, or that is explained by the word *tijaratan*. The meaning would be: "except that the wealth be a trade," or "except that the trade be a trade by mutual consent from you," as the poet said: *"If it is a day with a star, a bright one"*, meaning "if my day today is a day with a star." Abu 'Ubayd chose the Kufans' reading. The remaining seven read *tijaratun* with the nominative, on the basis that *kana* is *tammah* (complete, i.e., does not require a predicate). Makki ibn Abi Talib said: the most common usage in Arabic speech is that their saying *illa an takuna* in the exception, without a pronoun in it, means "happens" or "occurs." This conflicts with Abu 'Ubayd's preference. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the completeness of *kana* is preferred by some, because it is a *silah* (a connecting element), so it is lowered from its rank when it is free of a *silah* and other things. This is a preference that is not strong, but it is good. This is the end of what he mentioned. This statement requires reflection, and perhaps something was lost from the copy that would make clear the meaning he intended. *'An taradin* (by mutual consent) is a qualifier of *tijarah*, meaning: a trade issuing from mutual consent.

* *

﴿and do not kill yourselves⦆ Its apparent meaning is the prohibition of a person killing himself, as some ignorant people do deliberately, or by exposing himself to a hazard by which he dies, as some rebels against kings do, for they kill the king and are killed without doubt. 'Amr ibn al-'As argued with this verse when he refrained from bathing in cold water, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approved his argument. It was said: it may be that the meaning is: do not do what makes you deserving of being killed, such as killing, apostasy, and adultery after being married. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the interpreters are agreed that the intent is the prohibition of some people killing others. al-Zamakhshari, citing al-Hasan, said: the meaning is "do not kill your brothers." On this meaning He attributed the killing to their selves, because they are like one soul, or of one kind, or of one substance, and because when one kills, he is killed in retaliation, as if he had killed himself. What Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned about the agreement of the interpreters, others have noted disagreement about. He said, in a summary: it may be that the literal meaning of killing is intended, so the meaning may be: let none of you kill another. It may be that the meaning is: let no one kill himself because of harm that befalls him, or injustice that afflicts him, or a wound that takes him out of the limit of uprightness. It may also be that the figurative meaning of killing is intended, that is: he consumes wealth by falsehood, or by pursuing wealth and being absorbed in it, or he puts himself at risk leading to destruction, or by committing these sins and persisting in them. Thus "killing" is used as a figure of speech for destruction, as in the saying: "A witness killed three: himself, the one he testified for, and the one he testified against," meaning: he destroyed. 'Ali and al-Hasan read *wa-la taqtulu* with the intensive form (*taqtilu*).

* *

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you⦆ in that He forbade you from destroying souls and from consuming the unlawful, and explained to you the avenue of lawfulness, which should be the foundation of the souls' sustenance and life through what is earned from it, because the goodness of earnings is the basis for the soundness and acceptance of acts of worship. Do you not see what has been transmitted: whoever performs the pilgrimage with unlawful wealth, when he says "Labbayk" (here I am), Allah says to him: "No Labbayk, no Sa'dayk, and your pilgrimage is rejected against you." And do you not see the one who calls upon his Lord while his food is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, how is it said: "How could he be answered?" The prohibition of consuming wealth by falsehood preceded the prohibition of killing themselves, because it occurs more often and is more widespread among people than killing, especially if the intent is the apparent meaning of the verse, that He forbade a person from killing himself, for this situation is rare. It was said: He is Merciful to you in that He did not require you to kill yourselves at the time of repentance, as He required the Children of Israel to kill themselves, and made that a repentance for them and an expiation of their sins.

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 30:

﴿And whoever does that in transgression and wrongdoing, We will drive him into a Fire.﴾ The reference of "that" (dhalika) is to what was forbidden in this sentence: consuming wealth falsely and killing souls. This is because the prohibitions of these two were given in a coherent, sequential manner, and then the threat came in accordance with the prohibition. A group of scholars held this view. Restricting the consumption of wealth falsely by "transgression and wrongdoing" according to this view does not mean that it occurs in a way that is not transgression and wrongdoing; rather, these are among the descriptions that the act can only be committed with. It has been said: He only said "transgression and wrongdoing" so that error and inadvertence are excluded, along with what is governed by ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) in legal rulings. As for restricting the killing of souls, on the interpretation of "killing one another" (as in 4:29), by His saying "transgression and wrongdoing," this is because killing occurs in that manner, and it also occurs by mistake and by retaliation (qisas). It has also been said that "that" refers to the nearest previous mention, which is "the killing of souls." This is the view of Ata, and it is the choice of al-Zamakhshari, who said: "That is a reference to killing, meaning: whoever undertakes the killing of souls in transgression and wrongdoing, not by mistake nor by retaliation." End of quote. This would be similar to His saying: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell﴾ [al-Nisa: 93]. Al-Tabari held that "that" refers to the prohibition that was not accompanied by a threat, which is from His saying: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion, nor to restrain them﴾ [al-Nisa: 19], up to this prohibition, which is: ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾. As for the prohibitions before that, they were accompanied by a threat. What al-Tabari held is very far-fetched, because each sentence is self-contained, and no connection appears for it with what follows except a connection of relevance, not a connection of necessity of meaning. Even further from al-Tabari's view is what a group held, that "that" refers to all the matters prohibited from the beginning of the surah up to the prohibition that is followed by His saying: ﴿and whoever does that﴾.
