Al-Maturidi permitted that "that" refers to consuming wealth falsely, and he said: "That returns to what preceded of consuming wealth falsely, or the killing of a soul without right, or both together." End of quote. According to this view, there are five opinions regarding what "that" refers to.

The accusative of ﴿transgression and wrongdoing﴾ is as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi, accusative of cause). They also permitted that both could be verbal nouns in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: transgressing and wronging. It was read as "i'dwanan" with a kasra. The majority read "nuslihi" with a damma on the nun. Al-Nakha'i and al-A'mash read it with a fatha, from salaha, and from it comes "shah musliyyah" (a roasted sheep). It was also read "nusalliihi" with doubling. It was read "yusliihi" with a ya', and the apparent subject is a pronoun referring to God, meaning: He will roast him, that is, God the Most High. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the pronoun refers to "that," saying: "because it is the cause of the one who is roasted." But there is remoteness in this. The implied meaning of "Fire" is unrestricted, and what is intended, God knows best, is restricting it by the attribute of intensity, or by what is proportionate to this great offence of consuming wealth falsely and killing souls.

﴿And that is easy for God﴾. "That" refers to His roasting him in the Fire, and its ease for Him, may He be exalted, is its facility, because His proof is conclusive and His judgment has no reverser. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Because wisdom calls for it, and nothing turns Him from it, such as injustice or the like." In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilism (i'tizal).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 31:

﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to an honorable entrance.﴾ The connection (munasabah) of this verse is evident, for when He, exalted is He, mentioned the threat concerning the commission of some major sins, He mentioned the promise concerning avoiding the major sins. It is apparent that sins are divided into major sins (kaba'ir) and misdeeds (sayyi'at), and these are what most scholars have expressed as minor sins (saghair). They differed regarding this. The majority (al-jumhur) held that sins are divided into major and minor sins. Among the minor sins are the glance, the touch, the kiss, and the like, of what falls under the name of prohibition. Minor sins are expiated by avoiding the major sins. A group of the usulis (scholars of legal theory), among them the teacher Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini, Abu al-Ma'ali, and Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim al-Qushayri, held that all sins are major sins, and that only some of them are called minor relative to what is greater than them, just as it is said: fornication is a minor sin in relation to disbelief, and the forbidden kiss is a minor sin in relation to fornication. No sin is forgiven by avoiding another sin; rather every sin is a major sin, and its doer and perpetrator is subject to the Will (of Allah), except for disbelief. They interpreted His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the major sins that you are forbidden﴾ as referring to the types of polytheism and disbelief. They said: this is supported by the reading (kabir) in the singular. And His saying ﷺ: "Whoever takes the right of a Muslim man by his oath, Allah has made the Fire obligatory for him and forbidden Paradise to him." A man said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, even if it is something trivial?" He said: "Even if it is a twig of arak-wood." So the threat has come concerning the trivial just as it has come concerning the great. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas the like of the view of these, he said: Everything Allah has forbidden is a major sin.

Those who held that sins are divided into major and minor, and that minor sins are expiated by avoiding major sins, according to what the apparent meaning of the verse requires and what is strengthened by the authentic hadith from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Sahih Muslim, from his saying: "There is no Muslim man for whom a prescribed prayer comes, and he performs its ablution, its humility and its bowing well, except that it is an expiation for what preceded it of sins, so long as he does not commit a major sin, and that is for all time." And in Sahih Muslim: "The five daily prayers, and Friday to Friday, and Ramadan to Ramadan, are expiations for what is between them, when the major sins are avoided."

They differed regarding the major sins. Ibn Mas'ud said: they are three: despair of Allah's mercy, despairing of Allah's spirit, and feeling secure from Allah's plan. It is also narrated from him that they are four: he added associating partners with Allah. 'Ali said: they are seven: associating partners with Allah, killing a soul, slandering a chaste woman, consuming the property of an orphan, consuming usury, fleeing on the day of battle, and becoming a desert-dweller (a'rabi) after the migration. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: the major sins are seven, like the saying of 'Ali, and for each one of them there is a verse in the Book of Allah, and he made the verse concerning becoming a desert-dweller: ﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them﴾ [Muhammad: 25], the verse. In al-Bukhari: "Avoid the seven destructive sins," and he mentioned these except becoming a desert-dweller, and in its place came sorcery. Some people held that these major sins are these seven that are established in al-Bukhari. Ibn 'Umar said: he mentioned these except sorcery, and he added heresy in the Sacred Mosque, and one who mocks his parents, from disobedience to parents. Ibn Mas'ud also said, with al-Nakha'i: they are all that has been forbidden from the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' up to thirty verses into it, and these are: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾. Ibn 'Abbas also said, in what is narrated from him: they are nearer to seventy than to seven. Ibn 'Abbas also said: the major sins are everything upon which a threat of Fire, or punishment, or curse, or what resembles that has come. To something similar to this went Abu Muhammad 'Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Sa'id ibn Hazm al-Farisi al-Qurtubi, who said: I have searched extensively for this for years, and it became clear to me that everything for which Allah has threatened the Fire is a major sin. We found that he, peace be upon him, included among the major sins, by the explicit wording, things other than those he mentioned in the hadith — meaning the one in al-Bukhari — among them: false speech, disobedience to parents, lying about him, and a man exposing his parents to abuse by insulting people's fathers. He, peace be upon him, also mentioned the severe threat of the Fire for arrogance, for ingratitude toward one who does good in truth, for wailing at funerals, shaving the hair there, tearing garments, tale-bearing, neglecting to guard oneself from urine, severing kinship ties, for wine, for torturing animals without slaughter to eat what is lawful to eat from them or what is permitted to eat from them, for letting the lower garment hang out of arrogance, for one who reminds of the good he does, for one who sells his goods by a false oath, for one who withholds surplus water from the traveller, for theft of booty, for leaders who follow worldly ends, so that if they are given from it they fulfil obligations to them and if they are not given from it they do not fulfil obligations to them, for one who takes by his oath the right of a Muslim man, for a leader who deceives his subjects, for one who claims a lineage other than his father, for a runaway slave, for one who steals, for one who claims what is not his, for one who curses one who does not deserve a curse, for hatred of the Ansar, for one who abandons the prayer, for one who abandons zakat, and for hatred of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. We found the severe threat in the text of the Qur'an has come against fornicators and against those who spread corruption in the land by brigandage, and thus the saying of Ibn 'Abbas is confirmed. End of his words. That is, his saying: they are nearer to seventy than to seven. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: they are nearer to seven hundred, because there is no minor sin with persistence, and no major sin with seeking forgiveness.

Those who held that minor sins are expiated by avoiding major sins differed over whether the expiation is certain (qat'i) or a matter of probable opinion (ghalib al-zann). A group of jurists and people of hadith held that it is certain, as the verse and the hadiths indicate. The usulis said it is based on probable opinion, and they said: if that were certain, minor sins would have the ruling of the permissible, about which it is certain there is no consequence. He described "entrance" (mudkhalan) with His saying "honorable" (kariman), and the meaning of its honor is its excellence, and the negation of defects from it, as you say: a garment is honorable, and so-and-so is of noble origin. The meaning of expiating misdeeds is removing what they deserve of punishments and making them as if they had not been, and this is ordered upon avoiding the major sins.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr read (in ijtinabu kabira), in the singular. We have mentioned those who argued from it that disbelief is intended. As for one who did not say that, it is for him a collective noun (jins).

al-Mufaddal, from 'Asim, read (yukaffir wa-yudkhilkum) with the ya', in the third person.

Ibn 'Abbas read (min sayyi'atikum) with the addition of (min).

Nafi' read (mudkhalan) here and in al-Hajj with a fatha on the mim, and it is narrated from Abu Bakr. The rest of the seven read it with a damma, and the accusative of the damma-vowelled mim is either as a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., idkhalan, with the object of entering omitted, meaning: and He will admit you into Paradise with an honorable admission; or as the place of entering, whereupon the disagreement that concerns (dakhala) arises: is it transitive to these places by way of making the object, or by way of the adverbial of place? When the causative hamzah is added, the disagreement stands. As for the accusative of the fatha-vowelled mim, it may be the verbal noun of (dakhl), the intransitive counterpart of (adkhala), the meaning being: and He will admit you, so you enter an honorable entering, the (fa-tadkhulun) being omitted because the intransitive verb indicates it, and because its verbal noun also indicates it. It may also be intended as the place, in which case it is accusative either by (yudkhilkum) or by the omitted (dakhaltum), according to the disagreement over whether it is an object or an adverbial.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 4, verses 32–33 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿And do not wish for that by which God has given some of you preference over others.﴾ Qatadah and al-Suddi said: When ﴿To the male, the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ (4:11) was revealed, the men said: "We hope to be preferred over women in good deeds, as in inheritance." And the women said: "We hope that the burden upon us will be half of what is upon the men, as in inheritance." Ikrimah said: The women said: "We wish that God had made fighting (ghazw) for us, so that we would obtain a share of reward equal to what the men obtain." Mujahid added that this was narrated from Umm Salamah (may God be pleased with her), and that she said: "We only have half of the inheritance," and so it was revealed. It is also narrated from her that she said: "If only we were men," and so it was revealed.

The connection (munasabah) of this verse with what precedes it is this: when God forbade consuming wealth falsely and killing souls, and what He forbade was a means to indulgence in the world, to exaltation within it, and to acquiring its trappings, He forbade them from wishing for what God has given some of them preference over others. Such wishing is an effective cause in acquiring worldly things and in the soul's longing for them by every means. He did not suffice with forbidding the acquisition of wealth falsely and the killing of souls, but forbade the cause that incites to that as well. Beginning with the prohibition of the effect (musabbab) was more emphatic because of its heinousness and gravity, so it was mentioned first. Then He followed it with the prohibition of the cause, to cut off the root of the effect, and so that the inner act would correspond with the outer act, and the inward and outward would be equal in abstaining from ugly deeds. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the prohibition of a person wishing for himself what another has been given preference in. Rather, he must be content with what God has apportioned to him.

To wish for that is to wish to have the like of what that preferred person has. Ibn Abbas and Ata said: it is to wish for the wealth of another. Al-Zamakhshari said: They were forbidden from envy, and from wishing for what God has given some people preference over others in rank and wealth, because that preference is a distribution from God, issuing from wisdom, governance, and knowledge of the circumstances of His servants, and of what suits each one to whom it is apportioned, whether by expansion in provision or by restriction, and so on. This is a fine statement. The apparent prohibition only applies to what God has given some of them preference over others. As for wishing for things that are good for a person in worldly circumstances, and for deeds by which he hopes for reward in the Hereafter, that is good and does not fall within the verse. There has come in a hadith: "I wish that I were killed in the way of God, then brought to life, then killed." And at the end of the verse: ﴿And ask God of His bounty﴾, which indicates the permissibility of that. If wishing in general for what God has given some of them preference over others is forbidden, then wishing for it on condition that the blessing of the one who is preferred be removed is forbidden by a greater degree of prohibition. The more fitting reading is that this is envy (hasad), which is forbidden in the Sharia, and from which refuge is sought in God in the text of the Qur'an. Scholars differ regarding a person who wishes for the attainment of a blessing like that of the preferred person for himself, without that blessing departing from the preferred one. The apparent meaning of the verse is prohibition, and this is the view of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun), because that blessing may be a corruption for him in his religion and a harm to him in this world. So it is not permissible to say: "O God, give me a house like the house of so-and-so, or a spouse like his spouse." Rather, one should ask God for what he wills without reference to the one who has been preferred. Some people have permitted it.

* * *

﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned.﴾ Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said: its meaning is from inheritance, because the Arabs did not give women inheritance. This view has been deemed weak, because the wording of "earning" (iktisab) is incompatible with it. Iktisab indicates exertion and seeking after what is earned, and this does not apply to inheritance, because it is wealth that the heir takes effortlessly without any exertion in it. Qatadah's interpretation is built upon what he said about the occasion of revelation of the verse. It was also said: "earning" is used to mean "obtaining," as it is narrated that one of the Arabs obtained a treasure, and his son said to him: "By God, O father, give me a share of your earnings (kasb)," meaning what you have obtained. From this is the saying of Khadijah (may God be pleased with her): "and you earn the destitute (al-ma'dum)." They said: from this is the saying of the poet:

*"If they earn for me a meager wealth, indeed I have earned for them praise that endures through time."*

Another group said: the meaning is that God has made for each of the two categories acquisitions that are specific to them, so no one should wish for what has been made for the other. Thus, for men was made jihad, spending for the livelihood, and bearing heavy obligations such as judgeship, leadership, and hisba (the office of enjoining good and forbidding evil in public life), and other such things. For women was made bearing and its hardship, good conduct toward a husband, guarding the husband's absence, and service of the household. It was also said: the meaning is "of what he has earned of the bliss of this world," so one should be content with what God has apportioned to him. These three statements relate to the affairs of this world. Another group said: the meaning is a share of reward and good deeds. Al-Zamakhshari said: what is apportioned to each of men and women has been made an earning for him according to what God knows of his condition that calls for expansion or restriction. End of quote.

Regarding his statement "what God knows (arafa) of his condition," there is a point to consider. It is not said of God that He is "ʿārif" (one who has ma'rifah). The scholars have stated this, because in the language ma'rifah requires a prior ignorance of the thing known, and that is different from knowledge (ʿilm), which does not require a prior ignorance. Also, calling what God has apportioned an "earning" (kasb) for him is also questionable, because iktisab entails exertion and seeking, as we have said. Unless we say that most of what is apportioned to a person requires an earning from the person himself, and so iktisab is applied to all that is apportioned to him by way of giving predominance to the majority. In linking the share (nasib) to earning (iktisab) there is an encouragement to action and an alert to earning good.

* * *

﴿And ask God of His bounty.﴾ That is, of the increase of His grace and blessings. When He forbade them from wishing for what He had given some of them preference over others, He commanded them to rely upon Him, may He be blessed and exalted, for an increase. The apparent meaning of His statement "of His bounty" is generality with regard to matters of this world and matters of the Hereafter, because the apparent meaning of His statement "do not wish for that which God has preferred" is also generality, and this is the view of the majority. Ibn Jubayr and Layth ibn Abi Sulaym said: this applies to acts of worship, religion, and righteous deeds, and not to the bounty of this world. In the statement "of His bounty" there is an indication that the thing sought is not specified; rather, one should ask God for whatever will be a cause for the rectification of his religion and his worldly life, in an unrestricted manner, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And among them is one who says: "Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good"﴾ (2:201).

Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read (وسَلُوا, wa-saluw) with the elision of the hamzah and transferring its vowel to the sin (s), and this is when it is an imperative addressed to the second person, and preceded by a waw or fa', such as: (فَسَلِ الَّذِينَ يَقْرَءُونَ) [fa-sali alladhina yaqra'una, "so ask those who read" (10:94)] and (فَسَلُوا أهْلَ الذِّكْرِ) [fa-saluu ahla al-dhikr, "so ask the people of remembrance" (16:43)]. The rest of the seven readers read with the hamzah. Ibn Atiyyah said: except in His statement ﴿And ask for what you have spent﴾ (60:10), since they all agreed on the hamzah in it. This statement attributed by Ibn Atiyyah is a mistake. Rather, the explicit statements of the reciters in their books place ﴿And ask for what you have spent﴾ (60:10) among the matters in which Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i differed from the rest. Ibn Shita explicitly stated this in his book al-Tidhkar. Perhaps he was misled in this by the statement of Ibn Mujahid in his book al-Sab'ah, where he said: they did not differ regarding His statement ﴿and let them ask for what they have spent﴾ (60:10), that it has a hamzah, because it is in the third person singular (for an absent party). End of quote.

Al-Kisa'i narrated from Isma'il ibn Ja'far, from Abu Ja'far and Shaybah, that both of them did not pronounce a hamzah in (سَلْ, sal) or (فَسَلْ, fasal), like the reading of al-Kisa'i. The elision of the hamzah in (سَلْ, sal) is the dialect of the Hijaz, and retaining it is the dialect of some of the Tamim tribe. Al-Yazidi narrated from Abu Amr that the dialect of Quraysh is (سَلْ, sal). When they introduce a waw or fa', they pronounce the hamzah. The verb (سَأَلَ, sa'ala, "to ask") takes two objects, and the second object in His statement "and ask God" is His statement "of His bounty," just as you say: "I fed Zayd some of the meat (min al-lahm), and I clothed him with some of the silk (min al-harir)," the sense being: "some of His bounty," "some of the meat," and "some of the silk." Some grammarians said: (مِن, min) is extra (ziyadah), and the sense is "ask God for His bounty." This is not permissible except according to the school of al-Akhfash.

Ibn Atiyyah said: It seems good to me that the object be understood as (أمانِيَكم, amaniyyakum, "your wishes"), since what preceded makes this meaning fitting.

* * *

﴿Indeed, God is ever Knowing of all things.﴾ That is: His knowledge encompasses all things. He knows what He has given some of you preference over others with, and what suits each of you of expansion or restriction. So beware of objecting with a wish or otherwise. He is also knowing of your asking Him for His bounty, so He responds to your supplication.

﴿And for each We have appointed heirs (mawali) of what the parents and close relatives leave. And those with whom your oaths have bound you—give them their share.﴾ When He forbade the aforementioned wishing and commanded asking God for His bounty, He informed them of something about the circumstances of inheritance, and that in His legislation there is a great benefit, namely the acquisition of wealth for the heir, which he did not strive for and did not toil to seek, for "often the one who sits receives from the one who strives." The word (كُلٌّ, kull, "each") is never used except in an annexed form, either to an explicit noun or to an implied one. They differed regarding what is implied here. It was said: the omitted term is "person" (insan). It was said: the omitted term is "wealth" (mal). The word (المَوْلى, mawla) is a term shared among many meanings, among them "heir," and this is the meaning that fits here, because it is suitable for supplying either "person" or "wealth." Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and others interpreted it this way: that the mawali are the agnatic kin ('asabah) and the heirs. If we take the meaning to be "for each person," there are several possibilities:

The first: (كُلٍّ, kullin) is related to (جَعَلْنا, ja'alna, "We appointed"), and the pronoun in (تَرَكَ, taraka, "left") refers to (كُلٍّ), which is annexed to "person." The sense is: "And He appointed for each person heirs of what he left." Then (مِمّا, mimma, "of what") is connected to what is implied in the meaning of mawali from the sense of a verb, or to an implied verb explained by the meaning: "they inherit of what he left." The sentence is complete at His statement "of what he left." The word (الوالِدانِ, al-walidani, "the two parents") is in the nominative by an implied element, as if it were said: "And who are the heirs?" It was answered: "They are the parents and close relatives as heirs." The utterance consists of two sentences.

The second possibility: the sense is "And We appointed for each person mawali," that is, heirs. Then a verb is implied, namely: "the mawali inherit of what the parents left," so the subject of "left" is the parents. It is as if, when He was vague in saying "And We appointed for each person mawali," He clarified that the person for whom heirs were appointed is the parents and close relatives; those heirs inherit of what their parents and relatives left, and the parents and relatives are the ones inherited from. In both of these possibilities there is no omitted implied verb in (ja'alna), and the object of (ja'alnahu, "We appointed him") is the word mawali. The utterance consists of two sentences.

The third possibility: the sense is "And for each people We have appointed them mawali," that is, heirs, a share of what their parents and close relatives left. Then (ja'alna, "We appointed") is a qualifier of (kull, "each"), and the pronoun from the qualifying clause is omitted, and it is the object of (ja'alna). (Mawali) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and the subject of (taraka, "left") is "the parents." The utterance is formed of a subject and predicate. So (لِكُلٍّ, li-kullin) is related to an omitted element, since it is the predicate of the omitted subject whose qualifier is the prepositional phrase, given that the sense is "a share of what he left." In that case the utterance is a single sentence, as you say: "for everyone whom God created as a human being there is a portion of God's provision," meaning "a portion of God's provision." If we take the meaning to be "for each wealth," and they said: the sense is "and for each wealth left by the parents and close relatives—We appointed mawali," that is, heirs who take charge of it and secure it. In this case (مِمّا تَرَكَ, mimma taraka) is in the position of a qualifier to (kull), and "the parents and close relatives" is the subject of (taraka), and they are the ones inherited from, and (li-kull) is related to (ja'alna). However, in this estimation there is a separation between the qualifier and the qualified by a sentence containing the prepositional phrase connected to the verb, and this is like your saying: "I passed by every Tamimi man (bi-kulli rijlin marartu Tamimiyyun)," and there is an inquiry regarding the permissibility of that.

The Scholars differed over what is meant by *al-mu'aqadah* (the pact) here. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, al-Suddi and others said: it is the *hilf* (the alliance oath). The Arabs used to inherit through the *hilf*, so this verse confirmed that, and then it was abrogated (*nusikha*) by His words: ﴿And blood relatives are closer to one another in the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 75]. He also reported that it is the *hilf*, and that the *nasib* (share) is mutual support in the right and in victory, and fulfilling obligations, not inheritance. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is the *mu'akhah* (brotherhood pact), by which they used to inherit until it was abrogated. He also said: the Emigrants used to inherit from the Helpers to the exclusion of their blood relatives, until this was abrogated by what was mentioned earlier, and two things remained: the share of support and assistance, and a share of wealth by way of recommendation in a bequest. Ibn al-Musayyib said: it is adoption (*tabanni*), and the share that we were commanded to give is the bequest, not inheritance (p-238). The meaning of "your oaths have made a pact" in this view is: your oaths have bound them to you, and you have rubbed hands with them. It was also said: they used to inherit through adoption for people who died before the bequest and its obligation, so the one making the bequest was commanded to hand it over to the heirs of the one to whom the bequest was made. It was also said: the *mu'aqadah* here is marriage, and marriage is called an *'aqd* (contract); so He mentioned parents and relatives, and mentioned with them the husband and the wife. It was also said: the *mu'aqadah* here is *wala'* (patronage). It was also said: it is the oath of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq that he would not give 'Abd al-Rahman any inheritance; when he embraced Islam, Allah commanded him to give him his share of the wealth. Abu Ruq said: both of these were revealed concerning them.

So from these opinions regarding the *mu'aqadah*, the views are: is it the oath that the one swearing will not be inherited from? Or the brotherhood pact? Or adoption? Or the stipulated bequest? Or marriage? Or *al-muwalah* (alliance)? Seven opinions. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the wording "*mu'aqadah*" and "oaths" favours that what is meant is the alliances, because what has been mentioned other than alliances does not, in its entirety, involve a *mu'aqadah* or oaths. End.

The manner of the *hilf* in the Jahiliyyah was: a man would make a pact with another man and say: "My blood is your blood, my ruin is your ruin, my fire is your fire, my war is your war, my peace is your peace; you inherit from me and I inherit from you; you seek vengeance for me and I seek vengeance for you; you pay blood-money on my behalf and I pay blood-money on your behalf." The ally would then have a sixth of the inheritance of his ally, and Allah abrogated that. On the earlier opinions the disagreement arose concerning His words (*wa-alladhina 'aqadat aymanukum*, "and those whom your oaths have bound"): is it abrogated or not? It has been used as evidence for the inheritance of the *mawla al-muwalah* (the client by alliance), and this is the view of Abu Yusuf, Abu Hanifah, Zufar and Muhammad. They said: whoever embraces Islam at the hand of a man, and allies himself with him and makes a pact with him, and then dies with no heir other than him, his inheritance goes to him. Something similar is reported from Yahya ibn Sa'id, Rabi'ah, Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Zuhri, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud. Malik, Ibn Shubrumah, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i said: his inheritance goes to the Muslims. Abu Bakr al-Razi extensively discussed this question, supporting the position of Abu Hanifah.

The Kufans read *'aqadat* with a light *qaf* and without an *alif*; Hamzah, through the narration of 'Ali ibn Kabshah, read it with a doubled *qaf*; and the rest read *'aqadat* with an *alif*. They allowed several possibilities in the *i'rab* (grammatical analysis) of *alladhina*: First, that it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and the predicate is *fa-atuhum* ("then give them"). Second, that it is in the accusative by way of *al-ishtighal* (the verb's object being a pronoun referring back to the topicalised noun), like "Zayd, strike him." Third, that it is in the nominative, conjoined to *al-walidan wa-al-aqrabun* ("the parents and the relatives"), and the pronoun in *fa-atuhum* refers back to *mawali* (heirs by alliance) if the parents and those conjoined to them are the ones inherited from; but if they are the inheritors, it is permissible for it to refer to *mawali*, and it is permissible for it to refer to the parents and the one conjoined to them. Fourth, that it is in the accusative, conjoined to *mawali*; this was said by Abu al-Baqa', who said: that is, "and We have made those whom your oaths have bound to be heirs," and this was and was abrogated. But it is not possible, on the supposition he proposed, for it to be conjoined to *mawali*, because the conjunction becomes corrupt, since the meaning would become: "For every person, or: for every item of wealth, We have made heirs..." and "those whom your oaths have bound." If it is a conjunction of sentences, with the second object omitted because the meaning indicates it, then it is possible: that is, "We have made heirs for every item of wealth," that is, for every person, and "We have made those whom your oaths have bound heirs." This is, after all, a strained interpretation. The object of *'aqadat* is an omitted pronoun, that is, "your oaths have bound them," and likewise in the reading *'aqadat*, it is omitted, its estimate being: "your oaths have bound their alliance or their covenant." Attributing the *mu'aqadah* or the *'aqd* to the oaths, whether by them is meant the swearing or the limb, is a metaphor; rather, the doer of that is the person himself.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, Witness﴾. When He mentioned the legislation of inheritance and commanded the giving of the share, He informed that He is aware of everything, so He is the One who recompenses for it. In this is a threat to the disobedient, a promise to the obedient, and an alert that He is a witness over the pact among you. Its connection is: "So fulfil the covenant."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 4, verses 32–33 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿And do not wish for that by which God has given some of you preference over others.﴾ Qatadah and al-Suddi said: When ﴿To the male, the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ (4:11) was revealed, the men said: "We hope to be preferred over women in good deeds, as in inheritance." And the women said: "We hope that the burden upon us will be half of what is upon the men, as in inheritance." Ikrimah said: The women said: "We wish that God had made fighting (ghazw) for us, so that we would obtain a share of reward equal to what the men obtain." Mujahid added that this was narrated from Umm Salamah (may God be pleased with her), and that she said: "We only have half of the inheritance," and so it was revealed. It is also narrated from her that she said: "If only we were men," and so it was revealed.

The connection (munasabah) of this verse with what precedes it is this: when God forbade consuming wealth falsely and killing souls, and what He forbade was a means to indulgence in the world, to exaltation within it, and to acquiring its trappings, He forbade them from wishing for what God has given some of them preference over others. Such wishing is an effective cause in acquiring worldly things and in the soul's longing for them by every means. He did not suffice with forbidding the acquisition of wealth falsely and the killing of souls, but forbade the cause that incites to that as well. Beginning with the prohibition of the effect (musabbab) was more emphatic because of its heinousness and gravity, so it was mentioned first. Then He followed it with the prohibition of the cause, to cut off the root of the effect, and so that the inner act would correspond with the outer act, and the inward and outward would be equal in abstaining from ugly deeds. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the prohibition of a person wishing for himself what another has been given preference in. Rather, he must be content with what God has apportioned to him.

To wish for that is to wish to have the like of what that preferred person has. Ibn Abbas and Ata said: it is to wish for the wealth of another. Al-Zamakhshari said: They were forbidden from envy, and from wishing for what God has given some people preference over others in rank and wealth, because that preference is a distribution from God, issuing from wisdom, governance, and knowledge of the circumstances of His servants, and of what suits each one to whom it is apportioned, whether by expansion in provision or by restriction, and so on. This is a fine statement. The apparent prohibition only applies to what God has given some of them preference over others. As for wishing for things that are good for a person in worldly circumstances, and for deeds by which he hopes for reward in the Hereafter, that is good and does not fall within the verse. There has come in a hadith: "I wish that I were killed in the way of God, then brought to life, then killed." And at the end of the verse: ﴿And ask God of His bounty﴾, which indicates the permissibility of that. If wishing in general for what God has given some of them preference over others is forbidden, then wishing for it on condition that the blessing of the one who is preferred be removed is forbidden by a greater degree of prohibition. The more fitting reading is that this is envy (hasad), which is forbidden in the Sharia, and from which refuge is sought in God in the text of the Qur'an. Scholars differ regarding a person who wishes for the attainment of a blessing like that of the preferred person for himself, without that blessing departing from the preferred one. The apparent meaning of the verse is prohibition, and this is the view of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun), because that blessing may be a corruption for him in his religion and a harm to him in this world. So it is not permissible to say: "O God, give me a house like the house of so-and-so, or a spouse like his spouse." Rather, one should ask God for what he wills without reference to the one who has been preferred. Some people have permitted it.

* * *

﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned.﴾ Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said: its meaning is from inheritance, because the Arabs did not give women inheritance. This view has been deemed weak, because the wording of "earning" (iktisab) is incompatible with it. Iktisab indicates exertion and seeking after what is earned, and this does not apply to inheritance, because it is wealth that the heir takes effortlessly without any exertion in it. Qatadah's interpretation is built upon what he said about the occasion of revelation of the verse. It was also said: "earning" is used to mean "obtaining," as it is narrated that one of the Arabs obtained a treasure, and his son said to him: "By God, O father, give me a share of your earnings (kasb)," meaning what you have obtained. From this is the saying of Khadijah (may God be pleased with her): "and you earn the destitute (al-ma'dum)." They said: from this is the saying of the poet:

*"If they earn for me a meager wealth, indeed I have earned for them praise that endures through time."*

Another group said: the meaning is that God has made for each of the two categories acquisitions that are specific to them, so no one should wish for what has been made for the other. Thus, for men was made jihad, spending for the livelihood, and bearing heavy obligations such as judgeship, leadership, and hisba (the office of enjoining good and forbidding evil in public life), and other such things. For women was made bearing and its hardship, good conduct toward a husband, guarding the husband's absence, and service of the household. It was also said: the meaning is "of what he has earned of the bliss of this world," so one should be content with what God has apportioned to him. These three statements relate to the affairs of this world. Another group said: the meaning is a share of reward and good deeds. Al-Zamakhshari said: what is apportioned to each of men and women has been made an earning for him according to what God knows of his condition that calls for expansion or restriction. End of quote.

Regarding his statement "what God knows (arafa) of his condition," there is a point to consider. It is not said of God that He is "ʿārif" (one who has ma'rifah). The scholars have stated this, because in the language ma'rifah requires a prior ignorance of the thing known, and that is different from knowledge (ʿilm), which does not require a prior ignorance. Also, calling what God has apportioned an "earning" (kasb) for him is also questionable, because iktisab entails exertion and seeking, as we have said. Unless we say that most of what is apportioned to a person requires an earning from the person himself, and so iktisab is applied to all that is apportioned to him by way of giving predominance to the majority. In linking the share (nasib) to earning (iktisab) there is an encouragement to action and an alert to earning good.

* * *

﴿And ask God of His bounty.﴾ That is, of the increase of His grace and blessings. When He forbade them from wishing for what He had given some of them preference over others, He commanded them to rely upon Him, may He be blessed and exalted, for an increase. The apparent meaning of His statement "of His bounty" is generality with regard to matters of this world and matters of the Hereafter, because the apparent meaning of His statement "do not wish for that which God has preferred" is also generality, and this is the view of the majority. Ibn Jubayr and Layth ibn Abi Sulaym said: this applies to acts of worship, religion, and righteous deeds, and not to the bounty of this world. In the statement "of His bounty" there is an indication that the thing sought is not specified; rather, one should ask God for whatever will be a cause for the rectification of his religion and his worldly life, in an unrestricted manner, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And among them is one who says: "Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good"﴾ (2:201).

Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read (وسَلُوا, wa-saluw) with the elision of the hamzah and transferring its vowel to the sin (s), and this is when it is an imperative addressed to the second person, and preceded by a waw or fa', such as: (فَسَلِ الَّذِينَ يَقْرَءُونَ) [fa-sali alladhina yaqra'una, "so ask those who read" (10:94)] and (فَسَلُوا أهْلَ الذِّكْرِ) [fa-saluu ahla al-dhikr, "so ask the people of remembrance" (16:43)]. The rest of the seven readers read with the hamzah. Ibn Atiyyah said: except in His statement ﴿And ask for what you have spent﴾ (60:10), since they all agreed on the hamzah in it. This statement attributed by Ibn Atiyyah is a mistake. Rather, the explicit statements of the reciters in their books place ﴿And ask for what you have spent﴾ (60:10) among the matters in which Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i differed from the rest. Ibn Shita explicitly stated this in his book al-Tidhkar. Perhaps he was misled in this by the statement of Ibn Mujahid in his book al-Sab'ah, where he said: they did not differ regarding His statement ﴿and let them ask for what they have spent﴾ (60:10), that it has a hamzah, because it is in the third person singular (for an absent party). End of quote.

Al-Kisa'i narrated from Isma'il ibn Ja'far, from Abu Ja'far and Shaybah, that both of them did not pronounce a hamzah in (سَلْ, sal) or (فَسَلْ, fasal), like the reading of al-Kisa'i. The elision of the hamzah in (سَلْ, sal) is the dialect of the Hijaz, and retaining it is the dialect of some of the Tamim tribe. Al-Yazidi narrated from Abu Amr that the dialect of Quraysh is (سَلْ, sal). When they introduce a waw or fa', they pronounce the hamzah. The verb (سَأَلَ, sa'ala, "to ask") takes two objects, and the second object in His statement "and ask God" is His statement "of His bounty," just as you say: "I fed Zayd some of the meat (min al-lahm), and I clothed him with some of the silk (min al-harir)," the sense being: "some of His bounty," "some of the meat," and "some of the silk." Some grammarians said: (مِن, min) is extra (ziyadah), and the sense is "ask God for His bounty." This is not permissible except according to the school of al-Akhfash.

Ibn Atiyyah said: It seems good to me that the object be understood as (أمانِيَكم, amaniyyakum, "your wishes"), since what preceded makes this meaning fitting.

* * *

﴿Indeed, God is ever Knowing of all things.﴾ That is: His knowledge encompasses all things. He knows what He has given some of you preference over others with, and what suits each of you of expansion or restriction. So beware of objecting with a wish or otherwise. He is also knowing of your asking Him for His bounty, so He responds to your supplication.

﴿And for each We have appointed heirs (mawali) of what the parents and close relatives leave. And those with whom your oaths have bound you—give them their share.﴾ When He forbade the aforementioned wishing and commanded asking God for His bounty, He informed them of something about the circumstances of inheritance, and that in His legislation there is a great benefit, namely the acquisition of wealth for the heir, which he did not strive for and did not toil to seek, for "often the one who sits receives from the one who strives." The word (كُلٌّ, kull, "each") is never used except in an annexed form, either to an explicit noun or to an implied one. They differed regarding what is implied here. It was said: the omitted term is "person" (insan). It was said: the omitted term is "wealth" (mal). The word (المَوْلى, mawla) is a term shared among many meanings, among them "heir," and this is the meaning that fits here, because it is suitable for supplying either "person" or "wealth." Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and others interpreted it this way: that the mawali are the agnatic kin ('asabah) and the heirs. If we take the meaning to be "for each person," there are several possibilities:

The first: (كُلٍّ, kullin) is related to (جَعَلْنا, ja'alna, "We appointed"), and the pronoun in (تَرَكَ, taraka, "left") refers to (كُلٍّ), which is annexed to "person." The sense is: "And He appointed for each person heirs of what he left." Then (مِمّا, mimma, "of what") is connected to what is implied in the meaning of mawali from the sense of a verb, or to an implied verb explained by the meaning: "they inherit of what he left." The sentence is complete at His statement "of what he left." The word (الوالِدانِ, al-walidani, "the two parents") is in the nominative by an implied element, as if it were said: "And who are the heirs?" It was answered: "They are the parents and close relatives as heirs." The utterance consists of two sentences.

The second possibility: the sense is "And We appointed for each person mawali," that is, heirs. Then a verb is implied, namely: "the mawali inherit of what the parents left," so the subject of "left" is the parents. It is as if, when He was vague in saying "And We appointed for each person mawali," He clarified that the person for whom heirs were appointed is the parents and close relatives; those heirs inherit of what their parents and relatives left, and the parents and relatives are the ones inherited from. In both of these possibilities there is no omitted implied verb in (ja'alna), and the object of (ja'alnahu, "We appointed him") is the word mawali. The utterance consists of two sentences.

The third possibility: the sense is "And for each people We have appointed them mawali," that is, heirs, a share of what their parents and close relatives left. Then (ja'alna, "We appointed") is a qualifier of (kull, "each"), and the pronoun from the qualifying clause is omitted, and it is the object of (ja'alna). (Mawali) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and the subject of (taraka, "left") is "the parents." The utterance is formed of a subject and predicate. So (لِكُلٍّ, li-kullin) is related to an omitted element, since it is the predicate of the omitted subject whose qualifier is the prepositional phrase, given that the sense is "a share of what he left." In that case the utterance is a single sentence, as you say: "for everyone whom God created as a human being there is a portion of God's provision," meaning "a portion of God's provision." If we take the meaning to be "for each wealth," and they said: the sense is "and for each wealth left by the parents and close relatives—We appointed mawali," that is, heirs who take charge of it and secure it. In this case (مِمّا تَرَكَ, mimma taraka) is in the position of a qualifier to (kull), and "the parents and close relatives" is the subject of (taraka), and they are the ones inherited from, and (li-kull) is related to (ja'alna). However, in this estimation there is a separation between the qualifier and the qualified by a sentence containing the prepositional phrase connected to the verb, and this is like your saying: "I passed by every Tamimi man (bi-kulli rijlin marartu Tamimiyyun)," and there is an inquiry regarding the permissibility of that.

[p. 239]

﴿Men are in charge of women, because Allah has made some of them to excel others, and because they spend from their wealth.﴾ It was said: the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse is that a woman was slapped by her husband, so she sought redress, and retaliation (qisas) was decreed for her, and then the verse was revealed. He (Allah) said: "You desired a matter and Allah desired something else." This was related by al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and others. Al-Tibrizi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned that she was Habiba bint Zayd ibn Abi Zuhayr, wife of al-Rabi' ibn 'Umar, and one of the Naqibs (chiefs) of the Ansar. They elaborated the story, and at its end it says: so retaliation between the man and the woman was lifted. Abu al-Kalbi said: she was Habiba bint Muhammad ibn Salama, wife of Sa'id ibn al-Rabi'. Abu Rawq said: she was Jamila bint 'Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, wife of Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas. It was also said that with her there was revealed: ﴿Do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is completed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114]. Regarding the cause concerning the woman herself, it is that her husband slapped her because of her disobedience (nushuz). It was also said that the occasion of revelation is the statement of Umm Salama mentioned earlier: when women wished for the rank of men, they came to know the aspect of excellence. It was said: what is meant by "men" here are those who possess firmness and resolve, not everyone who has a beard. For many a bearded man has neither benefit nor harm nor protection in him, and for this reason it is said: "a man clearly manifest in manliness (rujuliyya) and manhood (rujula)." For this reason some exegetes claimed that the sentence contains an omission, its estimate being: "Men are in charge of women if they are men." And he recited:

*"Do you think every man is a man,*
*and a fire kindled at night is fire?"*

What appears to be correct is that this is a statement about the genus, without considering its individual members, as if it were said: "This genus is in charge of that genus." Ibn 'Abbas said: "in charge" means empowered to discipline women in what is right. In support of this view is (their obedience to them is obedience to Allah). "Qawwam" is an intensive form (sigha mubalagha), and it is also said qayyam and qayyim, which is one who attends to a matter and guards it. In a hadith: "You are the Sustainer (qayyam) of the heavens and the earth and of whoever is in them." The "ba'" in (bima) indicates cause, and "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), meaning: "because of Allah's preference." Whoever takes it to mean "alladhi" (that which) has gone far, since there is no returning pronoun in the sentence, and an omitted estimate that would justify its omission is absent, so this is not permissible.

The pronoun in "ba'diahum" refers to men and women. It was stated with the masculine taking precedence over the feminine (taghlib). The first "some" refers to men, and the second to women. The meaning is: they are in charge over them because of Allah's preference of men over women, this is how they have established this meaning. They said: he turned away from the two pronouns and did not say "what Allah preferred over them," because mentioning "some" carries a vagueness that does not require general application of the pronoun, for many a female has excelled a male. In this is evidence that guardianship (wilaya) is earned through excellence, not through domination and overbearing. They mentioned several things by which men were preferred over women, as examples. Al-Rabi' said: the Friday prayer and congregation. Al-Hasan said: the maintenance (nafaqa) of them. This is contradicted by His saying: ﴿and because they spend﴾. It was said: disposal (of affairs) and trade. It was said: fighting in battle, and the perfection of religion and intellect. It was said: intellect, opinion, the permissibility of four wives, possession through marriage, divorce, revocation (raj'a), the perfection of acts of worship, the excellence of testimony, agnatic succession (ta'sib), the increase of the share in inheritance and blood money, eligibility for prophethood, the caliphate, the imamate, oratory, jihad, archery, the call to prayer, seclusion in the mosque (i'tikaf), surety (hamala), oath of fifty (qasama), descent of children, beards, the uncovering of faces, turbans which are the crowns of the Arabs, guardianship, giving in marriage, the summoning to bed, writing in most cases, the number of wives, and sexual relations through right of ownership (milk al-yamin).

* *

﴿and because they spend from their wealth﴾: its meaning is "upon them." "Ma" is a verbal-noun particle, or with the meaning of "alladhi," and the returning pronoun is omitted, with a justification for its omission. It was said: the meaning is "by what they expend because of marriage, from their dowries, and from the continuous maintenance upon them." Mu'adh related that he said: "If I were to command anyone to prostrate to anyone, I would command the woman to prostrate to her husband." Al-Qurtubi said: the majority understood from His saying ﴿and because they spend from their wealth﴾ that whenever he is unable to maintain her, he is not in charge over her, and if he is not in charge over her, she has the right to annul the contract, since the purpose for which marriage was legislated has ceased. In this there is clear evidence from this angle for the establishment of annulment of marriage on account of inability to provide maintenance and clothing, and this is the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: it is not annulled, based on His saying: ﴿And if someone is in hardship, then let there be postponement until ease﴾ [al-Baqara: 280].

* *

﴿So righteous women are obedient, guarding in secret what Allah has guarded﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: the righteous ones are those who are good to their husbands, for when they are good to their husbands their condition becomes sound with them. Ibn al-Mubarak said: those who deal in goodness. It was said: those whom Allah has made fit for their husbands, as He said: ﴿and We made his wife fit for him﴾ [al-Anbiya: 90]. It was said: those who have made their words and deeds right. It was said: righteousness here is religion.

These statements are close in meaning. The "qanitat" are those who are obedient to their husbands, or obedient to Allah in guarding their husbands and carrying out their commands, or obedient to Allah in all their conditions, or those who fulfil what is due to husbands from them, or those who pray. These are sayings, the last of which belongs to al-Zajjaj.

﴿guarding in secret﴾: 'Ata' and al-Suddi said: they guard what is hidden from their husbands, and what is obligatory for them of protecting themselves for them, and they do not speak about what occurred between them and between them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "al-ghayb" is everything that is hidden from the knowledge of her husband among what is concealed from him, and this covers both the husband's absence and his presence. Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-ghayb" is the opposite of "al-shahada" (witnessing), meaning: guarding the obligations of the absent state when the husbands are not present with them; they guard what is obligatory for them to guard in the state of absence concerning the husband, the homes, and the wealth. End of quote. The definite article in "al-ghayb" stands in place of a pronoun, and this substitution is common, as in His saying: ﴿and the head has glistened with white hair﴾ [Maryam: 4], meaning "my head." Dhu al-Rumma said:

*"Lamya', on her lips is a dark sheen, a blackness, and in her gums and in her fangs is a whiteness (shanab)."*

He means: "in her gums." Abu Hurayra related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The best of women is the woman who, when you look at her, pleases you; when you command her, she obeys you; and when you are absent from her, she guards you in her wealth and her self." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) recited with the nominative for the Divine Name (Allah), so the apparent reading is that "ma" is a verbal-noun particle, and the estimate is: "by Allah's guarding of them." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Mujahid. This guarding may have several meanings: that is, He guards them, meaning, by His granting them success to guard what is hidden; or by His guarding them when He enjoined upon husbands concern for them in His Book and commanded His Messenger (ﷺ), so he said: "Be good to women." Or by His guarding them when He promised them a great reward for guarding what is hidden, and threatened them with severe punishment for betrayal. They also allowed that "ma" means "alladhi," and the returning pronoun to "ma" is omitted, the estimate being: "by what Allah has guarded for them of their husbands' dowries and of maintenance upon them," as said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the meaning may be either Allah's guarding and His care, without which no matter is accomplished, or His commands and prohibitions for women, and it is as though these were His guarding, so the meaning is: women guard in accordance with that and in proportion to it. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "ma" be an indefinite qualified noun.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' recited with the accusative for the Divine Name (Allah), so the apparent reading is that "ma" means "alladhi," and in "hafiza" there is a nominative pronoun returning to "ma," meaning: by the obedience and piety which Allah has guarded in carrying out His command. It was said: the estimate is "by the command which guarded the right of Allah and His trust," and this is chastity, self-restraint, compassion toward men, and advising them. Ibn Jinni estimated it as: "by what guarded the religion of Allah, or the command of Allah." Omitting the governed noun (hadhf al-mudaf) is required in this estimate, because the Sacred Essence is not described as being guarded by anyone. It was said: "ma" is a verbal-noun particle, and in ﴿hafiza﴾ there is a nominative pronoun whose estimate is: "by what they (the women) guarded of Allah," and it returns to "al-salihat." It was said: that pronoun was omitted, and in its omission there is an ugliness that is not permitted except in poetry, as he said:

*"Indeed, calamities have destroyed them,"*

meaning: "they have destroyed them." The meaning is: they guard Allah in His command when they carry it out. The best view in this is that one should not say that he omitted the pronoun; rather it should be said that the pronoun returned to them in the singular, as though the genus were considered, and as though "al-salihat" carries the meaning of "man salaha" (whoever is righteous). All of this is an interpretation of an anomaly, which resulted from the statement of one who said that "ma" in this reading is a verbal-noun particle. There is no need for this view; the Qur'an should be exalted above it. In the reading of 'Abdullah and his codex: "So the righteous women are obedient, guarding in secret what Allah has guarded; then correct your conduct towards them." It is proper to understand it as an explanation, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Imam (the 'Uthmanic text) and contains an addition. It has been authentically transmitted from him by a report beyond doubt that he recited in conformity with the consonantal text, so for this reason this reading should be understood as explanation. Ibn Jinni said: the broken plural (taksir) is more fitting to the meaning, since it indicates multiplicity, and multiplicity is what is intended here. The meaning of his words "then correct your conduct towards them" is: "be good to them." "Aslihu" (correct) has been given the sense of "ahsinu" (be good), and for this reason it governs "ila" (to). In a hadith it is related: "The bird in the air, the fish in the sea, the angels in the heavens, and the beasts in the wildernesses seek forgiveness for the woman who obeys her husband." Umm Salama said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, are the women of this world better, or the houris? He said: The women of this world are better than the houris. I said: O Messenger of Allah, why? He said: For their prayers, their fasting, their worship, and their obedience to their husbands."

* *

﴿As for those from whom you fear disobedience, admonish them, forsake them in the beds, and strike them﴾. When Allah mentioned the righteous wives, that they are obedient and guard what is hidden, He mentioned their opposite, who are disobedient to their husbands. "Fear" here was said to mean certainty. This view holds that the commands which follow are required by the occurrence of disobedience, not by the expectation of it. In support of the possibility of using "fear" in place of certainty, they cited the words of Abu Mihjan al-Thaqafi, may Allah be pleased with him:

*"Do not bury me in the wasteland, for I fear that when I die I will not taste it."*

It was also said that "fear" retains its basic meaning of some suspicion. He said:

*"A saying came to me from Nusayb, saying,*
*and I did not fear, O Sallam, that you would blame me,"*

meaning: "and I did not think." In a hadith: "I was commanded to use the miswak until I feared I would lose my teeth." It was also said that "fear" retains its basic meaning, the opposite of security, so the meaning is: they are wary and expect, because admonition and what follows it concern the continuation of what has appeared of the beginnings of what is feared. "Nushuz" means that a woman becomes crooked, her character rises up, and she exalts herself over her husband. It is said: nusur with the sin and the ra' (unpointed), it is said: nusur, and it is said: nushus. A woman is called nashir and nashis. Al-A'sha said:

*"An old man covered her at night, and by morning she had become a Qudā'iyya going to the soothsayers, raising her head."*

Ibn 'Abbas said: "their nushuz" is their disobedience. 'Ata' said: her nushuz is that she no longer perfumes herself, withholds herself from him, and changes from things she used to adorn herself with for the husband. Abu Mansur said: her nushuz is her dislike for the husband. It was said: it is her refusal to remain with him in his house, and her staying in a place where he does not wish her to stay. It was said: her withholding herself from enjoyment of her when he seeks her for that. All these statements are close in meaning.

Wa-waʿzuhunna (admonishing them): reminding them of God's command to obey the husband, and informing them that God has permitted striking them when they disobey, and that God's punishment for disobedience is upon them. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Mujahid said: he says to her, "Fear God, and return to your bed." It was also said: he says to her that the Prophet ﷺ said: "If I were to order anyone to prostrate to anyone, I would order the woman to prostrate to her husband." The Prophet ﷺ also said: "Do not let him be refused her body, even if she is on a saddle." He ﷺ said: "Any woman who spends the night refusing her husband's bed, the angels curse her until morning." Others added that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Three whose prayer does not go beyond their ears: a runaway slave, a woman whose husband spent the night displeased with her, and a leader of a people who dislike him."

Wa-hajruhunna fi al-madajiʿ (and forsaking them in the beds): leaving them out of aversion in the sleeping places. Al-madjaʿ (the bed/place of lying) is the place where one lies on one's side. The root of al-iḍtijaʿ (lying down) is lying on the back; it is said: ḍajaʿa ḍujūʿan and iḍtajaʿa, meaning he lay on his back to sleep; and aḍjaʿtuhu, I made him lie down onto the ground; and everything you lay down from a vessel or other thing, you have aḍjaʿtahu. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr said: its meaning is, do not have intercourse with them. Al-Ḍaḥḥak and al-Suddi said: leave off speaking to them, and turn your backs to them in the bed. Mujahid said: separate from them in the bed, that is, sleep at a side in a bed other than their bed. ʿIkrima and al-Hasan said: say to them in the beds "hajran," that is, harsh speech. It was also said: forsake them in speech for three days or less. The beds are used as a metaphor for the houses, because every place may be a place for lying down. Al-Nakhaʿi, al-Shaʿbi, al-Suddi and al-Hasan said: it is from al-hijran, which is distance. It was said: forsake them by abandoning intercourse and companionship, showing sternness, and turning away from them for a period whose limit is a month, as the Prophet ﷺ did when he swore not to enter upon his wives for a month. It was also said: tie them with the hijar, and compel them to intercourse; from their saying: hajara the camel when he tied it with the hijar, which is a rope with which a camel is tied. This was said by al-Tabari, and he preferred it, and he criticized the other opinions. Al-Zamakhshari, regarding al-Tabari's view, said: this is the interpretation of the dull-witted, end of quote. It was also said that fi is for causation: that is, forsake them because of their staying away from the bed. Al-Aʿmash and al-Nakhaʿi read fi al-madjaʿi in the singular, and it carries the sense of the plural, because it is a generic noun.

Wa-ḍarbuhunna (and striking them): it is that it be non-severe and non-harmful, as came in the hadith. Ibn ʿAbbas said: with a siwak or the like. Non-severe striking is that which does not break a bone, does not destroy a limb, and leaves no lasting effect; and al-nahik is the one who goes to the extreme; and he should avoid the face. And from the Prophet ﷺ: "Hang your whip where your family can see it." And from Asma bint al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with her: I was the fourth of four wives of al-Zubayr; when he became angry with one of us, he would strike her with the stick of the clothes-rack until he broke it upon her. This contradicts the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. Likewise what Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik: that Asma, the wife of al-Zubayr, used to go out until she was reproached for that and blamed for it, and her co-wives too; so he tied the hair of one to the other, then struck both of them very hard. The co-wife was more careful to protect herself, while Asma did not guard herself from the blows, so the striking fell on her more. She complained to her father Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, and he said: "My daughter, be patient, for al-Zubayr is a righteous man, and perhaps he will be your husband in Paradise."

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that he admonishes, forsakes them in the bed, and strikes her whom he fears will rebel. Some hold that he may combine them, and begin with whichever he wishes, because the particle wa does not indicate order. The majority say: admonition is at the fear of rebellion, and striking is when it becomes evident. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: these admonition, forsaking and striking are stages; if obedience occurs at one of them, it does not proceed to the rest. Al-Zamakhshari said: he was commanded to admonish them first, then to forsake them in the beds, then to strike them if admonition and forsaking do not benefit them. Al-Razi said, in summary: one begins with gentle speech in admonition; if that does not benefit, then with harsher speech; then he leaves her bed; then turns away from her entirely; then with a light blow such as a slap, a poke or the like, which conveys contempt and removal of respect; then with striking with a whip or a soft stick or the like, by which pain and distress are caused but no breaking or shedding of blood results. If none of these benefits, he ties her with the hijar, which is the rope, and compels her to intercourse, because that is his right. Whichever of these brings her back from her rebellion according to the order we have set, it is not permissible for him to move on to another, because of His saying: "If they obey you, then do not seek a way against them" (4:34). End of quote. His words "if they obey you" mean: if they agree with you and submit to what God has made obligatory upon them of obedience to you. This indicates that they were disobedient by rebelling, and that rebellion from them had actually occurred; thus the command is not conditioned upon the fear of rebellion. Its final part indicates that it is conditioned upon their disobedience by rebellion, and this is what led to interpreting "fear" as meaning "certainty." In my view, the best is that there is an omitted conjunction here, understood from the meaning and its requirement, and its estimate is: "those whose rebellion you fear and who have rebelled." Just as it is omitted in His saying: "Strike the rock with your staff, and it burst forth" (2:60), its estimate being "so he struck, and it burst forth," because bursting forth is not caused by the command, but by the striking. Thus these commands are ordered according to what is expressed. The omitted part is: he is commanded to admonish at the fear of rebellion, and commanded to forsake and strike at the occurrence of rebellion.

The meaning of "fa-la tabghu" (then do not seek): then do not seek against them any way among the three permitted ways, which are: admonition, forsaking, and striking. Sufyan said: its meaning is, do not burden them with what is not within their power, namely inclination and love, for that is up to God. It was said: it may be that tabghu is from al-baghy, which is injustice, and the meaning is: do not transgress against them by any path. The accusative of sabilan in this case is by removal of the preposition. It was also said: the meaning is, if they obey you, then do not seek against them any way of transgression against them or harm to them, leading thereby to their rebellion; that is, if they are obedient, then do not do with them anything that leads to their rebellion. The word "against them" indicates this meaning. And sabilan is indefinite in a negative context, so it encompasses the prohibition of harm by word or deed.

* *

"Inna Allaha kana ʿaliyyan kabiran" (Indeed God is ever Most High, Most Great): since in disciplining them with what God commanded the husband there is a superiority of the husband over the woman, God concluded the verse with the attribute of loftiness and greatness, to alert the servant that the one truly characterized by this is God, the Exalted. He permitted you what He permitted by way of discipline for them, so do not exalt yourselves over them, and do not be arrogant toward them, for that is not prescribed for you. In this is a great admonition for husbands, and a warning that God's power over you is greater than your power over them. In the hadith of Abu Masʿud, when he struck a slave of his: "Know, Abu Masʿud, that God is more capable over you than you are over this slave." Or the meaning may be: you disobey Him, the Exalted, despite the loftiness of His station and the majesty of His dominion, then He forgives you; so it is fitting for you to pardon them when they obey you.

﴿And if you fear a breach between the two of them, send an arbiter from his people and an arbiter from her people.﴾ The disagreement regarding "fear" here is like its occurrence in ﴿And those from whom you fear disobedience [nushuz]﴾ [An-Nisa: 34]. The woman's state with her husband is either obedience (ta'a) or disobedience (nushuz). And disobedience is either followed by obedience, or it persists. If obedience follows it, she returns to being as she was at first, an obedient wife. If the disobedience persists and grows severe, the two arbiters (hakamān) are sent.

Al-shiqaq means mutual hostility (al-mushaqqah). The original form was shiqaqan baynahuma, which was extended and then made into a construct phrase (idafah). The meaning is adverbial (ʿalā al-zarf), as you say: "The journey of the moonlit night pleases me." Or it is used as a noun and the adverbial sense has disappeared. Or al-bayn here is treated as the condition of the two of them, their companionship and their association.

The address in ﴿And if you fear﴾ and in (fabʿathū, "then send") is to the judges (al-ḥukkām) and to whoever holds responsibility for settling disputes among people. It was also said that the address is to the guardians (al-awliyāʾ), because they are the ones who manage people's affairs in contracts and their dissolution, and it is for them to appoint the two arbiters. It was also said that the address is to the believers in general. Whoever holds that the address is to the spouses is far from correct, for if it were addressed to the spouses it would say: "And if they both fear a breach between them, let them both send [arbiters]," or it would say: "If you fear a breach between you." Rather, it shifts from addressing the spouses to addressing the one who has authority and the settling of disputes among people. al-Ḥasan and al-Suddi held that it is addressed to the spouses. The pronoun in baynihimā refers to the two spouses, though their names were not mentioned explicitly; what indicates them has preceded in the mention of men and women.

The ḥakam (arbiter) is the one who is fit for judgment (ḥukūmah) among people and for reconciliation (iṣlāḥ). The verse does not specify what the two arbiters are to decide upon. The requirement that they be from the family is because they know the inner state of affairs better, the soul is at ease with them, and each of the two spouses informs his or her arbiter of what is in their heart of love, hatred, and desire for companionship or separation. A group of scholars said: It is necessary that both be knowledgeable of the circumstances of the spouses, just, skilled in management and in considering how to achieve benefit, and knowledgeable of God's ruling concerning the case they judge. If there is no one from their families fit for this, then two just and knowledgeable persons are sent from outside them. This applies when their situation is unclear and they both desire someone who can separate them. Some scholars said: This condition applies only to the two arbiters appointed by the judge (al-ḥākim). As for the two arbiters appointed by the spouses themselves, the only conditions are that they be adult, sane, Muslim, of chaste and modest character, and that their sincere counsel be probable.

They differed regarding the scope within which the two arbiters examine. The majority held that they examine everything, they may impose on the wrongdoer, and they carry out whatever they see fit, whether continuation or separation. This was the view of Malik, al-Awzaʿi, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr, and it is related from ʿAli, ʿUthman, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Shaʿbi, al-Nakhaʿi, Mujahid, Abu Salama, and Tawus. Malik said: If they see separation, they separate, whether that agrees with the doctrine of the city's judge or contradicts it, whether or not the spouses delegated them, and the separation in that case is an irrevocable divorce (ṭalāq bāʾin). A group said: The two arbiters examine only what the spouses delegated to them and explicitly stated that they were giving them precedence over it. The two arbiters are then agents (wakīlān): one is an agent for the husband and the other for the wife, and separation does not occur except with the consent of both spouses. This is the doctrine of Abu Hanifa, and there are two opinions attributed to al-Shafiʿi. al-Ḥasan and others said: The two arbiters consider reconciliation and the giving and taking, except for separation, for that is not in their hands.

As for what the two arbiters say: a group said that the husband's arbiter says to him: "Tell me what is in your mind." If he says: "I have no need of her, take for me what you can and separate us," then it is known that the disobedience comes from him. If he says: "I love her; satisfy her from my property however you wish, and do not separate us," then it is known that he is not the one who is disobedient. The wife's arbiter says the same to her. When it becomes clear to them both that the disobedience comes from him, they admonish him, rebuke him, and forbid him.

* *

﴿If they both intend reconciliation, God will bring about harmony between them.﴾ The pronoun in (yurīdā, "they both intend") refers to the two arbiters, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and others. And in (baynihimā, "between them") it refers to the spouses. That is: if they both intend to reconcile the matter (iṣlāḥ dhāt al-bayn) and their intention is sound, and they give sincere counsel for the sake of God, God will bring harmony between the spouses, unite them, and place affection in their souls. It was also said that both pronouns refer to the arbiters: if they intend to reconcile the matter, God will bring harmony between them, so they will agree upon one word, and they will help each other in seeking agreement until the goal is achieved. It was also said that both pronouns refer to the spouses: if the spouses intend reconciliation between them and the end of enmity, God will remove that and bring them together. It was also said that the pronoun in (yurīdā) refers to the spouses and the pronoun in (baynihimā) refers to the arbiters: if the spouses intend reconciliation, God will bring harmony between the two arbiters, so they agree upon one word, reconcile, and give sincere counsel.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that sending the two arbiters is necessary, and this is the view of the majority.

It is related from Malik that one sending suffices. The verse does not address the justice of the two arbiters, so if they were not just, ʿAbd al-Malik said: Their ruling is annulled. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The sound view is that it is valid. The people of binding and loosing (ahl al-ḥall wa al-ʿaqd, the qualified scholars and notables whose agreement is authoritative) agreed that appointing the two arbiters is permissible. The Khawarij held that arbitration is not permissible. If the two arbiters separate the spouses, it is a khulʿ (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation) with the consent of the spouses. Is it valid without the authority of a ruler? al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sirin held that reconciliation is not permissible except in the presence of the ruler. ʿUmar, ʿUthman, Ibn ʿUmar, and a group of the Companions and the Successors held that it is valid without the ruler's authority, including Malik, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and al-Shafiʿi.

﴿Indeed God is ever Knowing, Acquainted.﴾ He knows what the two arbiters intend and how they bring together those who differ, and He knows the hidden things of what they say concerning the matter of the spouses.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 36:

﴿Worship God and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, and to relatives, orphans, and the needy.﴾ The connection of this verse with what precedes it: when God mentioned that men are guardians (qawwamun) over women because of God's preference of them over women and because of their spending of their wealth, and the implication of the title (mafhum al-laqab) showed that he is not a guardian over other than them, He clarified that, although he is a guardian over women, he is also commanded to be good to his parents and to those whom He joined with parents. So this verse comes as an exhortation to good conduct and as a digression into noble character. The believer does not limit his obligations of goodness to what concerns his wife alone; rather, he is also obliged to other things, such as kindness to parents and others. God opened the path to this with the command to single Him out in worship, since it is the origin of good from which righteous deeds follow. A parallel is: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: You shall not worship except God, and be good to parents﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. The explanation of His saying ﴿and be good to parents, and to relatives, orphans, and the needy﴾ has already been given, except that here it is "wa-bi-dhi" and there it is "wa-dhi," and repeating the preposition (ba') indicates emphasis and intensification. So intensification is applied in this verse because it concerns this community, and it is not intensified in that one because it concerns the Children of Israel. Attention to this community is greater than attention to others, since it is "the best community brought forth for mankind."
