Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "wa-bil-walidayni ihsanun" with the nominative (raf'), and it is either a mubtada' (subject) or a khabar (predicate), in which there is the meaning of command found in the accusative form, even if it is a declarative sentence, like his saying:

"So patience is beautiful, for each of us is tested."

﴿And the neighbor who is a relative﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, and others said: it is the neighbor who is a near kinsman, and "the distant neighbor" (al-jar al-junub) is the stranger neighbor, with whom there is no kinship between you and him. Bal'a' ibn Qays said:

"No neighbor ever disowns us, whether a kinsman or a distant neighbor."

Nawf al-Shami said: it is the Muslim neighbor.

* *

﴿And the distant neighbor﴾: it is the Jewish or Christian neighbor. For him, there is the kinship of Islam and the foreignness of disbelief. Another group said: it is the neighbor near in dwelling to you, and the "junub" is the one far in dwelling from you. It seems to be derived from the hadith in which it is said: "I have two neighbors, to which of them should I send a gift?" He said: "To the one whose door is nearer to you." Maymun ibn Mihran said: "the neighbor who is a relative" is meant as the near neighbor. Ibn 'Atiyya said: [p. 245] this is an error in language, because he gathered, according to its interpretation, between the definite article (al-) and the construct (idafa), whereas the proper wording would be: "wa-jari dhi al-qurba." End of quote. Maymun's statement can be made correct, without it being a combination of the definite article and the construct as Ibn 'Atiyya claimed, by making His saying "dhi al-qurba" a badal (substitute/apposition) of "wal-jar," with an omitted modifier, the estimated meaning being "and the neighbor of the neighbor who is a relative," so that "jar" is omitted because the first "jar" indicates it. The Arabs have omitted the badal in such cases. The poet said:

"May God have mercy on the bones they buried in Sijistan, the Talha of talhas."

He means: the bones of Talhat al-Talhat. And among the speech of the Arabs: "If they knew the great knowledge for a year," meaning: the knowledge of the great for a year. "Al-Junub" is the distant one; it is so named because of his distance from kinship. And he said: "So do not deprive me of a gift from a distant tribe." Mujawara is a man's residing beside another man in a quarter or a city, or the being of forty houses on every side; or it is determined by hearing the adhan or hearing the iqama. These are four opinions, the second of which is the saying of al-Awza'i. He related in this regard a hadith that he (ﷺ) commanded his crier to call out: "Verily forty houses constitute a neighborhood, and one whose neighbor does not feel safe from his harms will not enter Paradise." Neighborliness has degrees, some closer than others; the closest is the wife. Al-A'sha said:

"O neighbor of ours, separate, for you are divorced."

It was also read: "wal-jara dha al-qurba" (with the accusative). Al-Zamakhshari said: [it is] in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), as it was read: "Guard the prayers and the middle prayer" [al-Baqarah: 238], to draw attention to the magnitude of his right, because he has two rights: the right of neighborliness and the right of kinship. End of quote. 'Asim, in the narration of al-Mufaddal from him, read: "wal-jari al-janbi" with a fatha on the jim and sukun on the nun, and its meaning is the distant one. A Bedouin was asked about "the distant neighbor" and said: he is the one who comes and settles wherever your eye falls upon him.

* *

﴿And the companion by the side﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak said: it is the companion on a journey. 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, and Ibn Abi Layla said: it is the wife. Ibn Zayd said: it is the one who visits you and comes to you so that you benefit him. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the one who accompanies you by being at your side, either as a fellow traveler, or as an adjoining neighbor, or as a partner in learning a knowledge or a craft, or as one sitting at your side in an assembly or a mosque, or other forms of the least companionship that brings you and him together. So you must observe that right and not forget it, and make it a means to goodness. Mujahid also said: it is the one who accompanies you on a journey and at home. It was said: the righteous companion.

(And the wayfarer) its explanation has already been given.

﴿And what your right hands possess﴾. It was said: "ma" here applies to the rational being in terms of its category, as in His saying: ﴿Marry what is good for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]. It was also said: because "ma" is more general than "man," it includes animals in their unrestricted sense, whether slaves or others, and animals other than slaves are more numerous in human possession than slaves, so the aspect of abundance was given precedence. God therefore commanded goodness to every owned being, whether human or other animal. Several hadiths have come concerning the recommendation to treat slaves well, in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere. Among the strange interpretations is what is reported from Sahl al-Tustari, who said: "the neighbor who is a relative" is the heart; "the distant neighbor" is the self (nafs); "the companion by the side" is the intellect ('aql) that guides upon following the Sunna and the sharia; and "the wayfarer" is the obedient limbs.

* *

﴿Indeed, God does not love one who is self-conceited and boastful﴾. God negated His love for the one characterized by these two attributes: ikhtiyal, which is arrogance, and fakhr, which is counting one's virtues in a way that exalts oneself by them and magnifies oneself over people. Because whoever is characterized by these two attributes is led by them to neglect those mentioned in the verse who have need of him. Abu Raja' al-Harawi said: you will not find one of bad character except that you find him self-conceited and boastful, and you will not find one undutiful to parents except that you find him tyrannical and wretched. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-mukhtal is the vain, ignorant one who is arrogant toward honoring his relatives, companions, and servants, so he does not show them hospitality and does not turn to them. Another said: God mentioned self-conceit because the self-conceited person disdains his relatives when they are poor, his neighbors when they are weak, orphans because of their weakness, the needy because of their humiliation, the wayfarer because of his distance from his family and wealth, and his servants because they are captive in his hand. [p. 246] End of quote. These reports agree that the mention of these two attributes at the end of the verse came as an alert that whoever is characterized by self-conceit and boasting disdains goodness toward the categories mentioned, and that what drives him to that is his being characterized by these two attributes. What appears to me is that their context is other than the context they mentioned. When God commanded goodness toward the categories mentioned, and the showing of kindness and honor to them, it was customary that whoever is characterized by noble character would find in himself pride, conceit, and boasting in what proceeded from him of goodness. The Arabs often boasted of this and exalted themselves in their prose and poetry with it. So God intended to draw attention to adorning oneself with the attribute of humility, and that one should not see for himself superiority over the one he has benefited, nor boast over him, as He said: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264]. So God negated His love from the one who adorns himself with these two descriptions. The meaning would be: they were commanded to worship God, to be good to parents and those mentioned with them, and they were forbidden from self-conceit and boasting. It is as if it were said: "And do not be self-conceited and boastful toward those to whom you have been good; indeed, God does not love one who is self-conceited and boastful." However, what we have mentioned is only complete if "alladhina yabkhaluna" is a mubtada' cut off from what precedes it. If it is connected to what precedes it, the meaning mentioned by the commentators comes, and the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "alladhina yabkhaluna" comes, and with it the meaning they mentioned becomes clear. The meaning we have mentioned is, God willing, the Exalted's.

This verse was revealed concerning disbelieving people. It is related from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Hadrami that it was revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews, who were stingy about informing people of the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and concealed the knowledge they had about it. They enjoined stinginess in two ways: they commanded their followers to deny the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they said to the Ansar, "Why do you spend on the Muhajirun, so that you become poor?" It is also said that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and it is said that it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah.

Given the difference in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul, the specific event that prompted the verse), the commentators differed about who is meant by ﴿الَّذِينَ يَبْخَلُونَ﴾ (those who are stingy). It is said that the verse is general, applying to everyone who is stingy and enjoins stinginess, whether Jews or others. In the language of the Arabs, al-bukhl (stinginess) means withholding from a petitioner something of the wealth in the hand of the one asked, while having a surplus. Tawus said: "Al-bukhl is that a person is stingy with what is in his hand, and al-shuhh (miserliness) is that he is greedy for what is in the hands of people." In the sacred law (al-Shari'a, the divine law), al-bukhl means withholding what is obligatory. Al-Raghib said: "It does not mean stinginess with wealth alone, but with everything that has benefit for others." End of quotation.

When Allah, exalted is He, commanded kindness to the two parents and to those mentioned with them among the needy, by way of the specific command of Allah, He made clear that those who do not do so are of two kinds. The first: the stingy person who does not at all proceed to spend wealth, to the point of excess, and who enjoins stinginess. The second: those who spend their wealth to be seen by people, not for the purpose of obeying Allah's command, complying with it and submitting to Him. Allah, exalted is He, condemned both kinds: He followed the first kind with ﴿وأعْتَدْنا لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ (and We have prepared for the disbelievers), and followed the second with His saying: ﴿ومَن يَكُنِ الشَّيْطانُ لَهُ قَرِينًا﴾ (and whoever has Satan as a companion).

Stinginess has many kinds: stinginess with wealth, stinginess with knowledge, stinginess with food, stinginess with greeting, stinginess with speech, stinginess toward relatives rather than strangers, and stinginess with social standing. All of these are blameworthy defects and vices, condemned by reason and by the Shari'a. Hadiths have come praising generosity and condemning stinginess, among them: "Two qualities do not combine in a believer: stinginess and bad character."

The apparent sense of His saying ﴿بِالبُخْلِ﴾ (with stinginess) is that it is connected to His saying ﴿ويَأْمُرُونَ﴾ (and they enjoin), as you say: "I commanded Zayd with patience," so that stinginess is the thing commanded. It is also said that the object of the command is omitted, and the letter bā' in ﴿بِالبُخْلِ﴾ is circumstantial (indicating a state), and the meaning is: "and they enjoin people to be ungrateful to them while they are characterised by stinginess," which is like what the poet pointed to in his saying:

*You gathered two matters, between which prudence was lost:*
*the arrogance of kings and the deeds of slaves.*

The majority of readers recited ﴿بِالبُخْلِ﴾ with a ḍamma on the bā' and a sukun on the khā'. ʿĪsā ibn ʿAmr and al-Ḥasan recited it with a ḍamma on both. Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī recited it with a fatḥa on both. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Suddi and a group recited it with a fatḥa on the bā' and a sukun on the khā'. All of these are dialectal forms (lughat). Al-Farra' said: "The Asad tribe say al-bakhal (with the fatḥa on both and a heavy pronunciation), Tamim say al-bukhl (lightly), and the people of the Hijaz say al-bukhl. [Some] also lighten it, so their dialect and the dialect of Tamim become one, while some of Bakr ibn Wa'il say al-bakhl." Jarir said:

*You want us to be pleased, while you are stingy;*
*and who is it that pleases friends with stinginess?*

Al-Mufaddal recited to me:

*And most loyal of them at a time of stinginess*

This line is recited with two fatḥas and two ḍammas:

*Surely a man from whom good is not expected*
*has stinginess; each one is a burden on whoever keeps company with him.*

The scholars differed in the grammatical analysis (i'rab, the study of word endings and sentence function) of ﴿الَّذِينَ يَبْخَلُونَ﴾. It is said that it is in the accusative position, as a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿مَن كانَ﴾ (whoever was). It is said it is from His saying ﴿مُخْتالًا فَخُورًا﴾ (self-conceited and boastful). The verb kāna (was) and its predicate are in the singular according to the wording of man (whoever), and the relative ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ is in the plural as a matter of meaning. It is also said that it is in the accusative to express disapproval (dhamm). In my view, it is permissible for it to be an attribute (ṣifa) of man, though they did not mention this possibility. It is also said that it is in the nominative position, by supposing an omitted subject, meaning: "They are those who..." Abu al-Baqa' said: "It is permissible for it to be a substitute for the pronoun in fakhūran (boastful), but this is weak."

These are six possibilities in which ﴿الَّذِينَ يَبْخَلُونَ﴾ is connected to what precedes it, and the stingy are then described as not loved by Allah, exalted is He. In that case the verse concerns believers, and the meaning is: "Be kind, O believers, to those whom Allah has named, for Allah does not love whoever has the qualities that prevent kindness toward them: self-conceit, boasting, stinginess, enjoining it, and concealing what Allah has given them of provision and wealth."

It is also said that ﴿الَّذِينَ يَبْخَلُونَ﴾ is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and the scholars differed about the predicate (khabar): is it omitted or spoken? It is said it is spoken, and it is His saying ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَظْلِمُ مِثْقالَ ذَرَّةٍ وإنْ تَكُ حَسَنَةً يُضاعِفْها﴾ (Indeed, Allah does not wrong by the weight of an atom; and if it is a good deed, He doubles it) [an-Nisa': 40]. In that case the connecting pronoun (rābiṭ) is omitted, its estimate being: "by the weight of an atom for them," or "He does not wrong them by the weight of an atom." This is the view of al-Zajjaj, but it is remote and strained because of the many separations between the subject and the predicate, and because the predicate does not fit clearly with the subject in meaning. The context of the subject and what is conjoined to it is evident from His saying: ﴿والَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم رِئاءَ النّاسِ ولا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ ولا بِاليَوْمِ الآخِرِ﴾ (And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day) [an-Nisa': 38], and it does not suit that it be predicated by His saying: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَظْلِمُ مِثْقالَ ذَرَّةٍ وإنْ تَكُ حَسَنَةً يُضاعِفْها ويُؤْتِ مِن لَدُنْهُ أجْرًا عَظِيمًا﴾ (Indeed, Allah does not wrong by the weight of an atom; and if it is a good deed, He doubles it and gives from Himself a great reward) [an-Nisa': 40]. Rather, the course of ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَظْلِمُ﴾ is that it be a new statement, informing about His justice and His bounty, exalted and sanctified is He.

It is also said that the predicate is omitted, and al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "Those who are stingy, act, and make (things) are deserving of every blame." Ibn Atiyya estimated it as: "they will be punished or recompensed," or similar. Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as: "those are their companion, Satan," and also estimated it as: "they are hated." It is possible that the estimate is: "they are disbelievers," (and We have prepared for the disbelievers). If what precedes the predicate implies real disbelief, such as their interpretation of stinginess as stinginess with the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and with declaring his prophethood, and the enjoining of stinginess upon their followers, meaning concealing that, and their concealing what the Torah contained of his prophethood and his Shari'a, then His saying ﴿وأعْتَدْنا لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ is literal. If what precedes the predicate is ingratitude for blessing, such as their interpretation that it concerns believers, then His saying ﴿وأعْتَدْنا لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ is ingratitude for blessing. Each of these estimates has something appropriate in the verse. The verse under these estimates, and under the view of al-Zajjaj, concerns disbelievers, and the occasion of revelation mentioned earlier makes this clear. The explanation of stinginess, of enjoining it, and of concealment has already been given in this sense in the occasion of revelation.

﴿وأعْتَدْنا لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾: that is, We have prepared and made ready. Al-ʿatīd is the present and prepared; al-mahīn is that which contains disgrace and humiliation, and it is more painful and more severe for the one punished.

﴿Those who spend their wealth to be seen by people and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day﴾. The interpretation of a verse like this was already given in His words: ﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:264). Here it says "and not in the Last Day," and there it says "and the Last Day." Al-Suddi, al-Zajjaj, Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and the majority said: they are the hypocrites, and the verse was revealed about them. Their spending is giving the zakat and bringing out wealth on journeys for the raid, to be seen and to ward off harm from themselves, not out of faith or love for the religion. Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and Mujahid said: it was revealed about the Jews. al-Tabari weakened this view on the ground that they believe in Allah and the Last Day. Ibn 'Atiyya (p-248) explained this view by saying that they did not believe in the proper way; he treated their faith as no faith at all, since it does not benefit them. It was also said: they are the polytheists of Mecca, because they used to deny the resurrection. The spending of the Jews was what they gave to support Quraysh at the battle of Uhud and the battle of the Trench, and the spending of the polytheists of Mecca was what they spent in hostility to the Prophet ﷺ and in seeking victory over him.

As for the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿those who spend﴾, there are several possibilities. The first is that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, which may be estimated as "will be punished," or "their companion is Satan," and the conjunction then is a conjunction of sentences. The second is that it is conjoined to "the disbelievers," in which case it is in the genitive, as al-Tabari said. The third is that it is conjoined to "those who are stingy," in which case its i'rab is like the i'rab of "those who are stingy." In the last two cases the conjunction is a conjunction of single words.

Ri'a' (showing off) is a verbal noun of ra'a, or its accusative is as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi, an accusative giving the reason for the action), and it has its conditions, so it is better to avoid this. It was said that it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal, an accusative describing the state of the subject), as Ibn 'Atiyya said, and he mentioned no other. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿and do not believe﴾ is that it is conjoined to the relative clause (silah) of "those who," so it is part of the relative clause. Separating the parts of the relative clause by an element governed by the relative clause does no harm, since the accusative of ri'a' in both of its possibilities is governed by "they spend."

They also allowed that ﴿and do not believe﴾ could be in the position of a circumstantial clause, so the waw is the waw of circumstance, meaning "not believing," and the governing verb of it is also "they spend." al-Mahdawi related that it is permissible for ri'a' to be an accusative of circumstance from the relative pronoun itself, not from the pronoun in "they spend." On this view it is not permissible for "and do not believe" to be conjoined to the relative clause, nor a circumstance from the pronoun in "they spend," because of what would follow: separating parts of the relative clause, or separating an element of the relative clause by a foreign element, namely ri'a', which is accusative as a circumstance from the relative pronoun itself. Rather, "and do not believe" would be a new independent sentence (mustani'af). This is a strained view. The connection of ri'a' to "they spend" is clear, whether as an object of purpose or as a circumstance, so it is not right to deviate from it.

The repetition of the negative particle (la) and the preposition (ba') in His words ﴿and not in the Last Day﴾ serves to negate each of them: belief in Allah, and belief in the Last Day. For when you say, "I do not strike Zayd and 'Amr," it is possible that you do not strike them both together, and for this reason it is permissible to say afterwards, "rather one of them." It is also possible that you negate striking each of them, both together and separately. But when you say, "I do not strike Zayd nor 'Amr," the second possibility is fixed, which was present without the repetition.

﴿And whoever has Satan as a companion, what an evil companion he is﴾. When He, exalted is He, mentioned those who are characterized by stinginess, commanding it, concealing the bounty of Allah, spending to be seen, and the absence of faith in Allah and the Last Day, He mentioned that these are results of being accompanied by Satan, mixing with him and staying close to him for one who is characterized by them. This is because they are pure evil, since they combine bad belief, which gives rise to spending to be seen, and all those blameworthy attributes. For this reason He placed those attributes first, and then mentioned what they arise from, which is the absence of faith in the Creator and in the abode of recompense. Then He mentioned that all of this comes from the companionship of Satan. The word "companion" (qarin) here is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of mufa'il, like "companion" (jalis) and "associate" (khalit), meaning one who sits with and mixes with. "Satan" here is a generic noun, not meaning Iblis alone, and it is like His words: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a satan, and he is his companion﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:36). "For him" is connected to "companion," meaning a companion to him. The fa' is the answer of the conditional clause. "Sa'a" here is the one that means "bi'sa" (what an evil), for emphasis in blame, and its subject according to the Basran grammarians is a general pronoun, and "companion" is a specification (tamyiz, an accusative clarifying a vague noun) of that pronoun. The noun particularly receiving the blame is omitted, and it is what returns to Satan who is the companion. It is not permissible for "sa'a" here to be the transitive one with its object omitted and "companion" as a circumstance, because in that case it would be an inflected verb, and then the fa' could not enter it, or it would enter it accompanied by qad. Some allowed that "companion" be accusative as a circumstance, or as an accusative of separation (qat'), but this is weak. The blame of this companion was intensified by making him carry those blameworthy attributes. al-Zamakhshari and others said: it is also permissible that it be a threat to them, that Satan will be joined with them in the Fire. End. In that case the companionship would be in the Hereafter, when he is joined with him in the Fire, so they curse each other and hate each other, as He said: ﴿joined together in fetters﴾ (Ibrahim 14:49), and ﴿when they are cast into it in a narrow place, bound together﴾ (al-Furqan 25:13). (p-249) The majority said: this companionship is in this world, like His words: ﴿And We appointed for them companions who made their deeds seem fair to them﴾ (Fussilat 41:25), and ﴿We appoint for him a satan, and he is his companion﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:36), and ﴿His companion will say: Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾ (Qaf 50:27). Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-Tabari linked this verse to His words: ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾ (al-Kahf 18:50). This is rejected, because "badalan" (as an exchange) is a circumstance. In this there is room for consideration. What al-Tabari said is correct: "badalan" is a specification, not a circumstance, and it clarifies the pronoun hidden in "bi'sa" according to the Basran grammarians, and the noun particularly receiving the blame is omitted, its estimate being: they, that is Satan and his offspring. The Kufans went to the view that the accusative after "ni'ma" and "bi'sa" is a circumstance, with differences among them established in the science of grammar.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 4, verse 39:

﴿And what would it have cost them had they believed in Allah and the Last Day and spent from what Allah has provided them?﴾ The apparent sense of this statement is that it forms a single, unified whole. What is intended by it is blame, rebuke, and a reproach for their ignorance of the place of their happiness. Otherwise, all success and benefit lie in their being characterized by what Allah, the Exalted, has mentioned. On this apparent reading, the statement may be two sentences, and *law* (if) remains in its proper function as a particle indicating that what would have happened is conditional on the occurrence of something else. The implied meaning is: "What would it have cost them in faith in Allah and the Last Day and in spending in the way of Allah, had they believed in Allah and the Last Day and spent from what Allah has provided them? Happiness would have been theirs." It may also be a single sentence, according to the view of those who hold that *law* is a verbal particle (*masdariyya*) with the meaning of *an* (that). It is as if it were said: "What would it have cost them that they believe," i.e., in faith in Allah. In that case there is no answer (*jawab*) for it, and it is like the poet's words:

*"And what would it have cost him that I mentioned companions, like gazelles of the sand dunes in the sanctuaries of Aqyal?"*

They said: It is also permissible that the phrase "and what would it have cost them" be independent, with nothing dependent on it from what follows, and that what follows is a new sentence. That is: "And what would it have cost them on the Day of Resurrection of ruin and punishment by their being characterized by miserliness and those blameworthy qualities?" Then he began anew and said: "Had they believed," and he omitted the answer of *law*. Ibn ʿAtiyya (*Ibn ʿAtiyya*) said: The answer of *law* in His saying "*mâdhā*" (what), so it is a preceding answer (*jawab muqaddam*), end of quote. If he intended the apparent sense of this statement, then it does not agree with the statements of the grammarians, because interrogation does not occur as the answer of *law*, and because their saying "I honored you if Zayd had stood," if it is established that it is from the speech of the Arabs, is taken to mean that "I honored you" indicates the answer, and is not itself the answer, as they said regarding their saying "You are unjust if you do it." If he intended an explanation of the meaning, then what he said is possible.

*Wa-mādhā* (and what): It is possible that all of it is an interrogative, with the predicate in *ʿalayhim* (upon them). It is also possible that *mā* is the interrogative and *dhā* means *alladhī* (who/which), and it is the predicate, with *ʿalayhim* being the relative clause of *dhā*. And if "had they believed in Allah and the Last Day" is one of the complements of His saying "and what would it have cost them," then in that there is a sense of grief for them, concern, and compassion. The Mu'tazila have clung to this. Abu Bakr al-Razi (*Abu Bakr al-Razi*) said: It indicates the falsity of the doctrine of the Jahmiyya, the people of compulsion (*Jabriyya*), because if they were not able to believe in Allah and to spend, it would not be permissible to say this about them, since their excuse would be clear, namely that they were not empowered to do what they were called to, nor capable of it, just as one does not say to the blind man, "What would it have cost him had he seen?" nor says to the sick man, "What would it have cost him had he been healthy?" In that is the clearest proof that Allah has cut off their excuse in performing what He obligated them to, of faith and all other acts of obedience, and that they are empowered to perform them, end of his statement. This is the view of the Mu'tazila. The doctrines on this matter are four, as has been established: the Jabriyya, the Qadariyya, the Mu'tazila, and the People of the Sunna (*Ahl al-Sunna*). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: The resolution of the Mu'tazila's doubt is that what is demanded is their acquisition (*kasb*), their striving, and their turning toward faith, while as for origination (*ikhtiraʿ*), Allah alone is its sole agent, end of quote.

When He, the Exalted, described them with those blameworthy qualities, there was in this an ascent from one ugly quality to one uglier than it. So He began first with miserliness, then with commanding it, then with concealing Allah's bounty, then with spending to be seen by people, then with disbelief in Allah (p-250) and in the Last Day. When He rebuked them and gently invited them, He began with faith in Allah and the Last Day, since by that eternal happiness is attained. Then He joined spending to it, i.e., in the way of Allah, since by it there is negation of those ugly qualities of miserliness, commanding it, concealing Allah's bounty, and spending to be seen by people.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing of them.﴾ This is a statement that includes a warning and an alert to the evil of their inner states, and that He, the Exalted, is aware of what they have concealed within themselves.

* *

It has been said: These verses include kinds of eloquence, rhetoric, and figures of speech (*badiʿ*): repetition (*takrar*), found in: *"a share of what they have earned"* [An-Nisa: 32] and *"a share of what they have earned"* [An-Nisa: 32]; the invocation of the divine name in *"and ask Allah"* [An-Nisa: 32] and *"indeed Allah"*; *"an arbiter from his people"* [An-Nisa: 35] and *"an arbiter from her people"*; *"some of you over others"* [An-Nisa: 32]; *"and the neighbor who is near of kin and the neighbor who is a stranger"* [An-Nisa: 36]; and *"those who spend their wealth to be seen by people and do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day"* [An-Nisa: 38]. And His saying: *"had they believed in Allah and the Last Day and spent from what Allah has provided them"*; *(qarīnan)* (a companion) and *(sāʾa qarīnan)* (evil is the companion); the divine name in *"from what Allah has provided them"* and *"Allah was"*. Paronomasia that is varied (*tajnis mughayir*) in: *"guarding in the unseen what Allah has guarded"* [An-Nisa: 34], and in *"they are miserly"* and *"with miserliness."* The sequence of attributes without a conjunction in: *"obedient, guarding"* [An-Nisa: 34]. Coordination by particles following the method of mentioning the more emphatic before the less emphatic in: *"and to parents, do good"* and what follows it. Antithesis in meaning (*tibaq maʿnawi*) in: *"their disobedience"* [An-Nisa: 34], *"if they obey you"* [An-Nisa: 34]; and in *"a breach between the two"* [An-Nisa: 35] and *"Allah will bring about agreement"* [An-Nisa: 35]. Specification in His saying *"from his people"* [An-Nisa: 35] and *"from her people"*, and in His saying *"those whom your oaths have bound"*. Indefiniteness in His saying *"anything"* and *"good"*, and *"what their right hands possess"*; the generality of *"anything"*, *"good"*, and *"mā"* is clear. Allusion (*taʿrid*) in: *"arrogant, boastful"* [An-Nisa: 36]. By this He alluded to the blame of arrogance, which leads to distancing oneself from poor relatives, despising them, and despising those mentioned with them. Emphasis by attributing ownership to the right hand in: *"what your right hands possess"* [An-Nisa: 36]. Simile (*tamthil*) in: *"And whoever has Satan as a companion, then evil is the companion"* [An-Nisa: 38]. Ellipsis in a number of places.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom. And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward.﴾ ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and We bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ [An-Nisa: 41] ﴿On that Day, those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them, and they will not conceal from Allah a single statement.﴾ [An-Nisa: 42] ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying, nor in a state of major impurity, except while passing through, until you have bathed. And if you are ill or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have contact with women and find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands. Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ [An-Nisa: 43]

Al-mithqal (the weight): it is on the pattern of mif'al, derived from al-thiql (heaviness). The mithqal of anything is its weight. Do not think that it refers only to the dinar.

Al-dharrah (the atom): a small ant. It is said that it is the smallest it is when a year has passed over it. It is also said that it is described as "red." It is said that when a year has passed over it, it becomes small and moves. [A poet] said:

"Of the modest-gazing (women), if a young ant of the dust crawled upon the back of her camel's saddle, it would leave a mark."

Hassan said:

"If a yearling of the offspring of the ant were to crawl upon her, her wounds would have made her weep."

It is reported from Ibn Abbas that al-dharrah is the head of an ant. It is also reported from him that he put his hand into the dust, lifted it, then blew on it and said: "Each one of these is a dharrah." It is said: every part of the dust motes in a window's opening is a dharrah. It is also said that al-dharrah is the mustard seed.

Al-sukr (intoxication): the blocking of the path of discernment by drinking what intoxicates. It comes from their saying: "The eye of the falcon was intoxicated (sakarat)," when sleep overcame it. From this comes: "The river was blocked (sakara)" when its channels were obstructed, and "I blocked it (sakartuhu)." Al-sukr, with a dammah on the sin, also means a dam. [A poet] said:

"We continued over the drinking, treating the blockage with blockage."

Al-sakar, with a fathah, means that which intoxicates, that is, that which prevents discernment.

Al-ghait (the low ground): what is lowered of the earth; its plural is ghiytan. It is said: ʿayt and ghawt. Ibn Jinni claimed that ghayt is on the pattern of fa'il, since its origin, in his view, is ghayyit, like hayyin and sayyid when you lighten them. The correct view is that it is fa'l, just as ghawt is fa'l, because the Arabs said: ghata yaghuts and yaghit, so they used it once among the verbs with ya' and once among those with waw. They pluralized ghawt as aghwat. (p-251) It is said: taghawwata when he relieved himself, and ghata fi al-ard yaghit and yaghut, meaning he disappeared into it until none could see him except one who stood right over him. When a man wished to relieve himself, he would seek out a low ground from the earth in which he could conceal himself from people's eyes. Then the term ghait was used for the act of defecation itself, just as it was said: "the scale flowed" and "the river ran."

* *

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom.﴾ It was revealed concerning the first emigrants. It is also said: concerning disputants. It is also said: concerning the believers in general. The connection of this to what precedes it is clear: when He, exalted is He, commanded the worship of Him and good treatment of parents and those mentioned with them, then followed that with condemnation of miserliness and the attributes mentioned with it, then rebuked those who did not believe and did not spend in obedience to Allah, all of this was a preparation for mentioning the recompense for good deeds and bad deeds. So He informed of the attribute of His justice, that He, mighty and majestic, does not wrong in the least, then He informed of the attribute of beneficence, saying:

* *

﴿And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward.﴾ He struck the example of the smallest thing with the weight of an atom, and that is a great exaggeration in negating injustice altogether. The apparent meaning of His saying "mithqal dharrah" is that the atom has a weight. It is also said: the atom has no weight, and that He tested this and found it had no weight. Since Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom, then He is even more far from wronging beyond that. And since the atom is the smallest of existing things, it was used as an example of smallness. Ibn Mas'ud read: "mithqal namlah" (the weight of an ant), and perhaps that is by way of explanation of the atom.

Al-Zamakhshari said: In it is evidence that if He were to diminish from their reward the least and smallest thing, or increase in the punishment, that would be injustice. And He does not do it because it is impossible in wisdom, not because it is impossible in power. End. This is a Mu'tazili tendency. In Sahih Muslim it is established from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah does not wrong a believer a good deed, by which he is given in this world and recompensed for it in the Hereafter. As for the disbeliever, he is fed for his good deeds in this world for what he did, until when he arrives at the Hereafter he has no good deed by which he is recompensed."

The verb yuzlamu (is wronged) is transitive to one object, which is omitted, and its estimate is: "He does not wrong anyone with the weight of an atom." Mithqal is in the accusative as an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: injustice of the weight of an atom, just as you say: "I do not wrong (anyone) a little or a lot." It is also said: it has been made to carry the meaning of what is transitive to two objects, so mithqal is in the accusative as the second object, and the first is omitted, the estimate being: "He does not diminish, or usurp, or defraud anyone of the weight of an atom of good or evil."

﴿And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it.﴾

The noon of "tak" has been deleted because of frequency of use. The analogical expectation was to keep the waw, because the waw was only deleted due to the meeting of two sukun letters. So when it is deleted, the waw should return, and because the reason for its deletion has ceased to exist. The permissibility of deleting it, according to the school of Sibawayh, is conditional on two sukun letters meeting. If it meets something like: "lam yakun ibnuka qa'iman" (your son was not standing) or "lam yakun al-rajulu dhahiban" (the man was not going), its deletion is not permitted. Yunus permitted it. The condition for the permissibility of this deletion is the entry of a jussive particle on a mudari' verb that is declined and raised with a dammah. If it were built upon the nun of emphasis or the nun of feminine plurals, or raised by a nun, its deletion would not be permitted.

Al-Jumhur read: "hasanatan" with the accusative, so tak is naqisah (a defective verb), and its subject is a hidden pronoun in it referring to mithqal. He made the verb feminine because it refers to a noun annexed to a feminine noun, or by consideration of the meaning, since mithqal means weight, that is: "if it be (taku) the weight of an atom." Al-Hasan and the two Haramiyyan (the Meccan and Medinan readers) read: "hasanatun" with the nominative, so tak is complete (tammah), the estimate being: "if a good deed occurs or exists." The two Ibns read: "yudda'ifha," with shaddah and without alif. Abu Ali said: The meaning of both is one, and they are two dialects. This is indicated by the reading of one who read: "yudda'af lahu al-adhab did'ayn" and "fayudda'ifa lahu adh'afan kathirah." Abu Ubayda in Kitab al-Majaz and al-Tabari said: daa'afa implies many times, and dda'afa implies two times, while the speech of the Arabs implies the reverse of this, because al-mudda'afah (multiplication) implies the increase of a like amount; when it is intensified, the form implies multiplication beyond two times up to the furthest extent of the number. We have already discussed this earlier.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Its reward is multiplied, because it deserves its opposite, the reward, at every time of the future, unending times. The doubling of a good deed by ten of its like is recorded in the Book of Allah, and the doubling of expenditure to seven hundred, and hadiths have come about multiplication by a thousand and a million, and there is no contradiction in this, for the intended meaning is abundance, not limitation. And if limitation is intended, there is no contradiction either, because the one promised this is all believers, and it varies according to the variation of deeds. The apparent meaning of His saying: "Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom," etc., is that it is general for everyone, and restricting that to the emigrants is not apparent.

﴿From Himself (min ladunhu)﴾ means: from His presence, by way of bounty. Al-Zamakhshari said: He called it a reward because it follows the reward and does not remain except by its remaining. End. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd said: The reward here is Paradise. It is also said: it has no limit and no counting.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 41:

﴿Then how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ He is their prophet, who bears witness against them for what they did, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117]. The "nation" here refers to those to whom the Prophet ﷺ was sent, both believers in him and disbelievers. When Allah the Exalted informed of His justice and the bestowal of His grace, He followed this with a warning about the state in which they will be present for recompense and in which he will bear witness against them.

The (kayfa) is in the position of nominative if the omitted element is a subject (mubtada'), the estimate being: "then how is the state of these people previously mentioned, or how is their conduct?" This subject is then the governing element for (idha), or it is in the position of accusative if the omitted element is a verb, i.e.: "then how will they act, or how will they be?" The verb is also the governing element for (idha). Ibn 'Atiyyah reported from Makki that the governing element for (kayfa) is (ji'na, we brought). He said: "This is an error." The interrogation here is for rebuke and reproach, and the pointing with "these people" is to the community of the Messenger ﷺ. Muqatil said: it refers to the disbelievers. It was also said: to the Jews and Christians. It was said: to the disbelieving Quraysh. It was said: to those who denied. His witnessing is by his conveying (the message) to his community; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Juraij, al-Suddi and Muqatil. Or it is by their faith, as said by Abu al-'Aliyah, or by their deeds, as said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. The apparent meaning is that the testimony is against those who are witnessed against. It was also said: "'ala" carries the meaning of "li" (for), i.e.: "and We bring you for these people," but this is remote. Al-Zajjaji said: he bears witness for them and against them, and the witnessed-against is omitted in His saying: ﴿When We bring from every nation a witness﴾ because its mention ran through the prepositional phrase, so it was abbreviated, and the estimate is: from every nation a witness over its nation. The apparent contrast requires that the testimony be against them, not for them, and it is not against them unless those witnessed against were deniers and rejecters of what he testified to concerning them. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, whenever he recited this verse, his eyes would overflow, and likewise when Ibn Mas'ud recited it to him, his eyes shed tears and he wept. Allah knows best; it is compassion for his community and mercy toward them from the terror of that Day. The apparent meaning of His saying: "and We bring you" is that it is conjoined to His saying: "We bring from every nation." It was also said: it is a circumstantial clause (hal) with "qad" implied, i.e.: "and We have indeed brought."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 42:**

﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them.﴾ The tanwin in (يَوْمَئِذٍ, yawma'idhin) is *tanwin al-'iwad* (the tanwin of compensation), which replaces an omitted sentence. The implied meaning is: "On the Day when We bring from every community a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people, those who disbelieved (كَفَرُوا) and disobeyed the Messenger (وَعَصَوُا الرَّسُولَ) will wish..." That is, they disbelieved in Allah and disobeyed His Messenger. Here الرَّسُولُ (al-Rasul) is a generic noun (*ism jins*). It is also possible that the tanwin compensates for the last sentence, and that الرَّسُولُ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). The Messenger is mentioned explicitly rather than as "and disobeyed you" because of the honour of mentioning the Messenger and the elevation of the message, which is the noblest thing a human being can bear from Allah, since it is the cause of happiness in this world and the Hereafter. The word that governs (يَوْمَ, yawma) is (يَوَدُّ, yawaddu). The meaning of يَوَدُّ is "wishes" (يَتَمَنّى). The apparent reading of (وَعَصَوْا) is that it is coordinated with (كَفَرُوا). It has been said that it is governed by an implied different relative pronoun, meaning "and those who disobeyed," so that they are two groups. It has also been said that the و is the *waw* of circumstance (واوُ الحالِ), meaning "who disbelieved while they had disobeyed the Messenger." Al-Hawfi said: it is permissible for (يَوْمَ) to be indeclinable together with (إذْ), because when a time noun is annexed to an indeclinable noun, it may take the same indeclinable form. (إذْ) in this position is a noun and not an adverb of time, because when time nouns are annexed to it they take on the sense of nominality through specifying the noun annexed to them, just as nouns are specified, and they deserve the genitive case, and the genitive is not one of the markers of adverbs of time. He ended here, and this is a good statement.

The Jumhur (majority of reciters) read وَعَصَوُا الرَّسُولَ with a *damma* on the *waw*. Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Abu al-Sammal read (وَعَصَوِ الرَّسُولَ) with a *kasra* on the *waw*, following the original form for the meeting of two unvocalised letters (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read تُسَوّى with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a light *sin*, in the passive voice; it is the imperfect of سَوّى. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and a doubled *sin*; its original form is تَتَسَوّى, and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *sin*, and it is the imperfect of تَسَوّى. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (تَسَوّى) with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and a light *sin*, by omitting one *ta'*, since its original form is تَتَسَوّى, and it is the imperfect of تَسَوّى. According to the reading of those who read تَتَسَوّى and تُسَوّى, the earth is the subject. Abu 'Ubayda and a group said: its meaning is "if the earth were split and they were in it, and the earth itself were levelled over them," and the particle (بِ) is in the sense of (عَلى, 'ala, "over"). Another group said: its meaning is "if the earth were levelled together with them, in that they would become dust like the beasts," so the wording is as though the earth were the one levelling along with them, but the real meaning is that they become equal with the earth. There is thus an inversion (*qalb*) in the wording, like the expression "I put the cap on my head." According to the reading of those who read تُسَوّى in the passive, the meaning is that Allah does this according to the two meanings mentioned earlier. It has been said: the meaning is "if they were buried and the earth were levelled over them as the dead are levelled over," and the meaning of this statement is the same as that of the first. It has been said: the meaning is "if the earth were made equal to them," i.e., what is upon it would be taken from them as ransom (فِدْيَةً).

The governing element of ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ يَوَدُّ﴾, and the object of يَوَدُّ, is omitted; its implied form is "the levelling of the earth over them," which is indicated by His saying: "if the earth were levelled over them." (لَوْ, law) is a particle for what would have occurred because another thing occurred. Its answer is omitted, and the implied form is "they would have been delighted by that," and it is omitted because يَوَدُّ indicates it. Whoever permits (لَوْ) to be a verbal-source particle (مَصْدَرِيَّة), like (أنْ), as he permitted here, then it has no answer, and it stands in the position of the object of يَوَدُّ.

* *

﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement.﴾ It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is: "They wished, when their limbs testified against them, that they had not concealed from Allah their polytheism." It is also reported from him: "When their limbs bore witness against them, they did not conceal anything from Allah." Al-Hasan said: the Resurrection has stations. In one station they recognise the evil of their deeds and ask to be returned to the world, and in another station they conceal and say: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am 6:23]. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: this is a new sentence (كَلامٌ مُسْتَأْنَفٌ), not connected with His saying "and the earth is levelled over them." The meaning is: they cannot conceal the statement, because it is manifest before Allah. It has been said: they wished that the earth were levelled over them, and that they had not concealed from Allah any statement. It has been said: they did not believe that they were polytheists; rather they believed that worshipping idols was obedience. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these two statements. Al-Qadi said: they reported what they imagined, for they used to think they were not polytheists, and that does not exempt them from having lied. When the sentence is included under يَوَدُّ, the majority said: it is their saying ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am 6:23], meaning "we did not do any evil," and this relates to the Hereafter. 'Ata' said: it concerns the command of the Messenger, his description and his sending, and this relates to this world. He ended the summary taken from the book *al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir*.

Ibn 'Atiyya said, in a summarised form: He began a new statement and informed that they will not conceal any statement, because their limbs will speak all of it, until some of them say: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am 6:23], and then Allah says: "You have lied," and then their limbs speak, so they conceal no statement. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas. A group said something similar, except that they said: it is a new statement to inform that concealment does not benefit, and even if they concealed, Allah would know all their secrets. The meaning is: that terrifying station is not one in which concealment benefits. The difference between this and the first view is that the first implies that concealment does not happen in any way, whereas the other implies that concealment does not benefit, whether it occurs or not, just as you say: "This is a gathering in which no falsehood is said," while you mean that it does not benefit there and no one listens to it. Another group said: the whole statement is connected, and the meaning is: they wish that they had not concealed from Allah any statement. Their wish is nothing but regret for their lie when they said: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists." Another group said: these are stations and groups. He ended. Al-Zamakhshari said: they cannot conceal it, because their limbs bear witness against them.

It has also been said: the *waw* is for circumstance (لِلْحالِ): they wish that they were buried under the earth, and that they do not conceal from Allah any statement, and do not lie in their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am 6:23]. For when they say that and deny their polytheism, Allah then seals their mouths, and their hands and feet speak, testifying to their lie and to their polytheism against them. Because of the severity of the matter for them, they wish that the earth were levelled over them. He ended. What emerges from this sentence is that the *waw* in His saying "and they do not conceal" is either a *waw* of circumstance or a *waw* of coordination. If it is a *waw* of circumstance, the meaning is: on the Day of Resurrection they will wish, if they had died and the earth were levelled over them, while not concealing Allah any statement. Then it is a circumstantial clause (حال) from (بِهِمْ, "over them"), and the element governing it is (تُسَوّى, "is levelled"). This circumstance is valid if (لَوْ) is taken as a verbal-source particle with the sense of (أنْ). It is also valid if (لَوْ) is taken as a particle for what would have occurred because another thing occurred, meaning: "If the earth were levelled over them while not concealing Allah any statement, that would have been their aim and their desire." It may also be a circumstance from (الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا), with the governing element (يَوَدُّ) on the assumption that (لَوْ) is a verbal-source particle, meaning: "On the Day of Resurrection those who disbelieved will wish that, if the earth had been levelled over them, they would not conceal." This circumstance then restricts the wishing: the wish occurs from them in the state of not concealing, which is the state of acknowledging what they were in the world of disbelief and denial. Their acknowledgement would then occur in one station and not another, since it is reported that they do conceal; it is far-fetched for it to be a circumstance in this way. (لَوْ) is a particle for what would have occurred because another thing occurred, due to the separation between the circumstance and its governing element by a sentence.

If the *waw* in "and they do not conceal" is a *waw* of coordination, then it may be coordination of single words (مُفْرَدات) or of sentences (جُمَل). If it is coordination of single words, then it is coordinated with the object of يَوَدُّ, meaning: "they wish the levelling of the earth over them and the absence of concealment." The absence of concealment may be in this world, or in the Hereafter, which is their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am 6:23]. It is very far-fetched that it is coordinated with the omitted object of يَوَدُّ, given that (لَوْ) is a particle for what would have occurred because another thing occurred. If it is coordination of sentences, then it may be coordinated with يَوَدُّ, meaning: "they wish such-and-such, and they do not conceal Allah any statement." Then Allah informs about them with two statements: the wish, and the absence of concealment, and the absence of concealment would be in some stations of the Resurrection. It is also possible that the object of يَوَدُّ is omitted, as we established, (لَوْ) is a particle for what would have occurred because another thing occurred, and its answer is omitted, as was mentioned earlier. The sentence "and they do not conceal" is then coordinated with (لَوْ) and what it entails, and Allah has informed us of three sentences: the sentence of wishing, the conditional sentence of (لَوْ) with its answer, and the sentence of the absence of concealment.

﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying﴾. It is narrated that a group of the Companions drank wine before it was prohibited. Then the time of prayer came, and one of them led the prayer and recited, "Say: O disbelievers," and confused the recitation. So this verse was revealed. It was also said that it was revealed because of 'Umar's statement the second time: "O God, make clear to us a sufficient explanation regarding wine." They used to avoid it at the times of the prayers, but when they had prayed the 'Isha' they would drink it, and they would not wake in the morning except that the intoxication had left them. This continued until 'Umar asked a third time, and then the prohibition of it was revealed absolutely. This verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) according to the majority. Ibn 'Abbas held that it is mansukh (abrogated) by the verse of al-Ma'idah. More surprising than this is the statement of 'Ikrimah that His saying, ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾, is abrogated by His saying, ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and so on. That is, it was permitted for them to delay the prayer until the intoxication passed. Then this was abrogated, and they were commanded to pray in every state. Then the drinking of wine was abrogated by His saying, "So avoid it." God did not reveal this verse to permit wine, so it is not abrogated. Nor did He, after its revelation, permit combining prayer with intoxication. The reasoning of Ibn 'Abbas is that the implication (mafhum) of the address indicates the permissibility of intoxication, and that only approaching prayer in that state was prohibited. So what was understood as permitting drinking and intoxication was abrogated by the prohibition of wine.

The connection (munasabah) of this verse with what precedes it is this: when God commanded the worship of God and sincerity in it, and commanded kindness to parents and noble character, and censured stinginess, and digressed from that to some matters of the Resurrection, and some of the Muslims had caused confusion in the prayer, which is the head of worship, because of drinking wine, it was fitting that the prayer be purified from the impurities of turbidity that cause it to deviate from its proper form. So God commanded that it be performed in its proper form, free from whatever corrupts it, so that He might unite for them sincerity in the worship of the Truth with noble character among themselves and toward creation. The address with His saying "O you who believe" is directed to those who are sober, because the intoxicated person who has lost discernment due to his intoxication is not addressed. But he is addressed when he becomes sober, by performing what is obligatory upon him, and by making expiation for what he neglected during his intoxication of the rulings whose obligation had been established for him before intoxication. There is in this no imposing of what is beyond one's capacity, contrary to what some people have held.

God emphasized the prohibition against a believer praying while intoxicated by His saying, ﴿Do not approach prayer﴾, because the prohibition against approaching prayer is more emphatic than saying "Do not pray while you are intoxicated." Similar to it are: "and do not approach fornication" (wa la taqrabu al-zina), ﴿and do not approach indecencies﴾ [al-An'am: 151], ﴿and do not approach the property of the orphan﴾ [al-An'am: 152]. The meaning is: do not defile the prayer. It was also said that there is an omission of a noun, meaning: do not approach the places of prayer, based on His saying, ﴿nor [approach prayer] while in a state of major impurity, except for travelers﴾, according to one of the two interpretations of "travelers" (ʿabiri sabil), which will come, God willing. The places of prayer are the mosques, based on his saying (ﷺ): "Keep your children and your insane away from your mosques."

The majority hold that what is meant is: "while you are intoxicated from wine." Al-Dahhak said that what is meant is intoxication from sleep, based on his saying (ﷺ): "If one of you dozes during prayer, let him sleep until the sleep leaves him, for he does not know, perhaps he would seek forgiveness and would revile himself." 'Ubaydah al-Salmani said that what is meant by His saying, ﴿while you are intoxicated﴾, is when you are holding back urine (haqin), based on his saying (ﷺ), peace be upon him: "None of you should pray while holding back urine." In another narration: "while pressing his thighs together." The statements of al-Dahhak and 'Ubaydah were regarded as weak and unlikely. Al-Qurtubi said: their statements are sound in meaning, because what is required of the worshipper is to devote himself to the worship of God Most High with his heart and his body, by removing the causes that disturb him and diminish his humility, such as sleep, the urge to urinate, hunger, and other things that occupy the mind. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the prohibition against approaching prayer in a state of intoxication. It was also said that what is meant is the prohibition against intoxication itself, because prayer had been obligated upon them, and the times of intoxication were not protected or determined among them, since intoxication sometimes occurs with a little and sometimes with a lot. When the time of it was not fixed for them, they abstained from drinking as a precaution for performing the prayers obligated upon them. Also, intoxication differs according to the temperaments of drinkers: some become intoxicated with a lot, and some with a little.

Al-Jumhur read *sukara* (سُكارى) with a damma on the sin. They differed: is it a broken plural (jam' taksir) or a collective noun (ism jam')? The position of Sibawayh is that it is a broken plural. Sibawayh said in defining the broken plural of adjectives: "They sometimes break some of these into *fu'ala*, as in the statement of some of them: *sukara* and *ujala*." This is an explicit statement from him that *fu'ala* is a plural. But the Ustadh Abu al-Hasan Ibn al-Baddhish erred and attributed to Sibawayh that it is a collective noun, and that Sibawayh explained this in the chapter on patterns (al-abniyah). Ibn al-Baddhish said: this is the analogical view, because it came in a pattern in which no plural came at all. In the chapter on patterns there is nothing but Sibawayh's explicit statement that it is a broken plural, since he said: "*Fu'ala* occurs in nouns, such as *hubara*, *sumana*, and *kubara*, and it is not an adjective, unless the singular is broken into it for the plural, such as *ujala*, *sukara*, and *kusala*." Al-Sirafi reported both views regarding it and preferred that it is a broken plural, and that this is what the statement of Sibawayh indicates.

A group read *sukara* with a fatha on the sin, like *nadman* and *nadama*, and this is a broken plural. Al-Nakha'i read *sakra*. It may be an adjective for a feminine singular, like *imra'atun sakra*, and applied to a group, since its meaning is: "You are a group intoxicated." Ibn Jinni said: it is a plural of *sakran* in the pattern *fa'la*, like His saying (in the poem): *rawba niyaman* and like their saying: *halka* and *maydan*, plurals of *halik* and *ma'id*. A'mash read *sukra* with a damma on the sin, in the pattern of *hubla*, and its explanation is that it is an adjective for a group, meaning "you are a group intoxicated." Jannah ibn Hubaysh reported *kasla* and *kusla* with a damma and a fatha, as al-Zamakhshari said.

The meaning of "until you know what you are saying" is: until you become sober and then know. The cause is put as the limit (ghayah) of the cause, and what is meant is the cause. This is because, as long as one is intoxicated, he does not know what he is saying. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the intoxicated person does not know what he says. For this reason, 'Uthman, Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, 'Ata', al-Qasim, Rabi'ah, al-Layth, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and al-Muzani held that the intoxicated person is not bound by divorce (talaq). Al-Tabari chose this view. The scholars were unanimous that the divorce of one who is mentally impaired (ma'tuh) is not valid, and the intoxicated person is like one who is mentally impaired, just as one who is obsessed (al-muwaswas) is mentally impaired by obsession. They do not differ that the divorce of one whose mind has gone due to narcotics (bang) is not valid, so likewise one who is intoxicated by drink. It is narrated from 'Umar, Mu'awiyah, and a group of the Successors (tabi'un) that his divorce takes effect against him. This is the view of Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, and al-Awza'i. Abu Hanifah said: his actions and contracts are all valid, like the actions of the sober person, except for apostasy. If he apostatizes, his wife is not separated from him. Abu Yusuf said: he becomes an apostate during his intoxication. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, except that he does not kill him during his intoxication, nor does he ask him to repent. His view differed regarding divorce. Malik held the intoxicated person liable for divorce, retaliation for wounds (qawad fi al-jirah), and blood money (al-'aql), but did not hold him liable for marriage or sale. Al-Mawardi said: a rare narration has reached us from our school that his divorce is not binding. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: neither divorce nor manumission is binding upon him.

They differed about intoxication. It was said: it is that in which the person does not recognize a man from a woman. This was stated by a group of the early scholars, and it is the view of Abu Hanifah. The verse indicates this, since His saying, ﴿until you know what you are saying﴾, its apparent meaning indicates that the intoxication to which the ruling applies is that in which the person does not understand what he says. Al-Thawri said: intoxication is the disturbance of the intellect; so if he garbles his recitation and speaks what he does not understand its limit. Ahmad said: if his intellect changes in a state of health, he is intoxicated. Something similar is reported from Malik.

It was said: the verse indicates that drinking was permitted at the beginning of Islam, up to the point where its drinker reaches intoxication. Al-Qaffal said: it is possible that there was permitted for them of drink that which moves the disposition toward generosity, bravery, and zeal. As for what removes the intellect until its drinker reaches a state of madness or unconsciousness, that was not permitted to intend, and indeed, if one consumed it without intention, he would be excused for it.

* *

﴿Nor [approach prayer] while in a state of major impurity (junub)﴾. This is a state conjoined to His saying, "while you are intoxicated," since it is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah). The nominal sentence is more emphatic because of the repetition of the pronoun, so restricting by it is more emphatic in negation than restricting by the singular, which is "nor [approach prayer] while in a state of major impurity." The entry of *la* (not) indicates the observance of each restriction individually. And if the prohibition is against performing the prayer accompanied by each state separately, then the prohibition against performing it with both together is included in the prohibition. The *junub* is one who is not in a state of purity due to emission (of semen) or the passing of the circumcised part (khitan). This is the statement of the majority of the community. But some of the Companions held: there is no ghusl except for one who has ejaculated, and this was said by al-A'mash and Dawud. This is a question whose proofs are mentioned in the science of jurisprudence (fiqh).

*Junub* derives from *janabah*, which means distance, as if he has moved away from purity (janaba al-tuhr), or from *janb* (side), as if he lay down beside someone and touched with his side. Al-Zamakhshari said: *junub* is used for both the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine, because it is a noun that functions like the verbal noun *ijnab*. He concluded. What he mentioned is the well-known usage in the language and the eloquent usage, and the Qur'an came with it. They have made its plural with the sound masculine plural suffix (waw and nun): "qawm junubun" (a people in major impurity). They have also made its broken plural: "qawm ajnab." As for its dual, they say: *junuban*.

﴿Except for travelers (ʿabiri sabil)﴾. *Al-ʿubur* means passing through and crossing over. From it comes the expression *naqa 'ubr al-hawajir* (a she-camel that crosses the noon heat) and *'ubr asfar* (one that crosses journeys). He said (in verse):
*"A swift, long-striding she-camel, with lean and slender forelegs, crossing the noonday heat, like a dry-skinned, dyed camel."*
The *ʿabir sabil* is the one who passes through the mosque without staying in it. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, who said: he passes through it and does not sit in it. Al-Layth said: he does not pass through it except if its door opens onto the mosque. Ahmad and Ishaq said: if the junub performs ablution, there is no harm in his sitting in the mosque. Al-Zamakhshari said: whoever interpreted "prayer" as "the mosque" said: its meaning is: do not approach the mosque in a state of major impurity, except as those passing through it, when the path to water is through it, or the water is in it, or you have had a wet dream in it. It was also said that men of the Ansar had their doors opening onto the mosque, so they would become junub and find no passage except through the mosque, so they were granted a concession.

It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "He did not permit anyone to sit in the mosque to pass through it while in a state of major impurity, except 'Ali, because his house was in the mosque." 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Hakam, and others also said: *ʿabir sabil* means the traveler. So it is not valid for anyone to approach prayer while in a state of major impurity, except after performing ghusl, except for the traveler, who performs tayammum (dry ablution). This is the view of Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, and Zufar. They said: no one enters the mosque except one who is pure, whether he intends to sit in it or to pass through it. This is the view of Malik, al-Thawri, and a group. This view was preferred on the ground that His saying, ﴿do not approach prayer﴾, remains on its apparent meaning and literal sense, unlike the interpretation of "places of prayer," which is figurative (majaz), and one does not turn to it except after the literal meaning of the speech is impossible. There is no condition in the mosque that prevents entering it, since it is impossible for one who is intoxicated, whereas in the prayer there is a recitation which is a condition, and one is prevented from it on account of the impossibility of establishing the prayer. The traveler is called *ʿabir sabil* because he is on the road, just as he is called *ibn al-sabil* (son of the road).

وأفادَ الكَلامُ مَعْنَيَيْنِ: أحَدُهُما: جَوازُ التَّيَمُّمِ لِلْجُنُبِ إذا لَمْ يَجِدِ الماءَ والصَّلاةِ بِهِ. والثّانِي: أنَّ التَّيَمُّمَ لا يَرْفَعُ الجَنابَةَ، لِأنَّهُ سَمّاهُ جُنُبًا مَعَ كَوْنِهِ مُتَيَمِّمًا. وعَلى هَذا المَعْنى فَسَرَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ الآيَةَ أوَّلًا فَقالَ: إلّا عابِرِي سَبِيلٍ، الِاسْتِثْناءُ مِن عامَّةِ أحْوالِ المُخاطَبِينَ، وانْتِصابُهُ عَلى الحالِ. فَإنْ قُلْتَ: كَيْفَ جَمَعَ بَيْنَ هَذِهِ الحالِ والَّتِي قَبْلَها ؟ قُلْتُ: كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: لا تَقْرَبُوا الصَّلاةَ في حالِ الجَنابَةِ إلّا ومَعَكم حالٌ أُخْرى تُعْذَرُونَ فِيها وهي حالُ السَّفَرِ، وعُبُورُ السَّبِيلِ عِبارَةٌ عَنْهُ. ويَجُوزُ أنْ لا يَكُونَ حالًا ولَكِنْ صِفَةً كَقَوْلِهِ: جُنُبًا أيْ: ولا تَقْرَبُوا الصَّلاةَ جُنُبًا غَيْرَ عابِرِي سَبِيلٍ، أيْ: جُنُبًا مُقِيمِينَ غَيْرَ مَعْذُورِينَ. فَإنْ قُلْتَ: كَيْفَ تَصِحُّ صَلاتُهم عَلى الجَنابَةِ لِعُذْرِ السَّفَرِ ؟ قُلْتُ: أُرِيدَ بِالجُنُبِ الَّذِينَ لَمْ يَغْتَسِلُوا، كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: لا تَقْرَبُوا الصَّلاةَ غَيْرَ مُغْتَسِلِينَ حَتّى تَغْتَسِلُوا، إلّا أنْ تَكُونُوا مُسافِرِينَ انْتَهى كَلامُهُ. ومَن قالَ بِمَنعِ الجُنُبِ مِنَ المُرُورِ في المَسْجِدِ والجُلُوسِ فِيهِ تَعْظِيمًا لَهُ، فالأوْلى أنْ يَمْنَعَهُ والحائِضَ مِن قِراءَةِ القُرْآنِ، وبِهِ قالَ الجُمْهُورُ، فَلا يَجُوزُ لَهُما أنْ يَقْرَآ مِنهُ شَيْئًا سَواءٌ كانَ كَثِيرًا أمْ قَلِيلًا حَتّى يَغْتَسِلا، ورَخَّصَ مالِكٌ لَهُما في الآيَةِ اليَسِيرَةِ لِلتَّعَوُّذِ، وأجازَ لِلْحائِضِ أنْ تَقْرَأ مُطْلَقًا إذا خافَتِ النِّسْيانَ عِنْدَ الحَيْضِ، وذَكَرُوا هَذِهِ المَسْألَةَ ولا تَعَلُّقَ لَها في التَّفْسِيرِ بِلَفْظِ القُرْآنِ.
* *
﴿حَتّى تَغْتَسِلُوا﴾ هَذِهِ غايَةٌ لِامْتِناعِ الجُنُبِ مِنَ الصَّلاةِ، وهي داخِلَةٌ في الحَظْرِ إلى أنْ يُوقِعَ الِاغْتِسالَ مُسْتَوْعِبًا جَمِيعَهُ. والخِلافُ: هَلْ يَدْخُلُ في ماهِيَّةِ الغُسْلِ إمْرارُ اليَدِ أوْ شَبَهِها مَعَ الماءِ عَلى المَغْسُولِ ؟ فَلَوِ انْغَمَسَ في الماءِ أوْ صَبَّهُ عَلَيْهِ فَمَشْهُورُ مَذْهَبِ مالِكٍ: أنَّهُ لا يُجْزِئُهُ حَتّى يَتَدَلَّكَ، وبِهِ قالَ المُزَنِيُّ: ومَذْهَبُ الجُمْهُورِ: أنَّهُ يُجْزِئُهُ مِن غَيْرِ تَدَلُّكٍ. وهَلْ يَجِبُ في الغَسْلِ تَخْلِيلُ اللِّحْيَةِ ؟ فِيهِ عَنْ مالِكٍ خِلافٌ. وأمّا المَضْمَضَةُ والِاسْتِنْشاقُ في الغَسْلِ فَذَهَبَ أبُو حَنِيفَةَ إلى فَرْضِيَّتِهِما فِيهِ لا في الوُضُوءِ. وقالَ ابْنُ أبِي لَيْلى وإسْحاقُ وأحْمَدُ وبَعْضُ أصْحابِ داوُدَ: هُما فَرْضٌ فِيهِما. ورُوِيَ عَنْ عَطاءٍ، والزُّهْرِيِّ وقالَ مُجاهِدٌ وجَماعَةٌ مِنَ التّابِعِينَ، ومالِكٌ، والأوْزاعِيُّ، واللَّيْثُ، والشّافِعِيُّ، ومُحَمَّدُ بْنُ جَرِيرٍ: لَيْسا بِفَرْضٍ فِيهِما. ورُوِيَ عَنْ أحْمَدَ: أنَّ المَضْمَضَةَ سُنَّةٌ، والِاسْتِنْشاقَ فَرْضٌ، وقالَ بِهِ بَعْضُ أصْحابِ داوُدَ. وظاهِرُ قَوْلِهِ: ﴿حَتّى تَغْتَسِلُوا﴾ حُصُولُ الِاغْتِسالِ، ولَمْ يُشْتَرَطْ فِيهِ نِيَّةُ الِاغْتِسالِ، بَلْ ذُكِرَ حُصُولُ مُطْلَقِ الِاغْتِسالِ، وبِهِ قالَ أبُو حَنِيفَةَ وأصْحابُهُ في كُلِّ طَهارَةٍ بِالماءِ. ورَوى هَذا الوَلِيدُ بْنُ مُسْلِمٍ عَنْ مالِكٍ، ومَشْهُورُ مَذْهَبِهِ أنَّهُ لا بُدَّ مِنَ النِّيَّةِ، وبِهِ قالَ الشّافِعِيُّ وأحْمَدُ وإسْحاقُ وأبُو ثَوْرٍ.
* *
﴿وإنْ كُنْتُمْ مَرْضى أوْ عَلى سَفَرٍ أوْ جاءَ أحَدٌ مِنكم مِنَ الغائِطِ أوْ لامَسْتُمُ النِّساءَ فَلَمْ تَجِدُوا ماءً فَتَيَمَّمُوا صَعِيدًا طَيِّبًا فامْسَحُوا بِوُجُوهِكم وأيْدِيكُمْ﴾ (p-٢٥٨) قالَ الجُمْهُورُ: نَزَلَتْ بِسَبَبِ عَدَمِ الصَّحابَةِ الماءَ في غَزْوَةِ المُرَيْسِيعِ، حِينَ أقامَ عَلى التِماسِ العِقْدِ. وقالَ النَّخَعِيُّ: في قَوْمٍ أصابَتْهم جِراحٌ وأجْنَبُوا. وقِيلَ: كانَ ذَلِكَ عَبْدَ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنَ عَوْفٍ، و(مَرْضى) يَعْنِي في الحَضَرِ. ويَدُلُّ عَلى مُطْلَقِ المَرَضِ قَلَّ أوْ كَثُرَ، زادَ أوْ نَقَصَ، تَأخَّرَ بُرْؤُهُ أوْ تَعَجَّلَ، وبِهِ قالَ داوُدُ. فَأجازَ التَّيَمُّمَ لِكُلِّ مَن صَدَقَ عَلَيْهِ مُطْلَقُ الِاسْمِ. وخَصَّصَ العُلَماءُ غَيْرُهُ المَرَضَ بِالجُدَرِيِّ، والحَصْبَةِ، والعِلَلِ المَخُوفِ عَلَيْها مِنَ الماءِ فَقالُوا: إنْ خافَ تَيَمَّمَ بِلا خِلافٍ، إلّا ما رُوِيَ عَنْ عَطاءٍ والحَسَنِ: أنَّهُ يَتَطَهَّرُ وإنْ ماتَ، وهُما مَحْجُوجانِ «بِحَدِيثِ عَمْرِو بْنِ العاصِ في غَزْوَةِ ذاتِ السَّلاسِلِ، وأنَّهُ أشْفَقَ أنْ يَهْلَكَ إنِ اغْتَسَلَ فَتَيَمَّمَ، فَأقَرَّهُ الرَّسُولُ ﷺ عَلى ذَلِكَ»، خَرَّجَهُ أبُو داوُدَ والدّارَقُطْنِيُّ.
* *
وإنْ خافَ حُدُوثَ مَرَضٍ أوْ زِيادَتَهُ، أوْ تَأخُّرَ البُرْءِ، فَذَهَبَ أبُو حَنِيفَةَ ومالِكٌ: إلى أنَّهُ يَتَيَمَّمُ. وقالَ الشّافِعِيُّ: لا يَجُوزُ، وقِيلَ: الصَّحِيحُ عَنِ الشّافِعِيِّ أنَّهُ إذا خافَ طُولَ المَرَضِ جازَ لَهُ التَّيَمُّمُ. وظاهِرُ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿أوْ عَلى سَفَرٍ﴾ مُطْلَقُ السَّفَرِ، فَلَوْ لَمْ يَجِدِ الماءَ في الحَضَرِ جازَ لَهُ التَّيَمُّمُ عِنْدَ مالِكٍ وأبِي حَنِيفَةَ ومُحَمَّدٍ. وقالَ الشّافِعِيُّ والطَّبَرِيُّ: لا يَتَيَمَّمُ. وقالَ اللَّيْثُ والشّافِعِيُّ أيْضًا: إنْ خافَ فَوْتَ الوَقْتِ تَيَمَّمَ وصَلّى، ثُمَّ إذا وجَدَ الماءَ أعادَ. وقالَ أبُو يُوسُفَ وزُفَرُ: لا يَتَيَمَّمُ إلّا لِخَوْفِ الوَقْتِ. والسَّفَرُ المُبِيحُ عِنْدَ الجُمْهُورِ مُطْلَقُ السَّفَرِ، سَواءٌ أكانَ مِمّا تُقْصَرُ فِيهِ الصَّلاةُ أوْ لا تُقْصَرُ. وشَرَطَ قَوْمٌ سَفَرًا تُقْصَرُ فِيهِ الصَّلاةُ، وشَرَطَ آخَرُونَ أنْ يَكُونَ سَفَرَ طاعَةٍ. وقالَ أبُو حَنِيفَةَ: لَوْ خَرَجَ مِن مِصْرِهِ لِغَيْرِ سَفَرٍ فَلَمْ يَجِدِ الماءَ جازَ لَهُ التَّيَمُّمُ، وقَدْرُ المَسافَةِ أنْ يَكُونَ بَيْنَهُ وبَيْنَ الماءِ مَيْلٌ. وقِيلَ: إذا كانَ بِحَيْثُ لا يَسْمَعُ أصْواتَ النّاسِ، لِأنَّهُ في مَعْنى المُسافِرِ. فَلَوْ وجَدَ ماءً قَلِيلًا إنْ تَوَضَّأ بِهِ خافَ عَلى نَفْسِهِ العَطَشَ تَيَمَّمَ عَلى قَوْلِ الجُمْهُورِ، فَلَوْ وجَدَهُ بِثَمَنِ مِثْلِهِ فَلا خِلافَ أنَّهُ يَلْزَمُهُ شِراؤُهُ، أوْ بِما زادَ. فَمَذْهَبُ أبِي حَنِيفَةَ والشّافِعِيِّ: يَتَيَمَّمُ. ومَذْهَبُ مالِكٍ: يَشْتَرِيهِ بِمالِهِ كُلِّهِ ويَبْقى عَدِيمًا. فَلَوْ حالَ بَيْنَهُ وبَيْنَ الماءِ عَدُوٌّ أوْ سَبُعٌ أوْ غَيْرُ ذَلِكَ مِمّا يَحُولُ فَكالعادِمِ لِلْماءِ.
* *
ومَجِيئُهُ مِنَ الغائِطِ كِنايَةٌ عَنِ الحَدَثِ بِالغائِطِ، وحُمِلَ عَلَيْهِ الرِّيحُ والبَوْلُ والمَنِيُّ والوَدْيُ، لا خِلافَ أنَّ هَذِهِ السِّتَّةَ أحْداثٌ. وقَدِ اخْتَلَفُوا في أشْياءَ ذُكِرَتْ في كُتُبِ الفِقْهِ. وقَرَأ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ: (مِنَ الغَيْطِ)، وخُرِّجَ عَلى وجْهَيْنِ: أحَدُهُما: أنَّهُ مَصْدَرٌ إذْ قالُوا: غاطَ يَغِيطُ. والثّانِي: أنَّ أصْلَهُ فَيْعِلٌ، ثُمَّ حُذِفَ كَمَيِّتٍ. واخْتَلَفُوا في تَفْسِيرِ اللَّمْسِ، فَقالَ عَمْرُو بْنُ مَسْعُودٍ وغَيْرُهُما: هو اللَّمْسُ بِاليَدِ، ولا ذِكْرَ لِلْجُنُبِ إنَّما يَغْتَسِلُ أوْ يَدَعُ الصَّلاةَ حَتّى يَجِدَ الماءَ. قالَ أبُو عُمَرَ: لَمْ يَقُلْ بِقَوْلِهِمْ أحَدٌ مِن فُقَهاءِ الأمْصارِ لِحَدِيثِ عَمّارٍ، وأبِي ذَرٍّ، وعُمْرانَ بْنِ حَصِينٍ في تَيَمُّمِ الجُنُبِ. وقالَ عَلِيٌّ وابْنُ عَبّاسٍ والحَسَنُ ومُجاهِدٌ والسُّدِّيُّ: المُرادُ الجِماعُ، والجُنُبُ يَتَيَمَّمُ. ولا ذِكْرَ لِلّامِسِ بِيَدِهِ، وهو مَذْهَبُ أبِي حَنِيفَةَ. فَلَوْ قَبَّلَ ولَوْ بِلَذَّةٍ لَمْ يَنْتَقِضِ الوُضُوءُ. وقالَ مالِكٌ: المُلامِسُ بِالجِماعِ يَتَيَمَّمُ، وكَذا بِاليَدِ إذا التَذَّ فَإنْ لَمَسَ بِغَيْرِ شَهْوَةٍ فَلا وُضُوءَ، وبِهِ قالَ أحْمَدُ وإسْحاقُ. وقالَ الشّافِعِيُّ: إذا أفْضى بِشَيْءٍ مِن جَسَدِهِ إلى بَدَنِ المَرْأةِ نَقَضَ الطَّهارَةَ، وهو قَوْلُ ابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ، وابْنِ عُمَرَ، والزُّهْرِيِّ، ورَبِيعَةَ، وعُبَيْدَةَ، والشَّعْبِيِّ، وإبْراهِيمَ، ومَنصُورٍ، وابْنِ سِيرِينَ. وقالَ الأوْزاعِيُّ: إنْ كانَ بِاليَدِ نَقَضَ وإلّا فَلا. وقَرَأ حَمْزَةُ، والكِسائِيُّ: (لَمَسْتُمْ)، وباقِي السَّبْعَةِ بِالألْفِ، وفاعِلُ هُنا مُوافِقٌ فِعْلَ المُجَرَّدِ نَحْوَ: جاوَزْتُ الشَّيْءَ وجُزْتُهُ، ولَيْسَتْ لِأقْسامِ الفاعِلِيَّةِ والمَفْعُولِيَّةِ لَفْظًا، والِاشْتِراكُ فِيهِما مَعْنًى، وقَدْ حَمَلَها الشّافِعِيُّ عَلى ذَلِكَ في أظْهَرِ قَوْلَيْهِ.
فَقالَ: المَلْمُوسُ كاللّامِسِ في نَقْضِ الطَّهارَةِ.
* *
وقَوْلُهُ: ﴿أوْ عَلى سَفَرٍ﴾ في مَوْضِعِ نَصْبٍ عَطْفًا عَلى (مَرْضى). وفي قَوْلِهِ: أوْ جاءَ، أوْ لامَسْتُمْ دَلِيلُ عَلى جَوازِ وُقُوعِ الماضِي خَبَرًا لِكانَ مِن غَيْرِ قَدْ، وادِّعاءُ إضْمارِها تَكَلُّفٌ خِلافًا لِلْكُوفِيِّينَ لِعَطْفِها عَلى خَبَرِ كانَ، والمَعْطُوفُ عَلى الخَبَرِ خَبَرٌ.
