(p-٢٥٩) ﴿فَلَمْ تَجِدُوا ماءً﴾ الضَّمِيرُ عائِدٌ عَلى مَن أُسْنِدَ إلَيْهِمُ الحُكْمُ في الأخْبارِ الأرْبَعَةِ. وفِيهِ تَغْلِيبُ الخِطابِ إذْ قَدِ اجْتَمَعَ خِطابٌ وغَيْبَةٌ، فالخِطابُ: ﴿كُنْتُمْ مَرْضى﴾، ﴿أوْ عَلى سَفَرٍ﴾، ﴿أوْ لامَسْتُمُ﴾. والغَيْبَةُ قَوْلُهُ: ﴿أوْ جاءَ أحَدٌ﴾. وما أحْسَنَ ما جاءَتْ هَذِهِ الغَيْبَةُ، لِأنَّهُ لَمّا كَنّى عَنِ الحاجَةِ بِالغائِطِ كَرِهَ إسْنادَ ذَلِكَ إلى المُخاطَبِينَ، فَنَزَعَ بِهِ إلى لَفْظِ الغائِبِ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿أوْ جاءَ أحَدٌ﴾، وهَذا مِن أحْسَنِ المُلاحَظاتِ وأجْمَلِ المُخاطَباتِ. ولَمّا كانَ المَرَضُ والسَّفَرُ ولَمْسُ النِّساءِ لا يَفْحُشُ الخِطابُ بِها جاءَتْ عَلى سَبِيلِ الخِطابِ. وظاهِرُ انْتِفاءِ الوِجْدانِ سَبَقَ تَطَلُّبُهُ وعَدَمُ الوُصُولِ إلَيْهِ، فَأمّا في حَقِّ المَرِيضِ فَجَعَلَ المَوْجُودَ حِسًّا في حَقِّهِ إذا كانَ لا يَسْتَطِيعُ اسْتِعْمالَهُ كالمَفْقُودِ شَرْعًا، وأمّا غَيْرُهُ باقِي الأرْبَعَةِ فانْتِفاءُ وِجْدانِ الماءِ في حَقِّهِمْ هو عَلى ظاهِرِهِ. و﴿فَلَمْ تَجِدُوا﴾ مَعْطُوفٌ عَلى فِعْلِ الشَّرْطِ ﴿فَتَيَمَّمُوا صَعِيدًا طَيِّبًا﴾ هَذا جَوابُ الشَّرْطِ، أمَرَ اللَّهُ تَعالى بِالتَّيَمُّمِ عِنْدَ حُصُولِ سَبَبٍ مِن هَذِهِ الأسْبابِ الأرْبَعَةِ وفُقْدانِ الماءِ.

Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How did he (Allah) join in a single series the sick and the travellers, and the one who has a minor impurity (muhdith) and the one who is in a state of major impurity (junub), when illness and travel are two causes of concession (rukhsah), minor impurity is the cause that makes wudu' (ablution) obligatory, and major impurity is the cause that makes ghusl (full washing) obligatory?" I answer: Allah, glorified and exalted, intended to grant concession to those who are obliged to purify themselves but cannot find water, so that they perform tayammum (dry ablution) with earth. He first singled out their sick and their travellers, because they are the most entitled to the concession, owing to the frequency of illness and travel and their predominance over the other causes that call for concession. Then He extended it to every person who is obliged to purify himself and lacks water, whether from fear of an enemy, a beast of prey, a lack of the means of drawing water, exhaustion in a place where there is no water, or other circumstances that are not as frequent as illness and travel. End of quotation. In his commentary there is this: his explanation of ﴿or you have touched women﴾ is that it means sexual intercourse, which results in major impurity. He explained it this way according to the school of Abu Hanifa, and he did not report any other school's view.

The gist of what he elaborated on is this: he gave a reason for mentioning illness and travel first. Those who take touching (lams) in its literal sense say that this is an instance of ascending from the lesser to the greater, because the state of illness is less than the state of travel, the state of travel is less than the state of answering the call of nature, and the state of answering the call of nature is less than the state of touching a woman. Do you not see that the state of health is generally greater than the state of sickness, and likewise in the rest of the cases?

Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' said: al-sa'id is dust. Al-Layth said: al-sa'id is level ground with nothing on it of plants or vegetation. This is also the view of Qatada, who said: al-sa'id is smooth ground. Al-Khalil said: al-sa'id is what rises from the surface of the earth, meaning the surface of the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: al-sa'id is the surface of the earth, whether it is dust or something else, even if it is rock with no dust on it. Someone else added: or sand, or a mineral, or saline ground.

Al-tayyib (the pure) means the clean, and this is the interpretation of a group, and it is the view of Abu Hanifa and Malik and the choice of al-Tabari. From the same usage is ﴿those whom the angels take in death while they are pure﴾ [al-Nahl: 32], meaning clean from the filth of transgressions. Some people said: al-tayyib here means lawful (halal). This was said by Sufyan al-Thawri and others. Al-Shafi'i and a group said: al-tayyib means that which grows plants, and Ibn 'Abbas also said this, citing the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes out by the permission of its Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. On this view, al-sa'id is dust. Those who hold this view permit tayammum with other than this, so the area of consensus (ijma') is that one performs tayammum with clean dust that grows plants, not taken by force and not usurped. The area where there is consensus on prohibition is that one performs tayammum on pure gold, silver, ruby, emerald, or on foodstuffs such as bread and meat, or on impurity. There is a difference of opinion concerning minerals: they are permitted according to the school of Malik, and prohibited according to the school of al-Shafi'i. Regarding salt, snow, dust that has been carried away, things baked like brick, a wall, plants, wood, and trees, there is disagreement. Al-Thawri and Ahmad permitted tayammum with the dust on the hand. Ahmad and Abu Yusuf said that it is not permitted except with earth and sand. The majority permit it on saline ground, except Ibn Rahawayh. Ibn 'Ulayya and Ibn Kaysan permitted tayammum with musk and saffron.

* *

The apparent meaning of the words is that tayammum is wiping the face and the two hands with pure earth. Whenever this manner is achieved, tayammum is achieved. The conjunction with waw does not require sequence between the face and the hands. The preposition bi in ﴿your faces﴾ is one with which the verb is sometimes transitive by means of it, and sometimes transitive by itself. Sibawayh reports: "I wiped his head" and "I wiped with his head," and "I rubbed his chest" and "I rubbed with his chest," with the same meaning. The apparent meaning of wiping the face is comprehensiveness, so one wipes all of it, just as one washes all of it with water. Some permitted not tracing the creases. As for the two hands, the apparent meaning of wiping them is the comprehensiveness of what they denote, and linguistically the term extends to the shoulders. Ibn Shihab also held this, and he said: one wipes up to the armpits, and this was reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. In the Sunan of Abu Dawud: "that he (ﷺ) wiped up to the middle of his forearms." Ibn 'Atiyya said: as far as I have memorised, no one has held this hadith. End of quotation.

Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and their companions, al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Salama, and al-Layth held that one wipes up to reaching the elbows as an obligatory requirement. This is the view of Jabir, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, and Ibrahim. A group held that one extends it to the two wrists (al-kau'ayn), which are the joints, and this is the view of 'Ali, 'Ata', al-Sha'bi, Makhul, al-Awza'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Dawud ibn 'Ali, al-Tabari, al-Shafi'i in his earlier view, and it is reported from Malik. Al-Sha'bi held that one wipes only the palms, and this was said by some jurists of hadith, and this is the view that should be adopted because of its soundness in the hadith. In Muslim, from the hadith of 'Ammar: "It would have sufficed you to strike your hand on the earth, then blow on it, then wipe with it your face and your palms." And from him, in this hadith: "He struck his hand on the earth and shook off his hands, then wiped his face and his palms." In al-Bukhari: "He put the nearer of the two to his mouth, then wiped with them his face and his palms." In Muslim also: "Would it not suffice you to say with your hand thus, then he struck his hand on the earth with one strike, then wiped the left over the right, and the back of the palms and the face." In Abu Dawud: "He struck his hand on the earth and gathered it, then struck with his left on his right and with his right on his left on the palms, then wiped his face." These sound hadiths clarify what the verse left open regarding the place of wiping and its manner.

The apparent meaning of these sound hadiths and the apparent meaning of the verse indicate that one suffices with one strike for the face and the two hands. This is the view of 'Ata', al-Sha'bi in one report, al-Awza'i according to the most well-known report from him, Ahmad, Ishaq, Dawud, and al-Tabari. Malik in al-Mudawwana, al-Awza'i in one report, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and their companions, al-Thawri, al-Layth, and Ibn Abi Salama held that two strikes are obligatory: one strike for the face and one strike for the hands. Ibn Abi Layla and al-Hasan held that there are two strikes, and with each strike one wipes the face, the forearms, and the elbows. No one among the people of knowledge other than these two has said this.

The rulings and issues of tayammum are many and are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence. This surah did not mention them, but they are mentioned in al-Ma'idah. The verse in al-Ma'idah indicates the view of al-Shafi'i concerning transferring some of the material wiped with onto the face and palms, and this absolute (verse) is understood in light of that qualified one. For this reason Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What then will you do with His words in the surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿So wipe your faces and your hands with it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], meaning some of it? This is not feasible with bare rock that has no dust on it." I answer: They said that min here is for the beginning of the extent (ibtida' al-ghayah). If you say, "Their saying that min is for the beginning of the extent is a strained view, and no one among the Arabs understands from the saying of a speaker, 'I wiped his head with oil, with water, and with dust,' anything but the meaning of partiality (tab'id)," I answer: It is as you say, and submitting to the truth is more deserving than disputation.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ is a metaphor (kinayah) for concession and facilitation, because whoever is accustomed to pardon sinners and forgive them prefers to be one who makes things easy and not one who makes them difficult. End of his speech. What is strange about him is that he submitted to the truth, while it is not his habit. Rather, his habit is to distort speech from its apparent meaning and carry it to other than its intended meaning in order to support what is established in his school. Furthermore, his final statement, where he said without qualification that Allah pardons sinners and forgives them, is strange, since he did not restrict that by repentance according to his school and his habit in matters resembling this statement.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 44–45:

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning the Jews. In a report from Ibn Abbas: concerning Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut. It was also said: concerning others among the Jews. The connection (munasabah) of this verse with what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned some of the conditions of the Hereafter, and that the disbelievers at that time will wish that the earth would be leveled over them, and they will not conceal from Allah any statement, this verse came after that as an interjection (i'tiradh) between the mention of the conditions of the disbelievers in the Hereafter and the mention of their conditions in this world, and of their enmity toward the believers, and how they deal with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who comes as a witness over them and over others. Since the Jews were the most adamant in denying the truth and the furthest from accepting good, and since it had also preceded: ﴿those who are miserly and enjoin people to be miserly and conceal﴾ [al-Nisa: 37], and they are the people most characterized by these two qualities, He began to remind them of their particular distinction. The explanation of ﴿Have you not seen those who﴾ has preceded in His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who went out from their homes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 243], so it suffices without repeating it.

Al-nasib means the share or portion. As for ﴿min al-Kitab﴾ (of the Book), it may be connected to ﴿utu﴾ (were given), and it may be in the position of an adjective for nasiban. The apparent wording of ﴿those who were given﴾ includes both the Jews and the Christians, and "the Book" would be an expression for the Torah and the Gospel. It was also said: the Book here is the Torah, and the portion was said to be part of the knowledge of the Torah, not acting upon what is in it. It was said: it is the knowledge of what constitutes a proof against them from it, and nothing more. It was said: it is their disbelief in it. It was said: it is knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad.

﴿They purchase error﴾: the meaning is that they purchase error in exchange for guidance, as He said: ﴿Those are the ones who purchased error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16].

Ibn Abbas said: they exchanged error for faith. Muqatil said: they exchanged denial of the Prophet after his manifestation for their faith in him before his manifestation and their seeking victory through him, end quote. The word "purchase" indicates the preference of error over guidance, and this becomes a severe transgression on their part and a manifest rebuke to them, since they possess a share of the knowledge of the Torah and the Gospel, and yet they preferred disbelief over faith. Their scripture is full of the obligation to follow the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel. It was also said: the purchase of error here is what they used to give from their wealth to their rabbis to keep their religion firm; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

﴿And they wish that you would err from the way﴾: that is, it was not enough for them to have gone astray themselves, until their hopes became attached to your going astray, O believers, from the path of truth. Because they knew that they had departed from the truth to falsehood, they disliked that the believers should be exclusively following the truth, so they wished that you would go astray as they had gone astray, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be equal﴾ [al-Nisa: 89]. Al-Nakha'i recited: "wa-turidun" with two taa' from above. It was said: its meaning is "and you, O believers, wish that you would err from the way," i.e., you claim the correctness of avoiding them, and you think them not to be enemies of Allah. It was also read: "an yadillu" with the ya' and with fatha and kasra on the dad.

﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾: in it is an alert to the attribute contrary to wishing good to the believers, which is enmity. In it is also an indication of warning against them and a rebuke for relying on them and leaning toward them. The meaning: He, exalted is He, has informed of their enmity toward the believers, so it is obligatory to beware of them, as He said: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4]. And "a'lamu" is on its own pattern of the comparative, i.e., He is more knowing of your enemies than you are. It was also said: it carries the meaning of "knowing" (alim), i.e., He is knowing of your enemies.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as a Protector, and sufficient is Allah as a Helper﴾: whoever has Allah as his protector and helper does not care about enemies, so trust in His guardianship and support over them, or do not care about them, for He will grant you victory over them and suffice you against their plotting. It was also said: the meaning is a protector for His Messenger and a helper for His religion.

The ba' in (bi-Allah) is extra (za'idah), and it may be omitted, as the poet Suhaym said:

"Old age and Islam suffice a man as a restrainer."

Its addition to the agent of "kafa" and the agent of "yakfi" is regular, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for your Lord that He is witness over all things?﴾ [Fussilat: 53]. Al-Zajjaj said: the ba' entered the agent because the sense of the utterance is a command, i.e., be content with Allah. The words of al-Zajjaj imply that the ba' is not extra, and what he said of the meaning is not valid, because a command requires that its agent be the addressees, and "bi-Allah" would be connected to it. And the ba' entering the agent requires that the agent be Allah and not the addressees, which contradicts his statement. Ibn al-Sarraj said: its meaning is "sufficient is the contentment with Allah," and this also indicates that the ba' is not extra, since it is connected to the contentment, so contentment is the agent of "kafa." This also is not valid, because it involves omitting the verbal noun while leaving its object (ma'mul), which is not permitted except in poetry, such as the poet's words:

"Will you remember at the two monasteries your emigration, and your rubbing your backs, O Compassionate, for a sacrifice?"

The estimate: "and your saying, O Compassionate, a sacrifice." Ibn Atiyyah said: "bi-Allah" is in the position of nominative by estimating the addition of the governing particle, and the benefit of its addition is clarifying the meaning of the command in the form of a statement, i.e., they were content with Allah, so the ba' indicates the intended sense. What Ibn Atiyyah said is a patchwork, part of it from the words of al-Zajjaj, and it is more corrupt than al-Zajjaj's statement, because it added to the contradiction of the difference of the agent the difference of the meaning of the particle: regarding Allah being the agent it is extra, and regarding its meaning "they were content with Allah" it is not extra. Ibn Isa said: the ba' entered "kafa bi-Allah" because the agent was connected, and with the entry of the ba' it became connected in the manner of the annexed and the manner of the agent, because sufficiency from Him is not like sufficiency from others, so its wording was doubled in the manner its meaning is doubled; this is a statement requiring interpretation. The discussion of "kafa bi-Allah" has already preceded in His saying: ﴿So bear witness against them, and sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾ [al-Nisa: 6], but it is repeated here because of the additional reports it contains, some of which have been related. As for the accusative of "waliyyan" and "nasiran," it was said they are in the position of the circumstantial (hal). It was said they are in the position of the specification (tamyiz), and this is better, because "min" may enter.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 46 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Among those who are Jews are those who distort words from their places.﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is disconnected in its i'rab (grammatical analysis) from what precedes it, so that it is based on the omission of a qualifying noun which is the subject (mubtada'), with "min alladhina hadu" (among those who are Jews) as its predicate. The estimate is: "Among those who are Jews is a people who distort words." This is the view of Sibawayh and Abu 'Ali, and the omission of the qualified noun after "min" (among) is permissible, even if the qualifier is a verb, as in their saying: "Min-na za'ana" (among us [is one who] departed) and "Min-na aqama" (among us [is one who] stayed), meaning: "Min-na nafarun za'ana" (among us is a group who departed) and "Min-na nafarun aqama" (among us is a group who stayed). The poet said:

"And time is nothing but two turns; of them, I die, and another time I seek life, toiling."

He means: "Of them, a time in which I die." Al-Farra' interpreted it as the omission of the relative pronoun "man" (whoever), i.e., "Among those who are Jews are whoever distort words," but this is not permissible according to the Basrans. They interpreted what came in similar form as the omission of the qualified noun with the qualifier taking its place. Al-Farra' said: Similar to this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"So they remained, and among them his tear is flowing for her, and another wipes away the tear of the eye with the hand."

It is not necessary that the omitted element be a relative pronoun; rather it is more likely to be a qualified noun, since the indefinite "another" (akhar) is conjoined to it, so the estimate would be: "So they remained, and among them is a lover whose tear is flowing for her." It has also been said that it is based on an omitted subject, the estimate being: "They are among those who are Jews," and "yuharrifuna" (they distort) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "hadu" (they are Jews), and "min alladhina hadu" is connected to what precedes it. It was said that it is connected to "nasiran" (a helper), i.e., a helper from those who are Jews, and it governed it with "min" just as it governs it in: ﴿And We helped him against the people﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77] and ﴿Who will help us against the might of Allah?﴾ [Ghafir: 29], meaning "and We protected him" and "who will protect us." It was said that ﴿among those who are Jews﴾ is an explanation of His saying "your enemies," and what is between them is a parenthetical insertion. It was said that it is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yuridun" (they desire), as Abu al-Baqa' said. He said: It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "utu" (they were given), because one thing cannot have more than one circumstantial clause unless some circumstances are conjoined to others, and it is not a circumstantial clause from "alladhina" for this meaning. End. What he mentioned, that the one in circumstance, if not plural, does not require more than one circumstance, is a matter of disagreement, for some grammarians permitted that.

It was said: "Among those who are Jews" is an explanation of ﴿those who were given a portion of the Scripture﴾ [al-Nisa': 44], because they are Jews and Christians; and His saying ﴿And Allah knows your enemies best﴾ [al-Nisa': 45], ﴿And Allah suffices as a protector﴾ [al-Nisa': 45], ﴿And Allah suffices as a helper﴾ [al-Nisa': 45] are sentences interposed between the explanation and what is explained, by way of parenthesis, as al-Zamakhshari said, and he began with it. This is weakened by the fact that these are three sentences, and if al-Farisi prohibited parenthesis of two sentences, then it is even more prohibited with three.

﴿Distort words﴾ means: the words of the Torah, and this is the view of the majority; or the words of the Qur'an, and this is the view of a group; or the words of the Messenger (ﷺ), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. He said: The Jews used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and ask him about a matter, and he would inform them, and they would think (p-263) that they were taking his word, but when they left from his presence they distorted the speech. Likewise Makki said: it is the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ). So the distortion of the words of the Torah is by changing the wording, which is the less common, such as their distortion of (ruddy, medium height) in his description, peace be upon him, to (tall, brown) in its place, and their distortion of the stoning with iron for him; and by changing the interpretation, which is the more common, as al-Tabari said. They used to interpret the Torah in ways other than what the meanings of its words require, for matters they chose and by which they reached the wealth of their lowly ones. As for distortion in the words of the Qur'an or the words of the Messenger, it can only be in interpretation.

It was read: "yuharrifuna al-kilm" with a kasra on the kaf and sukun on the lam, the plural of "kalimah," a lightened form of "kalimah." Al-Nakha'i and Abu Raja' read: "yuharrifuna al-kalam" (the speech). Here came ﴿from its places﴾. In al-Ma'idah it came: ﴿from its places﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13], and it came: ﴿from after its places﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41].

Al-Zamakhshari said: As for ﴿from its places﴾, it is according to what we explained of removing it from its places, which the wisdom of Allah had required placing it in, by what their desires required of replacing it with something else. As for ﴿from after its places﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], the meaning is that it had places in which it was fitting for it to be, so when they distorted it they left it like a stranger that has no place after its places and its abodes. The two meanings are close. End. What appears is that they are two contexts: where they are described with intense rebellion and transgression, manifest enmity, buying error, and breaking the covenant, it came: ﴿distort words from their places﴾. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And they say: We hear and we disobey﴾, and His saying: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant We cursed them and made their hearts hard; they distort words from their places﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13]? So it is as if they did not leave the words undistorted from what is intended by them, and the words were not settled in their places, so the distortion would be after their settling; rather they hastened to distort them at the first instant. And where they are described with some softness, hesitation, and making the Messenger a judge in some matters, it came: ﴿from after its places﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41]. Do you not see His saying: ﴿They say: If you are given this, take it, and if you are not given it, beware﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], and His saying after it: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42]? So it is as if they did not hasten to distortion, rather distortion befell them after the words had settled in their places. It may be said that they are two things, but He omitted here and in the beginning of al-Ma'idah ﴿from after its places﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], because His saying ﴿from its places﴾ indicates settled places for it; and in the second of al-Ma'idah ﴿from its places﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13] was omitted, because distortion from after its places indicates that it is distortion away from its places. So the original is "They distort the words from after its places" [al-Ma'idah: 41]. Here he omitted the "after," and there he omitted "from." All of this is a broadening of expression, and the beginning here was with His saying "from its places," because it is more concise. In it is an explicit statement of "from" and of "places," and an indication of "after."

﴿And they say: We hear and we disobey﴾: that is, we hear your saying and we disobey your command; or they heard it openly and disobeyed it secretly — two opinions. The apparent meaning is that they addressed the Prophet (ﷺ) with the two phrases directly, as an exaggeration on their part in their obstinacy in disbelief, and following their custom with the prophets. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength and listen. They said: We hear and we disobey﴾ [al-Baqarah: 93].

﴿And hear, without being made to hear﴾: this statement is not directed, and it admits several aspects. The apparent meaning is that they intended by it the disliked sense, given the context of what precedes it, His saying "We hear and we disobey," so its meaning would be: "Hear, may you not hear." They invoked upon him death or deafness, and intended that inwardly, while outwardly intending to honor him by it, since it may mean: "Hear, without being commanded and without being fit to be heard when commanded." Al-Zamakhshari said: Or "Hear, without being answered to what you call to," and its meaning: "without being made to hear an answer that agrees with you," as if you heard nothing. End; and Ibn 'Abbas said the same. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or "Hear, without being made to hear a speech you would be pleased with," so your hearing of it is far off. It is also permissible on this that "ghayra musma'in" be the object of "isma'," i.e., "Hear a speech that is not made to hear by you, since your ear does not comprehend it out of aversion to it." It may also be taken as praise, i.e., "Hear what is not made to hear of disliked speech from your saying: asma'a fulanun fulanan (so-and-so made so-and-so hear) when he insulted him." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: As for the one who says "ghayra musma'in" means "not accepted from you," it is not supported by morphology, and al-Tabari related it from al-Hasan and Mujahid. End. The reason morphology does not support it is (p-264) that the Arabs do not say "asma'tuka" meaning "I accepted from you," rather they say "sami'tu minka" meaning "I accepted," so they express acceptance by hearing figuratively, not by causing to hear. If what al-Hasan and Mujahid said were intended, the wording would be: "wasma' ghayra masmu'in minka" (and hear, not being heard from you).

﴿And [they say] "Ra'ina," twisting with their tongues and defaming the religion﴾: The explanation of "ra'ina" has already passed in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not say "ra'ina"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 104]. The meaning of ﴿twisting with their tongues﴾ is: twisting them with them; and distorting from the truth to falsehood, where they put "ra'ina" in place of "unzurna" (look at us), and "ghayra musma'in" in place of "la usmi'ta makruhan" (may you not be made to hear anything disliked). Or they twist with their tongues what they conceal of insult into what they show of reverence, as hypocrisy. The accusative of "ghayra musma'in" is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "isma'," and al-Zamakhshari's parsing of it as an object in one of the estimates has already passed. The accusatives of "laiyan" and "ta'nan" are objects of purpose. It was said: they are both verbal nouns in the position of circumstance, i.e., "twisting" and "defaming." The meaning of "wa-ta'nan fi al-din" (defaming the religion) is by the tongue. Their defamation of it is denying his prophethood, changing his description, or finding fault with the rulings of his law, or ascribing ignorance to him. Their saying: "If he were a prophet he would know that we revile him," or their mockery, opposition, and casting doubt upon his followers — four opinions. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This twisting with the tongue toward the opposite of what is in the heart exists even now among the Children of Israel, and examples of it are preserved from them in our era, but it is not fitting to mention them in this book. End. He is reporting this about the Jews of al-Andalus, and we have witnessed them and witnessed the Jews of the land of Egypt in this manner, and it seems they raise their small children on it, having them memorize what they address to the Muslims which outwardly is reverence while they intend contempt. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how did they come with the ambiguous speech with two faces, after they had openly said "We hear and we disobey"? I say: all the disbelievers used to confront him with disbelief and disobedience, and did not confront him with abuse and calls for evil, and it is possible that they said that among themselves, and it is possible that they did not utter it; but since they did not believe in him, they were treated as if they had uttered it.

﴿Had they said "We hear and we obey; hear and look at us," it would have been better for them and more upright﴾: That is: if they had exchanged disobedience for obedience, and obedience includes belief in you, and had confined themselves to the word "hear," and exchanged "ra'ina" for their saying "wa-unzurna" (and look at us), so they had turned away from the expressions that indicate non-submission and suggest it, to what they were commanded, it would have been better for them (that speech) with Allah and more just, i.e., more upright and more correct. Ikrimah, Mujahid and others said: "unzurna" means "intazirna," i.e., wait for us, in the sense of "afhimna" (make us understand) and be patient with us until we understand from you and grasp your saying, as al-Hutay'ah said:

"And I have looked at you between two journeys, for five (nights) during which my wiping and my soothing lasted long."

Another group said: its meaning is "look at us," and it seems to be a request for attention and kindness from them. From it is the saying of Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat:

"Manifest in beauty and loveliness, they look as the gazelles look at the arak trees."

Ubayy read: "wa-anzirna," from al-inzar, which is respite. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: if the saying "We hear and we obey" had been established, that saying would have been better for them, more upright, more just, and more correct. End. So he made "that they said" into a verbal noun raised by "thabata" (be established) as its subject; this is the view of al-Mubarrad, unlike Sibawayh. For Sibawayh holds that "an" after "law" together with what it governs is estimated as a nominal subject, and whether the predicate is omitted or no predicate need be estimated because the predicate and subject are in the relative clause of "an" — two opinions, the more sound of which is this. Al-Zamakhshari agreed with the view of al-Mubarrad, which is a weak view in the science of grammar.

﴿But Allah cursed them for their disbelief﴾: that is, Allah removed them far from guidance because of their previous disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, He forsook them because of their disbelief and removed them far from His kindnesses. End. This is according to the method of the Mu'tazilah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 46 (part 2 of 2):

﴿So they believe not, except a few.﴾ This is an exception (istithna') from the object pronoun in "laʿanahum" (cursed them), meaning: except a few whom He did not curse, so they believed. Alternatively, it is an exception from the subject in "fa-la yu'minūna" (so they believe not), meaning: except a few who believed, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, Kaʿb al-Ahbar, and others. Or it refers back to the verbal noun (maṣdar) implied by "fa-la yu'minūna," meaning: except a little faith, which he (God) diminished, since they believed in the Oneness (tawhid) of God but disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) (p-265) and his laws (shara'i'). Al-Zamakhshari said: "except a little faith" means weak and feeble faith, not worth regarding, which is their belief in the One who created them alongside their disbelief in others. He intended by "little" the sense of "none," as in the line of poetry:

*"Little complaining about the worries that befall him,"*

meaning: one who does not complain at all. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: whoever uses "little" to express faith means that it is an expression for its absence, as in what Sibawayh (Sibawayh, the grammarian) related from their saying: "A land that rarely (qallamā) produces such-and-such," while it does not produce it at all. What al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyya mentioned, that paucity may mean non-existence, is correct in itself, but this exceptive construction is not one of its usages. When you say, "I do not stand except a little," this is not used to negate standing entirely; rather, it indicates that standing is negated from you except a little, which then occurs from you. When you say, "Hardly does anyone stand except Zayd (qallamā yaqūmu aḥadun illā Zaydun)," and "Few a man says that," this may mean paucity as opposed to abundance, and it may mean pure negation. It is as if you said: "No one stands except Zayd," and "No man says that." Either you negate and then affirm, and the affirmation after the negation indicates negation, so "illā" and what follows it under this reading would be superfluous, with no benefit, since negation has already been understood from your saying "I do not stand." What benefit is there in an affirmative exception that intends the negation already understood from the preceding clause? Furthermore, it leads to the post-"illā" element agreeing in meaning with what precedes it, whereas in the exceptive construction the post-"illā" element must not agree with what precedes it. The apparent sense of His saying "fa-la yu'minūna illā qalīlan," if we take it as referring to faith, is that faith admits of degrees of paucity and abundance, so it increases and decreases. The answer is that its increase and decrease are according to the paucity or abundance of its objects (mutaʿalliqāt).

These verses contain various kinds of eloquence (fasahah), rhetoric (balaghah), and embellishment (badi'). They said: The figurative use (tajawwuz) by applying a term to something close to its meaning is in His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong [anyone]﴾, where "wrong" (ẓulm) is applied to diminishing the reward, since the shortfall from what was promised is close in meaning to wronging. Alerting to the higher by means of the lower is in His saying: ﴿the weight of an atom﴾. The ambiguity (ibham) is in His saying: ﴿He doubles it﴾, since the amount of doubling in reward is not specified. Asking about what is already known is for rebuking the listener, or for making him confess to himself, in: ﴿Then how will it be when We bring﴾. The shift from one form to another for a meaning is in: ﴿with a witness, and We bring you as a witness over these﴾. Homogeneous paronomasia (tajnis mumathil) is in: ﴿and We bring﴾ and in ﴿and We bring﴾, and in ﴿with a witness﴾ and "shahīdan". Heterogeneous paronomasia (tajnis mughayir) is in: ﴿and hear, (though you are) not made to hear﴾. The figurative use by applying the place to what is in it is in: ﴿from the privy﴾. Metonymy (kinaya) is in: ﴿or you have touched women﴾. Inversion of order (taqdim and ta'khir) is in: ﴿except as travellers, until you have washed﴾ up to His saying: ﴿then perform tayammum﴾. The interrogative meant as wonder is in: ﴿Have you not seen﴾. Metaphor (isti'arah) is in: ﴿they purchase error﴾. Antithesis (tibaq) is in "(this)," i.e., with guidance, and the explicit antithesis is in: ﴿and we disobey﴾ and ﴿and we obey﴾. Repetition is in: ﴿and God suffices as a protector﴾ and "and God suffices," and in ﴿we hear﴾ and ﴿we hear﴾. Ellipsis occurs in a number of places.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 4, verse 47**

﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what you already have, before We obliterate faces and turn them back on their backs, or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath. The command of Allah is always carried out.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be set up with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. Whoever sets up partners with Allah has indeed fabricated a tremendous sin.﴾ [An-Nisa': 48] ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged by so much as a thread.﴾ [An-Nisa': 49] ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah, and that is sufficient as a manifest sin.﴾ [An-Nisa': 50] ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book? They believe in al-Jibt and al-Taghut, and they say of those who disbelieve, "These are better guided than those who believe, in the way."﴾ [An-Nisa': 51] ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed. Whomever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper.﴾ [An-Nisa': 52] ﴿Or do they have a share in the kingdom? If so, they would not give the people even a speck.﴾ [An-Nisa': 53] ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? We had already given the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom.﴾ [An-Nisa': 54] ﴿Among them is one who believed in it, and among them is one who turned away from it. Hell suffices as a blazing fire.﴾ [An-Nisa': 55] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our signs, We will surely cast them into the Fire. Whenever their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins, so that they may taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is Ever Mighty and Wise.﴾ [An-Nisa': 56]

*Tamas* (طَمَسَ) is both transitive and intransitive. One says: "The rain obliterated the landmarks" (طَمَسَ المَطَرُ الأعْلامَ), meaning it erased their traces. "The landmarks were effaced" (طُمِسَتِ الأعْلامُ) means they were worn away, and "the road was effaced" (طَمَسَ الطَّرِيقُ) means it was obliterated and its markers were gone. This is what Abu Zayd reported. From the transitive usage is the verse: ﴿When the stars are obliterated﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 8], meaning uprooted. Ibn 'Arafah said regarding the verse ﴿Obliterate their wealth﴾ [Yunus: 88] that it means to destroy it entirely. A blind man is called *ma'tus* (مَطْمُوسٌ), meaning his two eyes are closed. Ka'b said:

*From every she-camel that spurts sweat at the nape when she sweats, her sides glistening, the landmarks obliterated and unknown.*

*Tamas*, *tasm*, *talas* and *dars* all have closely related meanings.

*Fatil* (فَتِيلٌ) is on the pattern *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*. It is said to be the thread in the split of a date pit. It is also said to be the filth that comes out between your palms and fingers when you twist them.

*Jibt* (جِبْتٌ) was originally the name of an idol, and then it came to be used for every falsehood. For this reason, the exegetes differed considerably about it, as will come later. Qutrub said: *jibt* is *jibs* (جِبْسٌ), which means something with no good in it, and the *sin* was changed to a *ta'*. It is said that he only said this because *jibt* is an unusual word.

*Naqir* (نَقِيرٌ) is the small point on the back of the date pit from which the palm tree sprouts. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Dahhak said it is the white spot in its middle.

*Nudj* (النُّضْجُ) is the process of a thing beginning to break down and its parts separating. From it come the ripening of meat (*nudj al-lahm*) and the ripening of fruit (*nudj al-thamarah*). It is said: *nadija al-shay'u yandaju nudjan wa nidajan* (the thing ripened). *Jild* (الجِلْدُ) is well known.

﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what you have﴾: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited the rabbis of the Jews, among them al-A'mash ibn Suriya, to Islam, and said to them: "You know that what I have brought is true." They said: "We do not recognize that." Then this verse was revealed. This was reported by Ibn 'Abbas.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah gave them hope with His words ﴿If they had said﴾ [An-Nisa': 46] and so on, He addressed those among them whose faith was hoped for, commanding them to believe, and He coupled this with a severe threat for abandoning it, so that it would more strongly move them to faith and belief in it. Then He removed their fear of the consequences of the major sins they had committed earlier, with His words ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be set up with Him﴾ [An-Nisa': 48], and so on. And He informed them that their claiming purity for themselves through what Allah had not purified them with would not benefit them.

*Alladhina utu al-Kitab* (الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ) here refers to the Jews, and "the Book" is the Torah. This is the view of the majority. Or it refers to the Jews and Christians, as stated by al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyyah. The Book is the Torah and the Gospel. And ﴿what We have sent down﴾ is the Qur'an without dispute. "What you have" refers to the law and creed you possess, not to what they have of altered and changed material.

﴿before We obliterate faces and turn them back on their backs﴾: The majority read *natmisa* (نَطْمِسَ) with a *kasra* on the *mim*. Abu Raja' read it with a *damma*. Both are dialectal variants. The apparent meaning is that "faces" refers to their literal meaning. As for their obliteration, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' al-'Awfi said it means that the two eyes alone are removed from them and turned to the back of the neck. In that case, "turning them back on their backs" means they walk backwards. On this view, the verse involves an omitted noun, meaning: before We obliterate the eyes of faces, and it does not mean all faces. Rather, the meaning is "your faces."

A group said that obliterating the faces means that the traces of the senses are effaced from them, so that they become like the other limbs, free of traces of the senses. And "turning them back on their backs" means that they are, in meaning, left without senses, the face being effaced because it is passing through the senses. Al-Zamakhshari endorsed and clarified this view, saying: *"That We obliterate faces"* means that We erase the outlines of their forms, of eye, eyebrow, nose and mouth, *"and turn them back on their backs"*, so We make them like the backs of their heads, which are the napes, flattened in the same way. The *fa'* (فَ) indicates causation. If you take it to indicate sequence, on the basis that they were threatened with two punishments, one after the other, then turning them back after obliterating them is the meaning: *"that We obliterate faces and so turn them upside down,"* the faces turned backward and the napes forward. End of quote.

The meaning of obliteration as erasure, mentioned above, is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and was preferred by al-Qutabi. Qatadah and al-Dahhak said it means blinding their eyes. He mentioned "faces" but meant "eyes," because obliteration is a characteristic of the eye. Allah says: ﴿So We obliterated their eyes﴾ [Al-Qamar: 37]. This is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Farra' said: obliterating the faces means making them places of growth for hair, like the faces of monkeys. It is also said that it means changing them into an ugly form, like the faces of pigs and monkeys.

Mujahid, al-Suddi and al-Hasan said that this is figurative, and that what is meant is the faces of guidance and right direction. Obliterating them means the certainty of misguidance and turning away from them, and turning them back on their backs means returning them to disbelief.

Ibn Zayd said: the faces are their homelands and dwellings in their lands, from which they went out. Obliterating them means expelling them from them. And turning them back on their backs means returning to Syria from where they first came.

Al-Zamakhshari endorsed this view, saying: There is another interpretation, which is that obliteration means transformation and alteration, as when He obliterated the wealth of the Copts and turned it into stones. By "faces" is meant their heads and notables, meaning: before We change the conditions of their notables, depriving them of their prestige and standing, and covering them with humiliation and their backs, or We send them back to where they came from. This is Adhri'at in Syria, and he means the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir. End of quote.

﴿or curse them﴾: This is coordinated with the phrase "that We obliterate." The apparent meaning of cursing is the commonly understood one, as in His words: ﴿Whom Allah has cursed and with whom He is angry﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 60]. Al-Hasan said its meaning is that We transform them into apes and pigs, as We transformed the people of the Sabbath. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: they are the people of Ayla who transgressed on the Sabbath by hunting, and their curse was that they were transformed into pigs and apes. It is also said its meaning is that We will make them wander in the wilderness until most of them die.

The apparent meaning of His words "before We obliterate or curse" is that this happens in this world. For this reason it is reported that 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, when he heard this verse, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) before going to his family, with his hand on his face, and embraced Islam, saying: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not think I could reach you until my face was turned to my back." Malik said: the conversion of Ka'b al-Ahbar was that he passed by a man at night who was reciting this verse. He placed his palm on his face, returned backward to his house, and embraced Islam on the spot, saying: "By Allah, I feared I would not reach my house before my face was obliterated."

It is also said that obliteration means the transformation of the Jews into apes before the Day of Resurrection, and this is inevitable. It is also said that what is meant is that it will befall them on the Day of Resurrection, which would be more humiliating for them before the first and the last, and that this would be the first punishment hastened upon them. This applies if obliterating the faces is taken literally. If what is meant is the alteration of the conditions of their notables or the faces of guidance and right direction, then it has occurred. And if obliteration is other than that, then cursing has occurred, for they are cursed in every tongue.

Making faith conditional upon the occurrence of one of two things does not necessarily entail that both will occur. Rather, whenever one of them occurs, the conditional is valid, and it does not require specifying which one. It is also said that the threat is conditional upon faith, and some of them did believe.

*Min qabl* (مِن قَبْلُ) is connected to *amanu* (آمَنُوا, "believe"), and *'ala adbarih* (عَلى أدْبارِها) is connected to *fa-naruddaha* (فَنَرُدَّها, "and turn them back").

Abu al-Baqa' said: *'ala adbarih* is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun of "faces," and to the object pronoun in *nal'anahum*.

It is said that the pronoun refers to the faces, if what is meant is the notables, or it refers to the owners of the faces, because the meaning is "before We obliterate the faces of a people," or it refers to those who were given the Book, by way of *iltifat* (الِالتِفاتُ), the shift from direct address to third person. This is, in my view, the best. What motivates this *iltifat* is that when Allah addressed them, this was an honour for them, and He prepared their hearing for what He was about to convey to them. Then He imposed upon them the command to believe in what was sent down, then mentioned that what was sent down confirms what they have of the Book. This was more inviting to faith. Then He mentioned this severe threat and omitted the noun to which the pronoun is attached in His words: *"before We obliterate faces"* (p-268), meaning "your faces." Then He coordinated with it His words *"or curse them,"* and used the third-person pronoun, because when the threat concerned the obliteration of faces and the curse, the address should not remain to them. This keeps the gentle encouragement, concern, and invitation to faith free from the shock of a direct address that frightens the listener, distresses the heart, and makes him more inclined to reject. This is among the finest forms of address and the most excellent kind of discourse.

﴿And the command of Allah is always carried out﴾: *Al-amr* (الأمْرُ) here is the singular of *al-umur* (affairs). It was sufficient to use it because it indicates the genus, and it refers to created things, such as punishment, curse and forgiveness. It is also said that what is meant is the commanded thing, a verbal noun (maṣdar) used in the place of the passive participle (maf'ūl), and the meaning is: what He wills, He brings into being. It is also said that its meaning is that every matter whose occurrence is delayed will inevitably come to pass, and the meaning is that Allah is not hindered in anything He wishes to do. It is also said: this is information about the continuing practice of Allah in threatening earlier nations, and that this is inevitably going to happen, so beware and be wary of this threat. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: It is inevitable that one of the two matters will occur if they do not believe, namely the obliteration or the curse.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 48–49 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills.﴾ Ibn al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning Wahshi and his companions. Wahshi had been promised manumission (ʿitq) in exchange for killing Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with him, but the promise was not fulfilled for him. So he went to Makkah, and he and his companions regretted what they had done. They wrote to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "We have indeed regretted what we did, and what prevents us from embracing Islam is only that we heard you say in Makkah: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ [al-Furqan: 68] and the verses that follow, whereas we had invoked another god with Allah, killed the soul that Allah had forbidden, and committed fornication. Had it not been for these verses, we would have followed you." Then it was revealed: ﴿except for one who repents, believes and does righteousness﴾ [al-Furqan: 70] and the verses that follow. This was sent to them, and they wrote: "This is a severe condition; we fear that we will not do righteous deeds." Then it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾, the verse. This was sent to them, and they sent back: "We fear that we are not among those whom He wills." Then it was revealed: ﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 53] and the verses that follow. This was sent to them, and they entered Islam, and it was accepted from them. Then he (the Prophet ﷺ) said to Wahshi: "Tell me how you killed Hamzah." When he told him, he said: "Woe to you! Hide your face from me." So Wahshi went to al-Sham and remained there until he died.

The Muslims have unanimously agreed on the eternal abiding of the one who dies a disbeliever in the Fire, and on the eternal abiding of the one who dies a believer who never committed a sin in Paradise. As for a penitent who died upon his repentance, the majority hold that he is joined to the believer who never sinned, while the view of some of the theologians (mutakallimun) is that he is subject to Allah's will (fi al-mashiʾah). As for a sinner who died before repenting, the Khawarij say: he is eternally abiding in the Fire, whether he is a person of a major sin or of a minor sin. The Murjiʾah say: he is in Paradise by his faith, and his sins do not harm him. The Muʿtazilah say: if he is a person of a major sin, he is eternally abiding in the Fire. As for the People of the Sunnah, they say: he is subject to Allah's will; if He wills, He forgives him and admits him to Paradise from the very first, and if He wills, He punishes him, takes him out of the Fire, and afterwards admits him to Paradise, abiding in it eternally.

The cause of this difference is the conflict between the general (ʿumumat) wordings of the verses of threat (waʿid) and the verses of promise (waʿd). The Khawarij made the verses of threat general concerning sinners, whether disbelievers or believers who have not repented. The verses of promise they restricted to the believer who never sinned, or to the sinner who repented. The Murjiʾah made the verses of threat restricted to disbelievers, and the verses of promise restricted to the believer, whether pious or disobedient. The People of the Sunnah restricted the verses of threat to disbelief and to those among disobedient believers whom Allah had foreknown He would punish, and they restricted the verses of promise to the believer who never sinned, to the penitent, and to those among disobedient believers whom Allah had foreknown He would pardon. The Muʿtazilah restricted the verses of promise to the believer who never sinned and to the penitent, and the verses of threat to the disbeliever and to the person of a major sin who did not repent.

This verse is the decisive one by its text in the place of dispute; it removes doubt and refutes these three groups. His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾, its meaning being that whoever dies as a polytheist is not forgiven, is a principle agreed upon among the four groups. His saying ﴿but He forgives what is less than that﴾ is a refutation of the Khawarij and the Muʿtazilah, because "what is less than that" is general and includes major and minor sins. His saying "for whom He wills" is a refutation of the Murjiʾah, since its implication is that forgiveness of what is below polytheism is only for some people rather than others, as Allah wills, unlike their claim that every believer is forgiven. The evidences of these groups are mentioned in the science of the fundamentals of religion (ʿilm uṣul al-din). The Muʿtazilah and the Murjiʾah have attempted to turn this verse back to their doctrines through interpretations that are not sound, and which contradict what the verse indicates.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: it is established that Allah, Mighty and Exalted, forgives polytheism for one who repents from it, and that He does not forgive what is less than polytheism of major sins except through repentance, then what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾? I say: The sound interpretation is that both the negated verb and the affirmed verb are directed to His saying ﴿for whom He wills﴾, as if it were said: Indeed, Allah does not forgive for whom He wills polytheism, and He forgives for whom He wills what is less than polytheism. Moreover, the intended meaning of the first is one who does not repent, and of the second one who repents. A parallel to this is your saying: "The commander does not give a dinar, and gives a qintar to whomever deserves it." End of his words. Thus he interpreted the verse according to his own school.

As for his saying "It is established that Allah, Mighty and Exalted, forgives polytheism for one who repents from it," this is agreed upon. As for his saying "and that He does not forgive what is less than polytheism of major sins except through repentance," we say to him: where is this established? They only argue with general expressions that admit of specification, as in their argument with His saying: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ [al-Nisa': 93] and so on, which Ibn ʿAbbas specified as applying to one who considers it lawful, and such a person is a disbeliever. And his saying: "He said: 'Then its recompense is that Allah recompenses him.' And he said: 'Khulud (abiding) means a long stay, not perpetual eternity without end, and the speech of the Arabs bears witness to this.'" As for his saying that the sound interpretation is that both the negated and affirmed verbs are directed to "for whom He wills," if he means that the prepositional phrase is attached to both verbs, this is not correct. If he means that the first is restricted by the will just as the second is restricted, then this is an interpretation. What is understood from his words is that the subject of "wills" refers to "whoever" (man), not to "Allah," because in his view the meaning is: Allah does not forgive polytheism for whom He wills that He not forgive, by virtue of his having died in polytheism without repenting of it, and He forgives what is less than polytheism of major sins for whom He wills that He forgive, by virtue of his having repented of them. What the apparent meaning of the speech indicates is that the first verb has no restriction by will, even though, according to our school, all existent things depend in their existence upon His will. And the subject of "wills" refers to Allah, Exalted, not to "whoever," and the meaning is: He forgives what is less than polytheism for whom He wills to forgive. And in His saying, Exalted: ﴿for whom He wills﴾ there is a great deferment (tarjiʾah), in that whoever dies upon a sin other than polytheism would not be definitively condemned to punishment, even if he dies persisting in it.

Al-Aʿmash ibn ʿUmar said: In the time of the Messenger of Allah, when a man died upon a major sin, we would testify for him that he was among the people of the Fire, until this verse was revealed, and we refrained from such testimonies. In the end of the hadith of ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit (it is said): "Whoever commits any of those things, i.e., of the sins mentioned earlier, and Allah conceals it for him, his affair is up to Allah: if He wills, He pardons him, and if He wills, He punishes him." Recorded by Muslim. It is narrated from ʿAli and others among the Companions: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more beloved to us than this verse." In this verse is evidence that the Jew is called a polytheist in the usage of the Shariah; otherwise he would be other than the polytheist, and it would be obligatory that he be forgiven. Also, the connection of this verse with what precedes it is because it contains a threat to the Jews, and the Jews fall under the name of polytheism. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 69], then His saying: ﴿and those who associate partners﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 82], and His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists do not wish﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105], and ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not⟩ [al-Bayyinah: 1], the distinction occurs according to the lexical concept, while the unity occurs according to the Shariah concept.

Al-Zajjaj said: Every disbeliever is a polytheist, because when he disbelieves, for example, in a prophet, he claims that these signs which he brought are not from Allah, and so he attributes to other than Allah what can only belong to Allah, and thereby becomes a polytheist in this sense. According to this, the estimated meaning is: Indeed, Allah does not forgive the disbelief of one who disbelieves in Him, or in one of His prophets. And the intended meaning is: when one meets Allah with that, since faith removes from him the application of the description of the disbelief that preceded it, by consensus, and due to his saying, peace be upon him: "Islam erases what came before it."

﴿And whoever associates partners with Allah has indeed fabricated a tremendous sin﴾: i.e., he invented and fabricated what is impossible. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked: "Which sin is the greatest?" He said: "That you make a rival to Allah while He created you."

﴿Have you not seen those who justify themselves?﴾ The majority said: they are the Jews. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: they are the Christians. Ibn Mas'ud said: some of them praise others so that the kings and their lowly ones will turn toward them, and they will connect with them through bribery. ʿAṭiyyah related from Ibn ʿAbbas: they said: "Our fathers who died will justify us before Allah and intercede for us." Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi, among others, said: Marhab ibn Zayd, Bahri ibn ʿAmr, and a group of Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ with their children and said: "Is there any sin upon these?" He said: "No." They said: "We are like them: what we sin by night is expiated for us by day, and what we sin by day is expiated for us by night," and so it was revealed. It was also said: it is their saying: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." On the view that they are the Jews and the Christians, then "justify themselves" refers to themselves. ʿIkrimah, Mujahid and Abu Malik said: they used to put forward children who had not reached puberty, and they would pray with them and say: "They have no sins; so if the one forgiven leads us in prayer, we shall be forgiven." Qatadah and al-Hasan said: it is their saying: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved," and ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], and ﴿Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135]. In the verse is an indication of the reproach of one who justifies himself with his tongue and describes himself with increase in obedience, piety, and nearness to Allah. His saying (peace be upon him): "By Allah, I am trustworthy in heaven, trustworthy on earth," when the hypocrites said to him: "Be just in the distribution," is a rebuttal of them, since they described him contrary to what his Lord described him; and how far apart is one whom Allah testifies to be purified from one who testifies for himself, or whom one who does not know testifies for. Said by al-Zamakhshari, and there is some abridgment in it.

Al-Raghib said, in summary: Purification (tazkiyah) is of two kinds: by action, which is to deliberately do what shows it, and by speech, which is to report it and praise one with it. He forbade that a person purify himself, but rather that he purify another, except in a specific manner. So tazkiyah is a report of what a person harbours, and no one knows that except Allah, Exalted.

﴿Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills﴾: "Rather" is a turning away from their purifying themselves, since they are not deserving of that. Know that the one who purifies is Allah, Exalted, and that He, Exalted, is the one whose purification is relied upon, since He is the Knower of the inner realities of things and the One who is aware of their hidden matters. The meaning of "purifies whom He wills" is: whom He wills to purify, by making him pure and purified; that is what Allah, Exalted, describes as "purified" (muzakka).

﴿And they will not be wronged a whit (fatil)﴾: an indication to the least thing, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the weight of an atom﴾ [al-Nisa': 40]. If Allah, Exalted, does not wrong the measure of a fatil, how would He wrong what is greater than it? They permitted that the pronoun in "and they are not wronged" return to those who justify themselves, and that it return to "whom" according to meaning; for if it returned according to the wording it would be "and he is not wronged," which is more apparent, since it is the nearest mentioned referent, and because "rather" (bal) cuts off what follows from what precedes. It was also said: it refers to both mentioned: the one who justifies himself and the one whom Allah purifies. Ibn ʿAtiyyah mentioned no view other than this one.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ means: those who purify themselves will be punished for their self-purification to the full extent of their due punishment, or whoever He wills will be rewarded, and they will not be diminished from their reward or the like. So do not purify yourselves; He is most knowing of who is god-fearing." End of quotation.

The majority of readers recited ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾ (alam tara, "Have you not seen?") with a fatha on the rāʾ. Al-Sulami recited it with a sukun on the rāʾ, treating the pause form as applying in continuous recitation. It was said that this is the dialect of a people who do not suffice with jazm by dropping the final radical of the verb, but also make the middle radical of the verb quiescent after it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 48–49 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills.﴾ Ibn al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning Wahshi and his companions. Wahshi had been promised manumission (ʿitq) in exchange for killing Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with him, but the promise was not fulfilled for him. So he went to Makkah, and he and his companions regretted what they had done. They wrote to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "We have indeed regretted what we did, and what prevents us from embracing Islam is only that we heard you say in Makkah: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ [al-Furqan: 68] and the verses that follow, whereas we had invoked another god with Allah, killed the soul that Allah had forbidden, and committed fornication. Had it not been for these verses, we would have followed you." Then it was revealed: ﴿except for one who repents, believes and does righteousness﴾ [al-Furqan: 70] and the verses that follow. This was sent to them, and they wrote: "This is a severe condition; we fear that we will not do righteous deeds." Then it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾, the verse. This was sent to them, and they sent back: "We fear that we are not among those whom He wills." Then it was revealed: ﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 53] and the verses that follow. This was sent to them, and they entered Islam, and it was accepted from them. Then he (the Prophet ﷺ) said to Wahshi: "Tell me how you killed Hamzah." When he told him, he said: "Woe to you! Hide your face from me." So Wahshi went to al-Sham and remained there until he died.

The Muslims have unanimously agreed on the eternal abiding of the one who dies a disbeliever in the Fire, and on the eternal abiding of the one who dies a believer who never committed a sin in Paradise. As for a penitent who died upon his repentance, the majority hold that he is joined to the believer who never sinned, while the view of some of the theologians (mutakallimun) is that he is subject to Allah's will (fi al-mashiʾah). As for a sinner who died before repenting, the Khawarij say: he is eternally abiding in the Fire, whether he is a person of a major sin or of a minor sin. The Murjiʾah say: he is in Paradise by his faith, and his sins do not harm him. The Muʿtazilah say: if he is a person of a major sin, he is eternally abiding in the Fire. As for the People of the Sunnah, they say: he is subject to Allah's will; if He wills, He forgives him and admits him to Paradise from the very first, and if He wills, He punishes him, takes him out of the Fire, and afterwards admits him to Paradise, abiding in it eternally.

The cause of this difference is the conflict between the general (ʿumumat) wordings of the verses of threat (waʿid) and the verses of promise (waʿd). The Khawarij made the verses of threat general concerning sinners, whether disbelievers or believers who have not repented. The verses of promise they restricted to the believer who never sinned, or to the sinner who repented. The Murjiʾah made the verses of threat restricted to disbelievers, and the verses of promise restricted to the believer, whether pious or disobedient. The People of the Sunnah restricted the verses of threat to disbelief and to those among disobedient believers whom Allah had foreknown He would punish, and they restricted the verses of promise to the believer who never sinned, to the penitent, and to those among disobedient believers whom Allah had foreknown He would pardon. The Muʿtazilah restricted the verses of promise to the believer who never sinned and to the penitent, and the verses of threat to the disbeliever and to the person of a major sin who did not repent.

This verse is the decisive one by its text in the place of dispute; it removes doubt and refutes these three groups. His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾, its meaning being that whoever dies as a polytheist is not forgiven, is a principle agreed upon among the four groups. His saying ﴿but He forgives what is less than that﴾ is a refutation of the Khawarij and the Muʿtazilah, because "what is less than that" is general and includes major and minor sins. His saying "for whom He wills" is a refutation of the Murjiʾah, since its implication is that forgiveness of what is below polytheism is only for some people rather than others, as Allah wills, unlike their claim that every believer is forgiven. The evidences of these groups are mentioned in the science of the fundamentals of religion (ʿilm uṣul al-din). The Muʿtazilah and the Murjiʾah have attempted to turn this verse back to their doctrines through interpretations that are not sound, and which contradict what the verse indicates.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: it is established that Allah, Mighty and Exalted, forgives polytheism for one who repents from it, and that He does not forgive what is less than polytheism of major sins except through repentance, then what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾? I say: The sound interpretation is that both the negated verb and the affirmed verb are directed to His saying ﴿for whom He wills﴾, as if it were said: Indeed, Allah does not forgive for whom He wills polytheism, and He forgives for whom He wills what is less than polytheism. Moreover, the intended meaning of the first is one who does not repent, and of the second one who repents. A parallel to this is your saying: "The commander does not give a dinar, and gives a qintar to whomever deserves it." End of his words. Thus he interpreted the verse according to his own school.

As for his saying "It is established that Allah, Mighty and Exalted, forgives polytheism for one who repents from it," this is agreed upon. As for his saying "and that He does not forgive what is less than polytheism of major sins except through repentance," we say to him: where is this established? They only argue with general expressions that admit of specification, as in their argument with His saying: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ [al-Nisa': 93] and so on, which Ibn ʿAbbas specified as applying to one who considers it lawful, and such a person is a disbeliever. And his saying: "He said: 'Then its recompense is that Allah recompenses him.' And he said: 'Khulud (abiding) means a long stay, not perpetual eternity without end, and the speech of the Arabs bears witness to this.'" As for his saying that the sound interpretation is that both the negated and affirmed verbs are directed to "for whom He wills," if he means that the prepositional phrase is attached to both verbs, this is not correct. If he means that the first is restricted by the will just as the second is restricted, then this is an interpretation. What is understood from his words is that the subject of "wills" refers to "whoever" (man), not to "Allah," because in his view the meaning is: Allah does not forgive polytheism for whom He wills that He not forgive, by virtue of his having died in polytheism without repenting of it, and He forgives what is less than polytheism of major sins for whom He wills that He forgive, by virtue of his having repented of them. What the apparent meaning of the speech indicates is that the first verb has no restriction by will, even though, according to our school, all existent things depend in their existence upon His will. And the subject of "wills" refers to Allah, Exalted, not to "whoever," and the meaning is: He forgives what is less than polytheism for whom He wills to forgive. And in His saying, Exalted: ﴿for whom He wills﴾ there is a great deferment (tarjiʾah), in that whoever dies upon a sin other than polytheism would not be definitively condemned to punishment, even if he dies persisting in it.
