﴿Look how they invent lies against God﴾: this is an address to the Prophet ﷺ. Having first addressed him with "﴿Have you not seen﴾" [al-Nisa: 49], meaning "Do you not marvel at these people who purify themselves?", He now addresses him a second time, directing his attention to the manner in which they fabricate lies against God. He used the form yaftaruna (they fabricate), which indicates continuity and persistence. He did not restrict the lie to their self-purification but generalized it to that and to other things. And what sin is greater than one who fabricates lies against God? ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God﴾ [al-An'am: 21]. So who is more unjust than one who lies against God?

Kayfa (how) is an interrogative of state (hal), and its accusative position is circumstantial (hal), its governing element being yaftaruna, and the clause is in the accusative position governed by unzur, because unzur is suspended (mu'allaqah). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "How can it be in the accusative position governed by yaftaruna? It may also be in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being yaftaruna." As for his statement that it may be in the accusative position governed by yaftaruna, this is correct according to what we have established. As for his statement that it may be in the nominative position as a subject with the predicate being yaftaruna, no one has held this view, because kayfa is not among the nouns with which it is permissible to begin a sentence. Rather, in the structure "kayfa yaftaruna 'ala Allahi al-kadhib" it is like "kayfa yadribu Zaydun 'Amran." If it were permissible to begin with it, it would not be permissible for it to be the subject in this structure, because he stated that the predicate is the clause "yaftaruna," and there is no connecting pronoun in it linking this clause to the subject, and the clause is not in meaning the same as the subject, so no connector is needed. Therefore, what he said about it, "and it may be," is invalid under every interpretation.

﴿And sufficient is He as a manifest sin﴾: This wording has already been discussed in its parallel, "wa-kafa bihi." The pronoun in bihi refers to the fabrication (al-iftira'), which is what He has denounced. It was also said to refer to the lie (al-kadhib). Al-Zamakhshari said: "And sufficient is their claim (bi-za'mihim), because He said, 'How they fabricate lies against God' in their claim that they are pure before God. And sufficient is this claim of theirs as a manifest sin among all their other sins." He thus made their fabrication of lies specific to the self-purification, whereas we have stated that it applies to this and to other things. The accusative of ithman (sin) is as a specification (tamyiz), and the meaning of mubinan is clear, i.e., evident and obvious to everyone.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "And sufficient is He" is a statement containing within it amazement and an act of making one marvel at the matter, and for this reason the preposition bi- entered, to indicate the meaning of commanding astonishment that they should be satisfied with this lie as a sin and not seek for them anything beyond it, since it is a ruinous and destructive matter." Regarding what was mentioned, that the bi- entered to indicate the meaning of commanding astonishment, there is room for scrutiny, and we have elaborated on this in his statement [wa-kafa bi-Allahi waliyyan] (﴿And sufficient is God as a protector﴾ [al-Nisa: 45]), so refer to it there.

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in al-jibt and al-taghut?﴾ [al-Nisa: 51]. They agreed that it refers to the Jews. The occasion of its revelation: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and a group with them came to Makkah seeking an alliance with the Quraysh against the Messenger of God ﷺ. They said: "You are the People of the Book, and you are closer to Muhammad than we are, so we do not trust your deception. Prostrate to our gods so that we may feel secure with you." So they did. Abu Sufyan said: "Are we better guided in the way, or is Muhammad?" Ka'b said: "What does Muhammad say?" They said: "He commands the worship of God alone and forbids association." He said: "And what is your religion?" They said: "We are the custodians of the House, we give drink to the pilgrims, we host the guest, we free the captive," and they mentioned their deeds. He said: "You are better guided in the way." There is disagreement in some wordings of this occasion, as Ibn 'Abbas said. 'Ikrimah said: "Ka'b went out with seventy riders from the Jews to Makkah after the battle of Uhud." The Scripture here is the Torah according to the majority, and it is possible that it means both the Torah and the Gospel.

Al-jibt and al-taghut are two idols that belonged to the Quraysh, as said by 'Ikrimah and others. Or al-jibt here is Huyayy, and al-taghut is Ka'b, as also said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or al-jibt is sorcery and al-taghut is Satan, as said by Mujahid and al-Sha'bi. It is narrated from 'Umar: "al-jibt is the sorcerer and al-taghut is Satan," as said by Zayd ibn Aslam. Or al-jibt is the sorcerer and al-taghut is the soothsayer (kahin), as said by Rafi' and Ibn Jubayr. Or al-jibt is the soothsayer and al-taghut is Satan, also said by Ibn Jubayr. Or al-jibt is the soothsayer and al-taghut is the sorcerer, said by Ibn Sirin. Or al-jibt is Satan and al-taghut is the soothsayer, said by Qatadah. Or al-jibt is Ka'b and al-taghut is Satan who was in the form of a human being. Or al-jibt is the idols, and everything worshipped besides God, and al-taghut is Satan, said by al-Zamakhshari. Or al-jibt and al-taghut are every object of worship besides God, whether a stone, a image, or a devil, said by al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutaybah.

Some exegetes presented the disagreement separately, saying: al-jibt is sorcery, said by 'Umar, Mujahid, and al-Sha'bi. Or the idols, transmitted by 'Atiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas, and this was also said by al-Dahhak and al-Farra'. Or Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, transmitted by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and by Layth from Mujahid. Or the soothsayer, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and this was said by Makhul and Ibn Sirin. Or Satan, said by Ibn Jubayr in one narration, and by Qatadah and al-Suddi. Or the sorcerer, said by Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd. Abu Bishr narrated from Ibn Jubayr who said: "al-jibt is the sorcerer in the Abyssinian language, and as for al-taghut, it is Satan," said by 'Umar, Mujahid in the narration of al-Sha'bi, and Ibn Zayd. Or the interpreters standing before the idols, narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, or from Ka'b. Narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and this was said by al-Dahhak and al-Farra'. Or the soothsayer, said by 'Ikrimah, or the sorcerer, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Sirin, and Makhul. Or everything worshipped besides God, said by Malik.

Some people said: al-jibt and al-taghut are synonyms with one meaning. The majority, however, and the statements of the exegetes, are contrary to this, and hold that they are two. The Messenger of God ﷺ made speech about unseen matters a jibt, because the knowledge of the unseen belongs exclusively to God, the Exalted. Abu Dawud recorded in his Sunan from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he said: "Tarq (divination by striking lines), tiyarah (omen-taking), and 'iyafah (augury by drawing lines) are from al-jibt." Tarq is zajr (deterring by omens), and 'iyafah is drawing lines. For al-jibt and al-taghut are the idols or what is worshipped besides God. So believing in them means affirming that they are gods whom they associate with God in worship. And if it is Huyayy and Ka'b, or a group of the Jews, or the sorcerer, or the soothsayer, or Satan, then believing in them is an expression of obeying them and agreeing with them in what they are upon, and it is of the category of using the fruit of faith to mean faith itself, which is obedience.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 51–53:

﴿And they say to those who disbelieve, "These are better guided in the way than those who believe."﴾ The pronoun in *yaqulun* (they say) refers to those who were given (a portion of the Book). In the occasion of revelation, it is reported that Ka'b was the one who said this statement. The clause *yu'minuna* (they believe) is a circumstantial clause (hal), and *yaqulun* is conjoined to *yu'minuna*, so it is also a circumstantial clause. It is possible that it is a resumptive informative statement (isti'naf) expressing astonishment at them, as if he said: "Do you not marvel at the condition of those who were given a portion?" It is then as if it was said: "What is their condition, when they have been given a portion of the Book of Allah?" So he said: they believe in such-and-such, and they say such-and-such. That is, their conditions are contradictory. Their being given a portion of the Book requires that they not fall into what they fell into; but what drove them to that is envy. The *lam* in *lilladhina kafaru* (to those who disbelieve) is the *lam* of communication (li'l-tabligh), connected to *yaqulun*. Those who disbelieve are the Quraysh, and the indication by *ha'ulai* (these) points to them. Those who believe are the Prophet and his community. Apparently they used the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) without considering the sense of sharing in it, or they said that as a form of mockery because of their disbelief.

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed﴾: an indication of those who believed in *al-jibt* and *al-taghut* and said that statement. Allah the Exalted has distanced them and abhorred them.

﴿And whoever Allah curses, you will not find for him any helper﴾: that is, who will help him and protect him from the effects of the curse, which is the great punishment.

﴿Or do they have a share of the kingdom?﴾ *Am* here is disjunctive (munqati'ah) in its estimation: "Rather, do they have a share of the kingdom?" It shifted from speech to a complete speech, and the interrogative is for denial, that they should have a share of the kingdom. Ibn Qutaybah related that *am* is used in interrogation at the beginning. Some exegetes said: *am* here means *bal* (rather). They interpreted it as an informative statement that they are the kings of the people of the world, with arrogance and luxury, not seeking anything other than that; so they are stingy, eager that no superiority should be (granted) to anyone else. The meaning according to the first view is: "Rather, do they have a share of the kingdom? If they had a share of the kingdom, they would have been stingy with it." The kingdom is the kingdom of the people of the world, and this is the apparent meaning, or the kingdom of Allah, due to His saying: ﴿Say: If you possessed the treasures of the mercy of my Lord, then you would withhold them for fear of spending﴾ [al-Isra: 100]. It was also said: it is wealth, because by it kingdom is attained, and it is its foundation. It was said: it is the entitlement to obedience. It was said: it is prophethood (p-273), and it was said: it is truthfulness of insight, mentioned by al-Mawardi. The more eloquent view is the cancelling of *idhan* (then) after the conjunctions *wa* (and) and *fa* (so), and most readers hold this view.

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Abdullah ibn Abbas recited (*la yu'tuna*) with the deletion of the *nun*, based on the operation of *idhan* (as a particle governing the subjunctive). "The people" here means the Arabs, or the believers, or the Prophet, or among the Jews and others; there are several statements. *Al-naqir* is the spot on the back of the date stone; this was related by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid, Ata, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, al-Suddi, Muqatil, al-Farra', and Ibn Qutaybah, among others, said the same. It was also said: it is the husk in the middle of the stone; related by al-Tamimi from Ibn Abbas. Or it is the thread in the middle of the stone; reported from Mujahid. Or it is the man's pricking of a thing with the tip of his thumb; related by Abu al-Aliyah from Ibn Abbas. Or it is the seed of the stone which is in its middle; related by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid. Al-Azhari said: *al-fatil*, *al-naqir* and *al-qitmir* are struck as examples for a trivial, insignificant thing. The insignificant things were specified by His saying *fatilan* (a thread) in His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged even a thread (fatil)﴾, and here by His saying *naqiran* (a speck) for agreement with the similar word-endings (fawasil).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 54–56:

﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ (Am) is also disjunctive (munqati'ah), so it is to be estimated as (bal, "rather"). The hamza (alif of interrogation) is said to be for the transition from one speech to another. The hamza is for the interrogation that is accompanied by denunciation. He first denounced them for stinginess (bukhl), then secondly for envy (hasad). Stinginess is the withholding of the arrival of good from a person to another, and envy is the wish for the removal of what Allah has given a person of good, and His granting it to him. Allah the Exalted censured them for adorning themselves with these two blameworthy traits. And since envy is the worse of the two traits, it ascended to mentioning it after mentioning stinginess. "The people" here refers to the Prophet ﷺ. And "the bounty" is prophethood (al-nubuwwah), as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and Muqatil.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi also said: "The bounty is what was made permissible to him of women." The occasion of revelation of the verse according to them is that the Jews said to the disbelievers of the Arabs: "Look at this man who claims he was sent with humility, and that he does not fill his belly with food, his concern is only with women, and the like of this." So it was revealed. The meaning is: Why do you single him out for envy, and not envy the family of Ibrahim, meaning Sulayman and Dawud, in that they were given prophethood and the Book, and were given along with that a great kingdom in the matter of women; and this is what is related: that Sulayman had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and Dawud had a hundred wives. So "kingdom" in this view is the permissibility of women, as if that is the primary intended mention. Qatadah said: "The people" here are the Arabs, whom the Children of Israel envied because the Messenger ﷺ was from them, and "the bounty" here is the Messenger. The meaning: Why do they envy the Arabs for this Prophet, when their forefathers were given prophets and books such as the Torah and the Psalms, and wisdom, which is understanding in the religion of what the Book has not explicitly stated? It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "We are the people," meaning the Quraysh.

﴿For We had already given the family of Ibrahim the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom.﴾ That is, the kingdom of Sulayman, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: it is prophethood. Hammam ibn al-Harith, Abu Maslamah, and Ibn Zayd said: it is support with angels. It was also said: "the people" here are the Messenger, Abu Bakr and 'Umar. The Book: the Torah and the Gospel, or both and the Psalms, are opinions; and wisdom: prophethood, as said by al-Suddi and Muqatil, or the understanding of the religion, as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. It was said that the great kingdom is the combination of governing the world and the law of religion, mentioned by al-Mawardi. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or do they envy them for what Allah has given them of His bounty": the victory, the dominance, and the increase of honour and advancement every day. (For We had already given) is a binding argument against them with what they knew of Allah's giving the Book and wisdom to the family of Ibrahim, who are the forefathers of Muhammad ﷺ, and that it is no novelty that Allah gives him the like of what His forefathers were given. And from Ibn 'Abbas: the kingdom among the family of Ibrahim is the kingdom of Yusuf, Dawud and Sulayman. End of his words. And it is a good statement.

﴿So among them is he who believed in it, and among them is he who turned away from it.﴾ That is, among the family of Ibrahim is he who believed in Ibrahim, and among them is he who disbelieved, like His saying: ﴿So among them is one guided, and many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Hadid: 26]; said by al-Suddi. Or: among the family of Ibrahim is he who believed in the Book; or among the Jews addressed by His saying: ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down﴾ [al-Nisa: 47]. "He who believed in it" means in the Qur'an, and it is what he was commanded to believe in His saying "in what We have sent down"; said by Mujahid, Muqatil, al-Farra' and the majority. (p-274) Therefore the "tamas" was lifted and did not occur. Or among the Jews is he who believed in the bounty which the Messenger ﷺ was given, or the Arabs, as previously mentioned. Or among the Jews is he who believed in him; that is, in what was mentioned of the account of the family of Ibrahim. Or among the Jews is he who believed in the Messenger of Allah, and among them is he who denied his prophethood. The apparent meaning is that when He denounced the Jews for their envy of the people for the bounty of Allah which He had given them, He followed it with what comes after it by way of digression, reflection and argument against them: that it is not fitting for you to envy, for your forefathers have attained of nobility what makes it fitting that you not envy anyone.

This verse contains consolation for the Messenger ﷺ regarding their envying him and not following him; so He mentioned that they too, along with their forefathers and prophets, divided into believer and disbeliever. This being the case with their forefathers, how about a prophet who is not from them?

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Ya'mar and al-Jahdari read (wa-man ṣuddа 'anhu) with the ṣad raised, in the passive voice. Ubayy, Abu al-Hawra', Abu Raja' and al-Hawfi read with the ṣad kasra, in the passive voice. The doubled, assimilated triliteral verb has what is permitted in ba'a when built in the passive: you say ḥubba Zayd with a ḍamma, and ḥibb with a kasra. Ishmam is also permitted. The verb ṣadd is not the opposite of belief except in meaning; and the meaning, and Allah knows best, is: among them is he who believed in him and followed him, and among them is he who denied him and turned away from him.

﴿And Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire.﴾ That is, as a burning and a flaming, for whoever turns away from him. Sa'iran is a specification (tamyiz), and it is the intensity of the kindling of the fire. The estimate: "and sufficient is the blazing of Hell as a blaze"; and it is a metaphor for the severity of the punishment and chastisement.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved in Our signs—We will drive them into a Fire.﴾ When He mentioned His saying: ﴿And among them is he who turned away from it, and Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire﴾, He followed that with what Allah has prepared for the disbelievers in His signs; then afterward it is followed by what He has prepared for the believers, and it became like ﴿On the Day faces will be whitened and faces will be blackened; as for those whose faces were blackened﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]. The majority read ﴿nuṣlīhim﴾ from aṣlā. Ḥumayd read naṣlīhim from ṣaliya. Sallam and Ya'qub read ﴿nuṣlīhim﴾ with a ḍamma on the hā'.

﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins.﴾ Kullamā is in the accusative as an adverb of time, since it is annexed to mā, the verbal temporal (maṣdariyyah ẓarfiyyah), and its governing element is "We will replace them"; and it is a clause having the sense of a condition, and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its governing element is "nuṣlīhim". Replacement has two meanings: a replacement in attributes while the substance remains, and a replacement in essences, by which the substance departs and another substance comes in its place; one says: "this is the replacement (badal) of this." The apparent meaning of the verse is the second meaning. That is, when that skin is roasted and decays and perishes, another skin is brought in its place; for this reason He said: "other skins than them." Al-Suddi said: the skins are created from the flesh; so when one skin is burned, Allah replaces it with another skin from the flesh of the disbeliever. It was also said: it is the same skin restored after it is burned, as bodies are restored after decay in graves; so this returns to the attribute, not to the essence. Al-Fudayl said: the roasting is made into non-roasting. It was said: they are replaced seven times each day. Al-Hasan said: seventy times. And most remote is the one who holds that the skins are garments of tar which mix with their skins in a mixing that cannot be removed, so Allah replaces those garments every day a hundred times, or as it is said: a hundred thousand times. They are called "skins" because of their contact with the skins. Also most remote is the one who holds that this is a metaphor for permanence: whenever it ends, it has begun again from its beginning; that is, whenever they think they have been roasted, burned and reached destruction, We give them fresh strength of life, so that they think they have now become new and found; so the intended meaning is the explanation of the perpetuity of the punishment and its non-cessation. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah clothes them in white skins as if they were scrolls. 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya said: the people of the Fire wear skins which pain them while they themselves are not pained.

﴿That they may taste the punishment.﴾ That is, that replacement each time the skins are roasted is so that they may taste the pain of the punishment. He used the word "taste" (dhawq), which implies the first sensation and is more painful; so whenever the replacement occurs, it is for tasting the punishment, unlike one who has become accustomed to punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: "that they may taste the punishment" so that it may continue for them without ceasing; like your saying to the mighty: "May Allah honour you," that is, keep you in your honour and increase you in it.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Mighty and Wise.﴾ That is, Mighty (p-275), not overcome; Wise, placing things in their proper places. Al-Zamakhshari said: Mighty, nothing He wills against the criminals is withheld from Him; Wise, He does not punish except with justice whoever deserves it.

Hammam ibn al-Harith, Abu Maslamah, and Ibn Zayd said: it is support with angels. It was also said: "the people" here are the Messenger, Abu Bakr and 'Umar. The Book: the Torah and the Gospel, or both and the Psalms, are opinions; and wisdom: prophethood, as said by al-Suddi and Muqatil, or the understanding of the religion, as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. It was said that the great kingdom is the combination of governing the world and the law of religion, mentioned by al-Mawardi. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or do they envy them for what Allah has given them of His bounty": the victory, the dominance, and the increase of honour and advancement every day. (For We had already given) is a binding argument against them with what they knew of Allah's giving the Book and wisdom to the family of Ibrahim, who are the forefathers of Muhammad ﷺ, and that it is no novelty that Allah gives him the like of what His forefathers were given. And from Ibn 'Abbas: the kingdom among the family of Ibrahim is the kingdom of Yusuf, Dawud and Sulayman. End of his words. And it is a good statement.

﴿So among them is he who believed in it, and among them is he who turned away from it.﴾ That is, among the family of Ibrahim is he who believed in Ibrahim, and among them is he who disbelieved, like His saying: ﴿So among them is one guided, and many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Hadid: 26]; said by al-Suddi. Or: among the family of Ibrahim is he who believed in the Book; or among the Jews addressed by His saying: ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down﴾ [al-Nisa: 47]. "He who believed in it" means in the Qur'an, and it is what he was commanded to believe in His saying "in what We have sent down"; said by Mujahid, Muqatil, al-Farra' and the majority. (p-274) Therefore the "tamas" was lifted and did not occur. Or among the Jews is he who believed in the bounty which the Messenger ﷺ was given, or the Arabs, as previously mentioned. Or among the Jews is he who believed in him; that is, in what was mentioned of the account of the family of Ibrahim. Or among the Jews is he who believed in the Messenger of Allah, and among them is he who denied his prophethood. The apparent meaning is that when He denounced the Jews for their envy of the people for the bounty of Allah which He had given them, He followed it with what comes after it by way of digression, reflection and argument against them: that it is not fitting for you to envy, for your forefathers have attained of nobility what makes it fitting that you not envy anyone.

This verse contains consolation for the Messenger ﷺ regarding their envying him and not following him; so He mentioned that they too, along with their forefathers and prophets, divided into believer and disbeliever. This being the case with their forefathers, how about a prophet who is not from them?

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Ya'mar and al-Jahdari read (wa-man ṣuddа 'anhu) with the ṣad raised, in the passive voice. Ubayy, Abu al-Hawra', Abu Raja' and al-Hawfi read with the ṣad kasra, in the passive voice. The doubled, assimilated triliteral verb has what is permitted in ba'a when built in the passive: you say ḥubba Zayd with a ḍamma, and ḥibb with a kasra. Ishmam is also permitted. The verb ṣadd is not the opposite of belief except in meaning; and the meaning, and Allah knows best, is: among them is he who believed in him and followed him, and among them is he who denied him and turned away from him.

﴿And Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire.﴾ That is, as a burning and a flaming, for whoever turns away from him. Sa'iran is a specification (tamyiz), and it is the intensity of the kindling of the fire. The estimate: "and sufficient is the blazing of Hell as a blaze"; and it is a metaphor for the severity of the punishment and chastisement.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved in Our signs—We will drive them into a Fire.﴾ When He mentioned His saying: ﴿And among them is he who turned away from it, and Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire﴾, He followed that with what Allah has prepared for the disbelievers in His signs; then afterward it is followed by what He has prepared for the believers, and it became like ﴿On the Day faces will be whitened and faces will be blackened; as for those whose faces were blackened﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]. The majority read ﴿nuṣlīhim﴾ from aṣlā. Ḥumayd read naṣlīhim from ṣaliya. Sallam and Ya'qub read ﴿nuṣlīhim﴾ with a ḍamma on the hā'.

﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins.﴾ Kullamā is in the accusative as an adverb of time, since it is annexed to mā, the verbal temporal (maṣdariyyah ẓarfiyyah), and its governing element is "We will replace them"; and it is a clause having the sense of a condition, and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its governing element is "nuṣlīhim". Replacement has two meanings: a replacement in attributes while the substance remains, and a replacement in essences, by which the substance departs and another substance comes in its place; one says: "this is the replacement (badal) of this." The apparent meaning of the verse is the second meaning. That is, when that skin is roasted and decays and perishes, another skin is brought in its place; for this reason He said: "other skins than them." Al-Suddi said: the skins are created from the flesh; so when one skin is burned, Allah replaces it with another skin from the flesh of the disbeliever. It was also said: it is the same skin restored after it is burned, as bodies are restored after decay in graves; so this returns to the attribute, not to the essence. Al-Fudayl said: the roasting is made into non-roasting. It was said: they are replaced seven times each day. Al-Hasan said: seventy times. And most remote is the one who holds that the skins are garments of tar which mix with their skins in a mixing that cannot be removed, so Allah replaces those garments every day a hundred times, or as it is said: a hundred thousand times. They are called "skins" because of their contact with the skins. Also most remote is the one who holds that this is a metaphor for permanence: whenever it ends, it has begun again from its beginning; that is, whenever they think they have been roasted, burned and reached destruction, We give them fresh strength of life, so that they think they have now become new and found; so the intended meaning is the explanation of the perpetuity of the punishment and its non-cessation. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah clothes them in white skins as if they were scrolls. 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya said: the people of the Fire wear skins which pain them while they themselves are not pained.

﴿That they may taste the punishment.﴾ That is, that replacement each time the skins are roasted is so that they may taste the pain of the punishment. He used the word "taste" (dhawq), which implies the first sensation and is more painful; so whenever the replacement occurs, it is for tasting the punishment, unlike one who has become accustomed to punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: "that they may taste the punishment" so that it may continue for them without ceasing; like your saying to the mighty: "May Allah honour you," that is, keep you in your honour and increase you in it.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Mighty and Wise.﴾ That is, Mighty (p-275), not overcome; Wise, placing things in their proper places. Al-Zamakhshari said: Mighty, nothing He wills against the criminals is withheld from Him; Wise, He does not punish except with justice whoever deserves it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 54–56:

﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ (Am) is also disjunctive (munqati'ah), so it is to be estimated as (bal, "rather"). The hamza (alif of interrogation) is said to be for the transition from one speech to another. The hamza is for the interrogation that is accompanied by denunciation. He first denounced them for stinginess (bukhl), then secondly for envy (hasad). Stinginess is the withholding of the arrival of good from a person to another, and envy is the wish for the removal of what Allah has given a person of good, and His granting it to him. Allah the Exalted censured them for adorning themselves with these two blameworthy traits. And since envy is the worse of the two traits, it ascended to mentioning it after mentioning stinginess. "The people" here refers to the Prophet ﷺ. And "the bounty" is prophethood (al-nubuwwah), as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and Muqatil.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi also said: "The bounty is what was made permissible to him of women." The occasion of revelation of the verse according to them is that the Jews said to the disbelievers of the Arabs: "Look at this man who claims he was sent with humility, and that he does not fill his belly with food, his concern is only with women, and the like of this." So it was revealed. The meaning is: Why do you single him out for envy, and not envy the family of Ibrahim, meaning Sulayman and Dawud, in that they were given prophethood and the Book, and were given along with that a great kingdom in the matter of women; and this is what is related: that Sulayman had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and Dawud had a hundred wives. So "kingdom" in this view is the permissibility of women, as if that is the primary intended mention. Qatadah said: "The people" here are the Arabs, whom the Children of Israel envied because the Messenger ﷺ was from them, and "the bounty" here is the Messenger. The meaning: Why do they envy the Arabs for this Prophet, when their forefathers were given prophets and books such as the Torah and the Psalms, and wisdom, which is understanding in the religion of what the Book has not explicitly stated? Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 57:

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever.﴾ When the Exalted mentioned the threat against the disbelievers, He followed it with the promise to the believers. The sentence about the disbelievers was emphasized with "inna" (indeed), as a confirmation of the certainty of the threat. The sentence about the believers did not need that emphasis, and it was introduced with the "sin" (the future particle) which indicates that the period of respite is short, by way of bringing good near to the believer and giving him good news of it.

﴿For them therein are purified spouses.﴾ The explanation of the like of this has already passed.

﴿And We will admit them to a shade, deep and dense.﴾ Ibn 'Atiyya said: that is, it shields from heat and cold. It is also possible that it means that it is a shade that does not move, as the shade of this world does, so He emphasized it by saying "dense" (zalilan) for that reason. It is also possible to describe it as "dense" because of its extent, for he, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed in Paradise there is a tree, such that a rider traveling on a well-trained swift horse would not cross its shade in a hundred years." End of his words.

Abu Muslim said: "al-zalil" (the dense) is the strong, the firmly established. He said: describing a thing by a word derived from the same root as itself is intensive, like their saying: "laylun alyal" (a very dark night) and "dahiya dahya'" (a great calamity). Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: He only said "shade, deep and dense" because the lands of the Arabs are in extreme heat, so shade was among the greatest causes of rest for them. For this reason it was made a metonymy (kinaya) for rest, and describing it as "dense" is an intensification of rest.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "zalil" is an adjective derived from the word "zill" (shade), to confirm its meaning, as one says "laylun alyal" and "yawmun ayyam" and similar things. It is that which is leafy (fannan), without any gap (jawb) in it, and lasting, which the sun does not erase, and mild (sajsaj), with neither heat nor cold in it. And that is nothing but the shade of Paradise. May God grant us, by His success, what brings us near to reclining under that shade. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: (sa-yudkhiluhum) with the "ya" (third person). End of his words.

Al-Hasan said: It may be a shade that is not dense, into which heat and sun penetrate; for this reason He described the shade of Paradise as "dense."

From al-Hasan: The shade of the people of Paradise shields from heat and scorching wind, while the shade of the people of Hell is from a black smoke (yahmum), neither cool nor pleasant. It is said that the times of Paradise are all alike, a moderate state in which there is neither heat nor cold.

Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab recited (sa-yudkhiluhum) with the "ya", and likewise (wa-yudkhiluhum zillan). Whoever reads with "nun", and they are the majority, took into account His saying regarding the threat against the disbelievers: ﴿We will surely burn them in Fire﴾ [4:56]. Whoever reads with "ya" took into account His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Mighty and Wise﴾ [4:56], and so he kept it in the third person.

These noble verses include various kinds of eloquence, expression and rhetorical figures (badi'):

The interrogative used to express amazement in: "Have you not seen" in both places; the general address used to mean the specific in: ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down﴾ [4:47], which is the Messenger's call, peace be upon him, to Ibn Suriya, Ka'b and other rabbis to faith, according to what is in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul); the metaphor (isti'ara) in His saying: ﴿before We obliterate faces﴾ [4:47], according to the view of the one who said it is turning away from the truth; and in: ﴿that they may taste the punishment﴾, where the name of tasting, which is specific to the sense of the tongue and the roof of the mouth, is applied to the arrival of pain at the heart.

Antithesis (tibaq) in: ﴿and turn them back on their backs﴾ [4:47], for "face" is the opposite of "back of the neck." And in: ﴿those who disbelieve say of those who believe, "These are better guided than those who believe"﴾ [4:51]; and in: ﴿Indeed those who disbelieve in Our signs﴾ [4:56]; and in: "whoever believes" and "whoever turns away"; this is a semantic antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi).

Digression (istitrad) in: ﴿or curse them as We cursed the companions of the Sabbath﴾ [4:47].

Repetition (takrar) in: "forgives" (yaghfiru); in the name of Allah (lafz al-jalala); in the word "people" (al-nas); in: "We gave" (atayna) and "We gave them" (ataynahum); in: "among them" (fa-minhum) and "among them" (minhum); in: "their skins" (juludahum) and ﴿skins﴾ [4:56]; and in: "We will admit them" (sa-nudkhiluhum) and "We will admit them" (nudkhiluhum).

Homogeneous paronomasia (tajnis mumathil) in: "We curse them as We cursed" (nal'anahum kama la'anna). And in: ﴿does not forgive﴾ [4:48] and ﴿and forgives﴾ [4:48]; and in: ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾ [4:52] and "whoever Allah curses"; and in: ﴿they do not give people﴾ [4:53], ﴿has given them﴾ [4:54], ﴿We gave﴾ [4:54], and ﴿and We gave them﴾ [4:54]; and in: "they believe in the idol and the false deity (jibt)" and "believed are more guided."

Amazement expressed by the form of the imperative in His saying: "Look how they invent lies" [4:50]. The shift of address (talwin al-khitab) in: ﴿they invent﴾ [4:50], where the present tense is used in place of the past, to inform that they continue in that.

The interrogative whose meaning is reproach and rebuke in: ﴿Or do they have a share?﴾ [4:53]; and in: "Or do they envy?"

Demonstration (ishara) in: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed﴾ [4:52].

Division (taqsim) in: ﴿Among them are those who believed in him and among them are those who averted from him﴾ [4:55].

Indirect allusion (ta'ridh) in: ﴿then they would not give people a speck﴾ [4:53], which alludes to the severity of their stinginess.

Use of the plural for the singular in: ﴿Or do they envy the people?﴾ [4:54], if it is explained as referring to the Messenger.

Use of the indefinite in place of the definite to take into account commonality (shuyu').

Abundance (kathra) in: ﴿We will surely burn them in a Fire﴾ [4:56].

Restriction (ikhtisas) in: ﴿Mighty and Wise﴾ [4:56].

Ellipsis (hadhf) in several places.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 58:**

﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Excellent is that with which Allah instructs you. Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is best and most suitable in outcome.﴾ [An-Nisa: 59] ﴿Have you not considered those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, yet they desire to refer their disputes to the tyrant (taghut), although they were commanded to reject it? And Satan intends to lead them far astray.﴾ [An-Nisa: 60] ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion.﴾ [An-Nisa: 61] ﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have put forward? Then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation."﴾ [An-Nisa: 62] ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah knows, so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them about themselves a far-reaching word.﴾ [An-Nisa: 63]

Al-za'm (claim): a statement accompanied by a conjectural belief. It may be pronounced with a damma, fatha or kasra on the zay. The poet, who is Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali, said:

"If you claim that I was ignorant among you, then indeed I have bought forbearance after you with ignorance."

Ibn Duraid said: it most often applies to falsehood. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The mount of a man is 'they claim'" (za'amu). Al-A'sha said:

"I was told of Qays, though I had not tested him, as they claimed, the best of the people of Yemen."

So the one praised said what was nothing but a claim, and he was deprived of it. When Sibawayh says "Zaʿama al-Khalil" (al-Khalil claimed), he uses it for what al-Khalil alone held, and which was stronger. The author of al-'Ayn (Sahib al-'Ayn) mentioned that the better usage with za'ama is to follow it with "anna" (that), and he said: it may occur in poetry followed by a noun. He recited this verse of Abu Dhu'ayb and the words of another:

"She claimed me an old man, though I am not an old man; the old man is only the one who walks with slow steps."

It is said that za'ama means "to guarantee" (kafala) and "to lead" (ra's), so it may take one object at a time, or a prepositional phrase. It is said: za'imat al-shatu, meaning the sheep became fat, and also meaning it became lean; in this sense it is intransitive. Al-tawfiq (grant of success): a verbal noun from wafaqa, and al-wifaq and al-wafq are the opposite of opposition.

﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾: The occasion of its revelation, as narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and as said by Mujahid, al-Zuhri, Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil, is found in a lengthy account whose meaning is: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the key of the Ka'ba from its custodians, Uthman ibn Talha and his paternal cousin Shayba ibn Uthman, after Uthman had refused; and he had not yet embraced Islam. Al-Abbas asked the Messenger (ﷺ) to combine for him the office of providing water (al-siqaya) and the custodianship (al-sidana), so it was revealed, and he returned the key to them, and Uthman embraced Islam. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Take it, O sons of Talha, as a perpetual and inherited trust; none will take it from you except a wrongdoer."

Ibn Abi Talha narrated from Ibn Abbas, and Zayd ibn Aslam, Makhul said, and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi chose: it was revealed concerning rulers, that they render the trust in what Allah has entrusted them with regarding the affairs of their subjects. It was also said that it was revealed in general terms, and this is related from Ubayy, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that, when Allah mentioned the promise to the believers and mentioned righteous deeds, He drew attention to these two noble deeds: whoever is characterized by them is more fitting to be characterized by other righteous deeds. One of them is what concerns a person in his relation to himself and others, namely rendering the trust, which was offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and they refused to bear it. The second is what occurs between two parties, namely judging between them with just judgment free of desire, which is among the great deeds that Allah commanded His messengers, prophets and the believers. Since the correct order is that a person begins with himself in acquiring benefits and warding off harms, and then turns to the condition of others, he was commanded first with rendering the trust, and after it with commanding judgment by truth. The apparent meaning of "Allah commands you" is that the address is general to everyone regarding every trust.

Ibn Jurayj said: it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the key of the Ka'ba. Ali, Ibn Aslam, Shahr and Ibn Zayd said: it is an address specifically to the rulers of the Muslims; so it is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his commanders, and then it extends to those after them. Ibn Abbas said: concerning rulers, that they should admonish women regarding disobedience (nushuz) and the like, and return them to their husbands. It was also said: it is an address to the Jews, who were commanded to return what they held of the trust, which is the description of the Messenger (ﷺ), that they should make it manifest to its people, since the address with them preceded this verse. Al-Tabrizi related: that it is an address to the commanders of military expeditions (al-sara'a) regarding guarding the spoils and placing them with their rightful owners. It was also said that this is general concerning what the servant is obligated to in acts of worship. The more apparent view is what we have already mentioned: that the address is general and includes rulers regarding the trusts entrusted to them in the division of wealth, returning wrongs, and the justice of judgments; and below them, other people regarding deposits, loans and testimonies, and a man judging in a particular case. Ibn Abbas said: Allah did not permit anyone, rich or poor, to withhold a trust.

It was read: "an tu'addu al-amanata" (in the singular, al-amana), and "an tahkumu" (that you judge). Its apparent meaning is that it is conjoined to "an tu'addu" (that you render), and a separation was made between the conjunction particle and the conjoined element by "idha" (when). Some of our companions held this view, and they compared it to the words of Allah: "Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter" [Al-Baqara: 201]; "And We placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier" [Ya-Sin: 9]; "Seven heavens and of the earth the like of them" [At-Talaq: 12]. In this verse, the conjunction "wa" was separated from the conjoined element by a prepositional phrase. Abu Ali restricted this to poetry, and that is not correct. If the conjoined element is in the genitive, the preposition is repeated, as in: "pass by Zayd, and tomorrow by Amr." But the words "when you judge between people, to judge" are not among these verses, because the prepositional particle in these verses is related to the governing element of the conjoined term; here the adverbial phrase apparently is in the accusative governed by "an tahkumu." That is not possible, because the verb is within the relative clause of "an," and it cannot be in the accusative governed by "an tahkumu," since the command is not occurring at the time of judging. Some have analysed it on this basis. What appears is that "idha" is governed by an implied "an tahkumu," and the expressed "an tahkumu" explains that implied one; this is when we follow the view of the majority. As for the view of al-Farra', "idha" is in the accusative governed by the expressed "an tahkumu," since he permits: "The honey pleases me that it be drunk," where the complement of the relative clause of "an" precedes it.

﴿Indeed, Allah, excellent is that with which He instructs you﴾: Its original form is ni'ma ma, and "ma" is a complete definite (ma ma'rifa tamma) according to the view of Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i. It is as if he said: "the thing is excellent with which He instructs you," that is, what a thing He instructs you with. "Ya'izukum" is a qualifier of "shay'" (thing), and "shay'" is the one specified by praise. It is also a relative pronoun (mawsula) according to one of the two opinions of al-Farisi. The specified element is omitted; the estimate is: "Excellent is that which instructs you with it: rendering trusts and judging with justice." It is indefinite in the accusative position as a specificative (tamyiz), and "ya'izukum" is its qualifier according to one of the two opinions of al-Farisi, and the specified element is omitted, with the same estimate as the preceding. I have explained "ma" here in all these views, and its detailed verification belongs to the science of grammar (nahw). Ibn Atiyya said: the "ma" attached after ni'ma is only preparatory for the verb to attach to it, as it is in "rubba-ma" and "mimma," in the words: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was among those who moved his lips," and like the poet's words:

"Indeed we, of what strike the ram with a blow, on its head, the tongue falls out of the mouth."

And similar to this. In this case it is in the position of "rubba-ma," but it differs from it in meaning, since "rubba-ma" means diminution, while "mimma" means multiplication. Although "ma" here is a preparatory particle, it has the meaning of "alladhi" (which). Also "ma" prepares only when it is a noun, but the intention is only for what follows it of the meaning in the verb. End of his words. This is incoherent speech, because from the standpoint of making it a preparatory particle, it cannot be a noun; and from the standpoint of making it mean "alladhi," it cannot be preparatory; so the two contradict each other.

The majority read "ni'immā" with a kasra on the 'ayn, by assimilation to the vowel of the 'ayn. Some readers read "na'immā" with a fatha on the nun, according to the original form, since the original is na'ima on the pattern of shahida. It is ascribed to Abu 'Amr that the 'ayn is sukun; so it would be a combination of two consecutive unvocalized letters.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing﴾: that is, of your statements issued by you in judgments.

﴿Seeing﴾: of the return of trusts to their owners.

﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾. It was said that it was revealed concerning the commanders (umara') of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They related a lengthy account, the substance of which is this: Ammar granted protection (ijara) to a man who had embraced Islam, while his companions fled when they were warned of the raiding detachment (sariyya) and ran away. The man remained behind. The commander of the detachment, Khalid, seized the man and his property. Ammar informed him of the man's conversion to Islam and of the protection he had granted him. Khalid said: "And you grant protection?" They quarrelled, and they brought the matter before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He upheld Ammar's protection and forbade him from granting protection against a commander.

Its connection to what precedes it is that when He commanded the rulers (wulat) to judge with justice, He commanded the subjects (ra'iyya) to obey them. Ata said: "Obey Allah in His obligations, and the Messenger (ﷺ) in his Sunna." Ibn Zayd said: "In His commands and prohibitions; and the Messenger, as long as he is alive, and his Sunna after his death." It was said: "Obey Him in what He has legislated, and the Messenger (ﷺ) in what he has explained." Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: "Those in authority (ulu al-amr) are the commanders." Mujahid said: "They are the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ)." Al-Tabrizi said: "The Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar)." It was said: "The Companions and the Successors (tabi'un)." It was said: "The four Caliphs." Ikrima said: "Abu Bakr and Umar." Jabir, al-Hasan, Ata, Abu al-Aliya and Mujahid also said: "The scholars ('ulama')," and Malik adopted this view. Maymun, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: "The commanders of the detachments, or the imams from the People of the House (ahl al-bayt)," as the Shi'a have said. Or "Ali alone," which they also said. The apparent meaning is that it applies to everyone who holds authority over any matter by valid appointment (wilaya sahiha). They said: "Even a wife must obey her husband, a slave obeys his master, a child obeys his parents, and an orphan obeys his guardian (wasi), in what pleases Allah and in which there is benefit for him."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "What is meant by ﴿those in authority among you﴾ is the rulers of truth (umara' al-haqq), because the rulers of injustice (umara' al-jawr) are disavowed by Allah and His Messenger; so they are not to be coupled with Allah and His Messenger." The first of the Caliphs used to say: "Obey me as long as I act justly among you; if I deviate, then there is no obedience to me from you." And from Abu Hazim: Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik said to him: "Were you not commanded to obey us, in His saying: ﴿and those in authority among you﴾?" He replied: "Has it not been removed from you when you opposed the truth, in His saying: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾?" It was also said that they are the commanders of the detachments.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah, and whoever disobeys me has disobeyed Allah; whoever obeys my commander has obeyed me, and whoever disobeys my commander has disobeyed me." It was also said that they are the pious scholars who teach people the religion, enjoining upon them what is right and forbidding them what is wrong, and that ends the citation. Sahl al-Tustari said: "Obey the ruler in seven matters: the minting of dinars and dirhams, weights and measures, judgments, the Hajj, the Friday prayer, the two 'Eids, and jihad. If the ruler forbids the scholar to issue legal opinions (fatwa), then he is not permitted to issue them; if he does issue them, he is a disobedient sinner, even if the ruler is an unjust commander." It was said: "Sahl's statement should be understood to mean that he should refrain from issuing fatwas when he fears for his own life."

Ibn Khuwayzimandad said: "As for obedience to the ruler, it is obligatory in what contains obedience, and it is not obligatory in what contains disobedience. For this reason we have said that the commanders of our time are not to be obeyed, nor assisted, nor honoured; yet it is obligatory to campaign (ghazw) with them whenever they campaign, and the judgments issued on their behalf, and the appointment to the imamate and to hisba (the office of enjoining good and forbidding evil), and the establishment of these things in accordance with the Sharia. If they lead us in prayer, and they are sinful wrongdoers (fasaqa) because of their sins, the prayer behind them is valid; but if they are innovators (mubtadi'a), the prayer behind them is not valid, unless one fears them, in which case one prays with them out of caution (taqiyya), and then repeats the prayer afterwards." That ends the citation.

Some scholars used this verse to refute those who say: "There must be an infallible imam (imam ma'sum)." For the commanders and jurists are liable to error and forgetfulness, and yet we have been commanded to obey them. Infallibility is a condition of the imam, so this cannot apply to him. And it is not possible that the intended meaning is the imam, because He said in the continuation of the address: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾. Had there been an imam whose obedience was obligatory, referral to him would have been obligatory, and he would have resolved the dispute. Since He commanded that the matter in dispute be referred to the Book and the Sunna and not to an imam, this indicates the invalidity of the imamate. As for their interpretation that ulu al-amr means Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, it is invalid, because ulu al-amr is a plural, whereas Ali is singular. The people were commanded to obey ulu al-amr during the lifetime of the Messenger (ﷺ), and Ali was not an imam during his lifetime; so it is established that they were commanders.

Obedience to them is due from those under their authority as long as they do not command disobedience. Likewise, after their deaths, it remains binding to follow them in obedience as long as it is not disobedience. Abu Abd Allah al-Razi said: "﴿and those in authority among you﴾ is a reference to consensus (ijma'). The proof of this is that He commanded obedience to those in authority absolutely and decisively in this verse; and whoever is commanded to be obeyed absolutely and decisively must necessarily be protected from error, for otherwise, if he committed an error, he would be commanded to be followed while error is forbidden, which would lead to the combination of command and prohibition in a single act in one respect, and that is impossible. No one after the Messenger is protected from error except the community as a whole, the people who loose and bind (ahl al-aqd wa al-hall); and the consequence of this is that the consensus of the community is a proof (hujja)."

﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾. Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-A'mash and Maymun ibn Mihran said: "Refer it to the Book of Allah and to consulting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during his lifetime, and to his Sunna after his death." A group, including al-Asamm, said: "Its meaning is: say, 'Allah and His Messenger know best.'" Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you and those in authority among you differ over any matter of the religion, then refer it, that is, return to the Book and the Sunna," and that ends the citation. Those who deny analogy (qiyas) and those who affirm it have both used the words ﴿refer it to Allah and His Messenger﴾ as evidence, and this is a question discussed in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

﴿If you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ is a conditional clause (shart), and its response (jawab) is omitted; that is, ﴿refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾. It is a conditional intended to urge the following of truth, because He had first addressed them with ﴿O you who have believed﴾; so it is like saying: "If you are my son, obey me." It also implies a warning against whoever does not refer the matter to Allah and the Messenger.

﴿That is better and more favourable in outcome﴾. That referral is to the Book and the Sunna, or to saying: "Allah and His Messenger know best." Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: "Better in outcome (ahsan 'aqiba)." Mujahid said: "Better in reward (ahsan jaza')." It was said: "Better in interpretation (ahsan ta'wil) than your own interpretation." A group said: "The meaning is that Allah and His Messenger have a better view and a better interpretation than you when you act on your own interpretation alone."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 60–63:

﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, yet they desire to take their disputes for judgment to the false deity (al-taghut), though they were commanded to reject it? And Satan wishes to lead them far astray.﴾ Regarding the occasion of its revelation, a lengthy account is related, summarized as follows: Abu Burda al-Aslami was a soothsayer (kahin) who judged between the Jews. A group from Aslam disputed before him, or Qays al-Ansari, one of those who claimed to be Muslim, and a Jewish man appealed to the soothsayer. They left the Messenger ﷺ after the Jew had invited them to the Messenger, while the Ansari refused except for the soothsayer. Or a hypocrite and a Jew disputed. The Jew chose the Messenger ﷺ, and the hypocrite chose Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. The Jew refused, and they went to the Messenger, who ruled in favour of the Jew. They left, but the hypocrite followed him and said: "Let us go to Umar." They went to him, and the Jew said: "We have taken our dispute to the Messenger ﷺ, but he did not accept his judgment." The hypocrite admitted this before Umar, so Umar killed him and said: "This is how I judge for the one who does not accept the judgment of Allah and His Messenger."

The connection of this verse with what precedes it (p-280) is clear, because when He, exalted is He, commanded the believers to obey Allah, His Messenger, and those in authority (ulu al-amr), He mentioned that He marvels, after this command has come, at the state of those who claim faith and desire to take their disputes to the false deity and abandon the Messenger. The apparent meaning of the verse requires that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, because He said: "They claim that they believed in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you." If it were concerning Jews, or a believer and a Jew, this would be remote from the wording of the verse, unless it is taken distributively, so that "what was revealed to you" refers to a hypocrite, and "what was revealed before you" refers to a Jew, and both are included in the pronoun of "they claim," in which case it is possible. As-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites of Quraydhah and an-Nadir, who boasted because of the equality of their blood-money, for an-Nadir in the Jahiliyyah used to pay blood-money for whomever they killed, while Quraydhah paid half of it to them if they killed one of theirs. When Islam came, Quraydhah refused, and they sought arbitration. The believers among them invited them to the Prophet ﷺ, while the hypocrites invited them to Burda the soothsayer, so it was revealed. Al-Hasan said: the hypocrites sought judgment by the arrow-shafts used for divination at the idols, so it was revealed. Or, because of their disagreement concerning the occasions of revelation, they differed concerning the false deity. It was said: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. It was said: the idols. It was said: whatever is worshipped besides Allah. It was said: the soothsayers.

* *

﴿And they were commanded to reject it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) referring back to His words "they desire." And "they desire" is itself a circumstantial clause (hal), so this is an interlocking circumstantial construction (hal mutadakhila). Here the pronoun is returned in the masculine, while in His words ﴿They avoid the false deity, lest they worship it﴾ [az-Zumar: 17] it is returned in the feminine. Abbas ibn al-Fadl recited it here in the feminine, and returned the pronoun like the pronoun for a plural of rational beings in His words ﴿Their protectors are the false deities; they bring them out﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257].

﴿And Satan wishes to lead them far astray﴾: the word "dalal" (straying) does not follow the verb "yudilla-hum" in the same derivational pattern. It may be that it was used in place of "idlal" (leading astray), or it may be the verbal noun (masdar) of the intransitive form corresponding to "yudilla-hum," meaning "so they stray far astray." The majority recited "bima unzila ilayka" and "wa ma unzila" with the passive voice in both. It was also recited with the active voice in both.

﴿And when it is said to them: "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾: Al-Hasan recited "ta'aluu" with a dammah on the lam. Abu al-Fath said: its basis is that the final radical of the verb from ta'alayta was deleted for lightness, and the lam which is the middle radical of the verb was given a dammah because the plural wa'w came after it. Az-Zamakhshari compared the deletion of the final radical here with its deletion in their saying "ma balaytu bihi balata" (I did not care about it at all), whose original form is "baliyatun," like "afiyatun." He likened it to the view of al-Kisa'i regarding "ayah" (sign), whose original form is "aylah," with the lam deleted. He said: from this is the saying of the people of Makkah: "Ta'ali" with a kasra on the lam addressed to a woman. In the poetry of al-Hamdani:

"Ta'ali, uqasimuki al-humuma ta'ali"
("Come, let me share my worries with you, come")

The correct form is fatha on the lam. He concluded. As for az-Zamakhshari's statement that the saying of the people of Makkah "ta'ali" may be ancient Arabic, and may be something changed from its Arabic form and so not Arabic, and as for his quoted poem of al-Hamdani, some have stated that it belongs to Abu Firas. I examined his Diwan, collected by al-Husayn ibn Khalawayh, and did not find it in there. The Banu Hamdan are many, and among them are several poets. Even if this is proven to be in their poetry, there is no proof in it, because one does not cite the speech of the later (muwallad) poets as evidence. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿you see the hypocrites﴾ is that it is from sight with the eye, that they turned away openly and explicitly. It may also be from sight of the heart, meaning "known," and their turning away would then be deception, cunning and secret stealth, so that it would be known only through interpretation of it. "Sududa" is a verbal noun of "sadda," and here it is transitive with a prepositional particle, though it may be transitive without one, as in His words ﴿and He turned them away from the path﴾ [an-Naml: 24]. The regular verbal noun of "sadda" in the pattern "fa'ala" is "sadda-hu sadda." Ibn Atiyya related that "sududa" here is not a verbal noun, and that the verbal noun in his view is "sadd."

﴿So how will it be when a disaster befalls them because of what their hands have sent forward, then they come to you swearing by Allah: "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation"?﴾ Az-Zajjaj said: "kayfa" is in a position of accusative (nasb), its estimated form being "how do you see them," or in a position of nominative (raf'), meaning "so how is their conduct, and the disaster." Az-Zajjaj said: Umar was killed, the one who rejected the judgment of the Messenger ﷺ. It was also said: every disaster that befalls the hypocrites in this world and the Hereafter. Then the speech returns to what preceded, informing about their action, and He said: ﴿Then they come to you swearing by Allah﴾. It was also said: it refers to the demolition of the Masjid adh-Dirar, and the verse was revealed concerning it. They swore in defence of themselves that they intended by building the mosque nothing but obedience and agreement with the Book. It was also said: (it refers to) abandoning seeking help from them, and the humiliation that would befall them from His words ﴿Say: "You will never go out with me, and you will never fight an enemy with me"﴾ [at-Tawbah: 83]. "What their hands have sent forward" refers to their rejection of the Messenger's judgment, or their previous disobediences, or their hypocrisy and mockery: three opinions. It was also said regarding His words ﴿except good and reconciliation﴾: that is, what we intended by demanding the blood of our companion whom Umar killed was nothing but good toward us, and what agrees with the truth in our matter. It was said: what we intended by appealing to Umar was nothing but good toward our companion through a just judgment, and reconciliation between him and his opponent. It was said: they came apologising to the Messenger ﷺ for their submitting their dispute to someone else: "In our turning away from you we intended nothing but good, by bringing judgment closer, and reconciliation between the opponents, without compelling them toward the truth." In His words ﴿So how will it be when a disaster befalls them﴾ there is a warning to them for their action, and that they will regret it when the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, descends, when regret will not benefit them and apology will not avail them.

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts. So turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves﴾: that is, He knows the hypocrisy in their hearts. The meaning is: He knows it, and so He will recompense them for it, or He will recompense them for what they concealed of disbelief and what they displayed of false oaths. He expressed recompense by knowledge. "So turn away from them": that is, from rebuking them and occupying the mind with them, and from accepting their faith and their excuses. It was said: the meaning of turning away is treating them with gentleness and forbearance, and in this is a disciplining of them, which is their rebuke. Turning away does not mean boycott and severance, for His words "admonish them" prevent that. "Admonish them": that is, frighten them with the punishment of Allah and restrain them, and denounce them for returning to the like of what they did.

"A far-reaching word" is rebuke and deterrence. Al-Hasan said: it is a threat of killing if they persist in the state of hypocrisy. His words "concerning themselves" connect with "say" according to one of two meanings: that is, say to them, alone with them, with no one else present, in private, because counsel in private is more successful and is more likely to be accepted quickly. The meaning of "balighan" is: effective upon them. Or: say to them, concerning the meaning of their defiled selves that are shrouded in hypocrisy, a word that reaches them so as to restrain them from returning to what they did.

Az-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: with what is the phrase "concerning themselves" connected? I say: with the word "balighan," meaning: say to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves, effective upon their hearts, causing them to be deeply distressed, and to feel fear, namely a threat of killing and annihilation if hypocrisy emerges among them and raises its head, and informing them that what is in their souls of corruption and hypocrisy is known to Allah, and that there is no difference between you and the polytheists. This restraint is only for your display of faith and your concealment and hiding of disbelief. If you do what would expose your covering, nothing will remain but the sword. He concluded his words. Connecting "concerning themselves" to "far-reaching" is not permissible according to the school of the Basrans, because the complement of an adjective (ma'mul al-sifa) may not precede the modified noun in their view. If you said: "This is a man striking Zayd," it would not be permissible to say: "This Zayd is a man striking," because the complement must only occur in a position where its governing element occurs, and it is well known that an attribute does not precede the noun it describes, since it is a follower (tabi'), and the follower in this matter is according to the school of the Kufans. As for what az-Zamakhshari said after this, of lengthy discourse, it is a kind of oratory, and the imposing upon the wording of the Qur'an what it cannot bear, and attributing to Allah, exalted is He, what He did not say. That is his habit in his tafsir, which is the multiplication of words and the attribution of things to Allah, exalted is He, that Allah did not say, and that the wording does not indicate clearly. Tafsir (exegesis) in reality is only the explanation of a word that is obscure to the hearer, by what is clear to him, through a synonym or near synonym, or through something that indicates it by one of the ways of indication. It is related from Mujahid that His words "concerning themselves" are connected with "a disaster," and that it is placed later in meaning as if earlier. This is an opinion from which Mujahid should be held free, for it is utterly corrupt.

* *
