So turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves﴾: that is, He knows the hypocrisy in their hearts. The meaning is: He knows it, and so He will recompense them for it, or He will recompense them for what they concealed of disbelief and what they displayed of false oaths. He expressed recompense by knowledge. "So turn away from them": that is, from rebuking them and occupying the mind with them, and from accepting their faith and their excuses. It was said: the meaning of turning away is treating them with gentleness and forbearance, and in this is a disciplining of them, which is their rebuke. Turning away does not mean boycott and severance, for His words "admonish them" prevent that. "Admonish them": that is, frighten them with the punishment of Allah and restrain them, and denounce them for returning to the like of what they did.

"A far-reaching word" is rebuke and deterrence. Al-Hasan said: it is a threat of killing if they persist in the state of hypocrisy. His words "concerning themselves" connect with "say" according to one of two meanings: that is, say to them, alone with them, with no one else present, in private, because counsel in private is more successful and is more likely to be accepted quickly. The meaning of "balighan" is: effective upon them. Or: say to them, concerning the meaning of their defiled selves that are shrouded in hypocrisy, a word that reaches them so as to restrain them from returning to what they did.

Az-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: with what is the phrase "concerning themselves" connected? I say: with the word "balighan," meaning: say to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves, effective upon their hearts, causing them to be deeply distressed, and to feel fear, namely a threat of killing and annihilation if hypocrisy emerges among them and raises its head, and informing them that what is in their souls of corruption and hypocrisy is known to Allah, and that there is no difference between you and the polytheists. This restraint is only for your display of faith and your concealment and hiding of disbelief. If you do what would expose your covering, nothing will remain but the sword. He concluded his words. Connecting "concerning themselves" to "far-reaching" is not permissible according to the school of the Basrans, because the complement of an adjective (ma'mul al-sifa) may not precede the modified noun in their view. If you said: "This is a man striking Zayd," it would not be permissible to say: "This Zayd is a man striking," because the complement must only occur in a position where its governing element occurs, and it is well known that an attribute does not precede the noun it describes, since it is a follower (tabi'), and the follower in this matter is according to the school of the Kufans. As for what az-Zamakhshari said after this, of lengthy discourse, it is a kind of oratory, and the imposing upon the wording of the Qur'an what it cannot bear, and attributing to Allah, exalted is He, what He did not say. That is his habit in his tafsir, which is the multiplication of words and the attribution of things to Allah, exalted is He, that Allah did not say, and that the wording does not indicate clearly. Tafsir (exegesis) in reality is only the explanation of a word that is obscure to the hearer, by what is clear to him, through a synonym or near synonym, or through something that indicates it by one of the ways of indication. It is related from Mujahid that His words "concerning themselves" are connected with "a disaster," and that it is placed later in meaning as if earlier. This is an opinion from which Mujahid should be held free, for it is utterly corrupt.

* *

﴿We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah's permission.﴾ He, exalted is He, drew attention to the greatness of the messengers, and that all creation is obliged to obey them, and that the messenger among them must be obeyed. The lam in ﴿li-yuta'a﴾ is the lam of purpose (lam kay), and the construction is an exception of the restricted type (istithna' mufarragh) in the position of the object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). The meaning is: We did not send any messenger with anything except for the purpose of obedience. "By Allah's permission" means by His command, as Ibn 'Abbas said, or by His knowledge, His enabling and His guidance. The real meaning of permission (idhn) is enablement together with knowledge of the extent to which one is enabled. The apparent view is that ﴿by Allah's permission﴾ is connected to ﴿to be obeyed﴾. It has also been said that it is connected to ﴿We sent﴾, meaning: We did not send any messenger by Allah's command, that is, by His law, His religion and His worship, except to be obeyed. Ibn 'Atiyya said: On both interpretations the wording is general but the meaning is specific, because we are certain that Allah, blessed and exalted is He, willed that some of His creatures not obey Him. For this reason a group interpreted permission as knowledge, and another group interpreted it as guidance for some people rather than others, and this is a good interpretation, because when Allah knows that someone will believe, He enables him to do so, and so it is as if He has permitted him. End of quote.

What he mentioned, that the speech is general in wording but specific in meaning, does not necessarily follow, because His saying ﴿li-yuta'a﴾ is in the passive form whose subject is not named, and it does not follow from the deleted agent that it must be general. So the implied meaning is: ﴿so that the world would obey him﴾. Rather, the deleted agent should be specific to match what exists, so the original would be: ﴿except that those whom We wished to obey him should obey him.﴾ 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: The verse indicates that there is no messenger except that he has with him a law, so that he may be obeyed and followed in that law. For if he only called to the law of someone before him, he would not in reality be obeyed; rather, the one obeyed would be the earlier messenger who originated that law. Allah, exalted is He, has ruled concerning every messenger that he is obeyed. End of quote. I do not like his phrase "the one who originated that law." The better wording is: "the one who brought that law from Allah."

* *

﴿If they, when they wronged themselves, had come to you and asked Allah's forgiveness, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance, Merciful.﴾ They wronged themselves by their resentment of your judgment, or by seeking judgment from the false deity (taghut), or by all the sins that proceeded from them. "Came to you and asked Allah's forgiveness" means with sincerity, and apologized to you. "The Messenger asked forgiveness for them" means the Messenger interceded for them in the forgiveness of their sins. The word "idh" (when) is governed by ﴿came to you﴾, and there is a shift (iltifat) in the phrase ﴿and the Messenger asked forgiveness for them﴾. The pronoun of address was not used in ﴿came to you﴾, to magnify the status of the Messenger and to glorify his asking forgiveness, and to draw attention to the fact that the intercession of one whose name is "the Messenger" has a station with Allah, exalted is He, and that this noble attribute, namely that Allah sent him, requires obedience to him, and that he is included in the generality of His saying: ﴿We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah's permission.﴾ The meaning of "they would have found" is "they would have known," that is, by his informing them that He accepted their repentance and had mercy on them.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said, in summary: The benefit of joining the Messenger's asking forgiveness to their own asking forgiveness is that, by seeking judgment from the false deity, they opposed the judgment of Allah and harmed the Messenger (ﷺ), so it was obligatory for them to apologize and to ask the Messenger to seek forgiveness. Or, since they did not accept the judgment of the Messenger, rebellion appeared from them; so when they repent, it is necessary that what removes the rebellion appear from them, by going to the Messenger and asking him to seek forgiveness. Or, if they repent by repentance, they performed it in a flawed manner, so when the Messenger's (ﷺ) asking forgiveness is added to it, it becomes deserving. The verse indicates the acceptance of the repentance of one who repents, because He said after it: ﴿they would have found Allah﴾, and this does not apply to that statement unless the meaning of ﴿Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾ is the acceptance of his repentance. End of quote.

It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, that he said: After we had buried the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) three days, a Bedouin arrived and threw himself upon his grave, and poured some of its dust upon his head, then said:

Best of those buried in the earth, whose bones are within it, so that the plain and the hills are made fragrant by their fragrance.

My soul is the ransom for a grave in which you dwell, wherein is chastity, and wherein are generosity and nobility.

Then he said: You have spoken, O Messenger of Allah, and we heard your words; you received from Allah and we received from you. Among what Allah revealed to you is ﴿If they, when they wronged themselves, had come to you﴾ to the end of the verse. I have wronged myself and have come to ask Allah's forgiveness for my sin, so ask forgiveness for me from my Lord. Then a voice was heard from the grave saying: Indeed, you have been forgiven.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 65–66:

﴿So no, by your Lord, they will not truly believe until they make you judge in what is in dispute between them﴾. Mujahid and others said: it was revealed concerning those who wished to seek judgment from the taghut (false judge). Al-Tabari preferred this view, because it better fits the context (nasaq) of the verses. It was also said that it concerns the man who disputed with al-Zubayr over irrigation with the water of al-Harrah, and that the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Irrigate, O Zubayr, then send the water on to your neighbour." The man became angry and said: "Because he is the son of your paternal aunt?" The Messenger (ﷺ) became angry and gave al-Zubayr his full right, saying: "Hold back the water, O Zubayr, until it reaches the walls (al-jadr), then release the water." The man was one of the Ansar and a veteran of Badr (badri). (p-284) It was also said that it concerns him and Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah. It was also said that it was revealed negating the faith of the man whom Umar killed, because he rejected the judgment of the Prophet (ﷺ), and affirming Umar's excuse for killing him, since the Prophet said: "I did not think that Umar would dare to kill a believing man."

He swore by attributing the Lord to the second-person pronoun (kaf al-khitab), as a sign of honour for the Prophet (ﷺ). This is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person) referring back to His words "they came to you" (jaa'uka).

[The word] "la" in His words "fa-la" [is also discussed]. Al-Tabari said: it is a rejoinder to what was previously implied, meaning: "The matter is not as they claim, that they believe in what was revealed to you," and then He began the oath with His words: "by your Lord, they will not believe." Others said: He placed la before the oath for emphasis on the negation, then repeated it afterward to emphasise that concern for the negation. It would be correct to drop the second la and the greater part of the emphasis would remain with the first; and it would be correct to drop the first and the meaning of negation would remain, but the sense of emphasis would be lost. It was also said that the second la is superfluous (za'idah) and the oath is interposed between the negative particle and what is negated. Al-Zamakhshari said: la is superfluous, to reinforce the meaning of the oath, just as it is added in His words "that they may not know" (Al-Hadid: 29), to reinforce the obligation of knowledge. "They will not believe" is the answer (jawab) to the oath. (If you say): why not claim that it was added in order to support the la in "they will not believe"? (I say): the equal standing of negation and affirmation in it prevents this; and this is seen in His words: "So I swear by what you see and what you do not see, that it is the word of a noble Messenger" (Al-Haqqah: 38). End of his words. Similar to the verse is the poet's saying:

"No, by God, it will never be found as a remedy for what is in me, nor for what is in them."

Here "hatta" (until) marks a limit (ghayah): that is, faith is negated of them up to this limit; so when what follows the limit occurs, they will be believers. "Fima shajara baynahum" is general, covering every matter over which dispute and contention arise between them. The meaning of "yuhakkimukum" is "make you an arbiter (hakam)." In the speech there is an omitted implied element: "so that you judge between them."

﴿Then they will find within themselves no discomfort (haraj) regarding what you have decided, and they will submit with full submission﴾; that is, no constriction against your judgment. Mujahid said: doubt, because the doubter is in constriction about his matter until clarity appears to him. Al-Dahhak said: sin, that is, a cause of sin. The meaning is: there does not occur to their minds what would make them sinful through not being content. It was also said: grief and sorrow. "Wa-yusallimu" means: they yield and submit to your decree, not opposing it in anything; this was said by Ibn Abbas and the majority. It was also said that the meaning is: "they submit what they disputed to your judgment," reported by al-Mawardi. He reinforced the verb with a verbal noun (masdar) to indicate the genuine occurrence of submission; and its being a fasilah (rhyme-closing unit) made it good.

Abu al-Sammal read "fima shajra" with a sukun on the jim, and it seems he avoided a succession of vowels; but this is not strong, because the fatha is light, unlike the damma and kasra; the sukun in place of them is regular in the dialect of Tamim.

﴿And if We had prescribed for them: "Kill yourselves" or "Leave your homes," they would not have done it, except a few of them﴾. The Jews said, when the hypocrite did not accept the Messenger's judgment: "We have never seen anything more foolish than these people, who do not believe in Muhammad yet follow him and walk in his footsteps, then do not accept his judgment; while we were commanded to kill ourselves and we did so, and the killing among us reached seventy thousand." Then Thabit ibn Qays said: "If that had been prescribed for us, we would have done it," and so it was revealed. This cause (sabab) is reported in varying wording, but the meaning is close.

The meaning of the verse: that if He, exalted is He, had imposed upon them that they kill themselves, either by each slaying himself with his own hand, or by some killing others, or that they leave their homes, as He imposed that upon the Children of Israel when they were required to repent of worshipping the calf, only a few of them obeyed; and this carries a great rebuke, since only a few comply with God's command. Al-Sab'i said: when it was revealed, a man said: "If He had commanded us, we would have done it, and praise be to God who has spared us." This reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: "Among my community are men whose faith is firmer in their hearts than the towering mountains." Ibn Wahb said: the man who said that was Abu Bakr. It is also reported from him that he said: "If that had been prescribed for us, I would have begun with myself and the people of my household." al-Naqqash mentioned that it was Umar. Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi mentioned that the speaker among them was Ammar, Ibn Mas'ud, and Thabit ibn Qays.

The pronoun in "alayhim" is said to refer to the hypocrites; that is, only a few of them did it out of showing off and reputation, and at that point the matter becomes difficult for them and their disbelief is exposed. It was also said that it refers to the people in general, both believers and hypocrites. Abu 'Amr read the nun of "an" with a kasra and the waw of "aw" with a damma; Hamzah and 'Asim read both with a kasra; the rest of the seven read both with a damma. "An" here may be explanatory (tafsiriyyah), or it may be verbal (masdariyyah), according to their stipulation that "an" is connected to the imperative verb.

The verse is evidence of the difficulty of leaving one's homes, since God linked it with killing oneself. The Companions who emigrated left their homes and parted from their families when God commanded them to migrate. "Qalil" is in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for the waw in "fa'aluhu" according to the Basran school, and as a conjunct upon the pronoun according to the Kufan view; the majority read it in the nominative. Ubayy, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn 'Amir and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "illa qalilan" in the accusative. The grammarians stated that the preferred way in such a construction is to make what follows "illa" agree with what precedes it in case, in the manner of substitution or conjunction, according to the two views we have mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "illa qalilan" was also read in the accusative according to the basic (istithna') construction, or as "illa fi'lan qalilan" (except a little action). The basic exceptive accusative is what people have given as the basis for this reading. As for his statement "as illa fi'lan qalilan," it is weak, since the interpretation contradicts the reading in the nominative, and because of His words "from them"; for on this construction, if you say: "They did not strike Zayd except a little striking from them," it would not be good for "from them" to be attached to it, and its mention would serve no purpose. The accusative pronoun in "fa'aluhu" refers to one of the two verbal nouns implied in "an uqtulu" and "awi-khruju." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the reference in "ma fa'aluhu" is to killing and leaving together, because the act is one genus, even if its form differs. That is his statement, and it is not grammatical speech.

﴿And if they had done what they were admonished with, it would have been better for them and firmer in establishing them﴾. The pronoun in "wa-law annahum" is specific to the hypocrites, and it is not far-fetched that the beginning of the verse is general and its end specific. Al-Zamakhshari said: "what they are admonished with" means following the Messenger of God (ﷺ), obeying him, and submitting to what he sees and to his judgment, because he is the truthful, the trusted, who does not speak from desire; it would have been better for them in this world and the next, and firmer for their faith, and further from wavering in it.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "If these hypocrites had taken heed and turned back in repentance, it would have been better for them, and firmer (tathbit), meaning certainty and confirmation." Both of them explained "what they are admonished with" in a way contrary to what the apparent sense indicates, because what they are admonished with is not the following and obeying of the Messenger, and the meaning of what they are admonished with is not "they took heed and repented." It was said that "wa'z" here means command; that is, if they had done what they are commanded and refrained from what they are forbidden. In Ray al-Zam'an it says: "what they are admonished with," that is, what they are enjoined and commanded with of sincerity and submission. Al-Raghib said: He informed that if they had accepted the admonition it would have been better for them. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the intended meaning is that if they had done what they were charged with and commanded, and this charge and command was called admonition because God's obligations are coupled with promise and threat, desire and fear, reward and punishment, and whatever is like that is called admonition. Al-Maturidi said: it was also said that "what they are admonished with" is the command from the Qur'an.

All these are interpretations that contradict the apparent sense; because admonition is the reminder of what befalls one who opposes God's command of punishment; so the thing admonished with is the sentences indicating that, and it is not possible to carry it on this apparent sense, since they were not commanded to do the thing admonished with. Rather, the explanation of that came to them through what contradicts the apparent sense, because they attached the "ma yu'azuna" to "bihi," in the manner of what is understood from your saying "I admonished you with such-and-such," so the "ba'" enters upon the thing admonished with, namely the sentence that indicates the admonition. But if the meaning is that the "ba'" is causal (sababiyyah), then the wording is taken according to its apparent sense, the meaning holds, and the estimate is: "And if they had done the thing because of which they are admonished, that is, because of abandoning it." The mention of "wa-law annahum fa'aluu" indicates the omitted abandoning, and the word "yu'azuna" remains in its apparent sense, without needing what they have interpreted.

﴿It would have been better for them﴾; that is, they would obtain the good of both abodes, so it is not the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil). It is possible that it is the comparative; that is, it would have been more beneficial for them than otherwise. "And firmer in establishing them," because it is truth, so it is more lasting and more firmly established; or because obedience calls to its like; or because a person first seeks to attain good, and when he has attained it, he seeks its continuance. So His words "it would have been better for them" indicate the first state, and His words "and firmer in establishing them" indicate the second state; this was said by Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "what they are admonished with" means following the Messenger of God (ﷺ), obeying him, and submitting to what he sees and to his judgment, because he is the truthful, the trusted, who does not speak from desire; it would have been better for them in this world and the next, and firmer for their faith, and further from wavering in it.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "If these hypocrites had taken heed and turned back in repentance, it would have been better for them, and firmer (tathbit), meaning certainty and confirmation." Both of them explained "what they are admonished with" in a way contrary to what the apparent sense indicates, because what they are admonished with is not the following and obeying of the Messenger, and the meaning of what they are admonished with is not "they took heed and repented." It was said that "wa'z" here means command; that is, if they had done what they are commanded and refrained from what they are forbidden. In Ray al-Zam'an it says: "what they are admonished with," that is, what they are enjoined and commanded with of sincerity and submission. Al-Raghib said: He informed that if they had accepted the admonition it would have been better for them. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the intended meaning is that if they had done what they were charged with and commanded, and this charge and command was called admonition because God's obligations are coupled with promise and threat, desire and fear, reward and punishment, and whatever is like that is called admonition. Al-Maturidi said: it was also said that "what they are admonished with" is the command from the Qur'an.

All these are interpretations that contradict the apparent sense; because admonition is the reminder of what befalls one who opposes God's command of punishment; so the thing admonished with is the sentences indicating that, and it is not possible to carry it on this apparent sense, since they were not commanded to do the thing admonished with. Rather, the explanation of that came to them through what contradicts the apparent sense, because they attached the "ma yu'azuna" to "bihi," in the manner of what is understood from your saying "I admonished you with such-and-such," so the "ba'" enters upon the thing admonished with, namely the sentence that indicates the admonition. But if the meaning is that the "ba'" is causal (sababiyyah), then the wording is taken according to its apparent sense, the meaning holds, and the estimate is: "And if they had done the thing because of which they are admonished, that is, because of abandoning it." The mention of "wa-law annahum fa'aluu" indicates the omitted abandoning, and the word "yu'azuna" remains in its apparent sense, without needing what they have interpreted.

﴿It would have been better for them﴾; that is, they would obtain the good of both abodes, so it is not the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil). It is possible that it is the comparative; that is, it would have been more beneficial for them than otherwise. "And firmer in establishing them," because it is truth, so it is more lasting and more firmly established; or because obedience calls to its like; or because a person first seeks to attain good, and when he has attained it, he seeks its continuance. So His words "it would have been better for them" indicate the first state, and His words "and firmer in establishing them" indicate the second state; this was said by Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 67–70 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And then We would surely give them from Us a great reward, and We would surely guide them to a straight path.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Idhan* (then) is a response to an implied question, as if it had been said: 'And what would they have besides, after being made firm?' So it is said: 'And *idhan*, if they had remained firm, We would have given them,' because *idhan* is a response (*jawab*) and a conditional consequence (*jaza'*)." End of quotation.

The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words, "because *idhan* is a response and a conditional consequence," implies that it carries both meanings simultaneously in every case. This is a point of scholarly disagreement. Al-Farisi (Abu Ali al-Farisi) held that it may be a response only in one position, and both a response and a conditional consequence in a negative context. For example, in *idhan azunnuka sadiqan* ("then I think you are truthful") said to someone who says "I will visit you," it is purely a response. In *idhan ukrimuka* ("then I will honour you") said to someone who says "I will visit you," it is both a response and a consequence. Al-Ustadh Abu Ali held that it is always to be understood as both a response and a consequence in every position, adhering to the apparent wording of Sibawayh. The correct view is that of al-Farisi. This is a question discussed in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*).

"Reward" (*ajr*) is a metaphor for the recompense for obedience. Describing it as "great" (*'azim*) is either in terms of its abundance or in terms of its nobility. "The straight path" (*al-sirat al-mustaqim*) is faith that leads to Paradise; this was said by Ibn Atiyya. It was also said that it is the way to Paradise, and that it is righteous deeds. When Ibn Atiyya explained the straight path as faith, he said: "The arrangement of this verse is as it is." It is known that guidance precedes the giving of the reward, because the purpose is to enumerate what Allah bestowed upon them, without regard to order. Thus the meaning is: "And We had guided them before, so that they would be among those who are given the reward." End of Ibn Atiyya's words. However, if the guidance to the path here is interpreted as the way to Paradise or as righteous deeds, then the order becomes apparent.

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour: of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: "It was revealed concerning Thawban, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who loved the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intensely. One day he came to him, his complexion had changed and his body had become emaciated. He said: 'O Thawban, what has changed your colour?' He replied: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have no illness and no pain, except that when I do not see you, I long for you and feel a severe loneliness until I meet you. Then I remember the Hereafter, and I fear that I will not see you there, because I know that you will be raised with the prophets, and even if I enter Paradise, I would be in a station lower than yours, and if I do not enter Paradise, then that is the time when I will never see you.'" End of al-Kalbi's words.

Similar words to Thawban's were related from a group of the Companions, among them "Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Abd Rabbih al-Ansari, the one who was shown the call to prayer (*adhan*), who said: 'O Messenger of Allah, when you die and we die, you will be in the highest ranks (*'Illiyyin*), so we will not see you nor gather with you.' He mentioned his sorrow over this, and so it was revealed." Makki related from this Abdullah that when the Prophet ﷺ died, he said: "O Allah, make me blind so that I see nothing after him," and he became blind.

The meaning of "with" (*ma'a*) in "with the prophets" is that they are together in one abode, and everyone in it is granted contentment with his state, and they are in such a position that each of them can see the others, even if their places are far apart. It was also said that companionship here means that they are raised to the dwellings of the prophets whenever they wish, as an honour for them, and then they return to their own dwellings. It was also said that the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs descend to those below them so that they may discuss the blessings of Allah; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi in his large commentary. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "This verse points to two matters of the states of the Return: the first is the illumination of the spirits by the lights of knowledge; the second is their being with the prophets. This companionship is not meant in terms of rank, for that is impossible; rather its meaning is that imperfect spirits, when they have perfected their attachments together with perfect spirits in this world, those attachments remain after separation. Thus the light of some is reflected upon others, and their lights become extremely strong. This is what occurred to me." End of his words. This resembles what the philosophers said about spirits when they separate from bodies. The people of Islam reject these expressions and their implications, but whoever is overcome by something and loves it, it runs through his speech.

His words "with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour" are an explanation of His words: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7], and they are those mentioned in this verse. The apparent meaning is that His words "of the prophets" explain "those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour." It is as if it were said: "Whoever among you obeys Allah and His Messenger, Allah will join him with those who preceded him from among those upon whom He bestowed favour." Al-Raghib said: "Among the four groups upon whom He bestowed favour, in rank and reward: the prophet with the prophet, the truthful with the truthful, the martyr with the martyr, and the righteous with the righteous." Al-Raghib also permitted that "of the prophets" be connected to His words "whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger," meaning "of the prophets and those after them," and that His words "those are with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour" be an allusion to the Highest Assembly. Then he said: ﴿and excellent are those as companions﴾. This is confirmed by the Prophet's words at death: "O Allah, join me with the Highest Companion." This is clear, he said. End of his words.

But this view, which he considers clear, is corrupt in terms of meaning and in terms of grammar. As for its meaning: the Messenger here is Muhammad ﷺ. Allah informs that whoever obeys Him and obeys His Messenger is with those mentioned. If "of the prophets" were connected to "whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger," then "of the prophets" would be an explanation of "whoever" in "whoever obeys." It would then follow that there would be prophets in the time of the Messenger or after him who obey him, and this is impossible, because Allah has stated that Muhammad is the Seal of the Prophets. And he himself said: "There is no prophet after me."

As for grammar: what precedes the response *fa'* (the particle of consequence) does not govern what follows it. If you say: "If Hind rises, then Amr is going, laughing," it is not permissible.

The scholars differed concerning the three attributes that come after "the prophets." Some said that they are all attributes of one described entity, and they are overlapping attributes, for it is not impossible for one person to be truthful, a martyr and righteous. It was also said that each attribute refers to a category of people. As for "truthful" (*siddiq*), it is an intensive form (*fi'il*) of hyperbole, like *shirrib* (a great drinker); it was said that it means one who speaks truth abundantly, and it was said that it means one who gives charity abundantly. The commentators have several interpretations of it. The first: whoever believes in everything without any doubt entering into it is truthful, based on Allah's words: ﴿Those who believed in Allah and His messengers, those are the truthful﴾ [al-Hadid: 19]. The second: the distinguished companions of the Messenger. The third: the one who was foremost in affirming the Messenger, and thereby became an example for all people.

As for "martyr" (*shahid*): it is one who is killed in the cause of Allah, specially favoured with the honour of this death. The Law distinguishes their ruling regarding the omission of the ritual washing and the funeral prayer, because they are too honoured to be interceded for. The discussion of why they are named martyrs has already been presented, but the word "martyrs" in the verse includes all the kinds of martyrs mentioned by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "It is not permissible for martyrdom to be explained as a person being killed by unbelievers. Rather we say: *shahid* is an intensive form (*fa'il*) in the sense of an active participle (*fa'il*), meaning one who bears witness to the religion of Allah, sometimes by argument and clear proof, and sometimes by the sword and the spear. So the martyrs are those who uphold justice, and they are those whom Allah mentioned in His words: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]." As for "righteous" (*salih*): it is one who is righteous in his belief and his action. This composition according to this view comes in accordance with the descent from the highest to the lower, and then to what is lower than that. In this there is encouragement for believers to obey Allah and obey His Messenger, since they are promised companionship with the nearest of Allah's servants to Him, and the highest of them in rank with Him.

Al-Raghib said: "Allah divided the believers in this verse into four categories, and gave them four stations, some of which are below others, and He urged all people not to fall short of any one of these stations. The first: the prophets, whom the power of divinity sustains; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing directly from close by. For this reason Allah said: ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12]. The second: the truthful, who compete with the prophets in knowledge; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing directly from afar. It was this that the Commander of the Faithful (Ali) meant when it was said to him: 'Have you seen Allah?' He said: 'I would not worship a thing I had not seen,' and then he said: 'The eyes do not see Him by the witness of sight, but the hearts see Him by the realities of faith.' The third: the martyrs, who know a thing through proofs; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing in a mirror from a near place, like the state of Haritha, when he said: 'It is as if I am looking at the Throne of my Lord.' It was this that the Prophet ﷺ intended when he said: 'Worship Allah as if you see Him.' The fourth: the righteous, who know a thing by following and imitating those firmly grounded in knowledge; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing from afar in a mirror. It was this that the Prophet ﷺ intended by his words: 'Worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you.'" End of his words. This resembles the words of the Sufis.

Ikrimah said: "The prophets are Muhammad, the truthful are Abu Bakr, the martyrs are Umar, Uthman and Ali, and the righteous are the righteous of the community of Muhammad." End of quotation. It should be understood that this is by way of example, and not by way of restriction. The statement "whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger" does not, in its apparent wording, imply sufficiency with a single act of obedience, since the word denoting the attribute suffices, in affirmative contexts, for the occurrence of that named quality once, because hypocrites may enter into it, for they may perform a single act of obedience. Rather, it is taken in a non-literal sense, by interpreting obedience as the performance of all commanded acts and the abandonment of all forbidden acts.

﴿And excellent are those as companions.﴾ "Those" (*ula'ika*) refers to the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. He did not suffice with "companionship" until He made them *rufaqa'* (companions) for them. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, they agree with him and accompany him. The *rafiq* is the companion, named so because one benefits from him (*irtifaq*). On this basis, *rafiqan* may be in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of "those," or as a specificative accusative (*tamyiz*). If it is in the accusative as a specificative, it is possible that it is not transferred; then *min* (from) may be placed before it, and it would be the specified noun. It came in the singular either because *rafiq*, like *khalit* and *sadiq*, is used for the singular, dual and plural with a single form, or because the singular is used in the specificative construction for sufficiency while the plural is meant, and the fact that it is a verse-ending (*fasila*) makes this more appropriate here. It is also possible that it is transferred from the agent, in which case it is not the specified noun, and the implied meaning is: "and excellent is the companion of those," so *min* is not placed before it. It is also permissible that "those" refers to whoever (*man*) "obeys Allah and the Messenger," and it was pluralised in accordance with the meaning of *man*. The aforementioned possibilities for the accusative of *rafiqan* are also permissible.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah 4, verses 67–70 (part 2 of 2):

The majority of readers recited *wa-ḥasuna* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* (وحَسُنَ), which is the original form and the dialect of the Ḥijāz. Abū al-Sammāl recited *wa-ḥasna* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn* (وحَسْنَ), which is the dialect of Tamīm. It is also permissible to read *wa-ḥusnun* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn* and a *ḍamma* on the *ḥā'* (وحُسْنٌ), on the basis of transferring the vowel of the *sīn* to the *ḥā'*; this is the dialect of some of the Banū Qays.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "*Wa-ḥasuna ulā'ika rafīqan* (﴿And how good are those as companions﴾) carries the sense of wonder (ta'ajjub), as if it were said: 'How good are those as companions!' Because it stands independently with the meaning of wonder, it is read *wa-ḥasna* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn*, as the one who wonders says it. [Likewise one says] *wa-ḥasuna al-wajhu wajhuka* (وحَسُنَ الوَجْهُ وجْهُكَ) with *fatḥa* and *ḍamma*, along with the *sukūn*." That is the end of his words.

This is a confusion and a mixing of one school's view with another's. We say: the scholars differed regarding a verb used to express praise and blame. Al-Fārisī and most of the grammarians held that it is permissible to attach it to the category of *ni'ma* and *bi'sa* (the two verbs of praise and blame) only, so that its subject can only be what is the subject of those two. Al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad held that it is permissible to attach it to the category of *ni'ma* and *bi'sa*, so that its subject is treated like their subject; this applies when the sense of wonder does not enter into it. Others held that it is permissible to attach it to the verb of wonder (fi'l al-ta'ajjub), so that it does not operate like *ni'ma* and *bi'sa* in terms of the subject or the rest of their rules; rather, its subject is what would be the object of the verb of wonder, so one says: *la-ḍaraba-tu yadaka* (لَضَرَبْتُ يَدَكَ) and *la-ḍaraba-tu al-yada* (لَضَرَبْتُ اليَدَ). The discussion of these two positions, both affirming and refuting them, is mentioned in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-naḥw). Al-Zamakhsharī did not follow either of these two positions; rather, he mixed and combined them. He took the wonder from the position of al-Akhfash, and took the example *wa-ḥasuna al-wajhu wajhuka* from the position of al-Fārisī. As for his statement, "Because it stands independently with the meaning of wonder, it is read *wa-ḥusnun* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn*, and he mentioned that the one who wonders says *wa-ḥasuna* and *wa-ḥusnun*," this is worthless, because al-Farrā' mentioned that these are dialects of the Arabs; therefore the *sukūn* is not [an indication of wonder], nor is it, together with the transfer, the whole of wonder.

﴿That bounty is from Allah﴾. The apparent meaning is that the reference is to the condition of the obedient among the prophets and those joined with them, because that is what is judged in His saying: ﴿then they are with those whom﴾ [Allah has blessed]. It is as if this were in answer to a question: what causes them to be equal with the prophets in the Hereafter, when the difference between them in this world is clear? So He mentioned that this is by His bounty, not by any obligation upon Him. And although they are equal with them in Paradise, they differ in their ranks.

It has also been said that the reference is to the reward in His saying "a great reward." It has been said that it refers to obedience, and it has been said that it refers to companionship. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the great reward given to the obedient and the companionship of those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour are from Allah, because He bestowed them upon them as a complement to their reward. *Dhālika* (ذَلِكَ) is the subject (mubtada') and *al-faḍl* (الفَضْلُ) is its predicate, and *min Allāh* (مِنَ اللَّهِ) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is also permissible for *al-faḍl* to be a qualifier (ṣifa), with the predicate being *min Allāh*. It is also permissible for both to be predicates, according to the view of those who permit that.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as Knower﴾. When He mentioned obedience and mentioned the recompense of the one who obeys, He used the attribute of knowledge, which includes the recompense; that is, sufficient is He as one who rewards those who obey. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "In it is the meaning of saying: they included the act of Allah and His favour from objection to Him, and they were content with His knowledge of that and of other things; for this reason the *bāʾ* entered upon the name of Allah, the Exalted, to indicate the matter contained in His saying *wa-kafā* (and sufficed)," end of quote. We have already shown the corruption of the view of those who claim that your saying *kafā bi-Zaydin* (كَفى بِزَيْدٍ) means *iktafi bi-Zaydin* (اكْتَفِ بِزَيْدٍ), when commenting on His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Protector, and sufficient is Allah as Helper﴾ [al-Nisā': 45].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "*Wa-kafā bi-Allāhi ʿalīman* (And sufficient is Allah as Knower) of the recompense of the one who obeys Him. Or He intended the distinction of those upon whom He bestowed favour, and their excellence, from Allah, because they acquired it through His enabling and His guidance; and sufficient is Allah as Knower of His servants, so He grants them success according to their circumstances," end of quote. These are the expressions of the Muʿtazila.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 67–70 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And then We would surely give them from Us a great reward, and We would surely guide them to a straight path.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Idhan* (then) is a response to an implied question, as if it had been said: 'And what would they have besides, after being made firm?' The first: whoever believes in everything without any doubt entering into it is truthful, based on Allah's words: ﴿Those who believed in Allah and His messengers, those are the truthful﴾ [al-Hadid: 19]. The second: the distinguished companions of the Messenger. The third: the one who was foremost in affirming the Messenger, and thereby became an example for all people.

As for "martyr" (*shahid*): it is one who is killed in the cause of Allah, specially favoured with the honour of this death. The Law distinguishes their ruling regarding the omission of the ritual washing and the funeral prayer, because they are too honoured to be interceded for. The discussion of why they are named martyrs has already been presented, but the word "martyrs" in the verse includes all the kinds of martyrs mentioned by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "It is not permissible for martyrdom to be explained as a person being killed by unbelievers. Rather we say: *shahid* is an intensive form (*fa'il*) in the sense of an active participle (*fa'il*), meaning one who bears witness to the religion of Allah, sometimes by argument and clear proof, and sometimes by the sword and the spear. So the martyrs are those who uphold justice, and they are those whom Allah mentioned in His words: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]." As for "righteous" (*salih*): it is one who is righteous in his belief and his action. This composition according to this view comes in accordance with the descent from the highest to the lower, and then to what is lower than that. In this there is encouragement for believers to obey Allah and obey His Messenger, since they are promised companionship with the nearest of Allah's servants to Him, and the highest of them in rank with Him.

Al-Raghib said: "Allah divided the believers in this verse into four categories, and gave them four stations, some of which are below others, and He urged all people not to fall short of any one of these stations. The first: the prophets, whom the power of divinity sustains; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing directly from close by. For this reason Allah said: ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12]. The second: the truthful, who compete with the prophets in knowledge; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing directly from afar. It was this that the Commander of the Faithful (Ali) meant when it was said to him: 'Have you seen Allah?' He said: 'I would not worship a thing I had not seen,' and then he said: 'The eyes do not see Him by the witness of sight, but the hearts see Him by the realities of faith.' The third: the martyrs, who know a thing through proofs; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing in a mirror from a near place, like the state of Haritha, when he said: 'It is as if I am looking at the Throne of my Lord.' It was this that the Prophet ﷺ intended when he said: 'Worship Allah as if you see Him.' The fourth: the righteous, who know a thing by following and imitating those firmly grounded in knowledge; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing from afar in a mirror. It was this that the Prophet ﷺ intended by his words: 'Worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you.'" End of his words. This resembles the words of the Sufis.

Ikrimah said: "The prophets are Muhammad, the truthful are Abu Bakr, the martyrs are Umar, Uthman and Ali, and the righteous are the righteous of the community of Muhammad." End of quotation. It should be understood that this is by way of example, and not by way of restriction. The statement "whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger" does not, in its apparent wording, imply sufficiency with a single act of obedience, since the word denoting the attribute suffices, in affirmative contexts, for the occurrence of that named quality once, because hypocrites may enter into it, for they may perform a single act of obedience. Rather, it is taken in a non-literal sense, by interpreting obedience as the performance of all commanded acts and the abandonment of all forbidden acts.

﴿And excellent are those as companions.﴾ "Those" (*ula'ika*) refers to the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. He did not suffice with "companionship" until He made them *rufaqa'* (companions) for them. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, they agree with him and accompany him. The *rafiq* is the companion, named so because one benefits from him (*irtifaq*). On this basis, *rafiqan* may be in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of "those," or as a specificative accusative (*tamyiz*). If it is in the accusative as a specificative, it is possible that it is not transferred; then *min* (from) may be placed before it, and it would be the specified noun. It came in the singular either because *rafiq*, like *khalit* and *sadiq*, is used for the singular, dual and plural with a single form, or because the singular is used in the specificative construction for sufficiency while the plural is meant, and the fact that it is a verse-ending (*fasila*) makes this more appropriate here. It is also possible that it is transferred from the agent, in which case it is not the specified noun, and the implied meaning is: "and excellent is the companion of those," so *min* is not placed before it. It is also permissible that "those" refers to whoever (*man*) "obeys Allah and the Messenger," and it was pluralised in accordance with the meaning of *man*. The aforementioned possibilities for the accusative of *rafiqan* are also permissible.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah 4, verses 67–70 (part 2 of 2):

The majority of readers recited *wa-ḥasuna* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* (وحَسُنَ), which is the original form and the dialect of the Ḥijāz. Abū al-Sammāl recited *wa-ḥasna* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn* (وحَسْنَ), which is the dialect of Tamīm. It is also permissible to read *wa-ḥusnun* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn* and a *ḍamma* on the *ḥā'* (وحُسْنٌ), on the basis of transferring the vowel of the *sīn* to the *ḥā'*; this is the dialect of some of the Banū Qays.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "*Wa-ḥasuna ulā'ika rafīqan* (﴿And how good are those as companions﴾) carries the sense of wonder (ta'ajjub), as if it were said: 'How good are those as companions!' Because it stands independently with the meaning of wonder, it is read *wa-ḥasna* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn*, as the one who wonders says it. [Likewise one says] *wa-ḥasuna al-wajhu wajhuka* (وحَسُنَ الوَجْهُ وجْهُكَ) with *fatḥa* and *ḍamma*, along with the *sukūn*." That is the end of his words.

This is a confusion and a mixing of one school's view with another's. We say: the scholars differed regarding a verb used to express praise and blame. Al-Fārisī and most of the grammarians held that it is permissible to attach it to the category of *ni'ma* and *bi'sa* (the two verbs of praise and blame) only, so that its subject can only be what is the subject of those two. Al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad held that it is permissible to attach it to the category of *ni'ma* and *bi'sa*, so that its subject is treated like their subject; this applies when the sense of wonder does not enter into it. Others held that it is permissible to attach it to the verb of wonder (fi'l al-ta'ajjub), so that it does not operate like *ni'ma* and *bi'sa* in terms of the subject or the rest of their rules; rather, its subject is what would be the object of the verb of wonder, so one says: *la-ḍaraba-tu yadaka* (لَضَرَبْتُ يَدَكَ) and *la-ḍaraba-tu al-yada* (لَضَرَبْتُ اليَدَ). The discussion of these two positions, both affirming and refuting them, is mentioned in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-naḥw). Al-Zamakhsharī did not follow either of these two positions; rather, he mixed and combined them. He took the wonder from the position of al-Akhfash, and took the example *wa-ḥasuna al-wajhu wajhuka* from the position of al-Fārisī. As for his statement, "Because it stands independently with the meaning of wonder, it is read *wa-ḥusnun* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn*, and he mentioned that the one who wonders says *wa-ḥasuna* and *wa-ḥusnun*," this is worthless, because al-Farrā' mentioned that these are dialects of the Arabs; therefore the *sukūn* is not [an indication of wonder], nor is it, together with the transfer, the whole of wonder.

﴿That bounty is from Allah﴾. The apparent meaning is that the reference is to the condition of the obedient among the prophets and those joined with them, because that is what is judged in His saying: ﴿then they are with those whom﴾ [Allah has blessed]. It is as if this were in answer to a question: what causes them to be equal with the prophets in the Hereafter, when the difference between them in this world is clear? So He mentioned that this is by His bounty, not by any obligation upon Him. And although they are equal with them in Paradise, they differ in their ranks.

It has also been said that the reference is to the reward in His saying "a great reward." It has been said that it refers to obedience, and it has been said that it refers to companionship. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the great reward given to the obedient and the companionship of those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour are from Allah, because He bestowed them upon them as a complement to their reward. *Dhālika* (ذَلِكَ) is the subject (mubtada') and *al-faḍl* (الفَضْلُ) is its predicate, and *min Allāh* (مِنَ اللَّهِ) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is also permissible for *al-faḍl* to be a qualifier (ṣifa), with the predicate being *min Allāh*. It is also permissible for both to be predicates, according to the view of those who permit that.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as Knower﴾. When He mentioned obedience and mentioned the recompense of the one who obeys, He used the attribute of knowledge, which includes the recompense; that is, sufficient is He as one who rewards those who obey. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "In it is the meaning of saying: they included the act of Allah and His favour from objection to Him, and they were content with His knowledge of that and of other things; for this reason the *bāʾ* entered upon the name of Allah, the Exalted, to indicate the matter contained in His saying *wa-kafā* (and sufficed)," end of quote. We have already shown the corruption of the view of those who claim that your saying *kafā bi-Zaydin* (كَفى بِزَيْدٍ) means *iktafi bi-Zaydin* (اكْتَفِ بِزَيْدٍ), when commenting on His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Protector, and sufficient is Allah as Helper﴾ [al-Nisā': 45].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "*Wa-kafā bi-Allāhi ʿalīman* (And sufficient is Allah as Knower) of the recompense of the one who obeys Him. Or He intended the distinction of those upon whom He bestowed favour, and their excellence, from Allah, because they acquired it through His enabling and His guidance; and sufficient is Allah as Knower of His servants, so He grants them success according to their circumstances," end of quote. These are the expressions of the Muʿtazila.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 67–70 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And then We would surely give them from Us a great reward, and We would surely guide them to a straight path.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Idhan* (then) is a response to an implied question, as if it had been said: 'And what would they have besides, after being made firm?' So it is said: 'And *idhan*, if they had remained firm, We would have given them,' because *idhan* is a response (*jawab*) and a conditional consequence (*jaza'*)." End of quotation.

The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words, "because *idhan* is a response and a conditional consequence," implies that it carries both meanings simultaneously in every case. This is a point of scholarly disagreement. Al-Farisi (Abu Ali al-Farisi) held that it may be a response only in one position, and both a response and a conditional consequence in a negative context. For example, in *idhan azunnuka sadiqan* ("then I think you are truthful") said to someone who says "I will visit you," it is purely a response. In *idhan ukrimuka* ("then I will honour you") said to someone who says "I will visit you," it is both a response and a consequence. Al-Ustadh Abu Ali held that it is always to be understood as both a response and a consequence in every position, adhering to the apparent wording of Sibawayh. The correct view is that of al-Farisi. This is a question discussed in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*).

"Reward" (*ajr*) is a metaphor for the recompense for obedience. Describing it as "great" (*'azim*) is either in terms of its abundance or in terms of its nobility. "The straight path" (*al-sirat al-mustaqim*) is faith that leads to Paradise; this was said by Ibn Atiyya. It was also said that it is the way to Paradise, and that it is righteous deeds. When Ibn Atiyya explained the straight path as faith, he said: "The arrangement of this verse is as it is." It is known that guidance precedes the giving of the reward, because the purpose is to enumerate what Allah bestowed upon them, without regard to order. Thus the meaning is: "And We had guided them before, so that they would be among those who are given the reward." End of Ibn Atiyya's words. However, if the guidance to the path here is interpreted as the way to Paradise or as righteous deeds, then the order becomes apparent.

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour: of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: "It was revealed concerning Thawban, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who loved the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intensely. One day he came to him, his complexion had changed and his body had become emaciated. He said: 'O Thawban, what has changed your colour?' He replied: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have no illness and no pain, except that when I do not see you, I long for you and feel a severe loneliness until I meet you. Then I remember the Hereafter, and I fear that I will not see you there, because I know that you will be raised with the prophets, and even if I enter Paradise, I would be in a station lower than yours, and if I do not enter Paradise, then that is the time when I will never see you.'" End of al-Kalbi's words.

Similar words to Thawban's were related from a group of the Companions, among them "Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Abd Rabbih al-Ansari, the one who was shown the call to prayer (*adhan*), who said: 'O Messenger of Allah, when you die and we die, you will be in the highest ranks (*'Illiyyin*), so we will not see you nor gather with you.' He mentioned his sorrow over this, and so it was revealed." Makki related from this Abdullah that when the Prophet ﷺ died, he said: "O Allah, make me blind so that I see nothing after him," and he became blind.

The meaning of "with" (*ma'a*) in "with the prophets" is that they are together in one abode, and everyone in it is granted contentment with his state, and they are in such a position that each of them can see the others, even if their places are far apart. It was also said that companionship here means that they are raised to the dwellings of the prophets whenever they wish, as an honour for them, and then they return to their own dwellings. It was also said that the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs descend to those below them so that they may discuss the blessings of Allah; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi in his large commentary. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "This verse points to two matters of the states of the Return: the first is the illumination of the spirits by the lights of knowledge; the second is their being with the prophets. This companionship is not meant in terms of rank, for that is impossible; rather its meaning is that imperfect spirits, when they have perfected their attachments together with perfect spirits in this world, those attachments remain after separation. Thus the light of some is reflected upon others, and their lights become extremely strong. This is what occurred to me." End of his words. This resembles what the philosophers said about spirits when they separate from bodies. The people of Islam reject these expressions and their implications, but whoever is overcome by something and loves it, it runs through his speech.

His words "with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour" are an explanation of His words: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7], and they are those mentioned in this verse. The apparent meaning is that His words "of the prophets" explain "those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour." It is as if it were said: "Whoever among you obeys Allah and His Messenger, Allah will join him with those who preceded him from among those upon whom He bestowed favour." Al-Raghib said: "Among the four groups upon whom He bestowed favour, in rank and reward: the prophet with the prophet, the truthful with the truthful, the martyr with the martyr, and the righteous with the righteous." Al-Raghib also permitted that "of the prophets" be connected to His words "whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger," meaning "of the prophets and those after them," and that His words "those are with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour" be an allusion to the Highest Assembly. Then he said: ﴿and excellent are those as companions﴾. This is confirmed by the Prophet's words at death: "O Allah, join me with the Highest Companion." This is clear, he said. End of his words.

But this view, which he considers clear, is corrupt in terms of meaning and in terms of grammar. As for its meaning: the Messenger here is Muhammad ﷺ. Allah informs that whoever obeys Him and obeys His Messenger is with those mentioned. If "of the prophets" were connected to "whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger," then "of the prophets" would be an explanation of "whoever" in "whoever obeys." It would then follow that there would be prophets in the time of the Messenger or after him who obey him, and this is impossible, because Allah has stated that Muhammad is the Seal of the Prophets. And he himself said: "There is no prophet after me."

As for grammar: what precedes the response *fa'* (the particle of consequence) does not govern what follows it. If you say: "If Hind rises, then Amr is going, laughing," it is not permissible.

The scholars differed concerning the three attributes that come after "the prophets." Some said that they are all attributes of one described entity, and they are overlapping attributes, for it is not impossible for one person to be truthful, a martyr and righteous. It was also said that each attribute refers to a category of people. As for "truthful" (*siddiq*), it is an intensive form (*fi'il*) of hyperbole, like *shirrib* (a great drinker); it was said that it means one who speaks truth abundantly, and it was said that it means one who gives charity abundantly. It was this that the Prophet ﷺ intended when he said: 'Worship Allah as if you see Him.' It is also permissible that "those" refers to whoever (*man*) "obeys Allah and the Messenger," and it was pluralised in accordance with the meaning of *man*. The aforementioned possibilities for the accusative of *rafiqan* are also permissible.
