Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "In it is the meaning of saying: they included the act of Allah and His favour from objection to Him, and they were content with His knowledge of that and of other things; for this reason the *bāʾ* entered upon the name of Allah, the Exalted, to indicate the matter contained in His saying *wa-kafā* (and sufficed)," end of quote. We have already shown the corruption of the view of those who claim that your saying *kafā bi-Zaydin* (كَفى بِزَيْدٍ) means *iktafi bi-Zaydin* (اكْتَفِ بِزَيْدٍ), when commenting on His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Protector, and sufficient is Allah as Helper﴾ [al-Nisā': 45].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "*Wa-kafā bi-Allāhi ʿalīman* (And sufficient is Allah as Knower) of the recompense of the one who obeys Him. Or He intended the distinction of those upon whom He bestowed favour, and their excellence, from Allah, because they acquired it through His enabling and His guidance; and sufficient is Allah as Knower of His servants, so He grants them success according to their circumstances," end of quote. These are the expressions of the Muʿtazila.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 67–70 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And then We would surely give them from Us a great reward, and We would surely guide them to a straight path.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Idhan* (then) is a response to an implied question, as if it had been said: 'And what would they have besides, after being made firm?' So it is said: 'And *idhan*, if they had remained firm, We would have given them,' because *idhan* is a response (*jawab*) and a conditional consequence (*jaza'*)." End of quotation.

The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words, "because *idhan* is a response and a conditional consequence," implies that it carries both meanings simultaneously in every case. This is a point of scholarly disagreement. Al-Farisi (Abu Ali al-Farisi) held that it may be a response only in one position, and both a response and a conditional consequence in a negative context. For example, in *idhan azunnuka sadiqan* ("then I think you are truthful") said to someone who says "I will visit you," it is purely a response. In *idhan ukrimuka* ("then I will honour you") said to someone who says "I will visit you," it is both a response and a consequence. Al-Ustadh Abu Ali held that it is always to be understood as both a response and a consequence in every position, adhering to the apparent wording of Sibawayh. The correct view is that of al-Farisi. This is a question discussed in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*).

"Reward" (*ajr*) is a metaphor for the recompense for obedience. Describing it as "great" (*'azim*) is either in terms of its abundance or in terms of its nobility. "The straight path" (*al-sirat al-mustaqim*) is faith that leads to Paradise; this was said by Ibn Atiyya. It was also said that it is the way to Paradise, and that it is righteous deeds. When Ibn Atiyya explained the straight path as faith, he said: "The arrangement of this verse is as it is." It is known that guidance precedes the giving of the reward, because the purpose is to enumerate what Allah bestowed upon them, without regard to order. Thus the meaning is: "And We had guided them before, so that they would be among those who are given the reward." End of Ibn Atiyya's words. However, if the guidance to the path here is interpreted as the way to Paradise or as righteous deeds, then the order becomes apparent.

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour: of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: "It was revealed concerning Thawban, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who loved the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intensely. One day he came to him, his complexion had changed and his body had become emaciated. He said: 'O Thawban, what has changed your colour?' He replied: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have no illness and no pain, except that when I do not see you, I long for you and feel a severe loneliness until I meet you. Then I remember the Hereafter, and I fear that I will not see you there, because I know that you will be raised with the prophets, and even if I enter Paradise, I would be in a station lower than yours, and if I do not enter Paradise, then that is the time when I will never see you.'" End of al-Kalbi's words.

Similar words to Thawban's were related from a group of the Companions, among them "Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Abd Rabbih al-Ansari, the one who was shown the call to prayer (*adhan*), who said: 'O Messenger of Allah, when you die and we die, you will be in the highest ranks (*'Illiyyin*), so we will not see you nor gather with you.' He mentioned his sorrow over this, and so it was revealed." Makki related from this Abdullah that when the Prophet ﷺ died, he said: "O Allah, make me blind so that I see nothing after him," and he became blind.

The meaning of "with" (*ma'a*) in "with the prophets" is that they are together in one abode, and everyone in it is granted contentment with his state, and they are in such a position that each of them can see the others, even if their places are far apart. It was also said that companionship here means that they are raised to the dwellings of the prophets whenever they wish, as an honour for them, and then they return to their own dwellings. It was also said that the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs descend to those below them so that they may discuss the blessings of Allah; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi in his large commentary. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "This verse points to two matters of the states of the Return: the first is the illumination of the spirits by the lights of knowledge; the second is their being with the prophets. This companionship is not meant in terms of rank, for that is impossible; rather its meaning is that imperfect spirits, when they have perfected their attachments together with perfect spirits in this world, those attachments remain after separation. Thus the light of some is reflected upon others, and their lights become extremely strong. This is what occurred to me." End of his words. This resembles what the philosophers said about spirits when they separate from bodies. The people of Islam reject these expressions and their implications, but whoever is overcome by something and loves it, it runs through his speech.

His words "with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour" are an explanation of His words: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7], and they are those mentioned in this verse. The apparent meaning is that His words "of the prophets" explain "those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour." It is as if it were said: "Whoever among you obeys Allah and His Messenger, Allah will join him with those who preceded him from among those upon whom He bestowed favour." Al-Raghib said: "Among the four groups upon whom He bestowed favour, in rank and reward: the prophet with the prophet, the truthful with the truthful, the martyr with the martyr, and the righteous with the righteous." Al-Raghib also permitted that "of the prophets" be connected to His words "whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger," meaning "of the prophets and those after them," and that His words "those are with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour" be an allusion to the Highest Assembly. Then he said: ﴿and excellent are those as companions﴾. This is confirmed by the Prophet's words at death: "O Allah, join me with the Highest Companion." This is clear, he said. End of his words.

But this view, which he considers clear, is corrupt in terms of meaning and in terms of grammar. As for its meaning: the Messenger here is Muhammad ﷺ. Allah informs that whoever obeys Him and obeys His Messenger is with those mentioned. If "of the prophets" were connected to "whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger," then "of the prophets" would be an explanation of "whoever" in "whoever obeys." It would then follow that there would be prophets in the time of the Messenger or after him who obey him, and this is impossible, because Allah has stated that Muhammad is the Seal of the Prophets. And he himself said: "There is no prophet after me."

As for grammar: what precedes the response *fa'* (the particle of consequence) does not govern what follows it. If you say: "If Hind rises, then Amr is going, laughing," it is not permissible.

The scholars differed concerning the three attributes that come after "the prophets." Some said that they are all attributes of one described entity, and they are overlapping attributes, for it is not impossible for one person to be truthful, a martyr and righteous. It was also said that each attribute refers to a category of people. As for "truthful" (*siddiq*), it is an intensive form (*fi'il*) of hyperbole, like *shirrib* (a great drinker); it was said that it means one who speaks truth abundantly, and it was said that it means one who gives charity abundantly. The commentators have several interpretations of it. The first: whoever believes in everything without any doubt entering into it is truthful, based on Allah's words: ﴿Those who believed in Allah and His messengers, those are the truthful﴾ [al-Hadid: 19]. The second: the distinguished companions of the Messenger. The third: the one who was foremost in affirming the Messenger, and thereby became an example for all people.

As for "martyr" (*shahid*): it is one who is killed in the cause of Allah, specially favoured with the honour of this death. The Law distinguishes their ruling regarding the omission of the ritual washing and the funeral prayer, because they are too honoured to be interceded for. The discussion of why they are named martyrs has already been presented, but the word "martyrs" in the verse includes all the kinds of martyrs mentioned by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "It is not permissible for martyrdom to be explained as a person being killed by unbelievers. Rather we say: *shahid* is an intensive form (*fa'il*) in the sense of an active participle (*fa'il*), meaning one who bears witness to the religion of Allah, sometimes by argument and clear proof, and sometimes by the sword and the spear. So the martyrs are those who uphold justice, and they are those whom Allah mentioned in His words: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]." As for "righteous" (*salih*): it is one who is righteous in his belief and his action. This composition according to this view comes in accordance with the descent from the highest to the lower, and then to what is lower than that. In this there is encouragement for believers to obey Allah and obey His Messenger, since they are promised companionship with the nearest of Allah's servants to Him, and the highest of them in rank with Him.

Al-Raghib said: "Allah divided the believers in this verse into four categories, and gave them four stations, some of which are below others, and He urged all people not to fall short of any one of these stations. The first: the prophets, whom the power of divinity sustains; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing directly from close by. For this reason Allah said: ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12]. The second: the truthful, who compete with the prophets in knowledge; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing directly from afar. It was this that the Commander of the Faithful (Ali) meant when it was said to him: 'Have you seen Allah?' He said: 'I would not worship a thing I had not seen,' and then he said: 'The eyes do not see Him by the witness of sight, but the hearts see Him by the realities of faith.' The third: the martyrs, who know a thing through proofs; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing in a mirror from a near place, like the state of Haritha, when he said: 'It is as if I am looking at the Throne of my Lord.' It was this that the Prophet ﷺ intended when he said: 'Worship Allah as if you see Him.' The fourth: the righteous, who know a thing by following and imitating those firmly grounded in knowledge; their likeness is that of one who sees a thing from afar in a mirror. It was this that the Prophet ﷺ intended by his words: 'Worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you.'" End of his words. This resembles the words of the Sufis.

Ikrimah said: "The prophets are Muhammad, the truthful are Abu Bakr, the martyrs are Umar, Uthman and Ali, and the righteous are the righteous of the community of Muhammad." End of quotation. It should be understood that this is by way of example, and not by way of restriction. The statement "whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger" does not, in its apparent wording, imply sufficiency with a single act of obedience, since the word denoting the attribute suffices, in affirmative contexts, for the occurrence of that named quality once, because hypocrites may enter into it, for they may perform a single act of obedience. Rather, it is taken in a non-literal sense, by interpreting obedience as the performance of all commanded acts and the abandonment of all forbidden acts.

﴿And excellent are those as companions.﴾ "Those" (*ula'ika*) refers to the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. He did not suffice with "companionship" until He made them *rufaqa'* (companions) for them. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, they agree with him and accompany him. The *rafiq* is the companion, named so because one benefits from him (*irtifaq*). On this basis, *rafiqan* may be in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of "those," or as a specificative accusative (*tamyiz*). If it is in the accusative as a specificative, it is possible that it is not transferred; then *min* (from) may be placed before it, and it would be the specified noun. It came in the singular either because *rafiq*, like *khalit* and *sadiq*, is used for the singular, dual and plural with a single form, or because the singular is used in the specificative construction for sufficiency while the plural is meant, and the fact that it is a verse-ending (*fasila*) makes this more appropriate here. It is also possible that it is transferred from the agent, in which case it is not the specified noun, and the implied meaning is: "and excellent is the companion of those," so *min* is not placed before it. It is also permissible that "those" refers to whoever (*man*) "obeys Allah and the Messenger," and it was pluralised in accordance with the meaning of *man*. The aforementioned possibilities for the accusative of *rafiqan* are also permissible.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah 4, verses 67–70 (part 2 of 2):

The majority of readers recited *wa-ḥasuna* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* (وحَسُنَ), which is the original form and the dialect of the Ḥijāz. Abū al-Sammāl recited *wa-ḥasna* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn* (وحَسْنَ), which is the dialect of Tamīm. It is also permissible to read *wa-ḥusnun* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn* and a *ḍamma* on the *ḥā'* (وحُسْنٌ), on the basis of transferring the vowel of the *sīn* to the *ḥā'*; this is the dialect of some of the Banū Qays.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "*Wa-ḥasuna ulā'ika rafīqan* (﴿And how good are those as companions﴾) carries the sense of wonder (ta'ajjub), as if it were said: 'How good are those as companions!' Because it stands independently with the meaning of wonder, it is read *wa-ḥasna* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn*, as the one who wonders says it. [Likewise one says] *wa-ḥasuna al-wajhu wajhuka* (وحَسُنَ الوَجْهُ وجْهُكَ) with *fatḥa* and *ḍamma*, along with the *sukūn*." That is the end of his words.

This is a confusion and a mixing of one school's view with another's. We say: the scholars differed regarding a verb used to express praise and blame. Al-Fārisī and most of the grammarians held that it is permissible to attach it to the category of *ni'ma* and *bi'sa* (the two verbs of praise and blame) only, so that its subject can only be what is the subject of those two. Al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad held that it is permissible to attach it to the category of *ni'ma* and *bi'sa*, so that its subject is treated like their subject; this applies when the sense of wonder does not enter into it. Others held that it is permissible to attach it to the verb of wonder (fi'l al-ta'ajjub), so that it does not operate like *ni'ma* and *bi'sa* in terms of the subject or the rest of their rules; rather, its subject is what would be the object of the verb of wonder, so one says: *la-ḍaraba-tu yadaka* (لَضَرَبْتُ يَدَكَ) and *la-ḍaraba-tu al-yada* (لَضَرَبْتُ اليَدَ). The discussion of these two positions, both affirming and refuting them, is mentioned in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-naḥw). Al-Zamakhsharī did not follow either of these two positions; rather, he mixed and combined them. He took the wonder from the position of al-Akhfash, and took the example *wa-ḥasuna al-wajhu wajhuka* from the position of al-Fārisī. As for his statement, "Because it stands independently with the meaning of wonder, it is read *wa-ḥusnun* with a *sukūn* on the *sīn*, and he mentioned that the one who wonders says *wa-ḥasuna* and *wa-ḥusnun*," this is worthless, because al-Farrā' mentioned that these are dialects of the Arabs; therefore the *sukūn* is not [an indication of wonder], nor is it, together with the transfer, the whole of wonder.

﴿That bounty is from Allah﴾. The apparent meaning is that the reference is to the condition of the obedient among the prophets and those joined with them, because that is what is judged in His saying: ﴿then they are with those whom﴾ [Allah has blessed]. It is as if this were in answer to a question: what causes them to be equal with the prophets in the Hereafter, when the difference between them in this world is clear? So He mentioned that this is by His bounty, not by any obligation upon Him. And although they are equal with them in Paradise, they differ in their ranks.

It has also been said that the reference is to the reward in His saying "a great reward." It has been said that it refers to obedience, and it has been said that it refers to companionship. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the great reward given to the obedient and the companionship of those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour are from Allah, because He bestowed them upon them as a complement to their reward. *Dhālika* (ذَلِكَ) is the subject (mubtada') and *al-faḍl* (الفَضْلُ) is its predicate, and *min Allāh* (مِنَ اللَّهِ) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is also permissible for *al-faḍl* to be a qualifier (ṣifa), with the predicate being *min Allāh*. It is also permissible for both to be predicates, according to the view of those who permit that.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as Knower﴾. When He mentioned obedience and mentioned the recompense of the one who obeys, He used the attribute of knowledge, which includes the recompense; that is, sufficient is He as one who rewards those who obey. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "In it is the meaning of saying: they included the act of Allah and His favour from objection to Him, and they were content with His knowledge of that and of other things; for this reason the *bāʾ* entered upon the name of Allah, the Exalted, to indicate the matter contained in His saying *wa-kafā* (and sufficed)," end of quote. We have already shown the corruption of the view of those who claim that your saying *kafā bi-Zaydin* (كَفى بِزَيْدٍ) means *iktafi bi-Zaydin* (اكْتَفِ بِزَيْدٍ), when commenting on His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Protector, and sufficient is Allah as Helper﴾ [al-Nisā': 45].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "*Wa-kafā bi-Allāhi ʿalīman* (And sufficient is Allah as Knower) of the recompense of the one who obeys Him. Or He intended the distinction of those upon whom He bestowed favour, and their excellence, from Allah, because they acquired it through His enabling and His guidance; and sufficient is Allah as Knower of His servants, so He grants them success according to their circumstances," end of quote. These are the expressions of the Muʿtazila.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 71–72:

﴿O you who believe, take your precaution (khudhū ḥidhrakum), then go forth in separate groups (thubāt) or go forth all together.﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when God mentioned obedience to Him and to His Messenger, and among the most important acts of obedience is the revival of God's religion, He commanded them to undertake the revival of His religion and the elevation of His call. He ordered them not to rush upon their enemy in ignorance, so He said: "take your precaution" (khudhū ḥidhrakum). Thus He taught them the conduct of war. Since the hypocrites had been mentioned earlier, in this verse He warned the believers against accepting their statements and against their discouraging them from jihad. So He addressed them by the name of faith, as is His custom when He wishes to command or forbid the believers. "Al-ḥadhar" and "al-ḥadhar" (both forms) have the same meaning. They said: the construction "akhdh ḥidhrak" (take your precaution) has not been heard in the form "akhdh ḥidhrika" (in the second person feminine). The meaning of "khudh ḥidhrak" is: prepare yourself with all kinds of things by which one prepares to meet the one who confronts you, so that taking up weapons and other things is included in it. It is said: "akhadha ḥidhrahu" when he guarded himself against what is feared, as if he made caution his instrument by which he protects himself and seeks refuge. The meaning is: be on guard against the enemy. Then God commanded going out to jihad in groups, one group after another (sariyyah ba'da sariyyah, i.e., detachments following one another), or as one united battalion (kattībah wāḥidah mujtami'ah).

The majority of readers read "fa-infirū" (go forth) with a kasra on the fā' in both places. Al-A'mash read it with a ḍamma on it in both places, and "thubātan" and "jamī'an" are in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl). As far as we know, "thubātin" was not read except with a kasra on the tā'. Al-Farrā' said: the Arabs put a kasra on this tā' in the accusative and also use the accusative form. Someone recited to me:

"When [the calamities] uncovered them with days, they gathered in groups (thubātan), their humiliation and their sorrow upon them."

It is recited with a kasra and with a fatḥa on the tā'. The words "aw" and "aw infirū" (or go forth) are for choice (lil-takhyīr). Ibn ʿAbbās said: this verse was abrogated (naskh, abrogation) by:

﴿The believers should not all go forth together.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. It was said: by this is meant specification (takhṣīṣ), since going forth is not required of the whole community.

﴿And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind.﴾ The address is to the army of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Qatādah, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and others said: those who will certainly lag behind are the hypocrites, and they were described as being among the believers on the basis of kind, or lineage, or outward affiliation to faith. Al-Kalbī said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and his companions. It was also said: they are the weak among the believers. This view is made distant by His saying, at the calamity of the believers: ﴿God has bestowed favor upon me, since I was not present with them as a witness,﴾ and His saying: (p-291) ﴿As if there had never been any affection between you and him.﴾ [al-Nisā': 73]. Such a statement does not come from a believer; it comes only from a hypocrite. The lām in "la-yubaṭṭi'anna" is the lām of an omitted oath, and the intended meaning is: "by God, the one who will certainly lag behind." The two sentences, the oath and its answer, form a relative clause (ṣilah) for "man," and the returning pronoun (ʿā'id) is the concealed pronoun in "la-yubaṭṭi'anna."

They said: in this verse there is a refutation of some early grammarians who claimed that it is not permitted to connect a relative pronoun to an oath and its answer when the oath clause lacks a pronoun. So it is not permitted to say "jā'anī alladhī uqsimu billāhi laqad qāma abūhu" (the one by whom I swear to God, his father certainly stood up has come to me). There is no proof in it, because the oath clause is omitted; so it is possible that there is a pronoun in it returning to the relative pronoun, and it is possible that there is not. What admits of two possibilities provides no proof for determining one of them. A similar verse is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, to each your Lord will surely pay in full their deeds.﴾ [Hūd: 111], according to the reading of the one who puts the accusative on "kullan" and lightens the mīm of "lamā" (so that it reads "wa-inna kullan lamā"). That is: "and indeed, to each one, by the one who will certainly pay them in full," according to the best of the interpretations (takhārīj). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the lām in "la-yubaṭṭi'anna" is the lām of an oath according to the majority. It was also said: it is an emphatic lām after an emphatic lām. This second view is an error.

The majority read "la-yubaṭṭi'anna" with shaddah. Mujāhid read "la-yubaṭi'anna" without shaddah. Both readings may be understood as intransitive, since they say "abṭa'a" and "baṭṭa'a" with the meaning of "baṭua" (to be slow). They may also be understood as transitive, with the hamzah or the doubling of the middle radical, from "baṭua." On the intransitive reading the meaning is that he is sluggish and held back from going forth to jihad; on the transitive reading, most of the exegetes take this view.

﴿But if a calamity befalls you, he says: "God has indeed bestowed favor upon me, since I was not present with them as a witness."﴾ The calamity (muṣībah) is defeat. It was so named because of the reproach that befalls a person through turning the back and failing to stand firm. Among the Arabs there are those who prefer death over defeat, and the poet has said:

"If you are truthful, as you have related to me,
then you escaped the escape of al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām."

"He left his loved ones to fight on their behalf,
and escaped with the head of a swift horse and its bridle."

He reproached him with defeat and with fleeing from his loved ones. Another said in praise of steadfastness in war and of being killed in it:

"Escape from death had been easy, but the bitter guardianship and the harsh character turned him back to it.
So he planted his foot in the swamp of death, and said to it: 'The gathering place is beneath your sole.'"

It was also said: the calamity is being killed in the way of God. They called that a calamity according to their corrupt belief, or because all death is a calamity, as God named it. It was also said: the calamity is defeat and killing. The "shahīd" (witness) here means one present with them on the field of battle, or one killed in the way of God. The hypocrite says it mockingly, because he does not believe in the reality of witnessing in the way of God.

As far as we know, "thubātin" was not read except with a kasra on the tā'. Al-Farrā' said: the Arabs put a kasra on this tā' in the accusative and also use the accusative form. Someone recited to me:

"When [the calamities] uncovered them with days, they gathered in groups (thubātan), their humiliation and their sorrow upon them."

It is recited with a kasra and with a fatḥa on the tā'. The words "aw" and "aw infirū" (or go forth) are for choice (lil-takhyīr). Ibn ʿAbbās said: this verse was abrogated (naskh, abrogation) by:

﴿The believers should not all go forth together.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. It was said: by this is meant specification (takhṣīṣ), since going forth is not required of the whole community.

﴿And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind.﴾ The address is to the army of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Qatādah, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and others said: those who will certainly lag behind are the hypocrites, and they were described as being among the believers on the basis of kind, or lineage, or outward affiliation to faith. Al-Kalbī said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and his companions. It was also said: they are the weak among the believers. This view is made distant by His saying, at the calamity of the believers: ﴿God has bestowed favor upon me, since I was not present with them as a witness,﴾ and His saying: (p-291) ﴿As if there had never been any affection between you and him.﴾ [al-Nisā': 73]. Such a statement does not come from a believer; it comes only from a hypocrite. The lām in "la-yubaṭṭi'anna" is the lām of an omitted oath, and the intended meaning is: "by God, the one who will certainly lag behind." The two sentences, the oath and its answer, form a relative clause (ṣilah) for "man," and the returning pronoun (ʿā'id) is the concealed pronoun in "la-yubaṭṭi'anna."

They said: in this verse there is a refutation of some early grammarians who claimed that it is not permitted to connect a relative pronoun to an oath and its answer when the oath clause lacks a pronoun. So it is not permitted to say "jā'anī alladhī uqsimu billāhi laqad qāma abūhu" (the one by whom I swear to God, his father certainly stood up has come to me). There is no proof in it, because the oath clause is omitted; so it is possible that there is a pronoun in it returning to the relative pronoun, and it is possible that there is not. What admits of two possibilities provides no proof for determining one of them. A similar verse is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, to each your Lord will surely pay in full their deeds.﴾ [Hūd: 111], according to the reading of the one who puts the accusative on "kullan" and lightens the mīm of "lamā" (so that it reads "wa-inna kullan lamā"). That is: "and indeed, to each one, by the one who will certainly pay them in full," according to the best of the interpretations (takhārīj). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the lām in "la-yubaṭṭi'anna" is the lām of an oath according to the majority. It was also said: it is an emphatic lām after an emphatic lām. This second view is an error.

The majority read "la-yubaṭṭi'anna" with shaddah. Mujāhid read "la-yubaṭi'anna" without shaddah. Both readings may be understood as intransitive, since they say "abṭa'a" and "baṭṭa'a" with the meaning of "baṭua" (to be slow). They may also be understood as transitive, with the hamzah or the doubling of the middle radical, from "baṭua." On the intransitive reading the meaning is that he is sluggish and held back from going forth to jihad; on the transitive reading, most of the exegetes take this view.

﴿But if a calamity befalls you, he says: "God has indeed bestowed favor upon me, since I was not present with them as a witness."﴾ The calamity (muṣībah) is defeat. It was so named because of the reproach that befalls a person through turning the back and failing to stand firm. Among the Arabs there are those who prefer death over defeat, and the poet has said:

"If you are truthful, as you have related to me,
then you escaped the escape of al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām."

"He left his loved ones to fight on their behalf,
and escaped with the head of a swift horse and its bridle."

He reproached him with defeat and with fleeing from his loved ones. Another said in praise of steadfastness in war and of being killed in it:

"Escape from death had been easy, but the bitter guardianship and the harsh character turned him back to it.
So he planted his foot in the swamp of death, and said to it: 'The gathering place is beneath your sole.'"

It was also said: the calamity is being killed in the way of God. They called that a calamity according to their corrupt belief, or because all death is a calamity, as God named it. It was also said: the calamity is defeat and killing. The "shahīd" (witness) here means one present with them on the field of battle, or one killed in the way of God. The hypocrite says it mockingly, because he does not believe in the reality of witnessing in the way of God.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 73 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if a bounty from Allah should reach you, he will surely say, as if there had never been between you and him any affection: "Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have attained a great attainment."﴾ The "bounty" here means victory over the enemy and booty.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read *la-yaqulanna* with a fatḥah on the lām. Al-Hasan read *la-yaqulunna* with a ḍammah on the lām, in which a plural pronoun is implied, in keeping with the meaning of *man* (whoever) [p-292].

Ibn Kathir and Ḥafs read *ka-an lam takun* with the feminine tā' (*takun*), while the rest read it with the yā' (*yakun*). Al-Hasan and Yazid al-Nahwi read *fa-afūza* with a ḍammah on the zāy, coordinated with *kuntu* (*fa-akūnu ma'ahum wa-l-fawz*), so that being with them and sharing in the booty fall within the wish. Or it is read as a new sentence, meaning "so I attain," i.e., *fa-anā afūzu*. Al-Jumhur read it with a fatḥah on the zāy, as the answer to the wish (*jawāb al-tamannī*).

According to the doctrine of the majority of the Basrans, the fatḥah is due to a concealed *an* after the fā', and this fā' is a conjunction that links the verbal noun formed from the concealed *an* and the verb it governs in the accusative to a supposed verbal noun. According to the Kufans, it is accusative by the *khilāf* (the particle of opposition). According to al-Jarmi, it is accusative by the fā' itself. The *yā'* (in *yā layti*), according to some, is the vocative particle, and the vocative noun is omitted; its estimate is *yā qawmu layt-ī* (O my people, would that I...). Abu 'Ali held that *yā* is for alerting (*tanbīh*), that there is no omitted vocative noun in the sentence, and this is the sound view.

Here *ka-an* is the light form (*mukhaffafa*) of the heavy one. When a verbal sentence follows it, it is preceded by *qad*, as in the verse:

"Let not your warming yourself at the heat frighten you, for its danger is that *ka-an qad alamma* (as if it has indeed approached)."

Or it is preceded by *lam*, as in his saying *ka-an lam yakun* and Allah's saying ﴿as if it had not flourished yesterday﴾ [Yunus: 24]. I found in the poetry of 'Ammar al-Kalbi its beginning in his saying:

"The nights have scattered their unity, so it is as if they had not been there before."

One should pause over the permissibility of this until it is heard from the speech of the Arabs.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *ka-an* implies the meaning of comparison, but it is not like the heavy form in needing a subject and predicate; rather, sentences follow it. This statement is neither precise nor unrestricted. When it is lightened and is followed by what would follow the heavy form, the more common and eloquent usage is that this sentence is in the nominative as subject and predicate, the subject of *kāna* is an omitted pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*), and that sentence is in the place of nominative predicate of *kāna*. When the pronoun of the matter is not intended, it is permissible for the noun to be in the accusative if it is explicit, and the predicate to be nominative. This is the apparent sense of Sibawayh's words. This is not restricted to poetry; we say *ka-an Zaydan qā'imun* (as if Zayd is standing).

Sibawayh said: "One who is trustworthy told us that he heard from the Arabs one who says *in 'Umaru al-munṭaliqu* (indeed, 'Umar is the one who sets out)." The people of Medina recite *wa-in kullan lammā* (Hud: 111), lightening and putting it in the accusative, as he said: *ka-an thadyayhi ḥuqqān* (as if his two breasts are two bowls). That is because the particle is in the position of the verb; so when something is omitted from its own form, it does not change its governing, just as it did not change the governing of *lam yak* (he was not), and I was not concerned when it was omitted." The apparent sense of Sibawayh's comparison, with his saying *ka-an thadyayhi ḥuqqān*, is the permissibility of this in speech, and that it is not restricted to poetry.

The author of *Ru'us al-masa'il* transmitted that when *ka-an* is lightened, its governing is not permitted according to the Kufans, while the Basrans permitted it. According to the Kufan doctrine, Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement about *an*, like the lightened *an* not being like the heavy one in needing a subject and predicate, may hold. But according to the Basran doctrine it does not, since for them it must have a subject and predicate.

The sentence *ka-an lam yakun baynakum wa-baynahu mawaddah* (as if there had never been between you and him any affection) has been disputed by the commentators, and we shall recount the words of those whose statements we have encountered. We say: al-Zamakhshari said: it is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tirāḍ*) between the verb *la-yaqulanna* and its object, which is *yā layti*. The meaning is: as if there had not previously been between him and you any affection, because the hypocrites used to show affection to the believers and befriend them outwardly, though they were plotting harm against them inwardly. The apparent sense is that it is mockery, since they were the greatest enemies of the believers and the most envious of them. So how can they be described as having affection, except in the opposite sense, mocking their condition?

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the hypocrite offers affection to the believers, pledges to take on the burdens of Islam, then he lags behind out of hypocrisy, doubt and disbelief in Allah and His Messenger, and then he wishes, when the unseen is revealed, for the believers' victory. On this view, Allah's saying ﴿as if there had never been between you and him any affection﴾ comes as an eloquent *iltifāt* (shift of address) and an insertion between the speaker and the spoken words, with an expression that shows an increase in the ugliness of their act.

Al-Zajjaj said: this sentence is a parenthetical insertion; Allah informed of this because they used to show affection to the believers. He also said, and al-Maturidi followed him: this is according to the reversal of order; its estimate is: "If a calamity should befall you, he says: 'Allah has blessed me since I was not with them as a witness,' as if there had never been between you and him any affection, and if a bounty from Allah should reach you..."

Al-Raghib said: that is unseemly, for one does not separate the sentence from something related to another sentence. He also said, and Abu al-Baqa followed him: the place of the sentence is accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), as you say *marartu bi-Zayd* (I passed by Zayd), and *ka-an lam yakun baynaka wa-baynahu ma'rifah* (as if there had not been between you and him any acquaintance), let alone affection. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: this sentence is from the words of the hypocrites who made them stay behind from jihad, while they themselves went out.

﴿as if there had never been between you and him﴾, i.e., between you and the Prophet (ﷺ), any affection, so that he would bring you out with them to take from the booty, in order that they might thereby make the Messenger hateful to them. Abu 'Ali followed Muqatil in this. Muqatil said: its meaning is: as if he is not of your community, and there is no affection between you. He means: the laggard said to those among the hypocrites and weak believers who stayed behind from the expedition, and those who stayed behind with permission: "as if there had not been between you and Muhammad any affection, so that he would bring you out to jihad, and you would attain what they attained."

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: it is an insertion of the utmost beauty, because whoever loves a person rejoices at his joy and grieves at his grief; so when he reverses the matter, that is a display of enmity. We say: Allah related the hypocrite's joy at the time of the Muslims' misfortune, then He wished to relate his grief at the Muslims' dynasty because he missed the booty; so before finishing the speech in full, He placed his saying *ka-an lam yakun baynakum wa-baynahu* (as if there had never been between you and him...), and the intent is wonder. It is as if Allah says: "Look at what this hypocrite says, as if there had never been between you, O believers, any affection or any association at all." This is the meaning of the speech.

Qatadah and Ibn Juraij said: the hypocrite's saying "Oh, I wish I had been with them" is in the sense of envy on his part toward the believers in attaining what he desires.

What is summarized from these statements is that this sentence either has a place in grammar (*i'rāb*) as accusative, a circumstantial clause from the concealed pronoun in *la-yaqulanna*, or accusative as the object of *yaqulanna* by way of narration, so that it is part of the spoken words. The spoken words are the whole of the two sentences: the sentence of comparison and the sentence of wish. The pronoun of address refers to those who stayed behind from jihad, and the pronoun of absence in *wa-baynahu* refers to the Messenger. On the first view, the pronoun of address refers to the believers, and the pronoun of absence refers to the speaker.

Or it has no place in grammar, because it is in origin a parenthetical insertion between the conditional clause and the oath clause, and was postponed, its intent being to be placed between the two sentences. Or because it is a parenthetical insertion between *la-yaqulanna* and its governed element, which is the sentence of wish, and it is not a parenthetical insertion that relates to the content of this later sentence, but relates to the content of both sentences. The pronoun of address refers to the believers, and in *baynahu* it refers to the speaker. It was inserted in the middle of the last clause and was not postponed after it, although in terms of meaning it is postponed, since its meaning relates to the content of both sentences; for the governed element of the verb of saying is intended to come first, but its postponement was made good because it fell as a closing pause (*fāṣila*). Had the parenthetical clause been postponed, it would not have been good, since it is not a closing pause. The estimate is: "he says, 'Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would attain a great attainment,' as if there had never been between you and him any affection," since from him came his saying at the time of the calamity: "Allah has blessed me since I was not with them as a witness," and his saying at the time of the booty: "Oh, I wish I had been with them." This is the speech of one between whom and you there was never any affection.

In the two verses there is an indication that they count as gifts only the worldly goods; they rejoice in what they obtain from them, and they count as trials only their calamities, so they are pained by what befalls them from them, as in Allah's saying: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him...﴾ [al-Fajr: 15], and so on.

This sentence includes kinds of eloquence and rhetorical ornament: the entry of the conditional particle on what in reality is not a condition, in His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. The demonstratives in ﴿that is better﴾ [al-Nisa': 59], ﴿those are the ones whom Allah knows﴾ [al-Nisa': 63], ﴿then those are with those whom﴾ [al-Nisa': 69], ﴿and excellent are those as companions﴾ [al-Nisa': 69], ﴿that is the bounty from Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 70]. The interrogation intended as wonder in ﴿Have you not seen those who claim﴾ [al-Nisa': 60]. The varied paronomasia (*tajnīs mughāyir*) in ﴿that He should lead them astray with a far-off error﴾ [al-Nisa': 60], in ﴿a calamity afflicted them﴾ [al-Nisa': 62], in ﴿and say to them about themselves a far-reaching word﴾ [al-Nisa': 63], in ﴿they turn away from you with aversion﴾ [al-Nisa': 61], in ﴿and submit in full submission﴾ [al-Nisa': 65], in ﴿if a calamity should befall you﴾ [al-Nisa': 72], and in ﴿so I would attain a great attainment.﴾ The metaphor in ﴿and if you dispute﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]: the original sense of *munāza'ah* (dispute) is pulling by the hand, then it was borrowed for dispute in speech. In ﴿a far-off error﴾ [al-Nisa': 60], he borrowed "far" (*bu'd*), which is specific to times and places, for meanings specific to the hearts, because hearts remain fixed upon them. In ﴿in what has become confused among them﴾ [al-Nisa': 65], he borrowed what is intertwined and crowded of trees for the dispute in which some speech enters into other speech, borrowing the sensible for the intelligible.

Abu Hayyan's (al-Bahr al-Muhit) commentary on surah 4, verse 73 (part 2 of 2):

And His saying ﴿in their souls, a constriction﴾ [4:65]: he used the term *ḥaraj* (constriction), which describes trees when they become dense, for a matter that weighs heavily on the soul, because of the connection between them. It derives from *al-ḍayq* (narrowness) and from *al-tatmīm* (completion, meaning an addition to a sentence that intensifies and clarifies the intended meaning). This appears in His saying ﴿a far-reaching word﴾ [4:63], meaning that its pain reaches their hearts, or that it is far-reaching in rebuking them.

The addition of the particle for increased meaning appears in ﴿any messenger﴾ [4:64]. It comes to express comprehensiveness, since if *lā* (no) were not present, the meaning would be "one."

Repetition appears in *istaghfara* (he asked forgiveness) and *istaghfarū* (they asked forgiveness), in *anfusihim* (their souls), and in ﴿in their souls﴾ [4:63], and the name of God appears in several places. There is *iltifāt* (a shift in grammatical person) in ﴿and the Messenger asked forgiveness for them﴾ [4:64]. There is emphasis by the verbal noun in ﴿and submit fully﴾ [4:65]. There is an eloquent division in His saying ﴿of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous﴾ [4:69]. There is the attribution of a verb to something that cannot literally perform it, in ﴿a calamity has struck you﴾ [4:72] and ﴿bounty from God has come to you﴾. There is the designation of a thing as being part of something when it is not truly part of it, for a connection, in His saying ﴿Among you is one who surely lingers﴾ [4:72]. There is *i'tirāḍ* (an interjected parenthetical clause) against the view of the majority (*al-jumhūr*) in His saying ﴿as if there had never been any affection between you and him﴾. There is *ḥadhf* (ellipsis) in several places: ﴿Let those fight in the way of God who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter. And whoever fights in the way of God and is killed or overcomes, We will bestow upon him a great reward﴾ [4:74]. ﴿And why should you not fight in the way of God and of the oppressed men, women and children, who say: "Our Lord, bring us out of this city whose people are wrongdoers, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper"﴾ [4:75]. ﴿Those who believe fight in the way of God, and those who disbelieve fight in the way of the *ṭāghūt* (false deity). So fight against the allies of Satan. Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak﴾ [4:76]. ﴿Have you not seen those who were told, "Restrain your hands, establish prayer and give zakat"? But when fighting was prescribed for them, a faction of them feared people as they should fear God, or even more intensely. And they said, "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You would delay us to a near term." Say: "The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for one who fears God, and you will not be wronged even by a thread"﴾ [4:77]. ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you were in towers built up high. And if good befalls them, they say, "This is from God," but if evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you." Say: "All is from God." So what is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾ [4:78]

(p-٢٩٥) *Idrāk* (attaining) a thing means reaching it and obtaining it. *Al-burj* is a fortress, and it is said to be a palace. *Al-burūj* are the lunar mansions, and all of them derive from *baraja* (to appear, become visible). From the same root comes *al-tabarruj*, which is a woman displaying her beauties. *Al-baraj* in the eye is its widening. *Al-mushayyad* is that which is built with *al-shīd*, which is plaster. It is said: *shāda* and *shayyada*, with the middle radical doubled for emphasis, as in *kasartu al-'ūd* (I broke the stick once) and *kassartuhu* (I broke it in several places), and *kharaqtu al-thawb* (I tore the garment) and *kharraqtuhu* (I tore it in several places, when the tear is in several places). On this basis one says *shāda al-jidār* (he built the wall with plaster). From this is the poet's saying:

*He built it of marble and covered it with plaster, so for the birds in its heights are nests.*

*Al-mushayyad* also means the elevated and raised. One says *shayyada*, and *ashāda al-bināʾ* (he raised the building), meaning he lifted it and made it tall. From this comes *ashāda al-rajulu dhikr al-rajul* (he raised the mention of a man) when he elevated it. *Al-fiqh* is understanding. One says *faqihtu al-ḥadīth* when I understood the speech, and *faquha al-rajul* when the man became a *faqīh* (jurist).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 74:**

﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter﴾. It was said that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites who stayed behind from Uhud. "Yashrun" means "yashtarun" (buy). The meaning is: sincerely hold the faith in Allah and His Messenger, and then strive in the way of Allah. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the believers who stayed behind, and "yashrun" means "yabghun" (seek) and "yu'thirun" (prefer) the Hereafter (al-ajilah) over this world (al-'ajilah), and they exchange for it the command of Allah to fight, [namely] those weak believers who stayed behind.

﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or achieves victory, We will bestow upon him a great reward﴾. Then He promised those who fight in the way of Allah a great reward, whether he is martyred or is overcome. He mentioned the final outcome in both cases, because the final outcome of the one who is defeated in battle is that he is killed, and the final outcome of the one who kills is that he prevails and gains spoils. So the most honorable of the two cases is the one mentioned first, which is martyrdom in the way of Allah; next is that he kills the enemies of Allah; below that is attaining spoils; and below that is that he goes out to fight and neither strikes nor is struck. The term "jihad in the way of Allah" encompasses all these states. The "great reward" has been interpreted as Paradise. What appears to be the case is that it is an increase in reward from Allah, the Exalted, such as their being alive with their Lord, receiving provision; because Paradise is promised to enter by faith. It seems that the one who interpreted it as Paradise was looking at the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties, [promising] that for them is Paradise﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111], and so on.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿fal-yuqatil﴾ with the imperative lam sakin. A group read it with the lam kasr, according to the original form. The majority read ﴿fayuqtal﴾ in the passive voice. Muharib ibn Dithar read "fayaqtul" with the verb in the active voice. Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Hisham, and Khallad (with a variant from him) assimilated (yaghlib) into the fa' (fayaghlib), while the rest of the seven read it with clear separation. The majority read ﴿nu'tihi﴾ with the nun. Al-A'mash and Talhah ibn Musarrif read ﴿yu'tihi﴾ with the ya'.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 75:

﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight in the cause of Allah and of the oppressed men, women and children who say, "Our Lord, bring us out of this town whose people are wrongdoers, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper"?﴾ This interrogation contains urging and incitement to jihad (struggle, fighting) in the cause of Allah, and to the liberation of the oppressed. The apparent reading is that His saying ﴿do not fight﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Some have permitted that the construction be: "And what is the matter with you in not fighting," and then, when the preposition was deleted and "an" (that) was deleted, the verb took the nominative case. "And of the oppressed" is conjoined to the name of Allah; that is, "and in the cause of the oppressed." Al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: it is conjoined to "the cause of Allah"; that is, "in the cause of Allah and in the liberation of the oppressed."

Ibn Shihab read: fi sabili Allahi al-mustad'afina without the conjunctive waw. This may be explained either as the deletion of the conjunctive particle, or as an apposition (badal) to "the cause of Allah"; that is, "in the cause of Allah, the path of the oppressed," because it is the path of Allah the Exalted. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "al-mustad'afin" be in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), meaning: "and specifically [in] the liberation of the oppressed from the cause of Allah," because the cause of Allah is general in every good, and the liberation of the oppressed Muslims from the hands of the disbelievers is among the greatest and most specific of goods. The end of his words. There is no need to strain for its accusative case as specification, since it is contrary to the apparent meaning.

By "the oppressed" is meant those believers who were in Mecca under the humiliation and harm of the Quraysh, as they were unable to leave, and they could not bear to remain under the harm. Among the oppressed was Abdullah ibn Abbas and his mother. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed for deliverance for the oppressed believers, and he named among them: al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Salamah ibn Hisham, and Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah. His saying ﴿of the men and the women and the children﴾ specifies the oppressed.

The apparent meaning is that al-wildan (children) is meant as al-sibyan (young boys), and it is the plural of walid. It was said: it may also be the plural of walad, like warl and wirlan. He drew attention to the children to emphasize the extreme injustice of those who wronged them; for they are not obligated, so that their parents would be harmed by it, and because they used to associate their fathers in supplication seeking the mercy of Allah the Exalted and the deliverance of them from the harm of the disbelievers. They are closest to being answered, since they have no sins, as the people of Jonah did, and as is the practice in the going out of children on the festival; for walid is applied to a male slave and walidah to a female slave, and the masculine has prevailed over the feminine when the feminine is in the plural, as with istisqa'. It was also said that by His saying "of the men and the women" is meant the free, and by "the children" the slaves, since walid is applied to a male slave and walidah to a female slave, and the masculine prevailed. ﴿Who say, "Our Lord, bring us out"﴾: they had no strength or defense against the oppression except by supplication and seeking help from Allah the Exalted. The town here is Mecca by consensus.

They have discussed the agreement of ﴿al-zalim﴾ (the wrongdoer), which is masculine, with ﴿al-qaryah﴾ (the town), which is feminine, and this is from the obvious grammar. Al-Zamakhshari said: had it been feminine, saying al-zalimah, or plural, saying al-zalimin, and he answered this; but this was not recited, so it requires discussion. Were we to address what is permissible in Arabic in the constructions of the Qur'an, that would be lengthy and would take us out of the method of tafsir. He described its people as wrongdoers either because of their associating partners with Allah, or because of the severity of their oppression of the believers and their humiliation of them.

Ibn Atiyyah said: the verse encompasses the believers, the captives, and the centres of polytheism until the Day of Resurrection. When they called upon their Lord, He answered many of them in going out; some of them migrated to Medina, some fled to Abyssinia, and some remained until the conquest. The majority hold that Allah the Exalted answered their supplication; so He appointed for them from Himself the best of protectors and helpers, who is Muhammad; he cared for them in the best care and gave them the strongest victory. When he left Mecca, he appointed over them Attab ibn Usayd, who was twenty-one years old, and they saw from him the governance and the support they had asked for. Ibn Abbas said: he would give the weak his right against the strong, until they became more honoured by him than the oppressors.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 76:**

﴿Those who believe fight in the cause of Allah, and those who disbelieve fight in the cause of al-Taghut (the transgressor, i.e., false objects of worship). So fight the allies of Shaytan (Satan). Indeed, the plot of Shaytan is ever weak.﴾

When Allah, the Exalted, first commanded the believers to go forth to jihad, then secondly said, ﴿So let those fight in the cause of Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 74], and thirdly, by way of urging and exhortation, said, ﴿And why should you not fight?﴾ [An-Nisa: 75], He informed them in this verse, by way of division, that the believer is the one who fights in the cause of Allah, and the disbeliever is the one who fights in the cause of al-Taghut, so as to make clear to the believers the difference between them and the disbelievers, and to strengthen, encourage and incite them thereby. Whoever fights in the cause of Allah is the one who prevails, because Allah is his Protector and Helper. Whoever fights in the cause of al-Taghut is the one who is forsaken and defeated. Al-Taghut here means Shaytan, as shown by His saying, ﴿So fight the allies of Shaytan.﴾ Here there is an omitted element; the implied meaning is: ﴿So fight the allies of Shaytan,﴾ for indeed you, through your strength in Allah, [will prevail]. Then he gave the reason for this omitted element, which is your victory over them, by saying that the plot of Shaytan is weak, so it cannot withstand the help and support of Allah. How far apart are a resolve that returns to faith in Allah and in what He has promised for jihad, and a resolve that returns to delusion and false security!

The particle *kāna* (كان, "was") is in His saying, ﴿was weak﴾, to indicate that this attribute preceded the plot of Shaytan, and that it has always been weak. It has also been said that it means *ay* (أي, "that is"), i.e., it became weak through Islam. As for the statement of one who claims that it is a superfluous (*zā'ida*) particle, it is worth nothing. Al-Hasan said: He informed them that they would prevail over them, and for this reason [the plot] was weak.

**Qur'an 4:77:** ﴿Have you not seen those to whom it was said, "Restrain your hands, establish the prayer, and give the zakat"? But when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them feared the people as they would fear God, or with even greater fear.﴾

Al-Nasa'i recorded in his Sunan, from Ibn Abbas: "Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and some companions of his came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in Mecca and said: 'O Prophet of God, we were in honour while we were polytheists; now that we have believed, we have become humiliated.' He said: 'I have been commanded to pardon, so do not fight the people.' When God Most High moved him to Medina, He commanded him to fight, and they refrained. So God revealed this verse." Similar reports are transmitted from Qatada, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

It is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas that the verse was revealed describing the conditions of a people who lived in an earlier time. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: "It seems to allude to the story of those who said: ﴿Appoint for us a king﴾ (Qur'an 2:246)."

Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the Jews. Al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning the believers, based on His saying "they fear the people," meaning the polytheists of Mecca. Fear (khashyah) is the dread that human beings are naturally disposed to, not fear that leads to disobedience. This is similar to what al-Hasan said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "A party of them said, 'Enough,' not out of doubt in the religion nor aversion to it, but out of reluctance to risk their lives and fear of death. Some said: many of the Arabs had liked entering the religion with its obligations that came before fighting, such as prayer, zakat, and similar things, and the truce. When fighting was prescribed, this weighed heavily on them, and they recoiled from it, so the verse was revealed."

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is evident: since God commanded fighting when they requested it, obeying God's command became obligatory. When some of them shrank from it, God said: "Do you not marvel, O Muhammad, at people who asked for fighting and were then commanded to hold back? When it was prescribed for them, a party of them was frightened and recoiled." The meaning of ﴿restrain your hands﴾ is: from fighting, as indicated by "when fighting was prescribed for them." Abu Abd Allah al-Razi said: "The phrase 'restrain' is said only to those who are eager for it, and they are the believers. It has been said that it refers to the hypocrites. He said 'restrain' because they used to show eagerness for it." End of his words.

He also said: The verse indicates that the obligation of prayer and zakat preceded the obligation of jihad, and this order is the one consistent with reason, because prayer is an expression of glorifying God's command, and zakat is an expression of compassion toward God's creatures. There is no doubt that both precede jihad. The "party" is either hypocrites, or believers, or people of an earlier time, or people who had embraced Islam before the obligation of fighting was imposed, according to the differences in the occasion of revelation. "The people" here means the people of Mecca, according to the majority, or the disbelievers among the People of the Book and the polytheist Arabs.

**Grammar of ﴿لَمَّا﴾:** The particle *lamma* is, according to Sibawayh's view, a particle of necessary consequence (ḥarf wujūb li-wujūb), and according to Abu Ali's view, it is a time adverb meaning "when." If it is a particle, which is the correct view, its answer is the sudden *idhā* (*idhā al-fujā'iyyah*). If it is an adverb, it needs a governing element, which is difficult, because what follows the sudden *idhā* cannot govern what precedes it, and the verb that follows *lamma* cannot govern it, since *lamma* is attached to the sentence after it. Some said the governing element in *lamma* is the sense of "they feared," as if it were said "they recoiled." He said: "'They recoiled' is the governing element of *idhā*, with the implied sense of the future." He said: "This verse is problematic, because it contains two time adverbs, one for the past and one for the future." End of his words.

What we choose is Sibawayh's view regarding *lamma*, that it is a particle. We also choose that the sudden *idhā* is an adverb of place, which may be made the predicate of the nominative noun following it as a subject, and may also be made an object governed by the predicate. So if you say: *lamma jā'a Zaydun idhā 'Amrun qā'imun* ("when Zayd came, behold, 'Amr was standing"), it is permissible to put *qā'imun* in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). *Idhā* as a particle may be made nominative as a predicate, and it governs *idhā*. Here it is permissible for *idhā* to be an object governed by *yakhshawna* ("they fear"), and *yakhshawna* is the predicate of *firīq* ("party"). It is also permissible for it to be the predicate, with *yakhshawna* as a state (ḥāl) of *firīq*, and *minhum* ("of them") in both cases is an attribute of *firīq*.

Whoever claims that *idhā* here is an adverb of time referring to the future is wrong, because if what governs it is what precedes it, it is impossible, since *kutiba* ("was prescribed") is past, while *idhā* refers to the future. And if one allows that *idhā* be taken in the sense of *idh* ("when," past), then the meaning becomes: "when fighting was prescribed for them at the time of the fear of a party among them," and this requires an answer for *lamma*, but it has no answer. And if what governs it is what follows it, it needs an answer, which is the governing element of it, and it has no answer either.

Regarding the sudden *idhā*: is it a time adverb, or a place adverb, or a particle mentioned in the science of grammar?

The *kāf* in ﴿like the fear of God﴾ is in the accusative position. It has been said that it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a fear like the fear of God." According to what has been established from Sibawayh's view, it is a state (ḥāl) of the omitted pronoun referring to the fear: that is, "they fear it, the people," meaning they fear the fear of the people, resembling the fear of God.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the i'rab (grammatical position) of *ka-khashyati Allāh*? I say: its position is accusative as a state of the pronoun in *yakhshawna*, that is, 'they fear the people like the people of the fear of God,' i.e., resembling the people of the fear of God. *Aw ashadda khashyatan* ('or with greater fear') means: or with greater fear than the people of the fear of God. *Ashadda* is coordinated with the state. If you ask: why did you deviate from the apparent reading, which is that it is an attribute of the verbal noun, and why did you not assume: 'they fear a fear of God,' meaning 'as one fears God'? I say: the phrase 'or with greater fear' prevents that, because it and what is coordinated with it are under one ruling. If you were to say 'they fear the people with greater fear,' it would only be a state of the pronoun of the party, and it would not be accusative as a verbal noun, because you do not say 'so-and-so feared greater fear' with *khashyatan* in the accusative intending the verbal noun; you say *ashadda khashyatin* with the genitive. When you put it in the accusative, *ashadda khashyatan* would only be an expression of the agent in the accusative as a state from him. Unless you make the fear 'one who fears,' in the manner of the saying *jiddu jiddihi* ('the seriousness of his seriousness'), so that you claim its meaning is 'they fear the people with a fear like a fear greater than the fear of God.' It is permissible on this basis that the position of *ashadda* be genitive, coordinated with 'the fear of God,' meaning: 'like the fear of God, or like a fear greater than it.'" End of his words.

It is possible that *khashyatan* be correct without being a specifier (tamyīz), and then it does not entail what al-Zamakhshari committed himself to; rather, *khashyatan* is coordinated with the position of the *kāf*, and *ashadda* is accusative as a state, because it was an attribute of an indefinite noun that preceded it, so it became accusative as a state. The meaning is: "they fear the people like the fear of God, or a fear greater than it." We mentioned this explanation in His saying: ﴿or more intense in remembrance﴾ (Qur'an 2:200), and we clarified it there.

*Khashyatu Allāh* ("the fear of God") is a verbal noun annexed to its object, with the subject omitted, meaning "like their fear of God." The *aw* ("or") retains its original meaning of doubt regarding the addressee; it has also been said it is for ambiguity before the addressee, and it has been said it is for choice, and it has been said it means *wa* ("and"), and it has been said it means *bal* ("rather"). Similar views were mentioned regarding His saying: ﴿or harder than stone﴾ (Qur'an 2:74). If it were said that it is for emphasis, it would be a view, meaning: some of them fear the people as they fear God, and some of them fear them with a fear that exceeds their fear of God.

\* \*

**Qur'an 4:77 (continued):** ﴿And they said, "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us to a near term."﴾

The apparent view is that those who said this were hypocrites, because when God commands something, one whose faith is pure does not question its reason. For this reason the context following it says: ﴿If good befalls them, they say, "This is from God," but if evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you (O Muhammad)"﴾, and this is only said by a hypocrite. *Law-lā* here is for urging, meaning "why not," and it occurs frequently in the Qur'an. The "near term" here is their death in their beds, as the exegetes said. It is mentioned in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "If only You had delayed us to a near term, so that we would die a natural death and not be killed, and the enemies would be pleased by that." Whoever said it is the statement of the believers, meaning they requested a postponement of the prescription of fighting until the time when Islam became dominant and widespread, is far-fetched, because the phrase *lam* ("why") was directed against the beginning of God's command and their non-submission to it, together with their saying: "If evil befalls them, they say, 'This is from you.'"

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Law-lā akhkhartanā ilā ajalin qarībin*" is a request for an increase in the duration of restraint and a plea for a postponement to another time, like His saying: ﴿If only You had delayed me to a near term, so that I would give charity﴾ (Qur'an 63:10). Al-Raghib said: "And they said, 'Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us?' It is possible that they uttered it, and it is possible that they believed it and said it to themselves; God related it to inform that, since they found it difficult, their difficulty indicates that they were not confident in their own states."

\* \*

**Qur'an 4:77 (continued):** ﴿Say: "The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God."﴾

The discussion of the world's enjoyment being little was mentioned before in His saying: ﴿a little enjoyment﴾ (Qur'an 3:197). It is little because it is transient, whereas the bliss of the Hereafter is everlasting, so it is better for whoever fears God and obeys His command in what he loves and in what is hard, such as fighting and other things. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Kathir read ﴿they will not be wronged﴾ (Qur'an 4:49) with the *ya'* (third person), and the rest of the seven read it with the *ta'* (second person) as an address; this is an *iltifat* (shift of person), meaning: you will not be diminished from the rewards of your deeds, nor will the least hardship of the obligations be lost; so do not turn away from the reward.

\* \*

**Qur'an 4:78:** ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in towers built high.﴾

That is: this delay that they asked for is of no benefit, because there is no escape from death, whether by being killed or otherwise, so there is no benefit in weakness of nature and love of life. This sentence may be under the governance of *qul* ("say"), and it may be an independent statement from God that none escapes death.

The "towers" here are fortresses on the earth, as Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, and the majority said; or fortresses of iron, as related from Ibn Abbas; or palaces in the lowest heaven that are built, as al-Suddi said; or fortresses, hills, and strongholds, as Ibn Abbas said; or houses that are above fortresses, as some said; or the towers of the sky, which are the mansions of the moon, as al-Rabi', Anas, and al-Thawri said, and Ibn al-Qasim transmitted it from Malik. He said: "Do you not see His saying: ﴿By the sky with its towers﴾ (Qur'an 85:1), and He placed towers in it: ﴿And We have placed towers in the sky﴾ (Qur'an 15:16)?" And Zuhayr said:

*Whoever fears the causes of death will meet them, even if he tries to reach the causes of the sky with a ladder.*

*Mushayyadah* ("built high") means lofty; this was said by Abu Malik, Muqatil, Ibn Qutayba, and al-Zajjaj. Or it means plastered with *shid* (lime plaster), as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Or it means fortified, as said by Ibn Abbas and Qatada. Whoever said they are towers in the sky, it is because they are white, and he likened them to something plastered with lime; for this reason it was said that they are white palaces built in the sky.

The *jazm* (jussive) in *yudrikkum* is on the answer of the conditional, and *ayna-ma* indicates generality, as if it were said: "in whatever place you are, death will overtake you." *Law* here means *in* ("if"), and it came to dispel the assumption of escape from death by supposing: "if they were in towers built high," and to show the thoroughness of the generality in *ayna-ma*. Talha ibn Sulayman read *yudrikukumu* with the *ra'* and the *kaf* both in the nominative, and Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) explained it as the omission of the answer's *fa'* (the particle introducing the consequent), meaning *fa-yudrikukumu al-mawt* ("then death will overtake you"); it is a weak reading. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may be said: it was made to follow what occupies the position of *ayna-ma takūnū*, which is *ayna-ma kuntum*, just as *laysū muṣliḥīna* was made to follow what occupies its position, which is *laysū bi-muṣliḥīna* ("they are not reformers"). So it was put in the nominative, as Zuhayr put it in the nominative: *lā ghā'ibun mā lī wa-lā ḥaramun* ("there is no absent one for me, nor a sanctuary"). This is the view of a grammarian of the school of Sibawayh." End of his words.

He means: he made ﴿يُدْرِكُكُمُ﴾ (*yudrikukumu*, "will overtake you") in the nominative (*marfūʿ*, raised) because ﴿أَيْنَمَا تَكُونُوا﴾ (*ayna-ma takūnū*, "wherever you are") is, in meaning, ﴿أَيْنَمَا كُنْتُمْ﴾ (*ayna-ma kuntum*, "wherever you were"), by imagining that he had uttered it. This is because whenever the conditional verb (*fiʿl al-sharṭ*) is in the past form in pronunciation, the imperfect verb that follows it may be read in two ways. The first is *jazm* (the jussive mood, apocopated) in agreement with the response clause (*jawāb*). The second is *rafʿ* (the indicative). There is disagreement about how the *rafʿ* is to be justified. The most correct view is that it is not the response; rather, it is by way of inversion (*al-taqdīm wa al-taʾkhīr*), and the response is omitted. When the response is omitted, the conditional verb must be in the past form, so parsing this reading on that basis is contradicted by the conditional verb being imperfect. Taking it as a conjunction with ﴿وَلا ناعِبَ﴾ (*wa-la nāʿib*, "nor any caller") is not good, because ﴿وَلا ناعِبَ﴾ is a conjunction on the basis of an imagined form (*ʿaṭf ʿalā al-tawahhum*), and conjunction on the basis of an imagined form is not an analogically valid construction.

Al-Zamakhsharī also said: it is possible that it be connected to his saying ﴿وَلا تُظْلَمُونَ فَتِيلًا﴾ (*wa-la tuẓlamūna fatīlā*, "and you will not be wronged the thread's breadth"), i.e., you will not be diminished in anything of what has been decreed for your terms, wherever you are, in the battles of wars or otherwise. Then he began with his saying ﴿يُدْرِكُكُمُ الْمَوْتُ وَلَوْ كُنْتُمْ فِي بُرُوجٍ مُشَيَّدَةٍ﴾ (*yudrikukumu al-mawtu wa-law kuntum fī burūjin mushayyadah*, "death will overtake you even if you are in towers built high"). On this view, the pause is at ﴿أَيْنَمَا تَكُونُوا﴾. End of his words.

This parsing is not sound, either in meaning or in grammatical craft. As for meaning, it is not appropriate for it to be connected to ﴿وَلا تُظْلَمُونَ فَتِيلًا﴾, because the apparent negation of wronging is in the Hereafter, according to His saying ﴿قُلْ مَتاعُ الدُّنْيا قَلِيلٌ وَالْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ لِمَنِ اتَّقى﴾ (*qul matāʿu al-dunyā qalīl, wa-al-ākhiratu khayrun li-mani ittaqā*, "Say: the enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God").

As for grammatical craft, his words, on their apparent sense, indicate that ﴿أَيْنَمَا تَكُونُوا﴾ is connected to ﴿وَلا تُظْلَمُونَ﴾, which is what he explained with his saying: i.e., you will not be diminished in anything of what has been decreed for your terms, wherever you are, in the battles of war or otherwise. This is not permissible, because *ayna-ma* is a conditional noun (*ism al-sharṭ*), so its governing element is the conditional verb that follows it. Moreover, a conditional noun cannot be preceded by its governor, so it is impossible for ﴿وَلا تُظْلَمُونَ﴾ to govern it. Rather, when something like *iḍrib Zaydan matā jāʾa* ("strike Zayd whenever he comes") occurs, it is not permissible for the governor of *matā* to be *iḍrib*.

If it is said that a response is assumed for it, indicated by what precedes it, namely ﴿وَلا تُظْلَمُونَ﴾, just as it is assumed in *iḍrib Zaydan matā jāʾa*, so the estimate is: wherever you are, then you will not be wronged the thread's breadth, i.e., nothing of your terms will be diminished, and he omitted it because what precedes indicates it. It is said in reply: the response is not omitted except when the conditional verb is in the past form, and the conditional verb here is imperfect. The Arabs say *anta ẓālimun in faʿalta* ("you are a wrongdoer if you did"), and do not say *anta ẓālimun in tafʿal* ("you are a wrongdoer if you do").

Nuʿaym ibn Maysara read *mashīdatun* with a kasra on the *yāʾ*, as a description of the towers by their doer, metaphorically, as one says *qaṣīdatun shāʿirah* ("a poem that is poetic"), whereas the poet is actually its composer. (p. 300)
