*They came to me, but I was not pleased with what they had contrived, and they had come to me with an abhorrent matter.*

Al-Akhfash said: the Arabs say of a thing when it is determined: "bayyita." Abu Razin said: "bayyita" means "allafa" (arranged, composed). It was also said: it means "hayya'a" (prepared) and "zawwara" (fabricated), and it was said: it means "qasada" (intended), and from this is the poet's saying:

*When we came upon (tabayyatna) a brother of Tamim, he gave the gift of a stingy, base miser.*

That is, "qasadna" (we intended). It was also said that al-tabyit is al-tabdil (substitution) in the dialect of Tayy. Their poet said:

*And the altering (tabyit) of my word before the King: may Allah fight you, O ungrateful servant!*

**Al-tadabbur**: contemplating the matter and looking at its ends (adbar) and what it leads to in its outcome; then it came to be used for every kind of contemplation. **Al-dabar** is abundant wealth, so named because it remains for the descendants and the later generations (adhar), as al-Zajjaj and others said.

**Al-idha'a**: making a thing apparent and spreading it. One says *dha'a yadhi'u* and *adha'a*, and it is transitive by itself and with the preposition *bi*; in that case *adha'a* has the meaning of the unaugmented verb. Abu al-Aswad said:

*They spread it among the people until it was as if it were a fire kindled on a high place with fuel-points.*

**Al-istinbat**: extraction. *Al-nabat* is the water that emerges from a well when it is first dug, and *al-inbat* and *al-istinbat* are its extraction. The poet said:

*Yes, truthful, and one who acts, the speaker who, when he speaks a word, draws water forth in the dry earth.*

Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is said of a man who is far in might and protection, that his enemy cannot reach him: "nabatan." Ka'b said:

*Near, you see him, his enemy cannot reach him, to him a nabat, refusing humiliation, stern in aspect.*

*Al-nabat* are those who extract water and plants from the earth. Al-Farra' said: *nabata* is like *istanbata*, and *nabata al-ma'* (the water) is said as *yanbutu*, with *ba'* either damma or fatha.

**Al-tahrid**: urging. **Al-tankil**: inflicting punishments of various kinds and repeating them upon the one punished; it seems to be derived from *al-nikl*, which is the shackle. **Al-kifl**: a share; a share in good is more commonly used, while *al-kifl* in evil is more commonly used than in good. **Al-muqit**: the one empowered (al-muqtadir). Al-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Muttalib said:

*And one with rancor, I restrained myself from him, and he was, despite his offense, muqit (empowered).*

That is, empowered. Al-Samaw'al said:

*Would that I knew, and would they know, when they bring it forth unfolded and I am summoned?*

*Is the favour mine, or is it upon me, when I am called to account? Indeed I am, over the reckoning, muqit.*

Abu Ubayda said: *al-muqit* is the present one (al-hadir). Ibn Faris said: *al-muqit* is the empowered one, and *al-muqit* is also the guardian and the witness. Al-Nahhas said: it is derived from *al-qut*, and *al-qut* is the measure by which a person is protected from perishing.

**Al-tahiyya**: Abd Allah ibn Idris said it means sovereignty, and he recited:

*I aim with it at Abu Qabus until I make my camp, upon his sovereignty, with my army.*

Al-Azhari said: *al-tahiyya* means sovereignty, and means permanence, and then it became to mean safety. End. Its form is *taf'ila*, and assimilation (idgham) in this form is not obligatory according to the view of al-Mazini; rather, showing the letters separately (izhar) is permissible, as they said *a'iyya* with izhar, and *a'iyya* with idgham, in the plural of *ayy*. The majority held that idgham is obligatory in *tahiyya*. The discussion on both views is mentioned in the books of grammar.

﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah; and whoever turns away, then We have not sent you as a guardian over them.﴾ He said: "Whoever loves me has loved Allah." The Jews objected and said: "This Muhammad orders the worship of Allah, and in this statement he claims lordship." So this was revealed. In another narration: the hypocrites said, "He has come close to shirk." In another narration: they said, "This man only wants to be taken as a lord, just as the Christians took Jesus." The connection between the two obediences is that he commands only what Allah has commanded him, and forbids only what Allah has forbidden, so his obedience in that is the obedience of Allah. "And whoever turns away" in hypocrisy or in a matter; "then We have not sent you" — this is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), for had it continued on the Messenger it would have said "then He has not sent him." The guardian here means: one who holds to account for deeds, or one who preserves the deeds, or one who guards against sins, or one who guards against turning away, or one empowered among the guardians; these are the views. This verse includes turning away from those who turn away, and leaving them is a mercy from Allah, and this was before the revelation of fighting.

﴿And they say, "Obedience"﴾ It was revealed concerning the hypocrites by agreement; that is, when you command them with something they say, "Obedience," meaning our matter is obedience, or from us is obedience. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible to read it in the accusative, meaning "we obeyed you with obedience," and this is like the saying of one who is convinced: "hearing and obeying" (sam'an wa ta'atan). Sibawayh's saying is similar. We heard some trusted Arabs being asked, "How did you wake up?" and he would say, "Praise be to Allah and commendation to Him," as if he had said: "my matter and my affair is the praise of Allah." If he had put "praise of Allah and commendation to Him" in the accusative, it would have been on the verb. The nominative indicates the stability and firmness of obedience. End. There is no need to mention what has not been read with it, nor to justify it, nor to compare it with other things, especially in a book which he composed in brevity, not in lengthiness.

﴿So when they go out from your presence, a group of them plots other than what you say﴾; that is, when they leave you, they plan and arrange; that is, a group of them plots other than what they say to you, O Muhammad, of displaying obedience, while inwardly they are liars and disobedient. According to this, the pronoun in *taqulu* (you say) refers to the group, and this is the view of Ibn Abbas. It was also said it refers to the Messenger; that is, other than what he says and is ordered with, O Muhammad, which is the dissent and disobedience contained in their inner selves. This interpretation is supported by the reading of Abd Allah, *bayyata mubayyitun minhum ya Muhammad* (a planner from them, O Muhammad, planned). Yahya ibn Ya'mur read *yaqulu* with the ya'; so it may be that the pronoun refers to the Messenger, and it is an iltifat, since it shifted from the address pronoun in *min 'indika* (from your presence) to the third-person pronoun. It may also refer to the group, since it means "people" or "party," and their group was singled out for planning because they would not all gather in one house, or because it is a report about those whom Allah knew would remain in their disbelief and hypocrisy. Hamza and Abu Amr assimilated *bayyata ta'ifatun* (the letters), and the rest showed them separately (izhar).

﴿And Allah records what they plot﴾; that is, He writes it in the pages of their deeds, as the guardian angels record it, so that they may be recompensed for it. Al-Zajjaj said: He records it in His book to you; that is, He sends it down in the Qur'an and knows it, and is informed of their secret. It was also said: *yaktubu* means *yu'allimu* (teaches); he expressed knowledge by writing, because it is one of its fruits.

﴿So turn away from them, and put your trust in Allah, and Allah is sufficient as a Disposer of affairs﴾. This confirms His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away, then We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾; that is, do not let your soul speak of taking revenge upon them. The meaning is not "turn away from calling them to faith and from admonishing them." Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of "turn away from them" is: do not inform about their names, lest they confront you with enmity after courtesy in speech. Then He commanded him to continue trusting in Him, for He will take vengeance on your behalf against them. This too was before the revelation of fighting.

﴿Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an﴾ The majority read *yatadabbaruna* with a ya' and a ta' after it, according to the original form. Ibn Muhaysin read it with assimilation of the ta' into the dal. This is an interrogative with the meaning of denial; that is, they do not contemplate what was revealed to you of the Revelation, nor do they turn away from it; for in its contemplation its proof becomes manifest and its light shines, and that does not become apparent to one who turns away from it and does not consider it.

﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ The apparent reading is that the pronoun in *fihi* (in it) refers to the Qur'an. This, in the science of rhetoric (bayan), is the theoretical argument, and some people call it the theological method. The reasoning of this proof is that no speaker delivers a lengthy speech without finding in his speech much discrepancy: either in description and wording, or in meaning through contradictions of reports, or by occurring contrary to what is reported, or by containing what does not fit together, or by the possibility of its being opposed. The Great Qur'an contains none of that, for it is the speech of the One who encompasses everything, suitable in eloquence, miraculous, surpassing the powers of the eloquent, and combining true reports and sound meanings; so none can produce it except the One who knows what no one other than Him knows.

Ibn Atiyya said: if a doubt occurs to anyone and he thinks there is discrepancy, then it is obligatory that he suspect his own reasoning and ask one more knowledgeable than himself. As for what some obstinate heretics claimed, that in it there are differing rulings and words that do not agree, the scholars of Islam have refuted their claim. What has come in the Qur'an of difference in tafsir (exegesis) and ta'wil (interpretation), and in qira'a (recitation), and of abrogating and abrogated (naskh and mansukh), and of decisive (muhkam) and allegorical (mutashabih), and of general (amm) and specific (khass), and of absolute (mutlaq) and restricted (muqayyad), is not what is meant in the verse; rather these are among the sciences of the Qur'an that indicate the breadth of its meanings and the rulings of its structures. Al-Zajjaj held that the pronoun in *fihi* refers to what Allah informs him of what they plan and conceal, and the meaning is: you inform them of it in accordance with how it happens, and that is evidence that it is from Allah, an unseen matter of the unseen. In the mention of *yatadabbaru al-Qur'an* (reflecting on the Qur'an) there is a rebuttal of those among the Rafidites who say that the meaning of the Qur'an cannot be understood except through the explanation of the Messenger.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 83:

﴿When there comes to them news of security or fear, they spread it abroad.﴾ Muslim narrated from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, from Umar: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) withdrew from his wives, Umar entered the mosque and heard the people saying, 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has divorced his wives.' So he went in to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him, 'Have you divorced your wives?' He said, 'No.' So he went out and called out, 'Verily, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has not divorced his wives!' Then this was revealed." It was he who derived (istinbat, drawing out a ruling by inference) the matter. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that when the Messenger (ﷺ) sent out a detachment (sariyya, a small military expedition) from among the expeditions, and it either gained the upper hand or was defeated, they would talk about it and spread it, and would not be patient until he himself was the one to report it; so this was revealed.

The pronoun in ﴿came to them﴾ refers to the hypocrites, as Ibn Abbas and the majority say. Or it refers to some of the weaker believers, as al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj say. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned no other, or it refers to both of them, as transmitted by Ibn Atiyya. Or it refers to the Jews, as some have said. The "news of security or fear" is the outcome of the detachment: its victory and booty, or its failure and misfortune, so they hasten to spread it before the Messenger informs them of it. Or it refers to what descended of revelation with the promise of victory, or of a lightening from the side of the unbelievers; the Prophet (ﷺ) would confide that to them, and they would spread it, and this would cause harm to the Muslims. Or it refers to what the Prophet was resolved upon of truce and safety for a people. "Fear" refers to the news arriving that a people are gathering against the Prophet (ﷺ), so the Muslims are afraid of them; this was said by al-Zajjaj, al-Mawardi, and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Ibn Atiyya said: The meaning is that the hypocrites used to strain to hear whatever would distress the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning his expeditions. So when a rumour of security for the Muslims arose, or they were granted a conquest, they would belittle it and diminish its importance. End of quote. The pronoun in ﴿with it﴾ refers to the matter. It has been said that it may also refer to "security or fear," and the pronoun was made singular because (aw, "or") requires one of the two.

﴿If they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those among them who seek to draw out its meaning would have known it﴾: that is, if they had referred the matter that reached them to the Messenger and to those in authority, namely the four rightly-guided caliphs and those who follow their path. This was said by Ibn Abbas, or by Abu Bakr and Umar specifically, as said by Ikrima. Or it refers to the commanders of the detachments, as said by al-Suddi, Muqatil, and Ibn Zayd. Or it refers to the scholars among the Companions, as said by al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Jurayj. The meaning is: if they had refrained from plunging into what reached them, and had sought out the matter from the Messenger and those in authority, then whoever has inquiry, reflection, and experience would have known the true nature of that matter that had arrived; and they would have informed them of the reality of it, and that the matter does not proceed according to the first report that comes.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They were a group of the weaker Muslims who had no experience of conditions and no depth of insight into affairs. Whenever a report reached them about the expeditions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whether of security and safety or of fear and disorder, they spread it abroad, and their spreading of it was corrupting. Had they referred that report to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to those in authority among them, who are the senior Companions, discerning in affairs, or those among them who used to be appointed as commanders, the ones who seek to draw out its plan would have known it through the knowledge of the planning of what they reported; that is, those who extract its strategy by their shrewdness, their experience, their knowledge of the affairs of war and its stratagems. It was said that they would stop short of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those in authority, regarding security and confidence in victory over some enemies, or regarding fear and apprehension; so they would spread it and it would be publicised, reaching the enemies, and their spreading would return as corruption. Had they referred it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to those in authority, and entrusted it to them, acting as if they had not heard it, those who devise its plan would have known how to plan it, and what to do about it and how to handle it. It was also said that they would hear from the mouths of the hypocrites some report about the expeditions which was conjectural and of unverified accuracy, and then they would spread it; so that would return as harm upon the believers. Had they referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority, and said, "We will keep silent until we hear it from them, and know whether it is of what should be spread or not," those among them who seek to draw out its meaning would have known its accuracy, and whether it is of what these spreaders spread; those who seek to draw it out from the Messenger and those in authority, that is, they would receive it from them and extract its knowledge from their side. End of his words.

These are all good interpretations, and the most suitable to the flow of the speech is this last interpretation: that the meaning is that when a report arrives concerning the security of the Muslims or their fear, it should be disseminated and referred to the Messenger and those in authority, for they will inform about the reality of the matter, and whoever asks them will know it and extract it from their side, because what the Messenger and those in authority report is truth beyond doubt.

Abu Bakr al-Razi said: In this verse there is evidence for the obligation of holding to qiyas (analogical reasoning) and ijtihad (independent reasoning) of opinion in the rulings of new events, because it is a command to refer new events to the Messenger during his lifetime, when they were in his presence, and to the scholars after his death and absence from his presence. What is explicitly stated does not need deduction, so it is established by this that among the rulings there is what is embedded in the text, for which one is charged to reach knowledge of it through inference and deduction. Al-Razi elaborated at length on this question with objections and answers, and derived rulings from the verse.

He said: It also indicates the falsity of the claim of the one who asserts the imamate (of a specific person by explicit designation), because if every ruling were explicitly stated and known to the imam, the place of deduction would disappear, and the referral to those in authority would be void. Rather, the obligation would be to refer to the imam who knows the correctness of that from its falsehood by way of the explicit text.

Shaykh Jamal al-Din Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Sulayman ibn al-Naqib, compiler of the book al-Tahrir wa al-Tahbir li-Aqwal A'immat al-Tafsir, said in that book, in its exact words: It has become clear to me regarding this verse that there is ellipsis, inversion, and displacement in the speech, and that this speech is connected to what precedes it and refers back to it, and the implied meaning is: ﴿Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ (Surah al-Nisa: 82). Had they reflected upon it, they would have known that it is from the speech of Allah; and what is difficult for them of its ambiguous (mutashabih) parts, had they referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, the ones who draw it out from them would have known it, meaning: would have known the meaning of that ambiguous matter, those who derive it from them from the people of knowledge of the Book, except a few; and that is what Allah has kept to Himself of the knowledge of His Book and the hidden meaning of His address. Then he said: ﴿When there comes to them news of security or fear, they spread it abroad.﴾ And what made that attractive to them and adorned it for them is Satan. Then he turned to the believers and said: ﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you…﴾ (the verse). Abu Talib al-Makki alluded to something of this in his well-known book Qut al-Qulub, and said that His words "except a few" are connected to His words ﴿those among them who seek to draw out its meaning﴾, and on this basis the drawing out (istinbat) is extraction of the meaning of the ambiguous word through a kind of reflection, effort, and contemplation. End of his words. And it is, as you see, a composition and an arrangement different from the composition and arrangement of the Qur'an. This man very often mentions in the Qur'an displacement and inversion. More strange than that, he makes it one of the types of the science of eloquence (ilm al-bayan), whereas our companions and the skilled grammarians consider it among the poetic licences (darurat al-shi'r). How vast is the difference between the two sayings.

Abu al-Sammal read ﴿لَعَلْمَهُ﴾ with the lam sukun-ed. Ibn Atiyya said: That is like "shajar baynahum" (where the vowel is reduced), end of quote. But it is not like it, because the sukun of the vowel in the word ʿilm is a regular analogy in the dialect of Tamim, whereas shajar is not a regular analogy; it is only by way of anomaly. The sukun of ʿalm is like the sukun in the poet's line:

If you test him, he will grow restless, as a camel past its prime of the leathery kind grows restless, its flanks and its withers sore from the saddle.

﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would surely have followed Satan, except a few.﴾ This is an address to the believers by agreement of the commentators; so said Ibn Atiyya. He said: The meaning is, had it not been for Allah's guidance to you and His direction, you would have remained upon your disbelief, which is following Satan. It has been said that the grace is the Messenger. It has been said that it is Islam. It has been said that it is the Qur'an. It has been said that the mercy is the revelation. It has been said that it is gentleness. It has been said that it is favour. It has been said that it is divine success (tawfiq). The apparent reading is that the exception is from the subject of ﴿you would have followed﴾. Al-Dahhak said: He guided all of them to faith; among them were those in whom it was so firmly established that no doubt ever occurred to them, and no suspicion of uncertainty had any hold on them; and these are the few. The rest of the Arabs who embraced Islam were not free of passing thoughts, so had it not been for the grace of Allah in granting them pure guidance, they would have gone astray and followed Satan; and the grace would be specific, that is, the mission of Muhammad and the Qur'an, because all were guided by the grace of Allah in an absolute sense.

Some said: "except a few" refers to those who were before Islam, not following Satan, upon the religion of Ibrahim; they perceived with their intellects the knowledge of Allah and affirmed His unity before the Messenger was sent, like Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, who perceived the corruption of what the Jews, the Christians, and the Arabs were upon; so he affirmed the oneness of Allah and believed in Him. On this view the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), since they are not included among those addressed by His words ﴿you would have followed﴾.

Others said: The exception is only from the following (ittiba'), so al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "except a few instances of following," thus making it an exception from the verbal noun implied by the verb ﴿you would have followed﴾. Ibn Atiyya said regarding the possibility that it is an exception from the following: that is, you all would have followed Satan except in a few matters in which you would not follow him; so he explained the exception as concerning the thing followed, the implied object, not the following itself, and so it is an exception from the implied object of following, not from following itself, and it is an exhaustive exception (mufarragh), the estimate being: you would have followed Satan in everything except a few things in which you would not follow him. If Ibn Atiyya explained it in terms of meaning, then it is correct, because from the exception it follows that the few instances of following would mean that the thing followed is few. If he explained it in terms of grammatical technique (sina'a nahwiyya), then it is not good, because the phrase "except a few instances of following" is not synonymous with "except a few matters which you would not follow him in."

Others said: His words "except a few" are an expression for non-existence, meaning: you would all have followed Satan. Ibn Atiyya said: This is an unsettled view, and it does not resemble what Sibawayh recorded of their saying: "a land which rarely produces such-and-such," meaning it does not produce it; because the association of rarity with the exception requires its occurrence. But al-Tabari mentioned it, end of quote. What Ibn Atiyya mentioned is correct, but he himself permitted it in His words: ﴿But Allah cursed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe, except a few﴾ (Surah al-Nisa: 46), and it did not seem unsettled to him there, nor did he reject it. We have already refuted him there, so refer to that place.

It has been said that ﴿except a few﴾ (Surah al-Nisa: 46) is an exception from His words ﴿they spread it abroad﴾, the estimate being: they spread it abroad, except a few. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd, and was chosen by al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', Abu Ubayd, Ibn Harb, and a group of grammarians, and al-Tabari preferred it. It has been said that it is an exception from His words ﴿those among them who seek to draw out its meaning would have known it﴾; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatada, and chosen by Ibn Uyayna. Makki said: ﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you﴾: that is, His mercy and favour, since He protected you from what He afflicted these hypocrites with, the ones He described as those who plot by night and oppose.

﴿You would surely have followed Satan﴾ is an address to those to whom He said: ﴿Take your precaution and go forth in groups, or go forth all together﴾ (Surah al-Nisa: 71). It has been said that the address is general, and the excepted few are the community of the Messenger, because they are few in comparison with the disbelievers. And in the authentic hadith: "You are only like a white mark on a black ox."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 84:**

﴿So fight in the way of Allah; you are not held responsible except for yourself, and urge the believers.﴾ It was said that it was revealed concerning Badr al-Sughra (the Lesser Badr). He called the people to go out, and Abu Sufyan had arranged a meeting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there. Some of the people disliked going out, so this was revealed. He went out, and with him were only seventy men. He did not turn back to anyone, and even if no one had followed him, he would have gone out alone.

The occasion of this verse is that, when Allah mentioned in the verses before it their discouraging others from fighting, He digressed from that to the point that death overtakes every person, even if he takes refuge in the strongest refuge, so there is no benefit in fleeing from fighting. He followed this with what He followed it with of the evil speech of the hypocrites toward the Messenger, peace be upon him, and their conduct with him, showing obedience with words while opposing it in deed. He rebuked them for not reflecting on what the Messenger brought of the Qur'an, in which fighting was prescribed for them. Then He returned to the matter of fighting. This is the habit of Arabic speech: it speaks about one matter, then digresses from it to another matter that has relevance and connection to it, and then returns to the first.

Here, the fa' (فاء) is conjoining a sentence to a sentence that follows it. As for one who claims that the basis of the conjunction with fa' is that it is connected to His saying ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight?﴾ [An-Nisa: 75], or to His saying ﴿then We will give him a great reward﴾ [An-Nisa: 74], this is an interpretation based on meaning with an implied condition, i.e., "If you desire success, then fight." Or that it is conjoined to His saying ﴿So fight the allies of Satan﴾ [An-Nisa: 76], but that is far-fetched. The apparent meaning of the command is that it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, and this is reinforced by ﴿you are not held responsible except for yourself﴾. Al-Zamakhshari took it as having an implied condition, saying: "That is, if they abandon you and leave you alone, you are not held responsible except for yourself alone, that you advance it to jihad, for Allah is your helper, not the troops. So if He wills, He will help you alone, just as He helps you when there are thousands around you." End of quotation. Al-Zajjaj preceded him in this, saying: "He commanded him to wage jihad, even if he fights alone, because He guaranteed him victory." Ibn Atiyyah said: "We have never found in any report that fighting was obligatory upon the Prophet alone without the community even once. So the meaning, and Allah knows best, is that it is addressed to the Prophet in form, but it is an example of what is said to each individual concerning himself. That is, you, O Muhammad, and every one of your community, is told: 'So fight in the way of Allah.' For this reason, every believer should be inclined to strive, even if alone." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I will certainly fight them until my two neck-veins are alone [i.e., until I stand alone]" (p-309), and the saying of Abu Bakr at the time of the Ridda (apostasy wars): "Even if my right hand opposed me, I would fight it with my left."

As for the meaning of ﴿you are not held responsible except for yourself﴾: that is, you are not held responsible in fighting except for yourself; so fight even if you are alone. It was said that the meaning is "except your capacity and your ability." The word nafs (نفس, self) is used to express strength; it is said: "his nafs fell," meaning his strength fell. Al-Jumhur (the majority) read ﴿lā tukallafu﴾ (لا تُكَلَّفُ) as a statement in the passive voice. They said the clause is in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause. It is also permissible that it be an informative statement from Allah to His Prophet, not a circumstantial clause, establishing for him that he is not held responsible for the affairs of others among the believers; he is held responsible only for his own affair. It was read as ﴿lā nukallifu﴾ (لا نُكَلِّفُ) with the nūn and with kasra on the lām, and it admits both aspects of i'rab (grammatical analysis): the circumstantial and the resumptive (isti'nāf). ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar read ﴿lā tukallaf﴾ (لا تُكَلَّفْ) with the tā' and fatḥa on the lām and jazm (the apocopate), as a response to the command. Allah the Exalted commanded him to urge the believers to fight and to stir their resolve toward martyrdom.

﴿It may be that Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve﴾. Ikrimah and others said: "'Asā (عسى, "it may be") from Allah is binding, while from people it is an expectation and hope." Those who disbelieved are the disbelievers of Quraysh. Allah the Exalted did restrain their might, and Abu Sufyan showed a desire to abandon fighting. He said: "This is a year of drought, and they had nothing with them but sawiq (a kind of parched grain), and they would only meet in a year of abundance," so he returned with them. It was said that the restraint of might will occur at the descent of ʿIsa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him). It was said that it was on the day of al-Ḥudaybiyya. It was said it concerns those upon whom the jizya (poll tax) was imposed. The majority hold to what we have mentioned earlier, that this was at their going out to Badr al-Sughra. The apparent meaning in this is that the restraint of the might of those who disbelieved is not restricted to what they mentioned, and specifying it with something requires evidence.

﴿And Allah is stronger in might and stronger in punishment﴾. This is a strengthening of the hearts of the believers, and that Allah's might is greater than the might of the disbelievers. He had hoped for the restraint of their might, then mentioned what He has prepared for them of punishment, and that Allah the Exalted is the most severe in punishment. So He mentioned His strength and His power over them, and what their affair will lead to of torment. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "﴿and stronger in punishment﴾; that is, a humiliating punishment." The more apparent view is that the comparative form (af'al al-tafḍīl) here is in its usual use. It was said it is of the type: "Honey is sweeter than vinegar," because their might in relation to His might is nothing at all.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 85–86:

﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share in it, and whoever intercedes with an evil intercession will bear a portion of it.﴾ Some said: whoever is an intercessor for the single one (witr) of your companions, O Muhammad, in the jihad, so that he aids them in fighting their enemy, will have a share in the jihad; or whoever intercedes for the single one (witr) of Islam by assisting the Muslims, that is a good deed and he has a share in it. What led them to this interpretation is the earlier mention of fighting and the command to it. Al-Tabari said something close to this. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and others said: it concerns people's needs; whoever intercedes for a benefit will have a share, and whoever intercedes for a harm will bear a portion.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the good intercession is that in which the right of a Muslim is observed, by which harm is averted from him or good is brought to him, which is sought for the sake of God's countenance, for which no bribe is taken, and which concerns a permissible matter, not one of God's prescribed limits (hudud) or one of the rights. The evil one is what is contrary to that. End of quotation.

This is an elaboration of what al-Hasan said: the good intercession is in righteousness and obedience, and the evil one is in sins. It was also said that the good intercession is supplication (da'wah) for a Muslim, since it is in the sense of intercession to God Most High. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever prays for his brother in his absence, it is answered for him, and the angel says to him: 'And for you is the like of that share.'" And supplication against a Muslim is the opposite of that. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said: the good intercession here is reconciliation between two people, and the evil one is causing discord between them and spreading tale-bearing. It was also said that the good intercession is to intercede with a disbeliever so as to clarify for him the proofs, so that perhaps he will become Muslim, and the evil one is to intercede with a Muslim, perhaps he will apostatize or become a hypocrite. The apparent meaning is that (man) indicates cause: that is, a share of good because of it, and a portion of evil because of it. It was mentioned earlier in al-Mufradat that al-kifl means the share.

Aban ibn Taghlib said: al-kifl means the like. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it means the burden and sin. The word used for the share is different: it is expressed with the term kifl in the evil intercession, because it is most commonly used for evil, although it has been used for good in His saying: ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ [al-Hadid: 28]. They said: it is a metaphor from the kifl of a camel, which is a cloth turned around its hump so that one may ride upon it, and it was called kifl because it does not cover the whole back, but only a portion of it.

﴿And God is ever Muqit over all things﴾; that is, Muqtadir (All-Powerful), as said by al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and al-Kisa'i. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: Hafiz (Preserver) and Shahid (Witness). 'Abdullah ibn Kathir said: Wasib (Constant), a guardian over affairs. It was said: al-Muhit (the All-Encompassing). It was said: al-Hasib (the Reckoner). It was said: al-Mujazi (the Requiter). It was said: the one who is persistent over a thing, constantly upon it. Ibn Kathir said: this is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas. These sayings are close to one another, since some of them imply the meaning of others. Al-Tabari said, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am over the reckoning Muqit﴾, that it is from a meaning other than those mentioned earlier, and that it means mawquf (appointed). This is weakened by the fact that the form of the active participle would then carry the meaning of the passive participle. Others said: its meaning is Muqtadir.

﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it, or return it.﴾ The apparent meaning is that the greeting here is the salam, and that the one greeted is given the choice between returning something better than it or returning its equivalent, so the particle (aw) here is for choice. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: greet with better than it if he is a Muslim; or return it if a disbeliever greets you, and if he is a Magian, then the particle (aw) here is for variety. What appears is that the disbeliever is not returned the same greeting, because the prescribed reply to them is to say to them: "And upon you," and nothing is to be added to that. So His saying "when you are greeted" means "when the Muslims greet you." This is the view of 'Ata'. From al-Hasan: it is permissible to say to a disbeliever: "And upon you the salam," but not say "and the mercy of God," for that is an invocation of forgiveness. From al-Sha'bi: he said to a Christian who greeted him, "And upon you the salam and the mercy of God," and it was said to him, and he replied: "Does one not live in the mercy of God?" Those who held this view seem to have taken the generality of ﴿when you are greeted﴾, but that opposes the prophetic text: "Say: and upon you." The manner of returning the better greeting is that when he says "Salamun 'alayka," you reply "'Alayka as-salam wa rahmatullah." If he says "Salamun 'alayka wa rahmatullah," you say "'Alayka as-salam wa rahmatullah wa barakatuh." If a Muslim says this in full, it is returned to him in the same form. It is reported from 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and others that the furthest extent of the salam is to the blessing (barakah).

The verse indicates that returning the greeting is obligatory by the command, but it does not indicate that initiating it is obligatory; rather it is a strongly recommended sunnah. This is the position of most scholars, and the majority hold that the People of the Book should not be initiated with the salam; a group deviated and permitted it. Al-Zamakhshari and others have lengthily mentioned many branch rulings on the salam, whose subject is the science of jurisprudence (fiqh). Mujahid restricted this greeting to jihad, saying: when you are greeted in your journey with the greeting of Islam, (do not say to one who offers you the salam, "You are not a believer") for the rulings of Islam apply to them. Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim reported from Malik that this verse concerns the blessing of one who sneezes and the response to one who blesses him. Ibn 'Atiyyah and others among Malik's companions weakened this view. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: because there is no indication in the text for that. As for the response to one who blesses, it falls by analogy within the meaning of returning a greeting, and this is the direction of Malik, if that is correct. Others said that what is meant by the greeting here is guidance and kindness, and that the one who gives something of this kind has the right to be given its like or something better.

Ibn Khuwayzimanda said: it is permissible to interpret this verse as applying to a gift given as recompense. Some people have filled their compilation here with branch rulings on warfare, the salam, the blessing of one who sneezes and gifts, whose subject is the science of jurisprudence. They also mentioned, among what enters into greeting, what accompanies the salam at meeting and the handshake, and that the Messenger (ﷺ) commanded it and did it along with the salam and embracing, and that the first to establish it was Abraham (peace be upon him), and the kiss. From al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿compassionate among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29], he said: a man would meet his brother and would not part from him until he embraced him and kissed him. From 'Ali: the kiss of a child is mercy, the kiss of a wife is desire, the kiss of parents is righteousness, the kiss of a brother is religion, the kiss of a just ruler is obedience, and the kiss of a scholar is reverence for God Most High. Al-Qushayri said: in the verse there is instruction for them in good companionship and the manners of fellowship, and that whoever bestows a favour upon you, that becomes a debt upon you; if you exceed his action, well and good, otherwise do not fall short of its like.

﴿Indeed, God is ever Reckoner over all things﴾; that is, Hasib (Reckoning) from the reckoning (hisab), or Muhsib from ihsab, which is sufficiency (kifayah). Either it is fa'il for intensification, or it is in the sense of muf'il.

These verses contain, in terms of rhetoric (bayan) and figures of speech (badi'), the following types: the iltifat (shift of grammatical person) in His saying ﴿So We did not send you﴾ [al-Nisa': 80]; the repetition in ﴿whoever obeys﴾ [al-Nisa': 80], ﴿has indeed obeyed﴾ [al-Nisa': 80], and in bayyata and yubayyitun, and in the name of God in several places, and in ashadd, and in ﴿whoever intercedes with an intercession﴾. The paronomasia of identical roots (tajnis mumathil) in yut'i and ata'a, in bayyata and yubayyitun, and in ﴿huyyitum﴾ ﴿fahayyu﴾. The paronomasia of different roots (tajnis mughayir) in tawakkal and wakil, in ﴿whoever intercedes with an intercession﴾, and in ﴿when you are greeted with a greeting﴾. The interrogation intended as denial in ﴿Do they not reflect?﴾ [al-Nisa': 82]. Antithesis (tibaq) in ﴿of security or fear﴾ [al-Nisa': 83], and in ﴿a good intercession﴾ and ﴿an evil intercession﴾. Tawjih (double meaning) in ﴿other than what you say﴾ [al-Nisa': 81]. Theological argumentation, called the dialectical method (madhhab kalami), in ﴿had it been from other than God﴾ [al-Nisa': 82]. Address to the specific while meaning others in ﴿so fight﴾ [al-Nisa': 84]; metaphor in ﴿in the way of God﴾ [al-Nisa': 84] and in ﴿that God may restrain the might﴾ [al-Nisa': 84]; and af'al in other than comparison in ashadd. The application of the whole to a part in ﴿the might of those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Nisa': 84], where the wording is general and the meaning is Badr al-Sughra. And ellipsis in a number of places where the context requires it.
