﴿Allah, there is no god but Him. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ ﴿Why have you become two groups concerning the hypocrites, when Allah has reverted them for what they earned? Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has led astray? And whomever Allah leads astray, you will never find for him a way.﴾ [An-Nisa: 88] ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike. So do not take from them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from them any ally or helper.﴾ [An-Nisa: 89] ﴿Except those who reach a people between you and whom there is a covenant, or who come to you with their breasts constricted from fighting you or fighting their own people. And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you. So if they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you a way against them.﴾ [An-Nisa: 90] ﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people. Whenever they are returned to disorder, they are reverted into it. So if they do not withdraw from you, offer you peace, and restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you overtake them. Those – We have made for you against them a clear authority.﴾ [An-Nisa: 91] ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by error. And whoever kills a believer by error must free a believing slave and pay blood-money (diyah) to his family, unless they forgo it as charity. If he was from a people hostile to you and he was a believer, then [the penalty is] freeing a believing slave. And if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant, then blood-money must be paid to his family and a believing slave freed. But whoever does not find [the means], then fasting two consecutive months – a repentance from Allah. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ [An-Nisa: 92] ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment.﴾ [An-Nisa: 93]

Al-Irkas (الإرْكاس): returning and bringing back. It has been said that it is derived from its last part upon its first, and al-Rikss (الرِّكْس) is what is returned (refuse). From this is his saying concerning the dung: "This is rikss." Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"So they were reverted into the boiling fire, for they were sinners, and they uttered falsehood and lies."

Al-Kisa'i and al-Nadr ibn Shumayl related that rakasa and arkasa have one meaning, i.e., he returned them. It is said: rakkasa, with shaddah, has the meaning of arkasa, and irtakasa means he returned. It has also been said that arkasahu means he destroyed him. He said:

"By your ill omen you reverted me into vice, and you struck me with various kinds of hardship."

It has been said that it means he led them astray. The poet said:

"You reverted me from the path of guidance, and made me an example for enemies."

It has been said that it means he overturned him. This was said by al-Zajjaj, who said:

"They were reverted into a dark trial, like the blackness of night, followed by trials."

Al-Diyah (الدِّيَةُ): what is owed in money for killing. In the pre-Islamic period it had rulings and amounts, and in the Sharia it has rulings and amounts; some of them will be mentioned later. Its origin is a verbal noun (masdar) applied to the mentioned wealth. You say: from it, wada yadi wad'an and diyah, just as you say: washa yashi washyan and washiyah. Its pattern in the sound-lam form is: zinah and 'idah.

Al-Ta'ammud (التَّعَمُّد) and al-'Amd (العَمْد): intending a thing and aiming toward it.

﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, there is no doubt about it﴾. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning those who doubted the resurrection, so Allah swore that He would surely resurrect them. Its connection to what precedes it is clear: when He mentioned that Allah is ever Reckoner over all things, He followed it with informing about Allah's oneness, the gathering, and the resurrection from the graves for judgment. It is possible that "there is no god but Him" is a statement about Allah, and it is possible that it is a parenthetical clause, with the predicate being the clause sworn to. The oath has been omitted here because it is known. As for "ila" (إلى), it is either in its own sense, meaning the end point, and the gathering is into the graves; or the verb is taken to include the meaning of "li-yahshuranna" (He will surely assemble you), so it takes "ila." It has been said that "ila" may mean "fi" (in), as they interpreted it in the saying of al-Nabigha:

"So do not leave me with threats, as if I were among people a mangy camel coated with tar."

That is, "among the people." It has also been said that "ila" means "ma'a" (with). "Al-Qiyamah" and "al-Qiyam" have one meaning, like "al-Tilabah" and "al-Tilab." It has been said that the ta' marbutah was added for emphasis, because of the intensity of the terror that occurs in it. It was named thus either because of their standing up from the graves, or because of their standing for reckoning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6]. Since resurrection is possible by reason and obligatory by revelation, He confirmed it with the oath before it and with the sentence after it, His saying: "there is no doubt about it." The pronoun in "fihi" (فِيهِ) may refer to the Day, which is the apparent meaning, or it may refer to the verbal noun implied in His saying: "li-yajma'annakum." The explanation of "la rayba fihi" was already given at the beginning of al-Baqarah [2].

﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is negation; the implied sense is: no one is more truthful in statement than Allah. There are two views on explaining "hadith" (الحَدِيث) as "report" or "promise," and the more apparent here is "report." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is because falsehood enters human speech only due to fear, hope, or bad disposition, and these are negated with respect to Allah the Exalted. Truthfulness in its reality is that what flows on the tongue of the speaker agrees with what is in his heart and with the matter he reports about in its existence. End of quote. Al-Maturidi said: That is, you accept one another's speech while admitting its possibility of truth and falsehood; so if you accept the speech of one who is impossible to lie about, then in every matter he informs you of, it is all the more so. Al-Zamakhshari was lengthy here, to show his doctrine, and he said: Falsehood is impossible for Him, because lying is a disgraceful act that is avoided, and it is reporting about a thing contrary to what it is. Whoever lies does so only because he needs to lie to gain some benefit or repel some harm, or he is free from it but is ignorant of his independence, or he is ignorant of its ugliness, or he is foolish and does not distinguish between truth and falsehood in his reports, and does not care which he utters, and perhaps lying is sweeter on his palate than truth. It is related from some fools that he was rebuked for lying, so he said: "If your uvula gargled with it you would not leave it." It was said to a liar: "Have you ever spoken truthfully?" He said: "If I were not truthful in my saying, I would not have said it." So He is the Wise, the Self-Sufficient, to whom needs do not apply, the Knower of every known thing, exalted above it as He is exalted above all other ugliness. End of quote. His speech is excessive and does not suit this book, since it is a concise tafsir (exegesis).

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "aṣdaq" (أَصْدَقُ) with the sad pronounced as a zay-sound (ishmam), and likewise in every similar case where a sakin sad is followed by a dal, such as "yaṣduqun" and "taṣdiyah." As for changing it to a pure zay in that case, it is the dialect of Kalb. They recited:

"May Allah increase in his goods the protector of his family's honor, whose truthful ones are with him."

He means: "with his ṣādaqāt" (true ones).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 88:

﴿So what is the matter with you concerning the hypocrites, that you are divided into two groups?﴾ They have mentioned concerning its occasion of revelation various sayings, which they lengthened, and the summary of them is: They are a people who embraced Islam, then the climate of Medina disagreed with them (istawbaʾū al-Madīnah), so they left. It was said to them: "Do you not have in the Messenger an excellent example?" Or: some people who returned from Uhud when the Messenger went out, and this is in the Two Sahihs from the saying of Zayd ibn Thabit. Or: some people in Mecca who professed Islam while they were aiding the disbelievers, so they left Mecca. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: they went out for a need of theirs; then some of the Muslims said, "Go out to them and kill them, for they support your enemy."

Others said: "How can we kill them, when they have professed Islam?" This was narrated by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah from Ibn ʿAbbas. Or: a people who came to Medina, showed Islam, then returned to Mecca and openly displayed polytheism. Or: a people who announced faith in Mecca and refrained from emigration; this was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. Or: the ʿUrayniyyun who raided the herds and killed Yasar. Or: the hypocrites who spoke in the matter of the slander (ḥadīth al-ifk).

Whatever of these sayings implies that they were in Medina is refuted by His saying: ﴿until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾ [an-Nisa: 89], unless you take emigration to mean abandoning what Allah has forbidden. The meaning is: He, the Exalted, rebuked them for their disagreement about the hypocrisy of one who had openly displayed hypocrisy; that is, whoever openly displayed hypocrisy is definitively judged a hypocrite, even if their hypocrisy was not manifest; otherwise the name of hypocrisy would not be applied to him. ﴿Concerning the hypocrites﴾ is connected to what is connected to ﴿lakum﴾ (for you), and it is in a state of being, i.e., "what is the matter with you concerning the hypocrites." Or it is in the sense of ﴿fi'atayn﴾ (two groups), i.e., two factions regarding the affair of the hypocrites. ﴿Fi'atayn﴾ is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl) according to the Basrans, from the pronoun of address in ﴿lakum﴾, and its governing element is the governing element of ﴿lakum﴾. The Kufans held that it is accusative by the implied ﴿kāna﴾ (was), i.e., "you were two groups." They permit "mā laka al-shātima," meaning "you were the one reviling," but according to the Basrans this is not permitted, because for them it is a state (ḥāl), and a state cannot be definite.

﴿And Allah has reverted them (arkasahum) for what they earned﴾: i.e., He returned them and sent them back into their disbelief; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj chose: "He ruined them" (awbaqahum). It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "or He misguided them"; this was said by al-Suddi. Or: "He destroyed them"; this was said by Qatadah, or "He overturned them," said by al-Zajjāj. All of these are close in meaning. Whoever expressed it as destruction has taken up a necessary implication of reverting. The meaning of "for what they earned" is: by what Allah caused to occur among them of opposition; and that reverting is by the creation and origination of Allah, while it is attributed to the servant as acquisition (kasb).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "And Allah has reverted them": i.e., He returned them to the ruling of the polytheists, as they were, for what they earned of apostasy, joining the polytheists, and their scheming against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Or: He reverted them into disbelief by forsaking them until they committed it, since He knew the sickness of their hearts. End of quote. This is in accordance with his Muʿtazili creed; so he does not attribute reverting to Allah in reality, but interprets it in the sense of abandonment and withholding of grace, or as a judgment that they are of the polytheists, since they are the doers of disbelief and its originators, not Allah; exalted is Allah above their saying.

ʿAbd Allah read: "rakasahum" in the triliteral form. It was also read: "rakkasahum" with the doubling, and "rakasū fīhā." Al-Raghib said: al-riks and al-niks are abasement, and al-riks is more intense than al-niks, because al-niks is what has its lower part made its upper part, while al-riks originally is what returns as refuse after having been food; so it is like al-rijs (filth), and He described their deeds by it, as He said: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are unclean﴾ [at-Tawbah: 28]. And "arkasahu" is more intense than "rakasahu," just as "asqāhu" is more intense than "saqāhu." End of quote. This clause is in the position of a state, He rebuking them for their disagreement about these hypocrites, while Allah has already returned them into disbelief; and one whom Allah returns to disbelief is not disputed concerning his disbelief.

﴿Do you wish to guide one whom Allah has misguided?﴾ This is an interrogative of denial; that is, whomever Allah wills to be astray, no one wills his guidance, lest his will contradict the will of Allah, the Exalted; and whomever Allah has decreed for misguidance cannot be guided. Whoever Allah has misguided includes those who were reverted and others whom Allah has misguided; it is as if it were said: "Do you wish to guide these hypocrites, and whoever else Allah has misguided among others?" Their inclusion within the generality of ﴿man﴾ (whoever) after His saying ﴿and Allah has reverted them﴾ is by way of emphasis, since they were mentioned first specifically and second as included within the generality. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Do you wish to make them among those guided? Whom Allah has misguided: whom He has placed among the astray and judged so, or forsaken until he went astray," end of quote. This is in keeping with his Muʿtazili method, that he does not attribute misguidance to Allah in its true sense.

﴿And whoever Allah misguides, you will not find for him a way﴾: i.e., you will not find a way to his guidance. The meaning is: for the creation of guidance in his heart, and this is what is negated. Guidance in the sense of direction and clarification belongs to the Messengers. The address shifted from addressing them to addressing the Messenger, by way of emphasis regarding those in dispute; for if he does not have this, then it is more fitting that they do not have it. It was said: whoever Allah deprives of reward and Paradise, no one finds a way to them for him. It was said: whoever Allah destroys, there is no one with a way to his salvation from destruction. It was said: whoever Allah misguides, you will not find for him an exit or a proof.

They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so that you would be equal (﴿ودُّوا لَوْ تَكْفُرُونَ كَما كَفَرُوا فَتَكُونُونَ سَواءً﴾). Whoever holds that *law* (لَوْ, "if/would that") is a verbal noun particle (مَصْدَرِيَّة, *masdariyya*, a particle that turns the following verb into a verbal noun) takes the sense to be: "They wish for your disbelief as they have disbelieved." Whoever holds that *law* is a particle indicating that one thing would have happened because another thing would have happened, takes the object of *waddū* (ودُّوا, "they wish") to be omitted, and the answer of *law* (جَوابَ لَوْ) to be omitted. The sense is: "They wish for your disbelief, if you were to disbelieve as they have disbelieved, and you were to be equal, they would be delighted by that." The reason for their wishing this is either envy at the evident rise of Islam, as He says in its parallel: ﴿حَسَدًا مِن عِنْدِ أنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ ("out of envy from themselves," Qur'an 2:109), or preference for them to be worshippers of idols, since they see the believers as having no basis. This is a disclosure by God Most High of their corrupt belief, and a warning to the believers against them. *Fa-takūnūna* (فَتَكُونُونَ, "and you would be") is coordinated (مَعْطُوفٌ) on His saying *takfurūna* (تَكْفُرُونَ, "you disbelieve").

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It would also be permissible for it to be put in the subjunctive as the answer to the wish (جَوابِ التَّمَنِّي), and the meaning would be: 'They wish for your disbelief and your being with them in one way regarding the error they are upon and following the religion of the forefathers.'" End of quote. The fact that the wish is expressed by a verb, and that it would have an answer, is open to question. What is transmitted is that the verb is put in the subjunctive after the answer to a wish when it is with a particle, such as *layta* (لَيْتَ, "would that") and *law*, unless these two have taken on the meaning of wishing. But when it is with a verb, it requires a hearing (سَماع) from the Arabs. Rather, even if it came, the answering function would not be realised in it, because *waddа* (وَدَّ, "to wish"), which indicates wishing, has as its complement only verbal nouns, not entities. So when the verb is put in the subjunctive after the *fa* (فاء), the *fa* cannot be determined to be the *fa* of an answer, because it is possible that it is of the type of coordinating a supposed verbal noun onto an actually stated verbal noun; so it would be of the type of: *lalubsu ʿabāʾatin wa-taqarru ʿaynī* ("the wearing of a cloak and my eye being cooled").

﴿فَلا تَتَّخِذُوا مِنهم أوْلِياءَ حَتّى يُهاجِرُوا في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of God"). When He stated their disbelief, and that they wished you to be like them, their enmity became clear because of the difference of the two religions. So God Most High forbade that any of them be taken as an ally, even if they believe, until they openly show the true emigration (الهِجْرَةُ الصَّحِيحَةُ, *al-hijra al-ṣaḥīḥa*, emigration (*hijra*) from the land of disbelief to the land of Islam), which is the greater part of faith, not the greater part of worldly advantage. He limited the condition to emigration only, because it includes faith. In this verse there is evidence for the obligation of emigration (الهِجْرَةِ, *hijra*) to the Prophet ﷺ in Medina. Its ruling remained so until Mecca was conquered, and then it was abrogated (نُسِخَ, *nusikha*, abrogated; *naskh*, abrogation, the cancelling of a ruling by a later one) by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "There is no emigration after the conquest; but there is struggle (*jihād*) and intention, and when you are called to go forth, then go forth." Al-Hasan al-Basri (الحَسَنُ البَصْرِيُّ) disagreed, saying that it is obligatory and its ruling has not been abrogated, and it remains, so that residing in the land of polytheism after accepting Islam is forbidden. The consensus (إجْماعُ) of the legal schools (أهْلِ المَذاهِبِ) is against him. Qadi Abu Ya'la and others said: whoever is able to emigrate but is not able to openly practise his religion, emigration is obligatory for him, because of God Most High's saying: ﴿ألَمْ تَكُنْ أرْضُ اللَّهِ واسِعَةً فَتُهاجِرُوا فِيها﴾ ("Was not the earth of God spacious, so that you could emigrate therein?" Qur'an 4:97). Whoever is able to openly practise his religion, emigration is recommended (اسْتُحِبَّتْ) for him. Whoever is not able to openly practise his religion, nor able to move, like the decrepit old man and the chronically disabled, emigration is not recommended for him.

﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَخُذُوهم واقْتُلُوهم حَيْثُ وجَدْتُمُوهم ولا تَتَّخِذُوا مِنهم ولِيًّا ولا نَصِيرًا﴾ ("So if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them an ally or a helper"). That is: if they turn away from faith openly shown by true emigration, then their ruling is the ruling of disbelievers: they are to be killed wherever they are found (p-315) within the sacred and non-sacred areas, and they are to be totally avoided, even if they offer you alliance and support; so do not accept from them.

﴿إلّا الَّذِينَ يَصِلُونَ إلى قَوْمٍ بَيْنَكم وبَيْنَهم مِيثاقٌ أوْ جاءُوكم حَصِرَتْ صُدُورُهم أنْ يُقاتِلُوكم أوْ يُقاتِلُوا قَوْمَهُمْ﴾ ("except those who reach a people between whom and you there is a covenant, or who come to you with their hearts constricted about fighting you or fighting their own people," Qur'an 4:90). This is an exception (اسْتِثْناءٌ, *istithnāʾ*, exception) from His saying: ﴿فَخُذُوهم واقْتُلُوهُمْ﴾ ("seize them and kill them"). The *wuṣūl* (وُصُولُ, "reaching") here means: arriving at a people. It was said that its meaning is "they are related by lineage" (يَنْتَسِبُونَ), as Abu 'Ubayda said. And al-A'sha recited:

"When they joined, they said to Bakr ibn Wa'il, and Bakr had taken them captive, while the noses were humbled."

Al-Nahhas said: this is a tremendous error, because it goes to the view that God forbade the killing of anyone between whom and the Muslims there is lineage; yet between the polytheists and the earlier Muslims there were lineages; that is: the Messenger and those with him fought those who were related to them by true lineage, let alone by affiliation. Al-Nahhas said: More extreme in ignorance than this is the saying of one who said that it was abrogated, because the people of interpretation (أهْلَ التَّأْوِيلِ) are unanimous that its abrogating text is *Bara'a* (Surat al-Tawba), and it was revealed only after the conquest, and after wars had ended. Al-Tabari agreed with him on this.

Al-Qurtubi said: Some scholars took the meaning of "they are related" to be "security" (الأمانِ), or that they affiliate themselves with the people of security, not in the sense of lineage that is kinship. End of quote. Ikrima said: "a people" are the people of Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir al-Aslami, who made a truce with the Messenger on the condition that he would not help him, nor would he help against him, and whoever took refuge with them would have the same as Hilal. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that they are the Banu Bakr ibn Zayd Manat. The majority hold that they are Khuza'a and Dhu Khuza'a. Muqatil said: Khuza'a and Banu Mudlij. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This ruling was at the beginning of Islam, before the obedience of the people had become firm; so the Messenger of God ﷺ had made truces with Arab tribes such as the clan of Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir al-Aslami, Suraqa ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum, and Khuzayma ibn Amir ibn 'Abd Manaf. This verse decreed that whoever of the polytheists, who have no covenant between them and the Prophet ﷺ, reaches these people of the covenant, enters among them, and does as they do of truce, then there is no way against him. Ikrima, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: Then when Islam became strong and its helpers multiplied, this verse and the one after it were abrogated by what is in Surat Bara'a. End of quote. It was also said they are Khuza'a and Khuzayma ibn 'Abd Manaf. Those whose hearts were constricted are the Banu Mudlij; they joined the Quraysh and were with them.

From Ibn 'Abbas: they are a people from among the disbelievers who withdrew from the Muslims on the day of the conquest of Mecca; so they were neither with the disbelievers nor with the Muslims; then that was abrogated by the verse of fighting.

The basic form of the exception is that it be connected (مُتَّصِلًا, *muttaṣil*, connected exception, where the excluded item belongs to the same category as what precedes it), and the apparent meaning of the verse and of these sayings that preceded is that it is a connected exception. The meaning is: except the disbelievers who reach a people who are hostile, or who reach a people who came to you without fighting you, nor fighting their own people. If *jāʾūkum* (جاءُوكم, "came to you") is coordinated onto the position of the attribute of "a people," then both coordinations were permitted by al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, but they preferred coordination onto the relative clause (الصِّلَةِ). Ibn 'Atiyya, after mentioning coordination onto the relative clause, said: "It may also be on His saying: *bainakum wa-baynahum mīthāq* (بَيْنَكم وبَيْنَهم مِيثاقٌ, 'between you and them is a covenant'), and the meaning in the two coordinations is different." End of quote. The difference is that the excluded items are either two categories: one reaching a treaty partner, and one coming and refraining from fighting; or one category which differs according to whether the one reached is a treaty partner or one refraining. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This too is a ruling that was before the affairs of Islam became firm; so the polytheist who came to the abode of Islam peacefully, unwilling to fight his people with the Muslims, nor to fight the Muslims with his people, has no way against him. This too was abrogated by what is in *Bara'a*. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The better option is coordination on the reason (العِلَّةِ) for His saying: ﴿فَإنِ اعْتَزَلُوكم فَلَمْ يُقاتِلُوكُمْ﴾ ("if they withdraw from you and do not fight you," Qur'an 4:90), and so on, after His saying "seize them and kill them," so that He established that their refraining from fighting is one of the two causes that make them deserve the removal of any attack on them and the abandonment of striking them. If you say: each of the two connections has an effect on the validity of the exception, and the deserving of leaving them alone comes from connection to the treaty partners and connection to those refraining, so why not permit that coordination be onto the attribute of "a people," and that His saying "if they withdraw from you" be a confirmation of the ruling on their connection to the refrainers, their mixing with them, and their going along with their ways? I say: that is permissible, but the first is more apparent and more in line with the style of the discourse. It was more apparent and more in line with the style of the discourse because the excluded item is the subject spoken of and the one ruled for, unlike the ruling of the excluding item. When coordinated onto the relative clause, it is the subject spoken of; when coordinated onto the attribute, it is not the subject spoken of, but rather a qualification (تَقْيِيدًا) on the "people" who are the qualifier in the relative clause whose owner is the subject spoken of. Whenever it is unclear whether the relation should be predicative in meaning or qualifying, it is more appropriate to take it as predicative, because of the awkwardness that results from the qualifying reading. This is from the standpoint of grammatical craft. As for what results from each of the two coordinations in meaning: their refraining from fighting becomes the cause of abandoning any attack on them, and that is a near cause; and this is in coordination onto the relative clause. Their reaching a people who abandon fighting becomes a cause of abandoning any attack on them, and that is a distant cause; and this is in coordination onto the attribute. Attending to the near cause is better than attending to the distant one. On the view that the exception is connected from the object of "seize them and kill them," the meaning is: God Most High required the killing of the disbeliever, except if he is a treaty partner or included in the ruling of a treaty partner, or one who has abandoned fighting; for killing them is not permitted. The majority's view is that the two excluded groups are disbelievers.

Abu Muslim said: When God Most High required emigration of everyone who had accepted Islam, He excepted whoever had an excuse, saying: ﴿إلّا الَّذِينَ يَصِلُونَ﴾ ("except those who reach"). They are a people from among the believers who intended to reach the Messenger for emigration and support; but on their way there were disbelievers, so they could not find a way to him because of fear of those disbelievers; so they came to a people between whom and the Muslims there was a treaty, and they stayed with them until they could be delivered. Then He excepted, after that, those who came to the Messenger and the Companions, because he fears God regarding it, and also does not fight the disbelievers, because they are his relatives, or because his wives and children remained among them, so he fears that if he fought them they would kill his children and companions. These two groups of Muslims may not be fought, even if emigration has not occurred from them, nor fighting the disbelievers. End of quote. Al-Raghib (الرّاغِبُ) chose this view. On Abu Muslim's view, the exception is disconnected (مُنْقَطِعًا, *munqaṭiʿ*, disconnected exception, where the excluded item is not of the same category), because the believers did not fall under His saying: ﴿فَما لَكم في المُنافِقِينَ فِئَتَيْنِ﴾ ("What is the matter with you that you are two groups about the hypocrites?" Qur'an 4:88).

Al-Maturidi said: "except those who reach" means: if the hypocrites join those with whom there is no covenant between you and them, then kill them until they repent and emigrate; but if they join the people of the covenant, then do not fight them. Or "who come to you with their hearts constricted": this is an attribute of those already mentioned; so the exception concerns those who reach the people of the treaty, when their attribute is that their hearts are constricted from fighting both believers and disbelievers, either because of the aversion of their natures, or because of fulfilling the covenant, or because they are in a period of reflection to distinguish truth from falsehood. On this basis, God described all the treaty partners who resolved to fulfil the covenant: that they accepted the covenant and the protected status only because fighting the Muslims was impossible for them, and their souls refused to help the Muslims against their own people; so they did not become Muslims in reality, but made peace in exchange for accepting the covenant. End of quote. Al-Qaffal, after mentioning that whoever enters the covenant of one who was within your covenant is also within the covenant, said: It may also be that the verse includes a people who intend to come into the presence of the Messenger, peace be upon him, but that goal becomes impossible for them, so they seek refuge with a people between whom and the Messenger there is a covenant, until they find a way to him. End of quote.

In the codex (مُصْحَفِ) of Ubayy and his recitation: *mīthāqun jāʾūkum* (مِيثاقٌ جاءُوكم) without a *wāw* (واوٍ, "and"). Al-Zamakhshari said: Its reading may be that *jāʾūkum* is an explanation (بَيانًا) of *yaṣilūna* (يَصِلُونَ), or a substitute (بَدَلًا), or a new sentence (اسْتِئْنافًا), or an attribute after an attribute of "a people." End of quote. These are possible readings, but some of them are weak. The explanation and the substitute are weak: because explanation (البَيانُ) does not occur in verbs, and substitution (البَدَلُ) cannot be achieved, because it is neither the thing itself, nor a part of it, nor something comprising it.

The meaning of *ḥaṣirat* (حَصِرَتْ, "were constricted") is "became narrow," and the basic sense of *ḥaṣr* (الحَصْرِ, "constriction") is in place, then it was extended to be used in speech. He said:

"The slanderers surrounded me and found / a constriction in your secret, O Umayym, so I was withholding."

Another meaning of it is: they dislike fighting you along with their people. The meaning is: they dislike fighting you alongside their own people. It is also said that the meaning is: they will neither fight you nor fight their own people alongside you, so they will be neither against you nor with you.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read *ḥaṣirat* (حَصِرَتْ). Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ya'qub read *ḥaṣrah* (حَصْرَةٌ) on the pattern of *nabqah*. Al-Mahdawi also reported this from 'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs. It is related from al-Hasan that he read *ḥaṣirāt* (حَصِراتٍ). It has also been read *ḥāṣirāt* (حاصِراتٍ), and *ḥaṣrah* (حَصْرَةٌ) with a nominative vowel, as a predicate placed before its subject. The meaning would then be: *ṣudūruhum ḥaṣrah* ("their breasts are constricted"), and this is a nominal clause in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action).

As for the reading of the majority, the majority of grammarians hold that the verb is in the position of a circumstantial clause. Those who require *qad* before a past verb when it functions as a ḥāl claim that *qad* is implied. Those who do not hold this view do not need to posit an implied *qad*, since there is an uncountable number of examples of this construction without *qad*. What supports that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause is the reading of those who read it as an accusative noun.

Al-Mubarrad has two opinions. The first is that an omitted *thamma* (ثَمَّ, "there") is the ḥāl, and this verb is its description, meaning: "or they come to you as a people whose breasts are constricted." The second is that it is a supplication against them, and so it has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis). Al-Farisi rejected al-Mubarrad's view that it is a supplication against them, on the grounds that we were commanded to say: "O Allah, place enmity among the disbelievers," so that in the phrase "or they fight their own people," the meaning required by the supplication of the Muslims against them is included. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Al-Mubarrad's view may be understood as a supplication against them that they should not fight the Muslims, which is a way of rendering them powerless, and a supplication against them that they should not fight their own people, which is a way of belittling them, meaning: they are weaker and more contemptible, and one can do without them. This is like when you wish to express this meaning and say: "May Allah not make so-and-so over me, nor with me," meaning: "I can do without him and am independent of him."

Someone other than Ibn 'Atiyya said: It may be a question about their death, on the basis that the phrase "their people" (*qawmahum*) may be used to refer to those who are not of them, but rather to their enemies.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *ḥaṣirat* be in the genitive position as an adjective of *qawm* (people), with the *wāw* of *jā'ūkum* being parenthetical. He said: "This is indicated by the reading of the one who omits *aw* (أوْ, "or"), which is that of Ubayy." He also permitted that *ḥaṣirat* be a substitute (badal) for *jā'ūkum*. He said: "It is a badal of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because coming includes constriction and other things."

Al-Zajjaj said: *ḥaṣirat ṣudūruhum* is a predicate following another predicate. Ibn 'Atiyya said: One distinguishes between positing a ḥāl and a new predicate in your saying: "Zayd came, he rode the horse." If you intend "he rode the horse" as a ḥāl, you must posit *qad*. If you intend it as a predicate following a predicate, we do not need to posit it.

Al-Jurjani said: Its implied form is "if they come to you constricted," so the *in* (إنْ, "if") is omitted. What he claimed about the implied element is not agreed upon. Its implied form would be "from fighting you" (*'an an yuqātilūkum*).

{{Allah says}} ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you﴾ [An-Nisa: 90]. This is an affirmation to the believers of the magnitude of Allah's favour upon them. That is: if He had willed, He would have strengthened them and emboldened them against you. So, He has indeed favoured you by the truce, so accept it. This is when those who are excepted are disbelievers. But according to the view of those who say they are believers, the meaning is that He, exalted is He, displayed His favour upon the Muslims, and that if He had not guided them, they would have been among those given power over you.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how is it permissible for Allah to give the disbelievers power over the believers, when their being held back was nothing but Allah casting terror into their hearts? And if He willed, for a purpose that He sees, such as a trial or the like, He would not have cast it. Then they would have been empowered, fighting, and not restrained. That is the meaning of *taslīṭ* (empowerment). End of quote. This is in keeping with his Mu'tazili method (the Mu'tazilites being a theological school that emphasised human free will and divine justice).

What al-Zamakhshari said was also said by Abu Hashim before him. He said: Allah, exalted is He, informed of His power over what He wills to do. Allah's empowering of the polytheists over the believers is not a command from Him; rather, it is by removing the fear of the Muslims from their hearts and strengthening the causes of boldness against them. The purpose of empowering them over them consists of three matters. First: as discipline for them and a punishment for the sins they have committed. Second: as a trial of their patience and a test of the strength of their faith and sincerity, as He said: "and We shall surely test you" (الآية, the verse). Third: to raise their ranks and multiply their good deeds. Or all of these together, and this is closer to the truth. End of quote.

As for the other Mu'tazilites, al-Ju'ba'i said: We have shown that the people who were excepted are believers, not disbelievers, and according to this, the meaning of the verse is: "And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you by strengthening their hearts, so that they could defend themselves if you engaged them in fighting in the way of injustice." Al-Ka'bi said: He, exalted is He, informed that if He had willed, He would have done it. This only indicates that He is capable of injustice. This is our position, except that we say that He, exalted is He, does not commit injustice, and there is no indication in the verse that He willed or intended that. End of his words.

The people of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the Sunni orthodox position) said: In this verse there is evidence that it is not ugly (qabīḥ) for Allah to empower a disbeliever over a believer and to strengthen him against him.

The majority read *falaqātalūkum* (فَلَقاتَلُوكُمْ, "and they would have fought you") with the *alif* of *mufā'alah* (the form implying mutual action). Mujahid and a group read *falaqatalūkum* (فَلَقَتَلُوكم) on the pattern of *ḍaraba-ūkum*. Al-Hasan and al-Jahdari read *falaqattalūkum* with shaddah (doubling). The *lām* in *laqātalūkum* is the *lām* of the answer to *law* (لَوْ, "if"), because the element conjoined to the answer is itself an answer, just as if you said: "If Zayd had stood, 'Amr would have stood, and Bakr would have stood." Ibn 'Atiyya said: The *lām* in *lasallaṭahum* is the answer to *law*, and in ﴿falaqātalūkum﴾ it is the *lām* of correspondence and pairing (lām al-muḥādhāh wa-l-izdiwāj), because it stands in the place of the first one. If the first one did not exist, you would say *laqātalūkum*. End of quote. His naming of this *lām* "the *lām* of correspondence and pairing" is a strange designation, which I have not seen except in the expression of this man and in that of Makki before him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 90–91:

﴿So if they withdraw from you and do not fight you, and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you any way against them.﴾ If those excepted are unbelievers, then "withdrawal" (i'tizal) in its literal sense can only be realized in a state of confrontation in war. It is as if He says: if they withdraw from you by separating themselves from their people who fight you, then do not kill them. It was also said that by "withdrawal" here is meant truce (muhadanah), and it was called withdrawal because it is the cause of withdrawing from fighting. And "peace" (al-salam) here means submission (al-inqiyad), as said by al-Hasan, or reconciliation (al-sulh), as said by al-Rabi' and Muqatil, or Islam, as also said by al-Hasan. As for the one who says that those excepted are believers, the meaning is that since they have withdrawn from you and shown Islam, leave them alone. According to this, it refers to those who embraced Islam but whose faith was not yet firm, and the meaning of "a way" is a way to killing them and fighting them. Al-Jahdari read al-salm with a sukun on the lam. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam.

﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and to be secure from their own people. Whenever they are returned to disorder, they are plunged back into it.﴾ When He mentioned the description of those who were sincere in disengagement and eager to offer peace, He drew attention to another group who were deceptive, who wished to remain in their places with their families. They tell them: "We are with you and upon your religion," and they say the same to the Muslims whenever they find them. It was said that Asad and Ghatafan had this description, and this verse was revealed concerning them, as said by Muqatil. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i, who used to carry news between the Prophet (ﷺ) [and others]; this was said by al-Suddi. It was also said that it concerned a people who came from Mecca to the Prophet (ﷺ) out of showing off, displaying Islam, then returned to Quraysh as disbelievers; so Allah exposed them and made known that they were not in the state of those who came before; this was said by Mujahid. It was also said that they were from the people of Tihamah; this was said by Qatadah. And it was said that they were from the hypocrites; this was said by al-Hasan.

From His saying "You will find others" it appears that they are a people other than those excepted in His saying: "except those who join" (illa alladhina yasiluna). Some held that this verse is in the same position as the first verse, and that the people concerning whom it was revealed are the same people concerning whom the first was revealed. It came as an emphasis and confirmation of the meaning of the first. The sin in "you will find" (satajidun) is not for the future; they said it indicates the continuation of that act in the future time, like His saying: "The foolish among the people will say" (Al-Baqarah 2:142), which was revealed only after His saying: "What turned them from their qiblah" (Al-Baqarah 2:142), so the sin came to indicate continuation, end of quote. There is no precision in their saying that the sin is not for the future but indicates continuation; rather the sin is for the future, but not at the beginning of the action; it is in its continuation, that they would seek to be secure from you, i.e., seek to be safe from your harm and seek to be safe from the harm of their people. Here "fitnah" means the trial of openly displaying disbelief. The meaning of "they were plunged back into it" (urkisu fiha) is that they returned in the most ugly and shameful return, and they were worse in it than any enemy. It is reported that whenever they returned to their people, one of them would be told: "Say: my lord is the beetle, my lord is the monkeys, my lord is the scorpion," and similar, and he would say it. Ibn Thabbab and al-A'mash read "ruddu" with a kasra on the ra', since when it was assimilated he transferred the kasra to the ra'. Abdullah read "ruktsu" with a damma on the ra', without an alif, lightened. Ibn Jinni said from him: with the kaf doubled.

﴿So if they do not withdraw from you, nor offer you peace, nor restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them.﴾ Allah commanded that these be killed wherever one gains power over them, on the supposition that withdrawal, offering peace, and restraining hands are absent. The implication of the condition indicates that if they realize withdrawal, offering peace, and restraining hands, they are not to be seized or killed.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This verse is an incitement to kill these deceivers if they do not return from their state to the state of the others who withdraw and offer peace. Consider the eloquence of the speech in that He presented it, in the earlier formula before this, in the context of commanding withdrawal, commanding the offering of peace, and negating fighting, since they were in the right in that and sincere in it. Its context in this later formula is the context of negating withdrawal and negating the offering of peace, since they were false and deceptive in it; and the ruling is the same in both contexts, because those upon whom He has placed no way, if they had not withdrawn, their ruling would have been the ruling of those upon whom the clear authority was placed. Likewise, those upon whom the clear authority is placed, if they do not withdraw, had they withdrawn their ruling would have been the ruling of those with no way against them; but by this expression they are under killing if they do not withdraw, end of his words. And it is good. Since the matter of the first group was lighter, He arranged the negation of placing a way against them upon two causes: the existence of withdrawal and the offering of peace. And since the matter of this deceptive group was more severe, He arranged their seizure and killing upon the existence of three things: the negation of withdrawal, the negation of offering peace, and the negation of restraining harm. All of this is by way of emphasis regarding them and intensification.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 92 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And We have given you clear authority over them﴾ [an-Nisa: 91]; that is, a clear proof for seizing them and killing them, because of the evident nature of their enmity, the exposure of their condition in disbelief and treachery, and their harm to the people of Islam. Or it means a manifest proof, in that We have permitted you to kill them. ʿIkrimah said: wherever the word sultan (authority) occurs in the Book of Allah, what is meant by it is proof (ḥujjah).

﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾ It is narrated that ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿah, who was a maternal half-brother of Abu Jahl, embraced Islam and emigrated to Madinah out of fear of his people, and that was before the emigration of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His mother swore that she would neither eat nor drink, nor let any roof shelter her, until he returned. So Abu Jahl set out, and with him al-Harith ibn Zayd ibn Abi Unaysah, and they came to him while he was in a fortified tower. Abu Jahl seized him by the back of the neck and said: "Does Muhammad not urge you to maintain the ties of kinship? Return and be dutiful to your mother, and you may keep your religion." Until he came down and went with them. When they had gone far from Madinah, they bound him and each of them flogged him one hundred lashes. He said to al-Harith: "This is my brother; so who are you, O Harith? By Allah, if I find you alone, I will kill you." They brought him to his mother, and she swore that his bonds would not be undone unless he apostatised; so he did. Then he emigrated after that, and al-Harith also embraced Islam and emigrated. ʿAyyash met him at the outskirts of Quba, and he did not realise that he had become a Muslim, so he struck him down and killed him. Then he was informed of his Islam, and he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "I killed him, and I did not realise that he had embraced Islam." So this verse was revealed. It is also said that it was revealed concerning a man who was herding sheep, whom Abu al-Darda' killed during one of the expeditions while he was saying the testimony of faith, and he drove off his sheep; the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rebuked him, and so this verse was revealed. It is also said that it was revealed concerning Abu Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman when he was killed by mistake on the Day of Uhud. And it has been said other than that. End.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it: when Allah exhorted to fighting the disbelievers, He then mentioned what relates to warfare, and among that is that someone might suppose a man to be a combatant (harbi) when he is a Muslim, and so kill him. This construction has already occurred in His saying: ﴿No right has it for them to enter them except in fear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114], and in His saying: ﴿It is not for a prophet to defraud﴾ [Al ʿImran: 161]. The discussion there would have sufficed in place of the discussion here, but we have seen fit to gather here what those commentators whose words we have come across have said.

al-Zamakhshari said: "It is not for a believer" means: it is not fitting for him, nor proper, nor does it suit his condition, as in His saying: ﴿It is not for a prophet to defraud﴾ [Al ʿImran: 161], and "It is not for us to return" [cf. al-Aʿraf: 89]: that he kill a believer initially, not by way of retaliation, except by mistake, in the manner of error. If you ask: by what is "mistake" (khata') in the accusative? I say: it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu); that is, it is not proper for him to kill him for any cause among the causes except for mistake alone. It may also be a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: he does not kill him in any state except in the state of mistake; and it may be an adjectival modifier of a verbal noun, that is: except a killing by mistake.

The meaning is: it is among the nature of the believer that the forms of killing a believer initiated by him be entirely removed from him, except when a mistake proceeds from him without intent, such as shooting at a disbeliever and hitting a Muslim, or shooting a person thinking he is a disbeliever and he turns out to be a Muslim. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The majority of the people of exegesis said: it is not, by Allah's permission or by His command to the believer, that he kill a believer in any way; then He made an exception that is disconnected (istithna' munqati') from the first, the kind in which "illa" has the sense of "but" (lakin), and the sense is: but mistake may occur. It may also be taken in another way: that kana is understood in the sense of "to be established and to exist." As if He said: "Nor did it exist, nor was it established, nor was it lawful for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake, since he is at times overcome in it." On this reading the exception is not disconnected, and the verse on this view implies the magnification of the matter and the gravity of its affair, as you say: "It was not for you, O so-and-so, to speak of this except forgetfully," magnifying deliberate intent and purpose, while absolutely forbidding speaking of it.

al-Raghib said: If it is asked, "Is it permissible for a believer to be killed by mistake, such that it is said: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾?" It is said: does your saying "it is permissible" or "it is not permissible" apply? It is only said regarding deliberate voluntary acts; as for mistake, that is not said of it. "It was not for you to do such-and-such" and "you would not have done such-and-such" are close in meaning, though they are not used with the same sense; although the first is more common, because abstaining from it stems from one's own self. That is: the believer would not kill a believer except by mistake. For this reason, whoever stated its meaning intended: it is not proper for a believer to kill a believer deliberately, but it may happen from him by mistake. Likewise whoever said: it is not in Allah's ruling that a believer be killed except by mistake. Al-Asamm said: its meaning is that killing a believer is not left unaccounted for, except where the killing is by mistake.

Abu ʿAbdullah al-Razi said: "And it is not" means: in what Allah has given or entrusted, or at no time has this been for him; and the purpose of it is to show that the sanctity of killing was established from the first period of legal responsibility. Abu Hashim said: the construction of the verse is: "and it is not for a believer to kill a believer and remain a believer, except that he kill him by mistake; then he remains a believer in that case." What Abu Hashim said was also said by al-Suddi. Al-Suddi said: the killing of a believer by a believer takes him out of being a believer, except where it is by mistake; and this is not the doctrine of the people of the Sunnah and the community. It has also been said that it is a negation of the permissibility of killing a believer, and its meaning is a prohibition; and the entry of kana indicates that it has never ceased to be the ruling of Allah. al-Maturidi said: the difficulty is that Allah forbade the believer from killing absolutely, and made an exception of mistake; and an exception from a negation is an affirmation, and from a prohibition is a permission; yet killing by mistake is not permissible by consensus; and whether it is forbidden is a matter of dispute. End.

The summary of what has been built upon this is: if it is a negation and what is meant by it is the sense of a prohibition, then the exception is disconnected, since it cannot be connected, for the meaning would become: (p-321) "except by mistake, in which case he may kill him." And if it is a negation in which prohibition is intended, then the exception is connected, since the meaning becomes: except by mistake, by his knowing him to be a disbeliever and killing him, when the unseen reveals that he was a believer; thus it is permitted to undertake the killing of disbelievers even if among them is one who has embraced Islam, provided he was not aware of him; and the exception from the prohibition is then a permission. Some scholars said: the meaning is: "It is not for a believer to kill a believer, either deliberately or by mistake," so that "illa" is in the sense of "wa la" (and not). al-Farra' rejected this view and said: such a construction is not permissible unless a prior exception has preceded, and the second is a conjunction of exception upon exception, as in the verse of the poet:
"There is no house in Madinah other than one house, the house of the Caliph, except the house of Marwan."
Abu ʿUbaydah narrated from Yunus that he asked Ru'bah ibn al-ʿAjjaj about this verse, and he said: "It is not for him to kill him deliberately or by mistake; but he has placed 'illa' in the position of 'wa' (and)," and it is like the saying of the poet:
"And every brother who parts from his brother — by the life of your father, except the two Farqads."

What appears is that His saying "except by mistake" is a disconnected exception, and this is the view of the majority, among them Aban ibn Taghlib. The meaning: but a believer may kill a believer by mistake. According to Malik, killing is of two kinds, deliberate and by mistake; so retaliation is taken for a slap, a bite, or a blow with a whip, which generally does not kill. According to al-Shafiʿi: deliberate, and quasi-deliberate (shibh al-ʿamd). There is no retaliation for quasi-deliberate or mistaken killing. According to Abu Hanifah: deliberate, mistaken, quasi-deliberate, and that which is neither mistaken nor deliberate nor quasi-deliberate. Mistake is of two kinds: that he intends to shoot a polytheist or a bird and hits a Muslim, or he thinks him to be a polytheist because he bears the marks of the people of polytheism or is in their territory. Quasi-deliberate is what is done deliberately with something that does not generally kill, such as a stone or a stick; and what is neither mistaken nor deliberate nor quasi-deliberate is the killing of one who is heedless or asleep. The majority read khaṭṭā’ (خَطّاءً) on the pattern of baннā’ (بَنّاءٍ). al-Hasan and al-Aʿmash read it on the pattern of sama’ (سَماءٍ), with the alif extended. al-Zuhri read it on the pattern of ʿaṣā (عَصًا), shortened, either because he lightened the hamzah by replacing it with an alif, or by assimilation to dam (دَمٍ), or he deleted the hamzah by deletion in the manner in which the lam of dam (دَمٍ) was deleted. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the forms of mistake are many, and their common root is the absence of intent.

﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then the freeing of a believing slave and a blood-money paid to his family, unless they remit it as charity﴾. Taḥrīr (تَحْرِير) means emancipation; ʿatīq (عَتِيق) means noble, because nobility is in free persons just as baseness is in slaves. From this come ʿitāq al-ṭayr (noble birds) and ʿitāq al-khayl (noble horses), for their nobility. The face of a free person is the most honoured place of it. Raqabah (رَقَبَة, neck) is used to refer to the whole person, as it is referred to by "head" in the saying: "So-and-so owns such-and-such heads of slaves." The apparent meaning is that every neck that has the characteristic of being judged a believer falls under His saying ﴿a believing neck﴾, falling under it in the manner of general inclusion; so it includes one born between two Muslims, one of whose parents is a Muslim, whether young or old, and one taken captive by a Muslim from the abode of war before puberty.

Ibrahim said: only one who has reached puberty is acceptable. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, al-Nakhaʿi, Qatadah and others said: only a female who has fasted and understood the oaths is acceptable; a young girl is not acceptable in this. Abu Hanifah, al-Awzaʿi, Malik, al-Shafiʿi, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad ibn Ziyad and Zufar said: in expiation for killing, a child is acceptable if one of his parents is a Muslim. ʿAṭāʾ said: a young child born between two Muslims is acceptable. Malik said: one who prays and fasts is more beloved to me. There is no disagreement that His saying "whoever kills a believer" includes both the young and the old; and likewise it should be in "the freeing of a believing neck." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the people of knowledge agreed that one with a great defect, such as the cutting off of both hands or both feet, or a blind man, is not acceptable, as far as I have memorised; if the defect is slight, such that livelihood and earning are still possible, as with lameness and the like, then there are two opinions. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: there is no disagreement among the Muslim community that a blind person, a paralysed person, one who has lost both hands or both feet, or one whose two limbs are withered, is not acceptable in expiation; and they differed concerning the lame. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: one who has lost one hand or one foot is acceptable. Malik, al-Shafiʿi and most of them said: the permanently insane is not acceptable according to most of them, nor according to Malik one who is intermittently insane; and one who is freed upon a term of years is not acceptable, though according to al-Shafiʿi both are acceptable. The mudabbar (one freed upon the owner's death) is not acceptable according to Malik, al-Awzaʿi and the Ahl al-Ra'y; and it is acceptable according to the view of al-Shafiʿi and Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it. Malik said: one part of whom has been freed is not valid. They differed concerning the reason for the obligation of expiation in killing by mistake. It has been said: it is an expiation and purification for the sin of the killer, in that he left off caution and vigilance until a person whose blood is protected perished at his hands. It has also been said: when he took a soul that was a believer out of the category of the living, it became incumbent upon him to bring into the category of the free a soul like it; for its release from the bond of slavery is its life, because the slave is prevented from the dispositions of the free.

The apparent position is that the obligation of the freeing and the blood-money falls upon the killer, since it is established in the Book and the Sunnah that whoever does something in which an obligation of a penalty such as an expiation arises, that obligation falls only upon its doer. As for the freeing, it is from the killer's property. As for the blood-money, it falls upon the entire paternal kin (ʿāqilah) according to a group including al-Awzaʿi and al-Hasan ibn Salih. Whatever exceeds a third is so according to the majority: Abu Hanifah, Malik, al-Shafiʿi, al-Layth, Ibn Shubrumah and others. As for a third, it is from the property of the offender; and it is not obligatory upon them except by way of consolation. This is contrary to the analogy of the principles regarding penalties and damages. The blood-money was established in the pre-Islamic period. The poet said:
"We pay with our wealth the traces of our hands."

[p. 323] The verse does not specify the amount to be paid as blood-money (diyah), nor what it must consist of. Abu Hanifa held that it is one hundred camels, as its details will follow, or gold dinars and silver dirhams: one thousand dinars or ten thousand dirhams. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said that it may also be cattle, sheep and garments (ḥullah), and this was the view of a group of the Successors (tabi'un), and the opinion of the seven jurists of Madinah. Thus, from cattle, two hundred cows; from sheep, one thousand sheep; and from garments, two hundred sets of garments. This was the practice of Umar, who imposed on the people of each category what has been mentioned.

Malik said: the people of gold are the people of Syria and Egypt, the people of silver are the people of Iraq, and the people of camels are the people of the desert. Therefore, from the people of camels only camels are accepted, from the people of gold only gold, and from the people of silver only silver. A group, including Tawus and al-Shafi'i, said: it is one hundred camels and nothing else. Al-Shafi'i said: the dirhams and dinars are substitutes for them when they are unavailable. He also had another opinion: that twelve thousand dirhams or one thousand dinars are due.

Abu Bakr al-Razi said: the jurists of the regions, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and Malik, agreed that the blood-money for unintentional killing (diyat al-khata') is in five categories, but they differed regarding the ages of the camels. Our companions (the Hanafis) all said: twenty banu makhad (she-camels in their second year), twenty bint labun (she-camels in their third year), twenty hiqqah (she-camels in their fourth year), and twenty jadha'ah (she-camels in their fifth year). This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, and Ahmad also held it. Malik said: twenty hiqaq, twenty jidha', twenty bint labun, twenty ibn labun, and twenty bint makhad. This is reported from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Sulayman ibn Yasar, al-Zuhri, Rabi'ah and al-Layth.

Al-Shafi'i said: blood-money is of two kinds. The aggravated kind (mughallazah) is in three categories: thirty hiqqah, thirty jadha'ah, and forty khalifah (pregnant she-camels) in whose wombs are their young. The lighter kind (mukhaffafah) is in five categories, as in Malik's view. It is reported from Ata' that the blood-money for unintentional killing is in four categories: twenty-five hiqqah, twenty-five jadha'ah, twenty-five bint makhad, and twenty-five bint labun, like the ages of male camels. Umar and Zayd ibn Thabit said: for unintentional killing, thirty bint labun, thirty jadha'ah, twenty ibn labun, and twenty bint makhad. It was also reported from them that hiqqat are substituted for the jadha'ah.

The apparent position is that there is no difference between killing by mistake within the Sacred Precinct (haram) or in a sacred month, and killing outside it or outside a sacred month. Al-Awza'i was asked about killing in a sacred month or in the Sacred Precinct: is the blood-money aggravated for it? He said: we have been told that if one kills in a sacred month or in the Sacred Precinct, a third is added to the killer's payment, and it is increased in the case of quasi-intentional killing (shibh al-'amd) in the ages of the camels.

As for the 'aqilah (those who bear the blood-money), it is said that they are the four categories of paternal kinsmen (asabah): the father, the grandfather however high, the son, and the son's son however low. This is the view of Malik. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: they are the people of his register (diwan), not his relatives. If the killer is not among the people of the register, the payment is imposed on his 'aqilah, the nearest and then the next nearest, and tribes are added to them by lineage. Al-Shafi'i, as transmitted from him by al-Muzani in his Mukhtasar, said: the 'aqil falls on those of kinship, not the people of the register or the allies, on the nearest and then the next nearest of the sons of his father, then of his grandfather, then the sons of his grandfather's father.

As for the period in which the blood-money is paid, consensus (ijma') has been established, and sound hadiths have been transmitted to that effect: it is paid over three years. There are many rulings concerning blood-money and the 'aqilah, some of which were touched on by some exegetes, and they are recorded in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

The meaning of ﴿delivered to his family﴾ is: paid and handed over to the family of the one killed, that is, to his heirs (awliya'), who inherit him and divide it as an inheritance. There is no difference between it and the rest of the estate in everything: debts are settled from it, and bequests are carried out. If there is no heir, it goes to the public treasury (bayt al-mal). Sharik said: no debt is settled from the blood-money, and no bequest is carried out from it. Ibn Mas'ud said: every heir inherits from it except the killer. The meaning of His words ﴿unless they forgo it as charity﴾ is: unless his heirs pardon the blood-money, in which case there is no blood-money. The wording of "charity" (tasaddaq) was used to draw attention to the virtue of pardon and to encourage it, and to show that it is like giving charity, and that its reward is deferred and gained without seeking immediate worldly gain. This is the ruling for one who is killed by mistake within the abode of Islam. In His words ﴿unless they forgo it as charity﴾ there is evidence for the permissibility of discharging a debt by the wording of charity, and evidence that acceptance is not a condition for remission (ibra'), contrary to Zufar, who said: the debtor is not released from the debt unless he accepts the release.

The apparent position is that if a group jointly kill a man by mistake, they are not all liable except for one expiation (kaffarah), because of the generality of His words ﴿and whoever kills﴾, and the ordering of the freeing of one slave and the blood-money upon that. This was held by a group; so said Abu Thawr, and it was reported from al-Awza'i. But al-Hasan, Ikrimah, al-Nakha'i, al-Harith, Malik, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: each one of them must perform the expiation.

This exception has been said to be disjunctive (munqati'), and it has been said to be connected (muttasil). Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: with what is ﴿unless they forgo it as charity﴾ connected, and what is its position? I say: it is connected to 'alayhi (upon him), or to 'musallamah' (delivered). As if it were said: the blood-money is due from him or he delivers it, except when they give it up as charity to him. Its position is the accusative as an adverbial of time, with the time element omitted, like their saying: sit as long as Zayd is sitting. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal) from ahlihi (his family), meaning: except as those who give charity." End of his words. Both of these explanations are wrong. As for making "an" and what follows it an adverbial of time, this is not permitted; the grammarians have stated this, and that it is a feature peculiar to the verbal "ma". They prohibited saying: "I will come to you when the rooster crows," meaning at the time of the crowing of the rooster. As for forming from it a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause, they also stated that this is not permitted. Sibawayh said regarding the Arabs' saying: "You are the man who will fight (an tunazila) or dispute (an tukhasima)," meaning "You are the man of fighting and disputing": the accusative of this is the accusative of the object for which something is done (maf'ul min ajlih), because the future cannot be a circumstantial clause. On this basis, what we have established, that it is a disjunctive exception, is the correct view.

The majority read ﴿yassaddaqu﴾, and its original form is yatasaddaqu, with the ta' assimilated into the sad. Al-Hasan, Abu Abd al-Rahman, and Abd al-Warith, from Abu Amr, read "tassaddaqu" with the ta' as address to the present group. It was also read "tasaddaqu" with a single ta' and a lightened sad; its original form is tatasaddaqu, and one of the two ta's was dropped, with disagreement over which of them is the one dropped. In the codex of Ubayy and Abdullah it is "yatasaddaqu" with ya' and ta'.

* *

﴿If he is from a people hostile to you and he is a believer, then freeing a believing slave﴾. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Nakha'i, al-Suddi, Ikrimah and others said: the meaning is that if this man killed by mistake was a believer who had accepted faith and remained among his people, and they are disbelievers hostile to you, then there is no blood-money for him; his expiation is only the freeing of a slave. According to them, the reason for its revelation was that the armies of the Muslims used to pass by tribes of disbelievers, and so it happened that one who had believed but not emigrated, or who had emigrated and then returned to his people, was killed in the charges of battle, supposing him to be one of the disbelievers; so the verse was revealed. According to these scholars, the blood-money falls away because the heirs of the one killed are disbelievers, so they are not given anything by which they may strengthen themselves. Also, his sanctity, if he believed but did not emigrate, is slight, so there is no blood-money. If a believer is killed in the lands of the Muslims while his people are at war, then there is blood-money for the public treasury (bayt al-mal) and the expiation.

A group said: the reason for the falling away of the blood-money is that his heirs are disbelievers, whether the killing by mistake happened among the Muslims or between his own people, whether he did not emigrate or emigrated and then returned to his people. His expiation is only the freeing of a slave, because if he is killed among his own people, he has exposed himself; and if he is killed among the Muslims, his family do not deserve the blood-money, nor do the Muslims, because they are not his family. So it is not obligatory in either case. This is the view of Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr. Ibrahim said: if the believer killed by mistake is from a people of polytheists with whom there is no treaty between them and the Prophet, then on his killer is the freeing of a slave; or if (his people have a treaty), then his blood-money is paid to his kin who are under treaty.

One of the authors (of books) said: the jurists of the regions differed concerning one who accepted Islam in the abode of war and was killed before emigrating. Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf, according to the well-known report from him, said: if a Muslim who has been granted safe-conduct (musta'man) kills him, then there is expiation for the mistake; or if both were under safe-conduct, then on the killer there is blood-money and expiation for the mistake; or if both were captives, then on the killer is expiation for the mistake, according to Abu Hanifa's view. Muhammad and Abu Yusuf said: there is blood-money in intentional and unintentional killing. Malik said: on the killer of one who accepted Islam in the abode of war and did not leave, there is blood-money and expiation if it was a mistake. The verse was only about the treaty of the Prophet ﷺ with the people of Makkah, because whoever did not emigrate was not inherited from, since they used to inherit by emigration. Al-Hasan ibn Salih said: if he stayed in the abode of war while he was able to leave, he is judged by the rulings applied to the people of war regarding his person and his property; and if he joined the abode of war without having apostatized from Islam, then he is an apostate by abandoning the abode of Islam. Al-Shafi'i said: if he kills a Muslim in the abode of war during a raid, while not knowing him to be a Muslim, then there is neither 'aql (blood-money) nor qawd (retaliation) for it, and there is expiation. This applies whether the Muslim was a captive, or under safe-conduct, or a man who accepted Islam there. But if he knew him to be a Muslim and killed him, then there is retaliation for him. End of what this author transmitted. What appears from the implications of these statements is that Allah the Exalted clarified the rulings concerning the believer killed by mistake in these three statements; for this reason He contrasted them with His words ﴿and whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾. So the believer killed by mistake, if his family are believers or under treaty, then there is the freeing (of a slave) and the blood-money. The people under treaty were placed, regarding receipt of the blood-money, in the position of believers, because the rulings for believers apply to them; and if his family are at war, then there is only the freeing (of a slave).

﴿And if he is from a people between you and them there is a covenant, then blood-money delivered to his family and the freeing of a believing slave﴾. Al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd, Ibrahim and others said: if the one killed by mistake was a believer from a people with whom you have a treaty, then their covenant requires that they have more right to the blood-money of their companion; his expiation is the freeing (of a slave) and the payment of the blood-money to them. Al-Nakha'i said: his inheritance goes to the Muslims. It was recited by al-Hasan as "and if he is from a people between you and them there is a covenant, and he is a believer." This is also the view of Malik. Ibn Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Ibrahim as well, and al-Zuhri said: the one killed by mistake from among the people of the covenant, whether he was a believer or a disbeliever, if he is under the covenant of his people, then there is blood-money for him like the blood-money of a Muslim, and the freeing (of a slave).

Concerning this, the blood-money of a covenanted person (mu'ahad) differed. Abu Hanifa and others said: his blood-money is like the blood-money of a Muslim. This is reported from Abu Bakr and Umar. Malik and his companions said: half the blood-money of a Muslim. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: one-third of the blood-money of a Muslim. What appears from the indication of the partitive "min" (from) is that it is a restriction in the first clause, to being from a hostile people, and a restriction in the second clause, to being from a covenanted people; and the meaning concerns lineage, not religion, because he is a believer and they are disbelievers. When these two clauses are thus restricted, this indicates that the first is restricted to his being among the believers by lineage, namely one who killed a believer by mistake; as if it said: and his family are believers, not belligerents nor covenanted. It is not possible to take it on its absolute sense, because of the contradiction and opposition between it and the two verses that follow.

Abu Bakr al-Razi said: His saying, ﴿And if he was from a people hostile to you﴾, is a resumption of speech (isti'naf) that had no prior mention in the address, for it is not permissible to say "Give this to a man, and if he is a man, then give him." This is corrupt speech that no wise person would utter. Thus it is established that this believer mentioned by the conjunction (ma'tuf) with the first is not included in the address. Then he said: The apparent meaning of the verse, meaning ﴿And if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant﴾, requires that the slain person mentioned in the verse be one with a covenant, and that it is not permissible to supply belief for him except by evidence. Evidence for this: when He willed a believer from the people of the abode of war, He mentioned belief, saying "and he is a believer," because if He had left it unqualified, the unqualified wording would have implied that he was an unbeliever from a hostile people to you. End of his words.

As for his saying "It is a resumption that had no prior mention in the address," this is not correct. Rather, there was prior mention in the address in His saying: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake, and whoever kills a believer by mistake﴾. However, it is not a resumption; rather it is of the category of division (taqsim), as we have mentioned. He began first with the more honorable, namely the believer whose people are believers and are neither belligerents nor covenanted. As for his saying, "for it is not permissible to say, 'Give this to a man, and if he is a man, then give him,'" this is in no way like the verse; rather, the pronoun in "was" refers to the one slain by mistake, the believer, if he was from a people hostile to you. His saying "and he is a believer" comes as emphasis, not as restriction, since the restriction is understood from what precedes it in the exception and in the conditional clause. As for his saying "It indicates this..." through to the end, it does not indicate this, because, as we mentioned, the qualifier is emphatic, and the benefit of emphasizing it is that one not suppose the pronoun refers to the slain person in general, without the qualification of belief. And his saying, "for if it were unqualified, the unqualified wording would imply that he was an unbeliever from a hostile people," is not so; rather, had He not said "and he is a believer," the pronoun in "was" would still refer to the one slain by mistake, because the reference was not stripped of mention to anything else; so the pronoun does not refer to one who has not been mentioned, and its reference is left to what has been mentioned.

﴿So whoever does not find [a slave], then fasting for two consecutive months﴾, meaning a slave he does not own, and he has not found the means to acquire one; then he must fast two consecutive months. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that nothing other than this is obligatory, for if blood money were obligatory, He would have conjoined it with fasting. This was the view of al-Sha'bi and Masruq, while the majority held that blood money is obligatory. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: What al-Sha'bi and Masruq said is an error, because blood money is imposed on the 'aqilah (paternal kin) and not on the killer. End of his words. It is not an error; rather, it is the apparent meaning of the verse, as we have mentioned.

The meaning of consecutiveness (tatabu'): no break in fasting may intervene. If menstruation occurs in the midst of it, it is not considered a breaking, by consensus. He may not travel and break the fast. Illness is like menstruation according to Ibn al-Musayyab, Sulayman ibn Yasar, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata', Mujahid, Qatadah, Tawus, and Malik. Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i, al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, al-Hasan ibn Hayy, Abu Hanifah and his companions said: he begins anew if he breaks the fast due to illness. Al-Shafi'i has two positions. (p-326) Ibn Shubrumah said: he makes up only that day if the excuse is overwhelming, like fasting Ramadan.

﴿A repentance from Allah﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning a return from Him to ease and lightness, in that He moved you from freeing a slave to fasting. Or, "a repentance from Allah" means acceptance from Him and mercy toward whom Allah relents, if He accepts his repentance.
