The Exalted called the one who killed by mistake to repentance, because he did not take precaution, and it was his duty to be careful.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, meaning Knowing of whoever killed by mistake, Wise in that He ordained what He ordained upon this offence according to what His wisdom required, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 93:

﴿Whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein, and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment.﴾ It was revealed concerning Miqyas ibn Subaba, when he killed his brother Hisham ibn Subaba, a man from the Ansar. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took the blood-money (diyya) for him. Then, after that, he sent him with a man from Fihr on a certain matter, and Miqyas killed him, and he returned to Makkah as an apostate, and began reciting:

"I killed Fihr in return for him, and I carried his blood-price, the chiefs of Banu al-Najjar, the lords of Fari'."

"I have released through him my vengeance, and I have attained my revenge, and I was the first to return to the idols."

So the Prophet ﷺ said: "I will not grant him safety in sacred or non-sacred territory," and he ordered his killing on the day of the Conquest of Makkah while he was clinging to the Ka'ba. This occasion of revelation (sabab) restricts the generality of His saying "Whoever kills," so it is specific to the disbeliever. Or it is according to what Ibn Abbas said: he said, the meaning of "intentionally" (muta'ammidan) is "considering it lawful" (mustahillan), and this also leads to disbelief. As for if it is general, then this is on the supposition of a condition, like all the threats concerning all sins. The meaning: "His recompense, if He recompenses him," that is, that is what he deserves because of the greatness of his sin. This is the view of the Ahl al-Sunna. "Abiding" (khulud) would be a metaphor, concerning the sinful believer, for a long stay, not one joined with eternity, since it is only so concerning the disbelievers.

The Mu'tazila held the generality of this verse, and that it is restricted by its generality, based on His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa: 48]. They relied on what is narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit that he said: "The severe (verse) was revealed after the lenient," meaning: "Whoever kills a believer with an enemy..." and "He forgives what is less than that," so it is as if it was said: "and He forgives what is less than that except for one who kills intentionally." They disputed the implication of the conditional "whoever" for generality. It was said that it is a word that often occurs for specificity, like His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 44], and the one among the believers who judges by other than what Allah has revealed is not a disbeliever. The poet said:

"And whoever does not defend his pool with his weapon, it will be destroyed, and whoever does not wrong people, will not be wronged."

If the generality is granted, then specification has entered it by consensus (ijma') between the Mu'tazila and the Ahl al-Sunna concerning one who is witnessed to have killed intentionally, or who confesses that he killed intentionally, and comes to the ruler or the guardians, and the legal penalty (hadd) is established upon him and he is killed. This one is not followed (by punishment) in the Hereafter. And the threat (wa'id) is not applied to him, by consensus, due to the authentic hadith from Ubada: "Whoever is punished in this world, it is an expiation for him." This is a specification of the generality. And if specification has entered it, then it is specific to the disbeliever, and the occasion of revelation bears witness to this, as we have mentioned.

The verse does not address the repentance of the killer, and the commentators spoke about it here. A group said: his repentance is not accepted. This is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas. Ibn Abbas used to say: "Shirk and killing are two shares; whoever dies upon them will be eternally abiding." He used to say: "This verse is Medinan, and it abrogated (nasakha) the one in al-Furqan, because that one is Meccan." Ibn Shihab, whenever someone asked him who understood from him that he had killed, would say to him: "Your repentance is accepted," and to one who had not killed he would say: "There is no repentance for the killer." Something close to the words of Ibn Shihab is narrated from Ibn Abbas in the tafsir of Abd ibn Humayd. From Sufyan: the scholars, when they were asked, would say: "There is no repentance for him." Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is to be understood from them as following the Sunna of Allah in severity and harshness; otherwise every sin is erased by repentance, and enough for you is the erasure of shirk as proof." And in the hadith: "Whoever helps in the killing of a believing Muslim, even with half a word, will come on the Day of Resurrection with written between his eyes: 'despairing of the mercy of Allah.'"

How strange is the matter of people who recite this verse (p-327), see what is in it, hear these definitive hadiths and the saying of Ibn Abbas together with repentance, and yet their greediness and their empty covetousness and their following of their desires, and what their wishes conjure for them, do not leave them, so that they hope for pardon for the killer of a believer without repentance. ﴿Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad: 24]. Then Allah, exalted is He, mentioned repentance in the case of accidental killing, because of what may occur of some kind of negligence in what is required of caution and guarding against it, as a cutting-off of greed. And what a cutting-off it is! But there is no life for one you call out to.

If you say: Is there in it any evidence for the expulsion of those among the people of major sins who do not repent? I say: How clear the evidence is in it, and it is the encompassing of His saying "whoever kills," whatever killer he may be, Muslim or disbeliever, repentant or non-repentant, except that the evidence excluded the repentant one. Whoever claims the exclusion of the non-repentant Muslim, let him bring evidence like it. This is the end of his words. This is in keeping with his Mu'tazili method, and an attack on his opponents with abuse and vilification. As for his saying "how clear the evidence is in it," it is not clear, because the claimant asks whether there is in it evidence for the eternal abiding of one who does not repent of major sins, and this is general for major sins. The verse concerns a specific major sin: killing a believer intentionally. Its being the greatest of major sins after shirk is specific; so it is possible that the ruling for this specific major sin is other than the ruling for the rest of the major sins, its being the greatest of major sins after shirk being specific. So there is no evidence in the verse for what he mentioned.

Thus it becomes clear that his saying "how clear the evidence is in it" is not correct. They differed about what constitutes intentional killing, and about a free man who intentionally kills a believing slave, whether retaliation (qisas) is taken from him. That is explained in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh). "Intentionally" (muta'ammidan) is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun hidden in "yaqtul," and the meaning is: intending his killing. Abdan narrated from al-Kisa'i: the softening (sukun) of the ta' in "muta'ammidan," as if he saw successive vowels as burdensome. These verses contain kinds of eloquence, clarity and rhetorical ornamentation (badi'): the tatmim (completion) in ﴿And who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ [al-Nisa: 87]; the interrogative in the sense of denial in ﴿Why are you among the hypocrites?﴾ [al-Nisa: 88], and in ﴿Do you wish to guide one whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ [al-Nisa: 88]; the antithesis (tibaq) in ﴿guide one whom Allah has sent astray﴾ [al-Nisa: 88]; the perfect paronomasia (tajnis) in ﴿they wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾ [al-Nisa: 89], in ﴿between you and them﴾ [al-Nisa: 92], in ﴿that they fight you or fight their own people﴾ [al-Nisa: 90], in ﴿that they should be safe from you and be safe﴾ [al-Nisa: 91], and in "khata'an" and "khata'an" (by mistake, and as a sin). The metaphor (isti'ara) in ﴿between you and them﴾ [al-Nisa: 92], in ﴿their hearts are restrained﴾ [al-Nisa: 90], in ﴿if they withdraw from you﴾ [al-Nisa: 90] and ﴿and offer you peace﴾ [al-Nisa: 90], in "sabilan" (a way), and in ﴿every time they are returned to disorder, they are plunged into it; so if they do not withdraw from you﴾ [al-Nisa: 91], to the end of the verse. The parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh) in ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you﴾ [al-Nisa: 90]. Repetition (takrar) in several places. Division (taqsim) in "And whoever kills," to its end. Ellipsis (hadhf) in several places.

﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully, and do not say to one who gives you the greeting of peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of worldly life; for with Allah are abundant spoils. Thus were you before, and Allah conferred favor upon you. So investigate carefully. Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ [al-Nisa: 94]. ﴿Not equal are those believers who sit [at home] other than those with a disability and those who strive in the cause of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and lives over those who sit [at home] by a degree. And to each Allah has promised the best [reward], but Allah has preferred the strivers over those who sit [at home] with a great reward﴾ [al-Nisa: 95]. ﴿[as] ranks from Him and forgiveness and mercy. And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa: 96]. ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, [the angels] will say, "In what [condition] were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." They will say, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?" For those, their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾ [al-Nisa: 97]. ﴿Except the oppressed among men, women and children who are not able to devise a plan nor are they guided to a way﴾ [al-Nisa: 98]. ﴿For those, perhaps Allah will pardon them, and ever is Allah Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ [al-Nisa: 99]. ﴿And whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find on earth many [alternative] places of refuge and abundance. And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger and then death overtakes him, his reward has already become incumbent upon Allah. And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa: 100].

Al-maghnam (spoils): a noun of place from "ghanima"; it is suitable for time, place and the verbal noun, and it is applied to the booty (ghanima) by naming the object with the verbal noun, i.e., the thing gained, which is what a man obtains of the enemy's wealth in a raid. Al-muragham: the place of ragham, which is that each one of the disputants humiliates the other's nose by securing for himself a stronghold, by overcoming his desire; it is said: "I ragham'd so-and-so" when you part from him while he dislikes your parting, due to a humiliation that befalls him thereby. And al-ragham is humiliation and abasement, and its origin is the adhesion of the nose to the ragham, which is dust (p-328).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 94 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully and do not say to one who gives you [the greeting of] peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of worldly life. For with Allah are abundant gains.﴾ Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated: "A man from Sulaym passed by a group of the Companions, and with him was a flock of sheep. He greeted them with peace, and they said, 'He only greeted us with peace in order to seek refuge,' so they killed him, took his sheep, and brought them to the Messenger, and this [verse] was revealed." It was also said: the Messenger sent a military expedition in which was al-Miqdad; the people scattered, but a man remained who had much wealth and did not move, and he professed the testimony of faith (tashahhud); al-Miqdad killed him. He informed the Messenger, peace be upon him, of that, and he said: "Did you kill a man who said, 'There is no god but Allah'? How will you face 'There is no god but Allah' tomorrow?" It was also said: the Companions met the polytheists and defeated them; a man from among them pursued a man, and when the spear reached him he said, "I am a Muslim," but he killed him and took his property. This was reported to the Messenger, and he said: "You killed him when he claimed to be a Muslim?" He said: "He said it only to seek refuge." He said: "Why did you not split open his heart?" This is in a narrative whose end is: the killer died, and the earth rejected him twice or three times, so he was cast into one of the ravines. It was also said that this is the expedition in which Usamah ibn Zayd killed Mirdas ibn Nahik of the people of Fadak, and that is well known. It was also said: "The Messenger, peace be upon him, sent Abu Hadrad al-Aslami, Abu Qatadah, and Muhallam ibn Jaththamah in an expedition to Aslam. When they reached Amir ibn al-Adbat al-Ashja'i, he greeted them with the greeting of Islam; Muhallam killed him and took his spoils. When they returned, [the Prophet] said: 'Did you kill him after he said, "I have believed"?' Then this [verse] was revealed."

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is evident: when Allah mentioned the recompense of one who kills a believer deliberately, that for him is Hell, and mentioned Allah's wrath against him, His curse, and the preparation of a great punishment for him, He commanded the believers to be steadfast and to investigate, and not to let a person proceed to kill one who has shown faith, and not to shed a forbidden blood on the basis of a weak interpretation. He repeated this at the end of the verse as an emphasis that one should not proceed in the presence of doubts and uncertainty until the matter he is about to undertake becomes clear to him. Since the concealment of that is tied to journeys and raids, He said: "when you go forth in the land." Otherwise, steadfastness and investigation are obligatory in killing one who professes Islam, whether on a journey or at home. The meaning of "going forth" (ḍarb) was already explained in His saying: ﴿They cannot strike through the land﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273].

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read fa-tathabbatū with the letter thā' (with three dots), and the rest read fa-tabayyanū. Both are of the form tafa"ala with the meaning of istaf'ala, which is for seeking; i.e., seek the establishment of the matter and its clarification, and do not proceed without deliberation and clarity. Some said: "tabayyanū" is more emphatic and more intense than "fa-tathabbatū," because one who seeks steadiness may not attain clarity. al-Raghib said: because clarity rarely occurs except after steadiness, and steadiness may occur without clarity; and it has been contrasted with haste in his peace be upon him saying: "Clarity is from Allah and haste is from Satan." Abu Ubayd said: the two are close in meaning. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the correct view is what Abu Ubayd said, because a man's "tabayyun" does not necessarily imply that the matter has become evident; rather it implies an attempt at clarification, just as "tathabbut" implies an attempt at clarification; so they are the same. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "tathabbut" is the opposite of advancing, and what is meant is deliberation and steadiness, and it is more specifically suited to this context. What shows this is His saying: ﴿and more firm in strengthening﴾ [al-Nisa': 66]; that is, more firm in holding them back from what they were admonished to not undertake. The speech of people says: "Be steady in your affair" (tathabbat fi amrika). It has come: "Clarity is from Allah and haste is from Satan"; and the contrasting of haste with clarity indicates the closeness of the two expressions.

Most scholars hold that the killer was Usamah and Muhallam, and the one killed was Amir, as we have mentioned; and so it is in the biography of Ibn Ishaq, in the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, and in al-Isti'ab. It was said: the one killed was Mirdas and his killer was Usamah. It was said his killer was Ghalib ibn Fadalah al-Laythi. It was said the killer was Abu al-Darda'. It was said Abu Qatadah.

ʿĀṣim, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read al-salāma (al-salām) with an alif. al-Zajjaj said: it may be in the sense of greeting (taslim), and it may be in the sense of submission (istislam). Nafi', Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamzah, and Ibn Kathir (through some of his transmissions), and Jabalah from al-Mufaddal from ʿĀṣim, read it with a fatḥah on the sīn and lām without an alif, and it is from istislam. Abān ibn Zayd, from ʿĀṣim, read it with a kasrah on the sīn and sukūn on the lām, and it means submission and obedience. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it may be that by salām is meant withdrawal and abstention; al-Akhfash said: one says "Fulan is salām" when he does not mix with anyone. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: that is, do not say to one who has withdrawn from you and has not fought you, "You are not a believer"; and its origin is from safety (salāmah), because one who withdraws from people seeks safety. al-Jahdari read it with a fatḥah on the sīn and sukūn on the lām. Abu Ja'far read ma'manan with a fatḥah on the mīm, meaning: we do not grant you security for yourself; this is the reading of ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Abu al-ʿĀliyah, and Yahya ibn Yaʿmar. The meaning of the majority's reading is: "You do not have the reality of faith; you only embraced Islam out of fear of being killed." Abu Bakr al-Razi said: Allah has ruled for the validity of the Islam of one who professes Islam and commanded that he be treated according to the rulings of the Muslims, even if in the unseen it is otherwise. This is among the things by which the repentance of a zindiq is argued for when he professes Islam: he is a Muslim. End. The point here is what was with the one killed of booty, or of goods and property, according to the difference concerning the occasion of revelation.

The meaning is: you seek the spoil, which is a transient, quickly passing commodity. "Tabtaghun" (seeking) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "wa-lā taqūlū" (and do not say); and in that there is an indication that what prompts the abandonment of steadiness or clarification is your seeking the goods of this world. "For with Allah are abundant gains": this is a promise of what Allah will bestow upon them of spoils in their proper form, lawfully, without committing a forbidden act under a doubt and without steadiness; so said the majority. Mujahid said: it means what Allah has prepared for them in the Hereafter of abundant reward and lasting bliss, which is the greatest of gains.

﴿Thus you were before, and Allah bestowed favor upon you, so investigate carefully.﴾ Ibn Jubayr said: its meaning is: you were concealing your Islam from your people, fearful of them for yourselves; then Allah bestowed favor upon you by strengthening your religion. So they now, each of them, is fearful among his people, awaiting that you might reach him; so when he reaches you, it is not proper that you kill him until you investigate his matter.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: there is a difficulty in this, because the concealment of faith was not general among them. (The commentary continues:) There is no difficulty, because the Muslims at the beginning of Islam loved their religion; the comparison was made with that first state. Even granting that concealment of faith was not general among them, there is also no difficulty, because what was found among some of them is attributed to the whole group. Ibn Zayd said: "Thus you were disbelievers, then Allah bestowed favor upon you by your becoming Muslims; so do not deny that he may be a disbeliever who then becomes a Muslim at the moment he meets you; therefore his matter must be investigated." Most said: the meaning is that before the Hijrah, when you were among the disbelievers, you believed in the word "There is no god but Allah"; so accept that from them. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: there is a difficulty in this, because they could say: our faith was not like their faith, for we believed by choice, whereas these showed faith under the shadows of swords. End. There is no difficulty in this, because it does not necessarily follow that the comparison must be in all respects, for then the compared would be identical to that to which it is compared, which is impossible, nor in most respects. The comparison here occurred in some respects, namely: entry into Islam was by the word of testimony. al-Zamakhshari praised this view and greatly elaborated it. He said: "When you first entered Islam, I heard from your mouths the word of testimony, and I safeguarded your blood and property, without waiting for an examination of the harmony of your hearts with your tongues. Then Allah bestowed favor upon you with steadfastness, with being known for faith, and with progress. And if you have become leaders in it, then you must treat those entering Islam as you were treated, and you must regard the outward profession of Islam among all, and do not say that the utterance of this formula is only to avoid killing and not from sincerity of intention, so that you make it a pretext for permitting his blood and property, which Allah the Exalted has forbidden." End.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: what seems closer to me is that one who moves from one religion to another, at first there arises in him an inclination due to a weak cause, then that inclination continues to strengthen until it is complete, firm, and the transition takes place. So it is as if it were said to them: "You, at the beginning of Islam, only a weak inclination arose in you through weak causes toward Islam; then Allah bestowed favor upon you by strengthening that inclination and confirming aversion to disbelief. Likewise these, when a weak inclination toward Islam arose in them through this fear, accept from them this faith, for Allah confirms the sweetness of faith in their hearts and strengthens that desire in their breasts." End of his words. But not every one of the Companions who believed had an initial weak inclination toward Islam that then grew stronger; rather among the Companions were those who were made clear-sighted at once by the call of the Messenger, or by seeing the Messenger, such as Abu Bakr, Abu Dharr, ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, and others like them who were clear-sighted and waiting.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it may be that the meaning is an indication by that to killing before investigation; i.e., in this state of your jahiliyyah you did not stand firm until Islam came and Allah bestowed favor upon you. End. The apparent meaning is that His saying "then Allah bestowed favor upon you" is part of ﴿Thus you were before﴾. It was also said it is part of ﴿seeking the goods of worldly life﴾ and what precedes it; so the meaning is: He bestowed favor upon you by accepting your repentance from that reprehensible act; so said Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi.

﴿So investigate carefully﴾: it has already been mentioned that it was read as fa-tathabbatū. It is possible that this is an emphasis of the first; and it is possible that ﴿fa-tabayyanū﴾ in the reading of one who takes it from clarification means that the difference of emphasis is not tied to the clarification. The meaning of the first is: investigate the matter of the one you are about to kill; and in the second: investigate Allah's blessing upon you of Islam.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ That is, Acquainted with your intentions and aims; so be cautious in what you intend, seeking the command of Allah the Exalted. This contains a warning; so guard yourselves from the sources of error. The majority read inna with a kasrah on the hamzah as a new sentence. It has also been read with a fatḥah, so that it is governed by His saying ﴿fa-tabayyanū﴾.

﴿Not equal are those who sit [at home] among the believers, other than those with a disability, and those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives﴾ [al-Nisa': 95]. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: it was revealed concerning people who, whenever a military campaign came, would ask permission to sit back and stay behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. As for "other than those with a disability," its occasion was the saying of Ibn Umm Maktum: "What of one who cannot strive?"

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 94 (part 2 of 3):

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when God Most High encouraged the believers to fight in the way of God against the disbelieving enemies of God, He digressed from that to the killing of a believer, whether by mistake or intentionally, without interpretation or with interpretation. So He forbade anyone to proceed to kill him on the basis of an interpretation of a command that would lead him to regard him as a non-Muslim, when the apparent meaning indicates otherwise. He mentioned the explanation of the virtue of the mujahid (one who strives in jihad) over the qa'id (one who sits back), and the explanation of the difference between the two. The fact that jihad is a context in which a mujahid might mistakenly strike a believer, or a person who offers peace and whom he then kills under interpretation, does not prevent this virtue. So he (God) followed this with the virtue of jihad and the attainment, by those who engage in it, of what He mentioned in the verse of the degrees, forgiveness, mercy and great reward, to dispel this doubt.

Here "yastawi" (to be equal) is among the verbs that do not suffice with a single subject. Affirming it does not indicate general equality, and likewise negating it does not; rather, it means the negation of equality in virtue. In this there is an ambiguity for the listener, and it is more eloquent than defining the rank that lies between the one who sits back and the mujahid. So the one who reflects remains with his thought and continues to imagine the degrees between them, while the qa'id is the one who stays behind from jihad. He expressed this by "sitting" (qu'ud) because sitting is the posture of one who does not move toward the matter from which he sits back, for the most part. "Ulu al-darar" (those with a harm) are those who are unable to fight because of blindness, sickness, lameness or lack of equipment. The meaning is: the sitters who are able to go out to raid and the mujahidun are not equal.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read "ghayru" with a damma on the ra' (raising). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha (accusative), and they related this from 'Asim. Al-A'mash and Abu Haywah read it with a kasra. As for the reading with the raising, most of the grammarians construed it as an adjective (sifah), and this is the view of Sibawayh, just as it is in his view an adjective in "ghayri al-maghdubi 'alayhim" [Al-Fatihah: 7], meaning "not of those who have earned Your anger." Similar to it is the verse of Labid:

"And if you are repaid a loan, then repay it, for indeed a youth is only repaid by one who is other than the Jumal."

Thus Abu 'Ali related it, and it is also related as "laysa al-jamal" (is not the camel). Some grammarians permitted in it the substitution (badal). It has been said: this is the clear i'rab (grammatical analysis), because it came after a negation, and it is preferable to the adjective for two reasons. The first: they stated that the most eloquent option after a negation is the substitution, then the accusative as an exception (istithna'), then the adjective in a third rank. The second: it is established that "ghayr" is indefinite in its original usage, even if it is made genitive to a definite noun. This is the well-known position and the view of Sibawayh, though it may become definite in some contexts. So making it an adjective here removes it from its original usage, either by holding that it is definite, or by holding that since the sitters were not specific people, the alif and lam in it are generic, and so it is treated like indefinites until it is described by an indefinite. All of this is weak.

As for the reading with the accusative, it is an exception from "al-qa'iduna" (the sitters). It has been said it is an exception from "al-mu'minin" (the believers). The first is more apparent, because it is the one spoken about. It has been said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) from "al-qa'iduna." As for the reading with the genitive, it is an adjective of "al-mu'minin," like the one who construed "ghayri al-maghdubi 'alayhim" [Al-Fatihah: 7] as an adjective of "alladhina an'amta 'alayhim" [Al-Fatihah: 7]; and "min al-mu'minin" is in the position of a circumstantial from His saying "al-qa'iduna," meaning: being among the believers.

They differed over whether those with a harm are equal to the mujahidin or not. If we consider the implied meaning (mafhum) of the adjective, or we hold the more preferred view that an exception from a negation is an affirmation, then equality follows. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is rejected, because those with a harm are not equal to the mujahidin; their best outcome, if they are freed from the reproach and blame that befall sitters without an excuse, is enough. Ibn Jurayj likewise said: the exception is to remove punishment, not to attain reward. The excused person receives the same reward as the one who went out to jihad, since he would wish that, if he were able, he would have gone out. He said: He excepted the excused from the sitters, and an exception from a negation is an affirmation; therefore equality between the mujahid and the excused sitter is established. End of quote. But the negation of equality was stated concerning what is known to be necessarily absent, in order to remind of the great difference between the sitter without an excuse and the mujahid; so the sitter is ashamed of the lowering of his status and is stirred toward jihad and desires it. Similar to it is "Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" [Az-Zumar: 9], which is meant to stir the ignorant through his pride and his sense of honor, so that he may proceed to learning and rise from the depths of ignorance to the nobility of knowledge.

Some scholars said: the revelation of this verse was at the time when jihad was voluntary; otherwise "is not equal" would have no meaning, because one who abandons an obligation is not described as not being equal to the one who performs it; rather the threat falls upon the one who abandons it, and the one who performs it is promised reward. Al-Maturidi said: the negation of equality between the doer of jihad and the one who abandons it does not indicate that jihad was not an obligation at that time. Do you not see that His saying, "Is one who was a believer like one who was a sinner? They are not equal" [As-Sajdah: 18], negated equality between the believer and the sinner, and faith is obligatory? He also said: "Or do those who commit evil deeds think..." [Al-Jathiyah: 21], the verse, and "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" [Az-Zumar: 9], and knowledge in many matters is obligatory. Since negating equality between the doer of a voluntary act and the one who abandons it is permissible, it is all the more permissible between the doer of an obligation and the one who abandons it, by way of priority. The sin does not fall upon the one who abandons it only because it is a communal obligation (fard kifayah). End of quote. The apparent meaning is that this negation of equality is not specific to a sitter from a particular jihad, nor to a mujahid in a particular jihad; rather it is general.

From Ibn 'Abbas: "The sitters from Badr are not equal to those who went out to it." From Muqatil: "to Tabuk." Ibn 'Abbas and others said: those with a harm are the people of excuses, since harm has affected them until it prevented them from jihad. In a hadith: "Indeed, you left behind in Madinah people who did not march a march nor crossed a valley except that they were with you; the excuse held them back." Here the preceding of wealth over lives comes up. In His saying, "Indeed God has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth" [At-Tawbah: 111], lives precede wealth because the two aims are different; for the mujahid is a seller, so mentioning the lives is delayed to indicate that restriction in them is stronger, and so he does not agree to give them except in the last of ranks. And for the buyer, lives are mentioned first to indicate that desire for them is stronger; for one desires first the most precious of things.

"God has preferred the mujahidin with their wealth and their lives over the sitters by a degree" [An-Nisa: 95]. The apparent view is that those preferred over are the sitters other than those with a harm, because they are the ones whose equality was negated. So he mentioned what distinguishes them over them, which is their being preferred over them by a degree. So this sentence is an explanation of the first sentence, as an answer to an implied question, as if someone said: "What is wrong with them that they are not equal?" Then it was said: "God has preferred the mujahidin." The ones preferred over them with a single degree are the same as those preferred over them later with degrees and what follows, and they are the sitters other than those with a harm. The two preferences are repeated according to their objects. The first preference by a degree is what is given in this world of spoils, and the second preference is what He grants them in the Hereafter. So he indicated the first by using the singular, and the second by using the plural, to show that the reward of this world is small compared to the reward of the Hereafter. It has been said: the ranks of the mujahidin are equal in this world with regard to their circumstances, like the equality of the slayers with respect to taking the spoils of those they killed, and the equality of the share of each of the horsemen, and the share of each of the foot soldiers. But in the Hereafter they vary according to their faith; so they have degrees according to what they deserve. Some of them receive forgiveness, and some of them receive mercy only. So mercy is as if it were the lowest station, and forgiveness is above mercy, and then the distance of the degrees is according to the levels. On this he drew attention by His saying, "They are degrees with God" [Ali 'Imran: 163]. The stations of the Hereafter vary. It has been said: the degree is praise and honor, and the degrees are the stations of Paradise. It has been said: the ones preferred over at first are not the ones preferred over second. The first are the sitters with an excuse, and the second are the sitters without an excuse; therefore what the preference is by differs: in the first it is a degree, and in the second it is degrees. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj, who held that those with a harm and the mujahidun are not equal.

It has also been said that the two kinds of jihad differ, so what one is preferred by differs. That is because jihad is of two kinds: minor and major. The minor is striving against the disbelievers, and the major is striving against the self. Upon this His statement (peace be upon him) indicates: "We have returned from the minor jihad to the major jihad." The striving against the self is greater because whoever strives against his self has struggled against this world, and whoever overcomes this world finds the striving against enemies easy for him. So he specified the degrees for the striving against the self, to exalt it. Al-Zamakhshari has contradicted himself in explaining the sitters. He said: "God has preferred the mujahidin" is a sentence clarifying what was negated of the equality of the sitters and the mujahidin, as if it were said: "What is wrong with them that they are not equal?" So it was answered with that. And the meaning is "over the sitters other than those with a harm," because the sentence is an explanation of the first sentence that includes this description. Then he said: "If you say: God Most High mentioned those preferred by a degree and those preferred by degrees, who are they?" I say: As for those preferred by one degree, they are those who were preferred over the sitters who are sick, and as for those preferred by degrees, they are those preferred over the sitters who were permitted to remain behind, being content with others, because raiding is a communal obligation. End of his words. So he said first that the meaning is "over the sitters other than those with a harm," and in this answer he said "over the sick sitters," and this is a contradiction. The apparent view is that His saying "degrees" is not meant to indicate a specific number; rather it is according to the varying levels of the mujahidin. Ibn Zayd said: they are the seven mentioned in Bara'ah in His saying, "That is because they do not suffer thirst" [At-Tawbah: 120], and the verses. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: if the degrees of jihad were counted, they would be more than these. Ibn Muhayriz said: the degrees in Paradise are seventy degrees; between every two degrees is the distance of a swift horse galloping for seventy years. Muqatil went in a similar direction, and al-Tabari preferred it. In the authentic hadith: "Indeed in Paradise there are a hundred degrees which God Most High has prepared for the mujahidin in His way; between each degree and the next is as the distance between the heaven and the earth."

Some scholars held that His saying, "And God has preferred the mujahidin over the sitters with a great reward, degrees from Him" [An-Nisa: 95], is by way of emphasis, and that the meaning of "daraja" (a degree) is not different from the meaning of "darajat" (degrees) in meaning; rather the two are the same in meaning. God Most High said: "And the men have a degree over them" [Al-Baqarah: 228], which is not meant as one single thing, but as many things. He repeated the preference for emphasis and for encouragement toward the matter of jihad. Al-Maturidi went in this direction and said: In the verse there is evidence that jihad is a communal obligation, since it is discharged by the performance of some; though the address in His saying, "And fight in the way of God" [Al-Baqarah: 190] is general. End of quote.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And to each [of them] God has promised the best [reward]﴾ [An-Nisa: 95]; that is, (each) of those who sit back and those who strive. It was also said that "each" refers to those who sit back other than the disabled, and to the disabled and the strivers. Here "al-husna" (the best reward) means Paradise, by consensus. ʿAbd al-Jabbar said: "This promise does not befit the matter of the Hereafter." And when He mentioned the share of the strivers in immediate benefits, it was possible to suppose that, just as they were singled out for these blessings, they would likewise be singled out for the reward. So He made clear that those who sit back have, in the promise of the best reward, the same as the strivers, and then He made clear that they have a superiority of degrees, because if He had not mentioned that, it would have given the impression that their state regarding the promise of the best reward is equal. End of quote. "Kullan" is in the accusative as the first object of "wa'ada" (promised), and the second is "al-husna." It was also read as "wa-kullun" with the nominative, as a subject, with the returning pronoun omitted; that is, "and God has promised all of them."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 95–99 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And Allah has preferred those who strive (in jihad) over those who sit back, with a great reward﴾. ﴿Degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy. And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾. It was said: the "degrees" refer to the high ranks after entry into Paradise; the "forgiveness" refers to the covering of sin; and the "mercy" refers to entry into Paradise. The apparent meaning is that this special preference applies to the one who strives with his own self and his wealth, and that one who is distinguished by only one of these is not in that position. It is well known that one who strives, and one who spends his wealth in jihad, is not like one who strives with money from someone else.

Regarding the accusative case (intisab) of "daraja" (degree) and "darajat" (degrees), there are several views. The first: both are in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), since "daraja" takes the place of the single occurrence in the preference; it is as if it were said, "He preferred them with a preference of His own," just as you say, "I struck him with a whip" (sawtan), and "darajat" takes the place of "tafdilat" (preferences), just as you say, "I struck him with whips" (aswatan), meaning strikes. The second: both are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning "possessors of a degree" and "possessors of degrees." The third: the preposition is elided, meaning "by a degree" and "by degrees." The fourth: both are in the accusative with the sense of an adverb of place (zarf), since they occupy its position, meaning "in a degree" and "in degrees." It was also said that the accusative of "darajat" is in apposition (badal) to "ajran" (reward). It was said that "wa maghfiratan wa rahmatan" (and forgiveness and mercy) are conjoined to "darajat." It was said that both were put in the accusative by implying their verbs, meaning: He forgave their sin with forgiveness, and had mercy on them with mercy. As for the accusative of "ajran 'azima" (a great reward), it was said to be a verbal noun, because the meaning of "faddala" (He preferred) carries the meaning of "ajr" (reward), so it is a verbal noun derived from the meaning and not from the wording. It was said to be the elision of the preposition, meaning "with a reward." It was said to be the object of "faddalahum" (He preferred them), since the verb is made to include the meaning of "a'taahum" (He gave them). Al-Zamakhshari said: "And 'ajran 'azima' is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the indefinite noun, which is 'darajat,' placed before it." This does not appear correct, because if it were placed after, it could not be a qualifier (na't) due to lack of agreement, since "ajran 'azima" is singular, and it cannot be a qualifier of "darajat" because that is plural. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "'Darajat' is in the accusative either as an apposition to 'al-ajr' (the reward), or by implying a verb, or that it is an emphasis of 'al-ajr,' as when we say to you, 'I owe you a thousand dirhams, by acknowledgment (urfan)'; as if you said, 'I acknowledge it by acknowledgment.'" This requires consideration.

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, (the angels) will say, "In what (condition) were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." ﴾ Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "That some people from among the Muslims were with the polytheists, increasing their numbers during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). An arrow would be shot and strike one of them, or he would be struck and killed; so this was revealed." It was said: a group from the people of Makkah who had embraced Islam; when the Messenger (ﷺ) migrated (hijrah, emigration), they remained with their people, and a group of them was tempted; then on the day of Badr, some of them went out with the disbelievers and they were killed at Badr, so this was revealed. 'Ikrimah said: it was revealed concerning five who were killed on the day of Badr: Qays ibn al-Na'ihah ibn al-Mughirah, al-Harith ibn Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad ibn Asad, Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu al-'As ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj, and 'Ali ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf. Al-Naqqash said: "Along with others besides them who had embraced Islam, then went out to Badr; when they saw the paucity of the Muslims, they said, 'This (religion) has deluded these people.'"

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah mentioned the reward of those who advanced to jihad, He followed it with the punishment of those who stayed back from jihad and settled in the lands of disbelief. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: "Tawaffi (taking in death) here means the seizing of souls." Al-Hasan said: "The gathering (hashr) to the Fire." As for "al-malaikah" (the angels) here, it was said to refer to the Angel of Death, and this is a case of using a plural for a singular in order to exalt him and magnify his station, based on the saying of Allah: ﴿Say, the Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11]. This is the view of the majority. It was also said that what is meant is the Angel of Death and his assistants, who are six: three for the souls of the believers and three for the souls of the disbelievers. What supports this is: ﴿Our messengers take him in death, and they do not fail﴾ [al-An'am: 61]. Their wronging themselves is by abandoning hijrah and remaining with their people when they returned to fighting, or by returning to disbelief, or by doubt, or by assisting the polytheists; these are four views. "Tawaffahum" (took them) is in the past tense according to the reading of the one who read "tawaffatbum," without adding the feminine ta' due to separation and because the feminine of "malaikah" is metaphorical; or it is in the present tense, and its original form is "tatawaffahum."

Ibrahim recited "tuwaffahum" with a dammah on the ta', the present tense of "waffaytu" (I fully paid); and the meaning is: Allah fully pays the angels their souls, so they take them in death, that is, He enables them to take full possession of them, so they take them fully. The pronoun in "qalu" (they said) refers to the angels, and the clause is the predicate of "inna" (indeed), and the linking pronoun is an elided pronoun indicated by the meaning; the estimate is: They said, "They said to them, 'In what (condition) were you?'" This interrogative means rebuke and censure. The meaning is: in what matter of your religion were you? It was also said that the conditions of this world and their answer to the angels is an excuse for their staying behind from hijrah and their residing in the house of disbelief, and this is an invalid excuse.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: How is it correct that the statement 'We were oppressed in the land' comes as an answer to their saying 'In what (condition) were you?' whereas the proper answer would have been, 'We were in such-and-such,' and not 'in a thing'? I say: The meaning of 'In what were you?' is rebuke, that they were in nothing of the religion, since they were able to migrate and did not migrate; so they said, 'We were oppressed,' as an excuse for what they were rebuked with, and as a justification by oppression, and that they were not able to migrate, so that they would be 'in something'." That is the end of his words. What appears is that their saying "We were oppressed in the land" is an answer to "In what (condition) were you?" according to the meaning and not the wording, because the meaning of "In what (condition) were you?" is: In what state that prevented you from migrating were you? They said, "We were oppressed," that is, in a state of oppression in the land, such that we could not migrate. This answer is a lie. The "land" here is the land of Makkah.

﴿They said, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could have migrated therein?"﴾ This is a rebuke from the angels to them and a refutation of what they used as an excuse; that is, you were not oppressed, rather you had the ability to leave for some regions so that you could migrate and join the emigrants, as those did who migrated to Abyssinia (al-Habasha) and then later joined the believers in Madinah. The meaning of "so that you could have migrated therein" is: to some region of its regions, where you would be safe in your religion. It was said: "the earth of Allah" means Madinah, spacious and safe for you from the enemy, so that you might go out to it.

Were these people whom the angels took in death Muslims who went out with the polytheists in fighting and were killed, or hypocrites, or polytheists? There are three views. The third was stated by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The angels' saying to them after the taking of their souls indicates that they were Muslims; if they had been disbelievers, nothing of this would have been said to them. They were not mentioned among the Companions because of the severity of what they committed, and because no one among them was specifically identified as a believer, and because of the possibility of their apostasy." That is the end, summarized. Al-Suddi said: "On the day this verse was revealed, whoever embraced Islam and did not migrate was considered a disbeliever until he migrated, except those who are unable to devise a means and do not find a way." That is the end. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "What the principles require is that whoever apostatized from among those is a disbeliever, and his abode is Hell, for eternity. Whoever was a believer and died in Makkah without migrating, or was forcibly taken out and killed, is a disobedient one whose abode is Hell but not for eternity. The Mu'tazilah have no proof from this verse for declaring disbelief on account of sins." In the verse there is evidence that whoever cannot establish his religion in a land as he loves is obligated to make hijrah. And it has been narrated in a hadith: "Whoever flees with his religion from one land to another land, even if it is a span of land, I have made Paradise necessary for him, and he will be the companion of his father Abraham and of his Prophet Muhammad."

﴿Then those—their abode is Hell, and evil is it as a destination﴾. The "fa" (then) is for conjunction; it conjoins one clause to another clause. It was also said that "fa-ola'ika" (then those) is the predicate of "inna" (indeed), and the "fa" entered the predicate of "inna" by likening its subject to the subject of a conditional particle. They said: "In what (condition) were you?" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the angels, or a qualifier of "zalimi anfusihim" (wronging themselves), meaning: wronging themselves, while the angels said to them, "In what (condition) were you?" It was also said that the predicate of "inna" is elided, its estimate being: "They perished," then the perishing is explained by their saying: "In what (condition) were you?"

﴿Except the oppressed among men, women, and children, who have no power to devise a plan and are not guided to a way﴾. Among the men there are a number: such as 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, Salamah ibn Hisham, and al-Walid ibn al-Walid. Among the women there are a number: such as Umm al-Fadl, Umamah bint al-Harith, the mother of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas. Among the children: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas and others. If by "children" are meant the slaves and female slaves who have reached maturity, there is no difficulty in their being included among those excepted. If by "children" are meant young children, then they cannot be anything but incapable, so no threat is directed at them, unlike men and women, who may be incapable and may be not incapable. They are mentioned with men and women, even though the threat does not apply to them, on the basis that their incapacity is the incapacity of their fathers, the men and the women; because among the strongest causes of incapacity and lack of resourcefulness is that men and women are preoccupied with their children, devoted to them, and so they are unable to make hijrah because of their fear of losing their children. So the mention of children among those excepted is an alert to the greatest of the ways of incapacity for men and women, since the ways of incapacity are not limited; so by mentioning the incapacity of children, He alerts to the strength of the incapacity of the parents because of them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that what is meant is the adolescents among them, those who understand what men and women understand, so that they are joined to them in obligation." That is the end. This is not good, because the adolescent is not joined to the accountable at all, and there is no threat for him as long as he is not obligated. It was also said: it is possible that what is meant by "the oppressed" are the Muslim captives who are in the hands of the polytheists, who cannot devise a way to get out, and cannot find a way to free themselves. As for this exception, al-Zajjaj said: it is from the saying of Allah: "Their abode is Hell." Others said: it is as if it were said, "Those are in Hell, except the oppressed"; according to this, it is a connected exception. But what the analysis requires is that it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), because the saying of Allah: "Indeed, those whom the angels take in death" to its end, the pronoun in "mawahum" (their abode) returns to them, and they, according to the views of the exegetes, are either disbelievers or disobedient ones through staying back from hijrah, while being able to make it; so the oppressed who are excepted are not included among them, because they are incapable, so it is disjunctive.

﴿They have no power to devise a plan and are not guided to a way﴾. "Al-hilah" (plan, means) is a general term for kinds of means of escape. "Al-sabil" (the way) here is the road to Madinah, as said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The correct view is that it is general to all ways, meaning the ways that deliver from the land of disbelief." That is the end. It was also said: they do not know a road to go out, and this clause was said to be a new (independent) sentence, and it was said to be in the position of a circumstantial state (hal). Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a qualifier of 'the oppressed,' or of the men, women, and children." He said: "It is permissible for that, although the clauses are indefinite, because the qualified noun, even if it has the definite article, is not a specific thing, as in his saying:"

Indeed I pass by the base man who reviles me

That is the end of his words.

This is an explanation that some grammarians followed in the same manner in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37]. It also undermines the well-known rule that an indefinite noun is only described by an indefinite, and a definite noun is only described by a definite.

What appears to be correct is that it is a clause explaining His saying "the oppressed" (al-mustad'afin), because it carries the meaning of "except those who were oppressed," so it comes as a clarification and explanation of that. This is because oppression (al-istid'af) occurs in various ways, so He specified the kind of oppression that is an excuse for staying behind from the migration, which is the inability to find a means (of escape) and not being guided to a way. The second is included under the first, because the absence of the ability to find a means by which one could escape entails the absence of being guided to a way.

It has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent this verse to the Muslims of Makkah. Jundub ibn Damrah al-Laythi said, and it is also said "Jundu'" with an ayn, or Damrah ibn Jundub, to his sons: "Carry me, for I am not among the oppressed, and I am indeed guided on the way. By Allah, I will not spend the night in Makkah." So they carried him on a litter facing toward Madinah, and he was a very old man, and he died at al-Tan'im.

﴿So those, Allah may well pardon them﴾. "'Asa" (perhaps) is a word of hope and expectation. He used it, although from Allah it is binding, to indicate that abandoning the migration is a difficult matter with no leeway in it, to the extent that the one who is clearly compelled by necessity should say: "Perhaps Allah will pardon me." It is also said the meaning of that is that He will pardon them in the future, as if He promised them forgiveness of their sins, just as He said: "Indeed Allah has looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you."

﴿And Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving﴾. This is an emphasis on the certainty of His pardon of these people, and an indication that this hoped-for outcome is actually realized, because He, exalted is He, has never ceased to be characterized by pardon and forgiveness.

Among the women there are a number: such as Umm al-Fadl, Umamah bint al-Harith, the mother of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas. Among the children: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas and others. If by "children" are meant the slaves and female slaves who have reached maturity, there is no difficulty in their being included among those excepted. If by "children" are meant young children, then they cannot be anything but incapable, so no threat is directed at them, unlike men and women, who may be incapable and may be not incapable. They are mentioned with men and women, even though the threat does not apply to them, on the basis that their incapacity is the incapacity of their fathers, the men and the women; because among the strongest causes of incapacity and lack of resourcefulness is that men and women are preoccupied with their children, devoted to them, and so they are unable to make hijrah because of their fear of losing their children. So the mention of children among those excepted is an alert to the greatest of the ways of incapacity for men and women, since the ways of incapacity are not limited; so by mentioning the incapacity of children, He alerts to the strength of the incapacity of the parents because of them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that what is meant is the adolescents among them, those who understand what men and women understand, so that they are joined to them in obligation." That is the end. This is not good, because the adolescent is not joined to the accountable at all, and there is no threat for him as long as he is not obligated. It was also said: it is possible that what is meant by "the oppressed" are the Muslim captives who are in the hands of the polytheists, who cannot devise a way to get out, and cannot find a way to free themselves. As for this exception, al-Zajjaj said: it is from the saying of Allah: "Their abode is Hell." Others said: it is as if it were said, "Those are in Hell, except the oppressed"; according to this, it is a connected exception. But what the analysis requires is that it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), because the saying of Allah: "Indeed, those whom the angels take in death" to its end, the pronoun in "mawahum" (their abode) returns to them, and they, according to the views of the exegetes, are either disbelievers or disobedient ones through staying back from hijrah, while being able to make it; so the oppressed who are excepted are not included among them, because they are incapable, so it is disjunctive.

﴿They have no power to devise a plan and are not guided to a way﴾. "Al-hilah" (plan, means) is a general term for kinds of means of escape. "Al-sabil" (the way) here is the road to Madinah, as said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The correct view is that it is general to all ways, meaning the ways that deliver from the land of disbelief." That is the end. It was also said: they do not know a road to go out, and this clause was said to be a new (independent) sentence, and it was said to be in the position of a circumstantial state (hal). Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a qualifier of 'the oppressed,' or of the men, women, and children." He said: "It is permissible for that, although the clauses are indefinite, because the qualified noun, even if it has the definite article, is not a specific thing, as in his saying:"

Indeed I pass by the base man who reviles me

That is the end of his words.

This is an explanation that some grammarians followed in the same manner in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37]. It also undermines the well-known rule that an indefinite noun is only described by an indefinite, and a definite noun is only described by a definite.

What appears to be correct is that it is a clause explaining His saying "the oppressed" (al-mustad'afin), because it carries the meaning of "except those who were oppressed," so it comes as a clarification and explanation of that. This is because oppression (al-istid'af) occurs in various ways, so He specified the kind of oppression that is an excuse for staying behind from the migration, which is the inability to find a means (of escape) and not being guided to a way. The second is included under the first, because the absence of the ability to find a means by which one could escape entails the absence of being guided to a way.

It has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent this verse to the Muslims of Makkah. Jundub ibn Damrah al-Laythi said, and it is also said "Jundu'" with an ayn, or Damrah ibn Jundub, to his sons: "Carry me, for I am not among the oppressed, and I am indeed guided on the way. By Allah, I will not spend the night in Makkah." So they carried him on a litter facing toward Madinah, and he was a very old man, and he died at al-Tan'im.

It is also said the meaning of that is that He will pardon them in the future, as if He promised them forgiveness of their sins, just as He said: "Indeed Allah has looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you."

The apparent meaning is that this special preference applies to the one who strives with his own self and his wealth, and that one who is distinguished by only one of these is not in that position. It is well known that one who strives, and one who spends his wealth in jihad, is not like one who strives with money from someone else.

The first: both are in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), since "daraja" takes the place of the single occurrence in the preference; it is as if it were said, "He preferred them with a preference of His own," just as you say, "I struck him with a whip" (sawtan), and "darajat" takes the place of "tafdilat" (preferences), just as you say, "I struck him with whips" (aswatan), meaning strikes. The second: both are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning "possessors of a degree" and "possessors of degrees." The third: the preposition is elided, meaning "by a degree" and "by degrees." The fourth: both are in the accusative with the sense of an adverb of place (zarf), since they occupy its position, meaning "in a degree" and "in degrees." It was also said that the accusative of "darajat" is in apposition (badal) to "ajran" (reward). It was said that "wa maghfiratan wa rahmatan" (and forgiveness and mercy) are conjoined to "darajat." It was said that both were put in the accusative by implying their verbs, meaning: He forgave their sin with forgiveness, and had mercy on them with mercy. As for the accusative of "ajran 'azima" (a great reward), it was said to be a verbal noun, because the meaning of "faddala" (He preferred) carries the meaning of "ajr" (reward), so it is a verbal noun derived from the meaning and not from the wording. It was said to be the elision of the preposition, meaning "with a reward." It was said to be the object of "faddalahum" (He preferred them), since the verb is made to include the meaning of "a'taahum" (He gave them). Al-Zamakhshari said: "And 'ajran 'azima' is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the indefinite noun, which is 'darajat,' placed before it." This does not appear correct, because if it were placed after, it could not be a qualifier (na't) due to lack of agreement, since "ajran 'azima" is singular, and it cannot be a qualifier of "darajat" because that is plural. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "'Darajat' is in the accusative either as an apposition to 'al-ajr' (the reward), or by implying a verb, or that it is an emphasis of 'al-ajr,' as when we say to you, 'I owe you a thousand dirhams, by acknowledgment (urfan)'; as if you said, 'I acknowledge it by acknowledgment.'" This requires consideration.

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, (the angels) will say, "In what (condition) were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." ﴾ Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "That some people from among the Muslims were with the polytheists, increasing their numbers during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was said: a group from the people of Makkah who had embraced Islam; when the Messenger (ﷺ) migrated (hijrah, emigration), they remained with their people, and a group of them was tempted; then on the day of Badr, some of them went out with the disbelievers and they were killed at Badr, so this was revealed. 'Ikrimah said: it was revealed concerning five who were killed on the day of Badr: Qays ibn al-Na'ihah ibn al-Mughirah, al-Harith ibn Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad ibn Asad, Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu al-'As ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj, and 'Ali ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: "Tawaffi (taking in death) here means the seizing of souls." Al-Hasan said: "The gathering (hashr) to the Fire." Ibrahim recited "tuwaffahum" with a dammah on the ta', the present tense of "waffaytu" (I fully paid); and the meaning is: Allah fully pays the angels their souls, so they take them in death, that is, He enables them to take full possession of them, so they take them fully. It was also said that the conditions of this world and their answer to the angels is an excuse for their staying behind from hijrah and their residing in the house of disbelief, and this is an invalid excuse.

The Mu'tazilah have no proof from this verse for declaring disbelief on account of sins." In the verse there is evidence that whoever cannot establish his religion in a land as he loves is obligated to make hijrah. And it has been narrated in a hadith: "Whoever flees with his religion from one land to another land, even if it is a span of land, I have made Paradise necessary for him, and he will be the companion of his father Abraham and of his Prophet Muhammad."

﴿Then those—their abode is Hell, and evil is it as a destination﴾. The "fa" (then) is for conjunction; it conjoins one clause to another clause. It was also said that "fa-ola'ika" (then those) is the predicate of "inna" (indeed), and the "fa" entered the predicate of "inna" by likening its subject to the subject of a conditional particle. It was also said that the predicate of "inna" is elided, its estimate being: "They perished," then the perishing is explained by their saying: "In what (condition) were you?"

﴿And Allah has preferred those who strive (in jihad) over those who sit back, with a great reward﴾. ﴿Degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy. And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾. The apparent meaning is that this special preference applies to the one who strives with his own self and his wealth, and that one who is distinguished by only one of these is not in that position. It is well known that one who strives, and one who spends his wealth in jihad, is not like one who strives with money from someone else.

The first: both are in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), since "daraja" takes the place of the single occurrence in the preference; it is as if it were said, "He preferred them with a preference of His own," just as you say, "I struck him with a whip" (sawtan), and "darajat" takes the place of "tafdilat" (preferences), just as you say, "I struck him with whips" (aswatan), meaning strikes. The second: both are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning "possessors of a degree" and "possessors of degrees." The third: the preposition is elided, meaning "by a degree" and "by degrees." The fourth: both are in the accusative with the sense of an adverb of place (zarf), since they occupy its position, meaning "in a degree" and "in degrees." It was also said that the accusative of "darajat" is in apposition (badal) to "ajran" (reward). It was said that "wa maghfiratan wa rahmatan" (and forgiveness and mercy) are conjoined to "darajat." It was said that both were put in the accusative by implying their verbs, meaning: He forgave their sin with forgiveness, and had mercy on them with mercy. As for the accusative of "ajran 'azima" (a great reward), it was said to be a verbal noun, because the meaning of "faddala" (He preferred) carries the meaning of "ajr" (reward), so it is a verbal noun derived from the meaning and not from the wording. It was said to be the elision of the preposition, meaning "with a reward." It was said to be the object of "faddalahum" (He preferred them), since the verb is made to include the meaning of "a'taahum" (He gave them). Al-Zamakhshari said: "And 'ajran 'azima' is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the indefinite noun, which is 'darajat,' placed before it." This does not appear correct, because if it were placed after, it could not be a qualifier (na't) due to lack of agreement, since "ajran 'azima" is singular, and it cannot be a qualifier of "darajat" because that is plural. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "'Darajat' is in the accusative either as an apposition to 'al-ajr' (the reward), or by implying a verb, or that it is an emphasis of 'al-ajr,' as when we say to you, 'I owe you a thousand dirhams, by acknowledgment (urfan)'; as if you said, 'I acknowledge it by acknowledgment.'" This requires consideration.
