This verse indicates that the "qada'" in His saying: ﴿So when you have completed the prayer﴾ is only the making up of the Prayer of Fear.

Al-Hasan read *tahinū* with a fatḥah on the *hā'*, and this is a dialect form. The *hā'* was given a fatḥah just as the *dāl* of *yada'u* was, because it is a guttural letter (*ḥarf al-ḥalq*). The meaning is: do not weaken or falter out of cowardice in pursuing the people.

ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read *wa-lā tuhānū*, from *al-ihānah* (humiliation). They were forbidden from doing anything that would result in their being humiliated, such as inflicting harm on their enemies and thereby being humiliated, like their saying: "May we not see you here!" Then He encouraged them to pursue the people and placed the proof upon them. What they suffer of pain is shared, and you have the additional advantage that you hope for reward from God and for the victory of His religion through His true promise, while they do not hope for it. Therefore you should be braver than them and further from cowardice. If they endure pains, wounds and killing, though they hope for no reward in the Hereafter, then you are more deserving of endurance, if you endure. A parallel to mentioning this shared matter is the words of the poet:

*Fight the people, O Khidāʿ, and let not their killing deter you from fighting them*
*The people are like you: they have hair on their heads, and they will not be resurrected if they are killed.*

The word *rajāʾ* (hope) here retains its normal meaning. It has also been said that it means fear: that you fear from God's punishment what they do not fear, as in his words:

*When the bee has stung him, he does not hope for its sting*

meaning, he does not fear it. Al-Farrāʾ claimed that *rajāʾ* does not mean fear except when accompanied by negation, and one does not say *rajawtuka* meaning *khiftuka* (I feared you). Al-Aʿraj read *an takūnū* with a fatḥah on the hamzah, as an object of purpose (*maf'ūl min ajlihi*). Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read *tiʾlamūna* with a kasrah on the *tāʾ*. Ibn Wathhāb and Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir read *tiʾlamūna* with a kasrah on the *tāʾ* of the present-tense prefix in both places and on their *yāʾ*, and this is a dialect.

﴿And God is ever Knowing, Wise﴾; that is, Knowing of your intentions, Wise in what He commands you and forbids you.

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between the people by what God has shown you. And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾. The commentators elaborated at length on the occasion of revelation (*asbāb al-nuzūl*), and we have summarized from it the conclusion of what Qatādah and others said. It was revealed concerning Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq. He stole a coat of mail wrapped in a bag containing flour belonging to Qatādah ibn al-Nuʿmān, and hid it with a Jew. Ṭuʿmah swore: "I have no knowledge of it." They followed the trail of the flour to the house of the Jew, and the Jew said: "Ṭuʿmah gave it to me." It has also been said that a Jew had been entrusted with a coat of mail and betrayed the trust, and when he feared that they would discover it, he threw it into the house of Abū Malīk al-Anṣārī. Al-Suddī said: It has been said that the weapons and food belonged to Rifāʿah ibn Zayd, the paternal uncle of Qatādah, and that the sons of Ubayriq broke into his storeroom (*mashrubiyyah*, an upper room) and took those things. They were Bushayr (with a *ḍammah* on the *bāʾ*), Mubashshir and Bishr, and they gave the impression that the one who did this was a Jew named Labīd ibn Sahl. Qatādah complained about them to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the Messenger intended to argue on behalf of Ṭuʿmah or Ubayriq. It is also said Ṭuʿaymah.

Al-Kirmānī said: The commentators agreed that these verses were revealed concerning Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq, one of the Banū Ẓafar ibn al-Ḥārith, except Ibn Baḥr, who said: They were revealed concerning the hypocrites, and it is connected to His words: ﴿Why are you divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 88]. End of quotation. In this verse there is an honouring of the Messenger and a delegation of matters to him through His words: ﴿that you may judge between the people by what God has shown you﴾.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He had described the states of the hypocrites, and had connected with that the matters of war and the legal rulings related to it, He returned to the states of the hypocrites, for they betrayed the Messenger in ways that are not appropriate. So God informed him of that and commanded him not to turn toward them. Bushayr was a hypocrite who satirised the Companions and falsely attributed poetry to others. As for Ṭuʿmah, he apostatised. When He had clarified the many rulings, he (the Prophet) knew that all of them came from God, and that it was not permissible for the Messenger to deviate from any of them in pursuit of the pleasure of a people. Or it may be that since he fights the disbelievers, it is not permissible to attribute to them what they did not do, and his disbelief does not permit leniency in considering him. Rather, religious obligation requires that he judge for him or against him according to what God has revealed, and that no injustice be inflicted for the sake of pleasing the hypocrite.

The "Book" here is the Qur'an. "In truth" means without crookedness or deviation. "The people" here is general. "What God has shown you" means what He has taught you of revelation. It has also been said: by correct judgment, for it is guarded in his ijtihād (independent reasoning) and protected in his sayings and actions. It has been said: by what He cast into your heart of the lights of knowledge and the purity of the inner self. Ibn ʿAbbās (or ʿUmar) reported: "Let none of you say: I have judged by what God has shown me, for God has granted that only to His Prophet; the Prophet's opinion was correct because God was showing it to him." And what is required of us is conjecture and obligation, not neglect. Or it means: by that which has a praiseworthy outcome, for what does not have such an outcome is vain and false. Al-Māturīdī said: "In truth" means in accordance with what is true for the servants, and what is due to some of them from others, so that they may know this; or as a clarification of His command. Or it means a fixed, established truth, which is the Resurrection and the Last Day, so that they may prepare provision for it. Or by what its doer compels upon them, or by justice and truthfulness, which secures against alteration and change. Regarding "by what God has shown you": there is in it evidence for the permissibility of his ijtihād, and his ijtihād is like a text, for God informed that He shows him that, or does not show him anything other than what is right. End of his words.

﴿And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾; that is, do not be a disputant, like *jalīs* in the sense of *mujālis* (companion). This was said by al-Zajjāj, al-Fārisī and others. It may also be that it is an intensive form from *khaṣama*, and the plural *khā'inūn* (the treacherous). For the three sons of Ubayriq were the ones who broke into the storeroom, so the plural applies apparently to them; and even if the one who betrayed concerning the coat of mail, or stole it, was alone, the plural is used with regard to him and to those who testified to his innocence from among his people, such as Usayd ibn ʿUrwah, and whoever followed him in praising him. They were thus partners in his sin, especially those who knew that he was the thief. Or the plural came to include Ṭuʿmah and everyone who betrayed a trust, so that one should never dispute on behalf of a traitor, nor argue for him. *Khaṣīman* requires an omitted complement: i.e., *al-bará'* (those who are innocent). Who is the innocent party? This is disputed according to the difference in the occasion: is it the Jew to whom Ṭuʿmah gave the coat of mail, namely Zayd ibn al-Simīn; or Abū Malīk al-Anṣārī, in whose house Ṭuʿmah threw the coat when he feared exposure; or Labīd ibn Sahl? Yaḥyā ibn Sallām said he was a Jew. Al-Mahdawī mentioned that he was a Muslim, and Abū ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr included him in the book *al-Ṣaḥābah* (the Companions), which indicates his Islam, as al-Mahdawī mentioned. When these verses were revealed, Ṭuʿmah fled to Mecca, apostatised, and stayed with Sulāfah. Ḥassān (ibn Thābit) satirised him in a poem he composed, of which the following is part:

*Bint Saʿd had lodged him, and she has become (a woman) who wrestles him for the skin of her buttocks, and he wrestles her.*
*You thought that what you had done would remain hidden, while among us is a Prophet who holds the revelation close to him.*

So she expelled him and threw his baggage outside the dwelling, and said: "You never brought me any good; you brought me the poetry of Ḥassān." So he stayed with al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿIlāṭ, stole from him and was driven off. Then he broke into a house to steal from it, and the wall collapsed on him and he died. It has also been said that he followed a group of Arabs, stole from them, and they killed him.

﴿And seek forgiveness of God; indeed God is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾; that is, seek forgiveness for your sinful community who dispute falsely. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Seek forgiveness of God for what you intended regarding the punishment of the Jew." Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zajjāj said: "Seek forgiveness of God," that is, for your sin in disputing on behalf of the treacherous. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is not a sin, because he, peace be upon him, only defended according to the outward appearance, while believing their innocence. End of quotation. It has also been said that it is a command to seek forgiveness as a form of glorification, without any sin or intention of repentance, as a man says: "I seek God's forgiveness." It has been said that the address is in form to the Prophet while the intended ones are the sons of Ubayriq. It has also been said that the meaning is: seek forgiveness of God for what you intended before prophethood.

﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾. This is general, including the people of the incident, and it establishes their censure. The betrayal of oneself is something that returns upon them as punishment in the Hereafter and in this world, just as their injustice to themselves is mentioned. The prohibition of a thing does not require that the one prohibited be engaged in it. Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger disputed on behalf of Ṭuʿmah and stood up to make an excuse in a sermon. Qatādah and Ibn Jubayr reported that he intended to do so but did not do it.

﴿Indeed God does not love one who is a habitual betrayer, a sinner﴾. He used the intensive forms *khawwān* (habitual betrayer) and *athīm* (great sinner) regarding betrayal and sin, in order to exclude from it the one who committed it once, and the one whose betrayal came from heedlessness and lack of intention. In the two intensive attributes is evidence of Ṭuʿmah's excess in betrayal and his committing of sins. It has been said: When you find a man committing a bad deed, know that it has siblings. It is reported from ʿUmar that he ordered the cutting off of the hand of a thief, and his mother came weeping and said: "This is his first theft, so pardon him." He said: "You lie; God does not hold His servant accountable for the first time." The attribute of betrayal was mentioned before the attribute of sins because it is the cause of sin: he betrayed and thus sinned; and for the harmony of the verse-endings (*fawāṣil*).

﴿They hide from people, yet they do not hide from God, and He is with them when they plot by night what He does not approve of in speech﴾. The apparent reference of the pronoun in *yastakhfūna* is to those who betray, and in this is great censure and rebuke, since they commit disobedience concealing it from people, if people should find out about it; and whoever did the same as them entered among them in this. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the category that commits acts of disobedience, and these are included among them: the people of the mentioned betrayal and those who support them. It has been said that it refers to "whoever" (*man*) according to its meaning, and the clause is a qualifying description. "And He is with them" means: He knows them and is aware of them; nothing of their secrets is hidden from Him, and this is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah ḥāliyyah*). Al-Zamakhsharī said: This verse is enough to rebuke people for their lack of shame and of fear of their Lord, despite knowing, if they are believers, that they are in His presence, with no concealment, no heedlessness, and no hiding; there is nothing but open exposure and disgrace. End of quotation. This is like the words of the poet:

*Woe for the one who disobeys and claims, when they have believed in what the messengers brought!*
*He came with a combination of faith and disobedience, all of them false hopes driven by longing.*

That is, disobedience, all of it false hopes driven by longing. *Al-istikhfā'* is concealment, hiding. Ibn ʿAbbās said: *al-istiḥyā'* (to be shy) — he was shy, so he hid. "When they plot" (*idh yubayyitūna*): the operative element of *idh* is the same as the operative element of *maʿahum* (with them). "What He does not approve of in speech" refers to the saying by which they accused the innocent and defended the thief. The discussion of *tabyīt* (plotting by night) has already preceded.

﴿And God is ever encompassing of what they do﴾. This is a metaphor for intensive knowledge. Since the story of Ṭuʿmah combined an action and a statement, the verse says: ﴿He is with them when they plot by night what He does not approve of in speech, and God is ever encompassing of what they do﴾, thereby alerting that He knows their statements and their actions. This contains a severe warning and profound rebuke, since He, exalted is He, encompasses all statements and actions; so it would have been fitting for their ugly deeds to be hidden from Him by not committing them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 102–109 (part 3 of 3):

﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf in the life of this world; but who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be their guardian?﴾ The discussion of ﴿Ha antum ha'ulaa'﴾ (Here you are, these people) has already passed [in the commentary on surah Muhammad, verse 38], as has the discussion of the sentence that follows it, in terms of recitation (qira'ah) and grammatical analysis (i'rab), in surah Al 'Imran. The address is to those who show partisanship (ta'assub) for people of doubt and disobedience, and the people of the incident (al-nazilah) are included within this general meaning. The more apparent view is that this is an address to the partisans in the story of Tu'aymah, and whoever acted as they did is included in it. What strengthens this is that ﴿ha'ulaa'﴾ is a pointer to people present. 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him) read ﴿'anhu﴾ in both places, meaning 'an Ta'mah (on behalf of Ta'mah). In His saying ﴿Who will argue with Allah on their behalf?﴾ there is a pure threat; that is, Allah knows the reality of the matter, so it is not possible for anyone to deceive Him with argument or otherwise. The meaning of this interrogative is negation; that is, no one will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection when His punishment descends upon them. Al-wakil is the protector and advocate, and the one to whom a person entrusts his affairs. This interrogative likewise carries the meaning of negation; as if he said: no one will be a guardian over them who defends them and protects them. In these two sentences, what is negated in the first is argument, which is defense in action and support by strength.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 102–109 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Then let them stand behind you﴾: The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "fa-l-yakunu" (then let them be) refers to the ones who prostrated; the meaning is that when they finish the prostration they move to the guard duty and so they are behind you. Al-Zamakhshari said: "fa-l-yakunu" means: those who were not praying, behind you, guarding you. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted both readings, saying: It is possible that it refers to those who prostrated, and it is possible that it refers to the group that first stood facing the enemy. al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read (fa-li-taqum) with a kasra on the lam. Abu Haywa read (wa-li-ya'ti) with a yaʾ with two dots beneath it, in accordance with the masculine form of "ṭā'ifa" (group). There is a difference reported from Abu 'Amr concerning the assimilation of the taʾ into the ṭāʾ. In His saying: ﴿Then let a group stand﴾ there is evidence that they divided into two groups: a group guarding first, and a group praying first with him. Then the group that prayed first became the guarding group, and the guarding group that came first prayed with him. The apparent position is that the command to take up arms is obligatory, because in it is the tranquility of the one praying; this is the view of al-Shafi'i and the Zahiris. Most scholars held that it is recommended.
This manner mentioned in this verse indicates that one group prayed with the Messenger for part of a prayer, and there is no indication in it of the amount of what they prayed with him, nor of the manner of their completing it; rather, that came in the Sunnah.
We mention those manners briefly, since they explain what was summarized in the Qur'an. The first manner: one group prayed with him, and another group faced the enemy, and remained standing until their prayer was completed, and they went to face the enemy; the group that had been facing the enemy came first, and he prayed with them the remaining rak'a, then he remained seated until they completed for themselves, then he gave the salam with them. This was at Dhat al-Riqa'. The second manner: like the first, except that when he prayed the last group one rak'a, he gave the salam, then they completed after his salam. This is also narrated concerning Dhat al-Riqa'. The third manner: he arranged the army behind him in two rows, then he said takbir, and they all said takbir, and they all bowed with him, and they all raised from the bowing; then he prostrated with the row that was next to him while the others stood guarding them; when they had prostrated and stood, the others prostrated in their place, then they advanced to the positions of the front and the rear moved back to the positions of the rear, then they all bowed with him, then he prostrated and the row next to him prostrated with him; when he finished the prayer, the others prostrated, then he gave the salam with them all together. This was his prayer at 'Usfan while the enemy was in the direction of the qibla. The fourth manner: like this, except that he said: "The front row retreats backwards when they raise their heads from prostration, and the other advances and they prostrate in the positions of the first ones." The fifth manner: he prayed one rak'a with one of the two groups while the other faced the enemy; then they departed and stood in the place of their companions facing the enemy, and those came and he prayed with them one rak'a, then gave the salam; then he completed for these one rak'a and for those one rak'a at one time.
The sixth manner: he prays one rak'a with one group, then they turn toward the enemy, and the other comes and he prays with them one rak'a, then gives the salam, and those who are with him stand and complete; when they finish they go toward the enemy, and the other completes. The seventh manner: he prayed one rak'a with each group, and neither group completed anything extra beyond one rak'a. The eighth manner: he prayed two rak'as with each group, so he had four, and each man had two rak'as. The ninth manner: he prays one rak'a with one of the two groups, if the prayer is two rak'as, while the other faces the enemy; then this group stands facing the enemy, and the first comes and performs the rak'a without recitation, and completes its prayer, then guards; and the other comes and performs the rak'a with recitation, and completes its prayer; and likewise in Maghrib, except that he prays with the first two rak'as and with the second one rak'a. The tenth manner: one group stood with him, and another group opposite the enemy with their backs to the qibla; the two groups said takbir with him, then he bowed, and those with him bowed with him, and they prostrated likewise; then he stood, so those with him came to face the enemy, and those who had been facing the enemy came and bowed and prostrated while he was standing as he was; then they stood and he performed another rak'a, and they bowed with him and prostrated with him; then those facing the enemy came and bowed and prostrated while he was seated; then he gave the salam and the two groups gave the salam with him all together. This was in the Battle of Najd. The eleventh manner: he prayed two rak'as with one group and then gave the salam; then the other group came and he prayed two rak'as with them and gave the salam. This was in Batn Nakhl.
The variation in these manners refutes the statement of Mujahid that the Messenger prayed only twice: once at Dhat al-Riqa' in the land of Banu Sulaym, and once at 'Usfan while the polytheists were at Dikhyan between them and the qibla. Ibn 'Abbas mentioned that the Prayer of Fear occurred in the Battle of Dhi Qarad. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: It is reported from him that he prayed the Prayer of Fear twenty-four times, meaning in manner. Ibn Hanbal said: We do not know that anything has been reported concerning the Prayer of Fear except a sound, authentic hadith; so whichever hadith you pray according to, it suffices. Likewise al-Tabari said. He combined in taking the precaution (hadhar) and the weapons; for he made the hadhar that one protects oneself with it as one protects oneself with weapons, as came in: ﴿They settled in the abode and in faith﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], making faith the settled state because of their firmness in it.
﴿The disbelievers wish that you would neglect your weapons and your belongings, so they could attack you in one assault﴾. The discussion of (law) after (wadda) has preceded in His saying: ﴿One of them wishes he could be given a long life﴾ [al-Baqara: 96], meaning: they would charge at you with one charge. It was read: (wa-amti'atikum), and this is anomalous, since it is a plural of a plural, as they said: ashqiyat and a'tiyat for ashqiya and a'tiya, plurals of shaqa' and 'ata'. In this statement there is an alert and a warning against heedlessness, and he singled out the matter because it is more eloquent in conveying it.
﴿There is no blame upon you if you put down your weapons because of rain that is a discomfort to you, or if you are ill; but take your precaution﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf; he was ill, so he put down his weapon, and some people rebuked him. Since these two states are ones in which carrying weapons is difficult, leniency was granted in them: for the sick person, because carrying weapons is disliked for him and increases his illness. Leniency was granted for rain, because rain tires the enemy and prevents him from agility of movement for fighting. He said: If they are harmed by rain, the enemy generally suffers from its harm what the Muslims suffer, if the two are close in distance. Illness is either due to an earlier wound, or to weakness of constitution, or other things counted as illness. The repetition of the command to take precaution in prayer, and in these two states, indicates emphasis on readiness and guarding against the enemy; for an army is often struck due to negligence in precaution. Al-Dahhak said concerning His saying: ﴿and take your precaution﴾, meaning: gird on your swords, for that is the precaution of the warriors.
﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: The command to be cautious of the enemy gives the impression of expecting defeat and being deceived; so He removed that impression from them by informing them that Allah humiliates their enemy, forsakes them, and gives them victory over him, so that their hearts may be strengthened, and so that they know that the command to take precaution is not for that; rather it is an act of worship from Allah, as He said: ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾ [al-Baqara: 195].
﴿So when you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides; and when you are secure, establish the prayer﴾. The apparent meaning of "qadaytum al-salat" is: when you have finished from it. The prayer here is the Prayer of Fear, and to this the majority went, and Ibn 'Abbas likewise explained it. The remembrance commanded here is remembrance by the tongue immediately after the Prayer of Fear, in the manner in which they were commanded at the completion of the rites to remember Allah; so they were commanded to remember Allah through tahlil, takbir, tasbih, and supplication for victory and support in all circumstances; for what they are in, of anticipating the clash with the enemy, is worthy of remembrance and of turning to Allah. That is: when you are secure, establish the prayer; that is, complete it. Some people went to the view that the meaning of "qadaytum al-salat" is: you engaged in the prayer and began it. (p-342) The meaning of the command to remember is: pray it "standing" in a state of fighting at close quarters and mixing, "and sitting" kneeling from pain, "and on your sides" wounded with injuries; so these are states corresponding to conditions according to their details. When you are secure, when war lays down its burdens and you are safe, then establish the prayer; that is, make up what you prayed in those states, which are states of anxiety and disquiet; and with this view al-Zamakhshari began, and it is contrary to the apparent meaning. He said: This is apparent according to the school of al-Shafi'i, in his requirement of prayer upon the combatant in the state of fighting, walking, and agitation in battle when its time arrives; and when he is secure, he must make up. But according to Abu Hanifa, he is excused in leaving it until he is secure. It has been said that His saying: ﴿So when you have completed the prayer, remember﴾ is a command to pray in a state of safety after fear: standing for the healthy, and sitting for those unable to sit due to paralysis, injury, or illness that prevents sitting; ﴿and when you are secure﴾, that is, safe from fear, said by Qatada and al-Suddi; ﴿establish the prayer﴾, that is, pray it not as the Prayer of Fear, but as the prayer of safety while traveling. It has been said: ﴿and when you are secure﴾, that is, when you return from your journey to your home, then establish it complete, four rak'as.
﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers as a decree of specified times﴾; that is, obligatory at fixed times. Said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi, Qatada, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Ibn Qutayba. He did not say "mawqutatan" because "kitab" is a verbal noun, so it is masculine. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is obligatory obligation; so they are two words with one meaning. The apparent is the first; that is, an obligation distributed over times. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: Here He summarized those times and explained them as five times; and fixing them at five times is in the utmost beauty when viewed rationally; for events have five stages: the stage of occurrence, the stage of standing, the stage of maturity, in which there is a hidden decline, the stage of old age, and the fifth: that its traces remain after his death for a period and then are erased. These stages occur to the sun according to its rising and setting, so Allah made obligatory at each stage of its five states a prayer. End of what we have summarized from his words; he elaborated greatly on something the Qur'an does not indicate, nor does the Arabic language require; he mentioned that in his tafsir, so whoever wants it should consult it there.
﴿And do not be weak in pursuing the people; if you are suffering, indeed they are suffering as you are suffering, but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for﴾. It was said it was revealed concerning jihad in general. It was said concerning the departure of the Companions from Uhud, and the Messenger had ordered them to pursue Abu Sufyan and his companions; he ordered that none should go out except those who had been with him at Uhud, and they complained that there were wounds among them. This verse indicates that the "qada'" in His saying: ﴿So when you have completed the prayer﴾ is only the making up of the Prayer of Fear.

Al-Hasan read *tahinū* with a fatḥah on the *hā'*, and this is a dialect form. The *hā'* was given a fatḥah just as the *dāl* of *yada'u* was, because it is a guttural letter (*ḥarf al-ḥalq*). The meaning is: do not weaken or falter out of cowardice in pursuing the people.

ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read *wa-lā tuhānū*, from *al-ihānah* (humiliation). They were forbidden from doing anything that would result in their being humiliated, such as inflicting harm on their enemies and thereby being humiliated, like their saying: "May we not see you here!" Then He encouraged them to pursue the people and placed the proof upon them. What they suffer of pain is shared, and you have the additional advantage that you hope for reward from God and for the victory of His religion through His true promise, while they do not hope for it. Therefore you should be braver than them and further from cowardice. If they endure pains, wounds and killing, though they hope for no reward in the Hereafter, then you are more deserving of endurance, if you endure. A parallel to mentioning this shared matter is the words of the poet:

*Fight the people, O Khidāʿ, and let not their killing deter you from fighting them*
*The people are like you: they have hair on their heads, and they will not be resurrected if they are killed.*

The word *rajāʾ* (hope) here retains its normal meaning. It has also been said that it means fear: that you fear from God's punishment what they do not fear, as in his words:

*When the bee has stung him, he does not hope for its sting*

meaning, he does not fear it. Al-Farrāʾ claimed that *rajāʾ* does not mean fear except when accompanied by negation, and one does not say *rajawtuka* meaning *khiftuka* (I feared you). Al-Aʿraj read *an takūnū* with a fatḥah on the hamzah, as an object of purpose (*maf'ūl min ajlihi*). Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read *tiʾlamūna* with a kasrah on the *tāʾ*. Ibn Wathhāb and Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir read *tiʾlamūna* with a kasrah on the *tāʾ* of the present-tense prefix in both places and on their *yāʾ*, and this is a dialect.

﴿And God is ever Knowing, Wise﴾; that is, Knowing of your intentions, Wise in what He commands you and forbids you.

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between the people by what God has shown you. And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾. The commentators elaborated at length on the occasion of revelation (*asbāb al-nuzūl*), and we have summarized from it the conclusion of what Qatādah and others said. It was revealed concerning Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq. He stole a coat of mail wrapped in a bag containing flour belonging to Qatādah ibn al-Nuʿmān, and hid it with a Jew. Ṭuʿmah swore: "I have no knowledge of it." They followed the trail of the flour to the house of the Jew, and the Jew said: "Ṭuʿmah gave it to me." It has also been said that a Jew had been entrusted with a coat of mail and betrayed the trust, and when he feared that they would discover it, he threw it into the house of Abū Malīk al-Anṣārī. Al-Suddī said: It has been said that the weapons and food belonged to Rifāʿah ibn Zayd, the paternal uncle of Qatādah, and that the sons of Ubayriq broke into his storeroom (*mashrubiyyah*, an upper room) and took those things. They were Bushayr (with a *ḍammah* on the *bāʾ*), Mubashshir and Bishr, and they gave the impression that the one who did this was a Jew named Labīd ibn Sahl. Qatādah complained about them to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the Messenger intended to argue on behalf of Ṭuʿmah or Ubayriq. It is also said Ṭuʿaymah.

Al-Kirmānī said: The commentators agreed that these verses were revealed concerning Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq, one of the Banū Ẓafar ibn al-Ḥārith, except Ibn Baḥr, who said: They were revealed concerning the hypocrites, and it is connected to His words: ﴿Why are you divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 88]. End of quotation. In this verse there is an honouring of the Messenger and a delegation of matters to him through His words: ﴿that you may judge between the people by what God has shown you﴾.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He had described the states of the hypocrites, and had connected with that the matters of war and the legal rulings related to it, He returned to the states of the hypocrites, for they betrayed the Messenger in ways that are not appropriate. So God informed him of that and commanded him not to turn toward them. Bushayr was a hypocrite who satirised the Companions and falsely attributed poetry to others. As for Ṭuʿmah, he apostatised. When He had clarified the many rulings, he (the Prophet) knew that all of them came from God, and that it was not permissible for the Messenger to deviate from any of them in pursuit of the pleasure of a people. Or it may be that since he fights the disbelievers, it is not permissible to attribute to them what they did not do, and his disbelief does not permit leniency in considering him. Rather, religious obligation requires that he judge for him or against him according to what God has revealed, and that no injustice be inflicted for the sake of pleasing the hypocrite.

The "Book" here is the Qur'an. "In truth" means without crookedness or deviation. "The people" here is general. "What God has shown you" means what He has taught you of revelation. It has also been said: by correct judgment, for it is guarded in his ijtihād (independent reasoning) and protected in his sayings and actions. It has been said: by what He cast into your heart of the lights of knowledge and the purity of the inner self. Ibn ʿAbbās (or ʿUmar) reported: "Let none of you say: I have judged by what God has shown me, for God has granted that only to His Prophet; the Prophet's opinion was correct because God was showing it to him." And what is required of us is conjecture and obligation, not neglect. Or it means: by that which has a praiseworthy outcome, for what does not have such an outcome is vain and false. Al-Māturīdī said: "In truth" means in accordance with what is true for the servants, and what is due to some of them from others, so that they may know this; or as a clarification of His command. Or it means a fixed, established truth, which is the Resurrection and the Last Day, so that they may prepare provision for it. Or by what its doer compels upon them, or by justice and truthfulness, which secures against alteration and change. Regarding "by what God has shown you": there is in it evidence for the permissibility of his ijtihād, and his ijtihād is like a text, for God informed that He shows him that, or does not show him anything other than what is right. End of his words.

﴿And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾; that is, do not be a disputant, like *jalīs* in the sense of *mujālis* (companion). This was said by al-Zajjāj, al-Fārisī and others. It may also be that it is an intensive form from *khaṣama*, and the plural *khā'inūn* (the treacherous). For the three sons of Ubayriq were the ones who broke into the storeroom, so the plural applies apparently to them; and even if the one who betrayed concerning the coat of mail, or stole it, was alone, the plural is used with regard to him and to those who testified to his innocence from among his people, such as Usayd ibn ʿUrwah, and whoever followed him in praising him. They were thus partners in his sin, especially those who knew that he was the thief. Or the plural came to include Ṭuʿmah and everyone who betrayed a trust, so that one should never dispute on behalf of a traitor, nor argue for him. *Khaṣīman* requires an omitted complement: i.e., *al-bará'* (those who are innocent). Who is the innocent party? This is disputed according to the difference in the occasion: is it the Jew to whom Ṭuʿmah gave the coat of mail, namely Zayd ibn al-Simīn; or Abū Malīk al-Anṣārī, in whose house Ṭuʿmah threw the coat when he feared exposure; or Labīd ibn Sahl? Yaḥyā ibn Sallām said he was a Jew. Al-Mahdawī mentioned that he was a Muslim, and Abū ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr included him in the book *al-Ṣaḥābah* (the Companions), which indicates his Islam, as al-Mahdawī mentioned. When these verses were revealed, Ṭuʿmah fled to Mecca, apostatised, and stayed with Sulāfah. Ḥassān (ibn Thābit) satirised him in a poem he composed, of which the following is part:

*Bint Saʿd had lodged him, and she has become (a woman) who wrestles him for the skin of her buttocks, and he wrestles her.*
*You thought that what you had done would remain hidden, while among us is a Prophet who holds the revelation close to him.*

So she expelled him and threw his baggage outside the dwelling, and said: "You never brought me any good; you brought me the poetry of Ḥassān." So he stayed with al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿIlāṭ, stole from him and was driven off. Then he broke into a house to steal from it, and the wall collapsed on him and he died. It has also been said that he followed a group of Arabs, stole from them, and they killed him.

﴿And seek forgiveness of God; indeed God is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾; that is, seek forgiveness for your sinful community who dispute falsely. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Seek forgiveness of God for what you intended regarding the punishment of the Jew." Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zajjāj said: "Seek forgiveness of God," that is, for your sin in disputing on behalf of the treacherous. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is not a sin, because he, peace be upon him, only defended according to the outward appearance, while believing their innocence. End of quotation. It has also been said that it is a command to seek forgiveness as a form of glorification, without any sin or intention of repentance, as a man says: "I seek God's forgiveness." It has been said that the address is in form to the Prophet while the intended ones are the sons of Ubayriq. It has also been said that the meaning is: seek forgiveness of God for what you intended before prophethood.

﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾. This is general, including the people of the incident, and it establishes their censure. The betrayal of oneself is something that returns upon them as punishment in the Hereafter and in this world, just as their injustice to themselves is mentioned. The prohibition of a thing does not require that the one prohibited be engaged in it. Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger disputed on behalf of Ṭuʿmah and stood up to make an excuse in a sermon. Qatādah and Ibn Jubayr reported that he intended to do so but did not do it.

﴿Indeed God does not love one who is a habitual betrayer, a sinner﴾. He used the intensive forms *khawwān* (habitual betrayer) and *athīm* (great sinner) regarding betrayal and sin, in order to exclude from it the one who committed it once, and the one whose betrayal came from heedlessness and lack of intention. In the two intensive attributes is evidence of Ṭuʿmah's excess in betrayal and his committing of sins. It has been said: When you find a man committing a bad deed, know that it has siblings. It is reported from ʿUmar that he ordered the cutting off of the hand of a thief, and his mother came weeping and said: "This is his first theft, so pardon him." He said: "You lie; God does not hold His servant accountable for the first time." The attribute of betrayal was mentioned before the attribute of sins because it is the cause of sin: he betrayed and thus sinned; and for the harmony of the verse-endings (*fawāṣil*).

﴿They hide from people, yet they do not hide from God, and He is with them when they plot by night what He does not approve of in speech﴾. The apparent reference of the pronoun in *yastakhfūna* is to those who betray, and in this is great censure and rebuke, since they commit disobedience concealing it from people, if people should find out about it; and whoever did the same as them entered among them in this. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the category that commits acts of disobedience, and these are included among them: the people of the mentioned betrayal and those who support them. It has been said that it refers to "whoever" (*man*) according to its meaning, and the clause is a qualifying description. "And He is with them" means: He knows them and is aware of them; nothing of their secrets is hidden from Him, and this is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah ḥāliyyah*). Al-Zamakhsharī said: This verse is enough to rebuke people for their lack of shame and of fear of their Lord, despite knowing, if they are believers, that they are in His presence, with no concealment, no heedlessness, and no hiding; there is nothing but open exposure and disgrace. End of quotation. This is like the words of the poet:

*Woe for the one who disobeys and claims, when they have believed in what the messengers brought!*
*He came with a combination of faith and disobedience, all of them false hopes driven by longing.*

That is, disobedience, all of it false hopes driven by longing. *Al-istikhfā'* is concealment, hiding. Ibn ʿAbbās said: *al-istiḥyā'* (to be shy) — he was shy, so he hid. "When they plot" (*idh yubayyitūna*): the operative element of *idh* is the same as the operative element of *maʿahum* (with them). "What He does not approve of in speech" refers to the saying by which they accused the innocent and defended the thief. The discussion of *tabyīt* (plotting by night) has already preceded.

﴿And God is ever encompassing of what they do﴾. This is a metaphor for intensive knowledge. Since the story of Ṭuʿmah combined an action and a statement, the verse says: ﴿He is with them when they plot by night what He does not approve of in speech, and God is ever encompassing of what they do﴾, thereby alerting that He knows their statements and their actions. This contains a severe warning and profound rebuke, since He, exalted is He, encompasses all statements and actions; so it would have been fitting for their ugly deeds to be hidden from Him by not committing them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 102–109 (part 3 of 3):

﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf in the life of this world; but who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be their guardian?﴾ The discussion of ﴿Ha antum ha'ulaa'﴾ (Here you are, these people) has already passed [in the commentary on surah Muhammad, verse 38], as has the discussion of the sentence that follows it, in terms of recitation (qira'ah) and grammatical analysis (i'rab), in surah Al 'Imran. The address is to those who show partisanship (ta'assub) for people of doubt and disobedience, and the people of the incident (al-nazilah) are included within this general meaning. The more apparent view is that this is an address to the partisans in the story of Tu'aymah, and whoever acted as they did is included in it. What strengthens this is that ﴿ha'ulaa'﴾ is a pointer to people present. 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him) read ﴿'anhu﴾ in both places, meaning 'an Ta'mah (on behalf of Ta'mah). In His saying ﴿Who will argue with Allah on their behalf?﴾ there is a pure threat; that is, Allah knows the reality of the matter, so it is not possible for anyone to deceive Him with argument or otherwise. The meaning of this interrogative is negation; that is, no one will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection when His punishment descends upon them. Al-wakil is the protector and advocate, and the one to whom a person entrusts his affairs. This interrogative likewise carries the meaning of negation; as if he said: no one will be a guardian over them who defends them and protects them. In these two sentences, what is negated in the first is argument, which is defense in action and support by strength.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 102–109 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Then let them stand behind you﴾: The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "fa-l-yakunu" (then let them be) refers to the ones who prostrated; the meaning is that when they finish the prostration they move to the guard duty and so they are behind you. Al-Zamakhshari said: "fa-l-yakunu" means: those who were not praying, behind you, guarding you. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted both readings, saying: It is possible that it refers to those who prostrated, and it is possible that it refers to the group that first stood facing the enemy. al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read (fa-li-taqum) with a kasra on the lam. Abu Haywa read (wa-li-ya'ti) with a yaʾ with two dots beneath it, in accordance with the masculine form of "ṭā'ifa" (group). There is a difference reported from Abu 'Amr concerning the assimilation of the taʾ into the ṭāʾ. In His saying: ﴿Then let a group stand﴾ there is evidence that they divided into two groups: a group guarding first, and a group praying first with him. Then the group that prayed first became the guarding group, and the guarding group that came first prayed with him. The apparent position is that the command to take up arms is obligatory, because in it is the tranquility of the one praying; this is the view of al-Shafi'i and the Zahiris. Most scholars held that it is recommended.
This manner mentioned in this verse indicates that one group prayed with the Messenger for part of a prayer, and there is no indication in it of the amount of what they prayed with him, nor of the manner of their completing it; rather, that came in the Sunnah.
We mention those manners briefly, since they explain what was summarized in the Qur'an. The first manner: one group prayed with him, and another group faced the enemy, and remained standing until their prayer was completed, and they went to face the enemy; the group that had been facing the enemy came first, and he prayed with them the remaining rak'a, then he remained seated until they completed for themselves, then he gave the salam with them. This was at Dhat al-Riqa'. The second manner: like the first, except that when he prayed the last group one rak'a, he gave the salam, then they completed after his salam. This is also narrated concerning Dhat al-Riqa'. The third manner: he arranged the army behind him in two rows, then he said takbir, and they all said takbir, and they all bowed with him, and they all raised from the bowing; then he prostrated with the row that was next to him while the others stood guarding them; when they had prostrated and stood, the others prostrated in their place, then they advanced to the positions of the front and the rear moved back to the positions of the rear, then they all bowed with him, then he prostrated and the row next to him prostrated with him; when he finished the prayer, the others prostrated, then he gave the salam with them all together. This was his prayer at 'Usfan while the enemy was in the direction of the qibla. The fourth manner: like this, except that he said: "The front row retreats backwards when they raise their heads from prostration, and the other advances and they prostrate in the positions of the first ones." The fifth manner: he prayed one rak'a with one of the two groups while the other faced the enemy; then they departed and stood in the place of their companions facing the enemy, and those came and he prayed with them one rak'a, then gave the salam; then he completed for these one rak'a and for those one rak'a at one time.
The sixth manner: he prays one rak'a with one group, then they turn toward the enemy, and the other comes and he prays with them one rak'a, then gives the salam, and those who are with him stand and complete; when they finish they go toward the enemy, and the other completes. The seventh manner: he prayed one rak'a with each group, and neither group completed anything extra beyond one rak'a. The eighth manner: he prayed two rak'as with each group, so he had four, and each man had two rak'as. The ninth manner: he prays one rak'a with one of the two groups, if the prayer is two rak'as, while the other faces the enemy; then this group stands facing the enemy, and the first comes and performs the rak'a without recitation, and completes its prayer, then guards; and the other comes and performs the rak'a with recitation, and completes its prayer; and likewise in Maghrib, except that he prays with the first two rak'as and with the second one rak'a. The tenth manner: one group stood with him, and another group opposite the enemy with their backs to the qibla; the two groups said takbir with him, then he bowed, and those with him bowed with him, and they prostrated likewise; then he stood, so those with him came to face the enemy, and those who had been facing the enemy came and bowed and prostrated while he was standing as he was; then they stood and he performed another rak'a, and they bowed with him and prostrated with him; then those facing the enemy came and bowed and prostrated while he was seated; then he gave the salam and the two groups gave the salam with him all together. This was in the Battle of Najd. The eleventh manner: he prayed two rak'as with one group and then gave the salam; then the other group came and he prayed two rak'as with them and gave the salam. This was in Batn Nakhl.
The variation in these manners refutes the statement of Mujahid that the Messenger prayed only twice: once at Dhat al-Riqa' in the land of Banu Sulaym, and once at 'Usfan while the polytheists were at Dikhyan between them and the qibla. Ibn 'Abbas mentioned that the Prayer of Fear occurred in the Battle of Dhi Qarad. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: It is reported from him that he prayed the Prayer of Fear twenty-four times, meaning in manner. Ibn Hanbal said: We do not know that anything has been reported concerning the Prayer of Fear except a sound, authentic hadith; so whichever hadith you pray according to, it suffices. Likewise al-Tabari said. He combined in taking the precaution (hadhar) and the weapons; for he made the hadhar that one protects oneself with it as one protects oneself with weapons, as came in: ﴿They settled in the abode and in faith﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], making faith the settled state because of their firmness in it.
﴿The disbelievers wish that you would neglect your weapons and your belongings, so they could attack you in one assault﴾. The discussion of (law) after (wadda) has preceded in His saying: ﴿One of them wishes he could be given a long life﴾ [al-Baqara: 96], meaning: they would charge at you with one charge. It was read: (wa-amti'atikum), and this is anomalous, since it is a plural of a plural, as they said: ashqiyat and a'tiyat for ashqiya and a'tiya, plurals of shaqa' and 'ata'. In this statement there is an alert and a warning against heedlessness, and he singled out the matter because it is more eloquent in conveying it.
﴿There is no blame upon you if you put down your weapons because of rain that is a discomfort to you, or if you are ill; but take your precaution﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf; he was ill, so he put down his weapon, and some people rebuked him. Since these two states are ones in which carrying weapons is difficult, leniency was granted in them: for the sick person, because carrying weapons is disliked for him and increases his illness. Leniency was granted for rain, because rain tires the enemy and prevents him from agility of movement for fighting. He said: If they are harmed by rain, the enemy generally suffers from its harm what the Muslims suffer, if the two are close in distance. Illness is either due to an earlier wound, or to weakness of constitution, or other things counted as illness. The repetition of the command to take precaution in prayer, and in these two states, indicates emphasis on readiness and guarding against the enemy; for an army is often struck due to negligence in precaution. Al-Dahhak said concerning His saying: ﴿and take your precaution﴾, meaning: gird on your swords, for that is the precaution of the warriors.
﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: The command to be cautious of the enemy gives the impression of expecting defeat and being deceived; so He removed that impression from them by informing them that Allah humiliates their enemy, forsakes them, and gives them victory over him, so that their hearts may be strengthened, and so that they know that the command to take precaution is not for that; rather it is an act of worship from Allah, as He said: ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾ [al-Baqara: 195].
﴿So when you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides; and when you are secure, establish the prayer﴾. The apparent meaning of "qadaytum al-salat" is: when you have finished from it. The prayer here is the Prayer of Fear, and to this the majority went, and Ibn 'Abbas likewise explained it. The remembrance commanded here is remembrance by the tongue immediately after the Prayer of Fear, in the manner in which they were commanded at the completion of the rites to remember Allah; so they were commanded to remember Allah through tahlil, takbir, tasbih, and supplication for victory and support in all circumstances; for what they are in, of anticipating the clash with the enemy, is worthy of remembrance and of turning to Allah. That is: when you are secure, establish the prayer; that is, complete it. Some people went to the view that the meaning of "qadaytum al-salat" is: you engaged in the prayer and began it. (p-342) The meaning of the command to remember is: pray it "standing" in a state of fighting at close quarters and mixing, "and sitting" kneeling from pain, "and on your sides" wounded with injuries; so these are states corresponding to conditions according to their details. When you are secure, when war lays down its burdens and you are safe, then establish the prayer; that is, make up what you prayed in those states, which are states of anxiety and disquiet; and with this view al-Zamakhshari began, and it is contrary to the apparent meaning. He said: This is apparent according to the school of al-Shafi'i, in his requirement of prayer upon the combatant in the state of fighting, walking, and agitation in battle when its time arrives; and when he is secure, he must make up. But according to Abu Hanifa, he is excused in leaving it until he is secure. It has been said that His saying: ﴿So when you have completed the prayer, remember﴾ is a command to pray in a state of safety after fear: standing for the healthy, and sitting for those unable to sit due to paralysis, injury, or illness that prevents sitting; ﴿and when you are secure﴾, that is, safe from fear, said by Qatada and al-Suddi; ﴿establish the prayer﴾, that is, pray it not as the Prayer of Fear, but as the prayer of safety while traveling. It has been said: ﴿and when you are secure﴾, that is, when you return from your journey to your home, then establish it complete, four rak'as.
﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers as a decree of specified times﴾; that is, obligatory at fixed times. Said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi, Qatada, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Ibn Qutayba. He did not say "mawqutatan" because "kitab" is a verbal noun, so it is masculine. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is obligatory obligation; so they are two words with one meaning. The apparent is the first; that is, an obligation distributed over times. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: Here He summarized those times and explained them as five times; and fixing them at five times is in the utmost beauty when viewed rationally; for events have five stages: the stage of occurrence, the stage of standing, the stage of maturity, in which there is a hidden decline, the stage of old age, and the fifth: that its traces remain after his death for a period and then are erased. These stages occur to the sun according to its rising and setting, so Allah made obligatory at each stage of its five states a prayer. End of what we have summarized from his words; he elaborated greatly on something the Qur'an does not indicate, nor does the Arabic language require; he mentioned that in his tafsir, so whoever wants it should consult it there.
﴿And do not be weak in pursuing the people; if you are suffering, indeed they are suffering as you are suffering, but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for﴾. It was said it was revealed concerning jihad in general. It was said concerning the departure of the Companions from Uhud, and the Messenger had ordered them to pursue Abu Sufyan and his companions; he ordered that none should go out except those who had been with him at Uhud, and they complained that there were wounds among them. This verse indicates that the "qada'" in His saying: ﴿So when you have completed the prayer﴾ is only the making up of the Prayer of Fear.

Al-Hasan read *tahinū* with a fatḥah on the *hā'*, and this is a dialect form. The *hā'* was given a fatḥah just as the *dāl* of *yada'u* was, because it is a guttural letter (*ḥarf al-ḥalq*). The meaning is: do not weaken or falter out of cowardice in pursuing the people.

ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read *wa-lā tuhānū*, from *al-ihānah* (humiliation). They were forbidden from doing anything that would result in their being humiliated, such as inflicting harm on their enemies and thereby being humiliated, like their saying: "May we not see you here!" Then He encouraged them to pursue the people and placed the proof upon them. What they suffer of pain is shared, and you have the additional advantage that you hope for reward from God and for the victory of His religion through His true promise, while they do not hope for it. Therefore you should be braver than them and further from cowardice. If they endure pains, wounds and killing, though they hope for no reward in the Hereafter, then you are more deserving of endurance, if you endure. A parallel to mentioning this shared matter is the words of the poet:

*Fight the people, O Khidāʿ, and let not their killing deter you from fighting them*
*The people are like you: they have hair on their heads, and they will not be resurrected if they are killed.*

The word *rajāʾ* (hope) here retains its normal meaning. It has also been said that it means fear: that you fear from God's punishment what they do not fear, as in his words:

*When the bee has stung him, he does not hope for its sting*

meaning, he does not fear it. Al-Farrāʾ claimed that *rajāʾ* does not mean fear except when accompanied by negation, and one does not say *rajawtuka* meaning *khiftuka* (I feared you). Al-Aʿraj read *an takūnū* with a fatḥah on the hamzah, as an object of purpose (*maf'ūl min ajlihi*). Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read *tiʾlamūna* with a kasrah on the *tāʾ*. Ibn Wathhāb and Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir read *tiʾlamūna* with a kasrah on the *tāʾ* of the present-tense prefix in both places and on their *yāʾ*, and this is a dialect.

﴿And God is ever Knowing, Wise﴾; that is, Knowing of your intentions, Wise in what He commands you and forbids you.

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between the people by what God has shown you. And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾. The commentators elaborated at length on the occasion of revelation (*asbāb al-nuzūl*), and we have summarized from it the conclusion of what Qatādah and others said. It was revealed concerning Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq. He stole a coat of mail wrapped in a bag containing flour belonging to Qatādah ibn al-Nuʿmān, and hid it with a Jew. Ṭuʿmah swore: "I have no knowledge of it." They followed the trail of the flour to the house of the Jew, and the Jew said: "Ṭuʿmah gave it to me." It has also been said that a Jew had been entrusted with a coat of mail and betrayed the trust, and when he feared that they would discover it, he threw it into the house of Abū Malīk al-Anṣārī. Al-Suddī said: It has been said that the weapons and food belonged to Rifāʿah ibn Zayd, the paternal uncle of Qatādah, and that the sons of Ubayriq broke into his storeroom (*mashrubiyyah*, an upper room) and took those things. They were Bushayr (with a *ḍammah* on the *bāʾ*), Mubashshir and Bishr, and they gave the impression that the one who did this was a Jew named Labīd ibn Sahl. Qatādah complained about them to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the Messenger intended to argue on behalf of Ṭuʿmah or Ubayriq. It is also said Ṭuʿaymah.

Al-Kirmānī said: The commentators agreed that these verses were revealed concerning Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq, one of the Banū Ẓafar ibn al-Ḥārith, except Ibn Baḥr, who said: They were revealed concerning the hypocrites, and it is connected to His words: ﴿Why are you divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 88]. End of quotation. In this verse there is an honouring of the Messenger and a delegation of matters to him through His words: ﴿that you may judge between the people by what God has shown you﴾.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He had described the states of the hypocrites, and had connected with that the matters of war and the legal rulings related to it, He returned to the states of the hypocrites, for they betrayed the Messenger in ways that are not appropriate. So God informed him of that and commanded him not to turn toward them. Bushayr was a hypocrite who satirised the Companions and falsely attributed poetry to others. As for Ṭuʿmah, he apostatised. When He had clarified the many rulings, he (the Prophet) knew that all of them came from God, and that it was not permissible for the Messenger to deviate from any of them in pursuit of the pleasure of a people. Or it may be that since he fights the disbelievers, it is not permissible to attribute to them what they did not do, and his disbelief does not permit leniency in considering him. Rather, religious obligation requires that he judge for him or against him according to what God has revealed, and that no injustice be inflicted for the sake of pleasing the hypocrite.

The "Book" here is the Qur'an. "In truth" means without crookedness or deviation. "The people" here is general. "What God has shown you" means what He has taught you of revelation. It has also been said: by correct judgment, for it is guarded in his ijtihād (independent reasoning) and protected in his sayings and actions. It has been said: by what He cast into your heart of the lights of knowledge and the purity of the inner self. Ibn ʿAbbās (or ʿUmar) reported: "Let none of you say: I have judged by what God has shown me, for God has granted that only to His Prophet; the Prophet's opinion was correct because God was showing it to him." And what is required of us is conjecture and obligation, not neglect. Or it means: by that which has a praiseworthy outcome, for what does not have such an outcome is vain and false. Al-Māturīdī said: "In truth" means in accordance with what is true for the servants, and what is due to some of them from others, so that they may know this; or as a clarification of His command. Or it means a fixed, established truth, which is the Resurrection and the Last Day, so that they may prepare provision for it. Or by what its doer compels upon them, or by justice and truthfulness, which secures against alteration and change. Regarding "by what God has shown you": there is in it evidence for the permissibility of his ijtihād, and his ijtihād is like a text, for God informed that He shows him that, or does not show him anything other than what is right. End of his words.

﴿And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾; that is, do not be a disputant, like *jalīs* in the sense of *mujālis* (companion). This was said by al-Zajjāj, al-Fārisī and others. It may also be that it is an intensive form from *khaṣama*, and the plural *khā'inūn* (the treacherous). For the three sons of Ubayriq were the ones who broke into the storeroom, so the plural applies apparently to them; and even if the one who betrayed concerning the coat of mail, or stole it, was alone, the plural is used with regard to him and to those who testified to his innocence from among his people, such as Usayd ibn ʿUrwah, and whoever followed him in praising him. They were thus partners in his sin, especially those who knew that he was the thief. Or the plural came to include Ṭuʿmah and everyone who betrayed a trust, so that one should never dispute on behalf of a traitor, nor argue for him. *Khaṣīman* requires an omitted complement: i.e., *al-bará'* (those who are innocent). Who is the innocent party? This is disputed according to the difference in the occasion: is it the Jew to whom Ṭuʿmah gave the coat of mail, namely Zayd ibn al-Simīn; or Abū Malīk al-Anṣārī, in whose house Ṭuʿmah threw the coat when he feared exposure; or Labīd ibn Sahl? Yaḥyā ibn Sallām said he was a Jew. Al-Mahdawī mentioned that he was a Muslim, and Abū ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr included him in the book *al-Ṣaḥābah* (the Companions), which indicates his Islam, as al-Mahdawī mentioned. When these verses were revealed, Ṭuʿmah fled to Mecca, apostatised, and stayed with Sulāfah. Ḥassān (ibn Thābit) satirised him in a poem he composed, of which the following is part:

*Bint Saʿd had lodged him, and she has become (a woman) who wrestles him for the skin of her buttocks, and he wrestles her.*
*You thought that what you had done would remain hidden, while among us is a Prophet who holds the revelation close to him.*

So she expelled him and threw his baggage outside the dwelling, and said: "You never brought me any good; you brought me the poetry of Ḥassān." So he stayed with al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿIlāṭ, stole from him and was driven off. Then he broke into a house to steal from it, and the wall collapsed on him and he died. It has also been said that he followed a group of Arabs, stole from them, and they killed him.

﴿And seek forgiveness of God; indeed God is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾; that is, seek forgiveness for your sinful community who dispute falsely. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Seek forgiveness of God for what you intended regarding the punishment of the Jew." Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zajjāj said: "Seek forgiveness of God," that is, for your sin in disputing on behalf of the treacherous. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is not a sin, because he, peace be upon him, only defended according to the outward appearance, while believing their innocence. End of quotation. It has also been said that it is a command to seek forgiveness as a form of glorification, without any sin or intention of repentance, as a man says: "I seek God's forgiveness." It has been said that the address is in form to the Prophet while the intended ones are the sons of Ubayriq. It has also been said that the meaning is: seek forgiveness of God for what you intended before prophethood.

﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾. This is general, including the people of the incident, and it establishes their censure. The betrayal of oneself is something that returns upon them as punishment in the Hereafter and in this world, just as their injustice to themselves is mentioned. The prohibition of a thing does not require that the one prohibited be engaged in it. Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger disputed on behalf of Ṭuʿmah and stood up to make an excuse in a sermon. Qatādah and Ibn Jubayr reported that he intended to do so but did not do it.

﴿Indeed God does not love one who is a habitual betrayer, a sinner﴾. He used the intensive forms *khawwān* (habitual betrayer) and *athīm* (great sinner) regarding betrayal and sin, in order to exclude from it the one who committed it once, and the one whose betrayal came from heedlessness and lack of intention. In the two intensive attributes is evidence of Ṭuʿmah's excess in betrayal and his committing of sins. It has been said: When you find a man committing a bad deed, know that it has siblings. It is reported from ʿUmar that he ordered the cutting off of the hand of a thief, and his mother came weeping and said: "This is his first theft, so pardon him." He said: "You lie; God does not hold His servant accountable for the first time." The attribute of betrayal was mentioned before the attribute of sins because it is the cause of sin: he betrayed and thus sinned; and for the harmony of the verse-endings (*fawāṣil*).

﴿They hide from people, yet they do not hide from God, and He is with them when they plot by night what He does not approve of in speech﴾. The apparent reference of the pronoun in *yastakhfūna* is to those who betray, and in this is great censure and rebuke, since they commit disobedience concealing it from people, if people should find out about it; and whoever did the same as them entered among them in this. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the category that commits acts of disobedience, and these are included among them: the people of the mentioned betrayal and those who support them. It has been said that it refers to "whoever" (*man*) according to its meaning, and the clause is a qualifying description. "And He is with them" means: He knows them and is aware of them; nothing of their secrets is hidden from Him, and this is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah ḥāliyyah*). Al-Zamakhsharī said: This verse is enough to rebuke people for their lack of shame and of fear of their Lord, despite knowing, if they are believers, that they are in His presence, with no concealment, no heedlessness, and no hiding; there is nothing but open exposure and disgrace. End of quotation. This is like the words of the poet:

*Woe for the one who disobeys and claims, when they have believed in what the messengers brought!*
*He came with a combination of faith and disobedience, all of them false hopes driven by longing.*

That is, disobedience, all of it false hopes driven by longing. *Al-istikhfā'* is concealment, hiding. Ibn ʿAbbās said: *al-istiḥyā'* (to be shy) — he was shy, so he hid. "When they plot" (*idh yubayyitūna*): the operative element of *idh* is the same as the operative element of *maʿahum* (with them). "What He does not approve of in speech" refers to the saying by which they accused the innocent and defended the thief. The discussion of *tabyīt* (plotting by night) has already preceded.

﴿And God is ever encompassing of what they do﴾. This is a metaphor for intensive knowledge. Since the story of Ṭuʿmah combined an action and a statement, the verse says: ﴿He is with them when they plot by night what He does not approve of in speech, and God is ever encompassing of what they do﴾, thereby alerting that He knows their statements and their actions. This contains a severe warning and profound rebuke, since He, exalted is He, encompasses all statements and actions; so it would have been fitting for their ugly deeds to be hidden from Him by not committing them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 102–109 (part 3 of 3):

﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf in the life of this world; but who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be their guardian?﴾ The discussion of ﴿Ha antum ha'ulaa'﴾ (Here you are, these people) has already passed [in the commentary on surah Muhammad, verse 38], as has the discussion of the sentence that follows it, in terms of recitation (qira'ah) and grammatical analysis (i'rab), in surah Al 'Imran. The address is to those who show partisanship (ta'assub) for people of doubt and disobedience, and the people of the incident (al-nazilah) are included within this general meaning. The more apparent view is that this is an address to the partisans in the story of Tu'aymah, and whoever acted as they did is included in it. What strengthens this is that ﴿ha'ulaa'﴾ is a pointer to people present. 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him) read ﴿'anhu﴾ in both places, meaning 'an Ta'mah (on behalf of Ta'mah). In His saying ﴿Who will argue with Allah on their behalf?﴾ there is a pure threat; that is, Allah knows the reality of the matter, so it is not possible for anyone to deceive Him with argument or otherwise. The meaning of this interrogative is negation; that is, no one will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection when His punishment descends upon them. Al-wakil is the protector and advocate, and the one to whom a person entrusts his affairs. This interrogative likewise carries the meaning of negation; as if he said: no one will be a guardian over them who defends them and protects them. In these two sentences, what is negated in the first is argument, which is defense in action and support by strength.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 102–109 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Then let them stand behind you﴾: The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "fa-l-yakunu" (then let them be) refers to the ones who prostrated; the meaning is that when they finish the prostration they move to the guard duty and so they are behind you. Al-Zamakhshari said: "fa-l-yakunu" means: those who were not praying, behind you, guarding you. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted both readings, saying: It is possible that it refers to those who prostrated, and it is possible that it refers to the group that first stood facing the enemy. al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read (fa-li-taqum) with a kasra on the lam. Abu Haywa read (wa-li-ya'ti) with a yaʾ with two dots beneath it, in accordance with the masculine form of "ṭā'ifa" (group). There is a difference reported from Abu 'Amr concerning the assimilation of the taʾ into the ṭāʾ. In His saying: ﴿Then let a group stand﴾ there is evidence that they divided into two groups: a group guarding first, and a group praying first with him. Then the group that prayed first became the guarding group, and the guarding group that came first prayed with him. The apparent position is that the command to take up arms is obligatory, because in it is the tranquility of the one praying; this is the view of al-Shafi'i and the Zahiris. Most scholars held that it is recommended.
This manner mentioned in this verse indicates that one group prayed with the Messenger for part of a prayer, and there is no indication in it of the amount of what they prayed with him, nor of the manner of their completing it; rather, that came in the Sunnah.
We mention those manners briefly, since they explain what was summarized in the Qur'an. The first manner: one group prayed with him, and another group faced the enemy, and remained standing until their prayer was completed, and they went to face the enemy; the group that had been facing the enemy came first, and he prayed with them the remaining rak'a, then he remained seated until they completed for themselves, then he gave the salam with them. This was at Dhat al-Riqa'. The second manner: like the first, except that when he prayed the last group one rak'a, he gave the salam, then they completed after his salam. This is also narrated concerning Dhat al-Riqa'. The third manner: he arranged the army behind him in two rows, then he said takbir, and they all said takbir, and they all bowed with him, and they all raised from the bowing; then he prostrated with the row that was next to him while the others stood guarding them; when they had prostrated and stood, the others prostrated in their place, then they advanced to the positions of the front and the rear moved back to the positions of the rear, then they all bowed with him, then he prostrated and the row next to him prostrated with him; when he finished the prayer, the others prostrated, then he gave the salam with them all together. This was his prayer at 'Usfan while the enemy was in the direction of the qibla. The fourth manner: like this, except that he said: "The front row retreats backwards when they raise their heads from prostration, and the other advances and they prostrate in the positions of the first ones." The fifth manner: he prayed one rak'a with one of the two groups while the other faced the enemy; then they departed and stood in the place of their companions facing the enemy, and those came and he prayed with them one rak'a, then gave the salam; then he completed for these one rak'a and for those one rak'a at one time.
The sixth manner: he prays one rak'a with one group, then they turn toward the enemy, and the other comes and he prays with them one rak'a, then gives the salam, and those who are with him stand and complete; when they finish they go toward the enemy, and the other completes. The seventh manner: he prayed one rak'a with each group, and neither group completed anything extra beyond one rak'a. The eighth manner: he prayed two rak'as with each group, so he had four, and each man had two rak'as. The ninth manner: he prays one rak'a with one of the two groups, if the prayer is two rak'as, while the other faces the enemy; then this group stands facing the enemy, and the first comes and performs the rak'a without recitation, and completes its prayer, then guards; and the other comes and performs the rak'a with recitation, and completes its prayer; and likewise in Maghrib, except that he prays with the first two rak'as and with the second one rak'a. The tenth manner: one group stood with him, and another group opposite the enemy with their backs to the qibla; the two groups said takbir with him, then he bowed, and those with him bowed with him, and they prostrated likewise; then he stood, so those with him came to face the enemy, and those who had been facing the enemy came and bowed and prostrated while he was standing as he was; then they stood and he performed another rak'a, and they bowed with him and prostrated with him; then those facing the enemy came and bowed and prostrated while he was seated; then he gave the salam and the two groups gave the salam with him all together. This was in the Battle of Najd. The eleventh manner: he prayed two rak'as with one group and then gave the salam; then the other group came and he prayed two rak'as with them and gave the salam. This was in Batn Nakhl.
The variation in these manners refutes the statement of Mujahid that the Messenger prayed only twice: once at Dhat al-Riqa' in the land of Banu Sulaym, and once at 'Usfan while the polytheists were at Dikhyan between them and the qibla. Ibn 'Abbas mentioned that the Prayer of Fear occurred in the Battle of Dhi Qarad. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: It is reported from him that he prayed the Prayer of Fear twenty-four times, meaning in manner. Ibn Hanbal said: We do not know that anything has been reported concerning the Prayer of Fear except a sound, authentic hadith; so whichever hadith you pray according to, it suffices. Likewise al-Tabari said. He combined in taking the precaution (hadhar) and the weapons; for he made the hadhar that one protects oneself with it as one protects oneself with weapons, as came in: ﴿They settled in the abode and in faith﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], making faith the settled state because of their firmness in it.
