It was also said that it was revealed concerning the people of Tu'mah: they came, embraced Islam, then apostatised. The meaning of opposition (mushaqqah) has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿So they are in opposition﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137]. ﴿And whoever opposes﴾ is general, so Tu'mah and others among the opponents are included in it. ﴿After guidance has become clear to him﴾: i.e., the truth that is the cause of guidance has become evident to him. Had there been nothing but Allah informing His Prophet (peace be upon him) of the story of Tu'mah, and making him aware of what they had plotted and fabricated, he would have had in that the greatest restraint and the clearest explanation. The sin of one who knows the truth and deviates from it is greater than the sin of the ignorant, because one who does not know the truth deserves punishment for abandoning knowledge, since action is not obligatory on him until he knows it, or until someone who is trusted tells him. The scholar deserves punishment for abandoning the practice of what his knowledge requires; so his crime is greater when he has been made aware of the truth and acts contrary to what it requires, out of obstinacy towards Allah, the Exalted, since light has been given to him by which he could be guided. The way of the believers is the upright religion (al-din al-hanifi) which they follow. This conjoined clause is by way of emphasis, vilification and condemnation; for otherwise, whoever opposes the Messenger is necessarily following other than the way of the believers; but He began with the greater of the two sins and followed it with its necessary consequence as emphasis.

Al-Shafi'i and others used this verse as evidence that consensus (ijma') is a proof (hujjah). The scholars of usul al-fiqh have elaborated at length on the derivation of the proof from it and what objections are raised against that, and this is mentioned in the books of usul al-fiqh. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is evidence that consensus is a proof which may not be opposed, just as opposing the Book and the Sunnah may not be done; for Allah, the Exalted, combined following other than the way of the believers with opposing the Messenger in the condition, and made its recompense a severe threat; so following them is obligatory, like loyalty to the Messenger. End of his words.

What he mentioned is not the apparent meaning of the verse, which is arranged upon two attributes, and it does not follow that the consequence applies to each one of them separately. The threat in the verse is only applied to one who has both attributes: opposing the Messenger and following other than the way of the believers; for this reason the verb is conjoined to the verb and no conditional particle is repeated with it. Had the conditional particle been repeated, as it would be in: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him﴾ and whoever follows other than the way of the believers, there would have been a manifestation of what they claimed. All of this is on the assumption that His saying ﴿and follows other than the way of the believers﴾ is distinct from His saying ﴿and whoever opposes the Messenger﴾. We have said that it is not distinct; rather, it is a necessary consequence of opposing the Messenger, by way of hyperbole, emphasis, and magnifying the matter and its condemnation. After all this, the verse is a threat against the disbelievers; so there is no indication in it of the particular details of the branches of the issues of fiqh. This verse was also cited as evidence for the obligation of the infallibility (ismah) of the Messenger, and that every mujtahid is relieved of sin. As for the meaning of His saying ﴿We will leave him in what he has turned to﴾, Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is a threat that he will be left with his corrupt choice. Al-Zamakhshari said: He makes it with the ya' (i.e., yuwallihi), and "what he has turned to" of misguidance means that You forsake him and leave him between himself and what he has chosen, end of his words. This is according to his Mu'tazili approach. It was also read: ﴿wa-nuslihi﴾ with a fatha on the nun, from salahu. Ibn Abi 'Ayla read (yuwallihi) and (yuslihi) with the ya' in both, following His saying ﴿fasawfa yu'tihi﴾ with the ya'. Regarding the ha' in ﴿nuwallihi﴾ and ﴿nuslihi﴾: there is ishba' (full vowelling), ikhtilas (reduced vowelling), and iskan (sukun), and each has been read.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 110–116 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Whoever does evil or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness from Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ The apparent meaning is that they are two different things: "evil" (su') is the ugly act that harms others, as Ṭu'mah did to Qatadah and the Jew, while "wronging oneself" (ẓulm al-nafs) is that which affects only the person himself, such as a false oath. It has been said: "whoever does evil" refers to a sin other than shirk, "or wrongs himself" refers to shirk, end of quote. It has also been said: "evil" is a minor sin and "wronging oneself" is a major sin. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: he specified what is directed at others with the name "evil," because that usually is not an immediate harm, since a person does not bring harm upon himself. It has been said that "evil" here means theft, and it has been said that it means shirk, and it has been said that it means everything for which one incurs sin. It has been said that "wronging oneself" here means accusing an innocent person of a charge. It has been said that it means whatever sins fall short of shirk. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the two have one meaning, repeated with different wording for emphasis. The apparent meaning is that forgiveness and mercy for the sinner are conditioned merely upon seeking forgiveness, and that it is sufficient; this is qualified by Allah's will according to the People of the Sunnah. Some scholars required repentance (tawbah) along with seeking forgiveness, and some restricted this to sins between the servant and his Lord, excluding sins between the servant and other servants. It has been said that seeking forgiveness means repentance. In the phrase ﴿will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ there is an emphasis on forgiveness, as if forgiveness and mercy are prepared for one who seeks them, ready for him whenever he asks for them, and he finds them. This verse contains great kindness and a generous promise for sinners who seek forgiveness from Allah, and in it the repentance of the Banu Ubayriq and those who defended them is sought, and they are invited to it. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that it is among the most hopeful verses.

﴿And whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ "Ithm" (sin) encompasses the "evil" and "wronging oneself" mentioned earlier. (p-346) The meaning is: the burden of that falls upon him, not passing to anyone else, and this is an indication of the requital that befalls him in the Hereafter. He concluded it with the attribute of knowledge, because He knows all that one earns, nothing of it escaping Him. Then with the attribute of wisdom, because He places things in their proper places, so He requites that sin with what His wisdom requires. The two attributes indicate His knowledge of that sin and what its doer deserves for it. In the wording there is also an indication of the sin's dominance over him, its overpowering and subduing of him.

﴿And whoever earns a fault or a sin, then throws it upon an innocent person, has certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin.﴾ It has been said it was revealed about Ṭu'mah ibn Ubayriq when he stole the armour and threw it into the house of the Jew. Al-Ḍaḥḥak related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed about ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, when he slandered ʿĀʾishah with the lie (al-ifk). The apparent sense of the conjunction with "or" (aw) is difference: it has been said that "khaṭī'ah" (fault) is what occurs without intention, and "ithm" (sin) is what occurs intentionally; or that one is minor and the other major; or that one is restricted to the doer and the other extends to another. It has been said that "khaṭī'ah" is the theft of the armour, and "ithm" is his false oath. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "khaṭī'ah" is the thief's false oath, and "ithm" is the theft of the armour and throwing it upon the Jew. Al-Ṭabari said: "khaṭī'ah" may occur intentionally or unintentionally, while "ithm" occurs only intentionally. It has been said that they are two words with one meaning, repeated for emphasis. The pronoun in "bihi" (with it) refers to "ithm," and the item joined by "or" may have its pronoun refer to the first item of the conjunction, as in His saying: ﴿they dispersed toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], or to the second, as in this verse. The discussion of that has been treated more fully than this. It has been said that it refers to the earning understood from "yaksib" (earns). It has been said that it refers to what is earned. It has been said that it refers to one of the two mentioned, indicated by the conjunction "or," as if it were said: then throws one of the two mentioned. It has been said there is an elided element; its estimate: "whoever earns a fault and then throws it upon an innocent person, or a sin and then throws it upon an innocent person." These are the derivations of one who has not mastered anything of the science of grammar.

The innocent (al-bari') is one accused of a sin while not having committed it. The meaning of ﴿has certainly borne a slander﴾ is: by his throwing (the blame) upon the innocent, for he thereby slanders him, ﴿and a manifest sin﴾, that is, evident, for his earning of the fault or the sin. The meaning is that he deserves two punishments: the punishment for the earning and the punishment for the slander. Slander (buhtan) was mentioned first because of its nearness to His saying ﴿then throws it upon an innocent person﴾, and because it is a more heinous sin than earning a fault or a sin. The verb "iḥtamala" is more emphatic than "ḥamala" (to carry), because the "if'tala" form here indicates effort, like "i'tamala." It is possible that "if'tala" here is like the bare form, as in His saying: ﴿and they will surely carry their burdens﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 29:13], so it would be like "qadara" and "iqtadara." Since burden (wizr) is described by the verb, the mention of carrying and bearing came, and this is a metaphor: the one accused is treated as a carried load. The word "whoever" (man) indicates generality, so it should not be restricted to the Banu Ubayriq; rather they are included within it. Mu'adh ibn Jabal read "wa-man yakkisib" with a kasra on the kaf and a shaddah on the sin, its origin being "yaktasib." Al-Zuhri read "khaṭiyyatan" with a shaddah.

﴿Had it not been for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy, a party of them would have resolved to lead you astray, but they lead astray none except themselves, and they do not harm you at all.﴾ The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "minhum" (of them) refers to the Banu Zafar, who disputed and defended the Banu Ubayriq. That is: had it not been for His protection and His revelation to you of what they concealed, they would have resolved to mislead you from judging with the truth and pursuing the path of justice, while knowing that the wrongdoer is their own companion. It has been reported that some of them knew the reality of the story; this includes some words of al-Zamakhshari, and it is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas via al-Sa'ib: that it relates to the story of Ṭu'mah and his companions, when they confused the Messenger about the matter of their companion.

Al-Ḍaḥḥak related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed about "the delegation of Thaqif, who came to the Messenger (ﷺ) and said: 'We have come to pledge allegiance to you on condition that we are not gathered (for jihad) nor levied (for charity), and that you let us enjoy al-ʿUzza for a year.' He did not answer them, so this was revealed." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Allah granted success to His Prophet according to the measure of his protection, and that it is by a grace from Allah and His mercy. His saying "a party would have resolved" (lahammat) means: it would have made it its concern and occupation until it carried it out. This indicates that the wording is general beyond the people of the incident, for otherwise the ones who were angry on behalf of the Banu Ubayriq had their resolve, and it occurred and was established. The meaning: had it not been for Allah's protection of you, there would have been among people one who occupies himself with misleading you and makes it his personal concern, as these did, but protection (al-'ismah) nullifies the scheming of the group, end of quote. The apparent view is the first, as we mentioned, except that "resolve" requires a qualifier: that is, "a party of them resolved with a resolve that would affect you." This qualifier is necessary, because they truly resolved, meaning those disputing on behalf of the Banu Ubayriq; or it specifies misleading from the religion, so the resolve is to mislead you from your Law and your religion, and Allah's protection of you prevented them from entertaining that thought.

﴿They lead astray none except themselves﴾: that is, the burden of what they undertook of cooperating in sin, slander and false testimony falls only upon them. ﴿And they do not harm you at all﴾: "min" (at all) indicates generality explicitly, that is, they do not harm you in the slightest or the greatest. Al-Qaffal said: this is a promise of protection in the future.

﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom﴾: "the Book" is the Qur'an. "Wisdom" was explained earlier. The meaning: the one upon whom Allah sent down the Book and wisdom, and qualified him for that, and commanded him to convey it, is protected from falling into error and doubts.

﴿And taught you what you did not know﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil said: it is the Law (al-shar'). Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: the reports of the earlier and later peoples. Al-Mawardi mentioned: the Book and wisdom, and also mentioned the measure of your precious self. It has been said: the hidden matters and the secrets of hearts that none knows except by revelation. Al-Qaffal said: it may carry two aspects. The first: that what is meant is what relates to religion, as He said: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ [al-Shura: 42:52]. On this reading: He informed you of the secrets of the Book and wisdom and their realities, while you knew nothing; so likewise He will deal with you in the coming days, and no one of the hypocrites will be able to mislead you or make you slip. The second: what you did not know of the reports of the past generations, and likewise He teaches you of the tricks and schemes of the hypocrites what cannot be guarded against, end of quote. There is some abridgment in it. The apparent sense is generality, so it encompasses all that they mentioned. The meaning: the things you did not know, had He not informed you of them.

﴿And the grace of Allah upon you has been immense﴾: it has been said: it is the favour of faith. Abu Sulayman said: it is what He singled you out with. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: this is one of the greatest proofs that knowledge is the noblest of virtues and merits, for Allah did not give creation of knowledge except a little, and a person's share of the knowledge of creatures is small, yet He called that little "great."

These verses contain several kinds of eloquence, expressiveness and rhetorical embellishment (*badi'*). Among them is metaphor (*isti'arah*) in: ﴿When you travel in the land﴾ [4:101], and in: (﴿so they would incline﴾ [4:102]), where he used the metaphor of *inclining* for [turning toward] war. There is repetition (*takrar*) in: (*junah*, "blame") and (*la junaha*, "there is no blame"), due to the difference in what each is connected to; and in: ﴿let a group of them stand﴾ [4:102] and ﴿let another group come﴾ [4:102]; and in: the caution and the weapons; and in: (the prayer); and in: ﴿you suffer﴾ [4:104]; and in: the name of Allah. There is paronomasia of difference (*tajnis al-mughayir*) in: ﴿so they incline﴾ [4:102] and ﴿a single inclination﴾ [4:102]; and in: (*kafaru*, "they disbelieved") and ﴿indeed the disbelievers﴾ [4:101]; and in: (*takhtanuna*, "you betray") and (*khawwanan*, "treacherous"); and in: (*yastaghfiru*, "seek forgiveness") and (*ghafuran*, "Forgiving"). There is paronomasia of similarity (*tajnis al-mumathil*) in: ﴿fa-aqamta﴾ [4:102] and ﴿fal-taqum﴾ [4:102]; and in: ﴿lam yusalloo﴾ [4:102] and ﴿falyusalloo﴾ [4:102]; and in: ﴿yastakhfoon﴾ [4:108] and (*la yastakhfoon*); and in: (*jadaltum*, "you argued") and ﴿who will argue﴾ [4:109]; and in: (*yaksib*) and (*yaksib*); and in: (*yudilloonaka*, "they would mislead you") and (*yudilloon*, "they mislead"); and in: (*'allamaka*, "He taught you") and (*ta'lam*, "you knew").

It has been said: the general is intended as the particular, in: ﴿So when you have completed the prayer﴾ [4:103]. Its apparent meaning is generality, but they agreed that what is intended by it is specifically the prayer of fear, because the context indicates this; and for this reason the *al-* in it is for previous reference (*al-'ahd*). The end of the quotation. Now, if *al-* is for previous reference, then it is not an instance of the general intended as the particular, because *al-* of generality (*al-'umum*) and *al-* of previous reference (*al-'ahd*) are two distinct categories; so when it is used for one of the two categories, it is not established for the other.

There is ambiguity (*al-ibham*) in His saying: ﴿by what Allah showed you﴾ [4:105], and in: ﴿what you did not know﴾ [4:113]. There is address to a specific person while another is intended (*khitab 'ayn wa-yurad bihi ghayruhu*), in: ﴿And do not be a advocate for the treacherous﴾ [4:105]; for he (ﷺ) is protected by infallibility from disputing on behalf of the falsifiers. There is completion (*al-tatmim*) in His saying: ﴿while He is with them﴾ [4:108], for censure of them and emphasis on the ugliness of their act; because a person is more shy before one who accompanies him than before himself alone. The original meaning of *ma'iyyah* ("being with") is in companionship, and Allah, Exalted, is exempt from that; so He is "with" His servant through knowledge and encompassing. The application of the description of sin (*ijram*) to meanings [i.e., to speech and plotting] has carried the sense of slander (*buhtan*). There is ellipsis (*al-hadhf*) in several places.

(p-348) ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk, except for one who enjoins charity or what is good or reconciliation between people. And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah, We will give him a great reward﴾ [4:114]. ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers – We will give him what he has turned to and drive him into Hell, and evil is it as a destination﴾ [4:115]. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly gone far astray﴾ [4:116]. ﴿They invoke besides Him only female [deities], and they invoke only a rebellious devil﴾ [4:117]. ﴿Allah has cursed him, and he said, "I will take from among Your servants a determined portion"﴾ [4:118]. ﴿And I will mislead them, and I will arouse in them false hopes, and I will order them so they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will order them so they will alter the creation of Allah." And whoever takes Satan as an ally instead of Allah has certainly suffered a clear loss﴾ [4:119]. ﴿He promises them and arouses in them desires, but Satan promises them nothing except delusion﴾ [4:120]. ﴿Those – their refuge is Hell, and they will not find from it any escape﴾ [4:121]. ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ [4:122]. ﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Scripture. Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and he will not find for himself besides Allah any protector or helper﴾ [4:123]. ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer – those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged, [even] as much as a speck﴾ [4:124]. ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah while being a doer of good and follows the religion of Abraham, inclining [to truth]? And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend﴾ [4:125]. ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is ever, of all things, Encompassing﴾ [4:126].

*An-najwa* (secret talk) is a verbal noun like *ad-da'wa* (claim). It is said: "*najawtu al-rajul anjuhu najwa*" when one converses privately with him. Al-Wahidi said: *an-najwa* occurs only between two persons. Al-Zajjaj said: *an-najwa* is what a group or two persons keep to themselves, whether secretly or openly. The end. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is private conversation (*al-musarrah*), and *an-najwa* may also be applied to the people who are conversing privately, and this is of the type: "*qawmun 'adlun*" (a just people), where a description is given with the verbal noun. Al-Kirmani said: *najwa* is the plural of *najiyy* (confidant), and the discussion of this root has already occurred, and it is repeated here due to the special nature of the pattern.

*Marid* (rebellious): from *marada*, meaning he rebelled and excelled in cunning, and devoted himself to evil and misguidance. Ibn 'Isa said: its original meaning is smoothness, and from it [comes] "*shajarah marda'*", i.e., a smooth tree whose leaves have fallen off; and "*ghulam amrad*" is a boy without facial hair; and "*sarh mumarrad*" is a smooth palace on which nothing can be hung because of its smoothness; and "*marid*" is one who does not cling to any virtue.

*Al-batk*: splitting and cutting; he cuts (*yabtik*), and the intensive form is *battaka*; *al-batk* is cutting, and its singular is *batkah*. The poet said:
*Until, when the hand of the youth struck it, it flew away, and in his hand there was a piece of its feathers.*

*Mahis* (escape): a noun of place from *hasa yahis*, meaning he swerved in aversion; and from it: "*fahasu hay-sata himar al-wahsh*" (they fled in a scattering like wild donkeys). The poet's saying:
*And we did not know whether we would escape from death by a swerve, how long life remains and how long the duration is extended.*
It is also said *jada'* with the letters *jim* and *dad* (with a dot), and *al-muhas* is like *al-mahis*. The poet said:
*He sought escape from the judgment of death, striving, but there is no escape for men from the fates.*
And in the proverb: "They fell into *hay-sa bay-sa*" (a difficult predicament). *Hasa basa* means he fell into what he cannot escape from. It is said: *hasa yahus hawsan* and *hiyasan* when he fled and left the place where he was.
*Al-hawsu* in the eye is the narrowness of its inner corner.

*Al-Khalil* (intimate friend): *fa'il* from *al-khullah*, which is poverty and need; or from *al-khullah*, which is purity of affection; or from *al-khalal* (gap). Tha'lab said: he was called *khalil* because his love penetrates the heart, so it leaves no gap in it without filling it. He recited the verse of Bashshar:
*It has permeated the course of the spirit within me, and by it the Khalil was named Khalil.*

﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk, except for one who enjoins charity or what is good or reconciliation between people﴾. The pronoun in *najwahum* ("their secret talk") refers to the people of Tu'mah who were mentioned earlier; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. Muqatil said: they are a group of Jews who conspired with the people of Tu'mah and agreed with them on deceiving the Messenger regarding the matter of Tu'mah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it refers to all people.

These verses came in general terms, so the people of the incident were included in that generality, namely the people of Tu'mah, and this is of the type of conciseness and eloquence, since one expression encompasses both the past and the different. The end. This exception is disjunctive (*munqati'*) if *an-najwa* is a verbal noun, and it may be connected (*muttasil*) by omitting a noun: i.e., "except a secret talk concerning a matter", as said by Abu 'Ubaydah. If *an-najwa* means the people conversing privately, it is said: *man* in the genitive may be in two ways: it may be a modifier of *kathir* (much), or a modifier of *an-najwa*, just as you say: "There is no good in a group of the people except Zayd," – if you wish you may make Zayd follow the group, and if you wish you may make him follow the people. It is permissible for *man amara* to be in the genitive as a substitute (*badal*) for *kathir*, because it falls within the scope of negation, or as an adjective. If it is disjunctive, the meaning is: "But whoever enjoins charity, then the good is in his secret talk." *Amara* means urged and incited. *Sadaqah* (charity) includes obligatory and voluntary charity. *Al-ma'ruf* (what is good) is general for every act of righteousness. This was preferred by a group including Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and Ibn 'Atiyyah. Thus charity and reconciliation fall under it, but these two were singled out and specified for mention, out of concern, since they are the greatest nourishment for the welfare of servants. They were joined by *aw* ("or"), and so they were made like a separate category opposite to the general, to emphasize their singling out, until the category became a distinct category. It has been said: *al-ma'ruf* is the obligatory duty; this was reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. It has also been said: it is aiding the one who is distressed.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that *sadaqah* refers to what is obligatory and *al-ma'ruf* refers to what is given in charity voluntarily. The end.

In the authentic hadith: "Every word of the son of Adam is against him, not for him, except one who enjoins what is good, or forbids what is evil, or remembers Allah, the Exalted." Sufyan al-Thawri narrated this hadith to some people, and one of them said: "How severe this hadith is!" He said: "Have you not heard: 'Every good deed is charity, and among good deeds is that you meet your brother with a cheerful face'?"

Al-Hutay'ah said:
*Whoever does good will not lose its rewarder; good custom does not vanish between Allah and the people.*

The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿or reconciliation between people﴾ is that it applies to everything in which disagreement and dispute occur. It has also been said that it is specific to reconciling between Tu'mah and the Jew mentioned. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said, in summary: He mentioned three types, because doing good is either by repelling harm, to which the reference is in His saying: "or reconciliation between people"; or by delivering benefit, which is either physical, namely giving wealth, to which the reference is in His saying: "charity"; or spiritual, namely perfecting the theoretical faculty through knowledge, or the practical faculty through good deeds, and the totality of these is an expression of enjoining what is good, to which the reference is in His saying: "or what is good." The end.

Al-Raghib said: Whatever the intellect deems good and recognizes is called *ma'ruf* (known), and whatever it deems ugly and rejects is called *munkar* (rejected). The reason is that He, Exalted, placed in the intellects the knowledge of good and evil, and to this He alluded with His saying: ﴿the coloring of Allah﴾ [2:138] and ﴿the nature of Allah﴾ [30:30]; and based on this, that to which the soul is at peace is what it recognizes. The end.

This is a Mu'tazilite inclination in that the intellect makes things good and bad. It has been said that these three contain good deeds, and he began with the most beneficial of them, which is delivering benefit to others; and by *al-ma'ruf* he drew attention to the voluntary acts which are of kindness, generosity, and reconciliation between people for their governance, and what leads to unifying their affairs. The end.

He (peace be upon him) said: "Shall I not inform you of something better than the rank of prayer, fasting and charity?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Reconciliation between people."

He specified (*man amara*) with these matters, and implicit in that is that the one who performs them deserves more than the one who merely commands them; and if good is in the secret talk of one who enjoins it, then it is not in the one who does it by way of priority [i.e., it is even more so for the doer].

﴿And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah, We will give him a great reward﴾. When He mentioned that good is in the one who enjoins, He mentioned the reward of the one who does. It is permissible that He intends: "And whoever enjoins that," so He expresses the command by the verb, just as He expresses by it all other acts.

Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read *yu'tihi* with *ya'* (third person), while the rest read it with *nun* (first person plural), by way of *iltifat* (shift of person), to harmonize with what follows it: ﴿We will turn him to what he has turned to, and drive him into Hell﴾. Thus the attribution of reward and punishment is to the pronoun of the majestic speaker, which is more eloquent than attributing it to the pronoun of the absent. And the one who reads with *ya'* has considered the absent name in His saying "seeking the pleasure of Allah"; and in His saying "seeking the pleasure of Allah" is evidence that none of the deeds are accepted except what has in it the pleasure of Allah, Exalted, and its sincerity for Allah alone, without showing off or seeking reputation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 110–116 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him, and follows other than the way of the believers, We will leave him in what he has turned to, and We will burn him in Hell, and evil is it as a destination.﴾ It was revealed concerning Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq, when Allah exposed him for his theft and absolved the Jew. He apostatised and went off to Makkah, and his death and its cause preceded this. Among what has been said about him: he boarded a ship, stole some property from it, was discovered, and was thrown into the sea. It was also said that when he stole the armour of al-Hajjaj al-Sulami, al-Hajjaj was ashamed before him because he had been his guest, so he let him go. He then joined the Banu Sulaym's valley, worshipped an idol of theirs, and died in polytheism. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the people of Tu'mah: they came, embraced Islam, then apostatised. The meaning of opposition (mushaqqah) has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿So they are in opposition﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137]. ﴿And whoever opposes﴾ is general, so Tu'mah and others among the opponents are included in it. ﴿After guidance has become clear to him﴾: i.e., the truth that is the cause of guidance has become evident to him. Had there been nothing but Allah informing His Prophet (peace be upon him) of the story of Tu'mah, and making him aware of what they had plotted and fabricated, he would have had in that the greatest restraint and the clearest explanation. The sin of one who knows the truth and deviates from it is greater than the sin of the ignorant, because one who does not know the truth deserves punishment for abandoning knowledge, since action is not obligatory on him until he knows it, or until someone who is trusted tells him. The scholar deserves punishment for abandoning the practice of what his knowledge requires; so his crime is greater when he has been made aware of the truth and acts contrary to what it requires, out of obstinacy towards Allah, the Exalted, since light has been given to him by which he could be guided. The way of the believers is the upright religion (al-din al-hanifi) which they follow. This conjoined clause is by way of emphasis, vilification and condemnation; for otherwise, whoever opposes the Messenger is necessarily following other than the way of the believers; but He began with the greater of the two sins and followed it with its necessary consequence as emphasis.

Al-Shafi'i and others used this verse as evidence that consensus (ijma') is a proof (hujjah). The scholars of usul al-fiqh have elaborated at length on the derivation of the proof from it and what objections are raised against that, and this is mentioned in the books of usul al-fiqh. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is evidence that consensus is a proof which may not be opposed, just as opposing the Book and the Sunnah may not be done; for Allah, the Exalted, combined following other than the way of the believers with opposing the Messenger in the condition, and made its recompense a severe threat; so following them is obligatory, like loyalty to the Messenger. End of his words.

What he mentioned is not the apparent meaning of the verse, which is arranged upon two attributes, and it does not follow that the consequence applies to each one of them separately. The threat in the verse is only applied to one who has both attributes: opposing the Messenger and following other than the way of the believers; for this reason the verb is conjoined to the verb and no conditional particle is repeated with it. Had the conditional particle been repeated, as it would be in: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him﴾ and whoever follows other than the way of the believers, there would have been a manifestation of what they claimed. All of this is on the assumption that His saying ﴿and follows other than the way of the believers﴾ is distinct from His saying ﴿and whoever opposes the Messenger﴾. We have said that it is not distinct; rather, it is a necessary consequence of opposing the Messenger, by way of hyperbole, emphasis, and magnifying the matter and its condemnation. After all this, the verse is a threat against the disbelievers; so there is no indication in it of the particular details of the branches of the issues of fiqh. This verse was also cited as evidence for the obligation of the infallibility (ismah) of the Messenger, and that every mujtahid is relieved of sin. As for the meaning of His saying ﴿We will leave him in what he has turned to﴾, Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is a threat that he will be left with his corrupt choice. Al-Zamakhshari said: He makes it with the ya' (i.e., yuwallihi), and "what he has turned to" of misguidance means that You forsake him and leave him between himself and what he has chosen, end of his words. This is according to his Mu'tazili approach. It was also read: ﴿wa-nuslihi﴾ with a fatha on the nun, from salahu. Ibn Abi 'Ayla read (yuwallihi) and (yuslihi) with the ya' in both, following His saying ﴿fasawfa yu'tihi﴾ with the ya'. Regarding the ha' in ﴿nuwallihi﴾ and ﴿nuslihi﴾: there is ishba' (full vowelling), ikhtilas (reduced vowelling), and iskan (sukun), and each has been read.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 110–116 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Whoever does evil or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness from Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ The apparent meaning is that they are two different things: "evil" (su') is the ugly act that harms others, as Ṭu'mah did to Qatadah and the Jew, while "wronging oneself" (ẓulm al-nafs) is that which affects only the person himself, such as a false oath. It has been said: "whoever does evil" refers to a sin other than shirk, "or wrongs himself" refers to shirk, end of quote. It has also been said: "evil" is a minor sin and "wronging oneself" is a major sin. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: he specified what is directed at others with the name "evil," because that usually is not an immediate harm, since a person does not bring harm upon himself. It has been said that "evil" here means theft, and it has been said that it means shirk, and it has been said that it means everything for which one incurs sin. It has been said that "wronging oneself" here means accusing an innocent person of a charge. It has been said that it means whatever sins fall short of shirk. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the two have one meaning, repeated with different wording for emphasis. The apparent meaning is that forgiveness and mercy for the sinner are conditioned merely upon seeking forgiveness, and that it is sufficient; this is qualified by Allah's will according to the People of the Sunnah. Some scholars required repentance (tawbah) along with seeking forgiveness, and some restricted this to sins between the servant and his Lord, excluding sins between the servant and other servants. It has been said that seeking forgiveness means repentance. In the phrase ﴿will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ there is an emphasis on forgiveness, as if forgiveness and mercy are prepared for one who seeks them, ready for him whenever he asks for them, and he finds them. This verse contains great kindness and a generous promise for sinners who seek forgiveness from Allah, and in it the repentance of the Banu Ubayriq and those who defended them is sought, and they are invited to it. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that it is among the most hopeful verses.

﴿And whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ "Ithm" (sin) encompasses the "evil" and "wronging oneself" mentioned earlier. (p-346) The meaning is: the burden of that falls upon him, not passing to anyone else, and this is an indication of the requital that befalls him in the Hereafter. He concluded it with the attribute of knowledge, because He knows all that one earns, nothing of it escaping Him. Then with the attribute of wisdom, because He places things in their proper places, so He requites that sin with what His wisdom requires. The two attributes indicate His knowledge of that sin and what its doer deserves for it. In the wording there is also an indication of the sin's dominance over him, its overpowering and subduing of him.

﴿And whoever earns a fault or a sin, then throws it upon an innocent person, has certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin.﴾ It has been said it was revealed about Ṭu'mah ibn Ubayriq when he stole the armour and threw it into the house of the Jew. Al-Ḍaḥḥak related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed about ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, when he slandered ʿĀʾishah with the lie (al-ifk). The apparent sense of the conjunction with "or" (aw) is difference: it has been said that "khaṭī'ah" (fault) is what occurs without intention, and "ithm" (sin) is what occurs intentionally; or that one is minor and the other major; or that one is restricted to the doer and the other extends to another. It has been said that "khaṭī'ah" is the theft of the armour, and "ithm" is his false oath. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "khaṭī'ah" is the thief's false oath, and "ithm" is the theft of the armour and throwing it upon the Jew. Al-Ṭabari said: "khaṭī'ah" may occur intentionally or unintentionally, while "ithm" occurs only intentionally. It has been said that they are two words with one meaning, repeated for emphasis. The pronoun in "bihi" (with it) refers to "ithm," and the item joined by "or" may have its pronoun refer to the first item of the conjunction, as in His saying: ﴿they dispersed toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], or to the second, as in this verse. The discussion of that has been treated more fully than this. It has been said that it refers to the earning understood from "yaksib" (earns). It has been said that it refers to what is earned. It has been said that it refers to one of the two mentioned, indicated by the conjunction "or," as if it were said: then throws one of the two mentioned. It has been said there is an elided element; its estimate: "whoever earns a fault and then throws it upon an innocent person, or a sin and then throws it upon an innocent person." These are the derivations of one who has not mastered anything of the science of grammar.

The innocent (al-bari') is one accused of a sin while not having committed it. The meaning of ﴿has certainly borne a slander﴾ is: by his throwing (the blame) upon the innocent, for he thereby slanders him, ﴿and a manifest sin﴾, that is, evident, for his earning of the fault or the sin. The meaning is that he deserves two punishments: the punishment for the earning and the punishment for the slander. Slander (buhtan) was mentioned first because of its nearness to His saying ﴿then throws it upon an innocent person﴾, and because it is a more heinous sin than earning a fault or a sin. The verb "iḥtamala" is more emphatic than "ḥamala" (to carry), because the "if'tala" form here indicates effort, like "i'tamala." It is possible that "if'tala" here is like the bare form, as in His saying: ﴿and they will surely carry their burdens﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 29:13], so it would be like "qadara" and "iqtadara." Since burden (wizr) is described by the verb, the mention of carrying and bearing came, and this is a metaphor: the one accused is treated as a carried load. The word "whoever" (man) indicates generality, so it should not be restricted to the Banu Ubayriq; rather they are included within it. Mu'adh ibn Jabal read "wa-man yakkisib" with a kasra on the kaf and a shaddah on the sin, its origin being "yaktasib." Al-Zuhri read "khaṭiyyatan" with a shaddah.

﴿Had it not been for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy, a party of them would have resolved to lead you astray, but they lead astray none except themselves, and they do not harm you at all.﴾ The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "minhum" (of them) refers to the Banu Zafar, who disputed and defended the Banu Ubayriq. That is: had it not been for His protection and His revelation to you of what they concealed, they would have resolved to mislead you from judging with the truth and pursuing the path of justice, while knowing that the wrongdoer is their own companion. It has been reported that some of them knew the reality of the story; this includes some words of al-Zamakhshari, and it is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas via al-Sa'ib: that it relates to the story of Ṭu'mah and his companions, when they confused the Messenger about the matter of their companion.

Al-Ḍaḥḥak related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed about "the delegation of Thaqif, who came to the Messenger (ﷺ) and said: 'We have come to pledge allegiance to you on condition that we are not gathered (for jihad) nor levied (for charity), and that you let us enjoy al-ʿUzza for a year.' He did not answer them, so this was revealed." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Allah granted success to His Prophet according to the measure of his protection, and that it is by a grace from Allah and His mercy. His saying "a party would have resolved" (lahammat) means: it would have made it its concern and occupation until it carried it out. This indicates that the wording is general beyond the people of the incident, for otherwise the ones who were angry on behalf of the Banu Ubayriq had their resolve, and it occurred and was established. The meaning: had it not been for Allah's protection of you, there would have been among people one who occupies himself with misleading you and makes it his personal concern, as these did, but protection (al-'ismah) nullifies the scheming of the group, end of quote. The apparent view is the first, as we mentioned, except that "resolve" requires a qualifier: that is, "a party of them resolved with a resolve that would affect you." This qualifier is necessary, because they truly resolved, meaning those disputing on behalf of the Banu Ubayriq; or it specifies misleading from the religion, so the resolve is to mislead you from your Law and your religion, and Allah's protection of you prevented them from entertaining that thought.

﴿They lead astray none except themselves﴾: that is, the burden of what they undertook of cooperating in sin, slander and false testimony falls only upon them. ﴿And they do not harm you at all﴾: "min" (at all) indicates generality explicitly, that is, they do not harm you in the slightest or the greatest. Al-Qaffal said: this is a promise of protection in the future.

﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom﴾: "the Book" is the Qur'an. "Wisdom" was explained earlier. The meaning: the one upon whom Allah sent down the Book and wisdom, and qualified him for that, and commanded him to convey it, is protected from falling into error and doubts.

﴿And taught you what you did not know﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil said: it is the Law (al-shar'). Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: the reports of the earlier and later peoples. Al-Mawardi mentioned: the Book and wisdom, and also mentioned the measure of your precious self. It has been said: the hidden matters and the secrets of hearts that none knows except by revelation. Al-Qaffal said: it may carry two aspects. The first: that what is meant is what relates to religion, as He said: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ [al-Shura: 42:52]. On this reading: He informed you of the secrets of the Book and wisdom and their realities, while you knew nothing; so likewise He will deal with you in the coming days, and no one of the hypocrites will be able to mislead you or make you slip. The second: what you did not know of the reports of the past generations, and likewise He teaches you of the tricks and schemes of the hypocrites what cannot be guarded against, end of quote. There is some abridgment in it. The apparent sense is generality, so it encompasses all that they mentioned. The meaning: the things you did not know, had He not informed you of them.

﴿And the grace of Allah upon you has been immense﴾: it has been said: it is the favour of faith. Abu Sulayman said: it is what He singled you out with. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: this is one of the greatest proofs that knowledge is the noblest of virtues and merits, for Allah did not give creation of knowledge except a little, and a person's share of the knowledge of creatures is small, yet He called that little "great."

These verses contain several kinds of eloquence, expressiveness and rhetorical embellishment (*badi'*). Among them is metaphor (*isti'arah*) in: ﴿When you travel in the land﴾ [4:101], and in: (﴿so they would incline﴾ [4:102]), where he used the metaphor of *inclining* for [turning toward] war. There is repetition (*takrar*) in: (*junah*, "blame") and (*la junaha*, "there is no blame"), due to the difference in what each is connected to; and in: ﴿let a group of them stand﴾ [4:102] and ﴿let another group come﴾ [4:102]; and in: the caution and the weapons; and in: (the prayer); and in: ﴿you suffer﴾ [4:104]; and in: the name of Allah. There is paronomasia of difference (*tajnis al-mughayir*) in: ﴿so they incline﴾ [4:102] and ﴿a single inclination﴾ [4:102]; and in: (*kafaru*, "they disbelieved") and ﴿indeed the disbelievers﴾ [4:101]; and in: (*takhtanuna*, "you betray") and (*khawwanan*, "treacherous"); and in: (*yastaghfiru*, "seek forgiveness") and (*ghafuran*, "Forgiving"). There is paronomasia of similarity (*tajnis al-mumathil*) in: ﴿fa-aqamta﴾ [4:102] and ﴿fal-taqum﴾ [4:102]; and in: ﴿lam yusalloo﴾ [4:102] and ﴿falyusalloo﴾ [4:102]; and in: ﴿yastakhfoon﴾ [4:108] and (*la yastakhfoon*); and in: (*jadaltum*, "you argued") and ﴿who will argue﴾ [4:109]; and in: (*yaksib*) and (*yaksib*); and in: (*yudilloonaka*, "they would mislead you") and (*yudilloon*, "they mislead"); and in: (*'allamaka*, "He taught you") and (*ta'lam*, "you knew").

It has been said: the general is intended as the particular, in: ﴿So when you have completed the prayer﴾ [4:103]. Its apparent meaning is generality, but they agreed that what is intended by it is specifically the prayer of fear, because the context indicates this; and for this reason the *al-* in it is for previous reference (*al-'ahd*). The end of the quotation. Now, if *al-* is for previous reference, then it is not an instance of the general intended as the particular, because *al-* of generality (*al-'umum*) and *al-* of previous reference (*al-'ahd*) are two distinct categories; so when it is used for one of the two categories, it is not established for the other.

There is ambiguity (*al-ibham*) in His saying: ﴿by what Allah showed you﴾ [4:105], and in: ﴿what you did not know﴾ [4:113]. There is address to a specific person while another is intended (*khitab 'ayn wa-yurad bihi ghayruhu*), in: ﴿And do not be a advocate for the treacherous﴾ [4:105]; for he (ﷺ) is protected by infallibility from disputing on behalf of the falsifiers. There is completion (*al-tatmim*) in His saying: ﴿while He is with them﴾ [4:108], for censure of them and emphasis on the ugliness of their act; because a person is more shy before one who accompanies him than before himself alone. The original meaning of *ma'iyyah* ("being with") is in companionship, and Allah, Exalted, is exempt from that; so He is "with" His servant through knowledge and encompassing. The application of the description of sin (*ijram*) to meanings [i.e., to speech and plotting] has carried the sense of slander (*buhtan*). There is ellipsis (*al-hadhf*) in several places.

(p-348) ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk, except for one who enjoins charity or what is good or reconciliation between people. And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah, We will give him a great reward﴾ [4:114]. ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers – We will give him what he has turned to and drive him into Hell, and evil is it as a destination﴾ [4:115]. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly gone far astray﴾ [4:116]. ﴿They invoke besides Him only female [deities], and they invoke only a rebellious devil﴾ [4:117]. ﴿Allah has cursed him, and he said, "I will take from among Your servants a determined portion"﴾ [4:118]. ﴿And I will mislead them, and I will arouse in them false hopes, and I will order them so they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will order them so they will alter the creation of Allah." And whoever takes Satan as an ally instead of Allah has certainly suffered a clear loss﴾ [4:119]. ﴿He promises them and arouses in them desires, but Satan promises them nothing except delusion﴾ [4:120]. ﴿Those – their refuge is Hell, and they will not find from it any escape﴾ [4:121]. ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ [4:122]. ﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Scripture. Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and he will not find for himself besides Allah any protector or helper﴾ [4:123]. ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer – those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged, [even] as much as a speck﴾ [4:124]. ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah while being a doer of good and follows the religion of Abraham, inclining [to truth]? And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend﴾ [4:125]. ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is ever, of all things, Encompassing﴾ [4:126].

*An-najwa* (secret talk) is a verbal noun like *ad-da'wa* (claim). It is said: "*najawtu al-rajul anjuhu najwa*" when one converses privately with him. Al-Wahidi said: *an-najwa* occurs only between two persons. Al-Zajjaj said: *an-najwa* is what a group or two persons keep to themselves, whether secretly or openly. The end. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is private conversation (*al-musarrah*), and *an-najwa* may also be applied to the people who are conversing privately, and this is of the type: "*qawmun 'adlun*" (a just people), where a description is given with the verbal noun. Al-Kirmani said: *najwa* is the plural of *najiyy* (confidant), and the discussion of this root has already occurred, and it is repeated here due to the special nature of the pattern.

*Marid* (rebellious): from *marada*, meaning he rebelled and excelled in cunning, and devoted himself to evil and misguidance. Ibn 'Isa said: its original meaning is smoothness, and from it [comes] "*shajarah marda'*", i.e., a smooth tree whose leaves have fallen off; and "*ghulam amrad*" is a boy without facial hair; and "*sarh mumarrad*" is a smooth palace on which nothing can be hung because of its smoothness; and "*marid*" is one who does not cling to any virtue.

*Al-batk*: splitting and cutting; he cuts (*yabtik*), and the intensive form is *battaka*; *al-batk* is cutting, and its singular is *batkah*. The poet said:
*Until, when the hand of the youth struck it, it flew away, and in his hand there was a piece of its feathers.*

*Mahis* (escape): a noun of place from *hasa yahis*, meaning he swerved in aversion; and from it: "*fahasu hay-sata himar al-wahsh*" (they fled in a scattering like wild donkeys). The poet's saying:
*And we did not know whether we would escape from death by a swerve, how long life remains and how long the duration is extended.*
It is also said *jada'* with the letters *jim* and *dad* (with a dot), and *al-muhas* is like *al-mahis*. The poet said:
*He sought escape from the judgment of death, striving, but there is no escape for men from the fates.*
And in the proverb: "They fell into *hay-sa bay-sa*" (a difficult predicament). *Hasa basa* means he fell into what he cannot escape from. It is said: *hasa yahus hawsan* and *hiyasan* when he fled and left the place where he was.
*Al-hawsu* in the eye is the narrowness of its inner corner.

*Al-Khalil* (intimate friend): *fa'il* from *al-khullah*, which is poverty and need; or from *al-khullah*, which is purity of affection; or from *al-khalal* (gap). Tha'lab said: he was called *khalil* because his love penetrates the heart, so it leaves no gap in it without filling it. He recited the verse of Bashshar:
*It has permeated the course of the spirit within me, and by it the Khalil was named Khalil.*

﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk, except for one who enjoins charity or what is good or reconciliation between people﴾. The pronoun in *najwahum* ("their secret talk") refers to the people of Tu'mah who were mentioned earlier; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. Muqatil said: they are a group of Jews who conspired with the people of Tu'mah and agreed with them on deceiving the Messenger regarding the matter of Tu'mah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it refers to all people.

These verses came in general terms, so the people of the incident were included in that generality, namely the people of Tu'mah, and this is of the type of conciseness and eloquence, since one expression encompasses both the past and the different. The end. This exception is disjunctive (*munqati'*) if *an-najwa* is a verbal noun, and it may be connected (*muttasil*) by omitting a noun: i.e., "except a secret talk concerning a matter", as said by Abu 'Ubaydah. If *an-najwa* means the people conversing privately, it is said: *man* in the genitive may be in two ways: it may be a modifier of *kathir* (much), or a modifier of *an-najwa*, just as you say: "There is no good in a group of the people except Zayd," – if you wish you may make Zayd follow the group, and if you wish you may make him follow the people. It is permissible for *man amara* to be in the genitive as a substitute (*badal*) for *kathir*, because it falls within the scope of negation, or as an adjective. If it is disjunctive, the meaning is: "But whoever enjoins charity, then the good is in his secret talk." *Amara* means urged and incited. *Sadaqah* (charity) includes obligatory and voluntary charity. *Al-ma'ruf* (what is good) is general for every act of righteousness. This was preferred by a group including Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and Ibn 'Atiyyah. Thus charity and reconciliation fall under it, but these two were singled out and specified for mention, out of concern, since they are the greatest nourishment for the welfare of servants. They were joined by *aw* ("or"), and so they were made like a separate category opposite to the general, to emphasize their singling out, until the category became a distinct category. It has been said: *al-ma'ruf* is the obligatory duty; this was reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. It has also been said: it is aiding the one who is distressed.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that *sadaqah* refers to what is obligatory and *al-ma'ruf* refers to what is given in charity voluntarily. The end.

In the authentic hadith: "Every word of the son of Adam is against him, not for him, except one who enjoins what is good, or forbids what is evil, or remembers Allah, the Exalted." Sufyan al-Thawri narrated this hadith to some people, and one of them said: "How severe this hadith is!" He said: "Have you not heard: 'Every good deed is charity, and among good deeds is that you meet your brother with a cheerful face'?"

Al-Hutay'ah said:
*Whoever does good will not lose its rewarder; good custom does not vanish between Allah and the people.*

The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿or reconciliation between people﴾ is that it applies to everything in which disagreement and dispute occur. It has also been said that it is specific to reconciling between Tu'mah and the Jew mentioned. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said, in summary: He mentioned three types, because doing good is either by repelling harm, to which the reference is in His saying: "or reconciliation between people"; or by delivering benefit, which is either physical, namely giving wealth, to which the reference is in His saying: "charity"; or spiritual, namely perfecting the theoretical faculty through knowledge, or the practical faculty through good deeds, and the totality of these is an expression of enjoining what is good, to which the reference is in His saying: "or what is good." The end.

Al-Raghib said: Whatever the intellect deems good and recognizes is called *ma'ruf* (known), and whatever it deems ugly and rejects is called *munkar* (rejected). The reason is that He, Exalted, placed in the intellects the knowledge of good and evil, and to this He alluded with His saying: ﴿the coloring of Allah﴾ [2:138] and ﴿the nature of Allah﴾ [30:30]; and based on this, that to which the soul is at peace is what it recognizes. The end.

This is a Mu'tazilite inclination in that the intellect makes things good and bad. It has been said that these three contain good deeds, and he began with the most beneficial of them, which is delivering benefit to others; and by *al-ma'ruf* he drew attention to the voluntary acts which are of kindness, generosity, and reconciliation between people for their governance, and what leads to unifying their affairs. The end.

He (peace be upon him) said: "Shall I not inform you of something better than the rank of prayer, fasting and charity?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Reconciliation between people."

He specified (*man amara*) with these matters, and implicit in that is that the one who performs them deserves more than the one who merely commands them; and if good is in the secret talk of one who enjoins it, then it is not in the one who does it by way of priority [i.e., it is even more so for the doer].

﴿And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah, We will give him a great reward﴾. When He mentioned that good is in the one who enjoins, He mentioned the reward of the one who does. It is permissible that He intends: "And whoever enjoins that," so He expresses the command by the verb, just as He expresses by it all other acts.

Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read *yu'tihi* with *ya'* (third person), while the rest read it with *nun* (first person plural), by way of *iltifat* (shift of person), to harmonize with what follows it: ﴿We will turn him to what he has turned to, and drive him into Hell﴾. Thus the attribution of reward and punishment is to the pronoun of the majestic speaker, which is more eloquent than attributing it to the pronoun of the absent. And the one who reads with *ya'* has considered the absent name in His saying "seeking the pleasure of Allah"; and in His saying "seeking the pleasure of Allah" is evidence that none of the deeds are accepted except what has in it the pleasure of Allah, Exalted, and its sincerity for Allah alone, without showing off or seeking reputation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 110–116 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him, and follows other than the way of the believers, We will leave him in what he has turned to, and We will burn him in Hell, and evil is it as a destination.﴾ It was revealed concerning Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq, when Allah exposed him for his theft and absolved the Jew. He apostatised and went off to Makkah, and his death and its cause preceded this. Among what has been said about him: he boarded a ship, stole some property from it, was discovered, and was thrown into the sea. It was also said that when he stole the armour of al-Hajjaj al-Sulami, al-Hajjaj was ashamed before him because he had been his guest, so he let him go. He then joined the Banu Sulaym's valley, worshipped an idol of theirs, and died in polytheism. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the people of Tu'mah: they came, embraced Islam, then apostatised. The meaning of opposition (mushaqqah) has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿So they are in opposition﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137]. ﴿And whoever opposes﴾ is general, so Tu'mah and others among the opponents are included in it. ﴿After guidance has become clear to him﴾: i.e., the truth that is the cause of guidance has become evident to him. Had there been nothing but Allah informing His Prophet (peace be upon him) of the story of Tu'mah, and making him aware of what they had plotted and fabricated, he would have had in that the greatest restraint and the clearest explanation. The sin of one who knows the truth and deviates from it is greater than the sin of the ignorant, because one who does not know the truth deserves punishment for abandoning knowledge, since action is not obligatory on him until he knows it, or until someone who is trusted tells him. The scholar deserves punishment for abandoning the practice of what his knowledge requires; so his crime is greater when he has been made aware of the truth and acts contrary to what it requires, out of obstinacy towards Allah, the Exalted, since light has been given to him by which he could be guided. The way of the believers is the upright religion (al-din al-hanifi) which they follow. This conjoined clause is by way of emphasis, vilification and condemnation; for otherwise, whoever opposes the Messenger is necessarily following other than the way of the believers; but He began with the greater of the two sins and followed it with its necessary consequence as emphasis.

Al-Shafi'i and others used this verse as evidence that consensus (ijma') is a proof (hujjah). The scholars of usul al-fiqh have elaborated at length on the derivation of the proof from it and what objections are raised against that, and this is mentioned in the books of usul al-fiqh. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is evidence that consensus is a proof which may not be opposed, just as opposing the Book and the Sunnah may not be done; for Allah, the Exalted, combined following other than the way of the believers with opposing the Messenger in the condition, and made its recompense a severe threat; so following them is obligatory, like loyalty to the Messenger. End of his words.

What he mentioned is not the apparent meaning of the verse, which is arranged upon two attributes, and it does not follow that the consequence applies to each one of them separately. The threat in the verse is only applied to one who has both attributes: opposing the Messenger and following other than the way of the believers; for this reason the verb is conjoined to the verb and no conditional particle is repeated with it. Had the conditional particle been repeated, as it would be in: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him﴾ and whoever follows other than the way of the believers, there would have been a manifestation of what they claimed. All of this is on the assumption that His saying ﴿and follows other than the way of the believers﴾ is distinct from His saying ﴿and whoever opposes the Messenger﴾. We have said that it is not distinct; rather, it is a necessary consequence of opposing the Messenger, by way of hyperbole, emphasis, and magnifying the matter and its condemnation. After all this, the verse is a threat against the disbelievers; so there is no indication in it of the particular details of the branches of the issues of fiqh. This verse was also cited as evidence for the obligation of the infallibility (ismah) of the Messenger, and that every mujtahid is relieved of sin. As for the meaning of His saying ﴿We will leave him in what he has turned to﴾, Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is a threat that he will be left with his corrupt choice. Al-Zamakhshari said: He makes it with the ya' (i.e., yuwallihi), and "what he has turned to" of misguidance means that You forsake him and leave him between himself and what he has chosen, end of his words. This is according to his Mu'tazili approach. It was also read: ﴿wa-nuslihi﴾ with a fatha on the nun, from salahu. Ibn Abi 'Ayla read (yuwallihi) and (yuslihi) with the ya' in both, following His saying ﴿fasawfa yu'tihi﴾ with the ya'. Regarding the ha' in ﴿nuwallihi﴾ and ﴿nuslihi﴾: there is ishba' (full vowelling), ikhtilas (reduced vowelling), and iskan (sukun), and each has been read.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 110–116 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Whoever does evil or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness from Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ The apparent meaning is that they are two different things: "evil" (su') is the ugly act that harms others, as Ṭu'mah did to Qatadah and the Jew, while "wronging oneself" (ẓulm al-nafs) is that which affects only the person himself, such as a false oath. It has been said: "whoever does evil" refers to a sin other than shirk, "or wrongs himself" refers to shirk, end of quote. It has also been said: "evil" is a minor sin and "wronging oneself" is a major sin. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: he specified what is directed at others with the name "evil," because that usually is not an immediate harm, since a person does not bring harm upon himself. It has been said that "evil" here means theft, and it has been said that it means shirk, and it has been said that it means everything for which one incurs sin. It has been said that "wronging oneself" here means accusing an innocent person of a charge. It has been said that it means whatever sins fall short of shirk. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the two have one meaning, repeated with different wording for emphasis. The apparent meaning is that forgiveness and mercy for the sinner are conditioned merely upon seeking forgiveness, and that it is sufficient; this is qualified by Allah's will according to the People of the Sunnah. Some scholars required repentance (tawbah) along with seeking forgiveness, and some restricted this to sins between the servant and his Lord, excluding sins between the servant and other servants. It has been said that seeking forgiveness means repentance. In the phrase ﴿will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ there is an emphasis on forgiveness, as if forgiveness and mercy are prepared for one who seeks them, ready for him whenever he asks for them, and he finds them. This verse contains great kindness and a generous promise for sinners who seek forgiveness from Allah, and in it the repentance of the Banu Ubayriq and those who defended them is sought, and they are invited to it. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that it is among the most hopeful verses.

﴿And whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ "Ithm" (sin) encompasses the "evil" and "wronging oneself" mentioned earlier. (p-346) The meaning is: the burden of that falls upon him, not passing to anyone else, and this is an indication of the requital that befalls him in the Hereafter. He concluded it with the attribute of knowledge, because He knows all that one earns, nothing of it escaping Him. Then with the attribute of wisdom, because He places things in their proper places, so He requites that sin with what His wisdom requires. The two attributes indicate His knowledge of that sin and what its doer deserves for it. In the wording there is also an indication of the sin's dominance over him, its overpowering and subduing of him.

﴿And whoever earns a fault or a sin, then throws it upon an innocent person, has certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin.﴾ It has been said it was revealed about Ṭu'mah ibn Ubayriq when he stole the armour and threw it into the house of the Jew. Al-Ḍaḥḥak related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed about ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, when he slandered ʿĀʾishah with the lie (al-ifk). The apparent sense of the conjunction with "or" (aw) is difference: it has been said that "khaṭī'ah" (fault) is what occurs without intention, and "ithm" (sin) is what occurs intentionally; or that one is minor and the other major; or that one is restricted to the doer and the other extends to another. It has been said that "khaṭī'ah" is the theft of the armour, and "ithm" is his false oath. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "khaṭī'ah" is the thief's false oath, and "ithm" is the theft of the armour and throwing it upon the Jew. Al-Ṭabari said: "khaṭī'ah" may occur intentionally or unintentionally, while "ithm" occurs only intentionally. It has been said that they are two words with one meaning, repeated for emphasis. The pronoun in "bihi" (with it) refers to "ithm," and the item joined by "or" may have its pronoun refer to the first item of the conjunction, as in His saying: ﴿they dispersed toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], or to the second, as in this verse. The discussion of that has been treated more fully than this. It has been said that it refers to the earning understood from "yaksib" (earns). It has been said that it refers to what is earned. It has been said that it refers to one of the two mentioned, indicated by the conjunction "or," as if it were said: then throws one of the two mentioned. It has been said there is an elided element; its estimate: "whoever earns a fault and then throws it upon an innocent person, or a sin and then throws it upon an innocent person." These are the derivations of one who has not mastered anything of the science of grammar.

The innocent (al-bari') is one accused of a sin while not having committed it. The meaning of ﴿has certainly borne a slander﴾ is: by his throwing (the blame) upon the innocent, for he thereby slanders him, ﴿and a manifest sin﴾, that is, evident, for his earning of the fault or the sin. The meaning is that he deserves two punishments: the punishment for the earning and the punishment for the slander. Slander (buhtan) was mentioned first because of its nearness to His saying ﴿then throws it upon an innocent person﴾, and because it is a more heinous sin than earning a fault or a sin. The verb "iḥtamala" is more emphatic than "ḥamala" (to carry), because the "if'tala" form here indicates effort, like "i'tamala." It is possible that "if'tala" here is like the bare form, as in His saying: ﴿and they will surely carry their burdens﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 29:13], so it would be like "qadara" and "iqtadara." Since burden (wizr) is described by the verb, the mention of carrying and bearing came, and this is a metaphor: the one accused is treated as a carried load. The word "whoever" (man) indicates generality, so it should not be restricted to the Banu Ubayriq; rather they are included within it. Mu'adh ibn Jabal read "wa-man yakkisib" with a kasra on the kaf and a shaddah on the sin, its origin being "yaktasib." Al-Zuhri read "khaṭiyyatan" with a shaddah.

﴿Had it not been for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy, a party of them would have resolved to lead you astray, but they lead astray none except themselves, and they do not harm you at all.﴾ The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "minhum" (of them) refers to the Banu Zafar, who disputed and defended the Banu Ubayriq. That is: had it not been for His protection and His revelation to you of what they concealed, they would have resolved to mislead you from judging with the truth and pursuing the path of justice, while knowing that the wrongdoer is their own companion. It has been reported that some of them knew the reality of the story; this includes some words of al-Zamakhshari, and it is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas via al-Sa'ib: that it relates to the story of Ṭu'mah and his companions, when they confused the Messenger about the matter of their companion.

Al-Ḍaḥḥak related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed about "the delegation of Thaqif, who came to the Messenger (ﷺ) and said: 'We have come to pledge allegiance to you on condition that we are not gathered (for jihad) nor levied (for charity), and that you let us enjoy al-ʿUzza for a year.' He did not answer them, so this was revealed." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Allah granted success to His Prophet according to the measure of his protection, and that it is by a grace from Allah and His mercy. His saying "a party would have resolved" (lahammat) means: it would have made it its concern and occupation until it carried it out. This indicates that the wording is general beyond the people of the incident, for otherwise the ones who were angry on behalf of the Banu Ubayriq had their resolve, and it occurred and was established. The meaning: had it not been for Allah's protection of you, there would have been among people one who occupies himself with misleading you and makes it his personal concern, as these did, but protection (al-'ismah) nullifies the scheming of the group, end of quote. The apparent view is the first, as we mentioned, except that "resolve" requires a qualifier: that is, "a party of them resolved with a resolve that would affect you." This qualifier is necessary, because they truly resolved, meaning those disputing on behalf of the Banu Ubayriq; or it specifies misleading from the religion, so the resolve is to mislead you from your Law and your religion, and Allah's protection of you prevented them from entertaining that thought.

﴿They lead astray none except themselves﴾: that is, the burden of what they undertook of cooperating in sin, slander and false testimony falls only upon them. ﴿And they do not harm you at all﴾: "min" (at all) indicates generality explicitly, that is, they do not harm you in the slightest or the greatest. Al-Qaffal said: this is a promise of protection in the future.

﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom﴾: "the Book" is the Qur'an. "Wisdom" was explained earlier. The meaning: the one upon whom Allah sent down the Book and wisdom, and qualified him for that, and commanded him to convey it, is protected from falling into error and doubts.

﴿And taught you what you did not know﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil said: it is the Law (al-shar'). Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: the reports of the earlier and later peoples. Al-Mawardi mentioned: the Book and wisdom, and also mentioned the measure of your precious self. It has been said: the hidden matters and the secrets of hearts that none knows except by revelation. Al-Qaffal said: it may carry two aspects. The first: that what is meant is what relates to religion, as He said: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ [al-Shura: 42:52]. On this reading: He informed you of the secrets of the Book and wisdom and their realities, while you knew nothing; so likewise He will deal with you in the coming days, and no one of the hypocrites will be able to mislead you or make you slip. The second: what you did not know of the reports of the past generations, and likewise He teaches you of the tricks and schemes of the hypocrites what cannot be guarded against, end of quote. There is some abridgment in it. The apparent sense is generality, so it encompasses all that they mentioned. The meaning: the things you did not know, had He not informed you of them.

﴿And the grace of Allah upon you has been immense﴾: it has been said: it is the favour of faith. Abu Sulayman said: it is what He singled you out with. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: this is one of the greatest proofs that knowledge is the noblest of virtues and merits, for Allah did not give creation of knowledge except a little, and a person's share of the knowledge of creatures is small, yet He called that little "great."

These verses contain several kinds of eloquence, expressiveness and rhetorical embellishment (*badi'*). Among them is metaphor (*isti'arah*) in: ﴿When you travel in the land﴾ [4:101], and in: (﴿so they would incline﴾ [4:102]), where he used the metaphor of *inclining* for [turning toward] war. There is repetition (*takrar*) in: (*junah*, "blame") and (*la junaha*, "there is no blame"), due to the difference in what each is connected to; and in: ﴿let a group of them stand﴾ [4:102] and ﴿let another group come﴾ [4:102]; and in: the caution and the weapons; and in: (the prayer); and in: ﴿you suffer﴾ [4:104]; and in: the name of Allah. There is paronomasia of difference (*tajnis al-mughayir*) in: ﴿so they incline﴾ [4:102] and ﴿a single inclination﴾ [4:102]; and in: (*kafaru*, "they disbelieved") and ﴿indeed the disbelievers﴾ [4:101]; and in: (*takhtanuna*, "you betray") and (*khawwanan*, "treacherous"); and in: (*yastaghfiru*, "seek forgiveness") and (*ghafuran*, "Forgiving"). There is paronomasia of similarity (*tajnis al-mumathil*) in: ﴿fa-aqamta﴾ [4:102] and ﴿fal-taqum﴾ [4:102]; and in: ﴿lam yusalloo﴾ [4:102] and ﴿falyusalloo﴾ [4:102]; and in: ﴿yastakhfoon﴾ [4:108] and (*la yastakhfoon*); and in: (*jadaltum*, "you argued") and ﴿who will argue﴾ [4:109]; and in: (*yaksib*) and (*yaksib*); and in: (*yudilloonaka*, "they would mislead you") and (*yudilloon*, "they mislead"); and in: (*'allamaka*, "He taught you") and (*ta'lam*, "you knew").

It has been said: the general is intended as the particular, in: ﴿So when you have completed the prayer﴾ [4:103]. Its apparent meaning is generality, but they agreed that what is intended by it is specifically the prayer of fear, because the context indicates this; and for this reason the *al-* in it is for previous reference (*al-'ahd*). The end of the quotation. Now, if *al-* is for previous reference, then it is not an instance of the general intended as the particular, because *al-* of generality (*al-'umum*) and *al-* of previous reference (*al-'ahd*) are two distinct categories; so when it is used for one of the two categories, it is not established for the other.

There is ambiguity (*al-ibham*) in His saying: ﴿by what Allah showed you﴾ [4:105], and in: ﴿what you did not know﴾ [4:113]. There is address to a specific person while another is intended (*khitab 'ayn wa-yurad bihi ghayruhu*), in: ﴿And do not be a advocate for the treacherous﴾ [4:105]; for he (ﷺ) is protected by infallibility from disputing on behalf of the falsifiers.
