﴿Those—their refuge is Hell, and they will find no escape from it﴾: He informed that the place where they take refuge and settle is Hell, and that they will not find from it a way to turn aside to. "ʿAnhā" (from it) cannot be connected to an omitted verb, because it is not transitive with ʿan, nor to maḥīṣan (escape), even though the meaning depends on it, since it is a verbal noun; so it may be that this is a clarification by an implied "ʿannī" (away from me). They also permitted it to be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from maḥīṣ, connected to maḥīṣ, meaning "being away from it"; and had it been placed after, it would have been an attribute.

(p. 355) ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds—We will surely admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾: When He mentioned the abode of the disbelievers, He mentioned the abode of the believers, and attributed the verb to the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah), out of concern that He Himself is the One who takes charge of admitting them into Paradise, and as an honor for them. It was also read sa-yudkhiluhum with yāʾ. When He arranged the destiny of those who followed Iblīs as the Fire, because of their association and disbelief and their alteration of the rulings of Allah, the Exalted, here He arranged entry into Paradise upon faith and doing righteous deeds.

﴿The promise of Allah, in truth﴾: Since He mentioned that the promise of the devil is false delusion, He mentioned that this promise from Him, the Exalted, is the truth about which there is no doubt, and no uncertainty about its fulfillment. "Those who" is the subject (mubtada), and "We will admit them" is the predicate. It may also be from the construction of ishtighāl (where the verb is occupied by a pronoun referring to the object): i.e., "and We will admit those who believed, We will admit them." "The promise of Allah, in truth" is in the accusative as an infinitive emphasizing something other than itself: the promise of Allah emphasizes His saying "We will admit them," and "in truth" emphasizes the promise of Allah.

﴿And who is more truthful in speech than Allah?﴾: qīl and qawl are the same; i.e., no one is more truthful in speech than Allah. This clause also emphasizes what came before it. The benefit of these emphases is to intensify what Allah, the Exalted, informed His believing servants, in contrast to the promises of the devil and his false wishes, which lead to the failure of his own wishes.

﴿It is not according to your wishes, nor according to the wishes of the People of the Book﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Masrūq, Qatādah, al-Suddī, and others said: the address is to the community (the Muslims). Some of them said: they disputed with a group from the People of the Book, who said: "Our religion is older than yours and better; our prophet came before your prophet." The believers said: "Our book abrogates the books, and our prophet is the seal of the prophets," and similar argument, and so this was revealed. Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: the address is to the disbelievers of Quraysh, because they said: "We will not be resurrected, nor will we be punished; this is only our life, in which we have bliss, and then there is no punishment." The Jews said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." And other similar sayings of theirs.

(No one will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian) — Allah thus refuted both groups.

Al-Zamakhsharī said regarding "laysa" (it is not): its pronoun refers to the promise of Allah; that is, what Allah promised of reward is not attained by your wishes, nor the wishes of the People of the Book. The address is to the Muslims, because no one wishes for the promise of Allah except one who believes in Him; for this reason He mentioned the People of the Book alongside them, because they share with them in faith. It is reported from al-Ḥasan: "Faith is not by wishing; rather, it is what settles in the heart and what deeds confirm. Some people were distracted by wishes of forgiveness until they left this world without any good deed, and they said: 'We have good expectation of Allah'—and they lied. Had they truly had good expectation of Him, they would have done good deeds." It may also be that the address is to the polytheists, because of their saying: "If the matter is as these claim, we will surely be better than them and in a better state; we will be given wealth and children; indeed for me with Him is the best (ḥusnā)." The People of the Book used to say: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved; the Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days." The mention of the polytheists before reinforces this. End of quote.

On these sayings the disagreement arose concerning the subject of laysa (its noun). The pronoun returns preferably to the promise that He will admit them into Paradise; and next, it returns to the faith understood from His saying "those who believed and did righteous deeds," as al-Ḥasan held; then it returns to what the argument between the believers and the People of the Book was about, or what Quraysh and the People of the Book said, as already mentioned. Al-Ḥawfī said: the subject of laysa is a hidden pronoun in it, meaning: "Reward for good deeds is not, nor punishment for evil deeds, by your wishes; because entitlement comes only through deeds, not wishes." Abū al-Baqāʾ said: the subject of laysa is a hidden pronoun in it, with no prior mention, but the occasion of revelation indicates it: the Jews and Christians said, "We are the companions of Paradise," and the polytheists said, "We will not be resurrected." So He said: "It is not according to your wishes"; that is, what you claim is not according to your wishes. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah ibn Niṣāḥ, al-Ḥakam, and al-Aʿraj read bi-amānīkum and wa-lā amānī ahl al-kitāb with the yāʾ silent (sākinah), formed as the plural pattern faʿālil, like qarāqīr and qarāqir, the plural of qurqūr (a type of jar).

﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾: The majority said: the word is general, and both the disbeliever and the believer are recompensed for the evil they do. The disbeliever's recompense is the Fire, and the believer's is the afflictions of this world. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When it was revealed, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how severe this verse is, it breaks the back!' He said: 'It is only the calamities of this world.'" ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, gave a similar interpretation. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb also held it; al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād asked him about the meaning of the verse, and as if he feared it, he said to him: "I did not think you were more knowledgeable than what I see: a man is not struck by a scratch or anything else except for a sin, and what Allah pardons is more." al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd restricted it to the disbelievers, who are recompensed for minor and major sins. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it means the Jews, the Christians, the Magians, and the disbelieving Arabs; and these held that Allah promised the believers the expiation of their evil deeds. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jubayr restricted "evil" (sūʾ) to polytheism. It was said that "evil" is general in major sins.

﴿And they will not find for themselves besides Allah any protector or helper﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 173]: Ibn Bakkār reported from Ibn ʿĀmir: wa-lā yajidu with the nominative (rafʿ), as a resumption (qaṭʿ, a new clause).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 117–125 (part 3 of 3):

﴿Whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise﴾. (Min) in "min al-salihat" (of the righteous deeds) is partitive (lil-tab'id), because each person cannot do all the righteous deeds. He only does those that are obligatory for him and within his capacity. How many a responsible person (mukallaf) is not required to pay zakat, or to perform hajj or jihad, and prayer is dropped from him in some circumstances according to some schools of law. Al-Tabari reported from some people that (min) is extra (za'ida), meaning "whoever does the righteous deeds." But the addition of (min) in a conditional clause is weak, especially when it is followed by a definite noun. The second (min) is to clarify the vagueness in "whoever does" (man ya'mal). The discussion of (aw) has already been covered in His words: ﴿I will not let the work of any worker among you go to waste, whether male or female﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195]. The clause is circumstantial (jumla haliyya, a clause describing the state of the subject). The condition on human action is specified because, if a person performs righteous deeds, they will not benefit him unless he is a believer. Al-Zamakhshari said: "When God nullifies wishful thinking, and establishes that the whole matter is tied to righteous deeds, and that whoever improves his deeds is the successful one, and whoever spoils his deeds is the doomed one, the matter becomes clear and evident. It becomes obligatory to cut off wishful thinking, to end greed, and to turn to righteous deeds. But this is advice that ears do not heed and minds do not accept." End of quote. What the verse indicates is that faith is a condition for benefiting from deeds, because deeds are a condition for the soundness of faith.

﴿And they will not be wronged the least bit (naqir)﴾. Its apparent meaning is that it refers to the nearest previously mentioned group, who are the believers, and the ruling on the disbelievers is the same. Mentioning one of the two groups implies the other, that both will be rewarded according to their deeds. Also, wronging the evildoer would mean increasing his punishment, and it is known that God does not increase the punishment of the criminal, so mentioning it is unnecessary. The doer of good has a reward, and what follows the reward as God's bounty is treated as part of the reward, so it is possible that some of the bounty could be reduced. Thus the negation of wronging indicates that no reduction in the bounty occurs. It is also possible that the pronoun in "and they will not be wronged" refers to both groups: the doers of evil and the doers of righteous deeds. The reading of (yudkhalun), in the passive voice, here and in Maryam and the first two verses of Ghafir, is by Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr also read it so in the second verse of Ghafir. Abu 'Amr also read it so in Fatir. The rest read it in the active voice.

﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to God while being a doer of good﴾. The discussion of something similar has already been covered in the two readings of "who submits himself to God while being a doer of good."

﴿and follows the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾. The discussion of the religion of Abraham, a hanif, has already been covered in His words: ﴿Say: Rather, the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾ [al-Baqara: 135]. As for following him, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is in monotheism (tawhid). Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: it is in standing up for God with what He has obligated. It was also said: it is in all of his law except what has been abrogated (mansukh) from it.

﴿And God took Abraham as an intimate friend (khalil)﴾. This is a metaphor for his being chosen and singled out with a honor resembling the honor of a close friend with his friend. The derivation of "khalil" has already been mentioned in al-Mufradat. The majority hold that it comes from khulla, which is affection free of any defect (khalal). As for the statement of Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Hashimi, that he was only called khalil because he withdrew (takhallā) from everything other than his Friend, if he meant the explanation of the meaning, it is possible; but if he meant etymology, it is not correct, because the two roots are different. From the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he said: "O Gabriel, for what did God take Abraham as a khalil?" He said: "For his feeding people food." The honor with which God honored him was mentioned in a lengthy story from Ibn 'Abbas, the gist of which is (p-357) that God turned the sandy dunes into fine white flour for him, and he kneaded and baked it and fed the people from it.

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "God took Abraham as a khalil, and Moses as a najiy (confidant), and He took me as a habib (beloved), then He said: By My might and My majesty, I will surely prefer My beloved over My khalil and My najiy." When He praised those who follow the religion of Abraham, He informed them of his distinction with Him and his being chosen, so that this would be more encouraging to follow him. Because whoever God has singled out with friendship deserves to be followed. Or it is to make clear that this friendship was caused by Abraham's hanifiyya (turning away from all other religions toward the religion of truth), as in His words: ﴿And when his Lord tested Abraham with commands, and he fulfilled them, He said: Indeed I will make you a leader (imam) for the people﴾ [al-Baqara: 124], meaning a model for you to complete those commands. By this He alerted that whoever acts by his law has a share in his station. This sentence is not coordinated (ma'tuf) with the sentence before it, because the sentence before it is coordinated with the relative clause (silat) of (man), and this one is not suitable for the relative clause. Rather, it is coordinated with the interrogative sentence whose meaning is a statement, that is: no one is better in religion than the one who submits himself to God. It draws attention to the nobility of the source and the success of the follower.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the position of this sentence? I say: it is a parenthetical sentence (jumla i'tiradiyya) that has no place in the grammatical structure, like what comes in poetry, such as their saying: 'and calamities are many.' Its benefit is to emphasize the obligation to follow his religion, because whoever attained such closeness to God that He took him as a khalil deserves to have his religion and path followed." End of quote. If by "parenthetical" he means something other than the technical sense defined in al-Dawd, then his statement may be correct, as if he means: "I interjected the speech." But if by "parenthetical" he means the technical term, then it is not correct, because a parenthetical clause is only inserted between two elements that depend on each other, such as a relative clause and its relative, a condition and its response, an oath and what it is sworn upon, a follower and what it follows, or a governor and what it governs. As for his saying "like what comes in poetry, such as their saying: 'and calamities are many,'" what we know is that the phrase "calamities are many" only occurs between two dependent elements, as in his saying:

"And calamities have overtaken me while calamities were many,
The points of a people's spears, neither weak nor unarmed."

And as in the saying of another:

"Has it not reached them, while calamities were many,
That Imru' al-Qays ibn Tamlik Bayqara..."

We do not know of it occurring at the end of a sentence.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 117–125 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly strayed far astray.﴾ [al-Nisa: 116] The explanation of this verse has already been given, similar to the above. It was revealed concerning Tu'ma. It was also said concerning a group of Quraysh who had embraced Islam, then reverted to Makkah as apostates. It was also said concerning an old man who said: "I have not associated anything with Allah since I came to know Him, except that I used to commit sins. I repented and sought forgiveness." But the last part of the earlier verse, "then he has certainly committed a great sin," and the end of this one, "then he has certainly strayed far astray," each verse was concluded with what suits it.

That earlier verse concerned the People of the Book, who had knowledge from their scriptures of what they had no doubt about regarding the truth of the Messenger, the obligation to follow his law, and its abrogation (naskh) of all previous laws. Despite this, they associated others with Allah, even though they had what indicates the oneness of Allah (tawhid) and belief in what was revealed. Thus their conduct became a fabrication and a contradiction, extremely grave and an act of audacity against Allah.

This verse, however, concerns people who were polytheists, who were neither People of a Book nor possessors of knowledge. Nevertheless, guidance had come to them from Allah, and the path of right direction had become clear to them. Yet they associated others with Allah, and thereby they went astray in a manner that is hard to imagine occurring, or that is far from the right course. Therefore, after it comes: ﴿They call upon none besides Him except female deities﴾, and after those (verses) comes: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim their own purity?﴾ [al-Nisa: 49], and His saying: ﴿See how they fabricate lies against Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 50]. No one among the exegetes (mutawwilin) disagreed that the intended people here are the Jews, even though the wording is general.

Since shirk is among the greatest of major sins, the error arising from it is far removed from the right course, because other sins, though they are error, are close to the point where their perpetrator may return to the truth, since he has a capital (ra's mal) to return to, which is faith. This is not the case with the polytheist. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿He calls upon others besides Allah that which neither harms him nor benefits him. That is the far-reaching error﴾ [al-Hajj: 12]. And the mention of error here is appropriate because guidance preceded it.

﴿They call upon none besides Him except female deities﴾. The meaning is: they do not worship, and do not take as a god, anything besides Allah except things named with the names of females. He used "calling" (du'a') as a metaphor for worship, because whoever worships something calls upon it in his needs and interests. They used to adorn the idols with various kinds of jewelry and name them "female" (unthā). Ināth is the plural of unthā, as ribāb is the plural of ruba. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the intended meaning is wood and stones, which are feminine and do not reason, so they are spoken of as feminine things are spoken of. Thus His saying ﴿except female deities﴾ becomes an expression for inanimate objects. Abu Malik, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and others said: the Arabs named their idols with feminine names such as al-Lat, al-'Uzza, Manat and Nailah. This is objected to on the grounds that they also named them with masculine names, such as Hubal and Dhu al-Khalasah.

Al-Dahhak and others said: the intended meaning is what the Arabs believed about the angels being female, and their worship of them. It was said to them: this is for establishing the proof against their corrupt statement. Al-Hasan said: no tribe of the Arabs existed without having an idol that they worshipped, which they called "the female of such-and-such a clan." In this there is an expression of femininity to indicate deficiency and baseness in comparison with masculinity. Al-Raghib said: most of the idols worshipped by the Arabs were things that are acted upon, not acting. So Allah rebuked them: while they are acting in some respect, they worship what is wholly acted upon in every respect. Based on this, Ibrahim, peace be upon him, alerted them with his saying: ﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees?﴾ [Maryam: 42].

Abu Raja' recited ﴿in tad'una﴾ with the letter ta' as second-person address, and this is narrated from 'Asim. In the Mushaf of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, it reads "illa awthanan," the plural of wathan, which is an idol. Abu al-Sawwar and al-Hunna'i recited it this way. Al-Hasan recited "illa unthā" in the singular. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Haywa, al-Hasan, 'Ata', Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu Nahik and Mu'adh al-Qari recited "unthan." Al-Tabari said, reporting it: it is like thimar and thamar (plural forms). Others said: anath is the plural of anith, like gharir and garar. Al-Maghribi said: ﴿illa inathan﴾ means "except weak ones who have no power." It is said: sayf anith (a weak sword), and minathah with the ta' marbutah, and mainath, a blade that does not cut. The poet said:

*You tell me that reason in me is a crumbling stick, neither least nor weak.*

Anatha in his affair means he became soft (yielded). Anith means an effeminate weak man. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' recited "illa wathanan" with fatha on the waw and the tha', without hamzah. Ibn al-Musayyab, Muslim ibn Jundub, and what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar and 'Ata' recited "illa athanan," meaning wathanan, so the hamzah was substituted with waw. This is explained as a plural of a plural, since its origin is wathan, which was pluralized as withan (like jamal and jimal), then withan became wuthun (like mithal and mithul, and himar and humur). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is an error, because fi'al in the plural of fi'l is for multiplicity, and the plural that denotes multiplicity is not pluralized further; rather, the plurals of paucity are pluralized. The correct form would be: wuthn, the plural of wathan directly, like asad and usud. This is not a complete correction, for plurals in general cannot be made plural by analogy, whether they denote multiplicity or paucity; the grammarians have stated this explicitly. Ayyub al-Sijistani recited "illa wuthunan" with damma on the waw and tha', without hamzah, like shuqaq. A group recited "illa athnan" with sukun on the tha', and its origin is wathnan. Thus eight readings have been gathered in this word: inathan, unthan, awthanan, wathnan, wuthunan, ithnan, and athanan.

﴿And they call upon none but a rebellious devil﴾. ﴿Allah has cursed him﴾. The intended one is Iblis, as most scholars said, and this is the correct view, because what he said afterward clarifies that he is the one. It was also said that the devil is specific to each idol; it is singular in wording, but plural in meaning, since the singular denotes the genus. It was said that he would enter the bellies of the idols and speak to their callers. It is possible that "Allah has cursed him" is a description, or that it is a report about him. It was also said that it is a supplication. The two restrictions do not contradict each other, because calling upon idols arises from their calling upon the devil. When they worshipped the devil, he incited them to worship idols; or the two calls differ: the first is worship, and the second is obedience. Ibn 'Isa said: it is like His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ [al-Anfal: 17], meaning that attributing their calling upon idols is by way of metaphor, while in reality they call upon the devil.

﴿And he said: "I will surely take from among Your servants a designated portion"﴾. That is, a due portion, which I have set aside for myself, from their saying: "He was allotted (faraḍa) a share in the gift," and "the army's allotment" (fard al-jund) is their provision. The meaning is: I will surely single them out for my misguidance, and specially assign them to my leading astray, and they are the disbelievers and the disobedient. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-mafrud here means "allotted" (al-muntaḥaz), derived from farḍ, which is a notch in wood and other things. It may also mean "obligatory" if he takes it. The sending to the Fire is Iblis's portion. Al-Hasan said: out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine. They said: the word "portion" (naṣīb) applies only to a small quantity. But the text indicates that the followers of Iblis are the majority, as evidenced by: ﴿I will surely seize his descendants, except a few﴾ [al-Isra: 62], and ﴿they followed him except a party of the believers﴾ [Saba: 20]. This is contradictory.

It has been answered that the disparity arises only within the human species. But if you include the various kinds of angels with their great number alongside the believers, the majority belongs to the believers. Also, the believers, although few in number, have a great portion with Allah, the Exalted. The disbelievers and the corrupt, though many, are as if nonexistent. The summary of what has been answered ends here. What I say is: the word naṣīb does not indicate few or many, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and relatives leave﴾ [al-Nisa: 7], and so on. The waw here is said to be a conjunctive waw, and it is said to be the waw of circumstance (waw al-ḥāl).

﴿And I will surely mislead them, and I will surely arouse in them desires, and I will surely command them so that they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will surely command them so that they will alter the creation of Allah﴾. These are five things over which Iblis swore. The first: taking a portion of the servants of Allah, which is his choosing of them. The second: misguiding them, which is diverting them from guidance and its means. The third: arousing desires in them (tamniyah), which is enticement (taswil), and it is not restricted to one type, because he arouses in each person desires suited to his condition, such as long life, reaching one's goal, and other things, all of which are false and baseless desires. It was said that the desires are the postponement of repentance. It was said they are the belief that there is no Paradise, no Fire, no resurrection and no reckoning. Al-Zamakhshari said: "and I will surely arouse in them false desires, such as long lives, reaching aspirations, the mercy of Allah for the criminals without repentance, and leaving the Fire after entering it through intercession and the like." The end of his statement. This is according to his Mu'tazili tendency and his zeal in interpreting the Book of Allah according to it, without the wording of the Qur'an indicating what he says and deduces. The fourth: his command to them, from which comes the slitting of the ears of cattle, which is their practice with the baḥā'ir (she-camels whose ears were slit and who were left free), which they did to a she-camel when she bore five litters, and the fifth was a male; and they forbade themselves to benefit from them. This is narrated by 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Suddi. It was said that it contains an allusion to everything that Allah made complete in its natural disposition (fitrah), and man, through his mismanagement, made deficient. The fifth: his command to them, from which comes the alteration of the creation of Allah, the Exalted.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibrahim, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah and others said: he meant altering the religion of Allah. In this they argued with His saying: ﴿the natural disposition of Allah upon which He created mankind; there is no altering of the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30], that is, of the religion of Allah. Substitution (tabdil) takes the place of alteration (taghyir), although alteration is more general than it. The phrase ﴿there is no altering of the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30] is in the form of a report, but its meaning is a prohibition. A group, including al-Zajjaj, said: it is the disbelievers making for themselves gods out of what was created for reflection, such as the sun, fire, stones and other things they worshipped. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan said: it is tattooing and what is similar to it of cosmetic alteration for beautification. From this is the hadith concerning the curse upon: "those who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, those who pluck their facial hair and those who file their teeth for beauty, who alter the creation of Allah; and the curse upon the one who joins hair (al-wasilah) and the one who has her hair joined." The end.

Ibn ʿAbbās also said, as did Anas, ʿIkrimah, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Mujāhid, and Qatādah: it is castration (al-khiṣāʾ), and in the case of human beings it is forbidden. Anas disliked castrating sheep, though a group of scholars permitted it for the benefit of fattening the animal for food. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz permitted castrating horses. It was said to al-Ḥasan: "ʿIkrimah says it is castration." He replied: "ʿIkrimah lied; it is the religion of Allah, the Exalted." It was also said that it is takhannuth (effeminacy). Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is gouging out the eye of the protected animal (al-ḥāmī) and making it exempt from riding, end of quote. This is consistent with what he mentioned, namely the slitting of the ears of cattle, so it is fitting that the alteration be this. It was said that changing the creation of Allah means that whatever Allah has created for a virtuous purpose, a person uses for a base purpose, and thereby changes His creation. Included in its general meaning is what Allah has placed in human beings of sexual desire for intercourse, so that it may be a means of procreation in a specific manner. If a person uses it for illicit intercourse (al-sifāḥ) and sodomy (al-liwāṭ), that is changing the creation of Allah. Likewise, the effeminate man who plucks out his beard and veils himself to imitate women, and the girl who acts like a man to imitate young men. Whatever Allah has made lawful, they forbid; or what Allah has forbidden, they make lawful. On this basis is the verse: ﴿Say: Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made some of it unlawful and some lawful?﴾ [Yunus: 59]. The commentators pointed to this sense, and therefore they said: it is changing the rulings of Allah. It was also said that it is changing a person's lineage through attribution (al-istilḥāq) or denial (al-nafy). It was said that it is dyeing grey hair black. It was said that it is the rulers punishing some of the criminals by cutting off their ears, slitting their nostrils, gouging out their eyes, and cutting off their testicles. Whoever interprets it as tattooing, castration, or other things specific to alteration, that is by way of example (al-tamthīl), not restriction (al-ḥaṣr).

In the ḥadīth of ʿIyāḍ al-Mujāshiʿī: "Indeed I created My servants all as ḥanīfs (upright in faith), but the devils led them astray and turned them away from their religion. They made unlawful for them what I had made lawful for them, and commanded them not to associate with Me what I had not sent down any authority for, and commanded them not to change My creation."

The second object of amara (commanded) is omitted; that is: "I will surely command them to slit the ears, and they will surely slit them; and I will surely command them to alter (creation), and they will surely alter it." It was omitted because what follows indicates it. Abū ʿAmr read: ﴿wa-la-āmurannahum﴾ without an alif (wa-la-amurannahum); thus Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reported it. Ubayy read: ﴿wa-la-uḍillannahum﴾ (and I will surely lead them astray), ﴿wa-la-umanniyannahum﴾ (and I will surely give them false hopes), and ﴿wa-la-āmurannahum﴾, end of quote. In that case these are clauses spoken (by Iblīs), not an oath sworn upon them. The arrangement of these clauses sworn upon is in the utmost eloquence: he began first with the devil taking a portion from them and choosing them; then second, with misguiding them, which refers to what occurs in their beliefs of disbelief; then third, with giving them false wishes and empty hopes; then fourth, with slitting the ears of cattle, which is a ruling Allah did not permit; then fifth, with changing the creation of Allah, which includes slitting and other rulings that He has legislated for them. He began with the command to slit the ears, though it falls under the general meaning of alteration, so that this would serve as a lure toward what comes after it of general alteration, and as a way for Iblīs to learn of their obedience in the first thing he cast to them, so that he would know their acceptance of him. When they accept that, he commands them with all the alterations he wants from them, just as a person does with one he intends to deceive: he first commands him with something easy; when he sees that he has accepted what he has put to him of this, he commands him with everything he wants from him. Iblīs's oath upon these things that he would certainly do them requires knowledge of that, and that they will happen, either because of the saying of Allah, the Exalted:

﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together﴾ [Ṣād: 85]; or because he knew that from the angels; or because, when he made Adam slip, he knew that his descendants were weaker than him.

﴿Whoever takes the devil as a protector besides Allah has surely suffered a manifest loss﴾: that is, whoever prefers the share of the devil over his share from Allah. It is as if, when Iblīs said: "I will surely take from Your servants a portion," and it was mentioned that he would choose them for himself, He informed that they accepted that taking and submitted to it; so they took him as a protector besides Allah. The word walī (protector) here: Muqātil said it means lord (rabb). Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī said it is from muwālāh (allegiance). He ordered the manifest loss upon this taking, because whoever abandons his share from Allah for the share of the devil, his transaction has been ruined. His saying "besides Allah" is a necessary restriction, because it is impossible to take the devil as a protector unless one has not taken Allah as a protector, and it is impossible to take the devil as a protector while also taking Allah as a protector, since these are two divergent paths that do not combine: guidance and misguidance. This conditional clause is a warning against following the devil.

﴿He promises them and gives them false hopes﴾: two closely related words. The meaning is that what he swore to, namely that he would give them false hopes, has happened by Allah's informing about it; and He was content with the information about the occurrence of those clauses which Iblīs swore to, since they are clear and evident. Since promising and giving false hopes are matters of the inner self, Allah informed about them. The meaning is that he promises them with false matters, deceptive adornments, and that there is no reward and no punishment.

﴿And the devil promises them nothing but delusion﴾: al-Aʿmash read wa-mā yaʿiduhum with the dāl sukūn (sukūn), made light because of the successive vowels. The explanation of ghurūr (delusion) has already been given; its meaning here is the deceptions that are thought to be beneficial, while the unseen reveals that they are harmful. The accusative (naṣb) may be a second object, or an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlih), or an infinitive not of its own verb (maṣdar ʿalā ghayr al-ṣadr), since "yaʿiduhum" is taken to imply "yaghurruhum" (deceives them); and there would be an omitted qualifier, meaning "nothing but manifest delusion" or similar, or an adjective for an omitted infinitive, meaning "a promise of delusion," i.e., one possessing delusion.

﴿Those—their refuge is Hell, and they will find no escape from it﴾: He informed that the place where they take refuge and settle is Hell, and that they will not find from it a way to turn aside to. "ʿAnhā" (from it) cannot be connected to an omitted verb, because it is not transitive with ʿan, nor to maḥīṣan (escape), even though the meaning depends on it, since it is a verbal noun; so it may be that this is a clarification by an implied "ʿannī" (away from me). They also permitted it to be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from maḥīṣ, connected to maḥīṣ, meaning "being away from it"; and had it been placed after, it would have been an attribute.

(p. 355) ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds—We will surely admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾: When He mentioned the abode of the disbelievers, He mentioned the abode of the believers, and attributed the verb to the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah), out of concern that He Himself is the One who takes charge of admitting them into Paradise, and as an honor for them. It was also read sa-yudkhiluhum with yāʾ. When He arranged the destiny of those who followed Iblīs as the Fire, because of their association and disbelief and their alteration of the rulings of Allah, the Exalted, here He arranged entry into Paradise upon faith and doing righteous deeds.

﴿The promise of Allah, in truth﴾: Since He mentioned that the promise of the devil is false delusion, He mentioned that this promise from Him, the Exalted, is the truth about which there is no doubt, and no uncertainty about its fulfillment. "Those who" is the subject (mubtada), and "We will admit them" is the predicate. It may also be from the construction of ishtighāl (where the verb is occupied by a pronoun referring to the object): i.e., "and We will admit those who believed, We will admit them." "The promise of Allah, in truth" is in the accusative as an infinitive emphasizing something other than itself: the promise of Allah emphasizes His saying "We will admit them," and "in truth" emphasizes the promise of Allah.

﴿And who is more truthful in speech than Allah?﴾: qīl and qawl are the same; i.e., no one is more truthful in speech than Allah. This clause also emphasizes what came before it. The benefit of these emphases is to intensify what Allah, the Exalted, informed His believing servants, in contrast to the promises of the devil and his false wishes, which lead to the failure of his own wishes.

﴿It is not according to your wishes, nor according to the wishes of the People of the Book﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Masrūq, Qatādah, al-Suddī, and others said: the address is to the community (the Muslims). Some of them said: they disputed with a group from the People of the Book, who said: "Our religion is older than yours and better; our prophet came before your prophet." The believers said: "Our book abrogates the books, and our prophet is the seal of the prophets," and similar argument, and so this was revealed. Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: the address is to the disbelievers of Quraysh, because they said: "We will not be resurrected, nor will we be punished; this is only our life, in which we have bliss, and then there is no punishment." The Jews said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." And other similar sayings of theirs.

(No one will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian) — Allah thus refuted both groups.

Al-Zamakhsharī said regarding "laysa" (it is not): its pronoun refers to the promise of Allah; that is, what Allah promised of reward is not attained by your wishes, nor the wishes of the People of the Book. The address is to the Muslims, because no one wishes for the promise of Allah except one who believes in Him; for this reason He mentioned the People of the Book alongside them, because they share with them in faith. It is reported from al-Ḥasan: "Faith is not by wishing; rather, it is what settles in the heart and what deeds confirm. Some people were distracted by wishes of forgiveness until they left this world without any good deed, and they said: 'We have good expectation of Allah'—and they lied. Had they truly had good expectation of Him, they would have done good deeds." It may also be that the address is to the polytheists, because of their saying: "If the matter is as these claim, we will surely be better than them and in a better state; we will be given wealth and children; indeed for me with Him is the best (ḥusnā)." The People of the Book used to say: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved; the Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days." The mention of the polytheists before reinforces this. End of quote.

On these sayings the disagreement arose concerning the subject of laysa (its noun). The pronoun returns preferably to the promise that He will admit them into Paradise; and next, it returns to the faith understood from His saying "those who believed and did righteous deeds," as al-Ḥasan held; then it returns to what the argument between the believers and the People of the Book was about, or what Quraysh and the People of the Book said, as already mentioned. Al-Ḥawfī said: the subject of laysa is a hidden pronoun in it, meaning: "Reward for good deeds is not, nor punishment for evil deeds, by your wishes; because entitlement comes only through deeds, not wishes." Abū al-Baqāʾ said: the subject of laysa is a hidden pronoun in it, with no prior mention, but the occasion of revelation indicates it: the Jews and Christians said, "We are the companions of Paradise," and the polytheists said, "We will not be resurrected." So He said: "It is not according to your wishes"; that is, what you claim is not according to your wishes. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah ibn Niṣāḥ, al-Ḥakam, and al-Aʿraj read bi-amānīkum and wa-lā amānī ahl al-kitāb with the yāʾ silent (sākinah), formed as the plural pattern faʿālil, like qarāqīr and qarāqir, the plural of qurqūr (a type of jar).

﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾: The majority said: the word is general, and both the disbeliever and the believer are recompensed for the evil they do. The disbeliever's recompense is the Fire, and the believer's is the afflictions of this world. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When it was revealed, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how severe this verse is, it breaks the back!' He said: 'It is only the calamities of this world.'" ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, gave a similar interpretation. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb also held it; al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād asked him about the meaning of the verse, and as if he feared it, he said to him: "I did not think you were more knowledgeable than what I see: a man is not struck by a scratch or anything else except for a sin, and what Allah pardons is more." al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd restricted it to the disbelievers, who are recompensed for minor and major sins. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it means the Jews, the Christians, the Magians, and the disbelieving Arabs; and these held that Allah promised the believers the expiation of their evil deeds. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jubayr restricted "evil" (sūʾ) to polytheism. It was said that "evil" is general in major sins.

﴿And they will not find for themselves besides Allah any protector or helper﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 173]: Ibn Bakkār reported from Ibn ʿĀmir: wa-lā yajidu with the nominative (rafʿ), as a resumption (qaṭʿ, a new clause).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 117–125 (part 3 of 3):

﴿Whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise﴾. (Min) in "min al-salihat" (of the righteous deeds) is partitive (lil-tab'id), because each person cannot do all the righteous deeds. He only does those that are obligatory for him and within his capacity. How many a responsible person (mukallaf) is not required to pay zakat, or to perform hajj or jihad, and prayer is dropped from him in some circumstances according to some schools of law. Al-Tabari reported from some people that (min) is extra (za'ida), meaning "whoever does the righteous deeds." But the addition of (min) in a conditional clause is weak, especially when it is followed by a definite noun. The second (min) is to clarify the vagueness in "whoever does" (man ya'mal). The discussion of (aw) has already been covered in His words: ﴿I will not let the work of any worker among you go to waste, whether male or female﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195]. The clause is circumstantial (jumla haliyya, a clause describing the state of the subject). The condition on human action is specified because, if a person performs righteous deeds, they will not benefit him unless he is a believer. Al-Zamakhshari said: "When God nullifies wishful thinking, and establishes that the whole matter is tied to righteous deeds, and that whoever improves his deeds is the successful one, and whoever spoils his deeds is the doomed one, the matter becomes clear and evident. It becomes obligatory to cut off wishful thinking, to end greed, and to turn to righteous deeds. But this is advice that ears do not heed and minds do not accept." End of quote. What the verse indicates is that faith is a condition for benefiting from deeds, because deeds are a condition for the soundness of faith.

﴿And they will not be wronged the least bit (naqir)﴾. Its apparent meaning is that it refers to the nearest previously mentioned group, who are the believers, and the ruling on the disbelievers is the same. Mentioning one of the two groups implies the other, that both will be rewarded according to their deeds. Also, wronging the evildoer would mean increasing his punishment, and it is known that God does not increase the punishment of the criminal, so mentioning it is unnecessary. The doer of good has a reward, and what follows the reward as God's bounty is treated as part of the reward, so it is possible that some of the bounty could be reduced. Thus the negation of wronging indicates that no reduction in the bounty occurs. It is also possible that the pronoun in "and they will not be wronged" refers to both groups: the doers of evil and the doers of righteous deeds. The reading of (yudkhalun), in the passive voice, here and in Maryam and the first two verses of Ghafir, is by Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr also read it so in the second verse of Ghafir. Abu 'Amr also read it so in Fatir. The rest read it in the active voice.

﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to God while being a doer of good﴾. The discussion of something similar has already been covered in the two readings of "who submits himself to God while being a doer of good."

﴿and follows the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾. The discussion of the religion of Abraham, a hanif, has already been covered in His words: ﴿Say: Rather, the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾ [al-Baqara: 135]. As for following him, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is in monotheism (tawhid). Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: it is in standing up for God with what He has obligated. It was also said: it is in all of his law except what has been abrogated (mansukh) from it.

﴿And God took Abraham as an intimate friend (khalil)﴾. This is a metaphor for his being chosen and singled out with a honor resembling the honor of a close friend with his friend. The derivation of "khalil" has already been mentioned in al-Mufradat. The majority hold that it comes from khulla, which is affection free of any defect (khalal). As for the statement of Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Hashimi, that he was only called khalil because he withdrew (takhallā) from everything other than his Friend, if he meant the explanation of the meaning, it is possible; but if he meant etymology, it is not correct, because the two roots are different. From the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he said: "O Gabriel, for what did God take Abraham as a khalil?" He said: "For his feeding people food." The honor with which God honored him was mentioned in a lengthy story from Ibn 'Abbas, the gist of which is (p-357) that God turned the sandy dunes into fine white flour for him, and he kneaded and baked it and fed the people from it.

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "God took Abraham as a khalil, and Moses as a najiy (confidant), and He took me as a habib (beloved), then He said: By My might and My majesty, I will surely prefer My beloved over My khalil and My najiy." When He praised those who follow the religion of Abraham, He informed them of his distinction with Him and his being chosen, so that this would be more encouraging to follow him. Because whoever God has singled out with friendship deserves to be followed. Or it is to make clear that this friendship was caused by Abraham's hanifiyya (turning away from all other religions toward the religion of truth), as in His words: ﴿And when his Lord tested Abraham with commands, and he fulfilled them, He said: Indeed I will make you a leader (imam) for the people﴾ [al-Baqara: 124], meaning a model for you to complete those commands. By this He alerted that whoever acts by his law has a share in his station. This sentence is not coordinated (ma'tuf) with the sentence before it, because the sentence before it is coordinated with the relative clause (silat) of (man), and this one is not suitable for the relative clause. Rather, it is coordinated with the interrogative sentence whose meaning is a statement, that is: no one is better in religion than the one who submits himself to God. It draws attention to the nobility of the source and the success of the follower.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the position of this sentence? I say: it is a parenthetical sentence (jumla i'tiradiyya) that has no place in the grammatical structure, like what comes in poetry, such as their saying: 'and calamities are many.' Its benefit is to emphasize the obligation to follow his religion, because whoever attained such closeness to God that He took him as a khalil deserves to have his religion and path followed." End of quote. If by "parenthetical" he means something other than the technical sense defined in al-Dawd, then his statement may be correct, as if he means: "I interjected the speech." But if by "parenthetical" he means the technical term, then it is not correct, because a parenthetical clause is only inserted between two elements that depend on each other, such as a relative clause and its relative, a condition and its response, an oath and what it is sworn upon, a follower and what it follows, or a governor and what it governs. As for his saying "like what comes in poetry, such as their saying: 'and calamities are many,'" what we know is that the phrase "calamities are many" only occurs between two dependent elements, as in his saying:

"And calamities have overtaken me while calamities were many,
The points of a people's spears, neither weak nor unarmed."

And as in the saying of another:

"Has it not reached them, while calamities were many,
That Imru' al-Qays ibn Tamlik Bayqara..."

We do not know of it occurring at the end of a sentence.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 117–125 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly strayed far astray.﴾ [al-Nisa: 116] The explanation of this verse has already been given, similar to the above. It was revealed concerning Tu'ma. It was also said concerning a group of Quraysh who had embraced Islam, then reverted to Makkah as apostates. It was also said concerning an old man who said: "I have not associated anything with Allah since I came to know Him, except that I used to commit sins. I repented and sought forgiveness." But the last part of the earlier verse, "then he has certainly committed a great sin," and the end of this one, "then he has certainly strayed far astray," each verse was concluded with what suits it.

That earlier verse concerned the People of the Book, who had knowledge from their scriptures of what they had no doubt about regarding the truth of the Messenger, the obligation to follow his law, and its abrogation (naskh) of all previous laws. Despite this, they associated others with Allah, even though they had what indicates the oneness of Allah (tawhid) and belief in what was revealed. Thus their conduct became a fabrication and a contradiction, extremely grave and an act of audacity against Allah.

This verse, however, concerns people who were polytheists, who were neither People of a Book nor possessors of knowledge. Nevertheless, guidance had come to them from Allah, and the path of right direction had become clear to them. Yet they associated others with Allah, and thereby they went astray in a manner that is hard to imagine occurring, or that is far from the right course. Therefore, after it comes: ﴿They call upon none besides Him except female deities﴾, and after those (verses) comes: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim their own purity?﴾ [al-Nisa: 49], and His saying: ﴿See how they fabricate lies against Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 50]. No one among the exegetes (mutawwilin) disagreed that the intended people here are the Jews, even though the wording is general.

Since shirk is among the greatest of major sins, the error arising from it is far removed from the right course, because other sins, though they are error, are close to the point where their perpetrator may return to the truth, since he has a capital (ra's mal) to return to, which is faith. This is not the case with the polytheist. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿He calls upon others besides Allah that which neither harms him nor benefits him. That is the far-reaching error﴾ [al-Hajj: 12]. And the mention of error here is appropriate because guidance preceded it.

﴿They call upon none besides Him except female deities﴾. The meaning is: they do not worship, and do not take as a god, anything besides Allah except things named with the names of females. He used "calling" (du'a') as a metaphor for worship, because whoever worships something calls upon it in his needs and interests. They used to adorn the idols with various kinds of jewelry and name them "female" (unthā). Ināth is the plural of unthā, as ribāb is the plural of ruba. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the intended meaning is wood and stones, which are feminine and do not reason, so they are spoken of as feminine things are spoken of. Thus His saying ﴿except female deities﴾ becomes an expression for inanimate objects. Abu Malik, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and others said: the Arabs named their idols with feminine names such as al-Lat, al-'Uzza, Manat and Nailah. This is objected to on the grounds that they also named them with masculine names, such as Hubal and Dhu al-Khalasah.

Al-Dahhak and others said: the intended meaning is what the Arabs believed about the angels being female, and their worship of them. It was said to them: this is for establishing the proof against their corrupt statement. Al-Hasan said: no tribe of the Arabs existed without having an idol that they worshipped, which they called "the female of such-and-such a clan." In this there is an expression of femininity to indicate deficiency and baseness in comparison with masculinity. Al-Raghib said: most of the idols worshipped by the Arabs were things that are acted upon, not acting. So Allah rebuked them: while they are acting in some respect, they worship what is wholly acted upon in every respect. Based on this, Ibrahim, peace be upon him, alerted them with his saying: ﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees?﴾ [Maryam: 42].

Abu Raja' recited ﴿in tad'una﴾ with the letter ta' as second-person address, and this is narrated from 'Asim. In the Mushaf of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, it reads "illa awthanan," the plural of wathan, which is an idol. Abu al-Sawwar and al-Hunna'i recited it this way. Al-Hasan recited "illa unthā" in the singular. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Haywa, al-Hasan, 'Ata', Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu Nahik and Mu'adh al-Qari recited "unthan." Al-Tabari said, reporting it: it is like thimar and thamar (plural forms). Others said: anath is the plural of anith, like gharir and garar. Al-Maghribi said: ﴿illa inathan﴾ means "except weak ones who have no power." It is said: sayf anith (a weak sword), and minathah with the ta' marbutah, and mainath, a blade that does not cut. The poet said:

*You tell me that reason in me is a crumbling stick, neither least nor weak.*

Anatha in his affair means he became soft (yielded). Anith means an effeminate weak man. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' recited "illa wathanan" with fatha on the waw and the tha', without hamzah. Ibn al-Musayyab, Muslim ibn Jundub, and what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar and 'Ata' recited "illa athanan," meaning wathanan, so the hamzah was substituted with waw. This is explained as a plural of a plural, since its origin is wathan, which was pluralized as withan (like jamal and jimal), then withan became wuthun (like mithal and mithul, and himar and humur). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is an error, because fi'al in the plural of fi'l is for multiplicity, and the plural that denotes multiplicity is not pluralized further; rather, the plurals of paucity are pluralized. The correct form would be: wuthn, the plural of wathan directly, like asad and usud. This is not a complete correction, for plurals in general cannot be made plural by analogy, whether they denote multiplicity or paucity; the grammarians have stated this explicitly. Ayyub al-Sijistani recited "illa wuthunan" with damma on the waw and tha', without hamzah, like shuqaq. A group recited "illa athnan" with sukun on the tha', and its origin is wathnan. Thus eight readings have been gathered in this word: inathan, unthan, awthanan, wathnan, wuthunan, ithnan, and athanan.

﴿And they call upon none but a rebellious devil﴾. ﴿Allah has cursed him﴾. The intended one is Iblis, as most scholars said, and this is the correct view, because what he said afterward clarifies that he is the one. It was also said that the devil is specific to each idol; it is singular in wording, but plural in meaning, since the singular denotes the genus. It was said that he would enter the bellies of the idols and speak to their callers. It is possible that "Allah has cursed him" is a description, or that it is a report about him. It was also said that it is a supplication. The two restrictions do not contradict each other, because calling upon idols arises from their calling upon the devil. When they worshipped the devil, he incited them to worship idols; or the two calls differ: the first is worship, and the second is obedience. Ibn 'Isa said: it is like His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ [al-Anfal: 17], meaning that attributing their calling upon idols is by way of metaphor, while in reality they call upon the devil.

﴿And he said: "I will surely take from among Your servants a designated portion"﴾. That is, a due portion, which I have set aside for myself, from their saying: "He was allotted (faraḍa) a share in the gift," and "the army's allotment" (fard al-jund) is their provision. The meaning is: I will surely single them out for my misguidance, and specially assign them to my leading astray, and they are the disbelievers and the disobedient. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-mafrud here means "allotted" (al-muntaḥaz), derived from farḍ, which is a notch in wood and other things. It may also mean "obligatory" if he takes it. The sending to the Fire is Iblis's portion. Al-Hasan said: out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine. They said: the word "portion" (naṣīb) applies only to a small quantity. But the text indicates that the followers of Iblis are the majority, as evidenced by: ﴿I will surely seize his descendants, except a few﴾ [al-Isra: 62], and ﴿they followed him except a party of the believers﴾ [Saba: 20]. This is contradictory.

It has been answered that the disparity arises only within the human species. But if you include the various kinds of angels with their great number alongside the believers, the majority belongs to the believers. Also, the believers, although few in number, have a great portion with Allah, the Exalted. The disbelievers and the corrupt, though many, are as if nonexistent. The summary of what has been answered ends here. What I say is: the word naṣīb does not indicate few or many, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and relatives leave﴾ [al-Nisa: 7], and so on. The waw here is said to be a conjunctive waw, and it is said to be the waw of circumstance (waw al-ḥāl).

﴿And I will surely mislead them, and I will surely arouse in them desires, and I will surely command them so that they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will surely command them so that they will alter the creation of Allah﴾. These are five things over which Iblis swore. The first: taking a portion of the servants of Allah, which is his choosing of them. The second: misguiding them, which is diverting them from guidance and its means. The third: arousing desires in them (tamniyah), which is enticement (taswil), and it is not restricted to one type, because he arouses in each person desires suited to his condition, such as long life, reaching one's goal, and other things, all of which are false and baseless desires. It was said that the desires are the postponement of repentance. It was said they are the belief that there is no Paradise, no Fire, no resurrection and no reckoning. Al-Zamakhshari said: "and I will surely arouse in them false desires, such as long lives, reaching aspirations, the mercy of Allah for the criminals without repentance, and leaving the Fire after entering it through intercession and the like." The end of his statement. This is according to his Mu'tazili tendency and his zeal in interpreting the Book of Allah according to it, without the wording of the Qur'an indicating what he says and deduces. The fourth: his command to them, from which comes the slitting of the ears of cattle, which is their practice with the baḥā'ir (she-camels whose ears were slit and who were left free), which they did to a she-camel when she bore five litters, and the fifth was a male; and they forbade themselves to benefit from them. This is narrated by 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Suddi. It was said that it contains an allusion to everything that Allah made complete in its natural disposition (fitrah), and man, through his mismanagement, made deficient. The fifth: his command to them, from which comes the alteration of the creation of Allah, the Exalted.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibrahim, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah and others said: he meant altering the religion of Allah. In this they argued with His saying: ﴿the natural disposition of Allah upon which He created mankind; there is no altering of the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30], that is, of the religion of Allah. Substitution (tabdil) takes the place of alteration (taghyir), although alteration is more general than it. The phrase ﴿there is no altering of the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30] is in the form of a report, but its meaning is a prohibition. A group, including al-Zajjaj, said: it is the disbelievers making for themselves gods out of what was created for reflection, such as the sun, fire, stones and other things they worshipped. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan said: it is tattooing and what is similar to it of cosmetic alteration for beautification. From this is the hadith concerning the curse upon: "those who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, those who pluck their facial hair and those who file their teeth for beauty, who alter the creation of Allah; and the curse upon the one who joins hair (al-wasilah) and the one who has her hair joined." The end.

Ibn ʿAbbās also said, as did Anas, ʿIkrimah, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Mujāhid, and Qatādah: it is castration (al-khiṣāʾ), and in the case of human beings it is forbidden. Anas disliked castrating sheep, though a group of scholars permitted it for the benefit of fattening the animal for food. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz permitted castrating horses. It was said to al-Ḥasan: "ʿIkrimah says it is castration." He replied: "ʿIkrimah lied; it is the religion of Allah, the Exalted." It was also said that it is takhannuth (effeminacy). Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is gouging out the eye of the protected animal (al-ḥāmī) and making it exempt from riding, end of quote. This is consistent with what he mentioned, namely the slitting of the ears of cattle, so it is fitting that the alteration be this. It was said that changing the creation of Allah means that whatever Allah has created for a virtuous purpose, a person uses for a base purpose, and thereby changes His creation. Included in its general meaning is what Allah has placed in human beings of sexual desire for intercourse, so that it may be a means of procreation in a specific manner. If a person uses it for illicit intercourse (al-sifāḥ) and sodomy (al-liwāṭ), that is changing the creation of Allah. Likewise, the effeminate man who plucks out his beard and veils himself to imitate women, and the girl who acts like a man to imitate young men. Whatever Allah has made lawful, they forbid; or what Allah has forbidden, they make lawful. On this basis is the verse: ﴿Say: Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made some of it unlawful and some lawful?﴾ [Yunus: 59]. The commentators pointed to this sense, and therefore they said: it is changing the rulings of Allah. It was also said that it is changing a person's lineage through attribution (al-istilḥāq) or denial (al-nafy). It was said that it is dyeing grey hair black. It was said that it is the rulers punishing some of the criminals by cutting off their ears, slitting their nostrils, gouging out their eyes, and cutting off their testicles. Whoever interprets it as tattooing, castration, or other things specific to alteration, that is by way of example (al-tamthīl), not restriction (al-ḥaṣr).

In the ḥadīth of ʿIyāḍ al-Mujāshiʿī: "Indeed I created My servants all as ḥanīfs (upright in faith), but the devils led them astray and turned them away from their religion. They made unlawful for them what I had made lawful for them, and commanded them not to associate with Me what I had not sent down any authority for, and commanded them not to change My creation."

The second object of amara (commanded) is omitted; that is: "I will surely command them to slit the ears, and they will surely slit them; and I will surely command them to alter (creation), and they will surely alter it." It was omitted because what follows indicates it. Abū ʿAmr read: ﴿wa-la-āmurannahum﴾ without an alif (wa-la-amurannahum); thus Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reported it. Ubayy read: ﴿wa-la-uḍillannahum﴾ (and I will surely lead them astray), ﴿wa-la-umanniyannahum﴾ (and I will surely give them false hopes), and ﴿wa-la-āmurannahum﴾, end of quote. In that case these are clauses spoken (by Iblīs), not an oath sworn upon them. The arrangement of these clauses sworn upon is in the utmost eloquence: he began first with the devil taking a portion from them and choosing them; then second, with misguiding them, which refers to what occurs in their beliefs of disbelief; then third, with giving them false wishes and empty hopes; then fourth, with slitting the ears of cattle, which is a ruling Allah did not permit; then fifth, with changing the creation of Allah, which includes slitting and other rulings that He has legislated for them. He began with the command to slit the ears, though it falls under the general meaning of alteration, so that this would serve as a lure toward what comes after it of general alteration, and as a way for Iblīs to learn of their obedience in the first thing he cast to them, so that he would know their acceptance of him. When they accept that, he commands them with all the alterations he wants from them, just as a person does with one he intends to deceive: he first commands him with something easy; when he sees that he has accepted what he has put to him of this, he commands him with everything he wants from him. Iblīs's oath upon these things that he would certainly do them requires knowledge of that, and that they will happen, either because of the saying of Allah, the Exalted:

﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together﴾ [Ṣād: 85]; or because he knew that from the angels; or because, when he made Adam slip, he knew that his descendants were weaker than him.

﴿Whoever takes the devil as a protector besides Allah has surely suffered a manifest loss﴾: that is, whoever prefers the share of the devil over his share from Allah. It is as if, when Iblīs said: "I will surely take from Your servants a portion," and it was mentioned that he would choose them for himself, He informed that they accepted that taking and submitted to it; so they took him as a protector besides Allah. The word walī (protector) here: Muqātil said it means lord (rabb). Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī said it is from muwālāh (allegiance). He ordered the manifest loss upon this taking, because whoever abandons his share from Allah for the share of the devil, his transaction has been ruined. His saying "besides Allah" is a necessary restriction, because it is impossible to take the devil as a protector unless one has not taken Allah as a protector, and it is impossible to take the devil as a protector while also taking Allah as a protector, since these are two divergent paths that do not combine: guidance and misguidance. This conditional clause is a warning against following the devil.

﴿He promises them and gives them false hopes﴾: two closely related words. The meaning is that what he swore to, namely that he would give them false hopes, has happened by Allah's informing about it; and He was content with the information about the occurrence of those clauses which Iblīs swore to, since they are clear and evident. Since promising and giving false hopes are matters of the inner self, Allah informed about them. The meaning is that he promises them with false matters, deceptive adornments, and that there is no reward and no punishment.

﴿And the devil promises them nothing but delusion﴾: al-Aʿmash read wa-mā yaʿiduhum with the dāl sukūn (sukūn), made light because of the successive vowels. The explanation of ghurūr (delusion) has already been given; its meaning here is the deceptions that are thought to be beneficial, while the unseen reveals that they are harmful. The accusative (naṣb) may be a second object, or an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlih), or an infinitive not of its own verb (maṣdar ʿalā ghayr al-ṣadr), since "yaʿiduhum" is taken to imply "yaghurruhum" (deceives them); and there would be an omitted qualifier, meaning "nothing but manifest delusion" or similar, or an adjective for an omitted infinitive, meaning "a promise of delusion," i.e., one possessing delusion.

﴿Those—their refuge is Hell, and they will find no escape from it﴾: He informed that the place where they take refuge and settle is Hell, and that they will not find from it a way to turn aside to. "ʿAnhā" (from it) cannot be connected to an omitted verb, because it is not transitive with ʿan, nor to maḥīṣan (escape), even though the meaning depends on it, since it is a verbal noun; so it may be that this is a clarification by an implied "ʿannī" (away from me). They also permitted it to be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from maḥīṣ, connected to maḥīṣ, meaning "being away from it"; and had it been placed after, it would have been an attribute.

(p. 355) ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds—We will surely admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾: When He mentioned the abode of the disbelievers, He mentioned the abode of the believers, and attributed the verb to the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah), out of concern that He Himself is the One who takes charge of admitting them into Paradise, and as an honor for them. It was also read sa-yudkhiluhum with yāʾ. When He arranged the destiny of those who followed Iblīs as the Fire, because of their association and disbelief and their alteration of the rulings of Allah, the Exalted, here He arranged entry into Paradise upon faith and doing righteous deeds.

﴿The promise of Allah, in truth﴾: Since He mentioned that the promise of the devil is false delusion, He mentioned that this promise from Him, the Exalted, is the truth about which there is no doubt, and no uncertainty about its fulfillment. "Those who" is the subject (mubtada), and "We will admit them" is the predicate. It may also be from the construction of ishtighāl (where the verb is occupied by a pronoun referring to the object): i.e., "and We will admit those who believed, We will admit them." "The promise of Allah, in truth" is in the accusative as an infinitive emphasizing something other than itself: the promise of Allah emphasizes His saying "We will admit them," and "in truth" emphasizes the promise of Allah.

﴿And who is more truthful in speech than Allah?﴾: qīl and qawl are the same; i.e., no one is more truthful in speech than Allah. This clause also emphasizes what came before it. The benefit of these emphases is to intensify what Allah, the Exalted, informed His believing servants, in contrast to the promises of the devil and his false wishes, which lead to the failure of his own wishes.

﴿It is not according to your wishes, nor according to the wishes of the People of the Book﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Masrūq, Qatādah, al-Suddī, and others said: the address is to the community (the Muslims). Some of them said: they disputed with a group from the People of the Book, who said: "Our religion is older than yours and better; our prophet came before your prophet." The believers said: "Our book abrogates the books, and our prophet is the seal of the prophets," and similar argument, and so this was revealed. Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: the address is to the disbelievers of Quraysh, because they said: "We will not be resurrected, nor will we be punished; this is only our life, in which we have bliss, and then there is no punishment." The Jews said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." And other similar sayings of theirs.

(No one will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian) — Allah thus refuted both groups.

Al-Zamakhsharī said regarding "laysa" (it is not): its pronoun refers to the promise of Allah; that is, what Allah promised of reward is not attained by your wishes, nor the wishes of the People of the Book. The address is to the Muslims, because no one wishes for the promise of Allah except one who believes in Him; for this reason He mentioned the People of the Book alongside them, because they share with them in faith. It is reported from al-Ḥasan: "Faith is not by wishing; rather, it is what settles in the heart and what deeds confirm. Some people were distracted by wishes of forgiveness until they left this world without any good deed, and they said: 'We have good expectation of Allah'—and they lied. Had they truly had good expectation of Him, they would have done good deeds." It may also be that the address is to the polytheists, because of their saying: "If the matter is as these claim, we will surely be better than them and in a better state; we will be given wealth and children; indeed for me with Him is the best (ḥusnā)." The People of the Book used to say: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved; the Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days." The mention of the polytheists before reinforces this. End of quote.

On these sayings the disagreement arose concerning the subject of laysa (its noun). The pronoun returns preferably to the promise that He will admit them into Paradise; and next, it returns to the faith understood from His saying "those who believed and did righteous deeds," as al-Ḥasan held; then it returns to what the argument between the believers and the People of the Book was about, or what Quraysh and the People of the Book said, as already mentioned. Al-Ḥawfī said: the subject of laysa is a hidden pronoun in it, meaning: "Reward for good deeds is not, nor punishment for evil deeds, by your wishes; because entitlement comes only through deeds, not wishes." Abū al-Baqāʾ said: the subject of laysa is a hidden pronoun in it, with no prior mention, but the occasion of revelation indicates it: the Jews and Christians said, "We are the companions of Paradise," and the polytheists said, "We will not be resurrected." So He said: "It is not according to your wishes"; that is, what you claim is not according to your wishes. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah ibn Niṣāḥ, al-Ḥakam, and al-Aʿraj read bi-amānīkum and wa-lā amānī ahl al-kitāb with the yāʾ silent (sākinah), formed as the plural pattern faʿālil, like qarāqīr and qarāqir, the plural of qurqūr (a type of jar).

﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾: The majority said: the word is general, and both the disbeliever and the believer are recompensed for the evil they do. The disbeliever's recompense is the Fire, and the believer's is the afflictions of this world. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When it was revealed, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how severe this verse is, it breaks the back!' He said: 'It is only the calamities of this world.'" ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, gave a similar interpretation. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb also held it; al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād asked him about the meaning of the verse, and as if he feared it, he said to him: "I did not think you were more knowledgeable than what I see: a man is not struck by a scratch or anything else except for a sin, and what Allah pardons is more." al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd restricted it to the disbelievers, who are recompensed for minor and major sins. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it means the Jews, the Christians, the Magians, and the disbelieving Arabs; and these held that Allah promised the believers the expiation of their evil deeds. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jubayr restricted "evil" (sūʾ) to polytheism. It was said that "evil" is general in major sins.

﴿And they will not find for themselves besides Allah any protector or helper﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 173]: Ibn Bakkār reported from Ibn ʿĀmir: wa-lā yajidu with the nominative (rafʿ), as a resumption (qaṭʿ, a new clause).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 117–125 (part 3 of 3):

﴿Whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise﴾. (Min) in "min al-salihat" (of the righteous deeds) is partitive (lil-tab'id), because each person cannot do all the righteous deeds. He only does those that are obligatory for him and within his capacity. How many a responsible person (mukallaf) is not required to pay zakat, or to perform hajj or jihad, and prayer is dropped from him in some circumstances according to some schools of law. Al-Tabari reported from some people that (min) is extra (za'ida), meaning "whoever does the righteous deeds." But the addition of (min) in a conditional clause is weak, especially when it is followed by a definite noun. The second (min) is to clarify the vagueness in "whoever does" (man ya'mal). The discussion of (aw) has already been covered in His words: ﴿I will not let the work of any worker among you go to waste, whether male or female﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195]. The clause is circumstantial (jumla haliyya, a clause describing the state of the subject). The condition on human action is specified because, if a person performs righteous deeds, they will not benefit him unless he is a believer. Al-Zamakhshari said: "When God nullifies wishful thinking, and establishes that the whole matter is tied to righteous deeds, and that whoever improves his deeds is the successful one, and whoever spoils his deeds is the doomed one, the matter becomes clear and evident. It becomes obligatory to cut off wishful thinking, to end greed, and to turn to righteous deeds. But this is advice that ears do not heed and minds do not accept." End of quote. What the verse indicates is that faith is a condition for benefiting from deeds, because deeds are a condition for the soundness of faith.

﴿And they will not be wronged the least bit (naqir)﴾. Its apparent meaning is that it refers to the nearest previously mentioned group, who are the believers, and the ruling on the disbelievers is the same. Mentioning one of the two groups implies the other, that both will be rewarded according to their deeds.
