And ever is Allah All-Encompassing and Wise.﴾ [An-Nisa: 130] ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you and [now] you, to fear Allah. But if you disbelieve - then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and ever is Allah Free of need and Praiseworthy.﴾ [An-Nisa: 131] ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ [An-Nisa: 132] ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others; and ever is Allah capable of that.﴾ [An-Nisa: 133] ﴿Whoever should desire the reward of this world - then with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. And ever is Allah Hearing and Seeing.﴾ [An-Nisa: 134] ﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more worthy of both. So do not follow [your own] desire, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ [An-Nisa: 135] ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger and the Scripture which He sent down before. And whoever disbelieves in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers and the Last Day has certainly strayed far away.﴾ [An-Nisa: 136] ﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, and then increased in disbelief - Allah will never forgive them nor guide them to a way.﴾ [An-Nisa: 137] ﴿Give tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment.﴾ [An-Nisa: 138] ﴿Those who take disbelievers as allies instead of believers. Do they seek with them honor? Indeed, honor belongs to Allah entirely.﴾ [An-Nisa: 139] ﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being denied and ridiculed, do not sit with them until they enter into another conversation. Indeed, you would then be like them. Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers in Hell all together.﴾ [An-Nisa: 140] ﴿Those who wait [and watch] for you. If you have a victory from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?" But if the disbelievers have a portion [of victory], they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you and protect you from the believers?" Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and never will Allah give the disbelievers over the believers a way.﴾ [An-Nisa: 141]. Ash-shuhh (stinginess): Ibn Faris said: it is stinginess combined with greed. And "tashaḥḥa al-rajulan fi al-amr" means the two men were greedy about a matter, not wanting it to escape them; it is pronounced with a damma or kasra on the shin. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ash-shuhh is strict holding onto beliefs and intention; so in aspirations and wealth and the like, when it is excessive, there is some blame in it. What reaches the sphere of legal rights and what manliness requires is bukhl (miserliness), which is a vice. Yet it may exist in a believer, and from it is the hadith: "It was said, O Messenger of Allah, can a believer be stingy? He said, Yes." As for shuhh, it is in every person, and this is indicated by: ﴿And souls are present with stinginess﴾ and ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]; every soul has shuhh. And the Prophet's saying (peace be upon him): "That you give charity while you are healthy and stingy," and he did not intend by it one specific person; and it is not praised to say here "that you give charity while you are healthy and miserly."

Al-mu'allaqah: she who is neither divorced nor has a husband. A man said: "Is it anything but a delay, a suspension, or a sham, or between that a suspension?" In the hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is 'Ashannaq: if I speak, I am divorced; and if I remain silent, I am left suspended." She likened the woman to a thing suspended from something, because it has settled neither on the ground nor on what it is hung from. And in the proverb: "Earth from the vehicle with suspension."

Al-khawd: entering into a thing. You say: "I waded into the water (khudtu al-ma' khawdan wa khiyadan)," and "I plunged into the torrents (ghamarat)," and "khadahu bi al-sayf" means he moved his sword against the one struck. "Takhawwadu fi al-hadith" means they discussed it. Al-makhadah is the place of wading. The poet, and he is 'Abd Allah ibn Shubrumah, said:
Whenever al-Jawza' rises and the star is rising, every ford of the Euphrates becomes a crossing.
Al-khawdah, with a fatha on the kha', is the pearl; ikhtada means the same as khada; and takhawwada means he burdened himself with wading. Al-istihwadh: domination and overpowering; said by Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj. It is said: ha'da yahud hawdan, and ahada with the same meaning as haada and ahaada. (p-359) This word is anomalous in that its middle radical is sound in al-naqqal; Abu Zayd al-Ansari analogized upon it.

﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them﴾. Occasion of revelation: some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, asked about the matter of women and their rulings concerning inheritance and other things. As for its connection (munasabah), it is likewise according to the Arab manner of speech in quadrants: it is about a matter, then it moves from it to something else, then returns to what it was about first. Thus is the Book of Allah: the rulings of His obligations are explained in it, then they are followed by promise and threat, encouragement and warning, then this is followed by mention of the opponents and obstinate ones who do not follow those rulings, then by what indicates the majesty and grandeur of Allah the Exalted, then it returns to clarify what relates to those earlier rulings. Here in this surah, it began with the rulings of women and inheritance and the mention of orphans; then secondly with mention of some of that in this verse; then finally with mention of some of the inheritance as well. Since women's matters were disregarded among the Arabs regarding inheritance and other things, and likewise orphans, He emphasized discussion of them repeatedly, so that they would return from the rulings of the Jahiliyyah. Al-istifta' is the seeking of a fatwa; and "aftahu ifta'an," and fatwa and fatwa; and "aftaytu fulanan fi ru'yahu" means I interpreted his dream for him. The meaning of ifta' is the manifestation of what is difficult to the questioner. Its root is from al-fata, the young man who has become strong and complete; so the meaning is: it is as if it is the clarification of what is unclear, so that it becomes established and strengthened. Al-istifta' does not concern the essences of women; rather, it concerns some of their rulings, which were not explained, so it is mujmal (general/ambiguous). The meaning of yuftikum fihinna is: He clarifies for you the state of what you asked about and its ruling.

* *

(p-360) ﴿And what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, while you desire to marry them, and concerning the oppressed among the children﴾; they mentioned in the place of "ma" in terms of i'rab: the nominative, the accusative, and the genitive. The nominative has three aspects. One: that it is coordinated with the name of Allah; i.e., Allah gives you a ruling, and what is recited in the Book concerns the meaning of the orphans. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means His saying: "And if you fear that you will not be just concerning orphans" [An-Nisa: 3], and it is like the saying "I was impressed by Zayd and his generosity," end. Two: that it is coordinated with the pronoun hidden in yuftikum, and the separation between them by the object and the prepositional phrase is acceptable. Three: that ma yutla is the subject, and fi al-kitab is its predicate, as a parenthetical clause (jumlah mu'taridah). The intended "Book" is the Preserved Tablet, as an exaltation of what is recited to them, and that justice and equity in the rights of orphans are among the great matters of high rank with Allah, which must be observed and preserved, and whoever neglects them is a wrongdoer who disregards what Allah has exalted. Similar to this is the exaltation of the Qur'an: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 4]. It has been said regarding this aspect: the predicate is omitted, and the estimate is: "what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women" is for you, or "yuftikum"; it is omitted because of what precedes it. On this estimate, "fi al-kitab" is with His saying "yutla alaykum," or it is in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in yutla, and "fi yatama" is a substitute (badal) for "fi al-kitab." Abu al-Baqa' said regarding the second: it is connected to what the first is connected to, because their meanings differ; the first is an adverbial of place, and the second means "bi" (because of), i.e., because of the orphans, as you say: "I came to you on Friday concerning the matter of Zayd." It is permissible for the second to be connected to "al-kitab," i.e., in what He prescribed regarding the rulings of orphans. It is also permissible for the second to be a circumstantial clause, connected to a hidden element. As for the accusative, it is by the estimate: "and He clarifies for you what is recited," because "yuftikum" in meaning is "yubayyinu," so it indicates it. As for the genitive, it is from two aspects. One: that the waw is for oath, as if he said: "And I swear by what is recited to you in the Book," and the oath is for exaltation; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. Two: that it is coordinated with the genitive pronoun in "fihinna"; this was said by Muhammad ibn Abi Musa, who said: Allah gave them a ruling concerning what they asked about, and concerning what they did not ask about. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this interpretation is weakened by what it contains of coordinating on a pronoun in the genitive without repeating the genitive particle. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not correct to coordinate on the genitive in "fihinna," because it is defective both in wording and in meaning, end.

What I choose is this aspect, although it is well known in the school of the majority of the Basran grammarians that this is not permissible except in poetry; but I have mentioned evidences for its permissibility in speech. I have elaborated on the evidences for this in the commentary on His saying "wa kufrun bihi" and "al-Masjid al-Haram." It is not defective in wording, because we have argued for its permissibility; nor is it defective in meaning as al-Zamakhshari claimed; rather the meaning supports it, and it is on an estimate of omission, i.e., He gives them a ruling concerning their recited matter (mutlaw), and what is recited to you in the Book concerning their (women's) matters is an admissible annexation (idafah), since annexation occurs for the slightest connection; when something is recited concerning them, the annexation to them is valid. Among this is the poet's saying:
When the star of al-Kharqa' appeared at dawn...

As for al-Zamakhshari's claim that the sentence is "defective in both wording and meaning," this is exactly the view of al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: "This is far-fetched, because it fails both in terms of wording and in terms of meaning. As for wording, it requires coordinating an overt noun with a pronoun (*'atf al-muzhar 'ala al-mudmar*), and that is not permissible, just as His saying ﴿whom you ask about, and the wombs﴾ [an-Nisa 1] is not permissible. As for meaning, Allah, exalted is He, gave a ruling on those matters, and taking the conjunction as applying to the pronoun would imply that He gave a ruling only on what is recited to you in the Book. It is well known that this is not the intended meaning. Rather, the intended meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, gives rulings on the questions they asked Him." End of his words.

We have already shown the soundness of the meaning if the deleted element is assumed and the word is read in the nominative as a conjunction to *Allah*, or as a conjunction to a pronoun that takes it out of the category of *ta'sis* (establishing a new ruling, i.e., a ruling that adds new content). Taking the whole sentence as a whole removes the entire sentence from *ta'sis*. The same applies to reading it in the genitive as an oath. Reading it in the accusative with a verb deleted, or as a conjunction to the pronoun, makes it *ta'sis*. If one intends both *ta'sis* and *ta'kid* (emphasis, i.e., repeating what is already known), then reading it as *ta'sis* is preferable, and one should not resort to *ta'kid* except when it is clear that *ta'sis* is not possible.

The discussion of the connection of His saying ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾ has already preceded. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, with what does His saying ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾ connect? I say: in the first mode, it is the complement of *yutla* (is recited), meaning, 'is recited to you concerning their meaning.' It is also permissible for ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾ to be a substitute (*badal*) for *fihinna* (concerning them). As for the last two modes, it is only a substitute, nothing else." End of his words.

By his words "in the first mode" he means that the phrase and what is recited are in the nominative position. As for what he permitted in this mode, that it is the complement of *yutla*, this can only be imagined if ﴿concerning the orphans﴾ is a substitute for ﴿concerning the Book﴾, or if *fi* is for causation (*lil-sabab*), so that two prepositional phrases with the same meaning do not attach to one verb. This is not permitted except by way of substitution or conjunction. As for what he also permitted in this mode, that *fi yatama* is a substitute for *fihinna*, the apparent view is that it is not permitted, because of the separation between the substitute and what it substitutes for by a conjunction. The parallel of this structure is: "Zayd resides in the house, and 'Amr in a part of it." Here one has separated *fi al-dar* from *fi kisr minha* by a conjunction and by the familiar structure: "Zayd resides in the house in a part of it, and 'Amr."

Those whose commentary on the exegesis we have examined agree that this verse refers back to what came earlier at the beginning of this sura, namely His saying: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾ [an-Nisa 4], His saying: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [an-Nisa 2], and His saying: (p. 362) ﴿…great. And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [an-Nisa 3]. ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "This verse, meaning ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans﴾ [an-Nisa 3], was revealed first. Then after it, some people asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the matter of women, and so this was revealed: ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them﴾, and ﴿what is recited to you﴾." According to what the exegetes said, and what was reported from ʿĀʾishah, the phrase ﴿gives you a ruling﴾ and the phrase ﴿is recited in it﴾ place the present tense in the position of the past tense, because the giving of rulings and the reciting had already preceded.

The annexation in *yatama al-nisa'* (orphan women) is of the type of annexing the specific to the general, because women divide into orphans and non-orphans. Al-Kufiyyun said: it is an annexation of the adjective to the modified noun, and this is not permitted according to the Basrans, and this is established in the science of grammar.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the annexation in *yatama al-nisa'*? I say: it is an annexation in the sense of *min* (of, from), which is the annexation of a thing to its genus, like your saying: 'ring of iron,' 'garment of silk,' and 'ring of silver.' It is permissible to separate, and to follow the genus to what precedes it, and to put it in the accusative or genitive with *min*. What appears in ﴿orphan women﴾ and in 'a scrubbed turban' is that it is an annexation in the sense of *li* (for, belonging to), and the meaning of *li* is specification (*ikhtisas*)." End of his words.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Madani read *fi yamama al-nisa'* with two *ya*'s. Ibn Jinni explained it on the basis that the original was *ayama*, so the hamza was replaced with a *ya*', as they said *Bahilat ibn Ya'sur*, when it was *A'sur*, named after his saying:

"Has it reached you that your father's color was changed
By the passing of nights and the alternation of epochs?"

They also said the reverse of this: "May Allah cut off his *ayd*," meaning his *yad* (hand), so the *ya*' was replaced with a hamza. *Ayama* is the plural of *ayyim* in the pattern *fa'il*, and it is among the forms peculiar to defective roots. Its original was *ayayim*, like *sayayid*, the plural of *sayyid*. The *lam* was moved to the position of the *ʿayn*, so it became *ayama*. The kasra was replaced with a fatha, and the *ya*' became an *alif* because it was vowelized and the letter before it was open. Ibn Jinni said: "If someone were to say: *ayyim* was broken into *ayma* in the pattern *sakra*, and then *ayma* was broken into *ayama*, it would be a good view."

As for the meaning of ﴿what has been prescribed for them﴾, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and a group said: it is the inheritance. Others said: it is the dowry. The addressee of His saying ﴿you do not give them﴾ are the guardians of the woman, who used to take women's dowries and give them nothing. It was also said: the guardians of orphans used to marry off the orphans under their care, and they did not act justly regarding their dowries. It was read: "what Allah has prescribed for them." Abu ʿUbaydah said: ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾; this wording can mean either desire or aversion. So the meaning, in the case of desire, is "you desire to marry them because of their wealth or their beauty," and in the case of aversion, "you turn away from marrying them because of their ugliness, so you keep them out of desire for their wealth." The first view is the view of ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and a group.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, used to direct people to the superior course in this meaning. When he asked a guardian about his ward and was told, "She is wealthy and beautiful," he would say to him, "Seek for her one better than you, and more beneficial to her." If he was told, "She is ugly and poor," he would say to him, "You are more entitled to her and to covering her faults than anyone else."

﴿The oppressed (al-mustada'afin)﴾ [an-Nisa 98] is conjoined to ﴿orphan women﴾. What was recited about them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾ [an-Nisa 11], and so on. This is because the Arabs did not give inheritance to a girl or to a small boy. The eldest would take the property alone, and they used to say: "Only one who protects the territory, repels the spoils, and fights for the sanctuary inherits." So Allah, exalted is He, assigned to each one his right. It is also permissible that this is an address to the guardians, like His saying: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾ [an-Nisa 2]. It was also said that the "oppressed" here are the slaves, male and female.

﴿And that you stand up for orphans with justice﴾ is in the genitive position, conjoined to what precedes it, meaning "and concerning your standing up for orphans with justice." What was recited in this sense is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾ [an-Nisa 2], and other matters mentioned concerning the property of the orphan. *Al-qist* means justice. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative, in the sense of 'and He commands you that you stand up...' It is an address to the leaders, that they look after them, secure their rights for them, and do not allow anyone to oppress them." End of his words. In *Rayy al-Zam'an* (Rayy al-Zam'an, a commentary), it says: "It may be read in the nominative, with 'that you stand up' as the subject, and its predicate is deleted, meaning: 'better for you.'" (p. 363) When it is possible to take it without deletion, by considering it conjoined to a genitive noun, this is preferable to positing a deleted governing verb, as al-Zamakhshari held. And preferable to taking it as the subject whose predicate is deleted.

﴿And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it﴾. Since the mention of women, orphan women, the oppressed among children, and standing up for orphans with justice had preceded, He followed this with the statement that He, exalted is He, knows the good that is done on account of those mentioned, and so He rewards it with abundant reward. He restricted the mention to doing good because it is what He encouraged, although He, exalted is He, knows whatever good or evil is done, and He rewards or punishes it accordingly.

﴿And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment (*nushuz*) or aversion, there is no blame upon them if they make a settlement between themselves in reconciliation﴾. It was revealed concerning Ibn Bi'kak and his wife, according to Mujahid. It was also revealed concerning Rafi' ibn Khadij and his wife Khawla bint Muhammad ibn Maslama. She had grown old, and he married a young woman over her and favored her. Khawla could not endure, so he divorced her, then took her back and said: "I have only one wife, so either you accept favoritism or I will divorce you." So she fled. This was reported by ʿUbaydah, Sulayman ibn Yasar, and Ibn al-Musayyab. Or it was revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ and Sawda bint Zam'a, who feared being divorced, so she said: "Do not divorce me, keep me with your wives, and do not allot me a night." So he did that, and this was revealed. This was reported by Ibn ʿAbbas and a group.

The fear here is in its literal sense, but it is not attained except through the appearance of signs that indicate the occurrence of what is feared. It was said that the meaning of "feared" is "knew." It was also said "suspected." It should not be taken away from its apparent meaning, since the meaning is correct with it. *Nushuz* means that he turns away from her by withholding himself from her, his maintenance, and the affection between them, and that he harms her by an offense or a beating. *Ia'rad* means that he reduces his conversation with her and his companionship, due to an objection about her age or ugliness, or a defect in character or appearance, or boredom, or the eye's longing for another, or other things. This is the lighter of the two kinds of *nushuz*. So Allah removes blame between them in reconciliation by all kinds of concessions from the husband to her, so that she will endure, or from her to him, so that he will favor her, or that he will not favor another, and she holds to the marriage bond, or in patience over favoritism and the like. All of this is permitted. He made the lifting of blame depend on the anticipation of fear and the appearance of signs of *nushuz* and aversion. It is even better when those things occur and are confirmed, because if reconciliation is permitted with the fear of them, then with their actual occurrence it is more strongly permitted, since in reconciliation the bond of affection and love remains. Among the forms of reconciliation is that she gives her day to another of his wives, as Sawda did, or that she agrees to his allotting her a long period once in a while, or that she gives him her dowry or part of it, or her maintenance. The right a woman has over her husband is the dowry and the maintenance, and the allotment of nights is also a right. Giving up any of this, or some part of it, on condition that he does not divorce her, is permissible.

The Kufans read *yuslihā* (they make peace) from *aslaḥa* in the pattern *akrama*. The rest of the seven read *yaṣṣālaḥā*, whose original is *yatasālaḥā*, and the *tā*' was assimilated into the *ṣād*. ʿUbaydah al-Salmani read *yuṣāliḥā* from the *mufā'ala* form. Al-Aʿmash read *in iṣṭalaḥā*, which is the reading of Ibn Masʿud, made into the past tense. Its original is *tasālaḥa* in the pattern *tafā'ala*, so the *tā*' was assimilated into the *ṣād*, and a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza) was added. *Al-ṣulḥ* (reconciliation) is not the verbal noun of the thing from these verbs that were read. If it is a noun for what one reconciles by, like *al-ʿaṭā'* (gift) and *al-karāma* (honor) with *a'ṭaytu* and *akramtu*, then its accusative case may be by dropping the preposition, meaning "reconciled by something upon which the two agree." It is also permissible that it be a verbal noun of these verbs by dropping the extra letters.

﴿And reconciliation is best﴾. Its apparent meaning is that *khayr* is a comparative form (elative), and that the thing compared against is the nushuz and aversion, so it is deleted because what precedes it indicates it. It was said the comparison is against separation. It was said against enmity. Here the *alif* and *lam* in *al-ṣulḥ* are for a previous reference (*'ahd*), meaning the reconciliation mentioned earlier, like His saying: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil 15], ﴿but Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil 16]. It was also said *al-ṣulḥ* is general. It was said *al-ṣulḥ* is the true reconciliation in which souls find rest and in which disagreement goes away, and the reconciliation of the spouses falls under it, so the meaning is: better than separation and disagreement. It was also said that *khayr* here is not a comparative, but its meaning is "good" in the sense of the goods (*khuyur*), just as enmity is an evil among evils.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 127–128 (part 3 of 3):

﴿Wa-uḥḍirati al-anfusu al-shuḥḥ﴾ (And souls have been made present to stinginess). This is a figure of speech of exaggeration (mubalagha): stinginess is treated as if it were a thing placed in a certain location. "And the souls were made present" (wa-uḥḍirat al-anfus), meaning they were driven toward it, and it did not come. Had stinginess been made to come to the souls, it would have been driven toward the souls; rather, the souls are driven toward it, because man is naturally disposed to stinginess and it is fixed in his nature. The exegetes singled out this word here. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr said: it is the wife's stinginess regarding her share from her husband and her wealth. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: it is the stinginess of each of the two regarding his or her right. Al-Maturidi said: it is possible that by shuḥḥ is meant ḥirṣ (greed), namely that each one is eager for his right. It is said: "he is shuḥḥ with your affection," i.e., eager to preserve it, and one does not say "bakhil" in this sense. Thus shuḥḥ and ḥirṣ are one in meaning, although originally shuḥḥ is for withholding and ḥirṣ for seeking. So shuḥḥ was applied to ḥirṣ, because each of them is a cause of the other, and because stinginess leads to greed and greed leads to stinginess. End.

Al-Zamakhshari said, regarding His words ﴿wa-l-ṣulḥu khayr﴾ (and reconciliation is best): this sentence is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ), and likewise His words ﴿wa-uḥḍirati al-anfusu al-shuḥḥ﴾. The meaning of the souls being made present to stinginess is that stinginess is made present to them, never absent from them, and they are never free of it; that is, they are naturally disposed to it. The point is that a woman hardly ever consents to have her turn allotted to her, or to be kept [by a husband] when he turns away from her and loves another. End.

His words ﴿wa-l-ṣulḥu khayr﴾ form a parenthetical clause, and likewise ﴿wa-uḥḍirati al-anfusu al-shuḥḥ﴾ is so considered on the basis that His words ﴿wa-in yatafarraqā﴾ (And if they separate) [al-Nisa: 130] are conjoined to His words ﴿fa-lā junaḥa ʿalayhimā an yuṣliḥā﴾ (there is no blame upon them if they reconcile). His words "the meaning of the souls being made present to stinginess is that stinginess is made present to them, never absent from them" — he made this a case of inversion (al-qalb), and it is not good. Rather, the Qur'anic construction requires that the souls are made present to stinginess, never absent from it, because al-anfus is the object that has not been named as agent, and it is the one that was the agent before the entry of the hamzat al-naql (causative hamza), for the original is: "the souls were present to stinginess." Yet according to the majority, in this construction it is permissible to place the second object in the position of the agent, with details on this matter, although the better practice according to them is to place the first. Thus it is possible that al-anfus is the second object and shuḥḥ the first, and the second has taken the place of the agent. But it is preferable to read the Qur'an according to the most eloquent and agreed-upon form. Al-ʿAdawi read "al-shiḥḥ" with a kasra on the shin, and this is a dialect.

﴿Wa-in tuḥsinū wa-tattaqū fa-inna Allāha kāna bi-mā taʿmalūna khabīran﴾ (And if you do good and fear God, then indeed God is ever Acquainted with what you do). He, exalted is He, urged good treatment in companionship toward women, even if they dislike it, out of regard for the right of companionship, and He commanded taqwa in their situation, because a husband may be carried by his dislike of his wife to harm her and to quarrel with her, especially since signs of dislike have appeared in him through disobedience (nushuz) and aversion. The Prophet ﷺ enjoined concern for them, saying: "for they are captives (ʿawān) with the husbands." Al-Maturidi said: "And if you do good" in that you give them more than their right, "and fear God" in that you do not diminish any of their right at all. Or: "do good" in fulfilling their right and in equality among them, and "fear God" (i.e., avoid) injustice, inclination, and favoring some over others. Or: "do good" in following what God has commanded you concerning obedience to them, and "fear God" by avoiding what He has forbidden you, namely disobedience to Him. End.

He concluded the end of this verse with the attribute al-Khabir (the All-Aware), which is knowledge of what is subtle in perception and fine; for between spouses there may be hidden matters that none knows but God, and it is not evident that this applies to everyone.

ʿImran ibn Hittan al-Kharijī was among the ugliest of people, and his wife was among the most beautiful of women. She cast her gaze upon his face and then continued praising God. He said: "What is wrong with you?" She said: "I praised God that you and I are among the people of Paradise." He said: "How?" She said: "Because you were given a wife like me and gave thanks, and I was given a husband like you and was patient, and God has promised Paradise to those who give thanks and those who are patient."

(p-358) ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, while you desire to marry them, and concerning the oppressed among the children, and that you should maintain justice for the orphans. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it."﴾ ﴿And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment (nushuz) or aversion (i'rad), there is no blame upon them both if they make a settlement between themselves; and settlement is best. And souls are present with stinginess (shuhh). And if you do good and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ ﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you should strive to do so. So do not incline completely [toward one] and leave her as if suspended. And if you amend and fear Allah, indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [An-Nisa: 129] ﴿And if they separate, Allah will compensate each of them from His abundance. And ever is Allah All-Encompassing and Wise.﴾ [An-Nisa: 130] ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you and [now] you, to fear Allah. But if you disbelieve - then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and ever is Allah Free of need and Praiseworthy.﴾ [An-Nisa: 131] ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ [An-Nisa: 132] ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others; and ever is Allah capable of that.﴾ [An-Nisa: 133] ﴿Whoever should desire the reward of this world - then with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. And ever is Allah Hearing and Seeing.﴾ [An-Nisa: 134] ﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more worthy of both. So do not follow [your own] desire, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ [An-Nisa: 135] ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger and the Scripture which He sent down before. And whoever disbelieves in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers and the Last Day has certainly strayed far away.﴾ [An-Nisa: 136] ﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, and then increased in disbelief - Allah will never forgive them nor guide them to a way.﴾ [An-Nisa: 137] ﴿Give tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment.﴾ [An-Nisa: 138] ﴿Those who take disbelievers as allies instead of believers. Do they seek with them honor? Indeed, honor belongs to Allah entirely.﴾ [An-Nisa: 139] ﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being denied and ridiculed, do not sit with them until they enter into another conversation. Indeed, you would then be like them. Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers in Hell all together.﴾ [An-Nisa: 140] ﴿Those who wait [and watch] for you. If you have a victory from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?" But if the disbelievers have a portion [of victory], they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you and protect you from the believers?" Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and never will Allah give the disbelievers over the believers a way.﴾ [An-Nisa: 141]. Ash-shuhh (stinginess): Ibn Faris said: it is stinginess combined with greed. And "tashaḥḥa al-rajulan fi al-amr" means the two men were greedy about a matter, not wanting it to escape them; it is pronounced with a damma or kasra on the shin. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ash-shuhh is strict holding onto beliefs and intention; so in aspirations and wealth and the like, when it is excessive, there is some blame in it. What reaches the sphere of legal rights and what manliness requires is bukhl (miserliness), which is a vice. Yet it may exist in a believer, and from it is the hadith: "It was said, O Messenger of Allah, can a believer be stingy? He said, Yes." As for shuhh, it is in every person, and this is indicated by: ﴿And souls are present with stinginess﴾ and ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]; every soul has shuhh. And the Prophet's saying (peace be upon him): "That you give charity while you are healthy and stingy," and he did not intend by it one specific person; and it is not praised to say here "that you give charity while you are healthy and miserly."

Al-mu'allaqah: she who is neither divorced nor has a husband. A man said: "Is it anything but a delay, a suspension, or a sham, or between that a suspension?" In the hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is 'Ashannaq: if I speak, I am divorced; and if I remain silent, I am left suspended." She likened the woman to a thing suspended from something, because it has settled neither on the ground nor on what it is hung from. And in the proverb: "Earth from the vehicle with suspension."

Al-khawd: entering into a thing. You say: "I waded into the water (khudtu al-ma' khawdan wa khiyadan)," and "I plunged into the torrents (ghamarat)," and "khadahu bi al-sayf" means he moved his sword against the one struck. "Takhawwadu fi al-hadith" means they discussed it. Al-makhadah is the place of wading. The poet, and he is 'Abd Allah ibn Shubrumah, said:
Whenever al-Jawza' rises and the star is rising, every ford of the Euphrates becomes a crossing.
Al-khawdah, with a fatha on the kha', is the pearl; ikhtada means the same as khada; and takhawwada means he burdened himself with wading. Al-istihwadh: domination and overpowering; said by Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj. It is said: ha'da yahud hawdan, and ahada with the same meaning as haada and ahaada. (p-359) This word is anomalous in that its middle radical is sound in al-naqqal; Abu Zayd al-Ansari analogized upon it.

﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them﴾. Occasion of revelation: some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, asked about the matter of women and their rulings concerning inheritance and other things. As for its connection (munasabah), it is likewise according to the Arab manner of speech in quadrants: it is about a matter, then it moves from it to something else, then returns to what it was about first. Thus is the Book of Allah: the rulings of His obligations are explained in it, then they are followed by promise and threat, encouragement and warning, then this is followed by mention of the opponents and obstinate ones who do not follow those rulings, then by what indicates the majesty and grandeur of Allah the Exalted, then it returns to clarify what relates to those earlier rulings. Here in this surah, it began with the rulings of women and inheritance and the mention of orphans; then secondly with mention of some of that in this verse; then finally with mention of some of the inheritance as well. Since women's matters were disregarded among the Arabs regarding inheritance and other things, and likewise orphans, He emphasized discussion of them repeatedly, so that they would return from the rulings of the Jahiliyyah. Al-istifta' is the seeking of a fatwa; and "aftahu ifta'an," and fatwa and fatwa; and "aftaytu fulanan fi ru'yahu" means I interpreted his dream for him. The meaning of ifta' is the manifestation of what is difficult to the questioner. Its root is from al-fata, the young man who has become strong and complete; so the meaning is: it is as if it is the clarification of what is unclear, so that it becomes established and strengthened. Al-istifta' does not concern the essences of women; rather, it concerns some of their rulings, which were not explained, so it is mujmal (general/ambiguous). The meaning of yuftikum fihinna is: He clarifies for you the state of what you asked about and its ruling.

* *

(p-360) ﴿And what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, while you desire to marry them, and concerning the oppressed among the children﴾; they mentioned in the place of "ma" in terms of i'rab: the nominative, the accusative, and the genitive. The nominative has three aspects. One: that it is coordinated with the name of Allah; i.e., Allah gives you a ruling, and what is recited in the Book concerns the meaning of the orphans. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means His saying: "And if you fear that you will not be just concerning orphans" [An-Nisa: 3], and it is like the saying "I was impressed by Zayd and his generosity," end. Two: that it is coordinated with the pronoun hidden in yuftikum, and the separation between them by the object and the prepositional phrase is acceptable. Three: that ma yutla is the subject, and fi al-kitab is its predicate, as a parenthetical clause (jumlah mu'taridah). The intended "Book" is the Preserved Tablet, as an exaltation of what is recited to them, and that justice and equity in the rights of orphans are among the great matters of high rank with Allah, which must be observed and preserved, and whoever neglects them is a wrongdoer who disregards what Allah has exalted. Similar to this is the exaltation of the Qur'an: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 4]. It has been said regarding this aspect: the predicate is omitted, and the estimate is: "what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women" is for you, or "yuftikum"; it is omitted because of what precedes it. On this estimate, "fi al-kitab" is with His saying "yutla alaykum," or it is in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in yutla, and "fi yatama" is a substitute (badal) for "fi al-kitab." Abu al-Baqa' said regarding the second: it is connected to what the first is connected to, because their meanings differ; the first is an adverbial of place, and the second means "bi" (because of), i.e., because of the orphans, as you say: "I came to you on Friday concerning the matter of Zayd." It is permissible for the second to be connected to "al-kitab," i.e., in what He prescribed regarding the rulings of orphans. It is also permissible for the second to be a circumstantial clause, connected to a hidden element. As for the accusative, it is by the estimate: "and He clarifies for you what is recited," because "yuftikum" in meaning is "yubayyinu," so it indicates it. As for the genitive, it is from two aspects. One: that the waw is for oath, as if he said: "And I swear by what is recited to you in the Book," and the oath is for exaltation; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. Two: that it is coordinated with the genitive pronoun in "fihinna"; this was said by Muhammad ibn Abi Musa, who said: Allah gave them a ruling concerning what they asked about, and concerning what they did not ask about. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this interpretation is weakened by what it contains of coordinating on a pronoun in the genitive without repeating the genitive particle. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not correct to coordinate on the genitive in "fihinna," because it is defective both in wording and in meaning, end.

What I choose is this aspect, although it is well known in the school of the majority of the Basran grammarians that this is not permissible except in poetry; but I have mentioned evidences for its permissibility in speech. I have elaborated on the evidences for this in the commentary on His saying "wa kufrun bihi" and "al-Masjid al-Haram." It is not defective in wording, because we have argued for its permissibility; nor is it defective in meaning as al-Zamakhshari claimed; rather the meaning supports it, and it is on an estimate of omission, i.e., He gives them a ruling concerning their recited matter (mutlaw), and what is recited to you in the Book concerning their (women's) matters is an admissible annexation (idafah), since annexation occurs for the slightest connection; when something is recited concerning them, the annexation to them is valid. Among this is the poet's saying:
When the star of al-Kharqa' appeared at dawn...

As for al-Zamakhshari's claim that the sentence is "defective in both wording and meaning," this is exactly the view of al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: "This is far-fetched, because it fails both in terms of wording and in terms of meaning. As for wording, it requires coordinating an overt noun with a pronoun (*'atf al-muzhar 'ala al-mudmar*), and that is not permissible, just as His saying ﴿whom you ask about, and the wombs﴾ [an-Nisa 1] is not permissible. As for meaning, Allah, exalted is He, gave a ruling on those matters, and taking the conjunction as applying to the pronoun would imply that He gave a ruling only on what is recited to you in the Book. It is well known that this is not the intended meaning. Rather, the intended meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, gives rulings on the questions they asked Him." End of his words.

We have already shown the soundness of the meaning if the deleted element is assumed and the word is read in the nominative as a conjunction to *Allah*, or as a conjunction to a pronoun that takes it out of the category of *ta'sis* (establishing a new ruling, i.e., a ruling that adds new content). Taking the whole sentence as a whole removes the entire sentence from *ta'sis*. The same applies to reading it in the genitive as an oath. Reading it in the accusative with a verb deleted, or as a conjunction to the pronoun, makes it *ta'sis*. If one intends both *ta'sis* and *ta'kid* (emphasis, i.e., repeating what is already known), then reading it as *ta'sis* is preferable, and one should not resort to *ta'kid* except when it is clear that *ta'sis* is not possible.

The discussion of the connection of His saying ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾ has already preceded. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, with what does His saying ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾ connect? I say: in the first mode, it is the complement of *yutla* (is recited), meaning, 'is recited to you concerning their meaning.' It is also permissible for ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾ to be a substitute (*badal*) for *fihinna* (concerning them). As for the last two modes, it is only a substitute, nothing else." End of his words.

By his words "in the first mode" he means that the phrase and what is recited are in the nominative position. As for what he permitted in this mode, that it is the complement of *yutla*, this can only be imagined if ﴿concerning the orphans﴾ is a substitute for ﴿concerning the Book﴾, or if *fi* is for causation (*lil-sabab*), so that two prepositional phrases with the same meaning do not attach to one verb. This is not permitted except by way of substitution or conjunction. As for what he also permitted in this mode, that *fi yatama* is a substitute for *fihinna*, the apparent view is that it is not permitted, because of the separation between the substitute and what it substitutes for by a conjunction. The parallel of this structure is: "Zayd resides in the house, and 'Amr in a part of it." Here one has separated *fi al-dar* from *fi kisr minha* by a conjunction and by the familiar structure: "Zayd resides in the house in a part of it, and 'Amr."

Those whose commentary on the exegesis we have examined agree that this verse refers back to what came earlier at the beginning of this sura, namely His saying: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾ [an-Nisa 4], His saying: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [an-Nisa 2], and His saying: (p. 362) ﴿…great. And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [an-Nisa 3]. ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "This verse, meaning ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans﴾ [an-Nisa 3], was revealed first. Then after it, some people asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the matter of women, and so this was revealed: ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them﴾, and ﴿what is recited to you﴾." According to what the exegetes said, and what was reported from ʿĀʾishah, the phrase ﴿gives you a ruling﴾ and the phrase ﴿is recited in it﴾ place the present tense in the position of the past tense, because the giving of rulings and the reciting had already preceded.

The annexation in *yatama al-nisa'* (orphan women) is of the type of annexing the specific to the general, because women divide into orphans and non-orphans. Al-Kufiyyun said: it is an annexation of the adjective to the modified noun, and this is not permitted according to the Basrans, and this is established in the science of grammar.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the annexation in *yatama al-nisa'*? I say: it is an annexation in the sense of *min* (of, from), which is the annexation of a thing to its genus, like your saying: 'ring of iron,' 'garment of silk,' and 'ring of silver.' It is permissible to separate, and to follow the genus to what precedes it, and to put it in the accusative or genitive with *min*. What appears in ﴿orphan women﴾ and in 'a scrubbed turban' is that it is an annexation in the sense of *li* (for, belonging to), and the meaning of *li* is specification (*ikhtisas*)." End of his words.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Madani read *fi yamama al-nisa'* with two *ya*'s. Ibn Jinni explained it on the basis that the original was *ayama*, so the hamza was replaced with a *ya*', as they said *Bahilat ibn Ya'sur*, when it was *A'sur*, named after his saying:

"Has it reached you that your father's color was changed
By the passing of nights and the alternation of epochs?"

They also said the reverse of this: "May Allah cut off his *ayd*," meaning his *yad* (hand), so the *ya*' was replaced with a hamza. *Ayama* is the plural of *ayyim* in the pattern *fa'il*, and it is among the forms peculiar to defective roots. Its original was *ayayim*, like *sayayid*, the plural of *sayyid*. The *lam* was moved to the position of the *ʿayn*, so it became *ayama*. The kasra was replaced with a fatha, and the *ya*' became an *alif* because it was vowelized and the letter before it was open. Ibn Jinni said: "If someone were to say: *ayyim* was broken into *ayma* in the pattern *sakra*, and then *ayma* was broken into *ayama*, it would be a good view."

As for the meaning of ﴿what has been prescribed for them﴾, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and a group said: it is the inheritance. Others said: it is the dowry. The addressee of His saying ﴿you do not give them﴾ are the guardians of the woman, who used to take women's dowries and give them nothing. It was also said: the guardians of orphans used to marry off the orphans under their care, and they did not act justly regarding their dowries. It was read: "what Allah has prescribed for them." Abu ʿUbaydah said: ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾; this wording can mean either desire or aversion. So the meaning, in the case of desire, is "you desire to marry them because of their wealth or their beauty," and in the case of aversion, "you turn away from marrying them because of their ugliness, so you keep them out of desire for their wealth." The first view is the view of ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and a group.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, used to direct people to the superior course in this meaning. When he asked a guardian about his ward and was told, "She is wealthy and beautiful," he would say to him, "Seek for her one better than you, and more beneficial to her." If he was told, "She is ugly and poor," he would say to him, "You are more entitled to her and to covering her faults than anyone else."

﴿The oppressed (al-mustada'afin)﴾ [an-Nisa 98] is conjoined to ﴿orphan women﴾. What was recited about them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾ [an-Nisa 11], and so on. This is because the Arabs did not give inheritance to a girl or to a small boy. The eldest would take the property alone, and they used to say: "Only one who protects the territory, repels the spoils, and fights for the sanctuary inherits." So Allah, exalted is He, assigned to each one his right. It is also permissible that this is an address to the guardians, like His saying: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾ [an-Nisa 2]. It was also said that the "oppressed" here are the slaves, male and female.

﴿And that you stand up for orphans with justice﴾ is in the genitive position, conjoined to what precedes it, meaning "and concerning your standing up for orphans with justice." What was recited in this sense is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾ [an-Nisa 2], and other matters mentioned concerning the property of the orphan. *Al-qist* means justice. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative, in the sense of 'and He commands you that you stand up...' It is an address to the leaders, that they look after them, secure their rights for them, and do not allow anyone to oppress them." End of his words. In *Rayy al-Zam'an* (Rayy al-Zam'an, a commentary), it says: "It may be read in the nominative, with 'that you stand up' as the subject, and its predicate is deleted, meaning: 'better for you.'" (p. 363) When it is possible to take it without deletion, by considering it conjoined to a genitive noun, this is preferable to positing a deleted governing verb, as al-Zamakhshari held. And preferable to taking it as the subject whose predicate is deleted.

﴿And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it﴾. Since the mention of women, orphan women, the oppressed among children, and standing up for orphans with justice had preceded, He followed this with the statement that He, exalted is He, knows the good that is done on account of those mentioned, and so He rewards it with abundant reward. He restricted the mention to doing good because it is what He encouraged, although He, exalted is He, knows whatever good or evil is done, and He rewards or punishes it accordingly.

﴿And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment (*nushuz*) or aversion, there is no blame upon them if they make a settlement between themselves in reconciliation﴾. It was revealed concerning Ibn Bi'kak and his wife, according to Mujahid. It was also revealed concerning Rafi' ibn Khadij and his wife Khawla bint Muhammad ibn Maslama. She had grown old, and he married a young woman over her and favored her. Khawla could not endure, so he divorced her, then took her back and said: "I have only one wife, so either you accept favoritism or I will divorce you." So she fled. This was reported by ʿUbaydah, Sulayman ibn Yasar, and Ibn al-Musayyab. Or it was revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ and Sawda bint Zam'a, who feared being divorced, so she said: "Do not divorce me, keep me with your wives, and do not allot me a night." So he did that, and this was revealed. This was reported by Ibn ʿAbbas and a group.

The fear here is in its literal sense, but it is not attained except through the appearance of signs that indicate the occurrence of what is feared. It was said that the meaning of "feared" is "knew." It was also said "suspected." It should not be taken away from its apparent meaning, since the meaning is correct with it. *Nushuz* means that he turns away from her by withholding himself from her, his maintenance, and the affection between them, and that he harms her by an offense or a beating. *Ia'rad* means that he reduces his conversation with her and his companionship, due to an objection about her age or ugliness, or a defect in character or appearance, or boredom, or the eye's longing for another, or other things. This is the lighter of the two kinds of *nushuz*. So Allah removes blame between them in reconciliation by all kinds of concessions from the husband to her, so that she will endure, or from her to him, so that he will favor her, or that he will not favor another, and she holds to the marriage bond, or in patience over favoritism and the like. All of this is permitted. He made the lifting of blame depend on the anticipation of fear and the appearance of signs of *nushuz* and aversion. It is even better when those things occur and are confirmed, because if reconciliation is permitted with the fear of them, then with their actual occurrence it is more strongly permitted, since in reconciliation the bond of affection and love remains. Among the forms of reconciliation is that she gives her day to another of his wives, as Sawda did, or that she agrees to his allotting her a long period once in a while, or that she gives him her dowry or part of it, or her maintenance. The right a woman has over her husband is the dowry and the maintenance, and the allotment of nights is also a right. Giving up any of this, or some part of it, on condition that he does not divorce her, is permissible.

The Kufans read *yuslihā* (they make peace) from *aslaḥa* in the pattern *akrama*. The rest of the seven read *yaṣṣālaḥā*, whose original is *yatasālaḥā*, and the *tā*' was assimilated into the *ṣād*. ʿUbaydah al-Salmani read *yuṣāliḥā* from the *mufā'ala* form. Al-Aʿmash read *in iṣṭalaḥā*, which is the reading of Ibn Masʿud, made into the past tense. Its original is *tasālaḥa* in the pattern *tafā'ala*, so the *tā*' was assimilated into the *ṣād*, and a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza) was added. *Al-ṣulḥ* (reconciliation) is not the verbal noun of the thing from these verbs that were read. If it is a noun for what one reconciles by, like *al-ʿaṭā'* (gift) and *al-karāma* (honor) with *a'ṭaytu* and *akramtu*, then its accusative case may be by dropping the preposition, meaning "reconciled by something upon which the two agree." It is also permissible that it be a verbal noun of these verbs by dropping the extra letters.

﴿And reconciliation is best﴾. Its apparent meaning is that *khayr* is a comparative form (elative), and that the thing compared against is the nushuz and aversion, so it is deleted because what precedes it indicates it. It was said the comparison is against separation. It was said against enmity. Here the *alif* and *lam* in *al-ṣulḥ* are for a previous reference (*'ahd*), meaning the reconciliation mentioned earlier, like His saying: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil 15], ﴿but Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil 16]. It was also said *al-ṣulḥ* is general. It was said *al-ṣulḥ* is the true reconciliation in which souls find rest and in which disagreement goes away, and the reconciliation of the spouses falls under it, so the meaning is: better than separation and disagreement. It was also said that *khayr* here is not a comparative, but its meaning is "good" in the sense of the goods (*khuyur*), just as enmity is an evil among evils.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 127–128 (part 3 of 3):

﴿Wa-uḥḍirati al-anfusu al-shuḥḥ﴾ (And souls have been made present to stinginess). This is a figure of speech of exaggeration (mubalagha): stinginess is treated as if it were a thing placed in a certain location. "And the souls were made present" (wa-uḥḍirat al-anfus), meaning they were driven toward it, and it did not come. Had stinginess been made to come to the souls, it would have been driven toward the souls; rather, the souls are driven toward it, because man is naturally disposed to stinginess and it is fixed in his nature. The exegetes singled out this word here. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr said: it is the wife's stinginess regarding her share from her husband and her wealth. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: it is the stinginess of each of the two regarding his or her right. Al-Maturidi said: it is possible that by shuḥḥ is meant ḥirṣ (greed), namely that each one is eager for his right. It is said: "he is shuḥḥ with your affection," i.e., eager to preserve it, and one does not say "bakhil" in this sense. Thus shuḥḥ and ḥirṣ are one in meaning, although originally shuḥḥ is for withholding and ḥirṣ for seeking. So shuḥḥ was applied to ḥirṣ, because each of them is a cause of the other, and because stinginess leads to greed and greed leads to stinginess. End.

Al-Zamakhshari said, regarding His words ﴿wa-l-ṣulḥu khayr﴾ (and reconciliation is best): this sentence is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ), and likewise His words ﴿wa-uḥḍirati al-anfusu al-shuḥḥ﴾. The meaning of the souls being made present to stinginess is that stinginess is made present to them, never absent from them, and they are never free of it; that is, they are naturally disposed to it. The point is that a woman hardly ever consents to have her turn allotted to her, or to be kept [by a husband] when he turns away from her and loves another. End.

His words ﴿wa-l-ṣulḥu khayr﴾ form a parenthetical clause, and likewise ﴿wa-uḥḍirati al-anfusu al-shuḥḥ﴾ is so considered on the basis that His words ﴿wa-in yatafarraqā﴾ (And if they separate) [al-Nisa: 130] are conjoined to His words ﴿fa-lā junaḥa ʿalayhimā an yuṣliḥā﴾ (there is no blame upon them if they reconcile). His words "the meaning of the souls being made present to stinginess is that stinginess is made present to them, never absent from them" — he made this a case of inversion (al-qalb), and it is not good. Rather, the Qur'anic construction requires that the souls are made present to stinginess, never absent from it, because al-anfus is the object that has not been named as agent, and it is the one that was the agent before the entry of the hamzat al-naql (causative hamza), for the original is: "the souls were present to stinginess." Yet according to the majority, in this construction it is permissible to place the second object in the position of the agent, with details on this matter, although the better practice according to them is to place the first. Thus it is possible that al-anfus is the second object and shuḥḥ the first, and the second has taken the place of the agent. But it is preferable to read the Qur'an according to the most eloquent and agreed-upon form. Al-ʿAdawi read "al-shiḥḥ" with a kasra on the shin, and this is a dialect.

﴿Wa-in tuḥsinū wa-tattaqū fa-inna Allāha kāna bi-mā taʿmalūna khabīran﴾ (And if you do good and fear God, then indeed God is ever Acquainted with what you do). He, exalted is He, urged good treatment in companionship toward women, even if they dislike it, out of regard for the right of companionship, and He commanded taqwa in their situation, because a husband may be carried by his dislike of his wife to harm her and to quarrel with her, especially since signs of dislike have appeared in him through disobedience (nushuz) and aversion. The Prophet ﷺ enjoined concern for them, saying: "for they are captives (ʿawān) with the husbands." Al-Maturidi said: "And if you do good" in that you give them more than their right, "and fear God" in that you do not diminish any of their right at all. Or: "do good" in fulfilling their right and in equality among them, and "fear God" (i.e., avoid) injustice, inclination, and favoring some over others. Or: "do good" in following what God has commanded you concerning obedience to them, and "fear God" by avoiding what He has forbidden you, namely disobedience to Him. End.

He concluded the end of this verse with the attribute al-Khabir (the All-Aware), which is knowledge of what is subtle in perception and fine; for between spouses there may be hidden matters that none knows but God, and it is not evident that this applies to everyone.

ʿImran ibn Hittan al-Kharijī was among the ugliest of people, and his wife was among the most beautiful of women. She cast her gaze upon his face and then continued praising God. He said: "What is wrong with you?" She said: "I praised God that you and I are among the people of Paradise." He said: "How?" She said: "Because you were given a wife like me and gave thanks, and I was given a husband like you and was patient, and God has promised Paradise to those who give thanks and those who are patient."

[p. 365]

﴿You will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you are eager to do so.﴾ Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It is narrated that this was revealed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and his inclination of heart toward ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her. End of quote. God (Exalted is He) alerts us that it is impossible to be able to be equitable and even between wives, so that no inclination whatsoever occurs, and no excess or deficiency in what is due to them. In this there is an excuse for men regarding the disparity that occurs in inward inclination of the heart, in attentiveness, in gazing, in companionship, and in pleasantry. Equality in these matters lies beyond the limit of what is within one's capacity. God made the impossibility of being able to achieve equality conditional upon a person's eagerness for it. It has been said that the meaning of "you will be equitable" is equality in love; this was said by ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Ḥasan. It has also been said that it refers to equal treatment and division of time. It has been said that it refers to sexual intercourse. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that: "He used to divide his time among his wives and act justly, and he would say: 'This is my division in what I possess, so do not hold me accountable for what You possess and I do not,' meaning love." This is because ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, was more beloved to him. ʿUmar used to say: "O Allah, this is my heart, which I cannot control; as for everything else, I hope to be just in it."

﴿So do not incline completely away, leaving her like one suspended.﴾ God (Exalted is He) forbade injustice toward the one who is desired; that is, if a shortfall in some measure of equality occurs from you, then do not commit complete injustice. The pronoun in "fa-tadharūhā" refers to the one from whom one inclines away, which is understood from His words: "So do not incline completely away."
Ubayy recited: "fa-tadhrūhā kal-mamsūnah" (leaving her like one imprisoned). ʿAbdullah recited: "fa-tadhrūhā ka-annahā muʿallaqah" (leaving her as if she were suspended). The explanation of "muʿallaqah" has already been mentioned in the section on vocabulary (al-mufradāt). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "like one confined without right." It has been said that the meaning of "like one suspended" is like one far from her husband, or from her right, as reported by al-Māwardī, derived from suspending a thing because it is distant from its resting place. "Tadharūhā" may be jussive, conjoined to "tamīlū," or it may be in the subjunctive, with an implied "an" after the prohibition. "Ka-l-muʿallaqah" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), so the particle "ka" is related to an implied element. In a hadith: "Whoever has two wives and inclines toward one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection with one side of him leaning." The meaning is that he inclines toward one of them completely, not merely inclining. "ʿUmar gave preference in the distribution of provision among the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but ʿĀʾishah refused and said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to act justly among us in the division, with his wealth and himself, so ʿUmar made them equal.'" Muʿādh had two wives; when he was with one of them, he would not perform ablution in the house of the other. Both died in the plague, and he buried them in one grave.

﴿And if you do right and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Al-Zamakhsharī said: "And if you set right what has passed from you, and make amends for it through repentance, and fear Allah regarding what is to come, Allah will forgive you." End of quote. In this there is a trace of Muʿtazilism (nazghat al-iʿtizāl, a tendency toward the Muʿtazilite school). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "And if you set right what you have spoiled through bad companionship, and abide by what is incumbent upon you of justice regarding what you possess, then indeed Allah is forgiving of what you possess, overlooking it." Al-Ṭabarī said: "Forgiving of what has passed from you of complete inclination before the revelation of this verse," end of quote. On this view, it is a forgiveness specific to particular people who committed the prohibited act during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ). This verse concludes with "ihsān" (excellence) in the earlier verse and with "iṣlāḥ" (setting right) here, because the former concerns something recommended, since one may choose not to do good and to be stingy, and to reconcile with what satisfies him, whereas this concerns something obligatory, since he has no option but to set things right, and indeed he is obligated to be just in what he possesses.

﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance.﴾ The pronoun in "yatafarraqā" refers to the two spouses mentioned in His words: "And if a woman fears ill-treatment or aversion from her husband" (4:128). The meaning: if each of them is stingy and they do not reconcile, and they separate by divorce, then Allah will enrich each of them from the other by His bounty and kindness, in wealth, in companionship, and in abundance and the attainment of what is sought. "Al-siʿah" means wealth and capability. This is a promise of sufficiency for each one if they separate, and it is known to occur by the will of Allah (Exalted is He). The attribution of the act to both of them indicates that each has a part in the separation, which is separation by bodies and the lengthening of the period through the dissolution of the marriage bond. It does not indicate separation by speech, which is divorce, because that is specific to the husband, and the wife has no share in verbal separation, so it is not attributed to her. This is contrary to those who held that separation here is by speech, which is divorce. Zayd ibn Aflaḥ recited "wa-in yatafāraqā" with the alif of mutual action (mufāʿalah), meaning: "and if each of them separates from the other." This verse is similar to His words: "Then either retain with kindness or release with good" (2:229), and to the saying of the Arabs: "If there is no agreement, there is divorce." Thus God alerted us that they may separate just as they may reconcile. This indicates permissibility. They said: In His words "Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance" there is an indication of wealth in property. It is reported that al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both, divorced many women; when he was asked about this, he said: "I have seen that Allah has tied sufficiency to two matters, when He said: 'And marry the single among you' (24:32), and He said: 'And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance.'"

﴿And Allah is ever All-Encompassing, All-Wise.﴾ This is fitting with the mention of abundance, since His abundance was mentioned earlier. "Al-wāsiʿ" (the All-Encompassing) is general in wealth, power, knowledge, and all other perfections. The mention of the attribute of wisdom is fitting, and wisdom is placing a thing in the place that suits it, because abundance without wisdom leads closer to corruption than to good; this was said by al-Rāghib. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "He means in what He decreed and admonished." al-Kalbī said: "In what He decreed upon the husband of retaining her with kindness or releasing her with good." al-Māturīdī said: "Or where separation is recommended when they disagree and there is no equality between them."

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ When God mentioned the abundance of His provision and His wisdom, He mentioned that He has dominion over whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth; so the wealth of no one diminishes what He has, nor does expansion upon Him add anything, because the one who possesses all of that is the absolutely Self-Sufficient.

﴿And We have certainly enjoined those who were given the Scripture before you and you [too], to fear Allah.﴾ "Waṣṣaynā" means We commanded or We charged them and you. "Min qablikum" may be connected to "ūtū" (were given), which is closer, or to "waṣṣaynā" (We enjoined). The meaning: the enjoining of piety is the practice of Allah with the earlier nations, so you are not singled out for this command. "Iyyākum" (and you) is conjoined to the relative pronoun, and the relative clause is mentioned first, because their enjoining preceded "waṣṣaynā," so this precedence is temporal. This kind of conjunction, meaning conjoining a detached object pronoun to a noun, is eloquent, occurs in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech, and is not restricted to poetry. Some of our companions and shaykhs erred in this, claiming it is permissible only in poetry, because one can express it connected, saying "I will come to you and Zayd." According to them, "I struck Zayd and you" is not permissible except in poetry. This is a gross error. Rather, it is a necessary consequence of the detachment of the pronoun that it can be conjoined; so "Zayd stood and you," and "Bakr went out and I," are permissible without dispute; likewise "I struck Zayd and you."
"Alladhīna ūtū l-kitāb" is general in divine books, and there is no necessity to restrict "those who were given the Scripture" to Jews and Christians, as some exegetes held, because God's command of piety has existed since He brought the world into being, so it is not restricted to Jews and Christians. "An ittaqū" may be a verbal particle (an maṣdariyyah), meaning "that fear Allah," or it may be explanatory (mufassirah), with the sense "fear Allah," because "waṣṣaynā" contains the meaning of saying.

﴿But if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ Its apparent meaning is address to those addressed in His words "and you," namely this nation. It is possible that it includes both those given the Scripture and the addressees, and the address is dominant, as established in the Arabic language, as you say: "I said that to Zayd: do not strike ʿAmr," and as you say: "Zayd and you go out."

﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth;﴾ that is, you are among those whom He possesses, and He is the one who disposes of you, since He is your Creator and the Bestower upon you of all kinds of blessings, and you are His possessions. It is therefore not fitting that you disbelieve in the One who owns you and oppose His command; rather, His right is that He be obeyed and not disobeyed, that His punishment be feared, and that His reward be hoped for. To Allah belongs whatever is in His heavens and His earth: those who worship Him as One and do not disobey Him.

﴿And Allah is ever Free of need;﴾ that is, free of His creation and their worship. Their obedience does not benefit Him, and their disbelief does not harm Him.

(Praiseworthy;) that is, deserving of being praised for the abundance of His blessings, even if you disbelieve in Him.

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ "Wakīl" is one who stands over affairs and carries out in them what he sees. Whoever possesses whatever is in the heavens and the earth is sufficient for whatever He disposes of, and does not rely on anyone else. He repeated His words "To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" three times according to the context. [p. 367] Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The first is an alert to the object of hope, that He guides those who are separated. The second is an alert to His independence from the servants. The third is a preface to the threat.
Al-Zamakhsharī said: The repetition of His words "To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" is an affirmation of what requires their piety, so that they fear Him, obey Him, and do not disobey Him, because fear and piety are the root of all good. Al-Rāghib said: The first is for consolation over what has passed. The second: that His enjoining is for His mercy, not for need, and that if they disbelieve in Him, they cannot harm Him at all. The third: an indication that He is Free of need. Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī said: The first is an affirmation that He is of vast generosity. The second is for exalting Him above the obedience of the obedient. The third is for His power to annihilate and to originate. The purpose of this is to affirm that He is capable of many implications, so it is fitting to mention the proof for each of its implications, and this repetition is better and more excellent than suffice with mentioning the proof once, because, in his view, repeating the proof brings to mind what necessitates knowledge of the implication, and the knowledge gained of that implication is stronger and more exalted; thus it is clear that this repetition is at the height of perfection. Makkī said: We alerted first to His dominion and vastness; second, to our need for Him and His independence; and third, to His preservation of us and His knowledge of our management.

﴿If He wills, He can take you away, O people, and bring others.﴾ Its apparent meaning is that the address is to those previously addressed. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The address is to the polytheists and the hypocrites, and the meaning is: "and bring others from among you." Close to this is what al-Zamakhsharī transmitted: that it is an address to those among the Arabs who opposed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī said: The address is to the disbelievers, and it is a threat to them, as if He said: "If He wills, He will destroy you as He destroyed those before you when they disbelieved in His messengers." It has also been said: it is for the believers, to whom the name "people" applies; and the meaning is: if He wills, He will destroy you as He originated you, and originate other people who worship Him. Al-Ṭabarī said: The address is to those who interceded for Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq, and who disputed and argued on his behalf regarding his betrayal in the matter of the coat of mail and the flour. This interpretation is remote. The generality may appear, so that it is an address to the present person to whom the address and call are directed. "And bring others" means: bring people other than you; so what is brought is of the same kind as what is taken away, and therefore it is of the same kind as the addressed person being called, namely people.

Narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck Salman on the back with his hand and said: "They are this man's people," meaning Ibn Faris (the Persians). Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and others allowed that by "others" (ākharīn) is meant a kind of those addressed. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And He would bring others in your place, or a different creation other than mankind." Ibn Atiyya said: "It is possible that it is a warning to all of the children of Adam, and that the others are of a kind other than theirs, just as it has been narrated that there were angels on earth worshipping Allah before the children of Adam." End of quote. But what they permitted is not permissible, because the meaning of "ākhar" (other) in the language is a meaning not specific to the kind of what preceded. So if you say: "Zayd came and another (ākhar) with him," or "I passed by a woman and another (ukhrā) with her," or "I bought a horse and another (ākhar)," and "I made a race between a donkey and another (ākhar)," then ākhar, its feminine ukhrā, its dual, and its plural are only of the same kind as what comes before them. But if you say: "I bought a garment and another (ākhar)," meaning "a non-garment," it is not allowed. Therefore their permitting that the phrase "bi-ākharīn" be of a kind other than what preceded, namely people, is not correct. This is the distinction between ghayr (other) and ākhar (another): ghayr applies to what differs in kind or in attribute; so you say: "I bought a garment and ghayrahu (something else)," which may be a garment, and may be a non-garment. Few people know this distinction.

﴿And Allah is ever Capable of that﴾; i.e., capable of removing you and bringing others. He used the intensive form in describing the power, because nothing that He wills is impossible for Him. This is wrath against them, a warning, and an explanation of His power.
