The first contains only the negation of standing; the second contains the negation of the will and the intention for standing, and the negation of the will to stand necessitates the negation of standing. We have already discussed this at length in the surah of Ali 'Imran. Al-Zamakhshari said: [this is] a negation of forgiveness and guidance, which is kindness, in the manner of emphasis preceded by the lam; and the intended meaning by negating both is the negation of what necessitates them, namely sound and steadfast faith. End of his words. The apparent meaning of his statement is that he holds the view of the Kufans (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of the Kufa school), namely that they say: when you say "lam yakun Zayd liyaqum" (Zayd would not stand), the predicate of "lam yakun" is your phrase "liyaqum", and the lam is for emphasis, added in the negation, while the thing negated is the standing; and "an" is not implied, rather the lam itself is the one that governs the verb in the subjunctive. The Basrans (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of the Basra school) say: the subjunctive is by the implied "an", and from "an" (implied) and the verb following it, a verbal noun (masdar) is formed; that verbal noun cannot be the predicate, because it is a meaning, and the subject is a solid body. Rather, the predicate is elided, and the lam serves to strengthen the transfer of that predicate to the verbal noun, because it is a solid body. "An" is implied after it, and the lam became like a substitute for the omitted "an"; for this reason it is not permissible to delete this lam, nor to combine it with "an" when "an" is expressed. As for the statement, "the intended meaning by negating both is the negation of what necessitates them," the meaning is that they would not have been [in a state] to believe so that Allah would forgive them and guide them.

﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them there is a painful punishment﴾: The address is to the Messenger. The meaning of "give good news" (bashshir) is "inform," and the expression "give good news" is used in mockery of them, like His saying, ﴿So give them good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 21]; that is, what stands in for good news for them is the information of punishment, as the poet said:
"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."
Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the term "good news" is used here explicitly with its benefit (the pleasant outcome); therefore it is apt to use it for what is disliked. When it comes unrestricted, it is understood in reference to what is loved. In this verse there is evidence that the one before it [verse 136] concerns the hypocrites. Al-Maturidi said: "Give the hypocrites the good news" indicates that His saying, ﴿O you who believe, believe﴾ [al-Nisa: 136], is about the people of hypocrisy and show-off, because no mention of the hypocrites preceded except this verse. It is also possible that it is a beginning without any prior mention of the hypocrites.

﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾: That is, the Jews, the Christians, and the polytheists of the Arabs, as allies, helpers, and supporters, whom they ally with against the Messenger and the believers. He specified among the attributes of the hypocrites the most harmful of them to the believers, namely their alliance with the disbelievers and their discarding of the believers, and He drew attention to the corruption of this so that whoever might fall into some form of it among the believers, out of heedlessness, ignorance, or leniency, would abandon it. "Those who" is either a qualifier of the hypocrites, or in the accusative by way of censure, or in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject; that is, they are the ones who.

﴿Do they seek honour from them?﴾: That is, might, strength, and protection through their alliance, and through the saying of some of them to others, "The affair of Muhammad will not be completed." In this interrogation there is a warning that they have no honour; so how can you seek it from them? And a warning about the wickedness of their intention, which is seeking honour through the disbelievers and gaining strength through them.

﴿For honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾: That is, to His allies, whom He has decreed honour and victory over the Jews and others. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail." Indeed Allah is Strong, Mighty﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21]. And He said: ﴿Honour belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers, but the hypocrites do not know﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever desires honour, then to Allah belongs all honour﴾ [Fatir: 10]. The fa' in ﴿for honour belongs to Allah﴾ entered because of the meaning of a condition present in the statement; the meaning is: if you seek honour from these people, then [know that] honour belongs entirely to Allah. "Jami'an" (entirely) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

﴿And it has already been sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being disbelieved in and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a conversation other than it﴾: The address is to whoever shows belief, whether sincere or hypocritical. It has also been said that it is addressed to the hypocrites previously mentioned, and that this would be a shift (iltifat) in address. They used to sit with the rabbis (ahbar) of the Jews, who would discuss the Qur'an, and they would listen to them; so they were forbidden from this, and they were reminded of what had been sent down to them in Mecca, His saying: ﴿And when you see those who engage in discourse about Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a conversation other than it﴾ [al-An'am: 68].

The majority recited "wa-qad nuzzila" (and it has been sent down), with doubling of the z and the passive voice. 'Asim recited "nazzala" with doubling and the active voice. Abu Haywa and Humayd recited "nazala" without doubling, with the active voice. Al-Nakha'i recited "unzila" with a hamza, in the passive voice. The position of "an" is nominative or accusative according to the governing element: it is in the accusative in the reading of 'Asim, and in the nominative as the subject in the reading of Abu Haywa and Humayd, and as the deputy subject (the subject of the passive verb) in the reading of the rest. "An" here is the lightened form of the heavy "inna", and its subject, the implied pronoun of the matter (damir al-shan), is elided; its estimate is: "that it is when you hear." What Abu al-Baqa estimated, namely "that you, when you hear," is not good, because when it is lightened, "in" does not govern a pronoun except when it is a pronoun of matter and affair that is elided; and its governing of something other than that is a necessity of poetry, as in the verse:
"Had you, in the day of ease, asked me
for your divorce, I would not have withheld it, though you are a friend."
The predicate of "an" is the clause consisting of "idha" (when) and its response. An example of a conditional clause occurring as the predicate of the lightened "an" from the heavy "inna" is the verse of the poet:
"So I knew that whomever you fear,
he is the prey of a locust and the young of an eagle."
"Yukfaru biha" (it is disbelieved in) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial qualifier. The pronoun in "ma'ahum" (with them) refers to the elided element indicated by His saying, "it is disbelieved in and mocked"; that is, "do not sit with the disbelieving mockers." "Until" (hatta) is the limit of the prohibition on sitting with them. The implication of the limit is that if they engage in discourse other than disbelief and mockery, the prohibition is lifted, and it becomes permissible for them to sit with them. The pronoun refers to what the meaning indicates; that is, "in a conversation other than their conversation, which is disbelief and mockery." It is also possible that the pronoun be singular, even though it refers to the two concepts understood from His saying, "it is disbelieved in" and "it is mocked," because both return to one meaning; and because it treated the pronoun as the demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) in being singular, even though it refers to two.

﴿Indeed, you would then be like them﴾: He, the Exalted, judged that if they sit with them while they disbelieve in the verses of Allah and mock them, they are like them in disbelief, being able to deny; for they would be content with disbelief, and contentment with disbelief is disbelief. The address in "innakum" (indeed you) is in the same disagreement as before: is it addressed to the hypocrites, or to the believers? He, the Exalted, did not judge the Muslims who used to sit with the disbelieving polytheists engaged in such discourse in Mecca to be like the polytheists, because the Muslims at that time were unable to deny; this is in contrast to Medina, where Islam was dominant and supreme; so they were able to deny, and the listener to the blame is a partner of the speaker. How excellent is the saying of the poet:
"Guard your hearing from listening to the ugly,
as you guard your tongue from speaking it."
Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this likeness is not in all attributes, but it is a binding implication, likened to the judgment apparent from association, as in the saying of the poet:
"Do not ask about the man, but ask about his companion,
for every companion follows his associate." (p-375)

Narrated from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that he apprehended a group who were drinking wine. Someone said to him about one of those present: "He is fasting." So he disciplined him, and he recited: ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them.﴾

As for those who hold that the meaning of His words ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them﴾ is: if you wade into it as they wade, and agree with them in that, then you are disbelievers like them, that interpretation is rejected by the context of the speech. Rather, the meaning is what we have already mentioned: that if you sit with them, you are like them.

Here, idhan (then) is placed between the subject and the predicate, and mithl (like) is used in the singular because the meaning is: "Indeed, your disobedience is like their disobedience." So the meaning is taken as a verbal noun (masdar), as in His words: ﴿Shall we believe two humans like us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 47]. He used the plural in His words: ﴿then they will not be your likes﴾ [Muhammad: 38], and in His words: ﴿and [there are] wide-eyed maidens﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 22], ﴿like hidden pearls﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 23]. Both the singular and the agreement in dual or plural are permissible.

It was read irregularly as (mithlahum) with a fatha on the lam. The Basrans explained it as indeclinable (mabni) because it is annexed to an indeclinable word, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, it is the truth, just as you speak﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 23], according to the reading of the one who put a fatha on the lam. The Kufans permit that (mithl) be in the accusative in terms of its position (mahall), being an adverbial of place (zarf), so that according to them "Zayd is mithlaka" with the accusative is permissible, meaning "in the situation like your situation." According to their view, the accusative of "mithlahum" is by position, as an adverbial of place.

﴿Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hell, all of them﴾ because they took them as allies in the world; He gathered them together in the Hereafter in the Fire, and a person is with whom he loves. This is a warning from Him, exalted is He, which emphasizes the caution against sitting with them and mixing with them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 141:

﴿Those who wait on you: if there is a victory for you from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?" But if the disbelievers have a share, they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you and protect you from the believers?"﴾ The meaning: those who await for you the changes of circumstances, whether of victory for you or against you. If there is a victory for you from Allah, they say: ﴿"Were we not with you?"﴾ supporting you. The meaning: then give us a share of the spoils on the ground that we are believers. And if the disbelievers, that is the Jews, have a share, i.e. an attainment against the believers, they say: ﴿"Did we not gain mastery over you?"﴾; i.e., did we not overcome you and gain the power to kill and take you captive, and spare you, and protect you from the believers by hindering them from you? So give us a share on the ground that we are your allies, so we do not harm you and do not leave anyone to harm you. It has been said that the meaning is that the disbelievers and Jews intended to enter Islam, but the hypocrites warned them against that and exaggerated in repelling them, saying that the Messenger's affair would weaken; so when they obtained a share, they bestowed favour upon them by claiming they had guided them to these benefits. The estimated sense is therefore: "and we hindered you from following the believers and entering their religion; so give us a share." It has also been said that the meaning is: did we not inform you of the affair of Muhammad and his companions, and make you aware of their secret? It is related from Ibn Abbas: did we not protect you from behind? The phrase ﴿those who wait﴾ is either a substitute for ﴿those who take﴾, or an attribute of the hypocrites, or in the accusative for blame, or in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject.

The Exalted named the believers' victory a "conquest" (fath), making it a great favour to them, and said ﴿a conquest from Allah﴾; but the disbelievers' success He called a "share" and did not attribute it to Himself, as a way of belittling them and degrading what they gained from the believers, because the believers' victory is a great matter for which the gates of heaven are opened. As Abu Tammam said regarding al-Mu'tasim's conquest of Amorium, the land of the Romans:

"A conquest for which the gates of heaven are opened, and the earth appears in its fresh garments."

As for the disbelievers' victory, it is a worldly portion they obtain. Ibn Abi Ablah read ﴿wa-namna'akum﴾ with a fatha on the ʿayn, by an implied particle after the waw of plurality, and the meaning is: did we not combine gaining mastery over you with preventing you from the believers? A parallel is al-Hutay'a's verse:

"Was I not your neighbour, with love and brotherhood between me and you?"

Ibn Atiyya said: ﴿wa-namna'akum﴾ with a fatha on the ʿayn by way of ṣarf (the grammatical term for a verb being turned aside from its expected form, here from conjunction with what precedes), meaning ṣarf from the sharing of the same governing verb's case with the following verb in its i'rab (grammatical inflection). The accusative by ṣarf is not from the terminology of the Basrans. Ubayy read ﴿wa-manaʿnakum﴾, which is coordinated with the sense of the estimated sentence: because the meaning is "Did we not gain mastery over you and protect you," like His saying: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1] ﴿and We set down﴾ [al-Sharh: 2], since the meaning is: "Did We not expand for you your breast and set down?"

﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾; i.e. between you and them, and He will give you justice against all of them. It is possible that there is no conjunction, and the meaning of "between you" is: between the group of you and them, and the second person is predominant. This is a consolation to the believers and a comfort in what He has promised them.

﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾; meaning on the Day of Resurrection, as said by Ali and Ibn Abbas. It is related from Subay' al-Hadrami who said: I was with Ali when a man said to him: "O Commander of the Believers, what do you say about the saying of Allah, ﴿and Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾? How is that, when they fight us and prevail over us at times?" Ali said: "Its meaning is the Day of Resurrection, the Day of Judgement." Ibn Atiyya said: all the people of interpretation said this. Ibn al-Arabi said: this is weak, since the statement gives no benefit in that case, even though the beginning of the sentence may suggest that meaning, given His words ﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾. It has also been said: He, the Exalted, does not erase the community of Islam by disbelief, nor does He allow their egg (i.e. their territory) to be plundered, as came in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Thawban, who said: "I asked my Lord that He not give power over them to an enemy from other than themselves, so that he would plunder their egg, even if all who are in its regions gathered against them, until some of them destroy others and some of them take others captive."

It has also been said: the meaning is that they do not enjoin one another in falsehood, nor forbid one another from wrongdoing, and they lag behind in repentance; so the enemy's domination over them comes from their own side, as the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you is for what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30]. Ibn al-Arabi said: this is very clear, and His words in the hadith of Thawban confirm it: "until some of them destroy others." Because "until" (hatta) marks a limit, the apparent sense of the speech is that He does not give their enemy power over them to plunder them except when some of them destroy others and take others captive. This has occurred in these times through the strife among the Muslims, so the might of the disbelievers grew strong, and they seized the lands of the Muslims until only the least of Islam remained.

It has also been said: "a way" refers to a way by way of the Law; if one is found, it is contrary to the Law. It has been said: "a way" means a valid legal proof or a rational argument by which they seek support, except that it is refuted and overturned. It has been said: "a way" means dominance; this is said by al-Kalbi. It can be understood as lasting, comprehensive dominance, so its meaning reverts to their not plundering the egg of Islam; otherwise they have indeed prevailed in some places, such as Uhud, earlier.

These verses have included, in eloquence and rhetoric, the arts of paronomasia (tajnis) of a different kind in: ﴿an yusliha bayna-huma sulhan﴾ [al-Nisa: 128], and in: "fa-la tamilu kulla al-mayl," and in: "fa-qad dalla dalalan," and in: "kafaru" and "kafaru." And paronomasia of the same kind in: "yastaftunaka" and "yuftikum," in: "sulhan" and "al-sulh," and in: "jami'" and "jami'an." And repetition in: the word "women," and in the word "orphans," and "the orphans and His Messenger," and the word "the Book," and in "believed then disbelieved," and in "the hypocrites." And simile in: "like the suspended one." And a word that admits of two opposites in: ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ [al-Nisa: 127]. And metaphor in: "nushuzan," and in: ﴿and souls are presented to stinginess﴾ [al-Nisa: 128], and in: "fa-la tamilu," and in: "qawwamina," and in: ﴿and if you distort or turn away﴾ [al-Nisa: 135], and in: ﴿that He would not forgive them nor guide them to a way﴾ [al-Nisa: 137], and in: "yatarabbasun," and in: "fath min Allah," and in: ﴿did we not gain mastery﴾, and in: "sabilan." All of these are bodily things borrowed for meanings. And antithesis in: ﴿rich or poor﴾ [al-Nisa: 135], and in: ﴿do not follow desire lest you deviate﴾ [al-Nisa: 135], and following desire is deviation; and in "the disbelievers" and "the believers." And specification in: "bi-ma ta'malun khabiran," which specified the action. And iltifat (shift of address) in: ﴿and He has already sent down to you﴾ [al-Nisa: 140], if the address is to the hypocrites. And ellipsis in many places.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 142–143:

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites deceive Allah, but He is the One who deceives them. And when they stand up for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to the people and not remembering Allah except a little.﴾ ﴿Wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those. And whomever Allah leaves astray, you will never find for him a way.﴾ . Al-kasal (laziness): sluggishness, reluctance, and lethargy regarding a thing. It is said: aksala al-rajul, when a man has intercourse and then lassitude overtakes him without his ejaculating. Al-dhabdhabah (wavering): agitation such that one does not remain in one state; this is what Ibn 'Arafah said, and it is hesitation between two matters. Al-Nabigha said:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah has given you a sura, in which every kingdom other than it wavers?⁠﴾

(p-377) Another said:

﴿A phantom for Umm al-Salsabil, and between her and it, a journey of a month for the wavering mail-rider.⁠﴾

With the second dhal kasra. Ibn Jinni said: that is, the anxiety that does not settle. It has been said that its root is al-dhabb (driving away), which is triliteral in origin; it was doubled, so it became dhabbab, then one of the two doubled letters, the second ba', was replaced by dhal, so it became dhabdhab. This is according to the Kufans. As for the Basrans, it is quadriliteral in their view, like dahraja.

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites deceive Allah, but He is the One who deceives them﴾: the explanation of "they deceive Allah" has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqarah. As for "He is the One who deceives them": that is, He inflicts deception upon them, and this is an expression for a punishment which He named by the name of the sin. Their punishment in this world is their humiliation and fear, and in the Hereafter, the torment of Jahannam; this is said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj and others among the exegetes said: this deception is that He, the Exalted, gives this community on the Day of Resurrection a light for every believer or hypocrite; the hypocrites rejoice and think they have been saved. But when they come to the Sirat, the light of every hypocrite is extinguished, and the believers rise up. That is the saying of the hypocrites: "Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light" (57:13), and that is the deception which befalls the hypocrites.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He is the One who deceives them" means that He does to them what the dominant one does in deception: He left them with their blood and property protected in this world, and prepared for them the lowest level of the Fire in the Hereafter, and in the immediate life He did not spare them from disgrace, the descent of might, vengeance, and perpetual terror. The one who deceives (khadi') is one who, when you deceive someone, you overcome him, and you were more deceptive than him. End of quotation. Part of it is borrowed from the words of al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: when He commanded the acceptance of what they showed outwardly, He was deceiving them by that. Maslamah ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nahwi read "khadi'hum" with a sukun on the 'ayn, for lightening, and to find the move from kasra to damma burdensome. This clause is coordinated upon the predicate of "inna" (indeed). Abu al-Baqa' said: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿And when they stand up for prayer, they stand lazily﴾: that is, sluggish, having no energy in it, because they only pray for appearance and as a pretence. The believer should guard himself against this trait for which the hypocrites were blamed, and should approach his prayer with energy, a free heart, and deliberation in performing it, and not hold back from it as the hypocrite does, who prays out of reluctance, not with good will and desire. In every age there have been hypocrites who conceal themselves with Islam and attend the prayers, like the philosophizers present in our time. Some of our scholars alluded to them in a poem he composed, in which he incorporated part of the verse. He said concerning Abu al-Walid Ibn Rushd al-Hafid, and those like him among the philosophizers of Islam:

﴿For the followers of the philosophers is a belief by which they see the dissolving of the Shariah.
They permitted every forbidden prohibition, and considered it lawful for themselves.
They did not ascribe themselves to Islam except to preserve their blood from being shed.
So they commit the abominations with energy, and come to prayer while they are lazy.⁠﴾

Al-Jumhur read "kusala" with a damma on the kaf, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Al-A'raj read "kasala" with a fatha on the kaf, and this is the dialect of Tamim and Asad. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "kaslá" on the pattern of "fa'lá," described with what is said of a singular feminine, in consideration of the group, like the reading: "and you see people as drunk (sukra)".

﴿Showing off to the people﴾: that is, by their prayer they intend showing off and reputation, and that they are Muslims. It is of the pattern of mufa'alah: the one who shows off displays to people his beautifying himself with acts of obedience, while they show him their approval of that deed. It may also be of the pattern fa'ala in the sense of fa'ala, as in ni'mah and na'imah. Abu Zayd related: "the woman looked at the mirror (ra'at al-mir'ah)" when she held it up to see her face. It was also read "yur'ūna" with a damma on the hamza and shadda between the ra' and the waw. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is stronger in meaning than "yurā'ūna," because its meaning is that they cause people to see them, and they display the prayer to them while concealing hypocrisy. Al-Zamakhshari attributed this reading to Ibn Abi Ishaq, (p-378) except that he said he read "yur'awnahum" with a shadda on the hamza, like "yur'awnahum," meaning they let them see their deeds, and show them likewise.

﴿And they do not remember Allah except a little﴾: al-Hasan said: "little," because he was working for other than Allah. Qatadah said something to the effect that it is little because it was not accepted; what Allah rejects, its abundance is little, and what He accepts, its little is abundant. Others said: "little" in relation to their immersion in falsehood and their saying of vain and disbelieving things. Al-Zamakhshari said: "except a little," because they never pray out of the sight of people except what they do openly, and what they do openly is little, because they found no escape from pretending what is not in their hearts, so they did not pretend; or they do not remember Allah with tasbih and tahlil except a little remembrance. It is possible that by the paucity is meant non-existence. End of quotation. It is not permissible to mean by it non-existence, because the exception (istithna') prevents it, and we have refuted this view and that of Ibn 'Atiyyah in this surah. It was said that "little" is because they intended by it the world and its splendour, since "the enjoyment of the world is little." It was also said that there is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: they do not remember the punishment of Allah and His reward except a little, due to their absorption in the world and the dominance of heedlessness over their hearts. The apparent meaning is that the remembrance here is with the tongue, and that they rarely mention Allah, unlike the sincere believer, for the remembrance of Allah the Exalted predominates in his states.

﴿Wavering between that﴾: that is, agitated. Al-Zamakhshari said: Satan and desire made them waver between faith and disbelief, moving between the two in bewilderment, as if they were being driven away from both sides; that is, they are repelled so that they do not settle on one side, as one says: "so-and-so is pelted by the rahawan (winds)." Except that dhabdhabah includes a repetition not present in dhabb: as if the meaning is that whenever he inclines to one side, he is driven away from it. End of quotation. He attributed the wavering to Satan, while the people of the Sunnah say that this life and the wavering only came about through Allah's creation. In a hadith: "The likeness of the hypocrite is the likeness of a goat wandering between two flocks." The reference by "that" is to the two states of disbelief and faith, as the Exalted said: "neither old nor young, but between that" (2:68), that is, between the virgin and the aged.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He indicated it, even though the mention of the apparent did not precede it, because it is implied in the speech, as in: "until it was hidden behind the veil" (38:32) and "everything upon it passes away" (55:26). End of quotation. It is not as he mentioned; rather, there precedes what the reference may properly point to: the two verbal nouns indicated by the mention of the disbelievers and the believers. So it is of the type: "when the foolish one speaks, he runs to him."

Ibn 'Abbas and 'Amr ibn Fa'id read "mudhabdhibina" with a kasra on the second dhal, taking it as an active participle: that is, making themselves or their religion wavering, or with the meaning of mutadhabdhibin, as "salsal" and "tasalsal" have the same meaning. Ubayy read "mutadhabdhibina," an active participle from tadhabdhaba: that is, to be agitated; likewise in the codex of 'Abd Allah. Al-Hasan read "mudhabdhabina" with a fatha on the mim and both dhals. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a rejected reading. End of quotation. Al-Hasan al-Basri is among the most eloquent of people, and his speech is cited as evidence; so his reading should not be rejected, and it has a basis in Arabic, namely that he made the vowel of the mim follow the vowel of the dhal; since they have made the vowel of the mim follow the vowel of the 'ayn of the word, as in "mintin," though there is a separating element between them, it is more fitting to make it follow without a separating element. Likewise they made the vowel of the 'ayn of munfa'il follow the vowel of the lam in the nominative case, so they said "munhadir," and this is more fitting, because the vowel of case-ending is not fixed, unlike the vowel of the dhal. All of this is a justification of an anomalous form. On the assumption that the transmission from al-Hasan is correct, he read with a fatha on the mim. Abu Ja'far read "mudabdibina" with an unpointed dal, as if the meaning is: they were seized at one time by a single path and at another in another path; so they do not continue on one path. The daba is the path, and it is in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "Follow the path of Quraysh and do not separate from the community," and one says: "leave me and my daba," that is, my way and my disposition. The poet said:

﴿Hapless, a babbler, whose eyes rarely close, upon a path like the tethered, hobbled beast.⁠﴾

The position of "mudhabdhabina" is as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "yura'una" or the subject of "wa la yadhkurun." Al-Zamakhshari said: "mudhabdhabina" is either a circumstantial clause from His saying "and do not remember" from the waw of "yura'unahum": that is, they show off to them while not remembering, wavering; or it is in the accusative as a dispraise.

﴿Neither to these nor to those﴾: the intended by one of the two indicated groups are the believers, and by the other the disbelievers. The meaning: they do not hold faith so as to be counted among the believers, nor do they persist in showing disbelief so as to be counted with the disbelievers. "Ila" is connected to an omitted element whose estimate is: not attributed to these nor to those, and this is the position of a circumstantial clause.

﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, you will never find for him a way﴾: that is, you will never find a way to his guidance, or you will never find a way to his guidance.

﴿O you who believe, do not take the disbelievers as allies in place of the believers﴾ (4:144): since this attribute is among the attributes of the hypocrites, and their blame for it has preceded, Allah the Exalted forbade the believers from this attribute. "The Ansar had, among the Banu Qurayzah, foster-relations, alliance and affection, and they said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Whom shall we ally with? He said: 'The Muhajirun.'" Al-Qaffal said: this is a prohibition to the believers against allying with the hypocrites; he says: "I have already made clear to you the characters of these hypocrites, so do not take from them allies," End of quotation. Upon this, are "the disbelievers" here the Jews or the hypocrites? There are two opinions. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His address to the believers includes, by the outward ruling, the hypocrites who manifest faith, and there is gentleness toward them in the wording, and this is what is meant by His saying: "Do you wish to give Allah a clear proof against yourselves?" (4:144). This reconciliation applies only to one who has some touch of the intellect that leads to this state, whereas the sincere believers have no touch of that. What strengthens this approach is His saying: "other than the believers" (4:144); that is, the believers who are knowing and sincere are absent from this alliance. This cannot be said of sincere believers; rather the meaning is: O you who have manifested faith and committed to its requirements. End of quotation. It was said: in the verse there is evidence that disbelievers are not entitled to any guardianship over a Muslim in any way, whether a relative or otherwise, and that one should not seek help from a dhimmi in a matter that involves support and guardianship, as in His saying: "Do not take as intimates those other than yourselves" (3:118). Some scholars disliked appointing a disbeliever as an agent in buying and selling, and giving him money to trade on a profit-sharing basis.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 142–143:

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites deceive Allah, but He is the One who deceives them. And when they stand up for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to the people and not remembering Allah except a little.﴾ ﴿Wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those. And whomever Allah leaves astray, you will never find for him a way.﴾ . Al-kasal (laziness): sluggishness, reluctance, and lethargy regarding a thing. It is said: aksala al-rajul, when a man has intercourse and then lassitude overtakes him without his ejaculating. Al-dhabdhabah (wavering): agitation such that one does not remain in one state; this is what Ibn 'Arafah said, and it is hesitation between two matters. Al-Nabigha said:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah has given you a sura, in which every kingdom other than it wavers?⁠﴾

(p-377) Another said:

﴿A phantom for Umm al-Salsabil, and between her and it, a journey of a month for the wavering mail-rider.⁠﴾

With the second dhal kasra. Ibn Jinni said: that is, the anxiety that does not settle. It has been said that its root is al-dhabb (driving away), which is triliteral in origin; it was doubled, so it became dhabbab, then one of the two doubled letters, the second ba', was replaced by dhal, so it became dhabdhab. This is according to the Kufans. As for the Basrans, it is quadriliteral in their view, like dahraja.

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites deceive Allah, but He is the One who deceives them﴾: the explanation of "they deceive Allah" has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqarah. As for "He is the One who deceives them": that is, He inflicts deception upon them, and this is an expression for a punishment which He named by the name of the sin. Their punishment in this world is their humiliation and fear, and in the Hereafter, the torment of Jahannam; this is said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj and others among the exegetes said: this deception is that He, the Exalted, gives this community on the Day of Resurrection a light for every believer or hypocrite; the hypocrites rejoice and think they have been saved. But when they come to the Sirat, the light of every hypocrite is extinguished, and the believers rise up. That is the saying of the hypocrites: "Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light" (57:13), and that is the deception which befalls the hypocrites.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He is the One who deceives them" means that He does to them what the dominant one does in deception: He left them with their blood and property protected in this world, and prepared for them the lowest level of the Fire in the Hereafter, and in the immediate life He did not spare them from disgrace, the descent of might, vengeance, and perpetual terror. The one who deceives (khadi') is one who, when you deceive someone, you overcome him, and you were more deceptive than him. End of quotation. Part of it is borrowed from the words of al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: when He commanded the acceptance of what they showed outwardly, He was deceiving them by that. Maslamah ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nahwi read "khadi'hum" with a sukun on the 'ayn, for lightening, and to find the move from kasra to damma burdensome. This clause is coordinated upon the predicate of "inna" (indeed). Abu al-Baqa' said: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿And when they stand up for prayer, they stand lazily﴾: that is, sluggish, having no energy in it, because they only pray for appearance and as a pretence. The believer should guard himself against this trait for which the hypocrites were blamed, and should approach his prayer with energy, a free heart, and deliberation in performing it, and not hold back from it as the hypocrite does, who prays out of reluctance, not with good will and desire. In every age there have been hypocrites who conceal themselves with Islam and attend the prayers, like the philosophizers present in our time. Some of our scholars alluded to them in a poem he composed, in which he incorporated part of the verse. He said concerning Abu al-Walid Ibn Rushd al-Hafid, and those like him among the philosophizers of Islam:

﴿For the followers of the philosophers is a belief by which they see the dissolving of the Shariah.
They permitted every forbidden prohibition, and considered it lawful for themselves.
They did not ascribe themselves to Islam except to preserve their blood from being shed.
So they commit the abominations with energy, and come to prayer while they are lazy.⁠﴾

Al-Jumhur read "kusala" with a damma on the kaf, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Al-A'raj read "kasala" with a fatha on the kaf, and this is the dialect of Tamim and Asad. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "kaslá" on the pattern of "fa'lá," described with what is said of a singular feminine, in consideration of the group, like the reading: "and you see people as drunk (sukra)".

﴿Showing off to the people﴾: that is, by their prayer they intend showing off and reputation, and that they are Muslims. It is of the pattern of mufa'alah: the one who shows off displays to people his beautifying himself with acts of obedience, while they show him their approval of that deed. It may also be of the pattern fa'ala in the sense of fa'ala, as in ni'mah and na'imah. Abu Zayd related: "the woman looked at the mirror (ra'at al-mir'ah)" when she held it up to see her face. It was also read "yur'ūna" with a damma on the hamza and shadda between the ra' and the waw. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is stronger in meaning than "yurā'ūna," because its meaning is that they cause people to see them, and they display the prayer to them while concealing hypocrisy. Al-Zamakhshari attributed this reading to Ibn Abi Ishaq, (p-378) except that he said he read "yur'awnahum" with a shadda on the hamza, like "yur'awnahum," meaning they let them see their deeds, and show them likewise.

﴿And they do not remember Allah except a little﴾: al-Hasan said: "little," because he was working for other than Allah. Qatadah said something to the effect that it is little because it was not accepted; what Allah rejects, its abundance is little, and what He accepts, its little is abundant. Others said: "little" in relation to their immersion in falsehood and their saying of vain and disbelieving things. Al-Zamakhshari said: "except a little," because they never pray out of the sight of people except what they do openly, and what they do openly is little, because they found no escape from pretending what is not in their hearts, so they did not pretend; or they do not remember Allah with tasbih and tahlil except a little remembrance. It is possible that by the paucity is meant non-existence. End of quotation. It is not permissible to mean by it non-existence, because the exception (istithna') prevents it, and we have refuted this view and that of Ibn 'Atiyyah in this surah. It was said that "little" is because they intended by it the world and its splendour, since "the enjoyment of the world is little." It was also said that there is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: they do not remember the punishment of Allah and His reward except a little, due to their absorption in the world and the dominance of heedlessness over their hearts. The apparent meaning is that the remembrance here is with the tongue, and that they rarely mention Allah, unlike the sincere believer, for the remembrance of Allah the Exalted predominates in his states.

﴿Wavering between that﴾: that is, agitated. Al-Zamakhshari said: Satan and desire made them waver between faith and disbelief, moving between the two in bewilderment, as if they were being driven away from both sides; that is, they are repelled so that they do not settle on one side, as one says: "so-and-so is pelted by the rahawan (winds)." Except that dhabdhabah includes a repetition not present in dhabb: as if the meaning is that whenever he inclines to one side, he is driven away from it. End of quotation. He attributed the wavering to Satan, while the people of the Sunnah say that this life and the wavering only came about through Allah's creation. In a hadith: "The likeness of the hypocrite is the likeness of a goat wandering between two flocks." The reference by "that" is to the two states of disbelief and faith, as the Exalted said: "neither old nor young, but between that" (2:68), that is, between the virgin and the aged.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He indicated it, even though the mention of the apparent did not precede it, because it is implied in the speech, as in: "until it was hidden behind the veil" (38:32) and "everything upon it passes away" (55:26). End of quotation. It is not as he mentioned; rather, there precedes what the reference may properly point to: the two verbal nouns indicated by the mention of the disbelievers and the believers. So it is of the type: "when the foolish one speaks, he runs to him."

Ibn 'Abbas and 'Amr ibn Fa'id read "mudhabdhibina" with a kasra on the second dhal, taking it as an active participle: that is, making themselves or their religion wavering, or with the meaning of mutadhabdhibin, as "salsal" and "tasalsal" have the same meaning. Ubayy read "mutadhabdhibina," an active participle from tadhabdhaba: that is, to be agitated; likewise in the codex of 'Abd Allah. Al-Hasan read "mudhabdhabina" with a fatha on the mim and both dhals. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a rejected reading. End of quotation. Al-Hasan al-Basri is among the most eloquent of people, and his speech is cited as evidence; so his reading should not be rejected, and it has a basis in Arabic, namely that he made the vowel of the mim follow the vowel of the dhal; since they have made the vowel of the mim follow the vowel of the 'ayn of the word, as in "mintin," though there is a separating element between them, it is more fitting to make it follow without a separating element. All of this is a justification of an anomalous form. On the assumption that the transmission from al-Hasan is correct, he read with a fatha on the mim. The daba is the path, and it is in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "Follow the path of Quraysh and do not separate from the community," and one says: "leave me and my daba," that is, my way and my disposition. The poet said:

﴿Hapless, a babbler, whose eyes rarely close, upon a path like the tethered, hobbled beast.⁠﴾

﴿Neither to these nor to those﴾: the intended by one of the two indicated groups are the believers, and by the other the disbelievers. The meaning: they do not hold faith so as to be counted among the believers, nor do they persist in showing disbelief so as to be counted with the disbelievers. "Ila" is connected to an omitted element whose estimate is: not attributed to these nor to those, and this is the position of a circumstantial clause.

﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, you will never find for him a way﴾: that is, you will never find a way to his guidance, or you will never find a way to his guidance.

﴿O you who believe, do not take the disbelievers as allies in place of the believers﴾ (4:144): since this attribute is among the attributes of the hypocrites, and their blame for it has preceded, Allah the Exalted forbade the believers from this attribute. Upon this, are "the disbelievers" here the Jews or the hypocrites? There are two opinions.
