Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 144–149 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Do you wish to give Allah a clear authority (sulṭān, meaning a manifest proof) against yourselves?﴾ That is, a clear and evident proof, through your allying yourselves with the disbelievers or the hypocrites, according to the view of al-Qaffal. The meaning is: if you ally yourselves with the disbelievers, He will seize you with retribution, and He has a clear proof against you in that, since He has already made their conditions clear to you and forbidden you from allying with them. It was said that sulṭān here means dominion and power. The meaning would then be: He will give them power over you because of your taking the disbelievers as allies. Al-Farra' said: it is used as feminine and as masculine. Some Arabs say: "The sulṭān has decided against you," and "The sulṭān has seized so-and-so." Among the eloquent, the feminine usage is more common, end of quotation. Whoever uses the masculine treats it as proof and argument, and whoever uses the feminine treats it as a hujjah (argument). The masculine was chosen here in the description, even though the feminine is more common, because the description falls at the end of the verse as a closing rhyme (fāṣilah). This is what favors the masculine over the feminine. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the masculine is more well known and is the language of the Qur'an wherever it occurs, and this contradicts what al-Farra' said. When the title is applied to the holder of the authority, it is by omission of a noun (ḥadhf muḍāf), and the estimated phrase is: "the possessor of authority," that is, the possessor of argument over people, since he is their manager and the one who looks after their interests and benefits. Al-Zamakhshari said: Do not imitate the hypocrites in taking the Jews and others among the enemies of Islam as allies. Sulṭān means a clear argument, meaning that allying with the disbelievers is a clear proof against the hypocrites. It is reported from Sa'sa'ah ibn Sawhan that he said to a nephew of his: "Be sincere to the believer, and deal courteously with the disbeliever and the wicked. The wicked will be content with you for good conduct, and it is incumbent upon you to be sincere to the believer."

﴿Indeed the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: the darak (depth) for the people of the Fire is like the darajah (degree) for the people of Paradise, except that the degrees are above one another, while the depths are below one another, end of quotation. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the darakāt are the layers, and their origin is from idrāk (overtaking), that is, they follow one another and are closely linked. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah said: they are coffins of iron hanging in the bottom of Hell. The Fire has seven depths. It was said that the first of them is Jahannam, then Laẓā, then al-Ḥuṭamah, then al-Sa'īr, then Saqar, then al-Jaḥīm, then al-Hāwiyah. All of them may be called by the name of the first layer, and some layers by the names of others, because the word "Fire" includes them all. Ibn 'Umar said: the most severely punished people on the Day of Resurrection are the hypocrites, and those who disbelieved among the People of the Table and the family of Pharaoh. Confirmation of this in the Book of Allah is this verse concerning the hypocrites, and ﴿I shall punish him with a punishment I shall not inflict upon anyone among the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 115], and ﴿Make the family of Pharaoh enter the most severe punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. The hypocrite is more severely punished than the other disbelievers because he is like them in disbelief, and he adds to disbelief the mockery of Islam and its people, the duplicity, and the disclosure of the secrets of the Muslims to the disbelievers. Thus he is more dangerous than the disbelievers and more capable of harming the Muslims.

The two Ḥaramis (the readers of Mecca and Medina) and the two Arab readers read ﴿fī al-darki﴾ with a fatḥah on the rā'. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash, and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read it with a sukūn on it, and this is reported differently from 'Asim. Al-A'mash and al-Barjamī narrated the fatḥah, and others narrated the sukūn. Abu 'Ali said: they are two dialects, like (الشَّمْعِ) and (الشَّمَعِ) (al-sham' and al-shama', both meaning "wax"). Some preferred the fatḥah because they say in the plural adrāk, like jamal and ajmāl (camel and camels), meaning that the pattern faʿal and afʿāl is regular, while the pattern faʿl is not regular. 'Asim said: if it were with a fatḥah, it would have been said al-suflā (the lowest, feminine). Some of them said: 'Asim held that the fatḥah is only as the plural of darakah, like baqarah and baqar (cow and cattle), end of quotation. What he mentioned about the feminine does not necessarily follow, because a collective noun whose singular takes the feminine ending (tā' marbūṭah) is feminine in the dialect of the Ḥijāz and masculine in the dialect of Tamīm and Najd, and the Qur'an has come with both, except where it is fixed as feminine or masculine. Darakah and darak are not among these. Accordingly, it is permissible to make darak masculine and feminine.

﴿And you will not find for them a helper.﴾ That is, one who prevents them from punishment, nor an intercessor who intercedes for them.

﴿Except those who repent, make amends, hold fast to Allah, and make their religion sincerely for Allah. Those are with the believers.﴾ That is: they repent from hypocrisy, reform their deeds, and hold fast to Allah and His Book, having no refuge or shelter except Allah, and they make their religion sincerely for Allah, that is, they seek by their acts of obedience nothing but the Face of Allah, the Exalted. Since the hypocrite is characterized by the defects of these attributes, namely disbelief, corrupt deeds, allying with the disbelievers, taking pride in them, and showing off before the believers, He made the condition of their repentance something opposed to those attributes, which is repentance from hypocrisy. This is the attribute that, in meaning, contains the rest of the attributes. Then He detailed what was summarized in it: reforming the future deeds in contrast to the corruption of their past deeds, then holding fast to Allah in the future, which is the opposite of allying with the disbelievers and relying on them in the past, then sincerity to the religion of Allah, which is the opposite of the showing-off they had in the past. Then, after the attainment of all these attributes, He pointed to them by saying that they are "with the believers." He did not judge them to be believers, nor among the believers, although they had become believers, in order to repel them from what they had been upon of the great disbelief of hypocrisy, and to honor the state of whoever was clothed with it. The meaning of "with the believers" is: their companions and associates in both abodes. The phrase ﴿those who repent﴾ is an exception from His saying ﴿in the lowest depth﴾. It was said it is an exception from His saying ﴿you will not find for them﴾ [al-Isra': 97]. It was also said it is in the nominative as a subject, with the predicate being ﴿then those﴾. Al-Ḥawfī said: the fa' entered because the speech carries a meaning of a condition connected to "those who."

﴿And Allah will soon give the believers a great reward.﴾ He used (سَوْفَ) (sawfa, "soon") because the giving of the reward is on the Day of Resurrection, a time in the future that is not near to the present time. They have said that (سَوْفَ) is more emphatic in deferral than the sīn. The pronoun did not return to them, so that it would be said "and He will give them," but rather He made that reward exclusively for the believers, and they are their companions, so they share in it and have a portion of it. The word (يُؤْتِ) was written in the Muṣḥaf without a yā', because when it was deleted in pronunciation to avoid the meeting of two unvocalized letters, it was also deleted in writing, and there are similar cases in the Qur'an. Ya'qub stopped on it with the yā', and the seven readers stopped without the yā', following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf. Stopping with the yā' has been narrated from Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Nafi'. Abu 'Amr said: it should not be stopped upon, because if one stops without the yā', one opposes the grammarians, and if one stops with the yā', one opposes the wording of the Muṣḥaf. The great reward is eternal dwelling in Paradise.

﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are thankful and believe?﴾ The address was said to be to the believers, and it was said to be to the disbelievers, and this is what the context of the speech requires. This is an interrogative whose meaning is negation, that is: He does not punish you if you are thankful and believe. The meaning is that there is no benefit for Him in that, nor any need, because punishment is only for something whose benefit returns or whose harm is averted from the one punished, and Allah, the Exalted, is far above that. His punishment of the evildoer is for a matter that His wisdom, the Exalted, has decreed. Whoever is thankful to Him and believes in Him, He does not punish.

The (ما) is interrogative, as we mentioned, in a position of accusative governed by a verb. The estimated meaning is: "What thing does Allah do with your punishment?" The (بِ) is for causation, whether seeking healing, enjoying the fire, bringing benefit, or repelling harm, and He, the Exalted, is far above all that. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that (ما) be negative, and said: the meaning is "He does not punish you." According to his view, the (بِ) would be superfluous, and the response of the condition would be omitted and indicated by what precedes it, that is: "If you are thankful and believe, then He will not do anything with your punishment."

It was mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant by thankfulness here is the affirmation of Allah's oneness (tawḥīd). Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why did He place thankfulness before faith? I say: because the rational person looks at the great blessing upon him in his creation and in his being exposed to benefits, so he gives thanks in a general way. When his reflection leads him to know the Benefactor, he believes in Him, and then he gives detailed thanks. Thus thankfulness precedes faith, and it is the basis and the axis of obligation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: true thankfulness is only accompanied by faith, but He mentioned faith for emphasis and to draw attention to its great standing, end of quotation. Those who went furthest astray said that it is by inversion and displacement, that is: "If you believe and are thankful."

﴿And Allah is Ever Thankful, All-Knowing.﴾ "Thankful" means: He rewards and fully pays your rewards. He used the description of thankfulness in the form of the active participle without intensification, to indicate that He accepts even the smallest deed and multiplies it. "All-Knowing" means He knows your thankfulness and your faith, so He recompenses you. In His saying "All-Knowing" there is a warning and an exhortation to sincerity to Allah, the Exalted. It was said that thankfulness from Allah is the continuation of blessings upon the one who is thankful.

[p-380] [p-381]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 144–149 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged.﴾ Mujahid said: A man was a guest of a people, and they treated him poorly. He complained about them, and he was rebuked, so this was revealed. Muqatil said: "A man insulted Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, while the Messenger (ﷺ) was present. Abu Bakr remained silent toward him several times, then responded to him. The Messenger (ﷺ) stood up. Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he insulted me and you said nothing, but when I responded to him you stood up.' He said: 'An angel was answering on your behalf, and when you responded to him, the angel left and the Shaytan came.'" So this was revealed. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the conditions of the hypocrites, their blameworthy qualities, and the exposure of their disgrace, and made clear their injustice and their oppression of the side of the believers, He here permitted the believers to remind them of the blameworthy qualities they possess. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Mention the wicked person for what is in him, so that people may beware of him."

The majority read ﴿مَن ظُلِمَ﴾ (man zulima, "one who has been wronged") in the passive form (mabni lil-maf'ul, the passive voice). Ibn Abbas and others said: "Except one who has been wronged, for he has the right to invoke (Allah) against the one who wronged him, and that is a concession from Allah to him; but if he is patient, that is better for him." Al-Hasan said: He should not invoke (Allah) against him, but let him say: "O Allah, help me against him. O Allah, extract my right. O Allah, prevent him from what he intends of my wronging." Ibn Jurayj said: He repays him with the like of his action and does not exceed it. It was also said: it means that he begins with insult and then responds to the one who insulted him. The statement of Mujahid has already preceded, that the verse concerns the guest who complains of the host's bad treatment toward him, and that this is attributed to injustice because it contradicts the Shari'ah and proper conduct.

Al-Munir said: Its meaning is: except one who is compelled to utter evil speech, such as disbelief or the like; that is permissible, and the verse concerns compulsion. This exception is connected (istithna' muttasil), on the assumption of an omitted noun (mudaf): i.e., "except the public utterance of one who has been wronged." It was also said that the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati', an exception whose excluded item does not belong to the category of what precedes it), and the sense is: "But the one who has been wronged has the right to obtain justice from his wrongdoer with what equals his injustice." This was said by al-Suddi, al-Hasan, and others.

﴿بِالسُّوءِ﴾ (bi-l-su') is linked to ﴿بِالجَهْرِ﴾ (bi-l-jahr, "the public utterance"), and it is a verbal noun (masdar) defined by the article al-, and its agent is omitted; ﴿بِالجَهْرِ﴾ is in the accusative position. Whoever permits the intention that this verbal noun be built for the object whose agent is not named (the passive) assumes that ﴿بِالسُّوءِ﴾ is in the nominative position. The sense is: "that it be uttered publicly in the passive voice, the agent not being named."

Some scholars allowed that ﴿مَن ظُلِمَ﴾ may be a substitute (badal, the grammatical substitute of a noun for a preceding one) for that omitted agent, with the sense: "No one, except the one who has been wronged." This is the view of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' permitted, in the construction "What stood except Zayd," that Zayd be a substitute for "one" (ahad). But according to the view of the majority, it is an exception whose verb is left without its object (al-mustathna alladhi faragha lahu al-'amil), so it is in the nominative case as the agent of the verbal noun. What makes this acceptable is that ﴿الجَهْرُ﴾ (al-jahr) falls within the scope of negation, as if it were said: "No one utters evil speech publicly except the one who has been wronged."

Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Ibn Jubayr, Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, al-Dahhak, Zayd ibn Aslam, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Muslim ibn Yasar, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, Qatada, and Abu Raja' read ﴿مَن ظَلَمَ﴾ (man zalama, "one who wronged") in the active voice, and this is a disconnected exception. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted it: "Because the wrongdoer commits what Allah does not love, so he utters evil speech publicly." Ibn Zayd said: The meaning is: "except one who wrongs in an action or a speech, so openly speak to him with evil speech," in the sense of forbidding his action, rebuking him, and responding to him. He said: That is because when Allah informed about the hypocrites that they are in the lowest level of the Fire, that was a report of evil speech. Then He said to them afterward: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment?﴾ and what follows, in the sense of establishing a fact and inviting them to gratitude and faith. Then He said to the believers: ﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech, except one who wrongs﴾ in his persistence in hypocrisy; for one may say to him: "Are you not the hypocrite, the unbeliever, for whom there is in the Hereafter the lowest level?" and similar statements.

Others said: its implied sense is: "But whoever is wronged, he utters evil speech publicly, and he is a wrongdoer in that." So in this disconnected exception there are three possible interpretations:
1. It refers to the first clause, "does not love": as if it were said, "But the wrongdoer loves the public utterance of evil speech, so he does it."
2. It refers to the agent of the public utterance: i.e., "Allah does not love that anyone utter evil speech publicly, but the wrongdoer utters evil speech publicly."
3. It refers to the omitted complement of the public utterance: i.e., "If any of you utters evil speech publicly to someone, then but whoever wrongs, you may utter evil speech publicly to him."

Ibn Atiyya said: The grammatical analysis of ﴿مَن﴾ (man) allows, in some of these interpretations, the accusative, and it allows the nominative as a substitute for the presumed ﴿أحد﴾ (ahad, "anyone"). End of quotation. By "ahad" presumed in the verbal noun he means that the sense is: "If anyone utters..." But what he mentioned, that the nominative as a substitute is permissible, is not correct. The disconnected exception is of two kinds. One kind permits a substitute, namely where the governing verb can be directed toward it, as in: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." Here a substitute is permitted in the dialect of Tamim, and the accusative as a disconnected exception is used in the dialect of the Hijaz. The substitute is permitted here because if you said, "There is in the house only a donkey," the meaning would be correct. The other kind requires the accusative as an exception and does not permit a substitute, namely where the governing verb cannot be directed toward it, as in: "The wealth increased only in loss." The sense: "But loss came to him." Here it is not possible for "increased" to apply to "loss," because if you said, "The wealth increased only the loss," the meaning would not be correct. The verse belongs to this second kind, because if you said, "Allah does not love that anyone utter evil speech publicly except the wrongdoer," then "utter" would be left without an object, and "the wrongdoer" could not be governed by it, and the meaning would not be correct.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ﴿مَن﴾ be in the nominative, as if it were said, "Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech except the wrongdoer," according to the dialect of one who says, "No one came to me except 'Amr," meaning, "No one came to me except 'Amr." From it is the verse: ﴿No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ (al-Naml 27:65). End of quotation.

What al-Zamakhshari permitted cannot be accepted, because it is not possible for the agent to be mentioned as superfluous, meaningless addition, and it is not possible for "the wrongdoer" to be a substitute for "Allah," nor "'Amr" a substitute for "Zayd." This is because the substitute in this construction returns in meaning to being a substitute of a part from a whole, either in the literal sense, as in: "No one of the people stood except Zayd," or in the figurative sense, as in: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." The substitute mentioned cannot apply here either in the literal or the figurative sense, because Allah is a proper name (alam), and so is Zayd; therefore it is not possible to imagine a generality in them, so that "the wrongdoer" would be a substitute for "Allah" and "'Amr" a substitute for "Zayd." What is permitted as a substitute in a disconnected exception is one in which a generality can be imagined in the preceding part, which is why the substitution is valid figuratively, even though what follows is not literally a part of what it excludes.

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "according to the dialect of one who says, 'No one came to me except 'Amr,'" we do not know of this dialect, except that in the book of Sibawayh, after he cited verses of the disconnected exception, the last of which is the saying of the poet:

"On the evening when spears cannot replace it, nor arrows, except the polished Indian sword."

Sibawayh's text reads: "This strengthens: 'No one came to me except 'Amr,' and 'Their brothers did not help him except his brothers,' because they are definite nouns, and the latter nouns are neither of them nor from them." End of Sibawayh's words. He did not state, nor even hint, that his saying "No one came to me except 'Amr" is from the speech of the Arabs. It was said that it is from the commentary on Sibawayh; so this strengthens "No one came to me except 'Amr," i.e., this should be established as part of their speech, because "arrows" is a definite noun, and it is not "the polished sword," just as Zayd is not 'Amr, and just as the brothers of Zayd are not your brothers. End of quotation. The example "No one came to me except 'Amr" is not a parallel to the verse of poetry, because in the poem a generality can be imagined in a figurative sense, as if it were said, "Weapons cannot replace it, except the polished sword," whereas in "No one came to me except 'Amr," no generality can be imagined at all in "No one came to me." Moreover, if this were heard from the speech of the Arabs, it would have to be interpreted so that the substitution is valid, so that it would be correct to say "No one came to me, nor anyone else, except 'Amr." The existence of this disconnected exception seems to indicate the omission of the conjunction; either it is because of the elimination of this agent and its addition, or because 'Amr is a substitute for Zayd. But neither is permitted, for the reason we have mentioned.

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "and of it is: ﴿Say: No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ (al-Naml 27:65)," it is not of the category mentioned, because it is possible that ﴿مَن﴾ (man) is the object and ﴿الغَيْبَ﴾ (al-ghayb, "the unseen") is a substitute of the kind called "substitution of inclusion" (badal ishtimal, where the substitute is part of the meaning of the first noun but not a part of it physically); i.e., "No one knows the unseen of those in the heavens and the earth except Allah," meaning what they conceal and hide, no one knows except Allah. And even if we grant that ﴿مَن﴾ is in the nominative, it is permissible that Allah be a substitute for ﴿مَن﴾ in the figurative sense regarding ﴿مَن﴾, because ﴿مَن فِي السَّماواتِ﴾ (man fi al-samawat, "those in the heavens") allows a generality to be imagined in it, as if it were said: "Say: No one knows what exists apart from the unseen except Allah." Or it is in the figurative sense of place as regards Allah, exalted is He, and this is why such expressions come from Him in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth﴾ (al-An'am 6:3), and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the One who is in the heaven a god, and in the earth a god﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:84). And in the hadith: "Where is Allah?" She said: "In the heaven." And from the speech of the Arabs: "No, by the One whose house is in the heaven," meaning Allah, exalted is He.

When the verse allows these aspects, it is not necessary to take it as meaning what has been mentioned. He singled out the public utterance for mention, either to present it in the form of an absent party, or to content Himself with the public utterance in place of its opposite, or because it is more shameful.

﴿And Allah is ever All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾: i.e., All-Hearing of what is publicly uttered of evil, All-Knowing of what is concealed of it. It was said: All-Hearing of the speech of the one wronged, All-Knowing of the wrongdoer. It was said: All-Hearing of the complaint of the one wronged, All-Knowing of the outcome for the wrongdoer, or All-Knowing of what is in the heart of the one wronged; so let him fear Allah and say only the truth. This sentence is a declarative statement, and its meaning is a threat and a warning.

﴿If you disclose good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, All-Powerful﴾: The apparent sense is that the pronoun in ﴿تُخْفُوهُ﴾ (tukhfuhu, "conceal it") refers to ﴿خَيْرًا﴾ (khayran, "good"). Ibn Abbas said: He means acts of righteousness such as fasting and charity. Some said: the pronoun in ﴿تُخْفُوهُ﴾ refers to ﴿السُّوءِ﴾ (al-su', "evil"). The meaning is: when Allah permitted the public utterance of evil for one who was wronged, He said to him and to his kind: "If you disclose good, in place of evil, or conceal evil, or pardon an evil." So pardon is better, though what is not pardoned is also permitted. He mentioned disclosing good and concealing it as a means toward that pardon, then joined pardon to them, to draw attention to its rank and to give it significance, even though it falls within disclosing good and concealing it. So He made it a separate category by conjunction, not a counterpart, out of concern for it. For this reason, He, glorified is He, attributed the quality of pardon and power to Himself, so that His example may be followed and one may take on something of His attributes. The meaning is: He pardons the offender while having the power to take revenge, and He is described with both qualities in an emphatic manner, to alert that the servant should increase in pardon while having much power to take revenge. In the authentic hadith: "Whoever suppresses anger while he is able to act upon it, Allah will fill his heart with security and faith." And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who restrain anger and pardon people﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:134). Al-Hasan said: The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, pardons the offenders while having the power to take revenge, so you should pardon. Al-Kalbi said: Its meaning is that I am more able to pardon your sins than you are to pardon your companion. It was also said: Pardoning toward one who pardons, and All-Powerful to deliver reward to him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 144–149 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Do you wish to give Allah a clear authority (sulṭān, meaning a manifest proof) against yourselves?﴾ That is, a clear and evident proof, through your allying yourselves with the disbelievers or the hypocrites, according to the view of al-Qaffal. The meaning is: if you ally yourselves with the disbelievers, He will seize you with retribution, and He has a clear proof against you in that, since He has already made their conditions clear to you and forbidden you from allying with them. It was said that sulṭān here means dominion and power. The meaning would then be: He will give them power over you because of your taking the disbelievers as allies. Al-Farra' said: it is used as feminine and as masculine. Some Arabs say: "The sulṭān has decided against you," and "The sulṭān has seized so-and-so." Among the eloquent, the feminine usage is more common, end of quotation. Whoever uses the masculine treats it as proof and argument, and whoever uses the feminine treats it as a hujjah (argument). The masculine was chosen here in the description, even though the feminine is more common, because the description falls at the end of the verse as a closing rhyme (fāṣilah). This is what favors the masculine over the feminine. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the masculine is more well known and is the language of the Qur'an wherever it occurs, and this contradicts what al-Farra' said. When the title is applied to the holder of the authority, it is by omission of a noun (ḥadhf muḍāf), and the estimated phrase is: "the possessor of authority," that is, the possessor of argument over people, since he is their manager and the one who looks after their interests and benefits. Al-Zamakhshari said: Do not imitate the hypocrites in taking the Jews and others among the enemies of Islam as allies. Sulṭān means a clear argument, meaning that allying with the disbelievers is a clear proof against the hypocrites. It is reported from Sa'sa'ah ibn Sawhan that he said to a nephew of his: "Be sincere to the believer, and deal courteously with the disbeliever and the wicked. The wicked will be content with you for good conduct, and it is incumbent upon you to be sincere to the believer."

﴿Indeed the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: the darak (depth) for the people of the Fire is like the darajah (degree) for the people of Paradise, except that the degrees are above one another, while the depths are below one another, end of quotation. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the darakāt are the layers, and their origin is from idrāk (overtaking), that is, they follow one another and are closely linked. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah said: they are coffins of iron hanging in the bottom of Hell. The Fire has seven depths. It was said that the first of them is Jahannam, then Laẓā, then al-Ḥuṭamah, then al-Sa'īr, then Saqar, then al-Jaḥīm, then al-Hāwiyah. All of them may be called by the name of the first layer, and some layers by the names of others, because the word "Fire" includes them all. Ibn 'Umar said: the most severely punished people on the Day of Resurrection are the hypocrites, and those who disbelieved among the People of the Table and the family of Pharaoh. Confirmation of this in the Book of Allah is this verse concerning the hypocrites, and ﴿I shall punish him with a punishment I shall not inflict upon anyone among the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 115], and ﴿Make the family of Pharaoh enter the most severe punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. The hypocrite is more severely punished than the other disbelievers because he is like them in disbelief, and he adds to disbelief the mockery of Islam and its people, the duplicity, and the disclosure of the secrets of the Muslims to the disbelievers. Thus he is more dangerous than the disbelievers and more capable of harming the Muslims.

The two Ḥaramis (the readers of Mecca and Medina) and the two Arab readers read ﴿fī al-darki﴾ with a fatḥah on the rā'. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash, and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read it with a sukūn on it, and this is reported differently from 'Asim. Al-A'mash and al-Barjamī narrated the fatḥah, and others narrated the sukūn. Abu 'Ali said: they are two dialects, like (الشَّمْعِ) and (الشَّمَعِ) (al-sham' and al-shama', both meaning "wax"). Some preferred the fatḥah because they say in the plural adrāk, like jamal and ajmāl (camel and camels), meaning that the pattern faʿal and afʿāl is regular, while the pattern faʿl is not regular. 'Asim said: if it were with a fatḥah, it would have been said al-suflā (the lowest, feminine). Some of them said: 'Asim held that the fatḥah is only as the plural of darakah, like baqarah and baqar (cow and cattle), end of quotation. What he mentioned about the feminine does not necessarily follow, because a collective noun whose singular takes the feminine ending (tā' marbūṭah) is feminine in the dialect of the Ḥijāz and masculine in the dialect of Tamīm and Najd, and the Qur'an has come with both, except where it is fixed as feminine or masculine. Darakah and darak are not among these. Accordingly, it is permissible to make darak masculine and feminine.

﴿And you will not find for them a helper.﴾ That is, one who prevents them from punishment, nor an intercessor who intercedes for them.

﴿Except those who repent, make amends, hold fast to Allah, and make their religion sincerely for Allah. Those are with the believers.﴾ That is: they repent from hypocrisy, reform their deeds, and hold fast to Allah and His Book, having no refuge or shelter except Allah, and they make their religion sincerely for Allah, that is, they seek by their acts of obedience nothing but the Face of Allah, the Exalted. Since the hypocrite is characterized by the defects of these attributes, namely disbelief, corrupt deeds, allying with the disbelievers, taking pride in them, and showing off before the believers, He made the condition of their repentance something opposed to those attributes, which is repentance from hypocrisy. This is the attribute that, in meaning, contains the rest of the attributes. Then He detailed what was summarized in it: reforming the future deeds in contrast to the corruption of their past deeds, then holding fast to Allah in the future, which is the opposite of allying with the disbelievers and relying on them in the past, then sincerity to the religion of Allah, which is the opposite of the showing-off they had in the past. Then, after the attainment of all these attributes, He pointed to them by saying that they are "with the believers." He did not judge them to be believers, nor among the believers, although they had become believers, in order to repel them from what they had been upon of the great disbelief of hypocrisy, and to honor the state of whoever was clothed with it. The meaning of "with the believers" is: their companions and associates in both abodes. The phrase ﴿those who repent﴾ is an exception from His saying ﴿in the lowest depth﴾. It was said it is an exception from His saying ﴿you will not find for them﴾ [al-Isra': 97]. It was also said it is in the nominative as a subject, with the predicate being ﴿then those﴾. Al-Ḥawfī said: the fa' entered because the speech carries a meaning of a condition connected to "those who."

﴿And Allah will soon give the believers a great reward.﴾ He used (سَوْفَ) (sawfa, "soon") because the giving of the reward is on the Day of Resurrection, a time in the future that is not near to the present time. They have said that (سَوْفَ) is more emphatic in deferral than the sīn. The pronoun did not return to them, so that it would be said "and He will give them," but rather He made that reward exclusively for the believers, and they are their companions, so they share in it and have a portion of it. The word (يُؤْتِ) was written in the Muṣḥaf without a yā', because when it was deleted in pronunciation to avoid the meeting of two unvocalized letters, it was also deleted in writing, and there are similar cases in the Qur'an. Ya'qub stopped on it with the yā', and the seven readers stopped without the yā', following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf. Stopping with the yā' has been narrated from Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Nafi'. Abu 'Amr said: it should not be stopped upon, because if one stops without the yā', one opposes the grammarians, and if one stops with the yā', one opposes the wording of the Muṣḥaf. The great reward is eternal dwelling in Paradise.

﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are thankful and believe?﴾ The address was said to be to the believers, and it was said to be to the disbelievers, and this is what the context of the speech requires. This is an interrogative whose meaning is negation, that is: He does not punish you if you are thankful and believe. The meaning is that there is no benefit for Him in that, nor any need, because punishment is only for something whose benefit returns or whose harm is averted from the one punished, and Allah, the Exalted, is far above that. His punishment of the evildoer is for a matter that His wisdom, the Exalted, has decreed. Whoever is thankful to Him and believes in Him, He does not punish.

The (ما) is interrogative, as we mentioned, in a position of accusative governed by a verb. The estimated meaning is: "What thing does Allah do with your punishment?" The (بِ) is for causation, whether seeking healing, enjoying the fire, bringing benefit, or repelling harm, and He, the Exalted, is far above all that. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that (ما) be negative, and said: the meaning is "He does not punish you." According to his view, the (بِ) would be superfluous, and the response of the condition would be omitted and indicated by what precedes it, that is: "If you are thankful and believe, then He will not do anything with your punishment."

It was mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant by thankfulness here is the affirmation of Allah's oneness (tawḥīd). Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why did He place thankfulness before faith? I say: because the rational person looks at the great blessing upon him in his creation and in his being exposed to benefits, so he gives thanks in a general way. When his reflection leads him to know the Benefactor, he believes in Him, and then he gives detailed thanks. Thus thankfulness precedes faith, and it is the basis and the axis of obligation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: true thankfulness is only accompanied by faith, but He mentioned faith for emphasis and to draw attention to its great standing, end of quotation. Those who went furthest astray said that it is by inversion and displacement, that is: "If you believe and are thankful."

﴿And Allah is Ever Thankful, All-Knowing.﴾ "Thankful" means: He rewards and fully pays your rewards. He used the description of thankfulness in the form of the active participle without intensification, to indicate that He accepts even the smallest deed and multiplies it. "All-Knowing" means He knows your thankfulness and your faith, so He recompenses you. In His saying "All-Knowing" there is a warning and an exhortation to sincerity to Allah, the Exalted. It was said that thankfulness from Allah is the continuation of blessings upon the one who is thankful.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 144–149 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged.﴾ Mujahid said: A man was a guest of a people, and they treated him poorly. He complained about them, and he was rebuked, so this was revealed. Muqatil said: "A man insulted Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, while the Messenger (ﷺ) was present. Abu Bakr remained silent toward him several times, then responded to him. The Messenger (ﷺ) stood up. Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he insulted me and you said nothing, but when I responded to him you stood up.' He said: 'An angel was answering on your behalf, and when you responded to him, the angel left and the Shaytan came.'" So this was revealed. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the conditions of the hypocrites, their blameworthy qualities, and the exposure of their disgrace, and made clear their injustice and their oppression of the side of the believers, He here permitted the believers to remind them of the blameworthy qualities they possess. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Mention the wicked person for what is in him, so that people may beware of him."

The majority read ﴿مَن ظُلِمَ﴾ (man zulima, "one who has been wronged") in the passive form (mabni lil-maf'ul, the passive voice). Ibn Abbas and others said: "Except one who has been wronged, for he has the right to invoke (Allah) against the one who wronged him, and that is a concession from Allah to him; but if he is patient, that is better for him." Al-Hasan said: He should not invoke (Allah) against him, but let him say: "O Allah, help me against him. O Allah, extract my right. O Allah, prevent him from what he intends of my wronging." Ibn Jurayj said: He repays him with the like of his action and does not exceed it. It was also said: it means that he begins with insult and then responds to the one who insulted him. The statement of Mujahid has already preceded, that the verse concerns the guest who complains of the host's bad treatment toward him, and that this is attributed to injustice because it contradicts the Shari'ah and proper conduct.

Al-Munir said: Its meaning is: except one who is compelled to utter evil speech, such as disbelief or the like; that is permissible, and the verse concerns compulsion. This exception is connected (istithna' muttasil), on the assumption of an omitted noun (mudaf): i.e., "except the public utterance of one who has been wronged." It was also said that the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati', an exception whose excluded item does not belong to the category of what precedes it), and the sense is: "But the one who has been wronged has the right to obtain justice from his wrongdoer with what equals his injustice." This was said by al-Suddi, al-Hasan, and others.

﴿بِالسُّوءِ﴾ (bi-l-su') is linked to ﴿بِالجَهْرِ﴾ (bi-l-jahr, "the public utterance"), and it is a verbal noun (masdar) defined by the article al-, and its agent is omitted; ﴿بِالجَهْرِ﴾ is in the accusative position. Whoever permits the intention that this verbal noun be built for the object whose agent is not named (the passive) assumes that ﴿بِالسُّوءِ﴾ is in the nominative position. The sense is: "that it be uttered publicly in the passive voice, the agent not being named."

Some scholars allowed that ﴿مَن ظُلِمَ﴾ may be a substitute (badal, the grammatical substitute of a noun for a preceding one) for that omitted agent, with the sense: "No one, except the one who has been wronged." This is the view of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' permitted, in the construction "What stood except Zayd," that Zayd be a substitute for "one" (ahad). But according to the view of the majority, it is an exception whose verb is left without its object (al-mustathna alladhi faragha lahu al-'amil), so it is in the nominative case as the agent of the verbal noun. What makes this acceptable is that ﴿الجَهْرُ﴾ (al-jahr) falls within the scope of negation, as if it were said: "No one utters evil speech publicly except the one who has been wronged."

Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Ibn Jubayr, Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, al-Dahhak, Zayd ibn Aslam, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Muslim ibn Yasar, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, Qatada, and Abu Raja' read ﴿مَن ظَلَمَ﴾ (man zalama, "one who wronged") in the active voice, and this is a disconnected exception. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted it: "Because the wrongdoer commits what Allah does not love, so he utters evil speech publicly." Ibn Zayd said: The meaning is: "except one who wrongs in an action or a speech, so openly speak to him with evil speech," in the sense of forbidding his action, rebuking him, and responding to him. He said: That is because when Allah informed about the hypocrites that they are in the lowest level of the Fire, that was a report of evil speech. Then He said to them afterward: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment?﴾ and what follows, in the sense of establishing a fact and inviting them to gratitude and faith. Then He said to the believers: ﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech, except one who wrongs﴾ in his persistence in hypocrisy; for one may say to him: "Are you not the hypocrite, the unbeliever, for whom there is in the Hereafter the lowest level?" and similar statements.

Others said: its implied sense is: "But whoever is wronged, he utters evil speech publicly, and he is a wrongdoer in that." So in this disconnected exception there are three possible interpretations:
1. It refers to the first clause, "does not love": as if it were said, "But the wrongdoer loves the public utterance of evil speech, so he does it."
2. It refers to the agent of the public utterance: i.e., "Allah does not love that anyone utter evil speech publicly, but the wrongdoer utters evil speech publicly."
3. It refers to the omitted complement of the public utterance: i.e., "If any of you utters evil speech publicly to someone, then but whoever wrongs, you may utter evil speech publicly to him."

Ibn Atiyya said: The grammatical analysis of ﴿مَن﴾ (man) allows, in some of these interpretations, the accusative, and it allows the nominative as a substitute for the presumed ﴿أحد﴾ (ahad, "anyone"). End of quotation. By "ahad" presumed in the verbal noun he means that the sense is: "If anyone utters..." But what he mentioned, that the nominative as a substitute is permissible, is not correct. The disconnected exception is of two kinds. One kind permits a substitute, namely where the governing verb can be directed toward it, as in: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." Here a substitute is permitted in the dialect of Tamim, and the accusative as a disconnected exception is used in the dialect of the Hijaz. The substitute is permitted here because if you said, "There is in the house only a donkey," the meaning would be correct. The other kind requires the accusative as an exception and does not permit a substitute, namely where the governing verb cannot be directed toward it, as in: "The wealth increased only in loss." The sense: "But loss came to him." Here it is not possible for "increased" to apply to "loss," because if you said, "The wealth increased only the loss," the meaning would not be correct. The verse belongs to this second kind, because if you said, "Allah does not love that anyone utter evil speech publicly except the wrongdoer," then "utter" would be left without an object, and "the wrongdoer" could not be governed by it, and the meaning would not be correct.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ﴿مَن﴾ be in the nominative, as if it were said, "Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech except the wrongdoer," according to the dialect of one who says, "No one came to me except 'Amr," meaning, "No one came to me except 'Amr." From it is the verse: ﴿No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ (al-Naml 27:65). End of quotation.

What al-Zamakhshari permitted cannot be accepted, because it is not possible for the agent to be mentioned as superfluous, meaningless addition, and it is not possible for "the wrongdoer" to be a substitute for "Allah," nor "'Amr" a substitute for "Zayd." This is because the substitute in this construction returns in meaning to being a substitute of a part from a whole, either in the literal sense, as in: "No one of the people stood except Zayd," or in the figurative sense, as in: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." The substitute mentioned cannot apply here either in the literal or the figurative sense, because Allah is a proper name (alam), and so is Zayd; therefore it is not possible to imagine a generality in them, so that "the wrongdoer" would be a substitute for "Allah" and "'Amr" a substitute for "Zayd." What is permitted as a substitute in a disconnected exception is one in which a generality can be imagined in the preceding part, which is why the substitution is valid figuratively, even though what follows is not literally a part of what it excludes.

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "according to the dialect of one who says, 'No one came to me except 'Amr,'" we do not know of this dialect, except that in the book of Sibawayh, after he cited verses of the disconnected exception, the last of which is the saying of the poet:

"On the evening when spears cannot replace it, nor arrows, except the polished Indian sword."

Sibawayh's text reads: "This strengthens: 'No one came to me except 'Amr,' and 'Their brothers did not help him except his brothers,' because they are definite nouns, and the latter nouns are neither of them nor from them." End of Sibawayh's words. He did not state, nor even hint, that his saying "No one came to me except 'Amr" is from the speech of the Arabs. It was said that it is from the commentary on Sibawayh; so this strengthens "No one came to me except 'Amr," i.e., this should be established as part of their speech, because "arrows" is a definite noun, and it is not "the polished sword," just as Zayd is not 'Amr, and just as the brothers of Zayd are not your brothers. End of quotation. The example "No one came to me except 'Amr" is not a parallel to the verse of poetry, because in the poem a generality can be imagined in a figurative sense, as if it were said, "Weapons cannot replace it, except the polished sword," whereas in "No one came to me except 'Amr," no generality can be imagined at all in "No one came to me." Moreover, if this were heard from the speech of the Arabs, it would have to be interpreted so that the substitution is valid, so that it would be correct to say "No one came to me, nor anyone else, except 'Amr." The existence of this disconnected exception seems to indicate the omission of the conjunction; either it is because of the elimination of this agent and its addition, or because 'Amr is a substitute for Zayd. But neither is permitted, for the reason we have mentioned.

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "and of it is: ﴿Say: No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ (al-Naml 27:65)," it is not of the category mentioned, because it is possible that ﴿مَن﴾ (man) is the object and ﴿الغَيْبَ﴾ (al-ghayb, "the unseen") is a substitute of the kind called "substitution of inclusion" (badal ishtimal, where the substitute is part of the meaning of the first noun but not a part of it physically); i.e., "No one knows the unseen of those in the heavens and the earth except Allah," meaning what they conceal and hide, no one knows except Allah. And even if we grant that ﴿مَن﴾ is in the nominative, it is permissible that Allah be a substitute for ﴿مَن﴾ in the figurative sense regarding ﴿مَن﴾, because ﴿مَن فِي السَّماواتِ﴾ (man fi al-samawat, "those in the heavens") allows a generality to be imagined in it, as if it were said: "Say: No one knows what exists apart from the unseen except Allah." Or it is in the figurative sense of place as regards Allah, exalted is He, and this is why such expressions come from Him in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth﴾ (al-An'am 6:3), and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the One who is in the heaven a god, and in the earth a god﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:84). And in the hadith: "Where is Allah?" She said: "In the heaven." And from the speech of the Arabs: "No, by the One whose house is in the heaven," meaning Allah, exalted is He.

When the verse allows these aspects, it is not necessary to take it as meaning what has been mentioned. He singled out the public utterance for mention, either to present it in the form of an absent party, or to content Himself with the public utterance in place of its opposite, or because it is more shameful.

﴿And Allah is ever All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾: i.e., All-Hearing of what is publicly uttered of evil, All-Knowing of what is concealed of it. It was said: All-Hearing of the speech of the one wronged, All-Knowing of the wrongdoer. It was said: All-Hearing of the complaint of the one wronged, All-Knowing of the outcome for the wrongdoer, or All-Knowing of what is in the heart of the one wronged; so let him fear Allah and say only the truth. This sentence is a declarative statement, and its meaning is a threat and a warning.

﴿If you disclose good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, All-Powerful﴾: The apparent sense is that the pronoun in ﴿تُخْفُوهُ﴾ (tukhfuhu, "conceal it") refers to ﴿خَيْرًا﴾ (khayran, "good"). Ibn Abbas said: He means acts of righteousness such as fasting and charity. Some said: the pronoun in ﴿تُخْفُوهُ﴾ refers to ﴿السُّوءِ﴾ (al-su', "evil"). The meaning is: when Allah permitted the public utterance of evil for one who was wronged, He said to him and to his kind: "If you disclose good, in place of evil, or conceal evil, or pardon an evil." So pardon is better, though what is not pardoned is also permitted. He mentioned disclosing good and concealing it as a means toward that pardon, then joined pardon to them, to draw attention to its rank and to give it significance, even though it falls within disclosing good and concealing it. So He made it a separate category by conjunction, not a counterpart, out of concern for it. For this reason, He, glorified is He, attributed the quality of pardon and power to Himself, so that His example may be followed and one may take on something of His attributes. The meaning is: He pardons the offender while having the power to take revenge, and He is described with both qualities in an emphatic manner, to alert that the servant should increase in pardon while having much power to take revenge. In the authentic hadith: "Whoever suppresses anger while he is able to act upon it, Allah will fill his heart with security and faith." And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who restrain anger and pardon people﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:134). Al-Hasan said: The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, pardons the offenders while having the power to take revenge, so you should pardon. Al-Kalbi said: Its meaning is that I am more able to pardon your sins than you are to pardon your companion. It was also said: Pardoning toward one who pardons, and All-Powerful to deliver reward to him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 144–149 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Do you wish to give Allah a clear authority (sulṭān, meaning a manifest proof) against yourselves?﴾ That is, a clear and evident proof, through your allying yourselves with the disbelievers or the hypocrites, according to the view of al-Qaffal. The meaning is: if you ally yourselves with the disbelievers, He will seize you with retribution, and He has a clear proof against you in that, since He has already made their conditions clear to you and forbidden you from allying with them. It was said that sulṭān here means dominion and power. The meaning would then be: He will give them power over you because of your taking the disbelievers as allies. Al-Farra' said: it is used as feminine and as masculine. Some Arabs say: "The sulṭān has decided against you," and "The sulṭān has seized so-and-so." Among the eloquent, the feminine usage is more common, end of quotation. Whoever uses the masculine treats it as proof and argument, and whoever uses the feminine treats it as a hujjah (argument). The masculine was chosen here in the description, even though the feminine is more common, because the description falls at the end of the verse as a closing rhyme (fāṣilah). This is what favors the masculine over the feminine. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the masculine is more well known and is the language of the Qur'an wherever it occurs, and this contradicts what al-Farra' said. When the title is applied to the holder of the authority, it is by omission of a noun (ḥadhf muḍāf), and the estimated phrase is: "the possessor of authority," that is, the possessor of argument over people, since he is their manager and the one who looks after their interests and benefits. Al-Zamakhshari said: Do not imitate the hypocrites in taking the Jews and others among the enemies of Islam as allies. Sulṭān means a clear argument, meaning that allying with the disbelievers is a clear proof against the hypocrites. It is reported from Sa'sa'ah ibn Sawhan that he said to a nephew of his: "Be sincere to the believer, and deal courteously with the disbeliever and the wicked. The wicked will be content with you for good conduct, and it is incumbent upon you to be sincere to the believer."

﴿Indeed the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: the darak (depth) for the people of the Fire is like the darajah (degree) for the people of Paradise, except that the degrees are above one another, while the depths are below one another, end of quotation. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the darakāt are the layers, and their origin is from idrāk (overtaking), that is, they follow one another and are closely linked. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah said: they are coffins of iron hanging in the bottom of Hell. The Fire has seven depths. It was said that the first of them is Jahannam, then Laẓā, then al-Ḥuṭamah, then al-Sa'īr, then Saqar, then al-Jaḥīm, then al-Hāwiyah. All of them may be called by the name of the first layer, and some layers by the names of others, because the word "Fire" includes them all. Ibn 'Umar said: the most severely punished people on the Day of Resurrection are the hypocrites, and those who disbelieved among the People of the Table and the family of Pharaoh. Confirmation of this in the Book of Allah is this verse concerning the hypocrites, and ﴿I shall punish him with a punishment I shall not inflict upon anyone among the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 115], and ﴿Make the family of Pharaoh enter the most severe punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. The hypocrite is more severely punished than the other disbelievers because he is like them in disbelief, and he adds to disbelief the mockery of Islam and its people, the duplicity, and the disclosure of the secrets of the Muslims to the disbelievers. Thus he is more dangerous than the disbelievers and more capable of harming the Muslims.

The two Ḥaramis (the readers of Mecca and Medina) and the two Arab readers read ﴿fī al-darki﴾ with a fatḥah on the rā'. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash, and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read it with a sukūn on it, and this is reported differently from 'Asim. Al-A'mash and al-Barjamī narrated the fatḥah, and others narrated the sukūn. Abu 'Ali said: they are two dialects, like (الشَّمْعِ) and (الشَّمَعِ) (al-sham' and al-shama', both meaning "wax"). Some preferred the fatḥah because they say in the plural adrāk, like jamal and ajmāl (camel and camels), meaning that the pattern faʿal and afʿāl is regular, while the pattern faʿl is not regular. 'Asim said: if it were with a fatḥah, it would have been said al-suflā (the lowest, feminine). Some of them said: 'Asim held that the fatḥah is only as the plural of darakah, like baqarah and baqar (cow and cattle), end of quotation. What he mentioned about the feminine does not necessarily follow, because a collective noun whose singular takes the feminine ending (tā' marbūṭah) is feminine in the dialect of the Ḥijāz and masculine in the dialect of Tamīm and Najd, and the Qur'an has come with both, except where it is fixed as feminine or masculine. Darakah and darak are not among these. Accordingly, it is permissible to make darak masculine and feminine.

﴿And you will not find for them a helper.﴾ That is, one who prevents them from punishment, nor an intercessor who intercedes for them.

﴿Except those who repent, make amends, hold fast to Allah, and make their religion sincerely for Allah. Those are with the believers.﴾ That is: they repent from hypocrisy, reform their deeds, and hold fast to Allah and His Book, having no refuge or shelter except Allah, and they make their religion sincerely for Allah, that is, they seek by their acts of obedience nothing but the Face of Allah, the Exalted. Since the hypocrite is characterized by the defects of these attributes, namely disbelief, corrupt deeds, allying with the disbelievers, taking pride in them, and showing off before the believers, He made the condition of their repentance something opposed to those attributes, which is repentance from hypocrisy. This is the attribute that, in meaning, contains the rest of the attributes. Then He detailed what was summarized in it: reforming the future deeds in contrast to the corruption of their past deeds, then holding fast to Allah in the future, which is the opposite of allying with the disbelievers and relying on them in the past, then sincerity to the religion of Allah, which is the opposite of the showing-off they had in the past. Then, after the attainment of all these attributes, He pointed to them by saying that they are "with the believers." He did not judge them to be believers, nor among the believers, although they had become believers, in order to repel them from what they had been upon of the great disbelief of hypocrisy, and to honor the state of whoever was clothed with it. The meaning of "with the believers" is: their companions and associates in both abodes. The phrase ﴿those who repent﴾ is an exception from His saying ﴿in the lowest depth﴾. It was said it is an exception from His saying ﴿you will not find for them﴾ [al-Isra': 97]. It was also said it is in the nominative as a subject, with the predicate being ﴿then those﴾. Al-Ḥawfī said: the fa' entered because the speech carries a meaning of a condition connected to "those who."

﴿And Allah will soon give the believers a great reward.﴾ He used (سَوْفَ) (sawfa, "soon") because the giving of the reward is on the Day of Resurrection, a time in the future that is not near to the present time. They have said that (سَوْفَ) is more emphatic in deferral than the sīn. The pronoun did not return to them, so that it would be said "and He will give them," but rather He made that reward exclusively for the believers, and they are their companions, so they share in it and have a portion of it. The word (يُؤْتِ) was written in the Muṣḥaf without a yā', because when it was deleted in pronunciation to avoid the meeting of two unvocalized letters, it was also deleted in writing, and there are similar cases in the Qur'an. Ya'qub stopped on it with the yā', and the seven readers stopped without the yā', following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf. Stopping with the yā' has been narrated from Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Nafi'. Abu 'Amr said: it should not be stopped upon, because if one stops without the yā', one opposes the grammarians, and if one stops with the yā', one opposes the wording of the Muṣḥaf. The great reward is eternal dwelling in Paradise.

﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are thankful and believe?﴾ The address was said to be to the believers, and it was said to be to the disbelievers, and this is what the context of the speech requires. This is an interrogative whose meaning is negation, that is: He does not punish you if you are thankful and believe. The meaning is that there is no benefit for Him in that, nor any need, because punishment is only for something whose benefit returns or whose harm is averted from the one punished, and Allah, the Exalted, is far above that. His punishment of the evildoer is for a matter that His wisdom, the Exalted, has decreed. Whoever is thankful to Him and believes in Him, He does not punish.

The (ما) is interrogative, as we mentioned, in a position of accusative governed by a verb. The estimated meaning is: "What thing does Allah do with your punishment?" The (بِ) is for causation, whether seeking healing, enjoying the fire, bringing benefit, or repelling harm, and He, the Exalted, is far above all that. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that (ما) be negative, and said: the meaning is "He does not punish you." According to his view, the (بِ) would be superfluous, and the response of the condition would be omitted and indicated by what precedes it, that is: "If you are thankful and believe, then He will not do anything with your punishment."

It was mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant by thankfulness here is the affirmation of Allah's oneness (tawḥīd). Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why did He place thankfulness before faith? I say: because the rational person looks at the great blessing upon him in his creation and in his being exposed to benefits, so he gives thanks in a general way. When his reflection leads him to know the Benefactor, he believes in Him, and then he gives detailed thanks. Thus thankfulness precedes faith, and it is the basis and the axis of obligation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: true thankfulness is only accompanied by faith, but He mentioned faith for emphasis and to draw attention to its great standing, end of quotation. Those who went furthest astray said that it is by inversion and displacement, that is: "If you believe and are thankful."

﴿And Allah is Ever Thankful, All-Knowing.﴾ "Thankful" means: He rewards and fully pays your rewards. He used the description of thankfulness in the form of the active participle without intensification, to indicate that He accepts even the smallest deed and multiplies it. "All-Knowing" means He knows your thankfulness and your faith, so He recompenses you. In His saying "All-Knowing" there is a warning and an exhortation to sincerity to Allah, the Exalted. It was said that thankfulness from Allah is the continuation of blessings upon the one who is thankful.

[p-380] [p-381]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 144–149 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged.﴾ Mujahid said: A man was a guest of a people, and they treated him poorly. He complained about them, and he was rebuked, so this was revealed. Muqatil said: "A man insulted Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, while the Messenger (ﷺ) was present. Abu Bakr remained silent toward him several times, then responded to him. The Messenger (ﷺ) stood up. Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he insulted me and you said nothing, but when I responded to him you stood up.' He said: 'An angel was answering on your behalf, and when you responded to him, the angel left and the Shaytan came.'" So this was revealed. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the conditions of the hypocrites, their blameworthy qualities, and the exposure of their disgrace, and made clear their injustice and their oppression of the side of the believers, He here permitted the believers to remind them of the blameworthy qualities they possess. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Mention the wicked person for what is in him, so that people may beware of him."

The majority read ﴿مَن ظُلِمَ﴾ (man zulima, "one who has been wronged") in the passive form (mabni lil-maf'ul, the passive voice). Ibn Abbas and others said: "Except one who has been wronged, for he has the right to invoke (Allah) against the one who wronged him, and that is a concession from Allah to him; but if he is patient, that is better for him." Al-Hasan said: He should not invoke (Allah) against him, but let him say: "O Allah, help me against him. O Allah, extract my right. O Allah, prevent him from what he intends of my wronging." Ibn Jurayj said: He repays him with the like of his action and does not exceed it. It was also said: it means that he begins with insult and then responds to the one who insulted him. The statement of Mujahid has already preceded, that the verse concerns the guest who complains of the host's bad treatment toward him, and that this is attributed to injustice because it contradicts the Shari'ah and proper conduct.

Al-Munir said: Its meaning is: except one who is compelled to utter evil speech, such as disbelief or the like; that is permissible, and the verse concerns compulsion. This exception is connected (istithna' muttasil), on the assumption of an omitted noun (mudaf): i.e., "except the public utterance of one who has been wronged." It was also said that the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati', an exception whose excluded item does not belong to the category of what precedes it), and the sense is: "But the one who has been wronged has the right to obtain justice from his wrongdoer with what equals his injustice." This was said by al-Suddi, al-Hasan, and others.

﴿بِالسُّوءِ﴾ (bi-l-su') is linked to ﴿بِالجَهْرِ﴾ (bi-l-jahr, "the public utterance"), and it is a verbal noun (masdar) defined by the article al-, and its agent is omitted; ﴿بِالجَهْرِ﴾ is in the accusative position. Whoever permits the intention that this verbal noun be built for the object whose agent is not named (the passive) assumes that ﴿بِالسُّوءِ﴾ is in the nominative position. The sense is: "that it be uttered publicly in the passive voice, the agent not being named."

Some scholars allowed that ﴿مَن ظُلِمَ﴾ may be a substitute (badal, the grammatical substitute of a noun for a preceding one) for that omitted agent, with the sense: "No one, except the one who has been wronged." This is the view of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' permitted, in the construction "What stood except Zayd," that Zayd be a substitute for "one" (ahad). But according to the view of the majority, it is an exception whose verb is left without its object (al-mustathna alladhi faragha lahu al-'amil), so it is in the nominative case as the agent of the verbal noun. What makes this acceptable is that ﴿الجَهْرُ﴾ (al-jahr) falls within the scope of negation, as if it were said: "No one utters evil speech publicly except the one who has been wronged."

Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Ibn Jubayr, Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, al-Dahhak, Zayd ibn Aslam, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Muslim ibn Yasar, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, Qatada, and Abu Raja' read ﴿مَن ظَلَمَ﴾ (man zalama, "one who wronged") in the active voice, and this is a disconnected exception. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted it: "Because the wrongdoer commits what Allah does not love, so he utters evil speech publicly." Ibn Zayd said: The meaning is: "except one who wrongs in an action or a speech, so openly speak to him with evil speech," in the sense of forbidding his action, rebuking him, and responding to him. He said: That is because when Allah informed about the hypocrites that they are in the lowest level of the Fire, that was a report of evil speech. Then He said to them afterward: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment?﴾ and what follows, in the sense of establishing a fact and inviting them to gratitude and faith. Then He said to the believers: ﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech, except one who wrongs﴾ in his persistence in hypocrisy; for one may say to him: "Are you not the hypocrite, the unbeliever, for whom there is in the Hereafter the lowest level?" and similar statements.

Others said: its implied sense is: "But whoever is wronged, he utters evil speech publicly, and he is a wrongdoer in that." So in this disconnected exception there are three possible interpretations:
1. It refers to the first clause, "does not love": as if it were said, "But the wrongdoer loves the public utterance of evil speech, so he does it."
2. It refers to the agent of the public utterance: i.e., "Allah does not love that anyone utter evil speech publicly, but the wrongdoer utters evil speech publicly."
3. It refers to the omitted complement of the public utterance: i.e., "If any of you utters evil speech publicly to someone, then but whoever wrongs, you may utter evil speech publicly to him."

Ibn Atiyya said: The grammatical analysis of ﴿مَن﴾ (man) allows, in some of these interpretations, the accusative, and it allows the nominative as a substitute for the presumed ﴿أحد﴾ (ahad, "anyone"). End of quotation. By "ahad" presumed in the verbal noun he means that the sense is: "If anyone utters..." But what he mentioned, that the nominative as a substitute is permissible, is not correct. The disconnected exception is of two kinds. One kind permits a substitute, namely where the governing verb can be directed toward it, as in: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." Here a substitute is permitted in the dialect of Tamim, and the accusative as a disconnected exception is used in the dialect of the Hijaz. The substitute is permitted here because if you said, "There is in the house only a donkey," the meaning would be correct. The other kind requires the accusative as an exception and does not permit a substitute, namely where the governing verb cannot be directed toward it, as in: "The wealth increased only in loss." The sense: "But loss came to him." Here it is not possible for "increased" to apply to "loss," because if you said, "The wealth increased only the loss," the meaning would not be correct. The verse belongs to this second kind, because if you said, "Allah does not love that anyone utter evil speech publicly except the wrongdoer," then "utter" would be left without an object, and "the wrongdoer" could not be governed by it, and the meaning would not be correct.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ﴿مَن﴾ be in the nominative, as if it were said, "Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech except the wrongdoer," according to the dialect of one who says, "No one came to me except 'Amr," meaning, "No one came to me except 'Amr." From it is the verse: ﴿No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ (al-Naml 27:65). End of quotation.

What al-Zamakhshari permitted cannot be accepted, because it is not possible for the agent to be mentioned as superfluous, meaningless addition, and it is not possible for "the wrongdoer" to be a substitute for "Allah," nor "'Amr" a substitute for "Zayd." This is because the substitute in this construction returns in meaning to being a substitute of a part from a whole, either in the literal sense, as in: "No one of the people stood except Zayd," or in the figurative sense, as in: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." The substitute mentioned cannot apply here either in the literal or the figurative sense, because Allah is a proper name (alam), and so is Zayd; therefore it is not possible to imagine a generality in them, so that "the wrongdoer" would be a substitute for "Allah" and "'Amr" a substitute for "Zayd." What is permitted as a substitute in a disconnected exception is one in which a generality can be imagined in the preceding part, which is why the substitution is valid figuratively, even though what follows is not literally a part of what it excludes.

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "according to the dialect of one who says, 'No one came to me except 'Amr,'" we do not know of this dialect, except that in the book of Sibawayh, after he cited verses of the disconnected exception, the last of which is the saying of the poet:

"On the evening when spears cannot replace it, nor arrows, except the polished Indian sword."

Sibawayh's text reads: "This strengthens: 'No one came to me except 'Amr,' and 'Their brothers did not help him except his brothers,' because they are definite nouns, and the latter nouns are neither of them nor from them." End of Sibawayh's words. He did not state, nor even hint, that his saying "No one came to me except 'Amr" is from the speech of the Arabs. It was said that it is from the commentary on Sibawayh; so this strengthens "No one came to me except 'Amr," i.e., this should be established as part of their speech, because "arrows" is a definite noun, and it is not "the polished sword," just as Zayd is not 'Amr, and just as the brothers of Zayd are not your brothers. End of quotation. The example "No one came to me except 'Amr" is not a parallel to the verse of poetry, because in the poem a generality can be imagined in a figurative sense, as if it were said, "Weapons cannot replace it, except the polished sword," whereas in "No one came to me except 'Amr," no generality can be imagined at all in "No one came to me." Moreover, if this were heard from the speech of the Arabs, it would have to be interpreted so that the substitution is valid, so that it would be correct to say "No one came to me, nor anyone else, except 'Amr." The existence of this disconnected exception seems to indicate the omission of the conjunction; either it is because of the elimination of this agent and its addition, or because 'Amr is a substitute for Zayd. But neither is permitted, for the reason we have mentioned.

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "and of it is: ﴿Say: No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ (al-Naml 27:65)," it is not of the category mentioned, because it is possible that ﴿مَن﴾ (man) is the object and ﴿الغَيْبَ﴾ (al-ghayb, "the unseen") is a substitute of the kind called "substitution of inclusion" (badal ishtimal, where the substitute is part of the meaning of the first noun but not a part of it physically); i.e., "No one knows the unseen of those in the heavens and the earth except Allah," meaning what they conceal and hide, no one knows except Allah. And even if we grant that ﴿مَن﴾ is in the nominative, it is permissible that Allah be a substitute for ﴿مَن﴾ in the figurative sense regarding ﴿مَن﴾, because ﴿مَن فِي السَّماواتِ﴾ (man fi al-samawat, "those in the heavens") allows a generality to be imagined in it, as if it were said: "Say: No one knows what exists apart from the unseen except Allah." Or it is in the figurative sense of place as regards Allah, exalted is He, and this is why such expressions come from Him in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth﴾ (al-An'am 6:3), and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the One who is in the heaven a god, and in the earth a god﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:84). And in the hadith: "Where is Allah?" She said: "In the heaven." And from the speech of the Arabs: "No, by the One whose house is in the heaven," meaning Allah, exalted is He.

When the verse allows these aspects, it is not necessary to take it as meaning what has been mentioned. He singled out the public utterance for mention, either to present it in the form of an absent party, or to content Himself with the public utterance in place of its opposite, or because it is more shameful.

﴿And Allah is ever All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾: i.e., All-Hearing of what is publicly uttered of evil, All-Knowing of what is concealed of it. It was said: All-Hearing of the speech of the one wronged, All-Knowing of the wrongdoer. It was said: All-Hearing of the complaint of the one wronged, All-Knowing of the outcome for the wrongdoer, or All-Knowing of what is in the heart of the one wronged; so let him fear Allah and say only the truth. This sentence is a declarative statement, and its meaning is a threat and a warning.

﴿If you disclose good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, All-Powerful﴾: The apparent sense is that the pronoun in ﴿تُخْفُوهُ﴾ (tukhfuhu, "conceal it") refers to ﴿خَيْرًا﴾ (khayran, "good"). Ibn Abbas said: He means acts of righteousness such as fasting and charity. Some said: the pronoun in ﴿تُخْفُوهُ﴾ refers to ﴿السُّوءِ﴾ (al-su', "evil"). The meaning is: when Allah permitted the public utterance of evil for one who was wronged, He said to him and to his kind: "If you disclose good, in place of evil, or conceal evil, or pardon an evil." So pardon is better, though what is not pardoned is also permitted. He mentioned disclosing good and concealing it as a means toward that pardon, then joined pardon to them, to draw attention to its rank and to give it significance, even though it falls within disclosing good and concealing it. So He made it a separate category by conjunction, not a counterpart, out of concern for it. For this reason, He, glorified is He, attributed the quality of pardon and power to Himself, so that His example may be followed and one may take on something of His attributes. The meaning is: He pardons the offender while having the power to take revenge, and He is described with both qualities in an emphatic manner, to alert that the servant should increase in pardon while having much power to take revenge. In the authentic hadith: "Whoever suppresses anger while he is able to act upon it, Allah will fill his heart with security and faith." And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who restrain anger and pardon people﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:134). Al-Hasan said: The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, pardons the offenders while having the power to take revenge, so you should pardon. Al-Kalbi said: Its meaning is that I am more able to pardon your sins than you are to pardon your companion. It was also said: Pardoning toward one who pardons, and All-Powerful to deliver reward to him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 144–149 (part 1 of 2):
