It is in *ghulf* ("uncircumcised" or "covered") and ﴿Rather, Allah has sealed it﴾ [al-Nisa: 155]. There is the addition of a particle for a meaning in *fa-bima naqdihim* ("so for their breaking").

There is the attribution of a verb to other than its doer, in ﴿so the thunderbolt seized them﴾ and ﴿clear proofs came to them﴾, and to one who approves of the act, in *wa-qatlihim al-anbiya'* ("and their killing of the prophets"), in ﴿and their saying against Mary a tremendous slander﴾, and in ﴿and their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah"﴾. There is good sequencing (*husn al-nasaq*) in *fa-bima naqdihim mithaqahum* ("so for their breaking their covenant") and in the conjoined terms that follow it, since they are linked with *waw*, which indicates only joint occurrence. Between these matters there are widely separated eras, yet their earlier and later generations are associated because the deeds of the former and the approval of the latter are the same. There is synecdoche (*itlaq ism kull 'ala ba'd*, the use of the name of a whole for a part) in their disbelief in ﴿the signs of Allah﴾, meaning the Qur'an and the Gospel. They did not disbelieve in any of the books except these two. It is also in their saying "Indeed, we killed," though only some of them said it. There is *ta'rid* (indirect reference) in *rasul Allah* ("the Messenger of Allah"), if we say that it is part of their speech. There is *tawjih* (grammatical versatility) in *ghulf*, since it may be a verbal noun, or the plural of *ghilaf* ("covering"), or the plural of *aghlaf*. There is the return of a pronoun to an unmentioned referent, in ﴿they will surely believe in him before his death﴾, according to those who take the pronouns to refer to something other than Jesus. There is *naql* (transfer) from the pattern *fa'il* to *fa'il*'s derived form *fa'il* in *shahid* ("witness"). There is ellipsis (*hadhf*) in several places.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 150–159 (part 1 of 4):**

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers﴾. Al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Juraij said: it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in Musa (Moses) and the Torah, and disbelieved in ʿIsa (Jesus) and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. The Christians believed in ʿIsa and the Injil (Gospel), and disbelieved in Muhammad and the Qur'an. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the Jews specifically: they believed in Musa, ʿUzayr and the Torah, and disbelieved in ʿIsa and the Injil, and in Muhammad and the Qur'an. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah had explained the bad character and blameworthy conduct of the hypocrites, He began to speak about the Jews and the Christians. He made their disbelief in some of the messengers a disbelief in all of the messengers, and their disbelief in the messengers a disbelief in Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And they wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers﴾: that is, they wish to separate belief in Allah from belief in His messengers. They say, "We believe in Allah, but we do not believe in so-and-so and so-and-so of the prophets."

﴿And they say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others"﴾: meaning, of the prophets. It was also said that this refers to the Jews' affirmation that Muhammad is a prophet, but only not to the Children of Israel. This is similar to their other divisions, which were out of obstinacy and evasion.

﴿And they wish to adopt a way between that﴾: that is, a middle path between disbelief and belief, though there is no intermediate position between the two.

﴿Those are the disbelievers in truth﴾. He emphasized it with the words "they" (hum), lest it be imagined that such belief would benefit them. He also emphasized it with the word "in truth" (ḥaqqan), which is an emphasis on the content of the declarative sentence, as when you say, "This is the servant of Allah in truth," meaning, "That is indeed the case, in truth." Or it is an adjective to an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a disbelief in truth," i.e., a disbelief that is established and certain, without doubt. Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), according to the view of Sibawayh. Similar examples have been mentioned before. Al-Wahidi criticized this interpretation and said: "Disbelief cannot be true in any way." This objection is not compelling, since it is not meant that ḥaqqan refers to the truth that is the opposite of falsehood; rather, the meaning is that it is a disbelief that is established and certain. The emphasis was used because the call to belief is shared by all the prophets, namely the manifestation of miracles at their hands. Thus their dividing [the prophets] in belief is evidence of their disbelief in all of them, since their belief in some of them did not arise from reflection on the evidence, but was rather by way of whim and trifling.

(And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.) This is a threat to them of humiliation in the punishment.

﴿But those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not make distinction between any of them﴾: these are the believers, the followers of Muhammad. The discussion of the use of (bayn) before (aḥad, "any") has already been covered in al-Baqara, in His words: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqara 2:285], so it is unnecessary to repeat it here.

(Those — We will give them their rewards.) He, exalted is He, explicitly promised these [believers] just as He explicitly threatened those [disbelievers]. Hafs read yu'tīhim with the yāʾ, so that it refers back to the name of Allah mentioned before it. The rest read it with the nūn (nu'tīhim), by way of iltifāt (a shift of grammatical person), and its counterpart is (wa-aʿtadnā, "and We have prepared"). As for the statement of Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi that the reading with nūn is preferable for two reasons, one being that it is more inclusive and the other that it is consistent with His words "and We have prepared," this is not a good argument, and there is no preference in this, because both readings are mutawātir (transmitted by mass transmission), and thus were revealed in this form.

(And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.) When He promised them reward, He added good news of pardon for their misdeeds and of His mercy toward them.

﴿The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down to them a book from the heaven﴾. al-Suddi said: The Jews said, "If you are truthful, then bring a book from the heaven all at once, just as Musa brought the Book." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi said: They said, "Bring tablets in which is your Book, just as Musa brought tablets in which was the Torah." Al-Hasan and Qatada said: They asked him to bring a book specifically for the Jews, commanding them to believe in Muhammad. Ibn Juraij said: They said, "We will not follow you in what you call us to, until you bring us a book from Allah to so-and-so and so-and-so, that you are the messenger of Allah." According to the view of Ibn Juraij, their request was like the request of ʿAbd Allah ibn Umayya al-Zuhri. It was also said that they asked for a book that they could witness until it descended. From among the Jewish questioners, he named Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and Finhas ibn ʿAzura. It was also said that the questioners were the Jews and the Christians, and their question was only by way of obstinacy. Al-Hasan said: If they had asked him in order that the truth might become clear, He would have given it to them, for what He has given you is sufficient.

﴿For they had asked Musa for greater than that, and said, "Show us Allah openly"﴾. Before this they assumed an omitted statement. Al-Zamakhshari made it a conditional clause whose answer is this, and its estimated sense is: "If you consider what they asked of you to be great, then they asked Musa for something greater than that." Ibn ʿAtiyya estimated it as: "So do not be concerned, O Muhammad, about their questioning and their hastiness, for this is their habit; they asked Musa." He attributed the question to them, although it had actually come from their forefathers, the seventy of their chiefs, because they were satisfied with the deeds of their forefathers and their ways, and resembled them in obstinacy. al-Hasan read akthara (greater) with the letter thāʾ (ث) instead of the bāʾ (ب) in the reading of the majority. The meaning of jahratan (openly) is: a direct seeing, manifest and clear. Jahratan is an attribute of the seeing. There is disagreement regarding the transmission from Ibn ʿAbbas. It is reported from him that jahratan is an attribute of the question, i.e., "they asked Musa [openly]." Or it is a circumstantial state of the subject of "they asked," meaning, "they asked him while openly declaring it." It is also reported from him that the estimate is: "They said openly, bluntly, 'Show us Allah,'" so it is an attribute of the saying.

﴿So the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing﴾: that is, for their obstinacy, and for their asking for what they had no right to ask. al-Zamakhshari said: "For their wrongdoing" means because of their asking to see [Allah]. If they had asked for something permissible, they would not have been called wrongdoers, and the thunderbolt would not have seized them. Just as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, asked to be shown the giving of life to the dead, and He did not call him a wrongdoer, nor did He strike him with the thunderbolt for the anthropomorphists, and the striking with thunderbolts [is for them]. End of quote. This is in line with the Muʿtazilite doctrine of the impossibility of seeing Allah according to them. The People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna) believe that they did not ask for something rationally impossible, but it is prohibited by the Law, since Allah, exalted is He, has informed through the tongues of His prophets that He is not seen in this worldly life, while seeing Him in the Hereafter is established from the Messenger through tawātur (mass transmission), and it is rationally possible. The discussion of the thunderbolt (al-ṣāʿiqa) has already been covered in al-Baqara. al-Sulami and al-Nakhaʿi read (fa-akhadhathum al-ṣaʿqa, "the stunning seized them"), while the majority read (al-ṣāʿiqa).

﴿Then they took the calf after the clear proofs had come to them﴾. Thumma ("then") here indicates sequence in the reports, not in the actual order of events. Then, the matter of their taking the calf was indeed after that, meaning that their forefathers, and those who were struck, were not the same as those who took the calf. The clear proofs (al-bayyināt) are the parting of the sea, the staff, the drowning of Pharaoh, and other things. al-Hufi said: He informed His prophet of their obstinacy and persistence. The meaning is: if what they asked for had descended upon them, they would have opposed the command of Allah, just as they opposed Him after Allah had revived them from their stunning, and worshipped the calf and took it as a god.

﴿Then We pardoned them for that﴾: that is, for their taking the calf as a god, and for all that preceded it of their opposition. The first explanation is more apparent, since in the story of the calf repentance was explicitly mentioned. "He" means: by what He tested them with, namely killing themselves, and then pardon was granted to the rest of them.

﴿And We gave Musa a clear authority﴾: that is, proof, domination, and manifest supremacy over them, when he commanded them to kill themselves until they would be forgiven. They obeyed him, sitting down in their courtyards while the swords fell upon them. How great a clear authority that is!

﴿And We raised over them the mount, because of their covenant﴾. What is meant by al-Ṭūr (the mount) has been discussed earlier. In al-Sham (Syria) there is a mountain known as al-Ṭūr, and this name became attached to it; it is the Ṭūr of Sinai. It is not the one that was lifted over the Children of Israel, because the raising of the mountain took place near the wilderness (al-tīh) on the side of the land of Egypt, while they were advancing with Musa, peace be upon him. The story of the raising of the Ṭūr was discussed in al-Baqara. The preposition "bi-" in "because of their covenant" indicates cause, namely the pact that Musa took from them after they had affirmed the Torah, that they would act upon what is in it. They broke their covenant and worshipped the calf, so Allah raised the mountain over them. There is an omitted statement that is estimated as: "because of their breaking of their covenant."

(And We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating.") The explanation of this phrase has been discussed in al-Baqara.

﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath"﴾. It was mentioned earlier when they transgressed, in His words: ﴿And you had already known those of you who transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-Baqara 2:65]. Warsh read (lā taʿaddū) with a fatḥa on the ʿayn and a shadda on the dāl, on the basis that the original was (taʿtadū), so the vowel of the tāʾ was transferred to the ʿayn and the tāʾ was assimilated into the dāl. Qalun read it with the vowel of the ʿayn suppressed and the dāl doubled, and the text (naṣṣ) with sukūn; its original is also (lā taʿtadū). The remaining readers of the seven read (lā taʿdū) with a sukūn on the ʿayn and a lightened dāl, from ʿadā yaʿdū. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-Aʿraf 7:163]. al-Aʿmash and al-Akhfash read (lā taʿtadū), from iʿtadā.

(And We took from them a firm covenant.) It was said that this is the first covenant, in His words "because of their covenant," and it is described as firm for emphasis. It is the one taken through Musa and Harun that they would take the Torah with strength, act upon everything in it, and transmit it to their children. It was also said: this covenant is other than the first, namely the second covenant that was taken from their prophets to affirm and believe in Muhammad. It is the one mentioned in His words: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets, "Whatever Book and wisdom I have given you..."﴾ [Aal ʿImran 3:81], and so on.

﴿So for their breaking of their covenant, and their disbelief in the signs of Allah, and their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying, "Our hearts are wrapped"﴾. Ibn ʿAtiyya, in what we have summarized of his words, said: This is informing about things they committed in opposition to what they were taken to account for. They broke the covenant by which the mountain was raised over them, and they replaced the faith contained in the command to enter the gate prostrating, which includes the humility that is the fruit of faith, with disbelief in the signs of Allah, and with withholding obedience and not complying with His command not to transgress in the Sabbath, the violation of the greatest sacred things, which is the killing of the prophets. They responded to the taking of the firm covenant with their ignorance and their saying, "Our hearts are wrapped," meaning in veils and coverings, so they do not understand. Allah, exalted is He, turned away from their saying and their lying, and informed that He had sealed their hearts because of their disbelief. End of quote. As for the covenant that was broken, was it their concealing of the description of the Messenger and their denial of what he brought, or their abandonment of acting upon what is in their Book, even though they had accepted and committed to acting upon it? There are two views. As for the signs of Allah that they disbelieved in, are they those that were revealed to them in their books, or all the books of Allah that were sent down? There are two views. The explanation of "Our hearts are wrapped" has been discussed in al-Baqara.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 150–159 (part 2 of 4):

﴿Rather, Allah has sealed their hearts because of their disbelief.﴾ Al-Kisa'i and Hamzah assimilated the lam of (bal) into the ta' of (ta-ba'a), while the rest of the Seven Readers made it clear (izhar). Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief﴾ is a statement whose meaning is blame, on the basis that their hearts are like things sealed, which never understand and never obey a messenger. Al-Zamakhshari said: They meant by their saying "Our hearts are wrapped (ghulf)" that Allah created our hearts wrapped, that is, in coverings that cannot be reached by any reminder or admonition, as Allah related about the polytheists: ﴿And they say, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 20]. The Mujbirah (the determinists), may Allah disgrace them, denied this, and it was said to them: Allah forsook them and withheld from them His favors because of their disbelief, so they became like what is sealed over, not that they were created wrapped and capable of receiving the reminder, nor able to accept it. End of quotation. This is in keeping with his Mu'tazili (rationalist) doctrine. As for Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah), they say: Allah truly sealed over them, as He informed, since there is no creator other than Him. The (ba') in ﴿so because of their breaking of their covenant﴾ is connected to an omitted element that al-Zamakhshari estimated as: "We did to them what We did." Ibn 'Atiyyah estimated it as: "We cursed them, humiliated them, and decreed eternal abiding in Hell upon those of them who died in that state." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The omission of the response to this statement is eloquent, left to the listener's understanding. End of quotation. Calling what the prepositional phrase depends upon a "response" (jawab) is a terminology not known in the science of grammar, and language does not support it, because it is not a response. They also permitted that it be connected to the phrase (We made unlawful for them) [Qur'an 4:160], with ﴿so because of an injustice from those who were Jews﴾ [An-Nisa': 160] being a substitute (badal) for ﴿so because of their breaking of their covenant﴾. This was said by al-Zajjaj, Abu Bakr, al-Zamakhshari and others. But this is far-fetched, because of the great distance between the substitute and what it substitutes, and because what is conjoined to a cause is itself a cause; so it would necessitate that some parts of the cause of the prohibition be delayed in time beyond the time of the prohibition, and it would then be impossible for it to be part of a cause or a caused effect except through a distant interpretation. The explanation of that is that their saying "against Mary a tremendous slander" and their saying "Indeed, we killed the Messiah" came later in time than (p. 389) the prohibition of the good things upon them. Therefore the better estimate is: "We cursed them," and this has been stated explicitly in the verse: ﴿So because of their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 13].

(﴿So they do not believe, except a few﴾) The explanation of this clause has already been given, so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿And because of their disbelief and their saying against Mary a tremendous slander﴾ Apparently, in His saying "And because of their disbelief and their saying," it is conjoined to His saying "so because of" and what follows it. Al-Zamakhshari also permitted that His saying ﴿and because of their disbelief and their saying﴾ be conjoined to "because of their disbelief." The repetition of the attribution of disbelief to them is according to its objects: for they disbelieved in Moses, then in Jesus, then in Muhammad (peace be upon him); so He conjoined some of their disbelief to some other. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or He conjoined the whole of the conjoined phrase to the whole of the phrase conjoined to, as if it was said: He gathered them between breaking the covenant, disbelieving in the signs of Allah, killing the prophets, their saying "Our hearts are wrapped," and their combining their disbelief and their slandering of Mary, and their boasting of killing Jesus (peace be upon him): We punished them. Or [it means]: "Rather, Allah sealed over them," and He gathered them between their disbelief and such and such. Al-Zamakhshari also said: If you say, "Why not suppose that the omitted element to which the preposition is attached is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿Rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief﴾?" I say: This estimate is not valid, because His saying "Rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief" is a rejection and denial of their saying "Our hearts are wrapped," so it is connected to that. End of quotation. This is a good answer, but there is another objection that prevents it: the conjunction with "bal" is for turning away from the first judgment and affirming a second in its place, by way of annulling the first, or moving on, as is common in the speech of Allah in reporting. So it is only used for moving on. The second clause conveys what the first clause does not. What al-Zamakhshari estimated does not allow what we have established, because His saying ﴿so because of their breaking their covenant﴾, ﴿and their disbelief in the signs of Allah﴾, and their saying: ﴿"Our hearts are wrapped." Rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief﴾ means the second clause conveys what the first clause conveyed, and this is not permissible. If you say, "Zayd passed by 'Amr, rather Zayd passed by 'Amr," it is not permissible. Abu al-Baqa' permitted this, and his estimate is: "so because of their breaking their covenant and their disbelief in the signs of Allah, and likewise their hearts were sealed over." It was also said the estimate is: "so because of their breaking their covenant, they do not believe except a few," and the (fa') is superfluous (muqhamah). The (ma) in His saying "so because of" is like the (ma) in His saying ﴿so by mercy﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 159], and the discussion of it has already passed. The tremendous slander is their accusing Mary (peace be upon her) of fornication despite their seeing the sign in the speech of Jesus (peace be upon him) in the cradle. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Otherwise, were it not for the sign, they would have been, in their saying, following the judgment of humans in denying a pregnancy without a male. End of quotation. It was described as "tremendous" because they persisted in it after the sign had appeared and the miracle of her innocence had been established. The accusation has been called "a tremendous slander" in His saying: ﴿Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander﴾ [An-Nur: 16].

﴿And their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah."﴾ Apparently "the messenger of Allah" is part of their saying: they said that in mockery, like the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 27], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning﴾ [Hud: 87]. It may also be that it is part of Allah's speech, placing a good mention in place of their ugly mention in relating it, as an elevation of Jesus (peace be upon him), as they used to mention him with it. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned both possibilities, while Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned only the second. He said: It is an information from Allah about the attribute of Jesus (peace be upon him), namely messengership, in order to show the sin of these who admitted to killing him, and the sin was incumbent upon them, though they did not kill Jesus. For they crucified that person thinking he was Jesus, and thinking Jesus was a liar who was not a messenger. But the sin was incumbent upon them because they believed that their killing had fallen upon Jesus; so it was as if they had killed him. Their belief that he was not a messenger does not remove the sin from them.

﴿But they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them.﴾ This is an information from Him, exalted is He, that they did not kill Jesus and did not crucify him.

The narrators differed (p. 390) about the manner of the killing and the crucifixion, and nothing has been established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it beyond what the Qur'an indicates.

The final outcome of Jesus's affair (peace be upon him) was that the Jews sought him, so he and the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) hid in a house. They were guided to him and came at night, and they were thirteen or eighteen. He dispersed them that night and sent them to the regions, and he and a man remained with him. Then Jesus was raised, and his likeness was cast upon the man, and he was crucified. It was said he was the Jew who had guided them to him. It was said he said to his companions: "Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him and be killed, and deliver these people, and he will be my companion in Paradise?" Sarjis said: "I," and the likeness of Jesus was cast upon him. It was said the likeness was cast upon all of them, and when they were brought out, one was missing from the count, so they took one of those upon whom the likeness was, and he was crucified. It is related that the king and those who handled it did not fail to know the matter of Jesus, because of what they saw of the missing from the count and the confusion of the affair; so that person was crucified, and the people were kept away from his cross for days until he changed; and no attribute of his remained. At that point the people approached him, and the disciples went about in the regions saying: "Jesus was crucified." It was said the likeness was not cast upon anyone; rather the meaning of ﴿but it was made to appear so to them﴾ is: the king, the deceiver, made it appear to them so that he would continue with the one missing from the count; he had hurried to crucify one person and kept people away from him, and said: "This is Jesus." This view is the one that should be held concerning His saying ﴿but it was made to appear so to them﴾. As for the likeness being cast upon a person, that has not been validly transmitted from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that one could rely upon it.

It has been differed about upon whom the likeness was cast, in many ways. It was said: the Jew who had guided them. It was said: the successor (khalifah) of Caesar who had been imprisoned with him. It was said: one of the Jews. It was said: he entered in order to kill him. It was said: a watchman whom the Jews had assigned to him. It was said: the likeness was cast upon all the disciples. It was said: the likeness was cast upon the face only, not the body. This uncertainty repels confidence in anything of that. For this reason some of them said: If it is permissible to say that Allah, exalted is He, casts the likeness of one human upon another human, then this opens the door to sophistry (sophistry: al-safsatah, fallacious reasoning). It was said the reason for the Jews' gathering to kill him was that a group of them insulted him and insulted his mother, so he invoked against them: "O Allah, You are my Lord, and by Your word You created me. O Allah, curse whoever insulted me and insulted my mother." So Allah transformed whoever insulted the two of them into monkeys and swine, and the Jews gathered to kill him. ﴿Was made to appear﴾ (shubbiha) has as its subject the prepositional phrase, like His saying: ﴿it was imagined to him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 66], but the resemblance occurred to them. It is permissible that it take as its subject the pronoun of the one killed, indicated by "we killed," i.e., but the one they killed was made to appear to them. It is not permissible that the pronoun refer to the Messiah, because the Messiah is the one likened to, not the one likened.

﴿And indeed, those who differed concerning it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it, except the following of assumption.﴾ The Jews differed about it: some of them said: he was not killed and not crucified; the face was the face of Jesus and the body was the body of another. It was said: they brought in someone to kill him, and the likeness was cast upon him, and he was crucified, and one was missing from the number. They had known the number of the disciples, so they said: If the crucified one is our companion, where is Jesus? And if it is Jesus, where is our companion? It was said: the common people said: "We killed Jesus," and those who witnessed his being raised to heaven said: he was not killed and not crucified. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The certainty that was transmitted by all in agreement from their senses is that a person was crucified, but whether he was Jesus or not is not a matter of the senses; therefore the transmission of it was not unanimous. The pronoun in "concerning it" refers to the killing; its meaning is: concerning his killing, and this is the apparent meaning indicated by what precedes and follows it. It was said the pronoun in "differed" also refers to the Jews, and their difference concerning him is the saying of some of them: he is a god, and the saying of some of them: he is the son of Allah, exalted is He. It was said their difference concerning him is that the Nestorians said: the crucifixion fell upon his humanity (nasut) and not his divinity (lahut). It was said the killing and crucifixion fell upon both. It was said it refers to the Jews and Christians, for the Jews said: he is the son of adultery, and the Christians said: he is the son of Allah. It was said their difference is from the aspect that the Christians said: the Jews killed him and crucified him; and the Jews who witnessed his being raised said: he was raised to heaven. The majority hold that ﴿except the following of assumption﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' munqati'), because the following of assumption is not of the kind of knowledge (p. 391), meaning: but rather they have the following of assumption.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It means: but they follow conjecture (al-zann). This is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis (i'rab)." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), since conjecture and knowledge are both included under beliefs of certainty (ma'taqadat al-yaqin). The one who conjectures may, in a figurative manner, say: 'My knowledge in this matter is that it is such-and-such,' meaning his conjecture." End of quotation. But this is not as he stated, because conjecture is not among the beliefs of certainty, for it is the preponderance of one of two possibilities (tarjih ahad al-ja'izayn). Whatever is a preponderance contradicts certainty, just as certainty contradicts the preponderance of one of two possibilities. And even assuming that conjecture and knowledge are included under that category, it would still not be a connected exception, because he did not make conjecture an exception from knowledge. The wording is not "they have no knowledge of it except conjecture"; rather the wording is "except the following of conjecture," and following conjecture is not included under knowledge, since the genus of what is mentioned is different.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "If you ask: Why are they described as doubters (shakk), when doubt is that neither of the two possibilities is preponderant? Then they are described as conjecturers (zann), and conjecture is that one of them is preponderant. So how can they be both doubters and conjecturers?" I answer: it is meant that they were doubters, having no knowledge at all, but signs appeared to them so they conjectured. End of quotation. This is an answer to his own question. However, it may be said that this question does not arise, because the Arabs apply the term doubt (shakk) to anything in which there is no certainty or conviction, so it includes everything that is wavering, whether equally balanced without preponderance or with preponderance of one side. If that is so, the question is dissolved.

**"And they did not kill him with certainty"** (﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا﴾). Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and a group said: the pronoun in "qatalūhu" refers to conjecture (al-zann). One says: "I killed this matter with knowledge" when you affirm it and assert it with the firm assertion that admits no doubt. The meaning is: their conjecture was not valid in their view, nor did they verify it with certainty, nor did they cut conjecture with certainty. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba said the pronoun refers to knowledge (al-'ilm), i.e., they did not kill knowledge with certainty. One says: "I killed knowledge and opinion with certainty" and "I killed it with knowledge," because killing a thing implies subjugation and domination. It is as if it were said: their knowledge of the killing of the Messiah was not knowledge that encompassed the matter; it was only conjecture. Al-Zamakhshari said: there is in this a mockery (tahakkum), because knowledge was negated from them entirely by the particle of comprehensiveness, and then it is said, "they did not know it with certainty and comprehension," which is nothing but mockery. End of quotation.

The apparent view, the view of the majority, is that the pronoun refers to Jesus (ʿIsā), by treating all the pronouns as referring to one thing, so they do not differ. The meaning is sound and eloquent. "Yaqīnan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "qatalūhu," i.e., "certain that it was Jesus, as they claimed in their saying: 'We killed the Messiah'," as al-Suddi said. Or it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., "a certain killing," which al-Zamakhshari allowed. Al-Hasan said: "And they did not kill him in truth." Its accusative status is then as an emphasis on the content of the negated sentence, like your saying: "They did not kill him in truth," meaning: the truth of the negation of his killing is true. As for what is related from Ibn al-Anbari, that in the speech there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) and that "yaqīnan" is governed by "rafaʿahu Allāh ilayhi" (﴿رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ﴾), with the meaning: "Rather, God raised him to Himself with certainty" — perhaps this is not correct from him. Al-Khalil has explicitly stated that this is an error, because what follows "bal" does not govern what precedes it.

**"Rather, God raised him to Himself"** (﴿بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ﴾). This is a refutation of their claim of his killing and crucifixion, and he is alive in the second heaven, as is authentically related from the Messenger (ﷺ) in the hadith of the Night Journey (al-Mi'raj). He remains there until God sends him down to the earth to kill the Dajjal (the Antichrist), and to fill it with justice as it was filled with injustice, and he will live on it for forty years and then die as humans die. Qatada said: God raised 'Isa to Himself, clothed him with feathers and garbed him with light, and cut off from him food and drink; so he became with the angels, and he is with them around the Throne. Thus he became a human, angelic, heavenly, and earthly being.

The pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to God, the Exalted, with the omission of an implied phrase: "to His heaven," and it has come as "wa rafi'uka ilayya" (Āl ʿImrān 3:55). It has also been said: "to where no judgment belongs except to Him." Supplication is directed only toward Him, and this returns to the first point. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: after mentioning that various trials reached 'Isa, God informed that He raised him to Himself, which shows that his being raised to Him is greater in conveying reward than Paradise and all its bodily pleasures; and this verse opens for you the door of knowing spiritual felicities. End of quotation. There is in this something of the speech of the philosophers.

**"And God is ever Mighty, Wise"** (﴿وكانَ اللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًا﴾). Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: by "mighty" is meant perfection of power, and by "wise" perfection of knowledge. He thereby draws attention to the fact that the raising of 'Isa, peace be upon him, from this world to the heavens, though it may seem nearly impossible for humans, is not beyond the reach of My power and My wisdom. End of quotation. Others said: "Mighty" means strong in exacting vengeance from the Jews; so He empowered Peter the Roman against them, and he killed among them a great slaughter. "Wise" means He decreed upon them curse and wrath. It was also said: "Mighty" means invincible, because the Jews attempted something against 'Isa, peace be upon him, and God willed the opposite. "Wise" means placing things in their proper places; so from His wisdom is His rescuing him from the Jews and raising him to heaven as He wills and as His wisdom, exalted is He, requires. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: God revealed to 'Isa at the age of thirty, then raised him when he was thirty-three, so his prophethood lasted three years. It has also been said: God sent Gabriel, peace be upon him, who brought him into a small door with an opening in its roof, and God raised him to heaven through that opening.

**"And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death"** (﴿وإنْ مِن أهْلِ الكِتابِ إلّا لَيُؤْمِنَنَّ بِهِ قَبْلَ مَوْتِهِ﴾). "In" here is negative (nāfiya), and the subject of the predication is omitted, its attribute standing in its place. The estimated meaning is: "There is not anyone from the People of the Book." As it is omitted in His saying: "There is not one of you but will come to it" (Maryam 19:71). The meaning: "There is none of the Jews." And His saying: "There is not one of us but has a known station" (al-Saffat 37:164), i.e., "there is not one of us but has a station," and "there is not one of you but will come to it." Al-Zajjaj said: "aḥad" is omitted because it is implied in every negation that admits an exception, as in "no one stood up except Zayd," meaning "no one stood up except Zayd." Al-Zamakhshari said: "la-yu'minanna bihi" is a clause of oath (jumla qasamiyya) occurring as an attribute of an omitted noun; its estimate is: "There is not from the People of the Book anyone (aḥad) except that he will surely believe in him," and similarly "There is not one of us but has a known station" and "There is not one of you but will come to it." The meaning: "There is none of the Jews who will not surely believe in him," end of quotation.

This is a gross error, for he claimed that "la-yu'minanna bihi" is an oath clause occurring as an attribute of an omitted noun, and so on to the end. The attribute of the omitted "aḥad" is only the prepositional phrase "from the People of the Book," and the estimate, as we have mentioned, is: "And there is no one (aḥad) from the People of the Book." As for His saying "la-yu'minanna bihi," it is not an attribute of a noun, nor is it an oath clause as he claimed; rather, it is the answer of the oath, the oath itself being omitted, and the oath together with its answer is in the position of the predicate (khabar) of the omitted subject "aḥad," since no predication can be formed from "aḥad" and the prepositional phrase, because it conveys no benefit; predication is formed only by the oath clause and its answer, and that is the locus of the benefit. Likewise the predicate is "illa lahu maqam" (al-Saffat 37:164), and likewise "illa wāriduhā," since nothing before "illa" forms a predicative structure. The apparent view is that both pronouns in "bihi" and "mawtihi" refer to 'Isa, and this is the context of the speech. The meaning is: from among the People of the Book who will be living at the time of his descent.

It is narrated that he descends from heaven at the end of time, and then no one of the People of the Book remains but believes in him, so that the religion becomes one, which is the religion of Islam. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Abu Malik. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan again, Mujahid and others: the pronoun in "bihi" refers to 'Isa, and in "mawtihi" refers to the Kitabi (the person of the Book). They said: no Jew dies until he believes in 'Isa and knows that he is a prophet; but at the moment of facing death, that belief is of no benefit, just as the belief of Pharaoh did not benefit him at the time of facing death. Al-Zamakhshari said something similar: the meaning is that there is not from the Jews and Christians anyone but will surely believe before his death in 'Isa, and that he is the servant of God and His messenger; meaning: when he witnesses (the truth) before his soul departs, at which time his belief will not benefit him, since the time of obligation has ended. Then there is related from Shahr ibn Hawshab and al-Hajjaj a lengthy narration, part of which touches on the exegesis: that when the Jew is present at death, the angels strike his back and his face and say: "O enemy of God, 'Isa came to you as a prophet and you denied him!" He says: "I believe that he is a prophet." And they say to the Christian: "'Isa came to you as a prophet and you claimed that he was God or the son of God!" He says: "I believe that he is the servant of God and His messenger," at a time when his belief does not benefit him. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he explained it thus; 'Ikrima said to him: "If a man comes to him and strikes his neck?" He said: "His soul does not leave until he moves his lips with it." He said: "And if he falls from a roof, or burns, or is eaten by a beast?" He said: "He speaks it in his fall, and his soul does not leave until he believes in him."

The recitation of Ubayy supports this: "illa la-yu'minunna bihi qabla mawtihim" with a damma on the nun, meaning: "And there is not one of them but they will believe in him before their death," since "aḥad" may be treated as plural. If you ask: What is the benefit of informing of their belief in 'Isa before their death? I answer: its benefit is warning, and it should be known that they will necessarily believe in him soon, at the time of witnessing, and that this will not benefit them; it is a reminder to them and an alert to dealing with belief in him at the time when it benefits, and it serves as an establishment of proof against them.

And likewise His saying:

**"And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them"** (﴿ويَوْمَ القِيامَةِ يَكُونُ عَلَيْهِمْ شَهِيدًا﴾). He testifies against the Jews that they denied him, and against the Christians that they called him the son of God. End of his words. He also said: It is possible that it means that not one of all the People of the Book remains but will surely believe in him, because God will revive them in their graves at that time, inform them of his descent and of what he descended for, and they will believe in him at a time when their belief will not benefit them. End of quotation. 'Ikrima said: the pronoun in "bihi" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), and in "mawtihi" to the Kitabi. He said: no Jew or Christian leaves this world without believing in Muhammad (ﷺ), even if he drowns or a wall falls upon him; he believes at that moment. It was also said: "bihi" returns to God, and "mawtihi" to one of the implied antecedents. Ibn Zayd said: when 'Isa, peace be upon him, descends to kill the Dajjal, no Jew or Christian will remain but will believe in God when they see the killing of the Dajjal, and all nations will become one upon the religion of Islam. This view is also attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada.

Al-Abbas ibn Ghazwan said: "Wa-inna min ahl al-kitab" (﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book﴾) is read with the nun doubled (*bi-tashdid al-nun*). This is a reading that is difficult to account for grammatically. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them﴾, meaning a witness against the People of the Book: against the Jews, for their denial of him and their disparagement of him, and against the Christians, for making him a god alongside Allah or a son of Him. The pronoun in *yakunu* ("he will be") refers to Jesus. Ikrimah said that it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ).

It has been said that these verses contain various kinds of eloquence and rhetorical ornament (*al-fasaha wa-al-badi'*). Among them is *tajnis mughayir* (heterogeneous paronomasia, i.e. a pun between words of different roots) in *yukhadi'una* ("they deceive") and *khadi'uhum* ("He deceives them"), and in *shakartum* ("you give thanks") and *shakiran* ("Thankful"). There is *tajnis mumathil* (homogeneous paronomasia, i.e. a pun between words of the same root) in *wa-idha qamu* ("and when they stand"). There is repetition (*al-takrar*) in the name of Allah, in *ha'ula'* ("these") and *hа'ula'*, in *yarawna* ("they see") and *yuridun* ("they desire"), in *al-kafirin* ("the disbelievers") and *al-kafirin*, in *ahl al-kitab* ("the People of the Book") and *kitaban*, and in *bi-mithaqihim* ("with their covenant") and *mithaqan*. There is *tibaq* (antithesis) in *al-kafirin* and *al-mu'minin* ("the believers"), in *in tubdu* ("if you reveal") and *yukhfuhu* ("or conceal it"), and in *nu'minu* ("we believe") and *nakfuru* ("we disbelieve"). There is *ikhtisas* (specification, i.e. a restriction of meaning) in *ila al-salah* ("to the prayer"), in ﴿the lowest depths of the Fire﴾ [al-Nisa: 145], and in ﴿public utterance of evil﴾ [al-Nisa: 148].

There is *isharah* (allusion) in the places of metaphor (*isti'arah*): in ﴿they seek to deceive Allah, but He is the One who deceives them﴾ [al-Nisa: 142], where the term "deception" is used metaphorically for requital. It is also in *sabilan* ("a way"), and in *sultanan* ("authority" or "proof") for the establishment of the argument. ﴿The lowest depths of the Fire﴾ [al-Nisa: 145] is metaphorical for the lowness of their ranks in the Fire. It is in *i'tasimu* ("hold fast") for seeking refuge. It is in ﴿to make distinction﴾ and in ﴿and they did not make distinction﴾. The root meaning is physical, but it is borrowed for abstract meanings. It is in *sultanan*, borrowed for "proof." It is in *ghulf* ("uncircumcised" or "covered") and ﴿Rather, Allah has sealed it﴾ [al-Nisa: 155]. There is the addition of a particle for a meaning in *fa-bima naqdihim* ("so for their breaking").

There is the attribution of a verb to other than its doer, in ﴿so the thunderbolt seized them﴾ and ﴿clear proofs came to them﴾, and to one who approves of the act, in *wa-qatlihim al-anbiya'* ("and their killing of the prophets"), in ﴿and their saying against Mary a tremendous slander﴾, and in ﴿and their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah"﴾. There is good sequencing (*husn al-nasaq*) in *fa-bima naqdihim mithaqahum* ("so for their breaking their covenant") and in the conjoined terms that follow it, since they are linked with *waw*, which indicates only joint occurrence. Between these matters there are widely separated eras, yet their earlier and later generations are associated because the deeds of the former and the approval of the latter are the same. There is synecdoche (*itlaq ism kull 'ala ba'd*, the use of the name of a whole for a part) in their disbelief in ﴿the signs of Allah﴾, meaning the Qur'an and the Gospel. They did not disbelieve in any of the books except these two. It is also in their saying "Indeed, we killed," though only some of them said it. There is *ta'rid* (indirect reference) in *rasul Allah* ("the Messenger of Allah"), if we say that it is part of their speech. There is *tawjih* (grammatical versatility) in *ghulf*, since it may be a verbal noun, or the plural of *ghilaf* ("covering"), or the plural of *aghlaf*. There is the return of a pronoun to an unmentioned referent, in ﴿they will surely believe in him before his death﴾, according to those who take the pronouns to refer to something other than Jesus. There is *naql* (transfer) from the pattern *fa'il* to *fa'il*'s derived form *fa'il* in *shahid* ("witness"). There is ellipsis (*hadhf*) in several places.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 150–159 (part 1 of 4):**

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers﴾. Al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Juraij said: it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in Musa (Moses) and the Torah, and disbelieved in ʿIsa (Jesus) and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. The Christians believed in ʿIsa and the Injil (Gospel), and disbelieved in Muhammad and the Qur'an. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the Jews specifically: they believed in Musa, ʿUzayr and the Torah, and disbelieved in ʿIsa and the Injil, and in Muhammad and the Qur'an. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah had explained the bad character and blameworthy conduct of the hypocrites, He began to speak about the Jews and the Christians. He made their disbelief in some of the messengers a disbelief in all of the messengers, and their disbelief in the messengers a disbelief in Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And they wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers﴾: that is, they wish to separate belief in Allah from belief in His messengers. They say, "We believe in Allah, but we do not believe in so-and-so and so-and-so of the prophets."

﴿And they say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others"﴾: meaning, of the prophets. It was also said that this refers to the Jews' affirmation that Muhammad is a prophet, but only not to the Children of Israel. This is similar to their other divisions, which were out of obstinacy and evasion.

﴿And they wish to adopt a way between that﴾: that is, a middle path between disbelief and belief, though there is no intermediate position between the two.

﴿Those are the disbelievers in truth﴾. He emphasized it with the words "they" (hum), lest it be imagined that such belief would benefit them. He also emphasized it with the word "in truth" (ḥaqqan), which is an emphasis on the content of the declarative sentence, as when you say, "This is the servant of Allah in truth," meaning, "That is indeed the case, in truth." Or it is an adjective to an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a disbelief in truth," i.e., a disbelief that is established and certain, without doubt. Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), according to the view of Sibawayh. Similar examples have been mentioned before. Al-Wahidi criticized this interpretation and said: "Disbelief cannot be true in any way." This objection is not compelling, since it is not meant that ḥaqqan refers to the truth that is the opposite of falsehood; rather, the meaning is that it is a disbelief that is established and certain. The emphasis was used because the call to belief is shared by all the prophets, namely the manifestation of miracles at their hands. Thus their dividing [the prophets] in belief is evidence of their disbelief in all of them, since their belief in some of them did not arise from reflection on the evidence, but was rather by way of whim and trifling.

(And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.) This is a threat to them of humiliation in the punishment.

﴿But those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not make distinction between any of them﴾: these are the believers, the followers of Muhammad. The discussion of the use of (bayn) before (aḥad, "any") has already been covered in al-Baqara, in His words: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqara 2:285], so it is unnecessary to repeat it here.

(Those — We will give them their rewards.) He, exalted is He, explicitly promised these [believers] just as He explicitly threatened those [disbelievers]. Hafs read yu'tīhim with the yāʾ, so that it refers back to the name of Allah mentioned before it. The rest read it with the nūn (nu'tīhim), by way of iltifāt (a shift of grammatical person), and its counterpart is (wa-aʿtadnā, "and We have prepared"). As for the statement of Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi that the reading with nūn is preferable for two reasons, one being that it is more inclusive and the other that it is consistent with His words "and We have prepared," this is not a good argument, and there is no preference in this, because both readings are mutawātir (transmitted by mass transmission), and thus were revealed in this form.

(And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.) When He promised them reward, He added good news of pardon for their misdeeds and of His mercy toward them.

﴿The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down to them a book from the heaven﴾. al-Suddi said: The Jews said, "If you are truthful, then bring a book from the heaven all at once, just as Musa brought the Book." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi said: They said, "Bring tablets in which is your Book, just as Musa brought tablets in which was the Torah." Al-Hasan and Qatada said: They asked him to bring a book specifically for the Jews, commanding them to believe in Muhammad. Ibn Juraij said: They said, "We will not follow you in what you call us to, until you bring us a book from Allah to so-and-so and so-and-so, that you are the messenger of Allah." According to the view of Ibn Juraij, their request was like the request of ʿAbd Allah ibn Umayya al-Zuhri. It was also said that they asked for a book that they could witness until it descended. From among the Jewish questioners, he named Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and Finhas ibn ʿAzura. It was also said that the questioners were the Jews and the Christians, and their question was only by way of obstinacy. Al-Hasan said: If they had asked him in order that the truth might become clear, He would have given it to them, for what He has given you is sufficient.

﴿For they had asked Musa for greater than that, and said, "Show us Allah openly"﴾. Before this they assumed an omitted statement. Al-Zamakhshari made it a conditional clause whose answer is this, and its estimated sense is: "If you consider what they asked of you to be great, then they asked Musa for something greater than that." Ibn ʿAtiyya estimated it as: "So do not be concerned, O Muhammad, about their questioning and their hastiness, for this is their habit; they asked Musa." He attributed the question to them, although it had actually come from their forefathers, the seventy of their chiefs, because they were satisfied with the deeds of their forefathers and their ways, and resembled them in obstinacy. al-Hasan read akthara (greater) with the letter thāʾ (ث) instead of the bāʾ (ب) in the reading of the majority. The meaning of jahratan (openly) is: a direct seeing, manifest and clear. Jahratan is an attribute of the seeing. There is disagreement regarding the transmission from Ibn ʿAbbas. It is reported from him that jahratan is an attribute of the question, i.e., "they asked Musa [openly]." Or it is a circumstantial state of the subject of "they asked," meaning, "they asked him while openly declaring it." It is also reported from him that the estimate is: "They said openly, bluntly, 'Show us Allah,'" so it is an attribute of the saying.

﴿So the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing﴾: that is, for their obstinacy, and for their asking for what they had no right to ask. al-Zamakhshari said: "For their wrongdoing" means because of their asking to see [Allah]. If they had asked for something permissible, they would not have been called wrongdoers, and the thunderbolt would not have seized them. Just as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, asked to be shown the giving of life to the dead, and He did not call him a wrongdoer, nor did He strike him with the thunderbolt for the anthropomorphists, and the striking with thunderbolts [is for them]. End of quote. This is in line with the Muʿtazilite doctrine of the impossibility of seeing Allah according to them. The People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna) believe that they did not ask for something rationally impossible, but it is prohibited by the Law, since Allah, exalted is He, has informed through the tongues of His prophets that He is not seen in this worldly life, while seeing Him in the Hereafter is established from the Messenger through tawātur (mass transmission), and it is rationally possible. The discussion of the thunderbolt (al-ṣāʿiqa) has already been covered in al-Baqara. al-Sulami and al-Nakhaʿi read (fa-akhadhathum al-ṣaʿqa, "the stunning seized them"), while the majority read (al-ṣāʿiqa).

﴿Then they took the calf after the clear proofs had come to them﴾. Thumma ("then") here indicates sequence in the reports, not in the actual order of events. Then, the matter of their taking the calf was indeed after that, meaning that their forefathers, and those who were struck, were not the same as those who took the calf. The clear proofs (al-bayyināt) are the parting of the sea, the staff, the drowning of Pharaoh, and other things. al-Hufi said: He informed His prophet of their obstinacy and persistence. The meaning is: if what they asked for had descended upon them, they would have opposed the command of Allah, just as they opposed Him after Allah had revived them from their stunning, and worshipped the calf and took it as a god.

﴿Then We pardoned them for that﴾: that is, for their taking the calf as a god, and for all that preceded it of their opposition. The first explanation is more apparent, since in the story of the calf repentance was explicitly mentioned. "He" means: by what He tested them with, namely killing themselves, and then pardon was granted to the rest of them.

﴿And We gave Musa a clear authority﴾: that is, proof, domination, and manifest supremacy over them, when he commanded them to kill themselves until they would be forgiven. They obeyed him, sitting down in their courtyards while the swords fell upon them. How great a clear authority that is!

﴿And We raised over them the mount, because of their covenant﴾. What is meant by al-Ṭūr (the mount) has been discussed earlier. In al-Sham (Syria) there is a mountain known as al-Ṭūr, and this name became attached to it; it is the Ṭūr of Sinai. It is not the one that was lifted over the Children of Israel, because the raising of the mountain took place near the wilderness (al-tīh) on the side of the land of Egypt, while they were advancing with Musa, peace be upon him. The story of the raising of the Ṭūr was discussed in al-Baqara. The preposition "bi-" in "because of their covenant" indicates cause, namely the pact that Musa took from them after they had affirmed the Torah, that they would act upon what is in it. They broke their covenant and worshipped the calf, so Allah raised the mountain over them. There is an omitted statement that is estimated as: "because of their breaking of their covenant."

(And We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating.") The explanation of this phrase has been discussed in al-Baqara.

﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath"﴾. It was mentioned earlier when they transgressed, in His words: ﴿And you had already known those of you who transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-Baqara 2:65]. Warsh read (lā taʿaddū) with a fatḥa on the ʿayn and a shadda on the dāl, on the basis that the original was (taʿtadū), so the vowel of the tāʾ was transferred to the ʿayn and the tāʾ was assimilated into the dāl. Qalun read it with the vowel of the ʿayn suppressed and the dāl doubled, and the text (naṣṣ) with sukūn; its original is also (lā taʿtadū). The remaining readers of the seven read (lā taʿdū) with a sukūn on the ʿayn and a lightened dāl, from ʿadā yaʿdū. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-Aʿraf 7:163]. al-Aʿmash and al-Akhfash read (lā taʿtadū), from iʿtadā.

(And We took from them a firm covenant.) It was said that this is the first covenant, in His words "because of their covenant," and it is described as firm for emphasis. It is the one taken through Musa and Harun that they would take the Torah with strength, act upon everything in it, and transmit it to their children. It was also said: this covenant is other than the first, namely the second covenant that was taken from their prophets to affirm and believe in Muhammad. It is the one mentioned in His words: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets, "Whatever Book and wisdom I have given you..."﴾ [Aal ʿImran 3:81], and so on.

﴿So for their breaking of their covenant, and their disbelief in the signs of Allah, and their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying, "Our hearts are wrapped"﴾. Ibn ʿAtiyya, in what we have summarized of his words, said: This is informing about things they committed in opposition to what they were taken to account for. They broke the covenant by which the mountain was raised over them, and they replaced the faith contained in the command to enter the gate prostrating, which includes the humility that is the fruit of faith, with disbelief in the signs of Allah, and with withholding obedience and not complying with His command not to transgress in the Sabbath, the violation of the greatest sacred things, which is the killing of the prophets. They responded to the taking of the firm covenant with their ignorance and their saying, "Our hearts are wrapped," meaning in veils and coverings, so they do not understand. Allah, exalted is He, turned away from their saying and their lying, and informed that He had sealed their hearts because of their disbelief. End of quote. As for the covenant that was broken, was it their concealing of the description of the Messenger and their denial of what he brought, or their abandonment of acting upon what is in their Book, even though they had accepted and committed to acting upon it? There are two views. As for the signs of Allah that they disbelieved in, are they those that were revealed to them in their books, or all the books of Allah that were sent down? There are two views. The explanation of "Our hearts are wrapped" has been discussed in al-Baqara.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 150–159 (part 2 of 4):

﴿Rather, Allah has sealed their hearts because of their disbelief.﴾ Al-Kisa'i and Hamzah assimilated the lam of (bal) into the ta' of (ta-ba'a), while the rest of the Seven Readers made it clear (izhar). Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief﴾ is a statement whose meaning is blame, on the basis that their hearts are like things sealed, which never understand and never obey a messenger. Al-Zamakhshari said: They meant by their saying "Our hearts are wrapped (ghulf)" that Allah created our hearts wrapped, that is, in coverings that cannot be reached by any reminder or admonition, as Allah related about the polytheists: ﴿And they say, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 20]. The Mujbirah (the determinists), may Allah disgrace them, denied this, and it was said to them: Allah forsook them and withheld from them His favors because of their disbelief, so they became like what is sealed over, not that they were created wrapped and capable of receiving the reminder, nor able to accept it. End of quotation. This is in keeping with his Mu'tazili (rationalist) doctrine. As for Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah), they say: Allah truly sealed over them, as He informed, since there is no creator other than Him. The (ba') in ﴿so because of their breaking of their covenant﴾ is connected to an omitted element that al-Zamakhshari estimated as: "We did to them what We did." Ibn 'Atiyyah estimated it as: "We cursed them, humiliated them, and decreed eternal abiding in Hell upon those of them who died in that state." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The omission of the response to this statement is eloquent, left to the listener's understanding. End of quotation. Calling what the prepositional phrase depends upon a "response" (jawab) is a terminology not known in the science of grammar, and language does not support it, because it is not a response. They also permitted that it be connected to the phrase (We made unlawful for them) [Qur'an 4:160], with ﴿so because of an injustice from those who were Jews﴾ [An-Nisa': 160] being a substitute (badal) for ﴿so because of their breaking of their covenant﴾. This was said by al-Zajjaj, Abu Bakr, al-Zamakhshari and others. But this is far-fetched, because of the great distance between the substitute and what it substitutes, and because what is conjoined to a cause is itself a cause; so it would necessitate that some parts of the cause of the prohibition be delayed in time beyond the time of the prohibition, and it would then be impossible for it to be part of a cause or a caused effect except through a distant interpretation. The explanation of that is that their saying "against Mary a tremendous slander" and their saying "Indeed, we killed the Messiah" came later in time than (p. 389) the prohibition of the good things upon them. Therefore the better estimate is: "We cursed them," and this has been stated explicitly in the verse: ﴿So because of their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 13].

(﴿So they do not believe, except a few﴾) The explanation of this clause has already been given, so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿And because of their disbelief and their saying against Mary a tremendous slander﴾ Apparently, in His saying "And because of their disbelief and their saying," it is conjoined to His saying "so because of" and what follows it. Al-Zamakhshari also permitted that His saying ﴿and because of their disbelief and their saying﴾ be conjoined to "because of their disbelief." The repetition of the attribution of disbelief to them is according to its objects: for they disbelieved in Moses, then in Jesus, then in Muhammad (peace be upon him); so He conjoined some of their disbelief to some other. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or He conjoined the whole of the conjoined phrase to the whole of the phrase conjoined to, as if it was said: He gathered them between breaking the covenant, disbelieving in the signs of Allah, killing the prophets, their saying "Our hearts are wrapped," and their combining their disbelief and their slandering of Mary, and their boasting of killing Jesus (peace be upon him): We punished them. Or [it means]: "Rather, Allah sealed over them," and He gathered them between their disbelief and such and such. Al-Zamakhshari also said: If you say, "Why not suppose that the omitted element to which the preposition is attached is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿Rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief﴾?" I say: This estimate is not valid, because His saying "Rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief" is a rejection and denial of their saying "Our hearts are wrapped," so it is connected to that. End of quotation. This is a good answer, but there is another objection that prevents it: the conjunction with "bal" is for turning away from the first judgment and affirming a second in its place, by way of annulling the first, or moving on, as is common in the speech of Allah in reporting. So it is only used for moving on. The second clause conveys what the first clause does not. What al-Zamakhshari estimated does not allow what we have established, because His saying ﴿so because of their breaking their covenant﴾, ﴿and their disbelief in the signs of Allah﴾, and their saying: ﴿"Our hearts are wrapped." Rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief﴾ means the second clause conveys what the first clause conveyed, and this is not permissible. If you say, "Zayd passed by 'Amr, rather Zayd passed by 'Amr," it is not permissible. Abu al-Baqa' permitted this, and his estimate is: "so because of their breaking their covenant and their disbelief in the signs of Allah, and likewise their hearts were sealed over." It was also said the estimate is: "so because of their breaking their covenant, they do not believe except a few," and the (fa') is superfluous (muqhamah). The (ma) in His saying "so because of" is like the (ma) in His saying ﴿so by mercy﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 159], and the discussion of it has already passed. The tremendous slander is their accusing Mary (peace be upon her) of fornication despite their seeing the sign in the speech of Jesus (peace be upon him) in the cradle. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Otherwise, were it not for the sign, they would have been, in their saying, following the judgment of humans in denying a pregnancy without a male. End of quotation. It was described as "tremendous" because they persisted in it after the sign had appeared and the miracle of her innocence had been established. The accusation has been called "a tremendous slander" in His saying: ﴿Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander﴾ [An-Nur: 16].

﴿And their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah."﴾ Apparently "the messenger of Allah" is part of their saying: they said that in mockery, like the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 27], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning﴾ [Hud: 87]. It may also be that it is part of Allah's speech, placing a good mention in place of their ugly mention in relating it, as an elevation of Jesus (peace be upon him), as they used to mention him with it. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned both possibilities, while Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned only the second. He said: It is an information from Allah about the attribute of Jesus (peace be upon him), namely messengership, in order to show the sin of these who admitted to killing him, and the sin was incumbent upon them, though they did not kill Jesus. For they crucified that person thinking he was Jesus, and thinking Jesus was a liar who was not a messenger. But the sin was incumbent upon them because they believed that their killing had fallen upon Jesus; so it was as if they had killed him. Their belief that he was not a messenger does not remove the sin from them.

﴿But they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them.﴾ This is an information from Him, exalted is He, that they did not kill Jesus and did not crucify him.

The narrators differed (p. 390) about the manner of the killing and the crucifixion, and nothing has been established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it beyond what the Qur'an indicates.

The final outcome of Jesus's affair (peace be upon him) was that the Jews sought him, so he and the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) hid in a house. They were guided to him and came at night, and they were thirteen or eighteen. He dispersed them that night and sent them to the regions, and he and a man remained with him. Then Jesus was raised, and his likeness was cast upon the man, and he was crucified. It was said he was the Jew who had guided them to him. It was said he said to his companions: "Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him and be killed, and deliver these people, and he will be my companion in Paradise?" Sarjis said: "I," and the likeness of Jesus was cast upon him. It was said the likeness was cast upon all of them, and when they were brought out, one was missing from the count, so they took one of those upon whom the likeness was, and he was crucified. It is related that the king and those who handled it did not fail to know the matter of Jesus, because of what they saw of the missing from the count and the confusion of the affair; so that person was crucified, and the people were kept away from his cross for days until he changed; and no attribute of his remained. At that point the people approached him, and the disciples went about in the regions saying: "Jesus was crucified." It was said the likeness was not cast upon anyone; rather the meaning of ﴿but it was made to appear so to them﴾ is: the king, the deceiver, made it appear to them so that he would continue with the one missing from the count; he had hurried to crucify one person and kept people away from him, and said: "This is Jesus." This view is the one that should be held concerning His saying ﴿but it was made to appear so to them﴾. As for the likeness being cast upon a person, that has not been validly transmitted from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that one could rely upon it.

It has been differed about upon whom the likeness was cast, in many ways. It was said: the Jew who had guided them. It was said: the successor (khalifah) of Caesar who had been imprisoned with him. It was said: one of the Jews. It was said: he entered in order to kill him. It was said: a watchman whom the Jews had assigned to him. It was said: the likeness was cast upon all the disciples. It was said: the likeness was cast upon the face only, not the body. This uncertainty repels confidence in anything of that. For this reason some of them said: If it is permissible to say that Allah, exalted is He, casts the likeness of one human upon another human, then this opens the door to sophistry (sophistry: al-safsatah, fallacious reasoning). It was said the reason for the Jews' gathering to kill him was that a group of them insulted him and insulted his mother, so he invoked against them: "O Allah, You are my Lord, and by Your word You created me. O Allah, curse whoever insulted me and insulted my mother." So Allah transformed whoever insulted the two of them into monkeys and swine, and the Jews gathered to kill him. ﴿Was made to appear﴾ (shubbiha) has as its subject the prepositional phrase, like His saying: ﴿it was imagined to him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 66], but the resemblance occurred to them. It is permissible that it take as its subject the pronoun of the one killed, indicated by "we killed," i.e., but the one they killed was made to appear to them. It is not permissible that the pronoun refer to the Messiah, because the Messiah is the one likened to, not the one likened.

﴿And indeed, those who differed concerning it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it, except the following of assumption.﴾ The Jews differed about it: some of them said: he was not killed and not crucified; the face was the face of Jesus and the body was the body of another. It was said: they brought in someone to kill him, and the likeness was cast upon him, and he was crucified, and one was missing from the number. They had known the number of the disciples, so they said: If the crucified one is our companion, where is Jesus? And if it is Jesus, where is our companion? It was said: the common people said: "We killed Jesus," and those who witnessed his being raised to heaven said: he was not killed and not crucified. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The certainty that was transmitted by all in agreement from their senses is that a person was crucified, but whether he was Jesus or not is not a matter of the senses; therefore the transmission of it was not unanimous. The pronoun in "concerning it" refers to the killing; its meaning is: concerning his killing, and this is the apparent meaning indicated by what precedes and follows it. It was said the pronoun in "differed" also refers to the Jews, and their difference concerning him is the saying of some of them: he is a god, and the saying of some of them: he is the son of Allah, exalted is He. It was said their difference concerning him is that the Nestorians said: the crucifixion fell upon his humanity (nasut) and not his divinity (lahut). It was said the killing and crucifixion fell upon both. It was said it refers to the Jews and Christians, for the Jews said: he is the son of adultery, and the Christians said: he is the son of Allah. It was said their difference is from the aspect that the Christians said: the Jews killed him and crucified him; and the Jews who witnessed his being raised said: he was raised to heaven. The majority hold that ﴿except the following of assumption﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' munqati'), because the following of assumption is not of the kind of knowledge (p. 391), meaning: but rather they have the following of assumption.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It means: but they follow conjecture (al-zann). This is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis (i'rab)." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), since conjecture and knowledge are both included under beliefs of certainty (ma'taqadat al-yaqin). The one who conjectures may, in a figurative manner, say: 'My knowledge in this matter is that it is such-and-such,' meaning his conjecture." End of quotation. But this is not as he stated, because conjecture is not among the beliefs of certainty, for it is the preponderance of one of two possibilities (tarjih ahad al-ja'izayn). Whatever is a preponderance contradicts certainty, just as certainty contradicts the preponderance of one of two possibilities. And even assuming that conjecture and knowledge are included under that category, it would still not be a connected exception, because he did not make conjecture an exception from knowledge. The wording is not "they have no knowledge of it except conjecture"; rather the wording is "except the following of conjecture," and following conjecture is not included under knowledge, since the genus of what is mentioned is different.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "If you ask: Why are they described as doubters (shakk), when doubt is that neither of the two possibilities is preponderant? Then they are described as conjecturers (zann), and conjecture is that one of them is preponderant. So how can they be both doubters and conjecturers?" I answer: it is meant that they were doubters, having no knowledge at all, but signs appeared to them so they conjectured. End of quotation. This is an answer to his own question. However, it may be said that this question does not arise, because the Arabs apply the term doubt (shakk) to anything in which there is no certainty or conviction, so it includes everything that is wavering, whether equally balanced without preponderance or with preponderance of one side. If that is so, the question is dissolved.

**"And they did not kill him with certainty"** (﴿وما قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا﴾). Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and a group said: the pronoun in "qatalūhu" refers to conjecture (al-zann). One says: "I killed this matter with knowledge" when you affirm it and assert it with the firm assertion that admits no doubt. The meaning is: their conjecture was not valid in their view, nor did they verify it with certainty, nor did they cut conjecture with certainty. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba said the pronoun refers to knowledge (al-'ilm), i.e., they did not kill knowledge with certainty. One says: "I killed knowledge and opinion with certainty" and "I killed it with knowledge," because killing a thing implies subjugation and domination. It is as if it were said: their knowledge of the killing of the Messiah was not knowledge that encompassed the matter; it was only conjecture. Al-Zamakhshari said: there is in this a mockery (tahakkum), because knowledge was negated from them entirely by the particle of comprehensiveness, and then it is said, "they did not know it with certainty and comprehension," which is nothing but mockery. End of quotation.

The apparent view, the view of the majority, is that the pronoun refers to Jesus (ʿIsā), by treating all the pronouns as referring to one thing, so they do not differ. The meaning is sound and eloquent. "Yaqīnan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "qatalūhu," i.e., "certain that it was Jesus, as they claimed in their saying: 'We killed the Messiah'," as al-Suddi said. Or it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., "a certain killing," which al-Zamakhshari allowed. Al-Hasan said: "And they did not kill him in truth." Its accusative status is then as an emphasis on the content of the negated sentence, like your saying: "They did not kill him in truth," meaning: the truth of the negation of his killing is true.
