﴿and their taking usury, though they had been forbidden it﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), which confirms the ugliness of their act and the evil of their conduct, since what God has forbidden must be kept far away. They said: usury is forbidden in all revealed laws.

﴿and their devouring the wealth of people falsely﴾: that is, the bribes they would take from their lowly people in distorting the Scripture. In this verse, the kinds of wrongdoing that necessitated the prohibition of good things are detailed. It was said: whenever they committed a sin, some good things were forbidden to them. The detail of the good things is omitted here; rather they are mentioned indefinitely and vaguely. In [surah] al-Ma'idah, He detailed the kinds of what was forbidden, but did not detail the cause. It is said: "That is because We recompensed them for their transgression." The preposition *ba'* is repeated in *wa-bisaddihim* (and because of their hindering) because it is distant from the thing it is coordinated with, separated by something that is not an object of what it is coordinated with, but rather of the governing word. It is not repeated in *wa-akhdhihim* (and their taking) and *wa-aklihim* (and their devouring), because the separation occurred by the object of what is coordinated. A parallel to repeating and omitting the particle is His words: "So because of their breaking their covenant..." [4:155]. The kinds of wrongdoing begin with what is most important, namely the matter of religion, which is hindering from the way of God; then the matter of worldly affairs, which is harm to some wealth; then he ascended to the most extreme in worldly wealth, which is consuming it falsely, that is, for free, with no exchange.

In mentioning this verse there is a favour upon the community of Muhammad, in that He did not treat them as He treated the Jews, by forbidding them good things in this world as a punishment for their sins.

﴿We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾ When He mentioned the punishment of this world, He mentioned what He had prepared for them in the Hereafter. Since that prohibition was general for the Jews because of the wrongdoing of those among them who did wrong, and its burden fell on their wrongdoers and non-wrongdoers alike, as He said: "And beware of a trial which will not strike only those among you who have done wrong" [8:25], He clarified that the painful punishment was prepared only for the disbelievers among them. For this reason it did not come as "We have prepared for them."

﴿But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and those who establish the prayer and give the zakat, and those who believe in God and the Last Day: those, We will give them a great reward.﴾ The coming of *lakin* (but) here is extremely elegant, because it falls between two opposites and their recompense: the disbelievers with the painful punishment, and the believers with the great reward. *Al-rasikhun* are the firm, the established, the steadfast, those who have insight, among them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like. *Al-mu'minun* (the believers) means among them, or the believers from the Emigrants and the Helpers. Apparently it is general to whoever believes.

*Al-rasikhun* is in the nominative as a beginning (*mubtada'*), and the predicate is *yu'minun* alone, because praise is not complete except after the sentence is complete. Whoever takes the predicate to be *ulaika sanu'tihim* (those, We will give them) has a weak view. *Al-muqimin* is in the accusative on the basis of praise (*al-madh*), and *wa-al-mu'tuna* is also in the nominative by an implied supposition, and they are by way of cutting (*al-qat'*, changing the grammatical case of a descriptive word) to the nominative. It is not permissible to coordinate it with the nominative before it, because when a descriptor is cut off in any part of it, what follows does not return to the case of the described word. This cutting is to show the excellence of the prayer and the zakat; so the description was multiplied by making it into separate clauses.

Ibn Jubayr, Amr ibn Ubayd, al-Jahdari, Isa ibn Umar, Malik ibn Dinar, Ismah from al-A'mash, and Yunus and Harun from Abu Amr read *wa-al-muqimuna* (with *-una* in the nominative) in the nominative, coordinated with the first. It is also so in the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud, as al-Farra' reported. It is narrated that it is so in the Codex of Ubayy. It was also said: rather it is in it *wa-al-muqimina al-salat*, as in the Codex of Uthman. It is reported from Aisha and Aban ibn Uthman that writing it with *ya'* is a scribal error in the codex; but this is not authentically reported from them, because they were both Arabs of eloquent speech; cutting of descriptors is more common in the language of the Arabs, and it is a broad topic, on which Sibawayh and others cited evidence; and Sibawayh explained this as cutting.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "We do not heed what they claim of its being a grammatical error in the orthography of the codex. Perhaps someone who looks in the book, and does not know the ways of the Arabs, might pay attention to it, and what they have in the accusative of specialisation (*al-nasb 'ala al-ikhtisas*) is from misguidance." By this he meant: the foremost early ones, whose likeness is in the Torah and whose likeness is in the Gospel, were more zealous in protecting Islam and in repelling its detractors, than to leave a breach in the Book of God which those after them would have to fill, or a tear which those who come after them would have to mend. End quote. By his words "one who does not look in the Book" he means the Book of Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, since the name *al-Kitab* is a proper name for it. And because of the ignorance of those who venture to interpret the Book of God and analyse its words without the rules of the science of grammar, they allowed several possibilities in the coordination of *wa-al-muqimin*:

First: that it is coordinated with *bima unzila ilayka* (what was sent down to you); that is, "they believe in the Books and in those who establish the prayer." They differed on this view as to who is meant by "those who establish the prayer." It was said: the prophets; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya mentioned this. It was said: the angels; Ibn Atiyya mentioned this. It was said: the Muslims, and the sense is: "and the encouragement of those who establish the prayer"; Ibn Atiyya mentioned its meaning.

Second: that it is coordinated with the pronoun in *minhum* (among them); that is, "those firm in knowledge among them and of those who establish the prayer." Ibn Atiyya mentioned this for a people he did not name.

Third: that it is coordinated with the *ka* in *ulaika* (those); that is, "what is sent down to you and to those who establish the prayer."

Fourth: that it is coordinated with the *ka* in *qablika* (before you), with an elided genitive; the estimate is: "and what was sent down before you," and it was said: "those who establish the prayer."

Fifth: that it is coordinated with the *ka* in *qablika*, meaning the prophets; Ibn Atiyya mentioned this.

Ibn Atiyya said: "There is a difference between the verse and the line of poetry" – meaning the line of al-Khirniq, which he had recited earlier – which is:

*"The ones who alight at every battlefield, and the ones who are good at tying knots of the waistcloths."*

"[The difference is] in the conjunction particle which is in the verse; for it is forbidden by some of them to estimate a verb." In this there is room for consideration. If anyone forbids that, he is refuted by the occurrence of that in the speech of the Arabs with a conjunction particle; and there is no room for consideration in that, as Ibn Atiyya said. The poet said:

*"And he takes refuge with women, bare and dishevelled, nursing infants like the ghouls."*

Likewise they allowed in His words, "and those who give the zakat" several possibilities other than the one we mentioned – namely that it is in the nominative on the predicate of an elided subject, by way of cutting the descriptors for praise:

First: that it is coordinated with *al-rasikhun* (the firm).

Second: on the hidden pronoun in *al-mu'minun* (the believers).

Third: on the pronoun in *yu'minun* (they believe).

Fourth: that it is a subject (*mubtada'*), and what follows it is the predicate, which is the demonstrative *ulaika* and what follows it. As for *al-mu'minuna bi-Allah* (the believers in God), it is coordinated with *wa-al-mu'tuna al-zakat* (and those who give the zakat), on the view we have chosen in raising *wa-al-mu'tuna*.

Since He first mentioned *wa-al-mu'minun* (and the believers), it included belief in what must be believed in. Then He informed about them and about the firm in knowledge that they believe in the Qur'an and in the revealed Books. Then He described them with qualities of praise, from carrying out the noblest of the outward physical attributes of faith, which is the prayer, and the financial one, which is the zakat. Then he ascended in praise to the noblest of the inward doctrinal attributes, which is belief in the One who sent down the Books, and who legislated in them the prayer and the zakat, and belief in the Last Day, which is resurrection and return, in which the fruit of faith appears and the carrying out of the commandments of the Law, such as prayer, zakat and others. Then, having completed that, He informed that He would give them a great reward, which is what He arranged for these glorious attributes with which He described them; and He pointed to them with *ulaika* (those) so as to indicate the totality of those attributes. Whoever parses *wa-al-mu'minuna bi-Allah* as a subject, with what follows as its predicate, is far removed from grasping eloquence. The better parsing is that *ulaika* is a subject. Whoever takes it in the accusative by a supposed verb whose explanation is what follows it – "He will give those, We will give them" – makes it [a case of] *al-ishtighal* (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring to the object, a construction in which the verb is elided and its object is topicalised), so his view is not preferred. This is because "Zayd, I struck him" is more eloquent and more common than "Zayda, a striking of him"; and because the object of what follows the future particle is disputed regarding its permissibility of being fronted in such constructions as "I will strike Zayd." Since that is so, *al-ishtighal* is not permitted. So the better course is to adopt what is not disputed.

Hamza read *sayu'tihim* with *ya'* (the third person), returning to His words, *wa-al-mu'minuna bi-Allah* (and the believers in God). The rest of the seven read it with the first person, by *al-iltifat* (a shift of grammatical person in the middle of a discourse). And [consider] the connection with *wa-a'tadna* (and We have prepared).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 160–167 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾. Ibn Abbas said: The occasion of its revelation was that Sukayn the rabbi and Adiyy ibn Zayd said: "O Muhammad, we do not know that God has sent down anything to a human after Moses, nor revealed to anyone." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: When [the verse] ﴿The People of the Scripture ask you﴾ [al-Nisa 4:153] was revealed, and it was recited to them, and they heard the account of their evil deeds, they said: "God has not sent down anything to a human, nor to Jesus," and they denied all of that. Then [the verse] ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said﴾ [al-An'am 6:91] was revealed, and so on. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾ is a reply to the People of the Scripture regarding their request that the Messenger of God ﷺ bring down a book to them from heaven, and their argument against him that his situation regarding revelation is like that of the other prophets who came before, end quote. He placed Noah first and singled him out from among them in the mention, because he is the second father (of mankind) and the first of the messengers, and his call was general to all who were on the earth at that time, just as the call of Muhammad is general to all who are on the earth.

﴿And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon﴾. God, exalted is He, singled these out for mention, honoring and magnifying them. He began with Abraham because he is the third father. He placed Jesus before those after him to lighten (the burden of) his prophethood, to cut off what the Jews assumed about him, to repel their belief, to magnify him in their eyes, and to make known the breadth of his mission. The lineages of Noah, Abraham and Aaron were mentioned earlier in the lineage of his brother Moses. As for Job, al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn al-Qadi al-Fadil Abd al-Rahim ibn Ali al-Nisaburi mentioned his lineage, saying: Job son of Amus son of Barih son of Tawrum son of al-Is son of Isaac son of Abraham, and his mother was from the descendants of Lot ibn Haran. As for Jonah, he is Jonah son of Matta. Nafi', in the transmission of Ibn Jammaz from him, read (يُونِسُ) with a kasra on the nun, and this is a dialect of some Arabs. al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read it with a fatha, and this is a dialect of some of Uqayl. Some Arabs apply hamza and kasra, and some of Asad apply hamza and damma to the nun. The dialect of the Hijaz is what the majority recited: leaving out the hamza and with a damma on the nun.

﴿And We gave David a Psalter﴾ (وآتَيْنا داوُدَ زَبُورًا), i.e., a book. Every book is called a zabur, but the term became dominant for the book that God revealed to David. It is on the pattern fa'ul with the meaning of maf'ul, like (halub) and (rakub), and it is not a regular pattern. It consists of one hundred and fifty surahs, in which there is no ruling, no prohibition, and no permission; rather, it contains wisdom and admonitions. I have read a portion of it in the lands of al-Andalus. It is said: Solomon was mentioned before David because of the abundance of his knowledge, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿So We gave Solomon understanding of it, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:79]. What appears to be the case is that He combined Jesus, Job and Jonah because they were people of trial and afflictions in this world, and He combined Aaron and Solomon because Aaron was beloved to the Children of Israel, esteemed and preferred, while Solomon was esteemed among the people, dominant over them, and deserving of what God mentioned in His Book; so the two were joined by being beloved and magnified. The mention of David was delayed to honor him by mentioning his book, and by presenting him and his book in a separate clause dedicated to him and to his book. Thus, what he lost of verbal precedence was compensated for by a doubling of moral honor.

Hamza read (زُبُورًا) with a damma on the zay. Abu al-Baqa said: In this there are two possibilities. One: it is a verbal noun like (al-qu'ud), and the revealed book of David is called by it. The second: it is the plural of (zabur) with the augmentative letter, which is the waw, removed. Abu Ali said: Just as they said (tariq) and (turuq), (karawan) and (kurawan), (warshan) and (wurushan), which are pluralized by removing the augmentative letter. What strengthens this interpretation is that broken plural is like diminutive, and this meaning has been regular in the diminutive of truncation, as in (azhar) and (zuhayr), (al-harith) and (huraythh), and (thabit) and (thubayt). The plural is similar to it in analogy, even if it is rarer in usage. Abu Ali said: It is also possible that it is the plural of (zubur), applied to what is written, just as they said: (darb al-amir) and (nasj al-yaman), and just as the written was called (kitab).

﴿And messengers We have related to you before﴾; i.e., We have mentioned their stories to you.

﴿And messengers We have not related to you﴾. It was narrated from the hadith of Abu Dharr that he asked about the messengers, and the Messenger of God ﷺ said to him: "The messengers were three hundred and thirteen." Al-Qurtubi said: This is the most authentic thing transmitted on this matter; al-Ajurri and Abu Hatim al-Busti recorded it in a sound musnad of his. In this hadith of Abu Dharr, he asked him: "How many were the prophets?" He said: "One hundred and twenty-four thousand prophets." It was narrated from Anas that the Messenger of God ﷺ was sent after eight thousand prophets, among them four thousand from the Children of Israel. It was narrated from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he said: The prophets are one million, four hundred thousand and twenty-four thousand. Ibn Atiyya said: What has been mentioned about the number of prophets is not sound, and God knows best their number, end quote.

The accusative of (رُسُلًا) is by an implied verb; i.e., "We have related messengers to you," so it is an instance of al-ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun). The clause ﴿We have related them﴾ explains that omitted verb. Evidence for this is the reading of Ubayy, and (رُسُلٌ) with the nominative in both places, as the subject of a new sentence. The beginning with an indefinite noun is permissible here because it is a place of detail, as they recited: "A garment I wore, and a garment I drag." Imru' al-Qays said:

"On one side, and a side with us that has not changed."

Among the arguments for the accusative over the nominative is that the conjunction is upon a verbal sentence, namely (wa-atayna Dawuda zaburan). Ibn Atiyya said: The nominative is by an implied (hum), i.e., "they are messengers," so in this case ﴿We have related them﴾ is a clause in the position of a qualifier. They also permitted the accusative of (رُسُلًا) for two reasons. One: it is accusative by meaning, because the meaning is: "We sent you and We sent messengers," since the rebuttal to the Jews is in their denial of the sending of messengers and the continuity of revelation.

﴿And God spoke to Moses directly﴾. This is information that God honored Moses by His speech, and it was emphasized by the verbal noun (taklim) to show that the verb occurs in its literal sense and not its figurative sense; this is the most common usage. Emphasis by the verbal noun does come in figurative usage, though rarely. Among that is the saying of Hind daughter of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir al-Ansari:

"The silk wept for Awf, and its skin denied it, and the cloaks of Judham cried out a crying."

Tha'lab said: Were it not for the emphasis by the verbal noun, it would be permissible to say: "I spoke to him for you," meaning "I wrote a note to him" or "I sent a messenger to him." So when He said (taklim), it was nothing but speech heard from God, exalted is He. The question of speech is one that the discussion has been lengthy about, and the scholars of Islam differed concerning it. By this question the science of the foundations of religion was called ('ilm al-kalam), speculative theology, and it is a question investigated in the foundations of religion. Ibrahim ibn Wathhab read (وكَلَّمَ اللَّهَ) with the accusative, so that Moses is the speaker. Among the peculiar tafsirs (exegesis) is that it derives from (al-kalm), wounding, and that its meaning is: "God wounded Moses with the claws of trials and the talons of afflictions." Ka'b said: God spoke to Moses in all the languages, so Moses kept saying: "My Lord, I do not understand," until He spoke to him in Moses' own language, the last of the languages.

﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾; i.e., they give glad tidings of Paradise to whoever obeys, and warn of the Fire to whoever disobeys. God intended by the messengers to cut off the argument of one who says: "If a messenger had been sent to me, I would have believed." In a hadith: "There is no one to whom excuse is more beloved than God; therefore He sent down the books and sent the messengers." Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: How can people have an argument against God before the messengers, when they are held accountable by the proofs God set up, whose reflection leads to knowledge, and the messengers themselves did not reach knowledge except by reflecting on those proofs, nor did they know they were messengers of God except by reflecting upon them? I say: The messengers forbid heedlessness and urge reflection, just as you see the scholars of justice and monotheism do, along with conveying what they carried of the detailed matters of religion, explaining the states of obligation, and teaching the laws. So their sending was a removal of the excuse and a completion of the establishment of the proof, lest they say: "Why did You not send us a messenger who would rouse us from the slumber of heedlessness and alert us to what it is obligatory to pay attention to," end quote. His saying "lest" (لِئَلّا) is like a reason for the two states: bearing good news and warning. The good news is of Paradise and the warning is of the Fire. Reward and punishment are not established by reason as obligatory; rather, reason only makes them permissible, and revelation came so that they became necessary to occur, and their obligation was learned only from the good news and the warning. So if the messengers had not given good news of Paradise to whoever complied with the legal obligations, nor warned of the Fire whoever did not comply, and if violations that entail punishment occurred without the obligated person being aware of them, since God does not send anyone to inform him that such is disobedience, then the person would have an argument when punished for something about which he had not been warned in advance regarding its performance and that punishment follows from it. As for the rational proofs God set up, they lead to knowledge and faith in God as is required; and the causes in the verse are other than knowledge and faith in God, so the question of al-Zamakhshari does not arise. The word (رُسُلًا) is in the accusative as an apposition (badal), which al-Zamakhshari expressed as being in the accusative by repetition. He said: The more correct view is that it is in the accusative by praise (madh). Others permitted that it be an object of an implied (arsalna), and that it be a preparatory circumstantial accusative (hal muwatti'a). The (لِئَلّا) is connected to (mundhirin) by the method of verbal government. It is also permitted that it be connected to an implied verb, i.e., "We sent them with that," meaning with the good news and warning, so that there would not be

﴿And God is ever Mighty and Wise﴾ (وكانَ اللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًا); i.e., nothing overpowers Him, and no one has an argument against Him, and His acts issue from wisdom, and so for that reason He cut off the argument by sending the messengers. It was said: Mighty in punishing the disbelievers, and Wise in giving excuse after the warning has preceded.

﴿But God bears witness to what He has sent down to you﴾. The corrective conjunction with (لَكِنْ) requires that an omitted clause precede it, because (لَكِنْ) cannot begin a sentence. So the estimate is what was narrated in the occasion of revelation: when ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾ was revealed, they said: "We do not bear witness to this for you, but God bears witness." God's witness to what He sent down to him is His establishing it by manifesting miracles, just as claims are established by evidence. As-Sulami and al-Jarrah al-Hakami read (لَكِنَّ اللَّهَ) with the shadda and the name of God in the accusative. Al-Hasan read (بِما أُنْزِلُ إلَيْكَ) in the passive voice.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 160–167 (part 3 of 3):

﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾. As-Sulami read: nazzalahu (with the doubled zay, "sent it down" in a gradual manner). Az-Zajjaj said: anzalahu wa-fihi 'ilmuhu (He sent it down, and in it is His knowledge). Abu Sulayman ad-Dimashqi said: anzalahu min 'ilmihi (He sent it down from His knowledge). Ibn Jurayj said: He sent it down to you with knowledge from Him that you are His chosen one from among His creation. It has also been said: He sent it down to you with His knowledge that you are worthy of its descent upon you, owing to your upholding its right, your knowledge of what is in it, your good call to it, and your urging of it. It has been said: with what the servants need. It has also been said: with His knowledge that you will convey it to His servants without alteration, addition, or deficiency. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This verse is among the strongest proofs relied upon by the People of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah) in affirming God's knowledge (ilm), in opposition to the Mu'tazila, who say: "Knowing without knowledge" (alim bila 'ilm). The meaning according to the People of the Sunnah is: He sent it down while knowing its descent and its revelation. The position of the Mu'tazila on this verse is that He sent it down accompanied by His knowledge, that is, that in it is His knowledge of hidden matters and commands and the like; so "knowledge" is an expression for the known things (al-ma'lumat) that are in the Qur'an, as in the saying of Khidr: "My knowledge and your knowledge have not decreased the knowledge of God except as this sparrow decreases this sea." Az-Zamakhshari said: He sent it down combined with His particular knowledge which no one else knows, namely its composition in an arrangement and style which every eloquent person and master of expression is unable to match; and its position relative to what precedes it is the position of an explanatory clause, since it is an explanation of the testimony to its authenticity, that He sent it down in an inimitable arrangement that exceeds all measure. It is also possible that He sent it down while knowing it, watching over it, guarding it from the devils with a watch of angels.

﴿And the angels bear witness﴾; that is, to what God has sent down to you. The angels' testimony follows God's testimony, and He is known to have testified to him by manifesting miracles at his hands. This is a consolation to him concerning the denial of the Jews: if the Jews deny you and deny what you have brought of revelation, do not mind, for God bears witness for you and so do His angels; so do not turn to their denial.

(And God suffices as a witness); that is, even if no one else bears witness. ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say: "God"﴾ [al-An'am: 19].

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of God have certainly strayed far astray﴾; that is, a straying from which their return is not near, nor their escape from it; for he believes about himself that he is right, then uses that straying to acquire wealth and status and to cast others into it, so it is straying in its utmost extent. Ikrima and Ibn Hurmuz read wa-suddu with a damma on the ṣad; it has been said that this refers to the Jews.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 160–167 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them, and because of their hindering many from the way of God,﴾ ﴿and their taking usury, though they had been forbidden it, and their devouring the wealth of people falsely. We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and those who establish the prayer and give the zakat, and those who believe in God and the Last Day: those, We will give them a great reward.﴾ ﴿We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him, and We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon, and We gave David the Psalms.﴾ ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you; and God spoke to Moses directly.﴾ ﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and as warners, so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers. And God is ever Mighty, Wise.﴾ ﴿But God bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness. And God suffices as a witness.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and hindered from the way of God have certainly strayed far astray.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and did wrong, God will not forgive them, nor will He guide them to a path,﴾ ﴿except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is easy for God.﴾ ﴿O mankind, the Messenger has come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe; it is better for you. But if you disbelieve, then indeed, to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and God is ever Knowing, Wise.﴾ ﴿O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion, and do not say about God except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of God and His word which He directed to Mary and a spirit from Him. So believe in God and His messengers, and do not say, "Three"; desist, it is better for you. God is but one God; glory be to Him that He should have a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is God as Trustee.﴾ ﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of God, nor will the angels who are near [to God]. And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant – He will gather them to Himself all together.﴾

*Al-ghuluww* (excess): exceeding the limit. From it comes *ghala al-si'r* (the price rose), and *ghawlat al-sahm* (the range of an arrow). *Al-istinkaf*: disdain and haughtiness, from *nakaftu al-damc* when you wipe away the tear with your finger from your cheek, and when you prevent it from flowing. [A poet] said:

*"So they spent the night; had it not been for remembrance of them from the 'Halq' [a place], a tear would not have been wiped from your eye."*

Abu al-Abbas [al-Mubarrad] was asked about *al-istinkaf*, and he said: "It is from *al-nakf*. It is said: 'He has no *nakf* nor *wakf* in this matter.' *Al-nakf* is that someone says something bad to him, and *istanka/a* means he repelled that evil."

﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ The meaning: "Because of a great wrongdoing," or "Because of wrongdoing of whatever kind." Omitting the adjective when the meaning is understood is permissible, as in the saying: "You have encountered meat – whatever kind of meat, a following one." It is connected to *harramna* (We forbade). The cause is mentioned before the effect to draw attention to the vileness of wrongdoing, to condemn it and to warn against it. The "good things" are those mentioned in His words, "And upon those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws" [6:146]. Milk, some birds and fish were forbidden to them. *Uhillat lahum* (that had been made lawful for them) is a description of *al-tayyibat* (good things) by what they were. This is clarified by the reading of Ibn Abbas: *tayyibatin kanat uhillat lahum* ("good things that had been made lawful for them").

﴿and because of their hindering many from the way of God﴾ That is, many people. So *kathiran* (many) is an object of the verbal noun; al-Tabari went this way. He said: "They hindered a great multitude of people by denying the command of Muhammad." Or it means: "He hindered many." Some have understood it as "a long time."

﴿and their taking usury, though they had been forbidden it﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), which confirms the ugliness of their act and the evil of their conduct, since what God has forbidden must be kept far away. They said: usury is forbidden in all revealed laws.

﴿and their devouring the wealth of people falsely﴾: that is, the bribes they would take from their lowly people in distorting the Scripture. In this verse, the kinds of wrongdoing that necessitated the prohibition of good things are detailed. It was said: whenever they committed a sin, some good things were forbidden to them. The detail of the good things is omitted here; rather they are mentioned indefinitely and vaguely. In [surah] al-Ma'idah, He detailed the kinds of what was forbidden, but did not detail the cause. It is said: "That is because We recompensed them for their transgression." The preposition *ba'* is repeated in *wa-bisaddihim* (and because of their hindering) because it is distant from the thing it is coordinated with, separated by something that is not an object of what it is coordinated with, but rather of the governing word. It is not repeated in *wa-akhdhihim* (and their taking) and *wa-aklihim* (and their devouring), because the separation occurred by the object of what is coordinated. A parallel to repeating and omitting the particle is His words: "So because of their breaking their covenant..." [4:155]. The kinds of wrongdoing begin with what is most important, namely the matter of religion, which is hindering from the way of God; then the matter of worldly affairs, which is harm to some wealth; then he ascended to the most extreme in worldly wealth, which is consuming it falsely, that is, for free, with no exchange.

In mentioning this verse there is a favour upon the community of Muhammad, in that He did not treat them as He treated the Jews, by forbidding them good things in this world as a punishment for their sins.

﴿We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾ When He mentioned the punishment of this world, He mentioned what He had prepared for them in the Hereafter. Since that prohibition was general for the Jews because of the wrongdoing of those among them who did wrong, and its burden fell on their wrongdoers and non-wrongdoers alike, as He said: "And beware of a trial which will not strike only those among you who have done wrong" [8:25], He clarified that the painful punishment was prepared only for the disbelievers among them. For this reason it did not come as "We have prepared for them."

﴿But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and those who establish the prayer and give the zakat, and those who believe in God and the Last Day: those, We will give them a great reward.﴾ The coming of *lakin* (but) here is extremely elegant, because it falls between two opposites and their recompense: the disbelievers with the painful punishment, and the believers with the great reward. *Al-rasikhun* are the firm, the established, the steadfast, those who have insight, among them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like. *Al-mu'minun* (the believers) means among them, or the believers from the Emigrants and the Helpers. Apparently it is general to whoever believes.

*Al-rasikhun* is in the nominative as a beginning (*mubtada'*), and the predicate is *yu'minun* alone, because praise is not complete except after the sentence is complete. Whoever takes the predicate to be *ulaika sanu'tihim* (those, We will give them) has a weak view. *Al-muqimin* is in the accusative on the basis of praise (*al-madh*), and *wa-al-mu'tuna* is also in the nominative by an implied supposition, and they are by way of cutting (*al-qat'*, changing the grammatical case of a descriptive word) to the nominative. It is not permissible to coordinate it with the nominative before it, because when a descriptor is cut off in any part of it, what follows does not return to the case of the described word. This cutting is to show the excellence of the prayer and the zakat; so the description was multiplied by making it into separate clauses.

Ibn Jubayr, Amr ibn Ubayd, al-Jahdari, Isa ibn Umar, Malik ibn Dinar, Ismah from al-A'mash, and Yunus and Harun from Abu Amr read *wa-al-muqimuna* (with *-una* in the nominative) in the nominative, coordinated with the first. It is also so in the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud, as al-Farra' reported. It is narrated that it is so in the Codex of Ubayy. It was also said: rather it is in it *wa-al-muqimina al-salat*, as in the Codex of Uthman. It is reported from Aisha and Aban ibn Uthman that writing it with *ya'* is a scribal error in the codex; but this is not authentically reported from them, because they were both Arabs of eloquent speech; cutting of descriptors is more common in the language of the Arabs, and it is a broad topic, on which Sibawayh and others cited evidence; and Sibawayh explained this as cutting.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "We do not heed what they claim of its being a grammatical error in the orthography of the codex. Perhaps someone who looks in the book, and does not know the ways of the Arabs, might pay attention to it, and what they have in the accusative of specialisation (*al-nasb 'ala al-ikhtisas*) is from misguidance." By this he meant: the foremost early ones, whose likeness is in the Torah and whose likeness is in the Gospel, were more zealous in protecting Islam and in repelling its detractors, than to leave a breach in the Book of God which those after them would have to fill, or a tear which those who come after them would have to mend. End quote. By his words "one who does not look in the Book" he means the Book of Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, since the name *al-Kitab* is a proper name for it. And because of the ignorance of those who venture to interpret the Book of God and analyse its words without the rules of the science of grammar, they allowed several possibilities in the coordination of *wa-al-muqimin*:

First: that it is coordinated with *bima unzila ilayka* (what was sent down to you); that is, "they believe in the Books and in those who establish the prayer." They differed on this view as to who is meant by "those who establish the prayer." It was said: the prophets; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya mentioned this. It was said: the angels; Ibn Atiyya mentioned this. It was said: the Muslims, and the sense is: "and the encouragement of those who establish the prayer"; Ibn Atiyya mentioned its meaning.

Second: that it is coordinated with the pronoun in *minhum* (among them); that is, "those firm in knowledge among them and of those who establish the prayer." Ibn Atiyya mentioned this for a people he did not name.

Third: that it is coordinated with the *ka* in *ulaika* (those); that is, "what is sent down to you and to those who establish the prayer."

Fourth: that it is coordinated with the *ka* in *qablika* (before you), with an elided genitive; the estimate is: "and what was sent down before you," and it was said: "those who establish the prayer."

Fifth: that it is coordinated with the *ka* in *qablika*, meaning the prophets; Ibn Atiyya mentioned this.

Ibn Atiyya said: "There is a difference between the verse and the line of poetry" – meaning the line of al-Khirniq, which he had recited earlier – which is:

*"The ones who alight at every battlefield, and the ones who are good at tying knots of the waistcloths."*

"[The difference is] in the conjunction particle which is in the verse; for it is forbidden by some of them to estimate a verb." In this there is room for consideration. If anyone forbids that, he is refuted by the occurrence of that in the speech of the Arabs with a conjunction particle; and there is no room for consideration in that, as Ibn Atiyya said. The poet said:

*"And he takes refuge with women, bare and dishevelled, nursing infants like the ghouls."*

Likewise they allowed in His words, "and those who give the zakat" several possibilities other than the one we mentioned – namely that it is in the nominative on the predicate of an elided subject, by way of cutting the descriptors for praise:

First: that it is coordinated with *al-rasikhun* (the firm).

Second: on the hidden pronoun in *al-mu'minun* (the believers).

Third: on the pronoun in *yu'minun* (they believe).

Fourth: that it is a subject (*mubtada'*), and what follows it is the predicate, which is the demonstrative *ulaika* and what follows it. As for *al-mu'minuna bi-Allah* (the believers in God), it is coordinated with *wa-al-mu'tuna al-zakat* (and those who give the zakat), on the view we have chosen in raising *wa-al-mu'tuna*.

Since He first mentioned *wa-al-mu'minun* (and the believers), it included belief in what must be believed in. Then He informed about them and about the firm in knowledge that they believe in the Qur'an and in the revealed Books. Then He described them with qualities of praise, from carrying out the noblest of the outward physical attributes of faith, which is the prayer, and the financial one, which is the zakat. Then he ascended in praise to the noblest of the inward doctrinal attributes, which is belief in the One who sent down the Books, and who legislated in them the prayer and the zakat, and belief in the Last Day, which is resurrection and return, in which the fruit of faith appears and the carrying out of the commandments of the Law, such as prayer, zakat and others. Then, having completed that, He informed that He would give them a great reward, which is what He arranged for these glorious attributes with which He described them; and He pointed to them with *ulaika* (those) so as to indicate the totality of those attributes. Whoever parses *wa-al-mu'minuna bi-Allah* as a subject, with what follows as its predicate, is far removed from grasping eloquence. The better parsing is that *ulaika* is a subject. Whoever takes it in the accusative by a supposed verb whose explanation is what follows it – "He will give those, We will give them" – makes it [a case of] *al-ishtighal* (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring to the object, a construction in which the verb is elided and its object is topicalised), so his view is not preferred. This is because "Zayd, I struck him" is more eloquent and more common than "Zayda, a striking of him"; and because the object of what follows the future particle is disputed regarding its permissibility of being fronted in such constructions as "I will strike Zayd." Since that is so, *al-ishtighal* is not permitted. So the better course is to adopt what is not disputed.

Hamza read *sayu'tihim* with *ya'* (the third person), returning to His words, *wa-al-mu'minuna bi-Allah* (and the believers in God). The rest of the seven read it with the first person, by *al-iltifat* (a shift of grammatical person in the middle of a discourse). And [consider] the connection with *wa-a'tadna* (and We have prepared).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 160–167 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾. Ibn Abbas said: The occasion of its revelation was that Sukayn the rabbi and Adiyy ibn Zayd said: "O Muhammad, we do not know that God has sent down anything to a human after Moses, nor revealed to anyone." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: When [the verse] ﴿The People of the Scripture ask you﴾ [al-Nisa 4:153] was revealed, and it was recited to them, and they heard the account of their evil deeds, they said: "God has not sent down anything to a human, nor to Jesus," and they denied all of that. Then [the verse] ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said﴾ [al-An'am 6:91] was revealed, and so on. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾ is a reply to the People of the Scripture regarding their request that the Messenger of God ﷺ bring down a book to them from heaven, and their argument against him that his situation regarding revelation is like that of the other prophets who came before, end quote. He placed Noah first and singled him out from among them in the mention, because he is the second father (of mankind) and the first of the messengers, and his call was general to all who were on the earth at that time, just as the call of Muhammad is general to all who are on the earth.

﴿And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon﴾. God, exalted is He, singled these out for mention, honoring and magnifying them. He began with Abraham because he is the third father. He placed Jesus before those after him to lighten (the burden of) his prophethood, to cut off what the Jews assumed about him, to repel their belief, to magnify him in their eyes, and to make known the breadth of his mission. The lineages of Noah, Abraham and Aaron were mentioned earlier in the lineage of his brother Moses. As for Job, al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn al-Qadi al-Fadil Abd al-Rahim ibn Ali al-Nisaburi mentioned his lineage, saying: Job son of Amus son of Barih son of Tawrum son of al-Is son of Isaac son of Abraham, and his mother was from the descendants of Lot ibn Haran. As for Jonah, he is Jonah son of Matta. Nafi', in the transmission of Ibn Jammaz from him, read (يُونِسُ) with a kasra on the nun, and this is a dialect of some Arabs. al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read it with a fatha, and this is a dialect of some of Uqayl. Some Arabs apply hamza and kasra, and some of Asad apply hamza and damma to the nun. The dialect of the Hijaz is what the majority recited: leaving out the hamza and with a damma on the nun.

﴿And We gave David a Psalter﴾ (وآتَيْنا داوُدَ زَبُورًا), i.e., a book. Every book is called a zabur, but the term became dominant for the book that God revealed to David. It is on the pattern fa'ul with the meaning of maf'ul, like (halub) and (rakub), and it is not a regular pattern. It consists of one hundred and fifty surahs, in which there is no ruling, no prohibition, and no permission; rather, it contains wisdom and admonitions. I have read a portion of it in the lands of al-Andalus. It is said: Solomon was mentioned before David because of the abundance of his knowledge, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿So We gave Solomon understanding of it, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:79]. What appears to be the case is that He combined Jesus, Job and Jonah because they were people of trial and afflictions in this world, and He combined Aaron and Solomon because Aaron was beloved to the Children of Israel, esteemed and preferred, while Solomon was esteemed among the people, dominant over them, and deserving of what God mentioned in His Book; so the two were joined by being beloved and magnified. The mention of David was delayed to honor him by mentioning his book, and by presenting him and his book in a separate clause dedicated to him and to his book. Thus, what he lost of verbal precedence was compensated for by a doubling of moral honor.

Hamza read (زُبُورًا) with a damma on the zay. Abu al-Baqa said: In this there are two possibilities. One: it is a verbal noun like (al-qu'ud), and the revealed book of David is called by it. The second: it is the plural of (zabur) with the augmentative letter, which is the waw, removed. Abu Ali said: Just as they said (tariq) and (turuq), (karawan) and (kurawan), (warshan) and (wurushan), which are pluralized by removing the augmentative letter. What strengthens this interpretation is that broken plural is like diminutive, and this meaning has been regular in the diminutive of truncation, as in (azhar) and (zuhayr), (al-harith) and (huraythh), and (thabit) and (thubayt). The plural is similar to it in analogy, even if it is rarer in usage. Abu Ali said: It is also possible that it is the plural of (zubur), applied to what is written, just as they said: (darb al-amir) and (nasj al-yaman), and just as the written was called (kitab).

﴿And messengers We have related to you before﴾; i.e., We have mentioned their stories to you.

﴿And messengers We have not related to you﴾. It was narrated from the hadith of Abu Dharr that he asked about the messengers, and the Messenger of God ﷺ said to him: "The messengers were three hundred and thirteen." Al-Qurtubi said: This is the most authentic thing transmitted on this matter; al-Ajurri and Abu Hatim al-Busti recorded it in a sound musnad of his. In this hadith of Abu Dharr, he asked him: "How many were the prophets?" He said: "One hundred and twenty-four thousand prophets." It was narrated from Anas that the Messenger of God ﷺ was sent after eight thousand prophets, among them four thousand from the Children of Israel. It was narrated from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he said: The prophets are one million, four hundred thousand and twenty-four thousand. Ibn Atiyya said: What has been mentioned about the number of prophets is not sound, and God knows best their number, end quote.

The accusative of (رُسُلًا) is by an implied verb; i.e., "We have related messengers to you," so it is an instance of al-ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun). The clause ﴿We have related them﴾ explains that omitted verb. Evidence for this is the reading of Ubayy, and (رُسُلٌ) with the nominative in both places, as the subject of a new sentence. The beginning with an indefinite noun is permissible here because it is a place of detail, as they recited: "A garment I wore, and a garment I drag." Imru' al-Qays said:

"On one side, and a side with us that has not changed."

Among the arguments for the accusative over the nominative is that the conjunction is upon a verbal sentence, namely (wa-atayna Dawuda zaburan). Ibn Atiyya said: The nominative is by an implied (hum), i.e., "they are messengers," so in this case ﴿We have related them﴾ is a clause in the position of a qualifier. They also permitted the accusative of (رُسُلًا) for two reasons. One: it is accusative by meaning, because the meaning is: "We sent you and We sent messengers," since the rebuttal to the Jews is in their denial of the sending of messengers and the continuity of revelation.

﴿And God spoke to Moses directly﴾. This is information that God honored Moses by His speech, and it was emphasized by the verbal noun (taklim) to show that the verb occurs in its literal sense and not its figurative sense; this is the most common usage. Emphasis by the verbal noun does come in figurative usage, though rarely. Among that is the saying of Hind daughter of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir al-Ansari:

"The silk wept for Awf, and its skin denied it, and the cloaks of Judham cried out a crying."

Tha'lab said: Were it not for the emphasis by the verbal noun, it would be permissible to say: "I spoke to him for you," meaning "I wrote a note to him" or "I sent a messenger to him." So when He said (taklim), it was nothing but speech heard from God, exalted is He. The question of speech is one that the discussion has been lengthy about, and the scholars of Islam differed concerning it. By this question the science of the foundations of religion was called ('ilm al-kalam), speculative theology, and it is a question investigated in the foundations of religion. Ibrahim ibn Wathhab read (وكَلَّمَ اللَّهَ) with the accusative, so that Moses is the speaker. Among the peculiar tafsirs (exegesis) is that it derives from (al-kalm), wounding, and that its meaning is: "God wounded Moses with the claws of trials and the talons of afflictions." Ka'b said: God spoke to Moses in all the languages, so Moses kept saying: "My Lord, I do not understand," until He spoke to him in Moses' own language, the last of the languages.

﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾; i.e., they give glad tidings of Paradise to whoever obeys, and warn of the Fire to whoever disobeys. God intended by the messengers to cut off the argument of one who says: "If a messenger had been sent to me, I would have believed." In a hadith: "There is no one to whom excuse is more beloved than God; therefore He sent down the books and sent the messengers." Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: How can people have an argument against God before the messengers, when they are held accountable by the proofs God set up, whose reflection leads to knowledge, and the messengers themselves did not reach knowledge except by reflecting on those proofs, nor did they know they were messengers of God except by reflecting upon them? I say: The messengers forbid heedlessness and urge reflection, just as you see the scholars of justice and monotheism do, along with conveying what they carried of the detailed matters of religion, explaining the states of obligation, and teaching the laws. So their sending was a removal of the excuse and a completion of the establishment of the proof, lest they say: "Why did You not send us a messenger who would rouse us from the slumber of heedlessness and alert us to what it is obligatory to pay attention to," end quote. His saying "lest" (لِئَلّا) is like a reason for the two states: bearing good news and warning. The good news is of Paradise and the warning is of the Fire. Reward and punishment are not established by reason as obligatory; rather, reason only makes them permissible, and revelation came so that they became necessary to occur, and their obligation was learned only from the good news and the warning. So if the messengers had not given good news of Paradise to whoever complied with the legal obligations, nor warned of the Fire whoever did not comply, and if violations that entail punishment occurred without the obligated person being aware of them, since God does not send anyone to inform him that such is disobedience, then the person would have an argument when punished for something about which he had not been warned in advance regarding its performance and that punishment follows from it. As for the rational proofs God set up, they lead to knowledge and faith in God as is required; and the causes in the verse are other than knowledge and faith in God, so the question of al-Zamakhshari does not arise. The word (رُسُلًا) is in the accusative as an apposition (badal), which al-Zamakhshari expressed as being in the accusative by repetition. He said: The more correct view is that it is in the accusative by praise (madh). Others permitted that it be an object of an implied (arsalna), and that it be a preparatory circumstantial accusative (hal muwatti'a). The (لِئَلّا) is connected to (mundhirin) by the method of verbal government. It is also permitted that it be connected to an implied verb, i.e., "We sent them with that," meaning with the good news and warning, so that there would not be

﴿And God is ever Mighty and Wise﴾ (وكانَ اللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًا); i.e., nothing overpowers Him, and no one has an argument against Him, and His acts issue from wisdom, and so for that reason He cut off the argument by sending the messengers. It was said: Mighty in punishing the disbelievers, and Wise in giving excuse after the warning has preceded.

﴿But God bears witness to what He has sent down to you﴾. The corrective conjunction with (لَكِنْ) requires that an omitted clause precede it, because (لَكِنْ) cannot begin a sentence. So the estimate is what was narrated in the occasion of revelation: when ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾ was revealed, they said: "We do not bear witness to this for you, but God bears witness." God's witness to what He sent down to him is His establishing it by manifesting miracles, just as claims are established by evidence. As-Sulami and al-Jarrah al-Hakami read (لَكِنَّ اللَّهَ) with the shadda and the name of God in the accusative. Al-Hasan read (بِما أُنْزِلُ إلَيْكَ) in the passive voice.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 160–167 (part 3 of 3):

﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾. As-Sulami read: nazzalahu (with the doubled zay, "sent it down" in a gradual manner). Az-Zajjaj said: anzalahu wa-fihi 'ilmuhu (He sent it down, and in it is His knowledge). Abu Sulayman ad-Dimashqi said: anzalahu min 'ilmihi (He sent it down from His knowledge). Ibn Jurayj said: He sent it down to you with knowledge from Him that you are His chosen one from among His creation. It has also been said: He sent it down to you with His knowledge that you are worthy of its descent upon you, owing to your upholding its right, your knowledge of what is in it, your good call to it, and your urging of it. It has been said: with what the servants need. It has also been said: with His knowledge that you will convey it to His servants without alteration, addition, or deficiency. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This verse is among the strongest proofs relied upon by the People of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah) in affirming God's knowledge (ilm), in opposition to the Mu'tazila, who say: "Knowing without knowledge" (alim bila 'ilm). The meaning according to the People of the Sunnah is: He sent it down while knowing its descent and its revelation. The position of the Mu'tazila on this verse is that He sent it down accompanied by His knowledge, that is, that in it is His knowledge of hidden matters and commands and the like; so "knowledge" is an expression for the known things (al-ma'lumat) that are in the Qur'an, as in the saying of Khidr: "My knowledge and your knowledge have not decreased the knowledge of God except as this sparrow decreases this sea." Az-Zamakhshari said: He sent it down combined with His particular knowledge which no one else knows, namely its composition in an arrangement and style which every eloquent person and master of expression is unable to match; and its position relative to what precedes it is the position of an explanatory clause, since it is an explanation of the testimony to its authenticity, that He sent it down in an inimitable arrangement that exceeds all measure. It is also possible that He sent it down while knowing it, watching over it, guarding it from the devils with a watch of angels.

﴿And the angels bear witness﴾; that is, to what God has sent down to you. The angels' testimony follows God's testimony, and He is known to have testified to him by manifesting miracles at his hands. This is a consolation to him concerning the denial of the Jews: if the Jews deny you and deny what you have brought of revelation, do not mind, for God bears witness for you and so do His angels; so do not turn to their denial.

(And God suffices as a witness); that is, even if no one else bears witness. ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say: "God"﴾ [al-An'am: 19].

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of God have certainly strayed far astray﴾; that is, a straying from which their return is not near, nor their escape from it; for he believes about himself that he is right, then uses that straying to acquire wealth and status and to cast others into it, so it is straying in its utmost extent. Ikrima and Ibn Hurmuz read wa-suddu with a damma on the ṣad; it has been said that this refers to the Jews.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 160–167 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them, and because of their hindering many from the way of God,﴾ ﴿and their taking usury, though they had been forbidden it, and their devouring the wealth of people falsely. We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and those who establish the prayer and give the zakat, and those who believe in God and the Last Day: those, We will give them a great reward.﴾ ﴿We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him, and We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon, and We gave David the Psalms.﴾ ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you; and God spoke to Moses directly.﴾ ﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and as warners, so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers. And God is ever Mighty, Wise.﴾ ﴿But God bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness. And God suffices as a witness.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and hindered from the way of God have certainly strayed far astray.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and did wrong, God will not forgive them, nor will He guide them to a path,﴾ ﴿except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is easy for God.﴾ ﴿O mankind, the Messenger has come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe; it is better for you. But if you disbelieve, then indeed, to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and God is ever Knowing, Wise.﴾ ﴿O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion, and do not say about God except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of God and His word which He directed to Mary and a spirit from Him. So believe in God and His messengers, and do not say, "Three"; desist, it is better for you. God is but one God; glory be to Him that He should have a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is God as Trustee.﴾ ﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of God, nor will the angels who are near [to God]. And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant – He will gather them to Himself all together.﴾

*Al-ghuluww* (excess): exceeding the limit. From it comes *ghala al-si'r* (the price rose), and *ghawlat al-sahm* (the range of an arrow). *Al-istinkaf*: disdain and haughtiness, from *nakaftu al-damc* when you wipe away the tear with your finger from your cheek, and when you prevent it from flowing. [A poet] said:

*"So they spent the night; had it not been for remembrance of them from the 'Halq' [a place], a tear would not have been wiped from your eye."*

Abu al-Abbas [al-Mubarrad] was asked about *al-istinkaf*, and he said: "It is from *al-nakf*. It is said: 'He has no *nakf* nor *wakf* in this matter.' *Al-nakf* is that someone says something bad to him, and *istanka/a* means he repelled that evil."

﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ The meaning: "Because of a great wrongdoing," or "Because of wrongdoing of whatever kind." Omitting the adjective when the meaning is understood is permissible, as in the saying: "You have encountered meat – whatever kind of meat, a following one." It is connected to *harramna* (We forbade). The cause is mentioned before the effect to draw attention to the vileness of wrongdoing, to condemn it and to warn against it. The "good things" are those mentioned in His words, "And upon those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws" [6:146]. Milk, some birds and fish were forbidden to them. *Uhillat lahum* (that had been made lawful for them) is a description of *al-tayyibat* (good things) by what they were. This is clarified by the reading of Ibn Abbas: *tayyibatin kanat uhillat lahum* ("good things that had been made lawful for them").

﴿and because of their hindering many from the way of God﴾ That is, many people. So *kathiran* (many) is an object of the verbal noun; al-Tabari went this way. He said: "They hindered a great multitude of people by denying the command of Muhammad." Or it means: "He hindered many." Some have understood it as "a long time."

﴿and their taking usury, though they had been forbidden it﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), which confirms the ugliness of their act and the evil of their conduct, since what God has forbidden must be kept far away. They said: usury is forbidden in all revealed laws.

﴿and their devouring the wealth of people falsely﴾: that is, the bribes they would take from their lowly people in distorting the Scripture. In this verse, the kinds of wrongdoing that necessitated the prohibition of good things are detailed. It was said: whenever they committed a sin, some good things were forbidden to them. The detail of the good things is omitted here; rather they are mentioned indefinitely and vaguely. In [surah] al-Ma'idah, He detailed the kinds of what was forbidden, but did not detail the cause. It is said: "That is because We recompensed them for their transgression." The preposition *ba'* is repeated in *wa-bisaddihim* (and because of their hindering) because it is distant from the thing it is coordinated with, separated by something that is not an object of what it is coordinated with, but rather of the governing word. It is not repeated in *wa-akhdhihim* (and their taking) and *wa-aklihim* (and their devouring), because the separation occurred by the object of what is coordinated. A parallel to repeating and omitting the particle is His words: "So because of their breaking their covenant..." [4:155]. The kinds of wrongdoing begin with what is most important, namely the matter of religion, which is hindering from the way of God; then the matter of worldly affairs, which is harm to some wealth; then he ascended to the most extreme in worldly wealth, which is consuming it falsely, that is, for free, with no exchange.

In mentioning this verse there is a favour upon the community of Muhammad, in that He did not treat them as He treated the Jews, by forbidding them good things in this world as a punishment for their sins.

﴿We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾ When He mentioned the punishment of this world, He mentioned what He had prepared for them in the Hereafter. Since that prohibition was general for the Jews because of the wrongdoing of those among them who did wrong, and its burden fell on their wrongdoers and non-wrongdoers alike, as He said: "And beware of a trial which will not strike only those among you who have done wrong" [8:25], He clarified that the painful punishment was prepared only for the disbelievers among them. For this reason it did not come as "We have prepared for them."

﴿But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and those who establish the prayer and give the zakat, and those who believe in God and the Last Day: those, We will give them a great reward.﴾ The coming of *lakin* (but) here is extremely elegant, because it falls between two opposites and their recompense: the disbelievers with the painful punishment, and the believers with the great reward. *Al-rasikhun* are the firm, the established, the steadfast, those who have insight, among them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like. *Al-mu'minun* (the believers) means among them, or the believers from the Emigrants and the Helpers. Apparently it is general to whoever believes.

*Al-rasikhun* is in the nominative as a beginning (*mubtada'*), and the predicate is *yu'minun* alone, because praise is not complete except after the sentence is complete. Whoever takes the predicate to be *ulaika sanu'tihim* (those, We will give them) has a weak view. *Al-muqimin* is in the accusative on the basis of praise (*al-madh*), and *wa-al-mu'tuna* is also in the nominative by an implied supposition, and they are by way of cutting (*al-qat'*, changing the grammatical case of a descriptive word) to the nominative. It is not permissible to coordinate it with the nominative before it, because when a descriptor is cut off in any part of it, what follows does not return to the case of the described word. This cutting is to show the excellence of the prayer and the zakat; so the description was multiplied by making it into separate clauses.

Ibn Jubayr, Amr ibn Ubayd, al-Jahdari, Isa ibn Umar, Malik ibn Dinar, Ismah from al-A'mash, and Yunus and Harun from Abu Amr read *wa-al-muqimuna* (with *-una* in the nominative) in the nominative, coordinated with the first. It is also so in the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud, as al-Farra' reported. It is narrated that it is so in the Codex of Ubayy. It was also said: rather it is in it *wa-al-muqimina al-salat*, as in the Codex of Uthman. It is reported from Aisha and Aban ibn Uthman that writing it with *ya'* is a scribal error in the codex; but this is not authentically reported from them, because they were both Arabs of eloquent speech; cutting of descriptors is more common in the language of the Arabs, and it is a broad topic, on which Sibawayh and others cited evidence; and Sibawayh explained this as cutting.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "We do not heed what they claim of its being a grammatical error in the orthography of the codex. Perhaps someone who looks in the book, and does not know the ways of the Arabs, might pay attention to it, and what they have in the accusative of specialisation (*al-nasb 'ala al-ikhtisas*) is from misguidance." By this he meant: the foremost early ones, whose likeness is in the Torah and whose likeness is in the Gospel, were more zealous in protecting Islam and in repelling its detractors, than to leave a breach in the Book of God which those after them would have to fill, or a tear which those who come after them would have to mend. End quote. By his words "one who does not look in the Book" he means the Book of Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, since the name *al-Kitab* is a proper name for it. And because of the ignorance of those who venture to interpret the Book of God and analyse its words without the rules of the science of grammar, they allowed several possibilities in the coordination of *wa-al-muqimin*:

First: that it is coordinated with *bima unzila ilayka* (what was sent down to you); that is, "they believe in the Books and in those who establish the prayer." They differed on this view as to who is meant by "those who establish the prayer." It was said: the prophets; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya mentioned this. It was said: the angels; Ibn Atiyya mentioned this. It was said: the Muslims, and the sense is: "and the encouragement of those who establish the prayer"; Ibn Atiyya mentioned its meaning.

Second: that it is coordinated with the pronoun in *minhum* (among them); that is, "those firm in knowledge among them and of those who establish the prayer." Ibn Atiyya mentioned this for a people he did not name.

Third: that it is coordinated with the *ka* in *ulaika* (those); that is, "what is sent down to you and to those who establish the prayer."

Fourth: that it is coordinated with the *ka* in *qablika* (before you), with an elided genitive; the estimate is: "and what was sent down before you," and it was said: "those who establish the prayer."

Fifth: that it is coordinated with the *ka* in *qablika*, meaning the prophets; Ibn Atiyya mentioned this.

Ibn Atiyya said: "There is a difference between the verse and the line of poetry" – meaning the line of al-Khirniq, which he had recited earlier – which is:

*"The ones who alight at every battlefield, and the ones who are good at tying knots of the waistcloths."*

"[The difference is] in the conjunction particle which is in the verse; for it is forbidden by some of them to estimate a verb." In this there is room for consideration. If anyone forbids that, he is refuted by the occurrence of that in the speech of the Arabs with a conjunction particle; and there is no room for consideration in that, as Ibn Atiyya said. The poet said:

*"And he takes refuge with women, bare and dishevelled, nursing infants like the ghouls."*

Likewise they allowed in His words, "and those who give the zakat" several possibilities other than the one we mentioned – namely that it is in the nominative on the predicate of an elided subject, by way of cutting the descriptors for praise:

First: that it is coordinated with *al-rasikhun* (the firm).

Second: on the hidden pronoun in *al-mu'minun* (the believers).

Third: on the pronoun in *yu'minun* (they believe).

Fourth: that it is a subject (*mubtada'*), and what follows it is the predicate, which is the demonstrative *ulaika* and what follows it. As for *al-mu'minuna bi-Allah* (the believers in God), it is coordinated with *wa-al-mu'tuna al-zakat* (and those who give the zakat), on the view we have chosen in raising *wa-al-mu'tuna*.

Since He first mentioned *wa-al-mu'minun* (and the believers), it included belief in what must be believed in. Then He informed about them and about the firm in knowledge that they believe in the Qur'an and in the revealed Books. Then He described them with qualities of praise, from carrying out the noblest of the outward physical attributes of faith, which is the prayer, and the financial one, which is the zakat. Then he ascended in praise to the noblest of the inward doctrinal attributes, which is belief in the One who sent down the Books, and who legislated in them the prayer and the zakat, and belief in the Last Day, which is resurrection and return, in which the fruit of faith appears and the carrying out of the commandments of the Law, such as prayer, zakat and others. Then, having completed that, He informed that He would give them a great reward, which is what He arranged for these glorious attributes with which He described them; and He pointed to them with *ulaika* (those) so as to indicate the totality of those attributes. Whoever parses *wa-al-mu'minuna bi-Allah* as a subject, with what follows as its predicate, is far removed from grasping eloquence. The better parsing is that *ulaika* is a subject. Whoever takes it in the accusative by a supposed verb whose explanation is what follows it – "He will give those, We will give them" – makes it [a case of] *al-ishtighal* (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring to the object, a construction in which the verb is elided and its object is topicalised), so his view is not preferred. This is because "Zayd, I struck him" is more eloquent and more common than "Zayda, a striking of him"; and because the object of what follows the future particle is disputed regarding its permissibility of being fronted in such constructions as "I will strike Zayd." Since that is so, *al-ishtighal* is not permitted. So the better course is to adopt what is not disputed.

Hamza read *sayu'tihim* with *ya'* (the third person), returning to His words, *wa-al-mu'minuna bi-Allah* (and the believers in God). The rest of the seven read it with the first person, by *al-iltifat* (a shift of grammatical person in the middle of a discourse). And [consider] the connection with *wa-a'tadna* (and We have prepared).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 160–167 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾. Ibn Abbas said: The occasion of its revelation was that Sukayn the rabbi and Adiyy ibn Zayd said: "O Muhammad, we do not know that God has sent down anything to a human after Moses, nor revealed to anyone." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: When [the verse] ﴿The People of the Scripture ask you﴾ [al-Nisa 4:153] was revealed, and it was recited to them, and they heard the account of their evil deeds, they said: "God has not sent down anything to a human, nor to Jesus," and they denied all of that. Then [the verse] ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said﴾ [al-An'am 6:91] was revealed, and so on. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾ is a reply to the People of the Scripture regarding their request that the Messenger of God ﷺ bring down a book to them from heaven, and their argument against him that his situation regarding revelation is like that of the other prophets who came before, end quote. He placed Noah first and singled him out from among them in the mention, because he is the second father (of mankind) and the first of the messengers, and his call was general to all who were on the earth at that time, just as the call of Muhammad is general to all who are on the earth.

﴿And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon﴾. God, exalted is He, singled these out for mention, honoring and magnifying them. He began with Abraham because he is the third father. He placed Jesus before those after him to lighten (the burden of) his prophethood, to cut off what the Jews assumed about him, to repel their belief, to magnify him in their eyes, and to make known the breadth of his mission. The lineages of Noah, Abraham and Aaron were mentioned earlier in the lineage of his brother Moses. As for Job, al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn al-Qadi al-Fadil Abd al-Rahim ibn Ali al-Nisaburi mentioned his lineage, saying: Job son of Amus son of Barih son of Tawrum son of al-Is son of Isaac son of Abraham, and his mother was from the descendants of Lot ibn Haran. As for Jonah, he is Jonah son of Matta. Nafi', in the transmission of Ibn Jammaz from him, read (يُونِسُ) with a kasra on the nun, and this is a dialect of some Arabs. al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read it with a fatha, and this is a dialect of some of Uqayl. Some Arabs apply hamza and kasra, and some of Asad apply hamza and damma to the nun. The dialect of the Hijaz is what the majority recited: leaving out the hamza and with a damma on the nun.

﴿And We gave David a Psalter﴾ (وآتَيْنا داوُدَ زَبُورًا), i.e., a book. Every book is called a zabur, but the term became dominant for the book that God revealed to David. It is on the pattern fa'ul with the meaning of maf'ul, like (halub) and (rakub), and it is not a regular pattern. It consists of one hundred and fifty surahs, in which there is no ruling, no prohibition, and no permission; rather, it contains wisdom and admonitions. I have read a portion of it in the lands of al-Andalus. It is said: Solomon was mentioned before David because of the abundance of his knowledge, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿So We gave Solomon understanding of it, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:79]. What appears to be the case is that He combined Jesus, Job and Jonah because they were people of trial and afflictions in this world, and He combined Aaron and Solomon because Aaron was beloved to the Children of Israel, esteemed and preferred, while Solomon was esteemed among the people, dominant over them, and deserving of what God mentioned in His Book; so the two were joined by being beloved and magnified. The mention of David was delayed to honor him by mentioning his book, and by presenting him and his book in a separate clause dedicated to him and to his book. Thus, what he lost of verbal precedence was compensated for by a doubling of moral honor.

Hamza read (زُبُورًا) with a damma on the zay. Abu al-Baqa said: In this there are two possibilities. One: it is a verbal noun like (al-qu'ud), and the revealed book of David is called by it. The second: it is the plural of (zabur) with the augmentative letter, which is the waw, removed. Abu Ali said: Just as they said (tariq) and (turuq), (karawan) and (kurawan), (warshan) and (wurushan), which are pluralized by removing the augmentative letter. What strengthens this interpretation is that broken plural is like diminutive, and this meaning has been regular in the diminutive of truncation, as in (azhar) and (zuhayr), (al-harith) and (huraythh), and (thabit) and (thubayt). The plural is similar to it in analogy, even if it is rarer in usage. Abu Ali said: It is also possible that it is the plural of (zubur), applied to what is written, just as they said: (darb al-amir) and (nasj al-yaman), and just as the written was called (kitab).

﴿And messengers We have related to you before﴾; i.e., We have mentioned their stories to you.

﴿And messengers We have not related to you﴾.
