﴿And that is ever easy for Allah﴾ [an-Nisa: 30]; that is, the withholding of His forgiveness, His guidance to them, and their being cast into the Fire is easy, with nothing to divert Him from it. This is a belittling of their affair, and that He, exalted is He, does not care for them and does not mind them.

O People, the Messenger has come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe; it is better for you. ﴿O mankind, the Messenger has come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe; it is better for you.﴾ This is an address to all people. Although the sura is Medinan, the command is general. Had it been specific to a legal obligation, the address would generally have been directed to the believers. Here "the Messenger" means Muhammad, and "the truth" is his sharia (revealed law). It has been interpreted as the Qur'an, as the religion, and as the testimony of monotheism. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning the polytheists.

Regarding the accusative (nasb) of ﴿khayran lakum﴾ (better for you) here, and in His saying ﴿Desist; it is better for you﴾ [An-Nisa: 171], there are three views on what the governing element is (the "nasib"):

The view of al-Khalil (Khalil ibn Ahmad) and Sibawayh is that it is governed by a verb that must be elided: "wa'tu khayran lakum" (وأْتُوا خَيْرًا لَكم), meaning "bring about what is better for you."

The view of al-Kisa'i and Abu Ubayda is that it is governed by "yakun" (يَكُنْ), "let it be," with the verb elided, as in ﴿if he be﴾ [An-Nisa: 135], so the sense is "let it be better for you."

The view of al-Farra' is that it is "iman khayran lakum" (إيمانًا خَيْرًا لَكم), "faith that is better for you," and "intiha'an khayran lakum" (انْتِهاءً خَيْرًا لَكم), "cessation that is better for you," with "khayran" being an adjective (na't) of an elided verbal noun (masdar) that is indicated by the preceding verb.

The preference among these views is discussed in the science of grammar (nahw).

﴿But if you disbelieve, then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾. The explanation of the like of this has already been given.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [An-Nisa: 17]: Knowing of what will come from you of disbelief and faith, and so He will recompense you for it; Wise in His imposing of obligations upon you, along with His exalted knowledge of what will come from you.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 4, Verse 171:**

﴿O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion﴾. It was said that it was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran; this is what Muqatil said. The majority of scholars said: it concerns Christians in general, for they believe in the *al-thalut* (the Trinity), saying: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God. It was also said that it concerns both the Jews and the Christians, and that He forbade them from transgressing the limit. The meaning is: in your religion which you are required to follow. The reference is not to their misguided religion, nor were they commanded to remain steadfast in it without excess. Rather, they were commanded to abandon excess in the religion of God absolutely. The Jews exceeded the limit in belittling Jesus, peace be upon him, removing him from his rank by claiming that he was born outside of lawful wedlock. The Christians exceeded the limit regarding him by making him a god. What appears is that His saying *O People of the Scripture* is addressed to the Christians, as indicated by the end of the verse. When God, exalted is He, answered the doubts of the Jews, who exaggerated in criticizing the Messiah, He turned to the matter of the Christians, who go to extremes in exalting the Messiah, to the point that they attributed to him what they attributed.

﴿And do not say about God except the truth﴾, which is to declare Him free from partners, offspring, indwelling (*hulul*), and union (*ittihad*).

﴿The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was but a messenger of God and His word which He directed to Mary and a soul (*ruh*) from Him﴾. Ja'far ibn Muhammad recited *innama al-Missih* on the pattern of *al-Sikkit* (i.e., with a doubled *sin*). The explanation of the word *kalima* (word) has already been given at *a word from Him whose name is the Messiah* (Al-Imran 3:45). Its meaning, *He directed it to Mary*, is that He brought this event into being in Mary and produced it within her. This clause was said to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*). It was also said to be a descriptive clause (*sifa*), on the assumption of intending separation, meaning: and a word from Him. The meaning of *a soul from Him* is that it proceeds from Him, because he is a living being who came into existence without being a part of a living being, like a drop of sperm separated from a living father; rather, he was originated by a unique origination from God and His power.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: Jesus is a soul from among the souls of God, exalted is He, whom He created and caused to speak by His saying: *Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes* (Al-A'raf 7:172). God sent him to Mary, and he entered (her).

Al-Tabari and Abu Rawq said: *and a soul from Him* means a breath from Him, since it came from Gabriel by His command. [Abu Hayyan] recited the verse of Dhu al-Rumma:

> *I said to him: "Gather it to yourself and give it life with your soul, and make for it a wick (qiyta) of a sparkling spark."*

He describes the falling of a spark of fire. It was called a *ruh* (soul) because it came into being from the breath of Gabriel.

It was also said: the meaning of *a soul from Him* is mercy. Compare *and He supported them with a soul from Him* (Al-Mujadila 58:22).

It was said: he was called a *ruh* because people are given life through him, just as they live by souls; for this reason the Qur'an is also called a *ruh*.

It was said: what is meant by *ruh* here is revelation, that is: and a revelation to Gabriel by breathing into her garment, or to the very being of Jesus: *Be!* And *ruh* is indefinite (*nakkara*) because the meaning is on the assumption of a description, not on the absolute sense of *ruh*; that is: a soul that is noble and precious from Him, exalted is He.

The particle *min* here is for the beginning of the limit (*ibtida' al-ghaya*), and it is not for partition (*tab'id*), as some Christians understood, who claimed that Jesus is a part of God, exalted is He. Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Wafid al-Marwazi refuted him when the Christian argued that the Qur'an contains what supports his doctrine, namely His saying: *and a soul from Him*. Ibn Wafid answered him with His saying: *And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all from Him* (Al-Jathiya 45:13). He said: if by this it must be that Jesus is a part of Him, then it must be that whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth is a part of Him. The Christian was silenced and embraced Islam. At that time Ibn Fayid composed the book *al-Nazair*.

*So believe in God and His messengers*, that is, those among whom are Jesus and Muhammad, upon both of them be peace.

﴿And do not say: Three﴾: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: the gods are three.

Al-Zamakhshari said: What the Qur'an indicates is the explicit statement from them that God, the Messiah, and Mary are three gods, and that the Messiah is the son of God from Mary. Do you not see His saying: *Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God?"* (Al-Ma'ida 5:116). The Christians said: The Messiah is the son of God. What is well-known and widely reported from them is that they say: in the Messiah there is divinity (*lahutiyya*) and humanity (*nasutiyya*), from the side of the Father and the mother. What indicates this is His saying: *The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary*, for it establishes that he is a son of Mary, connected to her in the way children are connected to their mothers, and that his connection to God, mighty and majestic is He, is because He is His messenger, and that he exists by His command; and that His originating him as a living body without a father negates that he is connected to Him in the way sons are connected to fathers. And His saying: *Glory be to Him that He should have a son* (An-Nisa 4:171), and God's report is more reliable than the report of others. This which al-Zamakhshari preferred is the view of Ibn Abbas, who said, meaning by the Trinity: God, exalted is He, and His wife, and His son.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: If the report about them is correct, that they say He is one substance (*jawhar*) with three hypostases (*aqanim*): the hypostasis of the Father, the hypostasis of the Son, and the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit; and that by the hypostasis of the Father they mean the Essence, by the hypostasis of the Son they mean Knowledge, and by the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit they mean Life, then its implied meaning is: God is three. End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that the implied meaning is: the Worshipped is three, or the gods are three, or the hypostases are three. And however the varied expressions of the Christians branch out, they differ according to that assumption. End of quotation.

Al-Zajjaj said: Its implied meaning is: gods, three. Al-Farra' and Abu Ubayd said: its implied meaning is: three, like His saying: *They will say: "They are three"* (Al-Kahf 18:22). Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: the implied meaning is: God is the third of three; the subject and the attributive noun (*mudaf*) are omitted. End of quotation. Abu Ali intended to agree with His saying: *They have certainly disbelieved who say: Indeed, God is the third of three* (Al-Ma'ida 5:73), that is: one of three gods.

What appears is that what they affirmed is the opposite of what is affirmed in the verse; and what is affirmed in the verse by way of restriction (*hasr*) is only the oneness of God, exalted is He, and His being declared free from having a son. So the implied meaning would be: Do not say, "God is three." The view of Abu Ali is preferred because it agrees with the verse we have mentioned, and with the saying of God, exalted is He: *Glory be to Him that He should have a son*. And although the sects of the Christians differ, they are all in agreement on the Trinity.

﴿Desist; it is better for you﴾. The discussion of the accusative *khayran* (better) has already been given. Al-Zamakhshari, in explaining the view of Sibawayh regarding its accusative case, said: when it urged them to faith, meaning in His saying *So believe; it is better for you* (An-Nisa 4:170), and to desisting from the Trinity, meaning in His saying *Desist; it is better for you*, it was known that He was leading them toward an action, so He said: *better for you*; that is: (pursue and bring about) what is better for you than what you are in of disbelief and Trinity, which is faith and monotheism. End of quotation. This is Sibawayh's explanation of the verse.

﴿Indeed, God is but one God﴾. Ibn Atiyya said: *innama* in this verse is restrictive (*hasira*); the meaning of the subject under discussion required that by reason, but the form *innama* does not by its structure require restriction. Rather, it is suited to restriction and to emphasis on the attribute, even when there is no restriction, as in: *Innama al-shuja'u 'Antara* ("The brave one is only 'Antara"), and other examples. End of his statement. Our discussion of *innama* was already extensively given in His saying: *We are only reformers* (Al-Baqara 2:11). Ibn Atiyya's statement here, that by its form it does not require restriction, is correct, although it is contrary to what is in the minds of many people.

﴿Glory be to Him that He should have a son﴾: its meaning is: declaring Him free from and exalting Him above having a son, as the Christians claim about Him, since they transferred the fatherhood of compassion and tenderness to the fatherhood of procreation. Al-Hasan recited *in yakunu lahu walad* with a kasra on the hamza and a damma on the nun of *yakunu*, on the basis that *in* is a negative particle; that is: a son is not to be had by Him. Thus the statement is a declaration of freedom from the Trinity and an informing of the negation of offspring, so the utterance is two sentences. In the recitation of the majority it is one sentence.

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: an announcement of His ownership of everything in them, so His ownership encompasses Jesus and others. Whatever is owned cannot be a part of the owner, given that partness is valid only for a body, while God, exalted is He, is declared free from body and accident.

﴿And sufficient is God as Disposer of affairs﴾ (An-Nisa 4:81): that is, sufficient in managing and preserving His creation, so there is no need for a consort, a son, or a helper. It was said: its meaning is: a guarantor for His allies. It was also said: the meaning is that creation entrusts their affairs to Him, so He is free of them, and they are poor in need of Him.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 4, verses 172–173:**

﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor will the angels brought near.﴾ It is narrated that "a delegation from Najran said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Why do you denounce our companion?' He said: 'And who is your companion?' They said: 'Isa.' He said: 'And what should I say?' They said: 'Say that he is the servant of Allah and His Messenger.' He said: 'There is no shame in his being a servant.' They said: 'Yes.'" Then it was revealed. That is: Isa does not disdain this, so do not you disdain it on his behalf. Had it been a matter for disdain, he would have been more entitled to disdain it, because shame clings more closely to him. That is: he will not be too proud, nor exalt himself, nor become arrogant. Ali read *ʿUbaydan lillah* (with the diminutive form). "Those brought near" means the *Karubiyyun* (the angels closest to the Throne), such as Jibril, Mikail, Israfil, and those in their rank, as al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn Abbas said they are the bearers of the Throne. al-Dahhak said they are those nearest to the seventh heaven. End of quotation. They are joined to Isa because some disbelievers worship the angels.

There is an ellipsis in the sentence. The estimated meaning is: "nor will the angels brought near disdain to be servants of Allah." If *ʿabd* is taken to mean "owned by Allah," then this estimate is not needed, and in that case *wa-la al-malaʾikatu* is a coordination of single words (*ʿatf al-mufradat*). Otherwise, if the unity of *ʿabd* is considered, then *wa-la al-malaʾikatu* is a coordination of clauses (*ʿatf al-jumal*) because the predicate differs. If the meaning of *wa-la al-malaʾikatu* is taken to be "nor any one of the angels," then it is a coordination of single words.

Some people have clung to this verse to claim that the angels are superior to the prophets. Ibn Atiyya said: "*Wa-la al-malaʾikatu al-muqarrabun*" adds weight to the argument and brings it closer to the mind. That is: nor do those who are at the highest ranks of created beings disdain this. How then could anyone else? In this verse there is clear evidence for the superiority of the angels over the prophets. End of quotation.

al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, 'From where does the words of the Exalted, *wa-la al-malaʾikatu al-muqarrabun*, indicate that the meaning is "nor those above him"?' I say: from the fact that the science of meanings (*ʿilm al-maʿani*, the branch of Arabic rhetoric) does not require anything else. The speech was only directed to refute the doctrine of the Christians and their excess in raising the Messiah above the rank of servanthood. So it was necessary to say to them: Isa will not rise above servanthood, nor will one who is higher than him in rank. As if it were said: the angels brought near will not disdain servanthood, so how about the Messiah? And the specification of 'those brought near' clearly and manifestly indicates this, because they are the highest of the angels in rank and the most exalted in station. An example of this is the saying of a poet:

*"Nor is his like among those who are generous like Hatim, nor is the sea with its waves surging in its depths."*

There is no doubt that he intended by 'the sea with its waves' what is above Hatim in generosity. Whoever has taste, let him taste with this verse the Exalted's words: *"Never will the Jews be pleased with you, nor the Christians"* (2:120), until he recognizes the clear distinction." End of his words.

The preference between prophets and angels is known only through revelation (*al-samʿ*), since we do not perceive the aspect of preference by reason. As for this verse, it may be said: whenever something is negated of two things, that does not indicate that the second is higher than the first, nor that this is a matter of gradual ascent (*al-tarakki*). If you say, "So-and-so will not disdain to prostrate to Allah, nor will ʿAmr," there is no indication in it that ʿAmr is superior to Zayd. Even if we accept that, the verse is not of this kind, because it set a singular against a plural, and did not set a singular against a singular, nor a plural against a plural. It may be said: the plural is superior to the singular, and the verse does not necessarily imply the preference of a plural over a plural, nor of a singular over a singular. And even if we accept that the conjoined term in the verse is higher than the term it is conjoined to, that would be according to what has been instilled in the minds of the Arabs and others of exalting the angel and raising him up, to the extent that they deny humanity to the one they praise and affirm angelhood for him. Their imagining that does not indicate that in reality he is superior and greater in reward. Among what was reported in accordance with what was instilled in minds is the saying of the Exalted, quoting the women who were struck by Yusuf's beauty: *"When they saw him, they were amazed at him and cut their hands, and said, 'Allah forbid! This is not a human; this is none but a noble angel'"* (12:31). And the poet said:

*"You are not a human, but an angel descended from the depths of the sky, bringing down (blessings)."*

al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, 'On what is *wa-la al-malaʾikatu al-muqarrabun* conjoined?' I say: either it is conjoined to *al-Masih*, or to the subject of *yakuna* (the pronoun in it), or to the implicit pronoun in *ʿabdan*, because of what it contains of the sense of description, as it indicates the meaning of worship. Your saying, 'I passed by a man, a servant whose father is...' Conjoining to *al-Masih* is the most apparent, because the other options lead to something with some deviation from the purpose, which is that the Messiah does not disdain to be (he and whoever is above him described as) servants, or to worship Allah (he and whoever is above him)." End of his words.

The deviation from the purpose he pointed to is that disdain would be specific to the Messiah, whereas the established meaning is that the angels share with the Messiah in the absence of disdain for servanthood. For it does not necessarily follow from his disdaining alone that he and the angels would be servants, or that he and they would worship their Lord, if they (the angels) disdained it. A person may be content that he and Zayd strike ʿAmr, but Zayd is not content with that. The preference between the two options is also apparent from the use of *la* (not). If the conjunction were intended to be with the pronoun in *yakuna*, or with the implicit pronoun in *ʿabdan*, *la* would not have been used. Rather the construction would have been without it. You say: "Zayd does not want him and his father to be standing," and you say: "Zayd does not want him and ʿAmr to reconcile." These and similar constructions are not places where *la* is used. So if *la* is found in Arabic usage in something like this, it is superfluous (*zaʾida*).

﴿As for whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant, He will gather them all to Himself.﴾ The pronoun in *yastankif* and *yastakbir* was first taken to agree with the wording of *man* (singular), then it was taken to agree with its meaning in *fa-sayahshuruhum* (plural). The pronoun refers to the meaning of *man*; this is the most apparent. It is possible that the pronoun is general, referring to all creation, because the gathering is not specific to the one who disdains, and because the detail that follows indicates this. The connection of the clause that is the answer to the conditional particle (*jawab al-shart*) is by the generality within it. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the meaning of *man*, and that a conjoined element was omitted because it corresponds to it. The estimated meaning is: "He will gather them and those who did not disdain to Him, all together," like His saying: *"Garments that protect you from the heat"* (16:81), meaning: and the cold. On these two possibilities, what is detailed afterwards (by *amma*) corresponds to what came before. On the first aspect, it does not correspond. The announcement of gathering to Him is a threat, since what is meant is the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, where the one who disdains and is arrogant will be humbled. al-Hasan read *fa-sanahshuruhum* with *nun* instead of *ya'* in *fa-sayahshuruhum*, and the *ba'* in *fa-yuʿadhdhibuhum* is read with light pronunciation (*takhfif*).

﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will pay them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty.﴾ That is: He will not diminish anyone's reward, whether small or great. The increase may be understood as the good deed being multiplied by ten up to seven hundred, and the multiplication that is not limited, as in His saying: *"Allah multiplies for whom He wills"* (2:261). Ibn Atiyya, may God have mercy on him, said this meaning.

﴿As for those who disdained and were arrogant, He will punish them with a painful punishment, and they will find for themselves besides Allah no protector or helper.﴾ This is a severe threat to those who abandon the worship of Allah out of pride and arrogance. Ibn Atiyya said: This disdain comes only from the disbelievers toward following the prophets and what is similar to that, like the behavior of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, his brother Abu Yasir, Abu Jahl, and others, toward the Messenger. If you suppose a human who knows Allah, it is impossible that you would find him disbelieving in Him out of arrogance toward Him. Rather, defiance only leads to it through arrogance toward humans, and with differences in ranks in the opinion of the arrogant. End of quotation.

He mentioned the reward of the believer first, because doing good to him is something that encompasses even the one who disdains, if he is included in the general category of punishment for him. So it is as if it was said: whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant, he will be punished by the gathering when he sees the rewards of those who did good, and by what befalls him of the punishment of Allah the Exalted.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 4, verses 172–173:**

﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor will the angels brought near.﴾ It is narrated that "a delegation from Najran said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Why do you denounce our companion?' He said: 'And who is your companion?' They said: 'Isa.' He said: 'And what should I say?' They said: 'Say that he is the servant of Allah and His Messenger.' He said: 'There is no shame in his being a servant.' They said: 'Yes.'" Then it was revealed. That is: Isa does not disdain this, so do not you disdain it on his behalf. Had it been a matter for disdain, he would have been more entitled to disdain it, because shame clings more closely to him. That is: he will not be too proud, nor exalt himself, nor become arrogant. Ali read *ʿUbaydan lillah* (with the diminutive form). "Those brought near" means the *Karubiyyun* (the angels closest to the Throne), such as Jibril, Mikail, Israfil, and those in their rank, as al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn Abbas said they are the bearers of the Throne. al-Dahhak said they are those nearest to the seventh heaven. End of quotation. They are joined to Isa because some disbelievers worship the angels.

There is an ellipsis in the sentence. The estimated meaning is: "nor will the angels brought near disdain to be servants of Allah." If *ʿabd* is taken to mean "owned by Allah," then this estimate is not needed, and in that case *wa-la al-malaʾikatu* is a coordination of single words (*ʿatf al-mufradat*). Otherwise, if the unity of *ʿabd* is considered, then *wa-la al-malaʾikatu* is a coordination of clauses (*ʿatf al-jumal*) because the predicate differs. If the meaning of *wa-la al-malaʾikatu* is taken to be "nor any one of the angels," then it is a coordination of single words.

Some people have clung to this verse to claim that the angels are superior to the prophets. Ibn Atiyya said: "*Wa-la al-malaʾikatu al-muqarrabun*" adds weight to the argument and brings it closer to the mind. That is: nor do those who are at the highest ranks of created beings disdain this. How then could anyone else? In this verse there is clear evidence for the superiority of the angels over the prophets. End of quotation.

al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, 'From where does the words of the Exalted, *wa-la al-malaʾikatu al-muqarrabun*, indicate that the meaning is "nor those above him"?' I say: from the fact that the science of meanings (*ʿilm al-maʿani*, the branch of Arabic rhetoric) does not require anything else. The speech was only directed to refute the doctrine of the Christians and their excess in raising the Messiah above the rank of servanthood. So it was necessary to say to them: Isa will not rise above servanthood, nor will one who is higher than him in rank. As if it were said: the angels brought near will not disdain servanthood, so how about the Messiah? And the specification of 'those brought near' clearly and manifestly indicates this, because they are the highest of the angels in rank and the most exalted in station. An example of this is the saying of a poet:

*"Nor is his like among those who are generous like Hatim, nor is the sea with its waves surging in its depths."*

There is no doubt that he intended by 'the sea with its waves' what is above Hatim in generosity. Whoever has taste, let him taste with this verse the Exalted's words: *"Never will the Jews be pleased with you, nor the Christians"* (2:120), until he recognizes the clear distinction." End of his words.

The preference between prophets and angels is known only through revelation (*al-samʿ*), since we do not perceive the aspect of preference by reason. As for this verse, it may be said: whenever something is negated of two things, that does not indicate that the second is higher than the first, nor that this is a matter of gradual ascent (*al-tarakki*). If you say, "So-and-so will not disdain to prostrate to Allah, nor will ʿAmr," there is no indication in it that ʿAmr is superior to Zayd. Even if we accept that, the verse is not of this kind, because it set a singular against a plural, and did not set a singular against a singular, nor a plural against a plural. It may be said: the plural is superior to the singular, and the verse does not necessarily imply the preference of a plural over a plural, nor of a singular over a singular. And even if we accept that the conjoined term in the verse is higher than the term it is conjoined to, that would be according to what has been instilled in the minds of the Arabs and others of exalting the angel and raising him up, to the extent that they deny humanity to the one they praise and affirm angelhood for him. Their imagining that does not indicate that in reality he is superior and greater in reward. Among what was reported in accordance with what was instilled in minds is the saying of the Exalted, quoting the women who were struck by Yusuf's beauty: *"When they saw him, they were amazed at him and cut their hands, and said, 'Allah forbid! This is not a human; this is none but a noble angel'"* (12:31). And the poet said:

*"You are not a human, but an angel descended from the depths of the sky, bringing down (blessings)."*

al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, 'On what is *wa-la al-malaʾikatu al-muqarrabun* conjoined?' I say: either it is conjoined to *al-Masih*, or to the subject of *yakuna* (the pronoun in it), or to the implicit pronoun in *ʿabdan*, because of what it contains of the sense of description, as it indicates the meaning of worship. Your saying, 'I passed by a man, a servant whose father is...' Conjoining to *al-Masih* is the most apparent, because the other options lead to something with some deviation from the purpose, which is that the Messiah does not disdain to be (he and whoever is above him described as) servants, or to worship Allah (he and whoever is above him)." End of his words.

The deviation from the purpose he pointed to is that disdain would be specific to the Messiah, whereas the established meaning is that the angels share with the Messiah in the absence of disdain for servanthood. For it does not necessarily follow from his disdaining alone that he and the angels would be servants, or that he and they would worship their Lord, if they (the angels) disdained it. A person may be content that he and Zayd strike ʿAmr, but Zayd is not content with that. The preference between the two options is also apparent from the use of *la* (not). If the conjunction were intended to be with the pronoun in *yakuna*, or with the implicit pronoun in *ʿabdan*, *la* would not have been used. Rather the construction would have been without it. You say: "Zayd does not want him and his father to be standing," and you say: "Zayd does not want him and ʿAmr to reconcile." These and similar constructions are not places where *la* is used. So if *la* is found in Arabic usage in something like this, it is superfluous (*zaʾida*).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verses 174–175:

﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light.﴾ The majority hold that the proof (burhan) is Muhammad (ﷺ), and it was called a proof because from him comes the proof (al-burhan), which is the miracle (mu'jizah). Mujahid said: the burhan here is the argument (hujjah). It was also said: it is Islam, and the clear light is the Qur'an.

﴿As for those who believed in Allah and held fast to Him, He will admit them into mercy from Him and bounty, and guide them to Himself on a straight path.﴾ The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (bihi, "to Him") refers to Allah, because it is closer and the meaning is sound, and because of His saying: ﴿And hold fast to Allah and devote their religion to Allah﴾ [an-Nisa': 146]. It may also refer to the Qur'an, which He expressed by His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you a clear light.﴾ And in the hadith: "The Qur'an is the strong rope of Allah; whoever holds fast to it is protected." The mercy and the bounty are Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿in mercy from Him and bounty﴾ means in a deserved reward and a grace. End of quote. The word "deserved" (mustahaqq) is one of the terms of the Mu'tazilah. It was also said: mercy is an increase in elevation and raising of ranks. It was said: mercy is divine success (tawfiq), and bounty is acceptance. The pronoun in (ilayhi, "to Him") refers to the bounty, and it is the guidance to the path of the Gardens, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He will guide them and set right their affairs and admit them﴾ [Muhammad: 5], because the guidance of direction had already preceded and been attained when they believed in Allah and held fast. On this view, the straight path is the path to the Garden. Al-Zamakhshari said: and guide them to His worship, so he made the pronoun refer to Allah the Exalted, and that is by omitting a noun in the genitive (mudaf); and this is the apparent meaning, because He is the one spoken of, whereas "in mercy from Him and bounty" is not a statement about them both. Abu 'Ali said: it refers back to the name of Allah the Exalted mentioned earlier; the meaning is: and guide them to His path. If we make "straight path" (sirat mustaqim) an accusative of state (hal), then the state is of this omitted noun. End of quote. He means the religion of Islam. It was also said: the pronoun refers to mercy and bounty, because they carry the sense of reward. It was also said: it refers to the Qur'an. It was also said: the meaning of "straight path" is righteous action.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 4, verse 176:

﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalalah (one who leaves neither ascendants nor descendants)."﴾ Al-Bara' ibn Azib said: It is the last verse to be revealed. Many of the Companions said: It is among the last of what was revealed. Jabir ibn Abdullah said: It was revealed on an occasion. The Prophet (ﷺ) visited me while I was ill, and I said: "O Messenger of Allah, how should I dispose of my wealth, for I have nine sisters and I have neither a child nor a father?" Then it was revealed. It is also said that Jabir met him on the road to Makkah in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage and said: "I have a sister; how much of her inheritance do I take if she dies?" Then it was revealed. The discussion of the word kalalah, both its derivation and its meaning, has already preceded, and its matter was problematic. Many narrations were related from him (Jabir) concerning its circumstances, and in his hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: The verse of summer that was revealed at the end of Surat al-Nisa suffices you." Abu Salamah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The one revealed in summer is: ﴿And if a man leaves an inheritance as kalalah...﴾ [an-Nisa: 12]." The apparent view is that it is ﴿They ask you for a ruling﴾, because al-Bara' said: It is the last verse to be revealed. Ibn Atiyyah said: The saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "The verse of summer suffices you from it," is a clarification that is sufficient and manifest. I do not know what in it was difficult for al-Faruq (may Allah be pleased with him), except that the indication of the wording was confused for many people; for this reason some said: the kalalah is the deceased himself, and others said: the kalalah is the wealth, and other differences of opinion. End of his words. This surah was concluded with this verse just as it began with the rulings on wealth in inheritance and other matters, so that the beginning and the end correspond; this occurs often in the surahs. It is related from Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) that in his sermon he said: "Surely the verse at the beginning of Surat al-Nisa, Allah revealed it concerning the child and the parent; the second verse Allah revealed concerning the husband and wife and the brothers from the mother; and the verse with which He concluded Surat al-Anfal Allah revealed concerning those with kinship ties (ulu al-arham)." The phrase "concerning the kalalah" is connected to ﴿yuftikum﴾ according to the method of giving effect to the second (of two competing verbs).

* *

﴿If a man dies leaving no child, and he has a sister, then for her is half of what he left.﴾ The intended "child" is the son. It is a common noun that may be used for male and female, because a son excludes the sister, whereas a daughter does not exclude her except according to the school of Ibn Abbas. The intended "sister" is the full sister, or the sister of the father rather than the sister of the mother, because Allah assigned her half and made her brother an agnatic heir (asabah), and He said: ﴿For the male is the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ [an-Nisa: 11]. As for the sister from the mother, she has a sixth in the verse of inheritance, equating her with her brother. The word ﴿imru'un﴾ is in the nominative as the subject of a verb omitted, which is explained by what follows it, and the clause ﴿he has no child﴾ is in the position of a qualifier (sifah) of ﴿imru'un﴾; that is: if a man dies who has no offspring. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of separating a qualifier from the qualified by an explanatory clause in the chapter of ishtighal (the verb-omission construction). On this view, "Zayd, I struck him, the wise one" is permitted. Whatever permits separation by a predicate permits it by an explanatory element. Al-Zamakhshari prevented the phrase ﴿he has no child﴾ from being a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "died," saying: the position of ﴿he has no child﴾ is nominative as a qualifier, not accusative as a circumstantial. Abu al-Baqa' permitted it, saying: ﴿he has no child﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial from the pronoun in "died," and ﴿and he has a sister﴾ is also a circumstantial clause. What analysis requires is that this is impermissible, because the actual predicated subject is the apparent noun governed by the omitted verb, and it is that which should be restricted, whereas the pronoun is in an explanatory clause with no place in the grammatical structure, so it is like an emphatic repetition of what preceded. When the following (ittiba') and the restriction contend, whether the emphasizer or the emphasized is qualified by the judgment, it belongs to the emphasized, since it is the basis of the original predication. Accordingly, if you say: "I struck Zayd, I struck Zayd the wise," then "the wise" should be a qualifier of Zayd in the first clause, not of Zayd in the second clause, because the second clause is an emphatic clause for the first. The intended predication is the first clause, not the second. It is said: there is an omitted conjoined element for brevity, and the sense of the speech indicates it. The estimate is: he has no child and no parent.

﴿And he inherits from her if she has no child﴾: that is, if the matter is reversed, with her death and his survival after her. The "child" here is the son, because a son excludes the brother but not the daughter. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: a son does not exclude a brother alone, since a father is similar to him in excluding, so why did it restrict itself to the negation of a child?" I answer: the ruling on the absence of a parent was left to the explanation of the Sunnah, namely his saying (peace be upon him): "Give the shares to their people, and what remains goes to the nearest male agnate," and the father is nearer than the brother. These are not the first two rulings, one of which was explained by the Book and the other by the Sunnah. It is permissible that the ruling on the absence of a child indicates the ruling on the absence of a parent, because the child is closer to the deceased than the parent. If the brother inherits when the nearer is absent, it is more fitting that he inherit when the more distant is absent. Also, kalalah covers the absence of both parent and child together, so mention of the absence of one indicates the absence of the other. End of his words. The pronoun in "he" (huwa) and in "inherits her" refers to what precedes it verbally but not in meaning; it is of the type of "I have a dirham and half of it," because the dead does not inherit, and the living is not inherited from. A parallel in the Qur'an is: ﴿Nor is a long-lived person granted length of life, nor is anything diminished from his lifespan﴾ [Fatir: 11]. This clause is independent and has no place in the grammatical structure, and it is the evidence for the response of the condition that follows it.

﴿But if there are two sisters, then for them are two-thirds of what he left﴾: They said: the pronoun in ﴿were﴾ (kanata) is the pronoun of two sisters, indicated by his saying ﴿and he has a sister﴾. It is established in the science of Arabic grammar that the predicate conveys what the noun does not convey. Abu Ali and others prevented: "The master of the slave-girl is her owner," because the predicate conveyed what the subject conveyed. The alif in ﴿kanata﴾ conveys the dual just as the predicate does, which is his saying ﴿two﴾ (ithnatayn). Al-Akhfash and others answered that his saying ﴿two﴾ indicates the absence of restriction by youth, age, or other qualities, so the two-thirds were earned by mere duality, free of conditions; for this reason it was informative. But what they said is nothing, because the alif in the pronoun for the two also indicates mere duality without regard to a condition, so the meaning of the alif and the meaning of ﴿two﴾ became the same, and the sense became: "If the two sisters were two," and it is known that two sisters are two. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: to whom does the dual and plural pronoun in His saying ﴿if they were two﴾ and ﴿if they were brothers﴾ refer? I answer: the original is: if the one who inherits by siblingship is two sisters, and if the one who inherits by siblingship is males and females. It is said ﴿if they were﴾ and ﴿if they were brothers﴾, as one says: 'Whichever mother she was to you,' so just as the pronoun of 'whoever' is feminine because of the feminine predicate, so too he made the pronoun of 'whoever inherits' dual and plural in 'were' and 'were,' because of the dual and plural of the predicate." End of his words. He follows others in this derivation, and it is a derivation that is not sound, and it is not like "whichever mother was your mother," because "whoever" is expressed and has both form and meaning. Whoever makes it feminine observes the meaning, since the intended sense is: "Whichever mother was your mother." The indicated meaning of the predicate here differs from the meaning of the noun, unlike the verse, where the two meanings are one. It was not made feminine in "whichever mother was your mother" because of the feminine predicate; it was made feminine out of regard for the meaning of "whoever," since it intended a female. Do you not see that you say "Who stood up?" and it is made feminine out of regard for the meaning when you intend to ask about a female, and there is no predicate here for which "stood" would be made feminine. What appears to me in the derivation of the verse is other than what has been mentioned. There are two aspects. The first: the pronoun in "were" does not refer to "two sisters," but refers to the two inheritresses, and there is an omitted qualifier, and "two," qualifying it, is the predicate. The estimate is: "If the inheriting females were two of the sisters, then for them are two-thirds of what he left," so the predicate then conveys what the noun does not convey, and omitting the qualifier is permissible when the meaning is understood. The second aspect: the pronoun refers to the two sisters as they said, and the predicate of "kana" is omitted for the indication of the meaning, though its omission is rare, and "two" is an emphatic circumstantial. The estimate is: "If there were two sisters belonging to him," that is, to the dead man. What indicates the omission of the predicate, which belongs to him, is "and he has a sister," so it is as if it were said: "If there were two sisters to him." A parallel would be: "If Zayd has a brother, his ruling is such-and-such, and if there are two brothers, their ruling is such-and-such," meaning "and if two brothers belong to him."

﴿And if they were brothers, men and women, then for the male is the equivalent of the share of two females﴾: that is, they take the wealth according to what was established in the inheritance of children, that the male has the share of two females. If the pronoun in "were" refers to the siblings, then the predicate conveys, through the detail including men and women, what the noun did not convey, since the noun is apparently for males. If it refers to the heir, then the predication of the predicate conveying what the subject conveys clearly appears. The intended meaning of "siblings" is brothers and sisters, and the masculine judgment prevailed. Ibn Abi Abla read: "fa-inna li-l-dhikri mithla hazzi al-unthayayn."

﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾: "lest you go astray" is an object of purpose, and the object of "makes clear" is omitted; that is: Allah makes clear to you the truth. Al-Basri, al-Mubarrad and others estimated it as "out of dislike that you go astray" (karahiyata an tadillu). The Kufan reader, al-Farra', al-Kisa'i, and al-Zajjaj following them read: "li-an la tadillu," omitting "la." Similar to this in their view is the verse of al-Qattami:

"We saw what the discerning among us saw, so we swore against it that it be sold,"

meaning: that it not be sold. Abu Ubayda related that he said: I told al-Kisa'i a hadith related by Ibn Umar in which: "Let none of you curse his child, lest it coincide with an answer from Allah," and he found it admirable, meaning: lest it coincide. Al-Zajjaj said: it is like His saying ﴿Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fatir: 41], meaning: lest they cease. Abu Ali preferred al-Mubarrad's view, saying that omitting the governed noun is more fitting and more common than omitting "la." It is also said that "lest you go astray" is an object: that is, Allah makes clear to you the error into which you should go astray.

﴿And Allah is knowing of all things﴾: He knows the interests of the servants in the beginning and the return, and in what He imposed on them of rulings. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: In this surah there is a wonderful subtlety: its beginning contains the perfection of Allah's transcendence and the vastness of His power, and its end contains the demonstration of perfect knowledge. These two attributes establish lordship, divinity, majesty and might, and by them the servant must be submissive to the obligations. These verses contain kinds of eloquence, rhetoric and figurative beauty. Among them is antithesis in: "We forbade" and "were made lawful" [al-Hajj: 30], and in "believe" and "if you disbelieve." Repetition is in: "they did not kill him" [an-Nisa: 157], in "We revealed," in "messengers" [an-Nisa: 164], in "bear witness" and "they bear witness," in "disbelieved," in "Mary," and in the name of Allah. Shift of person (iltifat) is in: "then We will give them," and in: "then We will gather them," and what follows "ma" in the reading of the one who reads with nun. Simile is in: "as We revealed" [an-Nisa: 163]. Metaphor is in: "the firmly grounded" [an-Nisa: 162], which is borrowed from solid bodies for firmness and establishment in knowledge; in "the way of Allah," in "bears witness," in "a way," in "do not exaggerate" [an-Nisa: 171], where ghuluw literally means the rise of prices; in "a guardian," borrowed for the encompassing of Allah's knowledge over them; and in "then He will pay them their wages" [an-Nisa: 173], borrowed for recompense. Paronomasia of the identical kind is in: "they ask you for a ruling" and "yuftikum." Detailed explanation is in: "As for those who believed" [an-Nisa: 175] and "As for those who disdained" [an-Nisa: 173]. Ellipsis is in a number of places.
